label: Seeker → Devotee → Initiate → Elder → High Priestess

programs.title: Hellenic: Your first thirty days
programs.summary: For someone new, in their first month, deciding whether this coven is right for them.
programs.description: A gentle first month: what the coven is and does, its tradition in brief, what membership asks and what your rights are, a first taste of practice, and a rite to attend. It ends with a decision, made openly with the coven’s head or your mentor: to carry on as a devotee, to take longer, or to part well.

stages.title: Arriving
stages.intro: Welcome. This first stage is short: read how these thirty days work, what a coven is and isn’t, and the rights you keep in any group, then say hello to your mentor or the High Priestess on this step.

tasks.title: Read: what a coven is, and how this month works
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "What a coven is, and what it isn’t".
2. Try the exercise at the end: write three lines in your own journal or Book of Shadows (why you looked for a coven, what you hope to find, what you fear). Keep them private; you will read them again at the end.
3. Tap "Mark done".

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Know your rights
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Your rights, red flags and green flags".
2. Say the five short "no" phrases aloud once each, so they feel familiar.
3. In the answer box, write in your own words the three rights that matter most to you, and one red flag you will keep an eye out for this month.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Say hello
tasks.instructions:
1. Open the conversation on this step.
2. Send your mentor or the High Priestess a short hello: your coven name, how you came to the coven, and what you hope to learn this month. Share only what you are comfortable sharing.
3. Ask who to talk to if you have questions, and which rite would be a good first one to attend.
4. In the answer box, note what they suggested, then send it for sign-off.

stages.title: Taking part
stages.intro: Now get to know the coven as it really is: read its own documents, go to a rite, and talk with its members. Take your time with this stage; it is the heart of the month.

tasks.title: Read the coven’s documents
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Getting to know this coven: attend, ask, read" and "What membership will ask of you".
2. Open the coven’s pages in the app and read its creed, rules, requirements and agreements, slowly, all the way through.
3. Note what you agree with gladly, what you are unsure of, and anything you disagree with or don’t understand.
4. In the answer box, write: the coven’s creed in two or three sentences of your own; what membership would ask of you in time, commitments and money; and your questions.
5. Send it for sign-off. Your mentor will answer your questions on this step’s conversation.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Learn how the coven gathers, online and in person
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Coven life online and in person".
2. Open each part of the coven in the app once: Rituals and rites, Altars, Messages, Petitions, Book of Shadows, and My standing.
3. Check Settings → Notifications & reminders → Covens and choose what you want to hear about.
4. Tap "Mark done".

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Attend a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Choose a rite with your mentor’s help and answer "Will you be there?" in the app.
2. Ask beforehand about anything you need to know: what to bring or wear, whether there is alcohol, access, smoke or pets.
3. Attend, in person or in the app. Follow quietly, and sit out any part you wish to.
4. Afterwards, while it is fresh, write in the answer box: what happened, what you liked, what puzzled you, how you felt before, during and after, and how people treated each other and you.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Meet members
tasks.instructions:
1. Start a conversation with a member (Messages → New message), or talk with them before or after a rite.
2. Ask open questions: how long they have been in the coven, what a typical month is like, what surprised them, what they would change.
3. Log each conversation. In the answer box, write a few lines on what you learned and how they spoke about the coven.
4. Do this with at least two different members.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Ask the High Priestess your questions
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Questions to ask the High Priestess".
2. Choose five to eight questions that matter most to you, from the lesson or your own.
3. Ask them on this step’s conversation, or in a call or meeting she agrees to.
4. In the answer box, write down her answers in your own words, and what reassured you or left you uneasy.
5. Send it for sign-off.

stages.title: Deciding
stages.intro: You have seen the coven from the inside. Now weigh it honestly, talk it through with the High Priestess, and choose: continue as a devotee, take longer, or part well. Every one of these is a good choice when it is made with care.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Look back over the lessons, especially "Your rights, red flags and green flags" and "What membership will ask of you".
2. Take the test. Choice questions are scored straight away; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor on this step, and try again.

tasks.title: Reflect on fit
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Does it fit? Values, people, practice, logistics".
2. Read again the three lines you wrote at the start, and your notes from the month.
3. Do the fit exercise: write what you have seen under Values, People, Practice and Logistics, and give each a mark from 1 to 5.
4. In the answer box, write your marks, a few lines on each, and one sentence on how you feel imagining yourself in this coven a year from now.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Talk it through with the High Priestess
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The decision: continue, take longer, or part well".
2. On this step’s conversation, write to the High Priestess: thank her for the month, say what you valued, say honestly what you are unsure of, and which way you are leaning. Ask any last questions.
3. Read her reply, and talk further if you need to.
4. In the answer box, note what you discussed, then send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Make your choice
tasks.instructions:
1. Sleep on it at least one night.
2. In the answer box, write your choice: "I will continue as a devotee", "I would like more time, until [date], because …" or "I will part with the coven".
3. Send it for sign-off. The High Priestess will confirm what happens next.
4. If you are parting, follow the steps for parting well in the lesson, and leave from My standing → Leaving when you are ready.
5. Mark the moment in your own way: a candle, a few lines in your journal, or a quiet minute.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

stages.title: A first taste of Hellenic practice
stages.intro: In your first thirty days you get a feel for the Hellenic tradition your coven keeps. Read three short lessons, try one simple practice at home, come to a rite if you can, and talk openly with your mentor or High Priestess about whether this path is for you.

tasks.title: Hellenic practice in brief
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Hellenic practice in brief".
2. Note anything that surprised you or that you want to ask about.
3. Mark this task done when you've read it.

tasks.title: Your first khernips and prayer
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Your first khernips and prayer to Hestia".
2. Do the practice at home, step by step: light Hestia's flame, make khernips, wash, pray, pour, be still, close.
3. Log each time. Do it three times on different days during your first month.

links.label: Journey: Hestia: The Fire at the Centre

tasks.title: Come to a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "What a rite is like, and what is asked of a devotee".
2. Ask your mentor which rite you could come to, and what to wear and bring.
3. Attend, in person or in the app. Watch and follow; you can say no to anything.
4. Send your mentor a message on this step afterwards with anything that puzzled you.

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Is this tradition for you?
tasks.instructions:
1. Reread the section "What is asked of a devotee".
2. In the answer box, write honestly: what appeals to you, what feels hard, whether the time and commitments fit your life, and what you'd like to ask before deciding.
3. Talk it through with your mentor or High Priestess.

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Take the short test. The choice questions are scored at once; your mentor reads the written answers.
2. You need 80% to pass. If you don't pass, look at the questions you missed and try again (the explanations show once you've passed); it's a check of understanding, not a hurdle.

docs.title: What a coven is, and what it isn’t
docs.summary: How these thirty days work, what a coven offers, what it should never be, and the people you’ll meet.
docs.body:
## Welcome

You have found a coven, and the coven has let you in to look around. For the next thirty days or so you are a *seeker*: someone who is getting to know this group, and letting the group get to know you, before either of you makes a promise. Nothing is expected of you yet except honesty and good manners. You are not on trial, and you are not signing up for anything by reading this.

This short course is here to help you decide well. Some people know within a week that they have found their people. Others need the whole month, or longer. Some realise it is not the right group, and that is a good outcome too: it is far better to find out now than after a year of half-hearted attendance.

## How these thirty days work

Everything in this course happens in the app, and the practice happens in your own life.

1. **Read.** Each step has short lessons like this one. Read them in your own time. Ten or twenty minutes is plenty for most.
2. **Take part.** You will be asked to attend a rite, read the coven’s own documents, and talk with some of its members.
3. **Write.** Some steps have an answer box. Write as much or as little as is true for you; there are no clever answers, only honest ones.
4. **Talk.** Every step has its own conversation, where you can message your mentor or the coven’s High Priestess about that step. Use it. A question asked is worth ten wondered about.
5. **Test.** There is one short test, mostly multiple choice, about your rights, what a healthy group looks like and what membership asks. Choice questions are scored straight away; the written answers are read and scored by your mentor or the High Priestess against a clear guide. You need 80% to pass, and you can try again.
6. **Decide.** At the end you choose: continue as a devotee, take longer, or part well.

> **Note:** "High Priestess" is the usual name for a coven’s leader in many modern traditions, and this course uses it throughout. Your coven may say High Priest, Elder, Gothi, Hierophant, Leader or something else. The person who leads the coven is who we mean.

## What a coven is

A **coven** is a small group of people who practise a magical or religious path together, regularly, under agreed ways of working. Most covens are between three and thirteen people, small enough that everyone knows everyone. They meet to hold **rites** (ceremonies with a purpose: marking a full moon or a festival, honouring gods or ancestors, working magic together), to learn, and to support one another’s practice.

The word is old, but the kind of group it now names is mostly modern. One of the earliest recorded uses is in the 1662 confessions of Isobel Gowdie in Scotland, given under interrogation in a witch trial, which speak of witches meeting in "covens" of thirteen. Whether such organised groups really existed then is doubtful; historians treat trial confessions with great caution. The covens you will meet today mostly descend, directly or by inspiration, from the revival of witchcraft and paganism in Britain and America from the 1950s onward, and from the many reconstructed traditions (Norse, Hellenic, Roman, Celtic, Slavic and others) that grew alongside it. Many of those groups use other words: grove, kindred, hearth, household, circle. It is all the same idea: people who choose to practise together.

A good coven usually offers:

- **Shared practice.** Rites are different with others. Many people find group ritual stronger, steadier or simply more joyful than practising alone.
- **Teaching.** Most covens train newer members, often through programs like this one, with a mentor who walks alongside.
- **Continuity.** A coven keeps its own customs, its calendar of holy days and its own Book of Shadows (its shared book of rites and lore).
- **Friendship and support.** Not always, and not with everyone, but often.
- **Accountability.** Practising with others keeps you honest and keeps you practising.

## What a coven isn’t

It helps just as much to know what a coven is not, because disappointment usually comes from expecting the wrong thing.

- **It isn’t a cult.** A healthy coven has no claim on your whole life, your money, your body, your relationships or your mind. You keep your own judgement. You can leave. A later lesson shows you how to tell the difference.
- **It isn’t therapy.** Members may care for each other well, but the coven cannot replace a doctor, counsellor or crisis service, and should never try to.
- **It isn’t a family you can’t leave.** It may come to feel like family, and that is lovely, but membership is always a choice you renew.
- **It isn’t a shop.** Shared costs (candles, room hire, food) are normal and should be open and modest. Paying for rank, for secrets or for "advancement" is not.
- **It isn’t a guarantee.** No group can promise you power, healing, wealth, love or enlightenment. Practice is something you do and experience; it is not a purchase.
- **It isn’t the only way.** Many people practise alone all their lives, and practise well. Joining a coven is one good path among several.

## The people you’ll meet

You will hear words for positions in the coven. They vary, but roughly:

- **The High Priestess** leads: she (or he, or they) holds the coven’s rites, keeps its customs and has the last word on who joins and who rises.
- **Elders** are experienced members who help lead, teach and care for others.
- **Initiates** have made the coven’s deeper commitment, usually after a year and a day of study.
- **Devotees** (or dedicants) have chosen the coven and are training in it.
- **Your mentor** is the person assigned to walk with you through your training: answering questions, reading your answers and signing off your work.
- **Seekers**, like you now, are looking around.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own names for its positions, and some covens have fewer or more of them. Look at the coven’s page in the app, or ask your mentor on this step: "What are the positions here, and what does each one do?"

## A word about pace and pressure

Thirty days is a guide, not a test of speed. If you are busy, unwell, grieving or simply slow to warm up, say so on the step’s conversation. A good coven will tell you to take your time. If anyone hurries you, makes you feel you will "miss your chance", or tells you that doubt is a sign of weakness, notice it: that is one of the red flags you will read about later.

> **Try this:** Before you go on, write three lines in your own journal (or in the app’s Book of Shadows): why you looked for a coven, what you hope to find, and what you are afraid of. Keep it. You will read it again at the end of the month, and it will help you decide.

docs.title: Your rights, red flags and green flags
docs.summary: The rights you keep in any group, how to use them in the moment, and the signs of a healthy or harmful coven.
docs.body:
## Your rights, here and in any group

Whatever coven you join, whatever tradition, whatever position anyone holds, these are yours. They are not favours; they are the floor beneath every healthy group. The app’s community guidelines expect every coven to honour them.

1. **Consent.** Nobody may touch you, work magic on you, or involve you in anything (a ritual act, a trance, a drink, a photograph) without your clear, freely given agreement. You may say no, and you may change your yes to no at any moment, even halfway through. You don’t owe anyone a reason.
2. **Privacy.** Your name, face, address, workplace, health, relationships and history are yours to share or keep. Nobody may demand them, and nobody may share what you’ve told them without your permission (with one narrow exception: when someone is in danger, which a later course for elders covers).
3. **Leaving.** You may leave at any time, for any reason or none, without permission, penalty or punishment. That includes magical punishment: threats of curses, bad luck or spiritual harm if you leave are a form of coercion, whatever words are used.
4. **Never pressured for money.** No one may demand payment, gifts or loans beyond the coven’s open, modest shared costs, and certainly not for rank, initiation, healing or secrets.
5. **Never pressured for sex.** No rank, rite, teaching or initiation ever requires sexual contact, nudity you have not freely chosen, or sending intimate images. A leader who suggests otherwise is abusing their position. This is true in every tradition.
6. **Never pressured for secrets.** No one may require you to reveal private things about yourself as a test of loyalty, or to hand over passwords, messages or information about others.
7. **To ask questions** and get honest answers about how the coven works.
8. **To be safe.** To step out of any rite, to have a non-alcoholic choice, and to be told about fire, herbs and anything else that could hurt you.

> **Safety:** Covens in the app are for adults only. If you believe someone in a coven may be under 18, report it (press and hold one of their messages and choose Report, with the reason "Someone may be under 18").

## How to use your rights in the moment

Knowing your rights is one thing; saying no in a room full of people is another. Practise these simple words until they feel natural:

- "No, thank you."
- "I’ll sit this part out."
- "I’m not comfortable with that."
- "I need to step out for a minute."
- "I’d like to think about it first."

Then do it:

1. Say the words, calmly. You don’t need to explain.
2. Step back physically if you need to.
3. If you are pressed, repeat the same words. You don’t have to find new reasons.
4. Afterwards, write down what happened.
5. Tell your mentor or the High Priestess, unless they were the one pressing you; then tell someone else you trust.

If something serious happens in the app (harassment, pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience, sexual advances, or someone at risk), press and hold the message and choose **Report**. Reports go to Salt & Sovereignty’s moderators, outside the coven. You can also **block** someone. If you are ever in danger, call your local emergency number; crisis and support lines are in the app under **More → Support**.

## Red flags

These are warning signs. One alone may be a misunderstanding; several together, or any of the serious ones, mean you should step back and talk to someone outside the group.

- **Pressure** to commit quickly, sign without reading, or decide before you are ready.
- **Secrecy about the basics:** how decisions are made, money, what happens to complaints, how to leave.
- **Money for rank, secrets, healing or access** to the leader.
- **Sexual pressure** of any kind, including "it’s part of the tradition".
- **Isolation:** being told your friends or family "won’t understand" and you should see less of them.
- **Fear of leaving:** stories about what happened to people who left, threats of curses or bad luck, or ex-members never spoken of.
- **A leader who can’t be questioned,** who claims special authority from the gods that overrides others’ consent, or who punishes doubt.
- **Love-bombing:** overwhelming warmth and flattery at first, which turns cold when you disagree.
- **Discouraging medical or psychological care,** or claiming magic can replace it.
- **Alcohol or drugs pressed on people,** or no non-alcoholic option.
- **Gossip and factions:** members running each other down, especially to newcomers.
- **Rules that apply to everyone but the leader.**

## Green flags

These are signs of a healthy group. You won’t find every one, but you should find most.

- You are encouraged to take your time, ask questions and look at other groups too.
- The documents say plainly how things work, and practice matches them.
- Consent is asked for, out loud, before touch, trance or anything personal.
- There is always a non-alcoholic choice, and nobody comments on what you choose.
- Costs are open, modest and optional for those who can’t pay.
- Members speak well of each other and can disagree respectfully.
- People who have left are spoken of kindly.
- The leader admits mistakes and has someone to answer to.
- Members have lives, friends and interests outside the coven, and that is welcomed.
- Mental and physical health are taken seriously, and professionals are recommended when needed.
- You leave gatherings feeling more yourself, not less.

> **Try this:** Take the two lists and, for each item, note "seen", "not seen" or "don’t know yet" for this coven. Every "don’t know yet" is something to watch or ask about over the rest of the month.

docs.title: Getting to know this coven: attend, ask, read
docs.summary: How to read the coven’s documents, go to a rite as a newcomer, and talk with members, step by step.
docs.body:
## Three ways to get to know a coven

You cannot judge a group from its description, any more than you can judge a person from their profile. You find out by spending time with it. There are three good ways, and you will use all of them this month:

- **Attend:** go to its gatherings and see what really happens.
- **Ask:** talk to the High Priestess, your mentor and the members, and listen to how they answer.
- **Read:** read what the coven has written down about itself: its creed, rules, requirements and agreements.

Each tells you something the others can’t. Documents say what a group intends; attendance shows what it does; conversation shows how it treats people. When all three agree, you can trust what you see. When they don’t, pay attention to the gap.

## Read: the coven’s documents

Every coven in the app can keep pages about itself. They usually come in four kinds:

- **Creed:** what the coven believes or holds sacred, and why it exists.
- **Rules:** how members are expected to behave, at rites and online.
- **Requirements:** what is asked of members: attendance, study, contributions.
- **Agreements:** things you sign. You may already have signed some to join; others may be asked of you later.

How to read them well:

1. Open the coven from the Coven tab and find its pages. Agreements you have signed, or are asked to sign, are also under **My standing → Agreements**.
2. Read each one slowly, all the way through, in a quiet moment. Give it twenty minutes rather than skimming on the bus.
3. As you read, note three kinds of thing on paper or in your journal: what you agree with gladly, what you are unsure about, and anything you disagree with or don’t understand.
4. Look especially for: how decisions are made, how complaints are handled, what is confidential, what costs money, and how someone leaves. Good documents answer these plainly.
5. Take your notes to the step’s conversation and ask about everything in the second and third lists.

> **Note:** Never sign an agreement you have not read or do not understand. It is always acceptable to say "I’d like to ask about this before I sign". A coven that pushes you to sign quickly is showing you something about itself.

## Attend: going to a rite as a newcomer

You will be asked to attend at least one rite this month. It might be in person, held online in the app, or both at once.

Before you go:

1. Find it under **Rituals and rites** on the coven’s page, and answer "Will you be there?" with Going, Maybe or Can’t make it, so the person leading knows who to expect.
2. Read what it says members should know or bring. If anything is unclear (what to wear, whether to bring food, whether there will be alcohol), ask on the step’s conversation or in the coven’s chat.
3. Ask your mentor what will happen, roughly, and whether there is anything a newcomer should not do. Most covens are glad to explain.

While you are there:

- **Arrive on time,** or a little early. Late arrivals can disturb a rite once it has begun.
- **Follow, don’t lead.** Watch what others do. If you are unsure, it is always fine to stand quietly.
- **You may sit out any part.** You never have to speak words you don’t mean, drink anything, be touched, or take part in anything that makes you uncomfortable. Simply step back. A good coven expects this of guests and will not mind.
- **Notice how you feel,** in your body and your mood, before, during and after. That is useful information.
- **Notice how people treat each other,** and how they treat you.

Afterwards, write down what happened while it is fresh: what you saw, what you liked, what puzzled you, how you felt.

## Ask: talking with members

Members are the people you would be practising with for years. Get to know some of them, not only the leader.

1. Use the coven’s chat to say hello, and reply when people talk to you.
2. Start a one-to-one conversation with two or three members (tap **Messages**, then **New message**). A simple opener works: "Hello, I’m new and looking around. How long have you been in the coven, and what do you like about it?"
3. Ask open questions: "What’s a typical month like?", "What surprised you when you joined?", "What would you change?"
4. Listen to *how* they answer as well as what they say. Do they talk freely, or nervously? Do they speak warmly of each other? Can they say something critical without looking over their shoulder?

You never have to share your phone number, address, real name or anything else personal to talk in the app. Share what you’re comfortable with, when you’re ready.

> **Your coven:** Some covens pair every seeker with a member who acts as a friendly guide. Others prefer that you talk mostly with the High Priestess or your mentor at first. Ask what your coven’s custom is.

## Bringing it together

At the end of each week, take ten minutes to ask yourself three questions and write the answers down:

1. What did I learn about this coven this week, from reading, attending and asking?
2. Did what they say, what they wrote and what they did agree?
3. How do I feel about it, honestly, in my body as well as my head?

By the end of the month you will have four short entries, and a much clearer picture than any first impression can give.

docs.title: What membership will ask of you
docs.summary: Time, commitments, confidentiality and money: what is usual, what isn’t, and how to check you have room.
docs.body:
## Knowing the cost before you commit

Every worthwhile commitment costs something: time, attention, a little money, some flexibility. It is far kinder to yourself and to the coven to know what membership asks *before* you say yes than to discover it later and quietly drift away. This lesson sets out the usual asks. Your coven’s own requirements are in its documents; read them alongside this.

## Time

Most covens ask for some mix of these:

- **Rites.** Often each full moon and the main holy days of the tradition: anywhere from eight to twenty-six gatherings a year, usually one to three hours each, plus travel if in person.
- **Training.** As a devotee you will probably read lessons, practise at home and log your practice in the app. Most programs expect between one and four hours a week.
- **Personal practice.** Many traditions ask for a short daily or weekly devotion: five to twenty minutes of prayer, meditation or an offering.
- **Service.** Covens run on volunteers. You may be asked to help set up, bring food, tidy, or later teach and lead.

A simple way to check whether you have room:

1. Look at your last two ordinary weeks. Where did the time go?
2. Find where three or four hours a week could realistically come from. Be honest: if it would come from sleep, it won’t last.
3. Look at the coven’s calendar for the next three months in the app. How many of its rites could you actually reach?
4. If the numbers don’t work, say so. Many covens can adapt, or suggest you take longer.

## Commitments

Beyond time, covens often ask for:

- **Reliability.** If you say you are Going to a rite, go, or tell the person leading as early as you can that you can’t. In the app you can change your answer to Can’t make it; that counts as sending word.
- **Keeping agreements.** If you sign an agreement, keep it, or talk to the High Priestess about changing it. Don’t simply ignore it.
- **Taking part in the coven’s way.** You may keep your own private practice too, but at coven rites you follow the coven’s form.
- **Respect for other members** online and in person.
- **Saying when something is wrong,** rather than letting it fester.

> **Note:** Commitments go both ways. The coven commits to you as well: to teach you honestly, to treat you fairly, to keep your confidences and to let you go well if you leave. If those aren’t written down, it is fair to ask about them.

## Confidentiality

Almost every coven asks members to keep certain things private. This is one of the oldest customs of the Craft, and it exists for good reasons:

- **To protect people.** Some members are not open about their spirituality at work or with family, and could be harmed if they were "outed". You never share who is in the coven, or anything that identifies them, without their permission.
- **To protect trust.** People speak openly in circle because they know it stays there. Personal things said in rites, in the coven’s chat or in conversations are not yours to repeat.
- **To keep some things for those who have trained.** Some traditions keep certain rites or teachings for initiates, who have the preparation to use them well. This is sometimes called being **oathbound**: bound by a promise not to share.

Confidentiality is *not*:

- **A cover for harm.** No promise of secrecy can require you to keep quiet about abuse, exploitation, crime or someone being in danger. Any group that says otherwise has shown you a serious red flag.
- **A ban on talking about your own life.** You can always tell a doctor, therapist, partner or friend about your own experiences and feelings, including if something troubled you.
- **A gag on seeking advice.** You can describe, in general terms, what kind of group you are in.

> **Your coven:** Ask on this step: "What exactly is confidential here, and what am I free to talk about?" A good coven can answer that clearly. Many write it in their rules or agreements.

## Money

Shared costs are normal: candles, incense, food, room hire, sometimes a small yearly sum toward the coven’s expenses. Healthy money looks like this:

- Costs are stated plainly, in advance, and are modest.
- You can see roughly what money is spent on.
- There is a quiet way to say "I can’t afford that right now" without shame, and an alternative (bring food instead, help set up).
- Nobody ever pays for a rank, an initiation, a secret or a leader’s attention.

## Your private life

A coven should ask nothing of your relationships, your body, your diet, your politics, your job or where you live, beyond what any decent group of people asks: be kind, be honest, be safe. If you are ever asked to cut off friends or family, to give up medical treatment, or to make a life decision because a leader says so, stop and talk to someone outside the group.

## Putting it together

Before you decide at the end of the month, write down in your journal:

1. How many hours a week membership would realistically take, and where they would come from.
2. Which commitments you are glad to make, and which you are unsure about.
3. What you understand to be confidential.
4. Any costs, and whether they are manageable.

If any answer is "I don’t know", that is your next question for the High Priestess.

docs.title: Coven life online and in person
docs.summary: What happens in the app and in person, how to join a rite in the app, notifications and your privacy.
docs.body:
## Two places to gather

Most covens in this app meet in two ways: in person, in a home, a garden, a hired room or out on the land; and online, in the app itself. Some are entirely online, with members in different countries. Some meet mostly in person and use the app for planning and messages. Knowing how your coven uses each will help you picture what membership would really be like.

## What happens in the app

Open the coven from the Coven tab. These are the main parts you will use:

- **Rituals and rites.** The coven’s calendar of gatherings. Each rite has a plan: its intention, what to bring, and its steps, some of which are given to particular people. You answer "Will you be there?", and when it begins you tap **Join the ritual**. Whoever leads moves through the steps, and when a step is yours, the app tells you.
- **Altars.** The coven’s shared altars, which everyone sees change as it happens. The ritual altar is where rites are held. Lighting a candle or placing an offering there is seen by everyone present.
- **Messages.** The coven’s chat, plus one-to-one and small group conversations. You never need to share a phone number.
- **Petitions.** Members can ask the circle to hold something for them (an exam, a sick friend, a hard week). Each petition has its own altar and candle, and members tend it while it is open.
- **Book of Shadows.** The coven’s own pages of rites and lore, written by members and approved before they go in.
- **Initiation and training.** Programs like this one, with stages, tasks, lessons, tests and a conversation on every step.
- **My standing.** Your position, the agreements you have signed, your record, and the button to leave.

Your own practice (your personal altar, journal, readings and so on) stays yours. The coven sees only what you choose to share with it.

## What happens in person

In-person rites are much like those in the app, but with real candles, real food and real voices. Ask before your first one:

1. Where it is, how to get there, and whether it is accessible to you.
2. What to wear and bring.
3. Whether there is food, drink or alcohol, and whether there is a non-alcoholic choice.
4. Whether there are pets, smoke or incense (important if you have allergies or asthma).
5. Whether you can leave early if you need to.

Some covens hold a rite in person while members far away join in the app at the same time. If you join that way, you will see the steps and the altar change as the people in the room move through them.

## Joining a rite in the app, step by step

1. Before the day, read the rite’s plan under **Rituals and rites**, and answer Going, Maybe or Can’t make it.
2. Prepare your space: a quiet corner, your phone charged, and anything the plan asks you to bring (a candle, a glass of water, a written intention).
3. Join a few minutes before it begins. Tap **Join the ritual**.
4. Follow along. Read the words for each step; speak them aloud if the coven does that, or quietly if you are not alone at home.
5. If a step is yours, the app will show you what to do: speak words, light a candle on the altar, place something.
6. When the rite ends, take a few minutes to come back to ordinary awareness: eat something, drink some water, stretch.
7. Write a note in your journal about it.

> **Safety:** If you light a real candle at home during an online rite, put it in a stable, heatproof holder away from curtains, paper and pets, and never leave it burning when you leave the room or fall asleep.

## Notifications

Covens can be busy. In **Settings → Notifications & reminders → Covens** you choose what reaches your phone: the coven’s chat, your conversations, gatherings put on the calendar, and so on. You can mute a single conversation from its ⓘ button. It is perfectly fine to turn things down; nobody expects you to answer instantly. If you are waiting on something important, such as a reply from the High Priestess on this step, make sure that kind of note is on.

## A first week in the app

If the app is new to you, take it slowly. A simple first week:

1. **Day one:** read the coven’s page and its documents.
2. **Day two:** open Messages, read back through the coven’s chat, and say hello.
3. **Day three:** look at Rituals and rites and answer for the next gathering.
4. **Day four:** visit the coven’s ritual altar, just to see it.
5. **Day five:** read a page or two of the coven’s Book of Shadows, if you can see it yet.
6. **Day six:** set your notifications.
7. **Day seven:** write a few lines in your journal about what you’ve seen.

The app’s own guide (More → How to use the app) explains every screen if you get stuck.

## Your privacy in the app

- Other members see the name you chose for your coven profile, not your account email.
- The coven’s leaders keep a record of who took part in rites and how studies are going; it shows counts and kinds, never what you wrote in conversations.
- You can report or block anyone from a message, and leave the coven at any time from **My standing**.

> **Your coven:** Every coven uses the app differently. Ask your mentor on this step: "What happens in the app, and what happens in person? Which would I be expected to join?"

docs.title: Questions to ask the High Priestess
docs.summary: How to ask, what to ask about the coven, training and safety, and what good and evasive answers sound like.
docs.body:
## Why ask the High Priestess directly

The High Priestess (or whoever leads your coven) shapes the coven more than anyone else. How she answers honest questions tells you a great deal about the group: whether it is open or secretive in the wrong ways, whether it respects people’s choices, and whether you would trust her with your training.

Good leaders like being asked. A thoughtful question shows that you are taking the coven seriously. You are not being rude by asking, and you do not need to ask everything at once.

## How to ask

1. **Choose the place.** Use the conversation on this step in the app, or ask for a call or a meeting in person. Writing gives both of you time to think; talking shows more of the person. Many people do both.
2. **Pick five to eight questions** from the lists below, the ones that matter most to you. Write them down beforehand.
3. **Ask one at a time** and let her answer fully. Don’t argue; you are gathering information.
4. **Write down what she said** soon afterwards, in your own words.
5. **Follow up** on anything vague: "Could you give me an example?" or "What would happen if…?"
6. **Thank her.** Answering takes time.

## Questions about the coven

- How did the coven begin, and how long has it run?
- What tradition does it follow, and how strictly? What is old, and what is the coven’s own?
- What does a typical month look like? How often do you meet in person, and how often in the app?
- How many members are there, and how long do people usually stay?
- Why have people left in the past? (A good leader can answer this without bitterness.)

## Questions about training and membership

- What happens after the first thirty days if I continue?
- How long does training take, and who will mentor me?
- What is required of members: attendance, study, contributions? What happens if I can’t meet them for a while?
- Are there costs? What are they for, and is there help for those who can’t afford them?
- What is confidential here, and what am I free to talk about outside?

## Questions about safety and fairness

- How are decisions made? Who has a say?
- What happens if two members fall out?
- If I had a complaint about a leader, including you, who would I take it to?
- Is alcohol ever used in rites? Is there always a non-alcoholic choice?
- Is there ever touch, nudity or trance work? How is consent asked for, and can I say no?
- How would I leave, if I decided to, and what would happen then?

## What good answers sound like

You are not looking for perfect answers. You are looking for these signs:

- **Plain and specific.** "We meet at each full moon in the app, and in person for the eight festivals. Most members make about two-thirds of rites." Not "We gather as the spirit moves us."
- **Open about limits.** "We’ve had two people leave this year: one moved away, one found we were too formal for them, and that’s fine."
- **Respectful of your choice.** "Take your time. If we’re not right for you, I’ll happily point you to other groups."
- **Clear on consent and safety.** "Anyone can step out of anything, at any time, no explanation needed."
- **Willing to be held to account.** "If you had a complaint about me, you could bring it to our elders, or report it to the app’s moderators."

## What evasive answers sound like

Be cautious, and talk to someone you trust, if you hear:

- "You’ll understand when you’re initiated" in answer to a question about **safety, money or rules.** Some lore is kept for initiates in many traditions, and that is normal; but how you will be treated is never a secret you must earn.
- "We don’t talk about people who left" when you asked *why* people leave.
- "There’s no need for complaints here; we’re all family."
- "That’s a very negative question." Questions about safety are not negative.
- Answers that change depending on who is in the room.
- Anger, sulking or coldness after you ask.

One awkward answer is not proof of anything; people have bad days and some questions catch them off guard. A pattern of evasion is a different matter.

> **Your coven:** Every coven keeps some things for its members, and some traditions keep certain rites and teachings for initiates only. It is fine to be told "That’s taught later". It is not fine to be told that you can’t know how decisions are made, what things cost, or what you are agreeing to.

## Questions to ask yourself

The High Priestess is not the only person with answers. Before and after your conversation, ask yourself:

- What do I most need from a coven: teaching, worship, friendship, structure, magic?
- What would make me leave? Knowing your own limits helps you spot them early.
- Am I hoping the coven will fix something in my life that it can’t?
- Have I told her honestly about anything that affects my taking part, such as health, access needs, work hours or caring duties, as far as I’m comfortable?

Your own honesty makes her answers more useful. If she knows you work nights, she can tell you plainly whether the coven’s rhythm will suit you.

## After the conversation

Write a short note for yourself: what did you learn, what reassured you, what left you uneasy? Bring anything still unclear back to the step’s conversation. You can ask the same question again in a different way; you can also ask your mentor or another member how they understand it.

docs.title: Does it fit? Values, people, practice, logistics
docs.summary: A clear way to weigh whether this coven suits you, with a simple marking exercise.
docs.body:
## Fit is not the same as quality

A coven can be safe, kind, well led and good at what it does, and still not be right for you. A brilliant formal ceremonial group will be wrong for someone who wants relaxed kitchen-table witchcraft, and the other way round. Deciding "this isn’t my coven" is not a judgement on it, or on you.

There are four things to weigh: **values, people, practice and logistics.** Each matters. A coven that fits three and fails badly on the fourth is usually not a good long-term home.

## Values

These are what the coven believes matters, and how it expects people to behave.

Ask yourself:

- Do I agree with the coven’s creed, or could I happily practise inside it?
- Do its ethics (about harm, consent, magic on others, honesty) match mine?
- Does it treat people the way I want to be treated, and the way I want to treat others?
- Is there anything in its documents I would have to pretend to believe?

A small difference ("they say the Goddess first; I tend to think of the gods together") is often fine. A deep one ("they think cursing is acceptable; I don’t") rarely is.

## People

You will spend years with these people, in vulnerable moments.

- Do I feel at ease with them, or on edge?
- Do I trust the High Priestess to teach me and treat me fairly?
- Could I imagine asking one of them for help?
- Is there anyone I would dread working closely with? (One difficult person in a big coven is manageable; in a coven of five it is a large part of your experience.)

Notice your body: tight shoulders and a sinking feeling before gatherings are information. So is looking forward to them.

## Practice

This is what the coven actually does.

- Do the rites move me, interest me, or at least feel worthwhile?
- Is the tradition one I want to learn deeply?
- Is the style right: formal or relaxed, scripted or spontaneous, solemn or playful?
- Does the coven focus on what I want to learn (devotion to gods, magic, seasonal celebration, community, study)?
- Is the pace of training right for me?

## Logistics

These are the practical things, and they sink more memberships than anything else.

- Can I get to the in-person gatherings, regularly, without strain?
- Do the times work with my job, family and health?
- Can I afford the costs?
- Is the coven’s way of using the app comfortable for me?
- Are its spaces accessible to me?

## A simple way to weigh it

1. On a page of your journal, write the four headings: Values, People, Practice, Logistics.
2. Under each, write what you have seen this month, good and bad. Use your notes from the rite you attended, your conversations and the documents.
3. Give each heading a mark from 1 to 5: 1 means "this really doesn’t fit", 3 means "it would do", 5 means "this fits me well".
4. Look for any 1s. A 1 anywhere is a serious problem, whatever the others say.
5. Look at the total. As a rough guide, 16–20 suggests a strong fit; 12–15 a reasonable one with questions to talk through; below 12, think carefully.
6. Then put the numbers aside and ask: when I imagine being in this coven a year from now, what do I feel? Relief? Excitement? Dread? Write one sentence about it.

The numbers are a tool for thinking, not an answer. Sometimes a 13 with real warmth is a better choice than an 18 that feels flat. But if the numbers and your feelings both say no, believe them.

> **Note:** Feeling nervous is normal and is not the same as a poor fit. Joining any group is a stretch. The question is whether, under the nerves, you feel welcome, respected and interested.

## An example

Here is how one seeker, Rowan, worked it through.

- **Values, 4:** "I agree with nearly all of the creed. They’re firmer than I am about only honouring the coven’s gods in rites, but I can live with that."
- **People, 5:** "Warm, funny, and they argue kindly. The High Priestess answered every question straight."
- **Practice, 4:** "The full moon rite moved me. The festivals are more formal than I expected."
- **Logistics, 2:** "Rites are on Thursday evenings, an hour’s drive away, and I work late two Thursdays a month."

Total: 15, with no 1s, but a 2 for logistics. Rowan’s sentence: "I feel excited, and a bit worried about the drive." Rowan took this to the High Priestess, who said members far away often join full moon rites in the app and come in person for festivals. Logistics rose to a 4, and Rowan chose to continue. Notice that the exercise didn’t make the decision; it showed which question to ask.

## When you can’t tell

If you have done all this and are still unsure, that is an answer too: you need more time. You can ask the High Priestess to extend your time as a seeker. Most covens will agree gladly, and it is better than committing to something you are unsure of.

> **Your coven:** Some covens can extend the seeker’s time; others prefer that you continue as a devotee with an understanding that you are still deciding. Ask on this step what your coven offers.

docs.title: The decision: continue, take longer, or part well
docs.summary: How to prepare to decide, talk it through with the High Priestess, and carry out each choice well.
docs.body:
## The end of the month

You have read, attended, asked and weighed. Now you choose. There are three good choices, and each can be made well:

1. **Continue as a devotee.** You want to dedicate yourself to this coven and begin its training.
2. **Take longer.** You are not ready to decide, and want more time as a seeker.
3. **Part well.** This coven is not right for you, and you will leave on good terms.

None of these is failure. A coven gains nothing from a member who joined out of politeness, and you gain nothing from staying somewhere that doesn’t fit.

## Preparing to decide

1. Read again the three lines you wrote at the start of the month: why you looked, what you hoped for, what you feared. What has changed?
2. Read your weekly notes and your fit marks.
3. Re-read your notes on red and green flags. Did anything worrying appear? Did anything reassure you?
4. Sleep on it at least one night.
5. Write your reflection in the answer box on the reflection step.

> **Safety:** If you saw serious red flags this month (pressure for money, sex or secrets, threats about leaving, isolation from friends or family), don’t decide alone. Talk to someone you trust outside the coven, and consider reporting it in the app. You can leave straight away; you don’t need to finish this course first.

It can help to imagine each choice in turn. Picture yourself telling the High Priestess "I’d like to continue", then "I need more time", then "I’m going to part". Notice which brings relief, which brings a sinking feeling, and which makes you want to argue. Your reactions are not the whole answer, but they are part of it.

## Talking with the High Priestess

Before you choose, talk your decision through with the High Priestess on the conversation for that step. This is not for permission; the choice is yours. It is so that she knows what you are thinking and can answer anything left over.

A simple shape for the message:

1. Thank her for the month.
2. Say what you valued.
3. Say honestly what you are unsure about, if anything.
4. Say which way you are leaning, and ask any last questions.

Then listen to her reply, and make your choice.

## If you continue

Tell the High Priestess, and write your choice in the answer box on the final step. She will usually move you into the devotee program and assign you a mentor. You may be asked to sign further agreements; read them before you do. Expect the next months to ask more of you: regular practice, study, rites. You can still leave at any time.

## If you take longer

Say so plainly: "I’m not ready to decide yet. Could I have another month as a seeker?" Say what you need the time for (to attend another rite, to see whether the times work, to think about a question of belief). Agree a time to talk again, and write it in your calendar. Then use the time; don’t simply drift.

## If you part well

Leaving well matters, for you and for the coven. A good parting:

1. **Tell the High Priestess first,** before you leave in the app, in the step conversation or in person. Don’t simply vanish.
2. **Thank them** for their time and welcome.
3. **Give a short, honest reason if you are comfortable,** framed about fit, not blame: "The times don’t work for my family", or "I’ve realised I’m drawn to a more solitary practice", or "The tradition isn’t quite mine." You don’t owe a reason, but a kind one helps the coven learn.
4. **Return anything you borrowed,** and keep any confidences you were given. Confidentiality outlasts membership.
5. **Say goodbye to the members you got to know,** if you’d like to.
6. **Leave in the app** from **My standing → Leaving** when you are ready.

An example message:

"Thank you so much for welcoming me this month. I’ve really valued the full moon rite and talking with everyone. I’ve realised the meeting times don’t work with my shifts, and I don’t want to join knowing I’d miss most rites. I’ll leave the coven this week. I wish you all well, and I’ll keep what I’ve learned."

A good coven will thank you and wish you well. If, instead, you are pressured to stay, guilted, or warned of bad consequences, that tells you that leaving was the right choice. Leave anyway; report it if it was serious.

## Common worries

- **"I’ll let them down if I leave."** A coven is better served by an honest goodbye than by a reluctant member.
- **"What if I regret it?"** Many covens welcome back people who left on good terms. Ask.
- **"I’m only staying because I don’t want to be alone in my practice."** That’s understandable, but not enough on its own. Solitary practice can be rich, and there are other covens.
- **"I feel pressured to decide now."** You never have to. Ask for more time. If it is refused with pressure or guilt, that is itself an answer.
- **"I want to continue, but I’m nervous."** Nerves are normal before any commitment. Name them to the High Priestess; she has seen them many times.

## After the decision

Whatever you chose, take a moment to mark it. Light a candle, write a few lines, or simply sit quietly and acknowledge that you made a real decision with care. That is itself a practice: choosing your path deliberately, rather than drifting into it.

docs.title: Hellenic practice in brief
docs.summary: A short, honest introduction to the Hellenic tradition your coven keeps: what it is, what it is not, and what a Hellenic coven actually does.
docs.body:
## Welcome

You are in your first thirty days with a coven that keeps Hellenic practice, finding out whether it is right for you. There is no pressure to decide quickly, and no wrong answer. This short course gives you a taste of the tradition: what it is, one simple practice to try, and what joining would ask of you. Your coven's general welcome lessons cover how the coven works, your rights and what to look out for in any group.

## What the Hellenic tradition is

Hellenic practice is the worship of the ancient Greek gods, revived and reconstructed in modern times. It is often called Hellenismos or Hellenic polytheism. "Polytheism" means honouring many gods; "Hellenic" means Greek.

The gods you would come to know include Zeus, Hera, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Hermes, Demeter, Persephone, Dionysus, Aphrodite and Poseidon, and three who are especially close to household practice:

- **Hestia**, goddess of the hearth and the home, who receives the first and last offering at every rite;
- **Hekate**, goddess of crossroads, thresholds and the night, honoured with a supper at the end of each month;
- **Zeus Ktesios**, Zeus as guardian of the household's stores.

At its heart, Hellenic practice is a religion of relationship. You honour the gods with small, regular gifts, purification, prayer and festivals, and over time a bond of goodwill grows. The Greeks called this bond kharis.

## What it is not

A few common misunderstandings, cleared away early:

- **It is not a role-play of ancient Greece.** You don't need to dress in costume, speak Greek or pretend to live in Athens. You practise as yourself, in your own life.
- **It is not only about myths.** The myths are stories told about the gods. Practice is what you do: purify, pray, offer, keep festivals.
- **It does not involve animal sacrifice.** The ancient Greeks sacrificed animals at great festivals. Modern Hellenic practitioners, almost without exception, do not. Offerings are food, drink, incense, flowers, songs and acts of kindness.
- **It is not closed.** You do not need Greek ancestry or anyone's permission to honour the Greek gods. What is asked is respect.
- **It is not mainly a system of magic.** Most Hellenic polytheists worldwide are not witches. Your coven combines Hellenic religion with witchcraft, and it will be clear with you about which is which.

## Honest about history

Greek religion was suppressed in the Roman Empire from the late 4th century CE, and public worship ended. What we know about it comes from ancient poems, hymns, inscriptions, art and archaeology, studied carefully. Modern practitioners rebuild practice from that evidence and fill gaps with careful judgement.

That means you will often hear your coven say "this is ancient", "this is our modern reconstruction", or "this is personal experience". That honesty is a feature, not a weakness. If anyone tells you a practice is ancient, it is fair to ask how we know.

## What a Hellenic coven does

A coven that keeps Hellenic practice typically:

- **meets for festivals** through the year, taken mainly from the calendar of ancient Athens: the Panathenaia for Athena, the Anthesteria for Dionysus and the dead, the Thargelia for Apollo and Artemis, and others;
- **keeps the monthly days**: Hekate's Deipnon at the dark moon, the Noumenia at the new moon, and the Agathos Daimon, the good spirit of the house, the day after;
- **holds rites in the Hellenic form**: procession, purification with khernips, prayer, libation and offering, with Hestia first and last;
- **shares meals**, because Greek rites often ended in a feast, and hospitality (xenia) is sacred;
- **teaches each member** to keep a small household shrine;
- **practises magic and divination** in the coven's own way.

Most members spend a few minutes a day at home with their shrine, keep the monthly days, and gather with the coven for festivals, in person or in the app.

> **Your coven:** Every Hellenic coven has its own balance of religion and magic, its own festivals and its own customs. Ask your mentor or High Priestess what yours is like, and which festivals are coming up in your first month.

## Is it for you?

People are drawn to Hellenic practice for many reasons: a love of the myths since childhood, a sense of being called by a particular god, a wish for a religion grounded in history, a love of household ritual, or a feeling that the Greek gods simply make sense. Some find, after a few weeks, that the tradition's emphasis on regular household worship suits them perfectly. Others find they want something different, and that is fine too.

As you read this course, notice:

- whether the practice of small daily offerings appeals to you or feels like a chore;
- whether the mix of careful history and personal devotion suits you;
- whether the gods feel like people you want to know;
- whether the coven feels like a place where you could belong.

> **Safety:** You are free to ask questions, take your time and say no. No one in a healthy coven will pressure you to join, demand money beyond agreed costs, ask for sex, or ask you to keep secrets that would hurt you. If anything feels wrong, talk to someone you trust, inside or outside the coven.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** the gods, purification, prayer, libation, offerings, festivals, the values of kharis and xenia.
- **Modern:** the revival itself, covens, and the combination of Hellenic religion with witchcraft.

docs.title: Your first khernips and prayer to Hestia
docs.summary: One simple practice to try at home: making khernips, washing, and saying a short prayer to Hestia, step by step, in about ten minutes.
docs.body:
## Start here

Every Hellenic rite, large or small, begins the same way: you purify yourself with khernips and you greet Hestia, goddess of the hearth. This lesson teaches you to do just that. It takes about ten minutes, needs almost nothing, and is the heart of Hellenic household worship. If you try only one thing in your first month, try this.

## What khernips is

Khernips (KHER-nips) is water made holy by quenching a flame in it. In ancient Greece, at every sacrifice, a burning brand from the altar fire was plunged into a basin of water, and worshippers washed their hands in it before approaching the gods. Bowls of this water stood at the entrances of temples. The poet Hesiod warned never to pour an offering to the gods "with unwashen hands", or they would not hear your prayers.

Khernips marks a clean break between ordinary life and time with the gods.

## Who Hestia is

Hestia is the goddess of the hearth: the fire at the centre of a home where food is cooked and people gather. She is the eldest of the Olympian gods, and she stays at home while the others travel. The Greeks gave her the first and last share of every offering. The ancient Homeric Hymn to Hestia says that without her there is no feast, because people always poured wine "to Hestia both first and last".

In a modern home, Hestia's hearth can be a candle, an oil lamp, or an electric light.

## What you need

- A small bowl of fresh water.
- A match, or a dried bay leaf and a match.
- A candle or tealight in a holder, or an electric candle.
- A small cup of water, juice or wine, and a saucer or second bowl to pour into.
- A towel.
- A quiet place: a shelf, a table, a windowsill.

## The practice, step by step

1. **Prepare.** Wash your hands and face as you normally would. Set out the bowl, the candle, the cup and the saucer. Put your phone on silent.
2. **Settle.** Stand or sit in front of them. Breathe in slowly for a count of four, and out for a count of six. Do this three times. Let your shoulders drop.
3. **Light Hestia's flame.** Light the candle, or switch on the electric one. Say: "Hestia, goddess of the hearth, be kindled here."
4. **Make the khernips.** Light the match (or the bay leaf from the candle). Hold it over the bowl of water. Say: "Begone, all that is unholy." Plunge the burning end into the water. You will hear a small hiss. The water is now khernips.
5. **Wash.** Dip your fingers in the khernips and rub your hands together. Touch a little water to your face: your forehead, eyes or lips.
6. **Dry your hands.**
7. **Pray to Hestia.** Raise your hands, palms up, if you are comfortable to, or rest them palms up in your lap. Say, aloud or in a whisper: "Hestia, eldest of the gods, keeper of the hearth, first and last of all: I am new to your worship, and I come with clean hands. Thank you for the shelter of this home. Keep it warm and safe."
8. **Pour.** Lift the cup and pour a little into the saucer. Say: "Hestia, this is for you."
9. **Be still.** Sit or stand quietly for a minute. Look at the flame. You don't have to think anything in particular.
10. **Close.** Say: "Hestia, first and last, thank you." Put out the candle.

## Afterwards

- Pour the used khernips outside on the earth, or down the drain. It has carried away impurity, so don't drink it.
- Leave the saucer with your offering until the next morning, then pour it onto the earth outside, a plant pot, or the drain, with a word of thanks.
- If you like, note in the app what you did and anything you noticed.

## What you might notice

People describe their first khernips and prayer in many ways: a feeling of calm, of settling, of being heard; a small chill or warmth; a sense of awkwardness at speaking aloud; or nothing at all. All of these are normal. Many people feel little at first, and only notice after weeks that the practice has become a place of quiet in their day. Khernips and prayer work as a practice whether or not you feel anything special.

## Common difficulties

- **"I feel silly talking aloud."** Almost everyone does at first. A whisper counts. It gets easier after a few times.
- **"I can't have a flame."** Use an electric candle for Hestia, and for khernips, wash your hands in clean running water with full attention and say the purification words.
- **"I forgot a step."** Nothing is spoiled. Do what you remember. The order becomes natural with practice.
- **"I don't know if I believe in Hestia."** You don't have to settle that now. Many people begin by acting as if, and find their understanding grows through the practice.

> **Safety:** Hold the lit match over the bowl, keep hair and sleeves back, and never leave a candle burning when you leave the room. Keep matches away from children. Water or juice is a perfectly good offering if you'd rather not use wine.

> **Try this:** Do this practice three times during your first month, on different days. After the third time, write a few sentences in the app: how did it feel the first time, and how did it feel the third?

> **Your coven:** Your coven may use slightly different words, a particular herb for the khernips, or a set prayer to Hestia. Ask your mentor to show you theirs.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** khernips, washing before approaching the gods, Hestia first and last, pouring a libation.
- **Modern:** the exact words and steps here, electric candles, and matches in place of a brand from the altar fire.

docs.title: What a rite is like, and what is asked of a devotee
docs.summary: What to expect at your first Hellenic coven rite, in person or in the app, how to take part, and what becoming a devotee would ask of you in time and commitment.
docs.body:
## Your first rite

During your first thirty days you will probably be invited to a coven rite: a festival, a monthly day, or a gathering for newcomers. This lesson tells you what it is likely to be like, so you can come relaxed, and what would be asked of you if you decided to become a devotee.

## Before you go

- **Ask what to expect.** Your mentor or the High Priestess will tell you which festival it is, roughly how long it will take, whether there is food afterwards, and what you might be asked to do.
- **Ask what to wear.** Usually just clean, comfortable clothes. Some covens like members to wear something pale or special for rites; as a guest, ordinary clean clothes are always fine.
- **Ask what to bring.** Often a small food offering for the shared meal, or nothing at all.
- **Wash** before you go, and arrive a little early.
- **Tell someone** you trust where you are going, as you would for any first meeting with a new group.

## What happens

A Hellenic rite follows a steady order. A festival rite might go like this:

1. **Welcome.** People greet you, offer you water, and settle. Phones go on silent.
2. **Briefing.** The leader explains the festival, its story and who does what.
3. **Procession.** Everyone walks to the altar, often carrying offerings. You may be handed something to carry; hold it with both hands and follow the person in front.
4. **Khernips.** A bowl of purified water comes round. Dip your fingers, wash your hands, touch your face. If you're unsure, watch the person before you.
5. **Barley and silence.** Grains may be scattered at the altar, and the leader calls for holy silence.
6. **Hestia first.** A prayer and offering to Hestia.
7. **Prayers and offerings** to the gods of the festival: prayer spoken aloud with arms raised, libations of wine, juice or water poured, incense and food offered.
8. **The festival's heart:** a myth read aloud, a hymn, a play, a working, a custom belonging to the day.
9. **Hestia last** and closing words.
10. **Shared meal.** Food and conversation. This is a good time to ask questions.

A rite usually lasts from half an hour to two hours, plus the meal.

### Online in the app

If the rite is online, each person stays at their own shrine with their own flame, khernips and cup. The leader guides each step, and everyone does it at the same time. Have your things ready before it starts, and a quiet room if you can.

## How to take part as a newcomer

- **Watch and follow.** No one expects you to know what to do.
- **You can always say no.** If you're offered a role and don't want it, or would rather watch a part, just say so. You never have to explain.
- **You don't have to pray aloud** or pour a libation if you're not ready. Standing quietly is a full way to take part.
- **Alcohol is optional.** Juice or water is always available, or you can pass the cup.
- **Ask afterwards** about anything that puzzled you.

> **Safety:** A healthy coven will tell you what a rite involves before you take part, will never require nudity, touch or anything sexual, and will never make you drink or take anything. If anything feels wrong, you may leave at any time. Tell your mentor or someone you trust.

## What is asked of a devotee

If you decide, at the end of your thirty days, to continue, the next step is to become a devotee: someone who has chosen this coven and its tradition and is learning its foundations, ending in a dedication. Here is roughly what that would ask of you.

### Time

- **A few minutes a day** at your household shrine: khernips, Hestia, a short prayer and libation. Five to ten minutes is enough.
- **The monthly days**: about an hour for Hekate's Deipnon (most of it cleaning), half an hour for the Noumenia, ten minutes for the Agathos Daimon.
- **Coven festivals and gatherings**: usually one or two a month, in person or in the app.
- **Study**: a few hours a month reading lessons, practising, and writing short answers for your mentor.

### Commitments

- **Keep a small household shrine** with a flame for Hestia, a bowl for khernips and a cup.
- **Work through the devotee course** at your own pace: energy and grounding, sacred space, Hellenic ritual, the tradition, household devotion, and finally a dedication.
- **Talk honestly with your mentor**, including about doubts and difficulties.
- **Keep confidential** what other members share with you.
- **Treat others with xenia**: respect, hospitality and care.

### What it does not ask

- Large sums of money. Agreed shared costs (food, candles, a venue) are normal; anything more is a red flag.
- Giving up other friends, family or interests.
- Believing anything you don't believe. Practice comes first; belief can grow or not.
- A lifelong promise. Dedication as a devotee is a commitment to the path for now, not an oath for life. You can always leave.

## Making your decision

Your thirty days end with a decision: continue as a devotee, take longer, or part kindly. Before then:

1. **Try the first practice** at least three times.
2. **Attend at least one rite**, if you can.
3. **Talk openly** with your mentor or the High Priestess about what you've liked, what puzzled you, and what worries you.
4. **Notice how you feel** in the days after practice and after the rite.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how long the devotee course usually takes in your coven, how often the coven meets, and what costs, if any, members share.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** the order of the rite, khernips, Hestia first and last, the shared meal, xenia.
- **Modern:** online rites, devotee courses, and the clear rights every member keeps.

quizzes.title: Your first thirty days: what you need to know
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on what a coven is, what membership asks, your rights and how to tell a healthy group. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor or the High Priestess scores the written ones. You need 80% to pass, and you can try again.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes a coven?
options: A small group who practise a magical or religious path together, regularly, under agreed ways of working
A group whose leader is responsible for every part of its members’ lives
A paid course that guarantees spiritual power at the end
A support group that replaces the need for counselling
questions.explanation: A coven is a small group practising together under agreed ways of working. It has no claim on your whole life, guarantees nothing, and is never a substitute for professional care.

questions.prompt: The modern coven is mostly a creation of the twentieth-century revival, even though the word "coven" appears in older witch-trial records.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The word appears in records such as Isobel Gowdie’s 1662 confession, but historians doubt such groups were organised as covens are now. Today’s covens mostly descend from the revival from the 1950s onward and from reconstructed traditions.

questions.prompt: Which of these are rights you keep in any coven? Choose all that apply.
options: To leave at any time without penalty
To say no to touch or a ritual act, even halfway through
To be told every initiate-only teaching before you join
Never to be pressured for money, sex or secrets
To have a non-alcoholic choice when drink is offered
questions.explanation: Leaving, consent, freedom from pressure for money, sex or secrets, and a non-alcoholic choice are rights in every group. Some traditions keep certain teachings for initiates; that is normal. What you may not be kept from is how the coven works, what it costs and what you are agreeing to.

questions.prompt: A member tells you that a promise of confidentiality means you must not tell anyone that a leader pressured another member for sex. What is true?
options: Confidentiality never covers abuse, exploitation, crime or someone in danger
Oaths of secrecy must always be kept, whatever they cover
You may only tell another initiate
You should wait until you have been in the coven a year
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects members’ privacy and the trust of the circle. It is never a cover for harm. A group that uses secrecy to hide abuse is showing a serious red flag. Tell someone you trust and report it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are red flags in a group? Choose all that apply.
options: Being told your friends and family won’t understand, and you should see less of them
Being encouraged to take your time and look at other groups too
Paying for rank or for access to secret teachings
Stories about bad luck or curses falling on people who left
Open, modest shared costs for candles and room hire
questions.explanation: Isolation, paying for rank or secrets, and fear about leaving are red flags. Being encouraged to take your time and modest, open shared costs are signs of a healthy group.

questions.prompt: At your first rite, the person leading invites everyone to take a drink of wine from a shared cup. You don’t want to. What do you do?
options: Politely decline or pass the cup on; it is always fine to sit out any part
Drink it so you don’t offend the coven
Leave the rite at once without a word
Ask the person beside you to drink your share
questions.explanation: You may sit out any part of a rite, including drinking. A simple "No, thank you" or passing the cup is enough. A healthy coven offers a non-alcoholic choice and doesn’t comment on what you choose.

questions.prompt: If you can’t make a rite you said you would attend, you should change your answer in the app or tell the person leading as early as you can.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Reliability is one of the usual commitments of membership. Changing your answer to "Can’t make it" lets the person leading plan, and counts as sending word.

questions.prompt: You ask the High Priestess how complaints about leaders are handled, and she replies, "You’ll understand when you’re initiated." What is the best way to understand this?
options: It is an evasive answer: how you will be treated is never a secret you must earn, so ask again or ask someone else
It is a normal answer, because all coven matters are oathbound
It means there are no complaints in this coven
It means you asked a rude question and should apologise
questions.explanation: Some lore is rightly kept for initiates, but how decisions are made, what things cost, how complaints are handled and how to leave should be answered plainly. One awkward answer is not proof of anything, but follow it up.

questions.prompt: In the fit exercise, you mark Values 5, People 5, Practice 4 and Logistics 1, because you can’t get to the gatherings. What does the lesson suggest?
options: A 1 anywhere is a serious problem: talk to the High Priestess about whether logistics can change, or think carefully
The total is 15, so join without further thought
Logistics never matter if the people are good
Ignore the marks and decide by how you feel on the day
questions.explanation: A coven that fits three areas but fails badly on the fourth is rarely a good long-term home. Logistics sink more memberships than anything else. Raise it: some covens can adapt, or you may need more time.

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of parting well? Choose all that apply.
options: Telling the High Priestess before you leave in the app
Keeping the confidences you were given
Posting a list of the coven’s faults in its chat
Returning anything you borrowed
Thanking them for their time
questions.explanation: Parting well means telling the leader first, thanking them, returning what you borrowed and keeping confidences, which outlast membership. If something serious went wrong, report it properly rather than airing it in the chat.

questions.prompt: In a few sentences, explain the difference between healthy confidentiality in a coven and secrecy that is a warning sign. Give one example of each.
questions.explanation: Healthy confidentiality protects members’ privacy (not outing anyone, not repeating what was said in circle) and may keep certain teachings for those trained to use them. Secrecy is a warning sign when it hides how the coven works, money, complaints or harm, or stops you seeking help.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): explains that healthy confidentiality protects people’s privacy and trust and/or keeps some teachings for initiates (1); explains that secrecy is a red flag when it hides basics (decisions, money, complaints, how to leave) or covers harm or abuse (1); gives one sound example of each, e.g. not revealing who is in the coven vs. being told not to tell anyone about pressure for sex (1). Give 2 if the examples are missing or muddled, 1 if only one side is explained.

questions.prompt: Imagine you have decided this coven is not right for you. Write the message you would send the High Priestess, and then say in two or three sentences why you wrote it that way.
questions.explanation: A good parting message thanks the coven, says honestly but kindly why you are leaving (about fit, not blame), tells the leader before you leave in the app, and leaves the door open to goodwill. You never owe a reason, but a kind one helps.
questions.rubric: Full marks (4): the message thanks the High Priestess or coven (1); gives a short, honest reason framed around fit rather than blame, or kindly says the writer prefers not to give one (1); is sent before leaving and says when they will leave (1); the explanation shows understanding of why parting well matters: goodwill, the coven can learn, confidences are kept, no need to justify at length (1). Take a mark off for blame, a list of grievances in place of a reason, or pressure on others to leave too. A brief, warm message can earn full marks.

quizzes.title: A first taste: test
quizzes.intro: Ten short questions on what Hellenic practice is, your first khernips and prayer, and what to expect at a rite. You need 80% to pass. Your mentor will read the written answers.

questions.prompt: What is Hellenic practice?
options: A role-play of life in ancient Athens
