The word daimon (DYE-mon) did not mean "demon" to the Greeks. It meant a divine power, sometimes a god, sometimes a lesser spirit, sometimes the force behind something that happens to you. Hesiod says the people of the Golden Age became daimones after death, kindly guardians who watch over mortals. Socrates spoke of a daimonion, a divine sign that warned him when he was about to make a mistake.

The daimon most important for household practice is the **Agathos Daimon** (AH-gah-thos DYE-mon), the Good Spirit of the house, its luck and its stores. He was often shown as a snake and paired with Agathe Tyche, Good Fortune. A cup of unmixed wine was poured to him at the end of a meal, and modern practitioners honour him on the second day of each month. The devotion lessons teach how.

The word was later used by Christian writers for evil spirits, which is where "demon" comes from. When you read daimon in a Hellenic context, put that meaning aside.

## Nymphs and spirits of place

Every spring, river, grove, cave and mountain could have its spirit. Nymphs were female spirits of nature: Naiads of springs and rivers, Dryads of trees, Oreads of mountains. They received offerings at caves and springs, and there are inscriptions from people who devoted themselves to them. Rivers were gods in their own right, and young people sometimes dedicated a lock of hair to the local river.

For a modern practitioner, this is the tradition's way of honouring the land where you actually live. You do not have to live in Greece. A stream, a park, an old tree near your home can be greeted with respect.

1. Visit the place a few times without asking anything. Just notice it.
2. Bring a small, safe offering: clean water, a song, an hour picking up litter.
3. Greet the spirit of the place in your own words.
4. Leave nothing harmful: no food that will hurt wildlife, no plastic, no candles.

Picking up litter is one of the best offerings you can make to a spirit of place.

## The dead

The Greeks cared deeply for their dead. A proper burial was a sacred duty; Sophocles' Antigone risks death to give her brother one. After a funeral, the family brought offerings to the grave on the third and ninth days, and again on the thirtieth, and then yearly. Athens held a festival of the dead called the Genesia in early autumn, and the last day of the Anthesteria in spring belonged to the dead.

Offerings to the dead were called choai (kho-EYE), libations poured into the earth: honey mixed with milk, wine, water, and sometimes oil. In the Odyssey, Odysseus pours honey and milk, sweet wine and water for the dead, and scatters white barley. These offerings were given away completely. The living did not drink or eat what had been given to the dead.

Ideas about the afterlife varied widely. Homer's dead are pale shadows in a gloomy underworld. The Eleusinian Mysteries promised initiates a better lot. Philosophers spoke of the soul's immortality or rebirth. Modern practitioners also differ, and you do not need to decide.

Most modern practitioners keep an ancestor shrine or shelf separate from the shrine of the gods, because of the old distinction between the deathless gods and the dead. The devotion lessons explain how to set one up and how to honour difficult or unknown ancestors.

> **Safety:** Ancestor work can bring up grief, sometimes unexpectedly. Go gently. If remembering someone becomes overwhelming, stop, ground yourself, eat something, and talk to your mentor or someone you trust. Religion can hold grief, but it does not replace a grief counsellor or doctor when you need one.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** hero cults, the Agathos Daimon, nymphs and river gods, offerings to the dead on set days, choai poured into the earth.
- **Modern:** honouring the spirits of non-Greek places, choosing personal heroes, and keeping a separate ancestor shrine at home (a sensible modern application of an ancient distinction).
- **Personal:** a sense that a place, ancestor or hero is present to you. Label it and treat it with care.

docs.title: How a Hellenic coven works
docs.summary: How Greeks worshipped together in households, cities and associations, how modern Hellenic groups work, and what to expect from a coven that keeps Hellenic practice.
docs.body:
## Worship was shared

In ancient Greece, almost no one worshipped entirely alone. Religion was something you did with your household, your neighbourhood, your city and, if you chose, a religious association. Understanding these circles helps you understand what a Hellenic coven is for.

## The ancient circles of worship

1. **The household (oikos).** The family worshipped at the hearth (Hestia), at the storeroom (Zeus Ktesios), at the courtyard altar (Zeus Herkeios) and at the door (Apollo Agyieus, Hermes and Hekate). The head of the household usually led, but women ran much of household religion, and some festivals belonged to women alone.
2. **The neighbourhood and kin group.** Athenians belonged to local districts (demes) and kin groups (phratries), each with its own festivals and sacrifices.
3. **The city (polis).** Great festivals like the Panathenaia were organised by the city, with priests, priestesses and officials.
4. **Associations.** People also formed voluntary groups to honour a particular god or hero together: a thiasos (a band of worshippers, often of Dionysus) or orgeones (members who met to honour a hero or god). These groups had members, rules, dues, shared meals and their own festivals. They are the closest ancient model to a coven.
5. **Mysteries.** Some rites, such as those at Eleusis, required initiation and secrecy.

## Modern Hellenic groups

Today, Hellenic polytheists gather in many ways: national organisations, local groups (often called a demos, from the word for a community), festival gatherings, online communities, and covens or temples that combine Hellenic worship with other practice. Some are strictly reconstructionist; others are freer. Many practitioners worship mainly at home and gather for festivals.

## What a Hellenic coven typically does

A coven that keeps Hellenic practice usually:

- **keeps the festival year**, gathering in person or in the app for the major Athenian festivals, and often for the monthly days;
- **holds rites in the Hellenic form**: procession, khernips, prayer, libation, offering and hymn, with Hestia first and last (taught step by step in the ritual lessons);
- **trains members** in household worship, so that each person keeps their own shrine between gatherings;
- **shares meals**, because a Greek rite often ended in a feast, and xenia is a sacred duty;
- **practises magic and divination** in whatever way the coven's witchcraft stream teaches;
- **cares for its members**, as an ancient association did, with rules, roles and mutual obligation.

## Roles you may meet

Ancient rites had many roles, and covens often borrow them. Your coven may use these names or its own.

- **Priest or priestess (hiereus, hiereia):** leads the rite and speaks the main prayers. In ancient Greece, priesthoods were often held for a set term, and many required no special training; the elder lessons explore this.
- **Herald (keryx):** calls for silence and announces each part of the rite.
- **Basket-bearer (kanephoros):** carries the basket of barley and offerings in procession.
- **Libation-bearer:** carries and pours the wine, juice or water.
- **Hymn-singer or reader:** leads the hymn.
- **Host:** looks after guests, food and the shared meal.

As a new member, you will probably be asked to carry something in procession, hold the khernips bowl, or read a hymn. Everyone starts there.

## The rhythm of a gathering

A coven gathering for a Hellenic festival often goes like this:

1. **Arrival and welcome.** Greetings, a drink of water, putting away phones.
2. **Briefing.** The leader explains the festival and who does what.
3. **Procession** to the altar, carrying offerings.
4. **Purification** with khernips and barley.
5. **Hestia first**, then prayer and offerings to the gods of the day.
6. **The heart of the festival:** a reading of myth, a hymn, a play, a working, or whatever belongs to that day.
7. **Hestia last** and closing.
8. **Shared meal** and conversation.

Online gatherings in the app follow the same order, each person at their own shrine with their own khernips, and a leader guiding the steps.

## Your part, and your rights

What is asked of you as a member:

- keep your own household shrine and simple daily practice;
- come to rites prepared and purified, and on time;
- keep what others share in confidence;
- help with the work: setting up, clearing, cooking, reading;
- be honest with your mentor about what is and isn't working.

What you can always expect:

- to be told what a rite will involve before you take part;
- to say no to anything, at any time, without explanation;
- never to be asked for sex, money beyond agreed costs, or secrets that would hurt you or others;
- to leave the coven if it is not right for you, and to be let go with kindness.

> **Safety:** In any group, beware of a leader who claims to speak for the gods in a way that cannot be questioned, demands money or devotion to themselves, isolates members from family and friends, or makes threats of divine punishment for leaving. Ancient priests served the gods; they did not own them. If you see these signs, speak to someone you trust outside the group.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor: which festivals does our coven keep together? Which do members keep at home? What roles might I take in my first rites? How do we meet in the app?

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** household, civic and association worship; the roles of priest, herald and basket-bearer; shared meals after rites.
- **Modern:** covens as such, online gatherings, and the blending of Hellenic religion with witchcraft.
- **Your part:** bringing your household practice into the life of the group, and the group's practice home.

docs.title: Household worship
docs.summary: The gods of the Greek household, Hestia first and last, Zeus Ktesios and his storage jar, the gods of the door, and how to set up a household shrine on little money and space.
docs.body:
## Religion begins at home

For most ancient Greeks, most of the time, religion happened at home. Great festivals came a few times a year; the household gods were honoured every day. The house (oikos) was a small religious community with its own gods, its own altar and its own rhythm. Modern Hellenic practice is built on the same foundation. Your household shrine is where your relationship with the gods grows.

## The gods of the house

Different gods watched over different parts of a Greek house.

- **Hestia** at the hearth, the centre. She is the fire that cooks, warms and gathers people, and so she is the heart of the home. She receives the first and last offering of every rite. Unlike the other gods, she does not travel; she stays at home.
- **Zeus Ktesios**, Zeus "of the property", guarded the storeroom and the household's wealth. He was honoured with a special jar, described below, and was sometimes imagined as a snake.
- **Zeus Herkeios**, Zeus "of the enclosure", had an altar in the courtyard, protecting the boundary of the house.
- **Apollo Agyieus**, Apollo "of the street", stood as a pointed pillar or stone by the front door.
- **Hermes** often stood by the door as a herm (a pillar with a head), guarding comings and goings.
- **Hekate** had small shrines (hekataia) at the door too, guarding the threshold.
- **The Agathos Daimon**, the Good Spirit, watched over the household's luck and stores.

You do not need to honour all of these. Many modern practitioners start with Hestia alone, add Zeus Ktesios and a god at the door, and grow from there.

## Hestia first and last

Hestia is the one god every Hellenic household honours. Her presence is a flame: a candle, an oil lamp, or an electric light. In ancient times the hearth fire was kept alight; when a new colony was founded, fire was carried from the mother city's hearth.

To honour Hestia daily:

1. Light her flame when you begin your devotions, and greet her.
2. Give her the first offering: a drop of oil, a pour of wine or water, the first bite of a meal set aside.
3. Do your other devotions.
4. Give her the last offering and thank her.
5. Put out the flame, or leave an electric light on.

A clean, welcoming home and generous hospitality honour her too. This agrees with her Living Library entry, which says she asks for steadiness and care rather than grand ceremony.

> **Safety:** Never leave a candle, lamp or flame unattended, even for Hestia. An electric candle or a small lamp is a perfectly respectful hearth, and many practitioners keep one lit for her all day. Real flames go out when you leave the room.

## Zeus Ktesios and the kadiskos

An ancient guide to religious practice, quoted by the writer Athenaeus, describes how to set up a shrine to Zeus Ktesios: take a new two-handled jar with a lid (a kadiskos), crown its handles with white wool and a strand of yellow, put into it whatever you find, and pour in "ambrosia", which the guide explains as pure water, olive oil and all kinds of fruits. The jar was kept in the storeroom.

Modern practitioners make a kadiskos like this:

1. **Choose a jar** with a lid: a clean jam jar, a small pottery pot, anything that closes.
2. **Wash it** and purify it with khernips.
3. **Decorate it**, if you like, with white and yellow thread or wool around the neck.
4. **Fill it** with small amounts of dried foods from your kitchen: a pinch of grain, a few dried beans, a little rice, dried fruit, a coin. Add a little water and olive oil if you follow the ancient recipe closely, or keep everything dry to avoid mould.
5. **Dedicate it**: "Zeus Ktesios, guardian of this house's stores, this is your jar. Keep our cupboards full and our household safe."
6. **Keep it** in or near your kitchen or pantry.
7. **Feed it** each Noumenia with a pinch of whatever you have bought or harvested that month, and pour a little libation over the lid or beside it.

Once a year, or when it gets full or stale, empty it into the earth or compost and start fresh.

> **Note:** Ancient sources do not tell us exactly how often households tended their kadiskos, or exactly what yellow strand was meant. The monthly feeding is a modern habit that suits the monthly cycle well.

## Gods at the door

The door is where the household meets the world, and the Greeks guarded it. You might:

- place a small stone or pillar by the door for Apollo Agyieus;
- put up a small image of Hermes, or a coin, near the door;
- keep a key, a small image or a candle for Hekate near the entrance;
- touch the door frame and greet the gods of the door as you leave and come home.

If you have a Hekate altar, the door is a natural place for it, since she was honoured there as Propylaia, "before the gate".

## Setting up a household shrine

You need very little. Here is how to make a shrine in an hour with things you probably have.

1. **Place.** A shelf, a windowsill, the top of a chest of drawers. It should be stable, at a height you can stand or sit before, and away from curtains. A corner of the kitchen is close to the hearth in spirit.
2. **Surface.** Clean it, and lay down a cloth or tile if you like.
3. **Hestia's flame.** A candle in a holder, a tealight in a jar, an oil lamp, or an electric light.
4. **Khernips bowl.** Any small bowl, kept for this.
5. **Libation cup.** A small cup or glass, kept for this.
6. **Offering bowl.** A bowl or saucer to pour and place offerings into.
7. **Images.** Optional. A printed picture, a postcard of a statue, a small figure, or a symbol: an owl for Athena, a key for Hekate, an olive branch, a seashell for Poseidon.
8. **Incense holder.** Optional, heatproof.
9. **Purify and dedicate** it as the ritual lessons describe.

Space is tight? A shoebox lid on a shelf holds all of this. Living with others who don't share your religion? An electric candle, a small bowl and a cup on a bookshelf can look like decoration and be a full shrine.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may suggest particular gods for every member's household shrine, or images to use. Ask your mentor. Some covens also keep a shrine in the app, which you can use alongside your physical one.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** Hestia at the hearth, Zeus Ktesios and the kadiskos, Zeus Herkeios, the gods of the door, small daily household offerings.
- **Modern:** electric candles, jam-jar kadiskoi, monthly feeding of the jar, and the household shrine as a single shelf combining what was spread across a whole ancient house.

docs.title: Daily practice
docs.summary: A simple morning and evening devotion, how to build a habit that lasts, the gods of the days of the month, and what to do when you miss days.
docs.body:
## Small and regular

Hesiod, the farmer-poet, gives this advice in Works and Days: "According to your means, do sacrifice to the deathless gods purely and cleanly ... and at other times propitiate them with libations and incense, both when you go to bed and when the holy light has come back." Morning and evening, with what you have, purely. That is daily Hellenic practice in one sentence.

Daily devotion is where kharis grows. It does not need to be long. Five minutes every day does more than an hour once a month.

## A morning devotion (5 minutes)

1. **Wash** your face and hands as you get up, or make khernips at your shrine.
2. **Light Hestia's flame** and greet her: "Hestia, good morning. Keep this house today."
3. **Pour a little water** or oil for her.
4. **Greet the gods** you honour, by name: "Hermes, Athena, Apollo, good day to you." If you like, add one line asking for help with the day: "Hermes, guide my journeys today."
5. **Pour to Hestia last**, and put out the flame (or leave an electric one on).

## An evening devotion (5 to 10 minutes)

1. **Make khernips** and wash.
2. **Light Hestia's flame** and pour her first offering.
3. **Burn a little incense**, if you use it.
4. **Give thanks** for the day: name one thing that went well, and thank a god for it.
5. **Pour a libation** to any god you are getting to know.
6. **Sit in stillness** for a minute or two.
7. **Pour to Hestia last**, and put out the flame.

Do one of these, or both. Many people find the evening easier to keep because the day's rush is over.

## At meals

The Greeks offered a little of their food and drink to the gods. You can:

- set aside the first bite of a meal for Hestia on a small dish, and give it to the earth later;
- pour a drop of your drink for the Agathos Daimon at the end of a meal;
- say a short line of thanks before eating.

## The days of the month

The Athenians gave several of the first days of each lunar month to particular gods. Modern practitioners use this as a gentle rhythm, honouring each god briefly on their day.

- **Day 1, Noumenia:** the household gods; the new month.
- **Day 2:** the Agathos Daimon.
- **Day 3:** Athena.
- **Day 4:** Hermes, Aphrodite, Herakles and Eros.
- **Day 6:** Artemis.
- **Day 7:** Apollo.
- **Day 8:** Poseidon and Theseus.
- **Last day:** Hekate's Deipnon.

You do not need to keep them all. Choose the days of the gods you honour, and add a short prayer and libation to your daily devotion on that day. The app's Hellenic calendar shows the Noumenia, Agathos Daimon and Deipnon each month; you can count the other days from the Noumenia.

> **Note:** The sacred days of the month are reconstructed by scholars from scattered ancient sources and are best attested for Athens. Different sources disagree on a few of them, and how widely ordinary households kept them is unknown.

## Building a habit that lasts

The hardest part of daily practice is not knowing what to do. It is doing it every day. These steps help.

1. **Attach it to something you already do.** After brushing your teeth; before your first coffee; when you get home from work.
2. **Make it easy.** Keep matches, bay leaves and a filled water jug next to the shrine. The fewer steps, the more likely you'll do it.
3. **Start small.** Two minutes, every day, beats twenty minutes when you feel like it.
4. **Log it.** Use the app to log each day. Seeing a run of days is encouraging.
5. **Set a reminder** on your phone if it helps.
6. **Review weekly.** At the end of each week, ask: what worked? What got in the way? Adjust.

### Common difficulties

- **Mornings are chaos.** Do the evening devotion instead, or a thirty-second greeting at the shrine on your way out.
- **Living with others.** Keep it quiet: an electric candle, a whispered prayer. A devotion can be invisible to everyone but you and the gods.
- **Travelling.** Take a tealight, a tiny bowl and a few bay leaves, or simply wash your hands with attention and speak a prayer.
- **Feeling nothing.** That is very common. Devotion is like tending a garden: most days you see no change. Keep going and, after a few months, look back.
- **Feeling too much.** If daily practice starts to feel overwhelming, frightening or compulsive, stop for a while, ground yourself, and talk to your mentor.

## When you miss days

You will miss days. Everyone does. The gods are not keeping a register, and there is no need for guilt or elaborate apology. When you come back:

1. Make khernips and wash.
2. Light Hestia's flame and greet her.
3. Say simply: "I have been away, and I have returned." Pour a libation.
4. Carry on as normal.

> **Safety:** Religious practice can sometimes slide into anxiety, perfectionism or compulsion, a feeling that something bad will happen if you skip a step. If you notice this, talk to your mentor. If it continues, please speak to a doctor or counsellor: obsessive worry about ritual is a recognised and treatable condition, and getting help is wise, not a failure of faith.

## Try this

> **Try this:** For the next thirty days, do a five-minute devotion every day, morning or evening. Log each one in the app. At the end, write down what has changed, if anything, in how you feel about the shrine, the gods and your days.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** morning and evening offerings, Hestia first and last, offerings at meals, the sacred days of the month.
- **Modern:** fixed short daily routines, habit-building methods, and logging.

docs.title: The monthly cycle: Noumenia and Agathos Daimon
docs.summary: How the Attic lunar month works, and how to keep the Noumenia and the Agathos Daimon at home step by step, with the Deipnon before them.
docs.body:
## A month that follows the moon

The ancient Athenian month was lunar. It began when the first thin crescent of the new moon was seen in the west after sunset, and ran for 29 or 30 days, until the moon disappeared again. The app's Hellenic calendar works this out for you and shows the monthly days each month.

Three days mark the turn of the month, and modern Hellenic practitioners keep them as a cycle:

1. **Hekate's Deipnon**, on the last day of the month, when the moon is dark: clearing out the old month and giving Hekate her supper. It has its own lesson, next.
2. **Noumenia**, the first day, when the new crescent appears: honouring the household gods for a good month.
3. **Agathos Daimon**, the second day: honouring the Good Spirit of the house.

The ancient Greeks called the last day of the month "the old and the new" (hene kai nea), because it stood between two months. Clearing out on the Deipnon and then welcoming the new month on the Noumenia gives the turn of each month a clean shape: close, clean, begin.

## Noumenia: the new month

Ancient writers called the Noumenia (noo-meh-NEE-ah) the holiest of days, and in Athens no other festival was held on it. Offerings were small and household-centred: incense, honey cakes, garlands for the household images. The philosopher Porphyry tells of Klearchos, the poor farmer whom the oracle at Delphi named as the most pious man in Greece, because every new moon he cleaned and crowned his images of Hermes and Hekate and offered them incense, barley cakes and small cakes. Small, regular and sincere: that is the spirit of the day.

### Keeping the Noumenia, step by step (20 to 30 minutes)

1. **Look for the moon.** At dusk, go outside or to a west-facing window and look for the thin crescent low in the sky, just after sunset. You may not see it: clouds, buildings and the moon's thinness all get in the way. That is fine; the calendar says it is there. If you see it, greet it: "Hail, new moon, the month begins."
2. **Refresh the shrine.** The Deipnon cleaning should already be done. Put out fresh water, fresh flowers or a bay sprig, and wipe the surfaces.
3. **Make khernips** and wash.
4. **Light Hestia's flame** and give her the first offering.
5. **Burn incense** for the household gods. Name them: "Hestia, Zeus Ktesios, Apollo Noumenios of the new moon, Hermes and Hekate at the door, and all the gods of this house."
6. **Offer** a honey cake, a little fruit, or barley. Garland or polish your images, as Klearchos did.
7. **Feed the kadiskos**, if you keep one: a pinch of something new from the month's shopping, and a libation.
8. **Speak one hope** for the month aloud: "Let this month bring health to this house." Keep it simple.
9. **Bless the rooms**, if you like: carry the incense through each room, pausing in each doorway.
10. **Hestia last**, and close.

Leave the food offering on the shrine until the next day, then give it to the earth or compost. The app has a ready-made Noumenia household blessing you can follow too.

### Small versions

On a busy day: light Hestia's flame, make khernips, burn one stick of incense, say "Gods of this house, bless this month", and pour to Hestia last. Five minutes.

## Agathos Daimon: the Good Spirit

The Agathos Daimon (AH-gah-thos DYE-mon) is the Good Spirit of the house, guardian of its luck, stores, vines and grain, often shown as a snake and often paired with Agathe Tyche, Good Fortune. The Greeks drank a small cup of unmixed wine to him at the end of a meal, before the main drinking began; Aristophanes' characters mention it as an everyday custom. House snakes were treated kindly as his presence.

Modern practitioners honour him on the second day of the month. The evidence for this day is thinner than for the Noumenia, and the Living Library and calendar note that honestly, but it is a gentle and well-loved custom.

### Keeping the Agathos Daimon, step by step (10 minutes)

1. **After the evening meal**, wash your hands, or make khernips.
2. **Pour a small cup** of unmixed wine, or grape juice, or water.
3. **Lift it and say**: "To the Agathos Daimon, good spirit of this house: thank you for our luck and our bread."
4. **Pour a few drops** into the offering bowl or onto the ground outside, and drink a sip.
5. **Leave the rest** by the shrine overnight, then pour it on the earth.
6. **Tend something** that brings the household luck: water the plants, tidy the pantry, put a coin in the savings jar.

## Fitting the cycle into a busy life

The cycle takes three days in a row every month. You do not have to do all of it at full length every time. A realistic pattern for a beginner:

- **Deipnon:** a quick clean of the shrine and the kitchen, and a small offering at the door.
- **Noumenia:** the full rite if you can, the short one if not.
- **Agathos Daimon:** a cup poured after dinner.

As your practice grows, you can lengthen each one.

> **Your coven:** Many covens gather, in person or in the app, for the Noumenia or the Deipnon. Ask your mentor which monthly days your coven keeps together, and how.

> **Safety:** Incense and candles go on a heatproof surface, away from curtains. Ventilate the room; smoke can trouble asthma and pets, especially birds. Juice or water is always a fine replacement for wine.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** the lunar month beginning with the crescent, the Noumenia as a holy day with small household offerings, the after-dinner cup for the Agathos Daimon, Hekate's suppers at the month's end.
- **Modern:** keeping all three as one monthly cycle in every household, and keeping the second day especially for the Agathos Daimon.

docs.title: Hekate's Deipnon and crossroads practice
docs.summary: What the ancient sources say about Hekate's monthly supper, and how to keep the Deipnon step by step: cleaning, reflection, the supper, the crossroads, and walking away, with safety for you and for animals.
docs.body:
## Hekate's supper

Deipnon (DAYP-non) means supper. On the last day of each lunar month, when the moon is dark, ancient Athenians sent a supper to Hekate at the crossroads. The same day was a time of household purification, when the sweepings and leftovers of the month's cleansing were carried out of the house. Modern Hellenists and many witches keep the Deipnon every month. If you keep a Hekate altar, this is the heart of your practice with her.

## What the ancient sources say

The evidence is scattered but real.

- **Aristophanes**, in his comedy Wealth (388 BCE), has a character say: ask Hekate whether it is better to be rich or poor, for the rich send her a supper every month, and the poor snatch it before it is even set down. The joke only works if everyone knew the custom.
- **Demosthenes**, in a court speech, mocks low people who eat the offerings left for Hekate.
- **Lucian**, centuries later, mentions Hekate's supper and the egg from a purification together, as things the hungry might pick up at the crossroads.
- **Theophrastus**, in his Characters, describes the "superstitious man" who keeps purifying his house because he thinks Hekate has been brought into it, and who pours oil on smooth stones at the crossroads.
- **The katharmata**, the leftovers of purification rites, and the sweepings of the house were taken out and left at the crossroads, according to several ancient writers.
- Foods named for Hekate's suppers by ancient or later writers, or by long modern custom, include **bread, small cakes, eggs, cheese, small fish such as red mullet, and garlic**.
- In Apollonius of Rhodes' Argonautica, Jason is told to make his night offering to Hekate and then walk away **without turning back**, whatever he hears. Theocritus describes a purification whose remains are thrown away by someone who then returns without looking back. Modern practitioners keep this custom at the Deipnon.

What we do not know: exactly what each household did, what was said, or how strictly the day was kept. The precise monthly rite most people follow today is a modern reconstruction from these pieces.

## Why the Deipnon matters

The Deipnon gathers together several things:

- **Closing the month.** The old month's dirt, worry and unfinished business are cleared out before the new month begins at the Noumenia.
- **Purification of the household.** The house is cleaned and cleansed.
- **Honouring Hekate** as guardian of thresholds and crossroads, who stands between the old and the new.
- **Remembering the restless dead.** Hekate was thought to travel with the restless dead, and some modern practitioners remember them on this night.
- **Care for the hungry.** In ancient Athens, the poor ate these suppers. Many modern practitioners give food or money to a food bank on the Deipnon in Hekate's name, and many consider this the most fitting offering of all.

## Keeping the Deipnon, step by step

The app shows the Deipnon each month and offers a gentle note on the day, and there is a ready-made Deipnon rite you can follow. Allow about an hour, most of it cleaning.

### 1. Clean the house (20 to 40 minutes)

In the afternoon or evening, clean: sweep, dust, wipe down the shrine and the kitchen, take out the rubbish. Many people work from the back of the house toward the front door. Gather anything broken, spoiled or finished with. Sweep the dust into a bag.

### 2. Cleanse (5 minutes)

Make khernips and sprinkle it in each room and at the threshold, or wash the front step. Some people burn a little incense and carry it through the house. Say something like: "Out goes the old month and all that is unclean."

### 3. Reflect (5 to 10 minutes)

Sit for a while and think through the month. What do you want to leave behind? What do you owe: an apology, a reply, a debt? What do you want to put down? Write it if you like. Settle what you can.

### 4. Prepare the supper (5 minutes)

On a plate or in a dish, set out a small supper for Hekate. For example:

- a piece of bread or a small cake;
- a boiled egg;
- a little cheese;
- a spoonful of honey;
- a clove of garlic, only if it will stay indoors or on your own step and be cleared promptly.

Light a candle beside it. Speak to Hekate in your own words, or use a hymn. For example: "Hekate of the crossroads, key-bearer, torch-bearer, guardian of the door: the month is ending, and the house is clean. This is your supper. Keep the doors of this house through the dark of the moon."

### 5. Carry it out (10 minutes)

Put out the candle. Never take a lit candle outside and leave it. Carry the supper, and the bag of sweepings, out of the house.

- **To a crossroads.** Ideally a place where three roads meet. In a town, a quiet three-way junction, the corner of a path, or a fork in a park track will do. Set the food down discreetly, at the edge, out of the way of traffic and feet, and put the sweepings in a bin there.
- **To your own threshold.** If there is no suitable crossroads, or it is not safe to go out, place the supper just outside your front door, on your step, or at the boundary of your garden. A doorstep is a threshold, and the threshold is Hekate's place.
- **To a household hekataion.** Some people keep a small shrine to Hekate by the front door, and leave the supper there.

### 6. Walk away without looking back (2 minutes)

Turn and walk home. Do not look back at the offering. It is hers now.

### 7. Wash (2 minutes)

As soon as you are in, wash your hands, in khernips or running water. The month is closed. Tomorrow is the Noumenia.

## What happens to the supper

The supper is given wholly away: it is not eaten by you or anyone in your household. What is hers is hers.

- If you left it at a crossroads, leave it. Animals or people may take it, as in ancient Athens.
- If you left it on your own step or in your garden, clear what is left the next morning, and compost, bury or respectfully bin it.
- If you left it at an indoor hekataion, clear it the next morning in the same way.

> **Safety:** Garlic, onion, chocolate, grapes, raisins and xylitol are toxic to dogs and cats. Never leave them where animals can reach them. Garlic is a traditional offering, so keep it indoors or on your own step and clear it at first light. Leave small portions, not heaps, so you don't attract rats.

> **Safety:** Going out alone after dark can carry risks. Go with someone if you can, carry a torch or phone light, tell someone where you are going, stay aware of traffic, and choose a well-lit place. Never leave a candle burning outdoors. Do not leave offerings on private property without permission, at memorials or shrines of other religions, or where they break littering rules. Your safety matters more than the exact location; the doorstep is always a fine crossroads.

## Common questions

**Is the Deipnon frightening?** No. Many people are told that Hekate is dangerous or that the dark moon is a perilous night. The Athenians treated the Deipnon as ordinary household religion, like taking out the rubbish with a prayer. Approach her with respect, not fear.

**Do I have to clean the whole house?** Clean what you can. A tidy kitchen and a clean shrine are a good start.

**I live in a flat with no outside space.** Use your front door, the landing if it is private and allowed, or a hekataion just inside your door, and clear it in the morning.

**What if I feel watched, or hear dogs, or sense something?** Many people report such experiences on the Deipnon. Note them in your journal as your own experience, without drawing big conclusions, and talk to your mentor. If you ever feel frightened, go home, wash, light Hestia's flame and ground yourself.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may keep the Deipnon together, in person or in the app, or have its own words and offerings. Ask your mentor.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** suppers for Hekate at the crossroads at the month's end, carrying out sweepings and katharmata, eggs and cakes among the foods, walking away without turning back (attested for Hekate and for purifications).
- **Modern:** the step-by-step rite, food bank gifts in her name, doorstep and indoor alternatives, and animal safety rules.
- **Personal:** what you feel or notice on the night. Label it as yours.

docs.title: Offerings in practice
docs.summary: What to offer which gods, offerings on a small budget, vows and votives, acts of service as offerings, and what not to offer.
docs.body:
## Giving well

The ritual lessons taught you how to pour a libation and how to dispose of offerings. This lesson is about choosing them: what to give, to whom, and how to make offerings a steady part of your life without strain.

## The principles

1. **Give what you can sustain.** Hesiod says to sacrifice "according to your means". Regular small gifts build kharis; occasional grand ones mostly build debt.
2. **Give what is fitting.** Each god has things they were traditionally given. Choosing well shows you know them.
3. **Give what is clean and good.** Not leftovers or stale food, but something you would be glad to serve a guest.
4. **Give something of yourself.** Time, effort, craft and attention are offerings too.
5. **Give freely.** An offering given resentfully, or because you feel forced, is not much of a gift.

## What suits which god

These suggestions agree with the Living Library entries in the app. Read the full entry for any god you honour.

- **Hestia:** the first and last of every offering; olive oil, bread, wine, water, incense; a clean and welcoming home.
- **Zeus:** libations of wine or water, frankincense, barley, honey cakes; hospitality to guests; a kept oath.
- **Hera:** flowers, especially lilies; incense; honour to marriages and commitments.
- **Athena:** olive oil, olives, honey; craftwork, study, weaving or mending.
- **Apollo:** bay leaves, frankincense, honey cakes; music, poetry, healing work.
- **Artemis:** round cakes, honey, fruit; time in wild places; care for wildlife and young people.
- **Hermes:** coins, olive oil, bread, honey, milk; a stone added to a roadside cairn; kindness to travellers; a good joke.
- **Demeter:** grain, bread, honey, fruit; growing food; giving food to the hungry.
- **Persephone:** pomegranate, flowers, honey; offerings that follow the seasons.
- **Dionysus:** wine or grape juice, ivy, figs; theatre, music, dance.
- **Aphrodite:** roses, myrrh, perfume, sweets; acts of love and beauty.
- **Poseidon:** a libation poured into the sea; care for waters and coasts.
- **Hekate:** bread, eggs, cheese, honey, olive oil, incense; the Deipnon supper; guarding boundaries; food for the hungry.
- **Hades and the chthonic powers:** honey, milk, water, wine poured into the earth; pomegranate; given wholly away.
- **The dead:** honey and milk, water, wine, flowers, a lit lamp; their names spoken aloud.

## Offerings on a small budget

Many of the best offerings cost nothing or very little.

- Fresh water, poured with care.
- A pinch of barley, oats or rice from the cupboard.
- The first bite of your own dinner.
- A flower or leaf gathered (where gathering is allowed).
- A hymn read aloud, or one you write.
- An hour's work for a cause the god cares about.
- Cleaning a public place, or picking up litter.
- A drawing, a poem, a song.

The story of Klearchos, the poor farmer named by the oracle as the most pious man in Greece for his monthly incense and small cakes, is the tradition's own answer to "can I afford this?"

## Acts as offerings

The Greeks offered songs, dances, plays and athletic contests to the gods. Modern practitioners widely dedicate acts too. To make an act an offering:

1. **Choose** something that suits the god: Athena and study, Apollo and music, Demeter and feeding people, Hermes and helping a traveller.
2. **Say beforehand** at your shrine or in your head: "I do this for you."
3. **Do it well.**
4. **Say afterwards**: "This was for you," and, if you like, pour a small libation.

## Vows and votives

A vow (euche) is a promise to give a god something if they help you: "If I pass this exam, I will give you a new image for your shrine." Greek sanctuaries were full of votive offerings (anathemata) set up when vows were fulfilled, many inscribed with the giver's thanks.

Vows are serious. Before you make one:

1. **Make it small and specific.** "I will pour you wine every Noumenia for a year," not "I will give you anything."
2. **Make it something you can certainly do.** A broken vow damages the relationship.
3. **Write it down**, with the date.
4. **Tell your mentor**, especially if it is a long or large vow.
5. **Keep it promptly** when the time comes.

If you find you truly cannot keep a vow, go to the god honestly, explain, offer what you can, and talk to your mentor. Honesty is better than pretending.

> **Safety:** No real god needs you to go into debt, give away money you need, or harm your health to keep a vow. If anyone, human or a voice in prayer, pressures you to make offerings you cannot afford, stop and talk to your mentor.

## What not to offer

- **Anything that harms an animal or person.** Modern Hellenic practice does not involve harming animals, and never involves harming people.
- **Anything that is not yours to give**, such as plants picked from protected land or someone else's possessions.
- **Food that harms wildlife or pets** if it will be left outside.
- **Plastic, glitter, balloons or anything that will litter.**
- **Spoiled or stale food.**
- **Your blood or anything that harms your body.** Some modern practices online suggest this. It is not Hellenic practice and is not safe.
- **Things for a god from a tradition that is not yours to take**, such as sacred objects of a closed tradition.

## Try this

> **Try this:** For one god you honour, write a short list: three traditional offerings, one zero-cost offering, and one act you could dedicate to them this month. Then make one of each over the next few weeks, and log them.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** offering according to means, fitting gifts for each god, vows and votives, music and contests as offerings.
- **Modern:** dedicating volunteer work and charity, litter-picking as an offering, and strict rules about animal safety.

docs.title: Ancestors and the dead
docs.summary: How the Greeks honoured their dead, how to set up an ancestor shrine separate from the gods', how to pour choai, and how to honour difficult, unknown and chosen ancestors.
docs.body:
## Caring for the dead

Caring for the dead was one of the great duties of Greek religion. Giving the dead proper burial and continuing to honour them afterwards was part of eusebeia, piety. Ancestor practice in a Hellenic context is a natural extension of that duty, and for many people it is deeply moving.

## How the Greeks honoured their dead

- **The funeral.** The body was washed and laid out (prothesis), mourned, and carried to burial or cremation (ekphora). Women led the lament.
- **The days after.** The family brought offerings to the grave on the third and ninth days after death, and again on the thirtieth.
- **Yearly.** The dead were remembered every year, and Athens held a state festival of the dead, the Genesia, in early autumn.
- **The Anthesteria.** On the last day of this spring festival, the dead were believed to walk among the living and were sent away at its end. The lore lessons tell this story in full.
- **Choai.** Offerings to the dead were poured into the earth: honey mixed with milk, wine, water, and sometimes oil. In the Odyssey, Odysseus pours honey and milk, sweet wine and water for the dead, and scatters white barley.
- **Tomb offerings.** Vases of oil (lekythoi), ribbons, wreaths and food were left at graves. Painted lekythoi often show family members visiting a tomb.

## The dead and the gods kept apart

The gods are deathless. The dead have died. Greek religion kept these apart: offerings to the dead went into the earth and were not shared; the dead were honoured at graves, not at the altars of the heavenly gods; those who had been touched by death were kept from temples for a time.

Most modern practitioners apply this by keeping an ancestor shrine separate from the shrine of the gods. It can be in the same room, but on a different shelf or surface.

## Setting up an ancestor shrine

1. **Choose a place** separate from your shrine to the gods. A shelf, a box, a small table.
2. **Clean it** and sprinkle it with khernips.
3. **Set out** photographs, names written on a card, or objects that belonged to your dead. A candle or lamp. A small bowl for choai.
4. **Dedicate it**: "This is a place for my dead, who came before me. Be welcome and be at peace."
5. **Pour a first choe**, a little water or honey and milk, into the bowl.

## Pouring choai, step by step

1. **Make khernips** and wash.
2. **Light the lamp** on the ancestor shrine.
3. **Speak the names** of those you honour, aloud. If you do not know names: "my mothers and fathers, and all who came before me".
4. **Lower your hands** toward the earth, or touch the floor, as the Greeks did for powers below.
5. **Pour** water, honey mixed with milk, wine or juice into the bowl, all of it.
6. **Speak** to them: share news, thank them, ask for their goodwill.
7. **Sit quietly** for a few minutes.
8. **Put out the lamp.**
9. **Pour the choe into the earth** later the same day or the next morning. Do not drink it.

Many people do this weekly, monthly, or on the anniversaries of their dead.

## Difficult ancestors

Not every ancestor was kind. Some families carry abuse, cruelty or great harm. You are under no obligation to honour anyone who hurt you or others.

- **Honour the dead as a group** ("all my ancestors who wish me well") rather than by name.
- **Leave someone out entirely**; piety does not require you to honour an abuser.
- **Honour those who loved you**, whether related or not.
- **Speak with your mentor** if ancestor practice stirs up painful memories.

## Unknown ancestors and chosen ancestors

Adopted people, people estranged from family, and people who simply don't know their family history can all keep ancestor practice:

- **Ancestors of blood** you do not know by name can be honoured as a group.
- **Ancestors of spirit**: teachers, writers, the founders of your coven's tradition, people whose lives shaped yours.
- **Ancestors of place**: the dead who lived where you live now. Honour them respectfully, without taking on the sacred practices of peoples whose traditions are closed.
- **Ancestors of craft**: people who did your work before you.

## Grief and pollution

In Greek religion, contact with death made a person ritually impure for a time: those who had attended a death or funeral did not approach the gods' altars for a set number of days. The next lesson explains this in detail. Many modern practitioners, after a death in the family or attending a funeral, pause their worship of the heavenly gods for a time, often a few days to forty days, while continuing to honour the dead. Others keep their usual practice. Your coven may have a custom.

Whatever you choose, grief itself is not shameful or impure. It is love with nowhere to go. Ancestor practice can give it somewhere.

> **Safety:** Ancestor work can bring grief to the surface without warning. If it becomes overwhelming, stop, eat something warm, ground yourself, and reach out to your mentor or someone you trust. Religion can hold grief, but it is not a substitute for bereavement support, counselling or medical help when you need them.

> **Note:** Some people believe they can contact their dead directly through divination or mediumship. Greek religion knew necromancy, but it was regarded with suspicion. If you try divination about your dead, keep it gentle, label what you receive as personal, and do not let it replace the slow work of grieving.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may keep a shared remembrance of members' dead, at the Anthesteria or another time. Ask your mentor how you can add the names of your dead.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** funerals, offerings on the third, ninth and thirtieth days, choai of honey, milk, wine and water poured into the earth, the Genesia, the separation of the dead from the heavenly gods.
- **Modern:** the household ancestor shrine on its own shelf, chosen and spiritual ancestors, and permission to leave out those who caused harm.

docs.title: Miasma and purification
docs.summary: What ritual pollution is and isn't, what caused it in ancient Greece, how modern practitioners handle it, and how to purify yourself and your home.
docs.body:
## Clean to approach the gods

The Greeks believed that certain events made a person ritually unclean, unfit to approach the gods until purified. This uncleanness is called miasma (mee-AZ-mah). Understanding it explains why khernips matters, why the Deipnon involves cleaning, and why some practitioners pause their worship after a funeral.

## Miasma is not sin

The most important thing to know about miasma is what it is not. It is not guilt, sin or moral failure. You could become polluted by doing nothing wrong at all. Attending a birth or caring for the dying were good and necessary acts, and they still brought miasma.

Think of it more like the way some things are kept apart in a kitchen: raw and cooked, clean and dirty. Miasma marks the boundaries between life and death, mortal and immortal, everyday and sacred. The gods are deathless; things touched by birth and death belong to the mortal world, and are kept apart from the gods for a while.

## What caused miasma

According to ancient sources, especially the sacred laws carved at sanctuaries:

- **Death:** contact with a dead body, attending a funeral, being in a house where someone has died.
- **Birth:** attending a birth, or giving birth.
- **Bloodshed:** killing a person brought the deepest miasma, which could spread to the whole city if left unpurified, as in the story of Oedipus.
- **Sex:** a short-lived pollution, removed by washing.
- **Certain foods**, at certain sanctuaries.

The length of impurity was set by sacred laws and varied: sometimes a day, sometimes forty days after a death, depending on the place and how close you were to the event.

## How the Greeks purified

- **Water:** washing with khernips, bathing, or sea water. Euripides has a character say that the sea washes away all human ills.
- **Fire and smoke:** fumigation. In the Odyssey, after the battle in his hall, Odysseus calls for fire and sulphur to purify the house.
- **Time:** waiting out the days of impurity.
- **Specialist rites:** for serious pollution, such as bloodshed, purifiers performed rites that we know only in part.
- **Carrying out the impurity:** the sweepings and remains of purification (katharmata) were carried out of the house, often to the crossroads, as at the Deipnon.

## How modern practitioners handle miasma

Modern Hellenists differ on how strictly to follow ancient purity rules. Common patterns:

1. **Khernips before every act of worship.** Almost universal.
2. **Washing after sex** before approaching the shrine. Very common.
3. **Not worshipping while bleeding** from a wound; bandage it and wash first. Common.
4. **A pause after death.** After a funeral or a death in the household, many pause worship of the heavenly gods for a period, often between a few days and forty days, while still honouring the dead and keeping Hestia's flame. Some keep worship going and simply wash with special care.
5. **Birth.** Some pause worship for a time after attending or giving birth. Many modern practitioners see no reason to.
6. **Menstruation.** Ancient evidence for menstruation as polluting is late and thin. Most modern practitioners do not treat it as polluting, and many regard rules about it as reflecting ancient attitudes to women rather than religion.

You get to decide where you stand, ideally after reading and talking with your mentor, and you can change your mind as you learn. What matters is that you approach the gods having made a deliberate break from ordinary life.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have its own purity customs, for example about attending rites after a bereavement. Ask your mentor. If anything about a purity rule feels shaming or excluding to you, say so; good covens listen.

## Purifying yourself, step by step

### Everyday purification

1. Make khernips and wash your hands and face. This is enough for daily worship.

### Fuller purification (before a festival, after a pollution, before a dedication)

1. **Bathe or shower**, with attention. Some add a handful of sea salt to a bath, or finish by pouring a jug of water over the head.
2. **Put on clean clothes.**
3. **Make khernips**, wash hands and face, and sprinkle a little over your head.
4. **Burn incense** (frankincense or bay) and let the smoke pass around you, if you use it.
5. **Say a line of purification**: "I wash away what is unclean, and come before the gods."

### After a time of impurity

1. Wait the period you have chosen.
2. Clean your shrine.
3. Do the fuller purification above.
4. Light Hestia's flame and pour her a libation: "I return to the gods."

## Purifying the home

1. **Clean** thoroughly, as for the Deipnon.
2. **Open windows** to let in fresh air.
3. **Sprinkle khernips** in each room, at each threshold.
4. **Burn incense** and carry it through the house, pausing in each doorway.
5. **Carry out the sweepings**, ideally on the Deipnon.

> **Safety:** Do not burn sulphur at home, despite the Odyssey: it produces toxic gas. Use incense, bay or rosemary, with ventilation. Do not mix cleaning products such as bleach and ammonia, which produce toxic fumes. Salt water can damage wood, metal and some stones, so test first.

## Miasma and hubris are different

Miasma is ritual uncleanness, removed by washing and time. Hubris is a moral wrong: treating others with arrogance or contempt. Purification does not remove the effects of wronging someone. For that, the Greek answer, like ours, was to make amends: apologise, repair the harm, and change your behaviour. Khernips cleans your hands; only you can clean up a wrong done to another person.

> **Safety:** If purity rules start to feel like obsessive anxiety, a need to wash again and again, or a constant fear of being unclean, please talk to your mentor and consider speaking to a doctor. Religious scrupulosity is a recognised form of obsessive-compulsive difficulty, and it is treatable.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** miasma from death, birth, bloodshed and sex; purification by water, fire, smoke and time; sacred laws setting periods of impurity.
- **Modern:** choosing your own purity rules, setting aside rules about menstruation, and household cleansing combined with the Deipnon.

docs.title: Discernment
docs.summary: How to tell real experiences from wishful thinking, how to test what you receive, ancient warnings about superstition, when to ask for help, and red flags in messages from any source.
docs.body:
## Telling true from wishful

As your practice deepens, you may start to have experiences: a sense of presence at the shrine, a vivid dream, a strong feeling that a god wants something, a run of coincidences. Discernment is the skill of weighing these honestly. It protects you from fooling yourself, from being fooled by others, and from mistaking ordinary anxiety for divine messages. It also helps you trust the experiences that are worth trusting.

## Piety and superstition

The Greeks had a word for a healthy fear of the gods (eusebeia, piety) and another for an unhealthy one: deisidaimonia, superstition. The philosopher Theophrastus wrote a famous sketch of "the superstitious man", who keeps purifying his house because he thinks Hekate has been brought into it, pours oil on every smooth stone at the crossroads, and runs to diviners whenever a mouse chews his flour sack. Plutarch wrote a whole essay against superstition, arguing that it is worse than disbelief because it makes people afraid of gods who are good.

This is an ancient warning worth hearing. The gods of Greek religion are not waiting to pounce on mistakes. A practice built on fear is not piety.

## Kinds of experience

People in Hellenic practice report many kinds of experience. All of these are common, and none of them proves anything on its own.

- **A sense of presence** at the shrine: warmth, a shift in the air, the feeling of being heard.
- **Dreams** of a god, or of their symbols.
- **Signs**: seeing a god's animal or symbol repeatedly, an overheard phrase that answers your question.
- **Inner words or images** during prayer.
- **Strong impressions** that a god likes or wants something.
- **Nothing at all**, for months or years, while practising faithfully. This is very common, and does not mean you are doing it wrong.

## Testing what you receive

When you have an experience you want to understand, take it through these steps.

1. **Write it down** soon after, plainly: what happened, when, what you were doing, how you felt. Label it UPG (unverified personal gnosis).
2. **Wait.** Do not act on it straight away. Give it a week. Things that matter tend to remain; passing feelings fade.
3. **Check it against the tradition.** Is it consistent with what we know of the god from ancient sources and the Living Library? A message from Hestia to hold a grand public spectacle would be odd; a message from her to tidy the kitchen would not.
4. **Check it against your own state.** Were you tired, anxious, hungry, unwell, longing for a particular answer? None of these makes the experience false, but they are worth noticing.
5. **Ask by divination**, using a method from your core divination lessons, or a traditional Greek one such as drawing a lot or listening for a chance word (kledon). Ask a clear question and record the answer honestly. Do not keep asking until you get the answer you want.
6. **Talk to your mentor.** A second person who knows you and the tradition can see what you cannot.
7. **Decide what to do**, if anything. Most experiences need nothing more than gratitude.

## What a real message does not ask

These are red flags. If you receive a message, from any source, inner or outer, that asks you to do any of the following, do not act on it. Stop, ground yourself, and talk to your mentor.

- Harm yourself or anyone else.
- Stop medical or psychological treatment, or medication.
- Cut yourself off from family, friends or support.
- Give away money you need, or give money to a particular person.
- Keep a secret that hurts you or someone else.
- Believe you are uniquely chosen and above others' advice.
- Feel constant terror of punishment.

> **Safety:** If you hear voices, see things others don't, feel that messages are coming at you from everywhere, or feel that you are being watched or controlled, please speak to a doctor promptly, as well as your mentor. These experiences can be signs of a health condition that is very treatable, and religious practice is not a substitute for care. Getting help does not mean your spiritual life is false. It means you are looking after the person who lives it.

## Ancient divination as a check

The Greeks constantly checked their decisions with the gods through divination. Common methods included:

- **Oracles** such as Delphi and Dodona, consulted with questions;
- **Dreams**, especially at healing sanctuaries of Asklepios;
- **Kledonomancy**: taking a chance word overheard as an answer;
- **Lots and dice**: drawing lots or throwing knucklebones (astragaloi) and reading the result from a list of answers;
- **Bird signs**.

Modern practitioners use similar methods alongside tarot and others. Divination is a way of asking, not a way of getting certainty. The elder and high priestess lessons explore leading divination for others.

## Labelling and sharing

When you share an experience with others in your coven or online:

- say plainly that it is your own experience ("I felt..." rather than "Hekate wants us all to...");
- do not present UPG as ancient fact;
- do not tell others what a god wants from them;
- receive other people's experiences with the same courtesy.

Hekate in particular attracts a lot of confident UPG online. Some of it may be meaningful; very little of it is ancient. Read it as other people's experience, not as instruction.

## When to ask for help

Talk to your mentor:

- before acting on any experience that would change your life, spend money or affect others;
- when an experience frightens or upsets you;
- when you are not sure what you experienced;
- when practice starts to feel compulsive or fearful;
- when you feel nothing for a long time and are discouraged.

You are never bothering your mentor by asking. That is what a mentor is for.

## Try this

> **Try this:** Keep a discernment journal for a month. For each experience, however small, write what happened, label it, wait a week, and then write a second note: does it still seem significant? Did anything confirm or contradict it? Share a few entries with your mentor.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** the distinction between piety and superstition, divination to test decisions, kledon, lots, dreams, oracles.
- **Modern:** the vocabulary of UPG and SPG, discernment journals, and the clear line between spiritual experience and health care.

docs.title: What dedication means
docs.summary: Dedication in the ancient Greek world, from votive gifts to young people's offerings at the threshold of adult life, and what it means to dedicate yourself as a devotee in a Hellenic coven.
docs.body:
## Setting something apart

To dedicate is to set something apart for the gods. The Greeks did it constantly. Their sanctuaries were crowded with dedications: statues, pots, tools, weapons, jewellery, little clay figures, locks of hair, inscribed stones, each set apart as belonging to a god. At the end of your devotee course you will dedicate yourself: you will set yourself apart, for a time, to the gods and the path of this coven. This lesson explains what that means.

## Dedication in the ancient world

### Votive gifts

An anathema (ah-NAH-theh-mah), literally "something set up", was a gift dedicated to a god and left in their sanctuary. Many were given to fulfil a vow: "If you heal my child, I will give you a statue." Others were thanks for a good harvest, a safe voyage, a victory, a birth. Many carried inscriptions naming the giver and the god. Once dedicated, an anathema belonged to the god; it was not to be taken back, sold or used for ordinary purposes. When sanctuaries filled up, old dedications were buried within the sacred precinct, not thrown away.

### Dedicating the self at life's thresholds

The Greeks also marked turning points of life with dedications of something of themselves.

- **Before marriage**, girls often dedicated their toys, a lock of hair or their girlhood clothes to Artemis, marking the end of one stage of life.
- **Young men** dedicated a lock of hair to a river god or to Apollo as they came of age.
- **Girls at Brauron** served Artemis for a time as "little bears", a period of service to the goddess before adulthood.
- **Craftspeople** dedicated their tools to a god on retirement.

What these share is a giving of something of yourself at a threshold, as a sign that you now belong, in some measure, to a god or to a new way of life.

### Service to a god

Some people held priesthoods, served in sanctuaries, or devoted themselves to a particular god for a set time or for life. But there was no general custom of "dedicating yourself" to a god in the way some modern practitioners do. Most people simply honoured the gods of their household and city, and some gods more closely than others.

## Dedication in this coven

When you dedicate as a devotee, you are doing something both ancient in spirit and modern in form:

- **Ancient in spirit**: you set something of yourself apart at a threshold, before the gods, with a gift, as Greeks did at the turning points of their lives.
- **Modern in form**: the dedication of a devotee to a coven's path is a coven custom, drawn from modern witchcraft's practice of dedicating before initiation.

A dedication says, before the gods and the coven:

1. I have chosen this path and this coven.
2. I will keep my household practice and continue to learn.
3. I give myself, for now, to the gods we honour together.

## What dedication is not

- **It is not initiation.** Initiation, if you later seek it, is a deeper threshold after a year and a day of further study and service, with its own oath. Dedication is the first commitment.
- **It is not a lifelong oath.** You are committing to the path as it is now, and to keep walking it in good faith. If, in time, the path or the coven proves not to be yours, you can leave with honour.
- **It is not ownership.** No one owns you by your dedication: not the coven, not the High Priestess or High Priest, not a god as imagined by another person. You remain free.
- **It is not a requirement to choose a patron god.** Some people dedicate themselves to a particular god as well; this is optional and should be done with care.

## Dedicating to a particular god

Some devotees feel called to dedicate themselves especially to one god, such as Hestia, Athena, Apollo or Hekate. This is a modern practice with ancient echoes in individuals who were especially close to a god. If you feel this pull:

1. **Wait.** Honour the god regularly for at least several months before considering a dedication.
2. **Learn.** Read their Living Library entry, their hymns, their myths and their festivals.
3. **Discern.** Use the discernment practices from your devotion lessons. Is the pull steady, or a passing enthusiasm?
4. **Talk to your mentor** before any dedication to a single god.
5. **Keep it within the household frame.** Dedication to one god never means neglecting Hestia or the household gods.

Many people with a Hekate altar feel a strong pull to dedicate to her. Take the same care: she has been honoured in many ways over many centuries, and a relationship built slowly through the Deipnon and the threshold is stronger than one built on a single intense experience.

> **Your coven:** Your coven decides what a devotee's dedication involves, when it happens and who leads it. Some covens hold it on a Noumenia, a festival, or a date the devotee chooses. Ask your mentor how it is done in your coven, and whether a dedication to a particular god can be part of it.

## Are you ready?

You are probably ready to dedicate when:

- you have kept a household practice for some months, imperfectly but steadily;
- you have completed or nearly completed the devotee lessons;
- you understand and accept what the coven asks of devotees;
- your mentor agrees;
- you want to, freely, without pressure.

If you feel pressured to dedicate before you are ready, say so. A good coven will wait.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** votive dedications (anathemata), vows, dedications of hair and childhood things at life's thresholds, periods of service to a god.
- **Modern:** the devotee's dedication to a coven's path, and dedication of oneself to a single patron god.

docs.title: Preparing for dedication
docs.summary: How to prepare in the weeks before your dedication: writing your words, choosing an anathema, purifying, and arranging the practical details with your mentor.
docs.body:
## Preparation is part of the rite

In Greek religion, coming before the gods was always preceded by preparation: washing, clean clothes, gathering offerings, walking in procession. Your dedication deserves the same. This lesson takes you through the weeks before, step by step.

## Three or four weeks before

1. **Agree a date** with your mentor and High Priestess or High Priest. The Noumenia, the start of the month, is a natural choice; a festival of a god you are close to is another.
2. **Ask about the shape of the rite**: where it will be, who will attend, how long it lasts, whether you will speak, what you should bring and wear. The next lesson gives the common shape; your coven will tell you its own.
3. **Ask any questions** about what you are committing to, so you can agree freely.
4. **Begin your words**: the statement you will speak at your dedication (see below).
5. **Choose your anathema**: the gift you will dedicate (see below).

## Writing your words

Many covens ask the devotee to speak a short statement of dedication. Even if yours provides set words, writing your own helps you know what you mean.

### Step by step

1. **Begin with whom you address.** Usually Hestia, the gods the coven honours, and any god you are especially close to. "Hestia, eldest of the gods, and all the gods of this coven..."
2. **Say who you are and where you have come from.** "I have kept your hearth these months, washed in khernips, poured to you first and last..." This is the argument of a Greek prayer, the reminder of the relationship.
3. **Say what you give.** "I set myself apart as a devotee of this path."
4. **Say what you will do.** Two or three specific commitments: "I will keep Hestia's flame and the monthly days. I will keep learning. I will treat my coven-mates with xenia." Make them things you can actually do.
5. **Ask for what you hope.** "Receive me, and guide me." Keep it simple.
6. **Read it aloud** at your shrine. Change anything that sounds false or grand.
7. **Wait a few days**, then read it again. Share it with your mentor.

Keep it short: a minute or two to speak is plenty.

### A sample

"Hestia, eldest of the gods, first and last; and all the gods we honour in this coven: I have kept your hearth these months, washed my hands before I came to you, and poured you wine and water. Now I set myself apart as a devotee of this path. I will keep your flame and the turning of the months, keep learning, and treat those who share this path with care and hospitality. Receive me, and walk with me."

## Choosing your anathema

An anathema is a gift dedicated to the gods and left with them. Your dedication is a natural moment to give one. It might be:

- **something you have made**: a woven cord, a small carving, a painted stone, a poem written out by hand;
- **something of yourself**: a lock of hair, as Greek youths gave at their thresholds;
- **something meaningful from your life**: a small object that marks the person you were before this path;
- **something for the coven's shrine**: a bowl, a lamp, a cloth, given to the gods of the coven.

Choose something modest, made or given with care. It will belong to the gods afterwards: kept on the shrine, buried in a garden, or kept in a box set apart.

## The week before

1. **Clean your home and shrine** thoroughly, as for the Deipnon. If the Deipnon falls in that week, keep it with special care.
2. **Keep your daily devotion** faithfully, and perhaps add an evening prayer telling the gods what is coming.
3. **Reread your devotee lessons** and your notes.
4. **Rest.** Sleep, eat well, and avoid overloading yourself.
5. **Abstain**, if your coven asks, from anything set aside before rites. No abstention should harm your health; tell your mentor if anything asked would.

## The day

1. **Bathe or shower** with attention. Put on clean clothes, or whatever your coven has asked you to wear.
2. **Make khernips** at your shrine, wash, and light Hestia's flame. Pour her a libation and tell her where you are going.
3. **Gather** your words, your anathema and anything else you were asked to bring.
4. **Eat something light** and drink water.
5. **Arrive in good time**, or log in early if the rite is in the app.

> **Safety:** If you are unwell, grieving or in crisis as the date approaches, it is entirely right to postpone. Dedication can wait; your wellbeing comes first.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may provide set words, ask for a particular anathema, or have customs for the day before. Ask your mentor and follow their guidance.

## Common worries

- **"What if I stumble over my words?"** Read from a card. Pause and start the sentence again. No one minds.
- **"What if I feel nothing?"** Many people feel the significance of a dedication only later. The act is real whether or not you feel it at the time.
- **"What if I'm not sure?"** Tell your mentor. Uncertainty is worth talking through before, not after. It may mean waiting, or it may be ordinary nerves.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** purification before approaching the gods, prayers that name the relationship, anathemata, offerings of hair at life's thresholds.
- **Modern:** the devotee's statement of dedication, and the coven's arrangements.

docs.title: The shape of the dedication rite
docs.summary: The common shape of a Hellenic dedication rite, step by step with sample words, for a coven gathering, an online gathering in the app, or a solitary dedication, for the coven to adapt.
docs.body:
## A rite in the Hellenic form

A dedication rite follows the shape of every Hellenic rite: procession, purification, Hestia first, prayer and offering, Hestia last, and a shared meal. Within that shape sits the dedication itself. This lesson gives the shape step by step, with sample words, so you know what to expect. Your coven will adapt it, and the leaders' version is the one that counts.

## Roles

In a coven dedication there are usually:

- **the leader**, the High Priestess or High Priest, or someone they ask, who speaks the main prayers and receives the dedication;
- **the mentor**, who presents the devotee and may stand beside them;
- **the herald**, who calls the procession and the silence;
- **the coven**, who witness and welcome;
- **the devotee**: you.

## The rite, step by step

### 1. Gathering (5 minutes)

The coven gathers. The devotee waits a little apart, or at the back, with their mentor, holding their anathema.

### 2. Procession (2 minutes)

The herald calls the procession. The coven walks to the altar with the offerings. The devotee walks with their mentor, carrying the anathema.

### 3. Khernips and barley (3 minutes)

The khernips is made and carried round. Everyone washes; the devotee washes last, or with special attention. Barley is scattered and the herald calls for holy silence.

### 4. Hestia first (2 minutes)

The leader pours to Hestia and prays: "Hestia, eldest of the gods, hearth of this coven, receive the first offering, and be present as we receive one who comes to the gods."

### 5. Invocation of the gods (5 minutes)

The leader invokes the gods the coven honours, and any god the devotee is especially close to, with prayer and libation.

### 6. The presentation (2 minutes)

The mentor presents the devotee: "I bring before the gods and this coven [name], who has kept the household fire and learned our ways these months, and who asks to be dedicated as a devotee."

### 7. The questions (2 minutes)

The leader may ask a few questions, so that the devotee's consent is spoken aloud. For example:

- "Do you come freely?"
- "Have you kept Hestia's flame and the turning of the months?"
- "Will you keep learning, and treat your coven-mates with care?"

The devotee answers in their own words, or "I do", "I have", "I will".

### 8. The dedication (3 minutes)

The devotee speaks their words of dedication, prepared beforehand. Then they offer their anathema, placing it on the altar: "I give this to the gods, as a sign that I set myself apart for this path."

### 9. Libation (2 minutes)

The devotee pours a libation to the gods they have addressed. The leader may pour one in response.

### 10. The welcome (5 minutes)

The leader receives the devotee: "The gods have heard, and this coven has witnessed. Be welcome as a devotee of this path." The coven welcomes them with words, a garland, a gift, a shared cup, or whatever the coven's custom is. This is xenia: the coven makes the new devotee its own.

### 11. Hestia last (2 minutes)

The leader pours to Hestia: "Hestia, first and last, keep this coven and all within it."

### 12. Closing and feast

The rite is closed, and everyone shares a meal. The new devotee is often served first.

## An online dedication in the app

If the coven meets online, each person keeps their own flame, khernips and cup at home. The devotee places their anathema on their own shrine. The steps are the same; the welcome might be words from each member in turn. Afterwards, the devotee keeps the anathema on their shrine.

## A solitary dedication

Some covens allow a devotee to dedicate alone, for example when distance makes gathering impossible, with the coven's leader joining by call or approving afterwards. A solitary dedication follows the same order, without the presentation and questions:

1. Prepare and purify.
2. Process to your shrine with your anathema.
3. Khernips, barley and silence.
4. Hestia first.
5. Invoke the gods.
6. Speak your dedication.
7. Place your anathema on the shrine.
8. Pour a libation.
9. Sit in stillness for five minutes.
10. Hestia last, and close.
11. Eat, drink and write it down.
12. Send your mentor a message the same day.

> **Your coven:** This is a common shape, not your coven's rite. Your High Priestess or High Priest may change the order, the words, the roles and the welcome. Ask your mentor to walk you through your coven's version beforehand, so nothing surprises you.

> **Safety:** A dedication rite should involve nothing you have not agreed to: no nudity, touch, substances or anything sexual, and no frightening ordeals. You may pause or stop at any time by saying so. If the rite uses candles and incense in a crowded room, keep flames well away from clothing, garlands and hair.

## What the anathema becomes

After the rite, the anathema belongs to the gods. If you placed it on the coven's altar, the coven keeps it. If it is on your shrine, keep it there, or in a box set apart. Do not use it for ordinary purposes or give it away. If it must one day be disposed of, bury it in the earth with a word of thanks, as ancient sanctuaries buried their old dedications.

## What's ancient and what's modern

- **Ancient:** procession, khernips, Hestia first and last, invocation, libation, anathemata, the shared feast, xenia.
- **Modern:** the presentation, questions and welcome of a devotee, online and solitary dedications.

docs.title: After dedication
docs.summary: Aftercare in the days after your dedication, what changes and what does not, keeping the anniversary, the path ahead, and what to do if the path proves not to be yours.
docs.body:
## The days after

Dedication is a beginning, not an ending. In the days after, look after yourself, and let the change settle.

### The first night

1. **Eat and drink** something substantial at the shared meal or when you get home.
2. **Ground yourself** if you feel light-headed, buzzing or very emotional: feet on the floor, slow breaths, a warm drink, as your core lessons taught.
3. **Pour to Hestia** when you get home: "I have returned, and I am dedicated."
4. **Write** in your book or the app what happened and what you felt, while it is fresh.
5. **Rest.**

### The first week

- **Keep your daily devotion.** It steadies you, and it is what you have just promised.
