*Cautions:* chamomile is in the daisy family; people allergic to ragweed may react to it. Take care with pets and in pregnancy.

### Mint

**Air, Mercury.** Prosperity, freshness, clear thinking, communication, healing.

*How to use:* fresh leaves in a money bowl; a sprig in your wallet; dried mint in jars for movement and increase. Mint grows vigorously in a pot.

*Cautions:* mint and especially **peppermint** essential oils are strong; peppermint oil is toxic to cats and must never go near the face of a baby or young child.

### Cinnamon

**Fire, Sun.** Prosperity, speed, success, passion, warmth, protection.

*How to use:* a stick in a money jar; a pinch in a sachet to “quicken” a working; a little ground cinnamon blown gently across the threshold from the outside in (a modern folk custom for drawing in good fortune).

*Cautions:* cinnamon irritates skin and eyes. Don’t blow powder near people, pets or anyone with asthma, and never put cinnamon oil on skin.

### Rose

**Water, Venus.** Love of every kind, self-love, compassion, beauty, healing, comfort in grief.

*How to use:* petals in a self-love jar or bath sachet (kept in a bag, not loose in the water); a single rose on the altar; rose water to anoint objects.

*Cautions:* florist roses are usually sprayed with pesticides. Use food-grade or home-grown petals for anything touching skin. Mind the thorns.

### Thyme

**Water, Venus.** Courage, purification, healing, restful sleep.

*How to use:* a sprig in a pocket before a hard day; dried thyme in a cleansing sachet; in floor washes with rosemary.

*Cautions:* thyme oil is irritating and must never touch skin undiluted.

### Garden sage

**Air, Jupiter.** Cleansing, wisdom, protection, blessing.

*How to use:* a dried bundle of garden sage, or loose leaves on a heat-proof dish, burned for smoke cleansing; leaves in protection jars.

*Cautions:* use **garden sage** (*Salvia officinalis*), which grows almost anywhere, not wild-picked white sage. White sage is sacred to particular Native American nations and is being over-harvested; the app’s guide to closed and living traditions explains why. Call what you do “smoke cleansing” rather than “smudging”, which names a specific Indigenous ceremony. Smoke can irritate lungs and pets.

### Lemon balm

**Water, Moon.** Comfort, emotional healing, cheer, gentle protection.

*How to use:* fresh leaves on the altar when you feel low; dried leaves in a comfort sachet; a pot by the door. It grows easily and smells of lemon when brushed.

*Cautions:* gentle for most people, but medicinal use can interact with some conditions and medicines. Keep magical use separate from treatment.

### Calendula (pot marigold)

**Fire, Sun.** Joy, success, being seen kindly, solar blessing, dreams.

*How to use:* dried petals in a joy or success jar; fresh flowers on a summer altar; petals scattered on an offering.

*Cautions:* in the daisy family, so it can trigger ragweed-type allergies. Traditionally avoided internally in pregnancy. Calendula (*Calendula officinalis*) is not the same plant as the French and African marigolds (*Tagetes*) sold for bedding, so check the label.

## How to use plants, step by step

Most herb magic uses a handful of simple methods:

1. **Choose.** Pick one to three plants whose meanings match your intention.
2. **Prepare.** Wash your hands. If you have learned to ground and centre (as you did in Grounding), do so now. Hold the herb and say, aloud or silently, what you are asking it to help with.
3. **Use it** in one of the ways listed below.
4. **Dispose with respect.** When a working is finished, return plant material to the earth: compost it, bury it, or put it in the garden waste. Don’t throw it into rivers or wild places where it may spread or harm wildlife.

The usual ways to use a plant:

- **A jar or sachet** (a small cloth bag tied shut) that you keep somewhere meaningful.
- **A bowl on the altar.**
- **A wash:** steep a handful in a litre of just-boiled water for ten minutes, cool and strain, and use it to wipe down a doorstep, windowsills or the altar.
- **A sprig** carried in a pocket or hung over a door.
- **Smoke,** only for herbs listed as safe to burn, in a fire-safe dish with a window open.

> **Note:** You can grow almost all of these on a windowsill. A herb you have grown, watered and talked to is, for many practitioners, the most powerful kind.

> **Your coven:** Your tradition may hold particular plants sacred (oak and mistletoe, laurel and olive, rue, birch, rowan and many more). Those are taught in your tradition’s own lessons; ask your mentor which the coven keeps.

docs.title: Building your own correspondences
docs.summary: How to build a personal correspondence list from your own experience and test it over time, so the language of magic becomes yours.
docs.body:
## Why make your own?

Published correspondence lists are a shared starting point. But the most powerful correspondences for you will often be your own: the smell of your grandmother’s garden, the stone you picked up on the day your life changed, the song that makes you brave. Experienced practitioners nearly all keep a personal list, built up over years, that sits alongside the traditional ones.

Building your own is not making things up at random. It is careful, honest observation of how things affect you, recorded and tested over time.

## Three sources for your own list

1. **Memory and association.** What does this thing already mean to you? A herb your family cooked with at celebrations may mean joy and gathering to you, whatever the books say.
2. **Direct experience.** What do you notice when you sit with it? Some practitioners feel warmth, coolness, tingling, heaviness, lightness, or images and moods arising. Others notice very little at first. Both are normal; you are learning to pay attention, as you began to in the lessons on energy.
3. **Results.** Which materials seem to work well in your workings? After months of keeping records, patterns appear.

## Step by step: a correspondence study

Do this with one item at a time: a herb, a stone, a colour, a tree you walk past every day.

1. **Prepare.** Sit somewhere quiet. Ground and centre as you learned in Grounding. Set a timer for ten minutes.
2. **Meet it with your senses.** Look closely at it for two minutes. Smell it, if it has a scent. Feel its texture, weight and temperature. If it is a food you know to be safe, you may taste a tiny amount; otherwise don’t.
3. **Notice your body.** With your eyes closed and the item in your hand or in front of you, breathe slowly (in for four, out for six) and notice any change in your body: warmth, coolness, relaxation, tension, energy, sleepiness.
4. **Notice your mind.** What thoughts, memories, images, words or colours come up? Don’t judge or chase them; just notice.
5. **Write it down straight away,** before you look anything up, using the pattern below.
6. **Then look it up.** Read the Living Library entry or a good book. Note where you agreed and where you differed.
7. **Repeat** on another day, in a different mood. A single session can be coloured by how you happened to feel.

The pattern for your notes:

- **Item:** what it is.
- **Date, time, moon phase:** when you sat with it.
- **Senses:** what you saw, smelt and felt.
- **Body:** what changed.
- **Mind:** images, memories, words.
- **It seems to suit:** your best guess at its purpose.

## Testing over time

When you use an item in a working, record what you used and what happened. Every few months, read back over your records. Ask:

- Which materials have I reached for again and again?
- Which workings felt strongest, and what was in them?
- Has anything surprised me?

If, over many uses, a herb consistently feels calming to you though the books call it fiery, trust your records. Write your meaning beside the book’s in your personal list.

## Keeping your list

Keep your correspondences in your Grimoire in the app, or in a notebook if you prefer paper. A simple layout works best:

- one page per item, or
- one page per intention (calm, courage, love, protection, money, clarity, rest), listing the colours, plants, stones, days and symbols that work for you.

Note where each entry came from: *traditional*, *coven*, or *mine*. This keeps you honest, and helps when you teach others later.

## A worked example

Here is how one trainee’s notes on thyme looked after three sessions.

- **Session one** (waxing Moon, a tired evening): smelt sharp and warm, like a roast dinner; felt my shoulders drop; remembered my grandfather’s garden; seemed to suit comfort and home.
- **Session two** (full Moon, a good morning): noticed how tough the little stems are; felt steadier and more awake; the word “keep going” came to mind; seemed to suit endurance and courage.
- **Session three** (waning Moon, after a hard day at work): felt calmer; slept well afterwards; seemed to suit rest and quiet courage.
- **The books said:** courage, purification, healing, sleep.

The trainee’s own entry read: “Thyme: quiet courage, comfort, keeping going. *Mine and traditional.*” Notice that her experience and the books mostly agreed, and that her own words, “keeping going”, will mean more to her in a working than any list.

## Common difficulties

- **“I don’t notice anything.”** Very common at first. Record that honestly, and record the senses: colour, smell, texture. Perception grows with practice, as you found in the lessons on energy.
- **“I just repeat what I’ve read.”** Do the study before you look anything up, and with things you haven’t read about: a weed from the pavement (looked at, not handled, if you can’t identify it), a pebble, the colour of your front door.
- **“My notes contradict each other.”** That is information. Things can have several sides, and your mood colours each session. Look for what stays the same.
- **“I can’t keep it up.”** One item a week is plenty. Correspondence lists grow over years.

## A word on humility

Personal correspondences are valuable, but they are personal. When you share them, say so: “For me, thyme is a sleep herb” rather than “Thyme is a sleep herb.” And when your coven or tradition has an established meaning for something in its shared rites, use the shared meaning there. A coven works best when everyone speaks the same symbolic language in the circle, even if each member also has a private dialect at home.

> **Your coven:** Some covens build a shared correspondence list together over years, adding what members find. If yours does, your notes may one day become part of it.

> **Try this:** Choose one intention that matters to you now (calm, courage, rest, friendship, focus). From your home, and without buying anything, gather one colour, one plant or food, one stone or natural object, and one sound or song that *feel* like that intention to you. Write them down as the first page of your personal correspondence list, with a line on why you chose each.

docs.title: Seven common stones
docs.summary: Seven easy-to-find stones, what they are used for, which must be kept out of water or sun, and how to care for and cleanse them safely.
docs.body:
## Stones in practice

Stones and crystals are popular in modern witchcraft. They are beautiful, they last, and holding one gives your hands and attention somewhere to rest. People use them on the altar, carry them in a pocket, place them in jars and sachets, sit with them in meditation, and lay them around a candle in a working.

Honesty first. Stones have been used as amulets and charms for thousands of years: carnelian and lapis in ancient Egypt, amber in northern Europe, jet in Roman Britain. But most of the specific meanings now given to crystals, especially for healing, come from New Age books of the 1980s onward. There is no scientific evidence that crystals heal illness. In magic, treat stones as **allies, symbols and focuses** for your intention, and never as a replacement for medical, psychological or practical help.

## The seven

These seven are cheap, easy to find, and between them cover most beginner needs. Their elements and planets follow the app’s Living Library.

### Clear quartz

**Spirit, Sun.** Clarity, amplification, holding an intention, cleansing. Often used as a stand-in for any other stone.

*Water:* safe to rinse. *Sun:* won’t fade, but a clear crystal can focus sunlight like a lens, so **never leave it in a sunny window near paper, curtains or anything that can catch fire**.

### Amethyst

**Air, Jupiter.** Calm intuition, dreams, meditation, spiritual protection, sobriety.

*Water:* safe to rinse. *Sun:* **fades** in strong sunlight over time; keep it out of sunny windows.

### Rose quartz

**Water, Venus.** Tenderness, self-love, compassion, forgiveness, gentle healing of the heart.

*Water:* safe to rinse. *Sun:* **fades** in strong sunlight.

### Black tourmaline

**Earth, Saturn.** Protection, grounding, boundaries, warding.

*Water:* a brief rinse is fine, but don’t soak it: pieces are often brittle and can split along cracks. *Sun:* fine.

### Citrine

**Fire, Sun.** Confidence, success, joy, abundance.

*Water:* safe to rinse. *Sun:* can fade over time. Note that much of the citrine sold is heat-treated amethyst; it can still be used, but it is fair to know what you are buying.

### Selenite

**Spirit, Moon.** Cleansing, peace, clarity, quiet.

*Water:* **never.** Selenite is a soft form of gypsum and dissolves, flakes and pits in water. Keep it away from damp, water bowls and bathrooms. Wash your hands after handling flaky pieces.

### Hematite

**Earth, Mars.** Grounding, focus, resilience, coming back into the body.

*Water:* **don’t soak**; hematite is an iron oxide and can rust. *Sun:* fine. Note that shiny magnetic “hematite” jewellery is usually a man-made material, not natural hematite.

## Quick rules for stone care

- **Out of water:** selenite, hematite, and also pyrite, malachite, and any soft, porous or flaky stone. When unsure, keep it dry.
- **Out of strong sun:** amethyst, rose quartz, citrine, and most coloured stones, which can fade.
- **Never in sun near anything flammable:** clear quartz and any clear crystal ball.
- **Never in drinking water:** don’t make “crystal elixirs” by soaking stones in water you drink. Some minerals, such as malachite, contain toxic metals, and many stones are dyed or treated.
- **Away from small children and pets:** small tumbled stones and chips are choking hazards.

## Cleansing a stone

Many practitioners **cleanse** a stone before using it and from time to time after, meaning they clear away whatever it has picked up so it is ready for new work. You don’t have to believe a stone “absorbs” anything to find this a useful habit: it marks the start of a new purpose.

Methods safe for every stone:

1. **Breath and intention.** Hold the stone, breathe in slowly for a count of four, and breathe out over it firmly, imagining anything stale blown away. Do this three times.
2. **Smoke.** Pass it through the smoke of a safe herb or incense three times, in a ventilated room.
3. **Sound.** Ring a bell, strike a singing bowl, or clap firmly over it.
4. **Earth or salt nearby.** Rest it on a dish of dry salt or rice, or on the soil of a pot plant, overnight. Don’t bury soft stones in damp soil or put any stone in salt water, which can damage many of them.
5. **Moonlight.** Leave it on a windowsill overnight. Moonlight won’t fade stones; just remember to bring the light-sensitive ones in before strong morning sun.

Then **dedicate** it: hold it, ground yourself, and say plainly what you would like it to help with. For example: “Amethyst, help me rest and dream clearly.” Keep it where you will see or touch it.

## Buying and sourcing

Stone mining can involve dangerous working conditions and child labour, and labels such as “ethically sourced” are often unverified. The app’s guide to sourcing explains more. Good habits: buy fewer stones; buy from sellers who can say where a stone was mined; consider second-hand stones; and remember that a pebble you found on a walk, which has meaning for you, is a perfectly good magical stone.

> **Your coven:** Some covens give each member a stone at dedication or keep stones on the coven altar. Ask your mentor how your coven uses them, if at all.

> **Try this:** Choose one stone you own, or a pebble from outside. Sit with it for five minutes. Notice its weight, temperature, texture and colour. Breathe slowly. Write down what you noticed, what (if anything) you felt, and what purpose it seems to suit. Then compare with the list above.

docs.title: Days of the week and planetary hours
docs.summary: How the seven days of the week came to be ruled by seven planets, what each day suits, and how planetary hours let you choose a time within a day.
docs.body:
## Seven planets, seven days

The ancient world could see seven moving lights in the sky that the Greeks called *planetes*, “wanderers”: the Sun, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. (The Sun and Moon were counted as planets in this old sense.) In the Hellenistic world, around two thousand years ago, each day of the week came to be ruled by one of them, and that system spread with the Roman Empire. You can still hear it in the names of the days.

- **Sunday:** the Sun. Success, vitality, confidence, health, recognition, blessing new ventures. Colours: gold, yellow, orange.
- **Monday:** the Moon (Moon-day; French *lundi*). Dreams, intuition, home and family, cleansing, emotional healing, divination. Colours: silver, white.
- **Tuesday:** Mars (French *mardi*; in English, Tiw’s day, after a Germanic war god). Courage, protection, energy, competition, cutting ties. Colour: red.
- **Wednesday:** Mercury (French *mercredi*; in English, Woden’s day). Communication, study, writing, business, travel. Colours: yellow, orange, sometimes purple.
- **Thursday:** Jupiter (French *jeudi*; in English, Thor’s day). Luck, growth, abundance, generosity, legal matters, learning. Colours: blue, purple.
- **Friday:** Venus (French *vendredi*; in English, Frigg’s day). Love, friendship, beauty, art, pleasure, harmony. Colours: green, pink.
- **Saturday:** Saturn. Boundaries, binding bad habits, endings, protection of the home, discipline, the ancestors. Colours: black, indigo, dark blue.

The English names come from the Germanic peoples matching their own gods to the Roman ones: Tiw for Mars, Woden for Mercury, Thor for Jupiter, Frigg for Venus. That matching is itself an old act of correspondence.

## Planetary hours

The same ancient astrologers also gave each *hour* a planet. This lets you choose not just a day but a time within it.

Here is how it works:

1. **The day and the night are each divided into twelve “hours”.** The time from sunrise to sunset is split into twelve equal parts, and the time from sunset to the next sunrise into another twelve. So in summer the daytime hours are long and the night hours short, and in winter the other way round. A planetary hour is rarely exactly sixty minutes.
2. **The first hour after sunrise belongs to the planet of the day.** On a Monday, the first hour belongs to the Moon; on a Friday, to Venus.
3. **The rest follow in a fixed order,** from the slowest planet to the fastest as the ancients saw them: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, then Saturn again, round and round.

This is in fact *why* the days of the week are in the order they are: if you run the hours on through twenty-four of them, the first hour of the next day lands on the next day’s planet.

You don’t need to work this out by hand. The app calculates planetary hours for where you are, shows you which planet rules the hour now, and finds the next hours of any planet you choose. It uses the same traditional meanings:

- **Sun:** success and vitality.
- **Moon:** dreams and intuition.
- **Mars:** courage and protection.
- **Mercury:** words and study.
- **Jupiter:** luck and growth.
- **Venus:** love and beauty.
- **Saturn:** boundaries and endings.

## Using days and hours

1. **Decide whether timing matters for this working.** For many small workings it doesn’t much. For a working you are planning ahead, it is a pleasant way to add one more layer of meaning.
2. **Find the planet that matches your intention.** A job interview: the Sun (success) or Mercury (words). A friendship: Venus. Protecting your home: Saturn or Mars.
3. **Choose the day,** if you can wait for it.
4. **Within the day, choose the planet’s hour,** using the app. If the day and the hour share the planet (a Venus hour on a Friday), many practitioners consider that especially fitting.
5. **If you can’t wait, use the hour alone.** Every planet has an hour on every day, so you can always find a Venus hour within a day or so.
6. **Write down the day and hour** in your record of the working, so you can compare results later.

## A worked example

Priya wants to bless a new friendship.

1. *Planet:* Venus, for friendship and harmony.
2. *Day:* Friday, Venus’s day.
3. *Hour:* she opens the app on Friday morning and sees that the next Venus hour starts at 1.40 in the afternoon, while she is at work, and the one after that late in the evening. She chooses the evening hour.
4. *Correspondences:* a pink candle (friendship), a pinch of rose petals (love of every kind), a piece of rose quartz.
5. *Record:* “Friday, hour of Venus, waxing Moon” goes at the top of her notes.

If Friday had been impossible, she could have used a Venus hour on any other day, or simply worked at a time that suited her. The timing is a gift to the working, not a condition of it.

## Common difficulties

- **“The hours don’t start on the hour.”** That is right: they run from sunrise and sunset, and their length changes through the year. Trust the app’s times for your location.
- **“The right hour falls in the middle of the night or my working day.”** Choose another hour of the same planet, or let the day alone carry the meaning.
- **“Different books give different colours for the days.”** Pick one list and be consistent.

> **Note:** Planetary days and hours come from the learned astrological tradition of the Mediterranean and Middle East, carried through medieval and Renaissance magic. They are genuinely old. Whether they suit your tradition is another question: some reconstructionist traditions don’t use them at all, and others use their own calendars. Your tradition’s lessons will say.

> **Your coven:** Covens often meet on the same weekday for practical reasons. Don’t worry if your coven’s meeting day doesn’t “match” the working. A coven’s regular rhythm has its own power.

> **Try this:** For one week, at some point each day, open the app and note which planet rules the day and the hour. Write one line on how the day felt. At the end of the week, read your notes back and see whether you noticed any pattern. Don’t worry if you didn’t; you are training attention, not proving anything.

docs.title: The Moon’s phases
docs.summary: What the Moon is actually doing through its month, the eight phases and their names, and how to find and recognise each one in your own sky.
docs.body:
## Why the Moon?

Of all the things in the sky, the Moon is the one people have watched most closely. It changes shape night by night, it is easy to see without any equipment, and its rhythm is short enough to live by: about a month from one full moon to the next. The word *month* itself comes from *moon*. Farmers, fishers, healers and priests in many cultures timed their work by it, and most modern witches do too.

Before we talk about magic, let’s be clear about what is happening in the sky. Knowing the real Moon will make your practice richer, not poorer.

## What the Moon is doing

The Moon gives off no light of its own. It is a ball of rock lit by the Sun, and half of it is always in sunlight, just as half the Earth is always in daytime. As the Moon travels around the Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half.

- When the Moon is roughly **between the Earth and the Sun**, its lit side faces away from us. We see little or nothing. This is the **new moon**.
- As it moves round, we see a growing sliver, then half, then most of the lit side. The Moon is **waxing** (growing).
- When the Moon is on the **far side of the Earth from the Sun**, we see the whole lit face. This is the **full moon**.
- Then the lit part shrinks again night by night. The Moon is **waning**.

One complete cycle, from new moon to new moon, takes about **29 and a half days**. This is called a *lunation* or *synodic month*.

The Earth’s shadow has nothing to do with the ordinary phases. (It only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, which you will meet in a later lesson.)

## The eight phases

The cycle is continuous, but it is usually divided into eight phases. These are the names the app uses.

1. **New Moon.** The Moon is close to the Sun in the sky and invisible, or nearly so. Some people call the last day or two before it the **dark moon**, and keep “new moon” for the first thin crescent; others use the words the other way round, or as one. Ask your coven which it uses.
2. **Waxing Crescent.** A thin, growing curve of light appears in the west just after sunset, a day or two after the new moon.
3. **First Quarter.** About a week after the new moon, half the face is lit. It is called a “quarter” because the Moon is a quarter of the way through its cycle, not because a quarter is lit. It is high in the south (in the northern hemisphere) around sunset.
4. **Waxing Gibbous.** More than half lit and still growing. *Gibbous* means “humped”.
5. **Full Moon.** About two weeks after the new moon, the whole face is lit. The full moon rises in the east around sunset and sets around sunrise, so it is up all night.
6. **Waning Gibbous.** More than half lit, now shrinking. It rises later each evening.
7. **Last Quarter** (also called third quarter). Half lit again, the other half this time. It rises around midnight and is seen in the morning sky.
8. **Waning Crescent.** A thin, shrinking curve seen in the east before dawn, until it disappears into the new moon again.

The Moon rises on average about fifty minutes later each day, which is why the waning Moon is a creature of the small hours and the morning, while the waxing Moon belongs to the evening.

## Which way round? The hemisphere matters

Where you live changes how the Moon looks.

- In the **northern hemisphere**, a waxing Moon is lit on the **right**, and a waning Moon on the **left**. A memory aid: the lit shape spells **D-O-C** through the month: a D shape (waxing), O (full), C shape (waning).
- In the **southern hemisphere** it is the other way round: waxing is lit on the left, waning on the right. The lit shape goes C-O-D.
- Near the **equator**, the crescent lies on its back like a bowl or a smile.

The phases themselves happen at the same moment for everyone on Earth. A full moon is full in London, Sydney and Nairobi at once; only the time on the clock differs. So covens meeting online across the world can share a full moon.

## Finding the phase

The app shows the current phase and the coming new, quarter and full moons in the sky view on the Today tab. Use it, and also *look up*. Even in a city, the Moon is usually visible when it’s above the horizon and the sky is clear.

> **Try this:** For one whole lunation (about a month), look for the Moon every day or night you can. Each time, note the date, time, where it was in the sky, what shape it was, and one word for how it made you feel. If you can’t see it because of cloud or because it isn’t up, write that down too. By the end, you will know the Moon’s rhythm in your body, not just from a chart.

## A note on the Moon and our bodies

You will hear many claims that the full moon makes people wilder, that hospitals are busier, or that menstrual cycles follow the Moon. Large studies have mostly not found these effects. The Moon does move the tides of the ocean, and many animals and plants, especially in the sea, time their breeding by it. For people, its effect seems to be mostly cultural and psychological, which is real enough: when you pay attention to the Moon, it shapes your month.

> **Your coven:** Many covens meet at the full moon, at the new moon, or both. These meetings are often called **esbats** (a word for a witches’ gathering, popularised in the twentieth century), to tell them apart from the seasonal festivals. Ask your mentor when your coven meets and what it calls its lunar gatherings.

docs.title: Working with the phases
docs.summary: What each phase is traditionally good for, how to shape any intention to fit the phase you’re in, and simple practices such as moon water and a moon journal.
docs.body:
## The basic idea

The principle behind lunar timing is simple: **as the Moon grows, work to grow things; as it shrinks, work to shrink things.** Bring in while it waxes; let go while it wanes. Use the full moon for things at their peak, and the new moon for rest and fresh starts.

## How old is this?

Folk practice in many parts of Europe timed planting, harvesting, cutting hair and wood, and even medical treatments by the Moon. Roman writers such as Pliny the Elder (first century) recorded advice about doing things at the waxing or waning Moon, and farmers’ almanacs still print it. So the idea of lunar timing is genuinely old.

The detailed system of eight phases, each with its own magical purpose, is much more recent. It developed in twentieth-century witchcraft and New Age writing. That doesn’t make it worse; it makes it a modern practice built on an old instinct. Use it as a helpful rhythm, not a rule.

## What each phase suits

These match the meanings the app gives for each phase.

- **New Moon:** rest, setting intentions, planting seeds in the dark. A time to decide what you want for the coming month.
- **Waxing Crescent:** beginnings, hope, first small steps. Start what you planned.
- **First Quarter:** action, courage, pushing through challenges. The first obstacles often appear; meet them.
- **Waxing Gibbous:** refining, building, nurturing. Adjust and tend what you have started.
- **Full Moon:** power, charging, celebration, divination, gratitude. Many people find this the strongest time for any working, and the best for thanks.
- **Waning Gibbous:** sharing, giving thanks, beginning to let go. Teach, give away, reflect.
- **Last Quarter:** release, breaking habits, clearing out. Cut ties, end things, clean.
- **Waning Crescent:** banishing, rest, reflection, preparing to begin again. Clear the decks before the new moon.

## Turning any intention to fit the phase

You don’t have to wait two weeks for the “right” Moon. Most intentions can be worded to fit whichever way the Moon is going.

1. **Write your intention plainly.** For example: “I want to stop feeling anxious about money.”
2. **Ask: what grows, and what shrinks?** Here, *security* should grow and *anxiety* and *debt* should shrink.
3. **If the Moon is waxing, word it as growth:** “My savings and my calm grow with the Moon.”
4. **If the Moon is waning, word it as release:** “My debt and my worry shrink with the Moon.”
5. **If it is full, word it as fulfilment or thanks:** “I give thanks for enough, and I welcome more security.”
6. **If it is new or dark, word it as a seed:** “I plant the seed of financial calm.”

This simple reframing is one of the most useful skills in lunar magic.

## A full-moon practice, step by step

This can be done alone, at home, in about twenty minutes.

1. **Prepare.** Choose a time when the full Moon is up (any time from sunset to sunrise on the night of the full moon, or the night before or after). Tidy a small space. If you can see the Moon from a window or outside, so much the better; if not, that is fine.
2. **Ground and centre,** as you learned in Grounding.
3. **Light a white or silver candle** in a safe holder, if you wish.
4. **Look at the Moon,** or close your eyes and picture it, for two minutes. Breathe slowly: in for four, out for six.
5. **Give thanks.** Say aloud three things that have gone well since the last full moon.
6. **Name what you want to bring to fullness.** One sentence.
7. **Sit in silence** for five minutes, open to whatever comes. Some people feel calm, some feel energised, some feel nothing in particular; all are fine.
8. **Close.** Thank the Moon, snuff the candle, eat or drink something, and write a few lines in your journal.

## Moon water

Moon water is water that has been left out under the Moon (usually the full Moon) to take on its qualities. It is a modern practice, very popular, and simple.

1. Fill a **clean glass jar with a lid** with tap or bottled water.
2. Hold it, and say what you would like it to carry (calm, clarity, blessing).
3. Put it on a windowsill or outside where the Moon will shine on it overnight, **with the lid on** to keep out dust and insects.
4. Bring it in before strong morning sun.
5. Use it to wipe the altar, anoint candles and stones, water plants, add to a cleansing bath, or sprinkle round a room.

> **Safety:** Don’t drink moon water unless it was clean drinking water in a clean, covered container and you use it within a day. Water left uncovered outdoors can carry bacteria, bird droppings and pollutants. If you want a drink of it, boil it first. Never put stones in water you will drink.

## Keeping a moon journal

A moon journal is the best way to learn how the Moon affects *you*.

1. Each day (or as often as you can), note the phase. The app shows it.
2. Write a line on your mood, energy, sleep and dreams.
3. Note any workings you did and their phase.
4. At the end of each lunation, read the month back.

After three or four months, many people notice patterns: perhaps your energy rises before the full moon, or you sleep badly at the dark of the Moon, or your divination seems clearer at a particular phase. These patterns are yours, and more useful than any book.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may hold particular rites at the full or new moon, call the Moon by names from its tradition, or honour a lunar god or goddess. Your tradition’s lessons will teach those. Ask your mentor whether you are expected to keep the full moon at home in the months you can’t gather together.

> **Try this:** At the next full moon, do the full-moon practice above and make a jar of moon water. Use the water over the following waning fortnight to cleanse your altar, and note how you feel each time.

docs.title: Signs, void-of-course and eclipses
docs.summary: A brief, honest introduction to the Moon’s zodiac sign, the void-of-course Moon and eclipses: what they are and how much weight to give them.
docs.body:
## Going deeper, briefly

Phases are the heart of lunar timing. But you will hear people talk about the Moon being “in Scorpio”, “void of course”, or about an eclipse coming up. The app shows all of these, so here is what they mean. You don’t need to use them yet. Think of this lesson as a map of what is further along the road.

## The Moon’s sign

As seen from Earth, the Moon travels through the same band of constellations as the Sun and the planets: the **zodiac**. Astrologers divide that band into twelve equal **signs** (Aries, Taurus, Gemini and so on). The Moon moves quickly, spending about two and a half days in each sign and going through all twelve in about a month.

In astrological magic, the Moon’s sign colours the mood of those days and suits certain workings. For example, the app describes the Moon in Taurus as steady and grounded, good for money and home blessings; the Moon in Gemini as curious and talkative, good for study and communication; the Moon in Scorpio as deep and intense, good for protection and transformation.

This comes from Hellenistic and later Western astrology, which is a long and learned tradition. It is also a tradition with no scientific support for its predictions. Use it, if you choose, as one more layer of symbolism, like a correspondence. Many excellent practitioners never consider it at all.

## The void-of-course Moon

The **void-of-course Moon** (often written *VOC*) is the stretch of time after the Moon has made its last major angle, or *aspect*, to another planet in one sign, and before it enters the next sign. The app calculates it for you. It can last a few minutes or, occasionally, more than a day.

The traditional advice from astrologers is that things *begun* during a void-of-course Moon tend to come to nothing, go off course, or have unexpected results. So some practitioners avoid starting new workings, signing contracts or making big decisions then, and use the time instead for rest, reflection, cleaning, meditation and finishing things.

How much weight to give it is up to you and your coven. Some ignore it entirely; some check it before every important working. A balanced approach:

1. If you are planning a significant working ahead of time and it is easy to avoid a void-of-course period, avoid it.
2. If you need to act now, act. Don’t let a void-of-course Moon stop you doing something urgent or kind.
3. Notice, in your records, whether workings begun during void-of-course periods turn out differently for you.

## Eclipses

A **lunar eclipse** happens when the Earth passes directly between the Sun and the full Moon, so the Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. It can only happen at a full moon. During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon often turns a coppery red. Lunar eclipses are completely safe to watch with the naked eye.

A **solar eclipse** happens when the new Moon passes directly between the Earth and the Sun and blocks some or all of the Sun’s light. It can only happen at a new moon.

> **Safety:** Never look directly at the Sun, during an eclipse or at any other time, without proper certified eclipse glasses or a safe projection method. Ordinary sunglasses, smoked glass and phone screens are not safe. Looking at the Sun can permanently damage your eyes in seconds.

Many cultures treated eclipses as omens, often frightening ones. In modern practice, people take different views: some find eclipses powerful times for deep change and release; others prefer not to work magic during them at all, treating them as unpredictable, and simply watch. Both are reasonable. If you work, keep it simple and ground well afterwards.

## Retrogrades, briefly

You will also hear people blame things on “Mercury retrograde”. A planet is **retrograde** when, seen from the moving Earth, it appears for a few weeks to drift backwards against the stars. Nothing actually reverses; it is an effect of our point of view, like a slower car seeming to slip backwards as you overtake it on a motorway. Mercury does this three or four times a year, for about three weeks each time.

Astrologers associate a planet’s retrograde with its affairs going awry or needing review: for Mercury, communication, travel, contracts and technology. Some practitioners use these weeks for revising, finishing and reflecting rather than starting. There is no evidence that emails go astray more often during Mercury retrograde, and it is not a reason to fear anything. The app notes retrogrades, and you can watch your own records to see whether they mean anything to you.

## A worked example

Alex wants to do a working to begin a new course of study. Opening the app, Alex sees that the Moon is waxing (good for beginnings), that it is in Gemini (curious, good for study), and that a void-of-course period begins at nine that evening and lasts until the next morning.

Alex decides to do the working at seven, during the waxing Moon in Gemini and before the void-of-course period starts, in an hour of Mercury found in the app. If none of this had lined up, Alex would simply have worked on the waxing Moon at a convenient time. The extra layers are a bonus, not a requirement.

## How these fit together

If you want a simple order of importance for a beginner:

1. **The phase** (waxing or waning, full or new). Use it often.
2. **The day and planetary hour,** which you met in Correspondences. Use it when you plan ahead.
3. **The Moon’s sign.** Optional, for extra colour.
4. **The void-of-course Moon.** Optional; avoid it for big new starts if it is easy to.
5. **Eclipses.** Rare; notice them, and decide with your coven how to treat them.

> **Your coven:** Some covens follow astrology closely and plan rituals around it; others don’t use it at all, and reconstructionist traditions may prefer their own historical calendars. Ask your mentor how your coven sees it.

> **Try this:** Open the app on three different days this week and note the Moon’s phase, sign, and whether a void-of-course period is coming. Write one line each time on how the day felt. Don’t try to prove anything; just get to know the sky.

docs.title: The Sun’s year and the seasons
docs.summary: The solstices, equinoxes and the days between, why seasons flip between the hemispheres, and how to tune your practice to the year where you actually live.
docs.body:
## The longer rhythm

If the Moon gives your practice a monthly rhythm, the Sun gives it a yearly one. Light lengthens and shortens; plants grow, flower, fruit and die back; animals breed and migrate; the weather turns. Almost every religious tradition on Earth marks the turning of the year with festivals, and your coven’s tradition will have its own calendar of holy days, taught in its own lessons. This lesson covers the astronomy and the general idea, so you can understand any calendar.

## Solstices and equinoxes

The Earth is tilted on its axis. As it travels round the Sun over a year, first one hemisphere and then the other leans towards the Sun. That tilt, not the Earth’s distance from the Sun, is what makes the seasons.

There are four turning points:

- **The summer solstice:** the longest day and shortest night. The Sun reaches its highest point at noon. In the northern hemisphere this falls around **21 June**; in the southern, around **21 December**.
- **The winter solstice:** the shortest day and longest night. The Sun is at its lowest. Around **21 December** in the north, **21 June** in the south.
- **The spring (vernal) equinox:** day and night are roughly equal, and days are lengthening. Around **20 March** in the north, **22 or 23 September** in the south.
- **The autumn equinox:** day and night roughly equal again, now with nights lengthening. Around **22 or 23 September** in the north, **20 March** in the south.

*Solstice* comes from Latin for “the Sun stands still”: for a few days around each solstice, the Sun’s rising point on the horizon seems to stop moving before turning back. *Equinox* means “equal night”.

The exact dates shift by a day or so from year to year, so check each year’s date in the app’s calendar or an almanac.

## The days between

Midway between each solstice and equinox lies a **cross-quarter day**, around the beginning of **February, May, August and November**. In the northern hemisphere these mark the first stirrings of spring, the start of summer, the first harvest, and the start of winter. Several old European festivals fall near them, and many modern calendars mark all eight points.

> **Note:** The “Wheel of the Year” that sets eight festivals at the solstices, equinoxes and cross-quarter days is a modern synthesis, put together by Wiccans and Druids in Britain in the 1950s to 1970s from older festivals of different peoples. It is a beautiful and widely used calendar, and it is honest to know it was assembled recently. Other traditions in this app keep their own historical calendars, some of which follow the Moon, the Sun, or a mixture.

## North and south

Because the seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres, a festival of the returning light belongs to December in Edinburgh and to June in Melbourne. Many practitioners in the southern hemisphere keep festivals by their own season rather than by the northern calendar date. Others keep the northern dates because of a tradition’s roots or a deity’s historical feast day. Both choices exist; your coven will have its own.

Near the equator, the seasons may be wet and dry rather than warm and cold, and practitioners there often build their year around rains, harvests and local festivals.

## Living by the seasons where you are

Books describe seasons in a particular place, usually Britain or North America. Your own place may be different. The best seasonal practice starts with paying attention to what is actually happening around you.

1. **Choose a spot outdoors** that you can visit often: a tree, a park bench, a stretch of river, a window box, the view from your window.
2. **Visit once a week.** Spend five minutes there. Notice the light, temperature, plants, birds, insects, smells and sounds.
3. **Write three lines** in your journal: what you saw, what changed since last week, and how you feel.
4. **Note the first and last of things:** the first frost, the first swallow, the first blossom, the last leaves.
5. **Over a year,** this becomes your own seasonal calendar. You will know when *your* spring really begins.

## Using the seasons in magic

Seasonal timing works much like lunar timing, on a larger scale:

- **Growing light (from the winter solstice to the summer one):** beginnings, growth, planting projects, building.
- **The peak of light (around the summer solstice):** strength, celebration, success, abundance.
- **Waning light (from the summer solstice to the winter one):** harvest, gratitude, letting go, rest, turning inward.
- **The depth of dark (around the winter solstice):** rest, endings, deep reflection, hope for the returning light.

Many practitioners combine the two: a working for a new project at a waxing Moon in spring, or a deep release at a waning Moon in late autumn.

## Marking a solstice or equinox at home

Before you learn your tradition’s own festivals, here is a simple way to mark one of the four turning points on your own. Allow about twenty minutes.

1. **Find the date and time** of the solstice or equinox for the year.
2. **Watch the Sun** if you can: its rising, its setting, or how high it stands at noon. Notice where on the horizon it rises or sets compared with a month ago.
3. **Gather something of the season** from where you live: a leaf, a flower, a seed head, a stone, snow in a bowl.
4. **Ground and centre,** then light a candle in a safe holder.
5. **Speak simply** of what the season means where you are: “Today is the longest night. From here the light returns.”
6. **Give thanks** for one thing the past season gave you, and name one thing you hope for in the next.
7. **Sit quietly** for a few minutes, then put out the candle, eat something, and write in your journal.

Your tradition will give you richer forms for its own holy days. This simple practice works for any of them and keeps you tied to the real sky.

> **Your coven:** Your coven’s holy days, and the customs of each, are taught in your tradition’s lessons on lore. Ask your mentor how your coven adjusts its calendar if members live in different hemispheres or climates.

> **Try this:** Choose your outdoor spot this week and make your first visit. Write down what you notice. Keep visiting once a week through this course.

docs.title: When timing matters, and when it doesn’t
docs.summary: How to decide how much timing a working needs, why urgent needs should never wait for the Moon, and how to layer timing without becoming ruled by it.
docs.body:
## Timing is a tool, not a gate

Once people learn about phases, days, hours, signs and seasons, some begin to feel they can’t do anything without consulting a chart. That is a trap. Timing is one way to add meaning and focus to a working. It is never a reason to leave someone without help, to avoid acting in ordinary ways, or to feel your magic has “failed” because you got the date wrong.

## When timing matters more

Timing is worth thinking about when:

- **You are planning ahead.** A working for a new project next month can easily be set for a waxing Moon on the right day.
- **The working is large or important to you.** Extra layers of meaning help you focus and treat it seriously.
- **It is a coven rite.** Shared timing (full moons, festivals) brings a group together in a common rhythm, which has a strength of its own.
- **Your tradition asks for it.** Some traditions keep particular days for particular gods, or particular hours for particular rites.
- **You are learning.** Paying attention to timing trains you to notice the world.

## When timing matters less, or not at all

- **When something is urgent.** If you or someone you love needs protection, comfort or healing *now*, act now. Every phase can be worded to suit (as you learned in Working with the phases), and every day has an hour of every planet.
- **For daily devotion and simple practices.** Grounding, prayer, offerings, a daily card: do them every day, whatever the Moon is doing.
- **When the alternative is not doing it at all.** A working done at the “wrong” time with care is worth more than a perfect working that never happens.

> **Safety:** Magic never replaces ordinary action in a crisis. If someone is in danger, ill or in distress, contact emergency services, a doctor or a crisis line first. Do your magic as well, at any time, but never instead.

## Layering timing

When you do want to plan, here is a simple order that keeps it manageable:

1. **Start with the phase.** Waxing for growth, waning for release, full for power and thanks, new for seeds and rest.
2. **Add the day,** if it is easy: Friday for love, Thursday for luck, Saturday for boundaries.
3. **Add the planetary hour,** if you want to: the app finds the next one.
4. **Check the void-of-course Moon,** if you or your coven use it, for big new beginnings.
5. **Stop there.** If all the layers won’t line up for weeks, pick the most important one (usually the phase) and go ahead.

## A worked example

Sam wants to do a working to find a new job.

1. *Intention:* “I find a job that suits me and pays fairly.”
2. *Phase:* it is a waning Moon. Sam can wait about ten days for the waxing Moon, or reword the intention for the waning Moon: “All that keeps me from the right job falls away.” Sam decides to do both: a release working now, and a drawing-in working when the Moon is waxing.
3. *Day and hour:* for the waxing working, Sam chooses a Sunday (success) in the hour of Mercury (applications and interviews), found in the app.
4. *Mundane action:* every week, whatever the Moon, Sam sends applications and updates their CV. The magic supports the action; it doesn’t replace it.
5. *Record:* Sam writes down both workings with their dates, phases, days and hours, and notes what happens over the following weeks.

## Common traps

- **Waiting for perfect timing.** All the layers rarely line up. If you find yourself putting a working off week after week, choose the phase alone and begin.
- **Anxiety about getting it wrong.** Timing is meant to add meaning and confidence, not fear. If checking the sky makes you anxious, step back to the phases only, or set timing aside for a while.
- **Blaming the timing.** When a working doesn’t go as hoped, it is tempting to blame the void-of-course Moon or a retrograde. Look first at the intention, the effort and the ordinary action you took, as you will learn in Spellcraft.
- **Letting timing replace care.** No phase or hour is ever a reason to delay helping someone, seeing a doctor, or keeping yourself safe.
- **Copying someone else’s calendar.** A book written for another hemisphere or tradition may not fit you. Use your own sky and your own coven’s calendar.

## Recording and learning

The only way to know how much timing matters *for you* is to keep records. For every working, note the date, time, phase, day, hour (and sign and void-of-course status if you use them). After six months, look back. Did workings at certain times feel stronger? Did they turn out differently? Your records, honestly kept, will teach you more than any book, including this one.

> **Your coven:** Covens often have to meet when people are free, not when the sky is perfect. Many covens hold their full-moon rite on the nearest convenient evening. Ask your mentor how strict your coven is about dates, and why.

> **Try this:** Think of something you would like to work for. Write the intention, then write it twice more: once worded for a waxing Moon and once for a waning Moon. Add the day and hour you would choose. Then write one ordinary, practical action you will take towards it this week, whatever the Moon.

docs.title: What divination is
docs.summary: What divination is and isn’t, a short honest history, the different ways practitioners understand it, how to ask a good question, and how to choose a system.
docs.body:
## Seeking insight

**Divination** is any practice of seeking insight or guidance through a system of signs: cards, runes, the fall of lots, a swinging pendulum, the patterns in water or smoke, the flight of birds, dreams. The word comes from Latin *divinare*, “to foresee” or “to be inspired by a god”.

Divination is one of the oldest and most widespread human practices. Babylonian priests read the livers of sacrificed animals. Greeks travelled to the oracle at Delphi. Romans watched the flight of birds before public business (the *augurs*). The Norse and other Germanic peoples, according to the Roman writer Tacitus, cast marked strips of wood to learn the will of the gods. Chinese diviners used the *Yijing* (I Ching). It is found on every continent.

In a coven, divination is used to look at a situation more clearly, to ask the gods or spirits for guidance, to check whether a working is wise before doing it, to reflect on your own path, and sometimes to help others.

## What divination can and can’t do

Be honest with yourself and with anyone you read for.

Divination **can**:

- help you see a situation from new angles;
- bring to the surface what you already half know;
- prompt good questions and better decisions;
- give a sense of guidance, comfort or warning;
- in many traditions, be a way of listening to gods, spirits and ancestors.

Divination **can’t**:

- tell you fixed facts about the future, as if it were already written;
- diagnose illness, predict pregnancy, settle legal questions, or tell you whether to take a medicine;
- tell you for certain what someone else is thinking or doing;
- replace doctors, lawyers, counsellors, or your own judgement.

There is no scientific evidence that divination predicts events. Practitioners who find it valuable usually speak of it as insight and guidance rather than prediction.

## How might it work?

Practitioners hold different views. You don’t need to choose one.

1. **As a mirror.** The symbols prompt your own intuition and unconscious mind. A card shows you a picture; what you see in it, and what you feel about it, tells you something you didn’t know you knew. The psychologist Carl Jung’s idea of *synchronicity* (meaningful coincidence) is often mentioned here.
2. **As a conversation.** Gods, spirits, ancestors or your own deeper self guide the fall of cards or runes to say something. This is the oldest understanding: in most ancient divination, the gods were the ones speaking.
3. **As a tool for thinking.** Even if nothing beyond chance is at work, a random prompt breaks habits of thought and helps you consider options you had overlooked.

Many practitioners use all three at different times.

## Asking a good question

The quality of a reading depends heavily on the question.

1. **Make it open, not yes or no.** “What do I need to know about this new job?” works better than “Will I get the job?”
2. **Make it about you,** or about something you have a right to know. “How can I improve my relationship with my sister?” rather than “What is my sister secretly thinking?”
3. **Make it about the near future or the present.** Readings are clearest about the next weeks or months, and about the forces at work now.
4. **Make it one question.** If you have three questions, do three readings.
5. **Write it down** before you begin, so you can read it back later.

Good starting forms: “What do I need to know about…?”, “What would help me with…?”, “What is the best approach to…?”, “What am I not seeing about…?”

## Choosing a system

There are hundreds of divination systems. For a beginner, it is best to learn **one** system well before trying others. A good choice:

- **Tarot** is the most widely used in modern witchcraft, has a rich picture language that beginners can read straight away, and is taught in depth in the next two lessons. The app has a full tarot deck with meanings.
- **Oracle decks** are simpler picture decks with no fixed structure; each comes with its own guidebook. They are gentle to start with but vary greatly.
- **Runes** suit Heathen and Germanic-leaning practitioners, and are taught briefly in a later lesson.
- **Ogham** suits Celtic-leaning practitioners, also taught briefly later.
- **Pendulum** is good for simple yes-or-no questions.
- **Scrying** (gazing into water, a mirror or flame) suits people who see images easily.

Choose what draws you, what fits your tradition, and what you can get easily. You can use the app’s cards and runes before buying anything.

## A first reading, before you know anything

You can begin today, before learning a single meaning.

1. Sit quietly and take five slow breaths.
2. Write an open question about your own life.
3. Draw one tarot card (from the app or a deck) without looking up its meaning.
4. Look at the picture for three minutes. Describe aloud or on paper everything you see: who is there, what they are doing, the colours, the weather, the mood.
5. Ask: if this picture were an answer to my question, what would it be saying?
6. Write your answer down. Only then look up the card’s meaning and compare.

Many beginners are surprised how much they find in the picture alone. That is the heart of reading: looking closely and listening to what arises.

## Common difficulties at the start

- **“I feel silly.”** Most people do at first. It passes with practice.
- **“I don’t trust what comes.”** That’s healthy. Write it down and see how it looks in a week.
- **“I want to read about everything.”** Keep to one question a day for now. Too many readings blur together.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may favour one system, especially one tied to its tradition: runes in Heathenry, ogham in Celtic paths, lots and omens in Hellenic and Roman practice, Psalms and Bible-opening in Christian folk magic. Ask your mentor which the coven uses and whether it has a reader you can learn from.

> **Safety:** If divination ever makes you anxious, obsessive (reading again and again on the same question) or frightened, stop for a while. Ground yourself, talk to your mentor, and remember that a reading shows possibilities, not fate.

docs.title: The tarot deck
docs.summary: The structure of a tarot deck: the 22 Major Arcana, the four suits and their elements, what the numbers and court cards mean, and a short honest history.
docs.body:
## A short history

Tarot cards first appear in northern Italy in the fifteenth century, as luxury hand-painted decks for a card game called *tarocchi*. The game is still played in parts of Europe. There is no evidence that tarot was used for divination for its first three hundred years or so.

In 1781 the French writer Antoine Court de Gébelin claimed that the tarot held the lost wisdom of ancient Egypt. He was wrong (the Egyptian language hadn’t yet been deciphered, and nothing connects the cards to Egypt), but the idea caught on. In 1789 a French occultist known as Etteilla published the first deck designed for fortune-telling. In the late nineteenth century the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn linked the cards to astrology, the Hebrew alphabet and the four elements.

In 1909 the artist **Pamela Colman Smith**, working with the occultist A. E. Waite, painted a deck in which every card, including the numbered ones, shows a scene. This **Rider–Waite–Smith** deck is the most influential tarot of the twentieth century, and most modern decks follow its structure and imagery. The app’s tarot uses it.

So tarot is old as a deck of cards, and a little over two centuries old as a divination system. It is a living, creative tradition, with thousands of decks made every year.

## The structure

A tarot deck has **78 cards**, in two parts.

### The Major Arcana: 22 cards

*Arcana* means “secrets”. The 22 Major Arcana show large themes, turning points and spiritual lessons. They are numbered 0 to 21. Read through them slowly; the keywords are the app’s.

- **0 The Fool:** beginnings, trust, the open road.
- **1 The Magician:** will, skill, the tools to hand.
- **2 The High Priestess:** secrets, intuition, the inner voice.
- **3 The Empress:** abundance, nurture, fruitfulness.
- **4 The Emperor:** structure, authority, steadiness.
- **5 The Hierophant:** tradition, teaching, belonging.
- **6 The Lovers:** love, union, a true choice.
- **7 The Chariot:** will, direction, victory.
- **8 Strength:** gentle courage, patience, compassion.
- **9 The Hermit:** solitude, inner light, seeking.
- **10 Wheel of Fortune:** cycles, fate, a turning point.
- **11 Justice:** fairness, truth, cause and effect.
- **12 The Hanged Man:** surrender, pause, a new way of seeing.
- **13 Death:** endings, transformation, clearing. Almost never a physical death.
- **14 Temperance:** balance, moderation, patience.
- **15 The Devil:** attachment, temptation, the shadow.
- **16 The Tower:** upheaval, revelation, sudden change.
- **17 The Star:** hope, renewal, calm.
- **18 The Moon:** illusion, fear, the unconscious.
- **19 The Sun:** joy, success, vitality.
- **20 Judgement:** awakening, reckoning, a calling.
- **21 The World:** completion, wholeness, arrival.

Many readers see the Major Arcana as a story, sometimes called **the Fool’s Journey**: the Fool sets out (0), meets teachers and powers (1 to 5), makes choices and gains mastery (6 to 10), faces trials, surrender and endings (11 to 16), and finds hope, illumination and completion (17 to 21).

> **Note:** In older decks such as the Tarot of Marseille, Strength is 11 and Justice is 8. Waite swapped them. Neither is wrong; just know which your deck uses.

### The Minor Arcana: 56 cards

The Minor Arcana are like ordinary playing cards: four suits, each with cards from Ace to Ten and four court cards. They show the everyday events, people, feelings and choices of life.

The four suits, with the elements most modern readers give them (from the Golden Dawn):

- **Wands** (also rods, staves): **fire.** Will, energy, creativity, ambition, work, passion. Equivalent to clubs in playing cards.
- **Cups:** **water.** Feelings, love, relationships, intuition, dreams. Equivalent to hearts.
- **Swords:** **air.** Thought, truth, words, conflict, decisions, difficulty. Equivalent to spades.
- **Pentacles** (also coins, disks): **earth.** Money, work, the body, home, the material world. Equivalent to diamonds.

> **Note:** A few decks and readers swap Wands and Swords, giving Wands to air and Swords to fire. If your deck’s book does this, follow it.

### The numbers

Each number has a general meaning, which combines with the suit:

- **Ace:** a seed, a beginning, the pure gift of the suit.
- **Two:** balance, choice, partnership.
- **Three:** growth, first results, cooperation.
- **Four:** stability, structure, rest (sometimes stagnation).
- **Five:** conflict, loss, challenge, disruption.
- **Six:** harmony restored, generosity, moving on.
- **Seven:** assessment, testing, a choice or a challenge to hold your ground.
- **Eight:** movement, effort, mastery or being caught.
- **Nine:** near-completion, fulfilment or its anxieties.
- **Ten:** completion, the end of a cycle, sometimes too much.

So the **Ace of Cups** is a new love or emotional beginning; the **Five of Pentacles** is material hardship; the **Ten of Wands** is the burden of carrying too much work.

### The court cards

Each suit has four court cards: **Page, Knight, Queen, King.** They can show:

- **a person** in your life, with the qualities of that rank and suit;
- **a part of you** you need to use;
- **a way of approaching** the situation.

A general guide:

- **Page:** a learner, messenger, beginner, curiosity.
- **Knight:** action, movement, pursuit (sometimes too fast or too much).
- **Queen:** mature, inward mastery of the suit; nurturing, understanding.
- **King:** mature, outward mastery of the suit; leadership, responsibility.

The **Queen of Cups** might be a deeply compassionate person, or a call to listen to your own feelings with care. The **Knight of Swords** might be someone rushing in with sharp words, or a call to act quickly on a clear idea.

Court cards are traditionally hard for beginners. Don’t worry about getting them “right”; notice what they suggest.

## Reversed cards

Some readers read cards that come out upside down as **reversed**, with a changed meaning: often the energy of the card blocked, delayed, turned inward, or overdone. The app gives reversed meanings for every card. Reading reversals is optional. Many good readers never use them. As a beginner, you may prefer to turn every card upright and add reversals later.

## Getting to know your deck

1. **Choose a deck.** The app’s Rider–Waite–Smith cards are a good start. If you buy a deck, choose one whose pictures you like and that follows the Rider–Waite–Smith structure, with scenes on every card.
2. **Look through every card,** slowly, without reading the meanings. Notice what catches your eye.
3. **Sort them** into Major Arcana and the four suits, and lay out each suit from Ace to King.
4. **Study one card a day.** Look at the picture for two minutes. Write what you see: people, colours, objects, weather, mood. Then read its meaning and write what you think it means *for you*.

There is a myth that your first tarot deck must be given to you as a gift. It needn’t. Buy, borrow or use the app’s.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have a preferred deck, or readers who use a particular one. Some covens cleanse and consecrate decks as tools (as you learned in Altar and tools). Ask your mentor.

docs.title: The daily draw and your reading journal
docs.summary: How to keep a daily one-card practice and a reading journal, what to record, and how reviewing your readings over time makes you a better reader.
docs.body:
## Little and often

The single best way to learn any divination system is a **daily draw**: one card (or rune, or ogham stave) each day, read and recorded. It takes five minutes. Over a few months, you will meet every card many times in the context of real days, which teaches you more than any book.

## The daily draw, step by step

1. **Choose a time.** Morning works well, so you can carry the card through the day and see how it fits. Some people prefer evening, as a reflection on the day just gone. Be consistent.
2. **Ground briefly.** Three slow breaths.
3. **Ask a simple question.** For example: “What do I need to know today?”, “What energy will help me today?”, or “What should I pay attention to?”
4. **Shuffle and draw one card.** Use your own deck or the app’s draw.
5. **Look first.** Spend a minute with the picture.
6. **Read the meaning.** Look it up if you need to.
7. **Write two or three lines:** the card, what you see in it, and one guess about how it might show up today.
8. **In the evening, add a line:** did it show up? How?

## Learning a card through the day

A daily card is a small teacher. To get the most from it:

1. **Describe it in your own words** before reading anything. “A man carrying ten heavy sticks towards a town, bent over, can’t see where he’s going.”
2. **Find the keyword that fits the picture.** For the Ten of Wands the app gives burden, responsibility, overload. You can see it in the picture.
3. **Make one guess.** “Today I might take on too much at work.”
4. **Watch.** During the day, notice anything that echoes the card: a conversation, a mood, a sight, a choice.
5. **Reflect in the evening.** Perhaps you did take on too much; perhaps you said no to something and felt relief; perhaps nothing matched. Write it down either way.

Over months, each card gathers real memories: the day the Ten of Wands was the shopping you carried home in the rain, the day the Star was the message from an old friend. Those memories become your meanings, and they are far easier to recall than lists.

## A worked week

Here is a trainee’s first week, as she wrote it in her journal.

- **Monday, Page of Cups:** a young person looking at a fish in a cup, surprised. *Guess:* a pleasant surprise. *Evening:* a colleague brought cake for no reason. Small, but it fitted.
- **Tuesday, Five of Swords:** someone walking off with swords, others defeated. *Guess:* an argument. *Evening:* I nearly snapped at my brother and didn’t. Maybe a warning heeded.
- **Wednesday, The Hermit:** an old man with a lantern alone on a mountain. *Guess:* I need time alone. *Evening:* cancelled plans and read; felt much better.
- **Thursday, Eight of Pentacles:** someone carefully making coins at a bench. *Guess:* steady work. *Evening:* finished a dull report properly. Felt good.
- **Friday, Three of Cups:** three women dancing with cups. *Guess:* friends. *Evening:* drinks with friends. Easy one.
- **Saturday, The Tower:** lightning, people falling. *Guess:* something sudden. *Evening:* the boiler broke. Annoying, not a disaster.
- **Sunday, Four of Swords:** a knight lying still in a church. *Guess:* rest. *Evening:* slept all afternoon.

Notice how ordinary it is. The daily draw is not about drama. It is about learning the cards through real life, and noticing your days more closely.

## Common difficulties

- **Missing days.** Don’t worry; start again the next day.
- **Drawing the same card often.** Take notice. A card that keeps returning may be pointing at something.
- **Every card seems to fit, whatever happens.** That can happen, because cards are broad. Make your morning guess specific, and be honest in the evening about whether it fitted.

## What to record

Keep every reading, daily draws and larger spreads alike, in one place: your Grimoire in the app, the app’s reading log, or a notebook. For each reading, write:

- the **date and time**, and the **Moon’s phase** (you will learn something from this);
- the **question**;
- the **spread** and the **cards** in their positions (and whether any were reversed);
- **what you saw** in the pictures and **what you felt**;
- your **summary**: the answer in a sentence or two;
- later, a **follow-up note**: what actually happened, and how the reading looks now.

## Reviewing your readings

Once a month, at the same phase of the Moon if you like, read back over the month’s readings.

1. **Count.** Which cards came up most? Which suits? Were there many Major Arcana? Repeated cards often point to a theme in your life.
2. **Check.** Read your follow-up notes. Which readings seem apt now? Which seem off? Can you see why?
3. **Learn.** Pick one card that confused you and study it again, looking at the picture and the app’s longer Grimoire page.
4. **Write a short summary** of the month: themes, lessons, how your reading is changing.

## Honest record-keeping

It is natural to remember the readings that “came true” and forget those that didn’t. That is how all human memory works. Writing everything down, including the misses, keeps you honest, helps you learn which kinds of question your system answers well, and protects you from both over-trusting and dismissing it.

> **Note:** If a daily card is hard (the Tower, the Five of Pentacles), don’t dread the day. Take it as a gentle warning: be careful with plans, look after your money, check in with yourself. Most days, nothing dramatic happens. Notice how the card shows up in small ways.

> **Your coven:** Some covens share a monthly card or rune with the whole group, or draw one at each esbat. Ask your mentor if yours does.

> **Try this:** Start your daily draw today. Keep it for the rest of this stage, recording each draw, and review the whole set at the end.

docs.title: Reading the cards: a three-card spread
docs.summary: How to prepare, shuffle, lay out and read a three-card spread step by step, with a worked example, common difficulties, and how to know you are improving.
docs.body:
## What a spread is

A **spread** is a pattern for laying out cards, where each position has a meaning. The positions turn a handful of cards into an answer you can read. There are many spreads, from one card to the famous ten-card Celtic Cross. The best one to learn first is the **three-card spread**: simple enough to learn quickly, rich enough to say something real.

## Three ways to read three cards

Choose one before you lay the cards.

- **Past, present, future:** what led here, where things stand, where they are heading if nothing changes.
- **Situation, challenge, advice:** what is going on, what stands in the way, what would help.
- **Mind, body, spirit:** what is happening in your thoughts, your physical life, and your spiritual life.

“Situation, challenge, advice” is especially good for beginners, because it always ends on something you can act on.

## Reading step by step

Allow about twenty minutes.

1. **Prepare the space.** Clear a table. Some people lay a cloth. Light a candle if you wish (safely). Switch off notifications.
2. **Ground and centre,** as you learned in Grounding. Take five slow breaths: in for four, out for six.
3. **Write your question** in your journal. Keep it open and about you (see What divination is).
4. **Shuffle.** Hold the cards and shuffle in whatever way is comfortable: overhand, riffle, or spread them face down on the table and swirl them. While you shuffle, hold the question in mind. Stop when it feels right, or after a count of your choice.
5. **Cut** the deck if you like (many readers cut into three piles with the left hand and restack), then take the top three cards. Or fan them out and pick three that draw you.
6. **Lay them face down,** left to right: position one, two, three.
7. **Turn them over** one at a time.
8. **Look before you read.** For each card, spend a minute just looking. What is happening in the picture? What is the mood? What catches your eye? What do you feel?
9. **Add the meaning.** Now recall or look up the card’s keywords. How do they fit the picture and the position?
10. **Read the cards together.** Look at all three. Is there a story moving left to right? Are there many cards of one suit (lots of Cups suggests feelings are the heart of it)? Many Major Arcana (a big, significant time)? Do people in the cards face towards or away from each other?
11. **Sum it up in one or two sentences.** This is the answer to your question.
12. **Write it down:** the date, question, spread, cards, what you saw, and your summary. If you’re using the app, you can save the reading.
13. **Close.** Thank whatever you feel helped (your deck, your gods, your own intuition), put the cards away, and drink some water.

## A worked example

**Question:** “What would help me feel settled in my new home?”

**Spread:** situation, challenge, advice.

1. **Situation: Four of Wands.** Garlands, people dancing at the gate: celebration, homecoming. The picture says this home is a good thing, a real arrival.
2. **Challenge: Eight of Swords.** A blindfolded woman surrounded by swords, though the way out is open. Feeling trapped, mostly by thoughts. The challenge isn’t the home; it’s worry.
3. **Advice: Six of Cups.** Children sharing flowers in an old courtyard: memory, kindness, simple pleasures. Bring things that feel like home from the past; be gentle; perhaps invite an old friend.

**Summary:** “The home is right. What unsettles me is worry, which is less real than it feels. Fill the place with familiar comforts and people I love.”

Notice that the reading didn’t predict anything. It gave a fresh way of looking at the situation and something to do.

## Common difficulties

- **“I can’t remember the meanings.”** Normal. Look them up, every time, for months. Meanings stick through use, not memorising lists. Lean on the pictures; they were drawn to be read.
- **“The cards don’t make sense together.”** Read each card alone first, then ask: if these three were a sentence, what would it say? If it still doesn’t fit, write it down and come back in a week. Many readings make sense only in hindsight.
- **“I got a scary card.”** Death, the Tower and the Devil are dramatic, but not curses. Death is endings and change; the Tower is upheaval that clears the ground; the Devil is unhealthy attachment. They show what is happening so you can respond.
- **“I keep drawing again because I don’t like the answer.”** Stop. Re-drawing until you get the answer you want teaches nothing. Write down the first reading and sit with it. Give the question a few days, at least, before asking again.
- **“I read what I want to see.”** Everyone does at first. Writing your reading down and checking it later is the cure.

## How you’ll know it’s working

You will not wake up one day with second sight. Instead, over weeks, you will notice: the meanings come faster; you see more in the pictures; your summaries get clearer; and when you look back at old readings, more of them seem apt. That is real progress.

> **Safety:** Don’t read about your health, a pregnancy, someone’s death, or legal and financial decisions in a way that replaces professional advice. If a reading frightens you, put it away, ground yourself, and talk to your mentor.

> **Try this:** Do a situation, challenge, advice reading on a small, real question in your life this week. Follow every step above and write it all down.

docs.title: Runes, ogham, pendulum and scrying
docs.summary: A short, honest introduction to four other common systems: what each is, where it comes from, and a simple way to begin.
docs.body:
## Other ways of seeing

Tarot is not the only way. This lesson introduces four other systems you may meet in your coven. Each could fill a course of its own; this is a first taste. The app’s Grimoire has fuller pages on the runes and ogham.

## Runes

**Runes** are the letters of the old Germanic alphabets. The oldest, the **Elder Futhark**, has 24 runes and was used from roughly the second to the eighth century, carved on stone, wood, metal and bone. It is named after its first six letters: *f, u, th, a, r, k*. Each rune is a letter, a sound and a name with a meaning: **Fehu** (cattle, wealth), **Uruz** (aurochs, strength), **Thurisaz** (giant, thorn), and so on.

**History, honestly.** The Roman writer Tacitus, around the year 98, described Germanic peoples casting strips of wood marked with signs to learn the will of the gods, but he doesn’t say the signs were runes. The old rune poems (Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic, written down in the Middle Ages) give each rune a short verse, and these are the main old source for meanings. Most modern methods of rune divination, and nearly all reversed (“merkstave”) readings, are twentieth-century inventions. The “blank rune” in many sets was added in 1982 and has no historical basis.

**A simple start:**

1. Make or buy a set of 24 runes. You can paint them on pebbles or write them on card, or use the app’s.
2. Ground and centre. Hold a question in mind.
3. Draw one rune from a bag without looking.
4. Read its name and meaning, and look at its shape. What does it say about your question?
5. Write it down.

> **Note:** Runes are sacred in Heathenry, and some runic symbols have been misused by hate groups. Learn them respectfully, from good sources. Your coven’s tradition lessons may teach them more fully.

## Ogham
