docs.title: Lughnasadh and Lammas
docs.summary: The first harvest at the start of August: Lugh and Tailtiu, Máire MacNeill’s record of Lughnasa hilltop gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, and keeping it with bread, thanks and the fruits of work.
docs.body:
## When

Lughnasadh, also called Lammas, is kept from the evening of 31 July into 1 August in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 January into 1 February in the south.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Lughnasadh

Lughnasadh (LOO-na-sa; Lúnasa in modern Irish, the name of the month of August) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the beginning of the harvest. Medieval Irish texts say it was founded by the god Lugh, a god of many skills, in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, who died after clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. The Óenach Tailten, a great assembly with games, horse races, trading and marriages, was held at Teltown in County Meath at this time.

### Máire MacNeill's Lughnasa

In 1962 the Irish folklorist Máire MacNeill published The Festival of Lughnasa, a study of how the festival survived in folk custom across Ireland. She found nearly two hundred places where people gathered at the start of August, usually on the last Sunday of July or the first of August, often called Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday or Height Sunday:

- **climbing hills** and mountains together;
- **picking bilberries** (also called fraughans or whortleberries), the first wild fruit, and eating or bringing them home;
- **visiting holy wells** and lakes;
- **dancing, music, courting** and sometimes faction fights;
- **the first new potatoes** dug and eaten.

The pilgrimage up Croagh Patrick on the last Sunday of July, and Puck Fair at Killorglin, where a wild goat is crowned king, are among the customs she linked to Lughnasa.

### The Anglo-Saxon Lammas

In England, 1 August was Hlafmæsse, "loaf mass", recorded from the 10th century. Bread baked from the first ripe grain was blessed in church. One Old English charm instructs that the blessed Lammas loaf be broken into four and the pieces put in the four corners of the barn to protect the stored grain. Lammas was also a quarter day for rents in Scotland.

### Harvest customs

Across Britain and Ireland, the end of the grain harvest (often later, in late August or September) had many customs: cutting the last sheaf, sometimes by throwing sickles at it so no one person "killed" it; plaiting it into a corn dolly or "kern baby" to keep through the winter; and a harvest supper for the workers. These belong to the harvest season as a whole, shared between Lammas and the autumn equinox.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Lughnasadh is a festival of the first harvest: gratitude for what has ripened, the fruits of work, and the first turn towards autumn. Common customs:

- **baking bread** from new grain, blessing it and sharing it;
- **giving the first piece** as an offering;
- **honouring Lugh** as a god of skill, for those drawn to him;
- **games and contests,** after the Óenach Tailten;
- **climbing a hill** and picking wild fruit;
- **making corn dollies** or wheat weavings;
- **giving thanks** for the work of the year, your own and others'.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Bake or buy a loaf,** ideally one you have made with your own hands. Even a simple soda bread counts.
2. **Decorate your altar** with ears of wheat or other grain, early fruit such as blackberries or bilberries, and a golden candle.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Hold up the loaf and say: "First bread of the harvest, gift of the land, the sun, the rain and many hands."
5. Name what you have harvested this year so far: the fruits of your work, learning, relationships.
6. Break off the first piece and give it as an offering. Break the rest and share it.
7. Name the people whose work feeds you: farmers, bakers, drivers, shop workers. Thank them.
8. **If you can, climb a hill** or walk somewhere with a view, and pick a few wild berries you can identify.

## Food and family

This is the festival of bread above all, so bake if you can: soda bread needs no yeast and takes under an hour. Shape the dough into a sheaf, a sun, a person or a simple plait. Early fruit, especially blackberries, bilberries and the first apples, and new potatoes with butter, suit the day. With children, baking together, making a simple corn dolly from a handful of wheat or long grass, and going blackberrying (with care about what they pick) all keep the festival. Games and races, after Lugh's games, are a good excuse to be outside.

Lugh himself is called Samildánach, "skilled in all the arts", in Irish legend. Some practitioners use Lughnasadh to show or celebrate a skill they have worked on this year: a craft, a song, a piece of writing. That fits the festival well.

## With the coven

Covens often bake bread together, hold a harvest feast, play games, or climb a hill. Many also give to a food bank, sharing the harvest with those in need.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Lughnasadh falls on 1 February, in late summer, at the height of many grain and fruit harvests. It suits the season well.

> **Safety:** Never eat wild berries you can't identify with certainty: some, such as deadly nightshade and yew, are poisonous. Hill walks need good shoes, water and an eye on the weather. Have gluten-free bread for those who need it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Lughnasadh, and whether it calls it Lammas, Lughnasadh or another name.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Lughnasadh, Lugh and Tailtiu, the Óenach Tailten, the folk Lughnasa gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, harvest customs and corn dollies.
- **Modern:** Lughnasadh as a pagan festival of the first harvest in this form, and corn dollies as altar decorations.

docs.title: The autumn equinox
docs.summary: The autumn equinox, when day and night stand equal again: the name Mabon and why it was chosen, Harvest Home, the last sheaf, the church harvest festival, Michaelmas and the harvest moon, and keeping it with gratitude, balance and letting go.
docs.body:
## When

The autumn equinox falls around 22 September in the northern hemisphere and around 20 March in the south. Day and night are nearly equal; from then on, the nights grow longer than the days.

## The roots

### The name Mabon

In the 1970s Aidan Kelly named the autumn equinox Mabon, after Mabon ap Modron, "Mabon son of Modron", a figure in the medieval Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, where he is a prisoner who must be rescued. Kelly later explained he chose the name because he liked its sound and wanted a Celtic-sounding name; there is no old connection between Mabon and the equinox. Some modern writers have linked Mabon's imprisonment to the waning year. That is a modern reading. Many practitioners prefer to call this festival Harvest Home, the autumn equinox, or Alban Elfed (the Druid name, from Iolo Morganwg).

### Harvest Home

In Britain and Ireland, there was no traditional folk festival at the equinox itself. But the weeks around it were the end of the grain harvest, and that had many customs:

- **The last sheaf:** the last of the grain to be cut was often treated specially: cut by all the reapers together, decorated, plaited into a figure called the corn dolly, the kern baby, the maiden or the hag, and kept until spring.
- **Crying the neck:** in Devon and Cornwall the reapers held up the last handful of wheat and cried out, a custom revived in some places today.
- **The harvest supper:** the farmer gave a feast for everyone who had worked the harvest, with drinking and songs.
- **Gleaning:** the poor were allowed to gather what was left in the fields.

### The church harvest festival

In 1843 the Reverend Robert Hawker of Morwenstow in Cornwall invited his parishioners to a service of thanksgiving for the harvest, with bread made from the new corn. The idea spread quickly, and the harvest festival, with churches decorated with produce later given to the poor, became one of the best-loved festivals in Britain. It is a Victorian creation, not a pagan survival.

### Michaelmas and the harvest moon

Michaelmas, 29 September, the feast of St Michael, was a quarter day for rents and the end of the farming year. Goose was eaten, and folklore said you must not pick blackberries after Michaelmas, because the devil had spat on them. The full moon nearest the autumn equinox is the harvest moon, which rises at almost the same time for several nights, giving light for harvesting late into the evening. The name is recorded in English from the early 18th century.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Because there is so little traditional equinox custom, this is the festival where modern practitioners have built the most. Common customs:

- **giving thanks** for the whole harvest of the year;
- **balance:** marking equal day and night, often with a light and a dark candle;
- **letting go:** releasing what you don't want to carry into the dark half of the year;
- **sharing:** giving to food banks, feeding others;
- **apples and the garden:** making cider, apple dishes, putting the garden to bed;
- **honouring the harvest's gods** for those drawn to them, such as Demeter and Persephone.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Decorate your altar** with apples, gourds, the last flowers of the garden, autumn leaves, and two candles, one light and one dark.
2. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
3. Light both candles: "Day and night, equal again."
4. Name, one by one, everything you are grateful for from this year's harvest: in your life, your work, your relationships, the land. Say thank you after each.
5. Then name something you want to let go of as the nights lengthen. Write it on a leaf, and later put it on the compost or bury it.
6. Share an apple: cut it across to show the five-pointed star of seeds inside, eat half, and give half as an offering.
7. **In the days around the equinox,** give food or time to someone in need, or to a food bank.

## Food and family

The autumn equinox is a time for apples, pears, plums, blackberries (before Michaelmas, if you keep the old saying), squash, nuts and the last of the garden: crumbles, pies, soups and cider or apple juice. With children, apple picking, pressing apples for juice, making a leaf crown and collecting conkers are good ways to keep the day. Taking a box of food together to a food bank teaches the heart of the festival: that a harvest is meant to be shared.

## With the coven

Covens often hold a harvest feast, give to a food bank, put a garden to bed together, or go apple picking. Some make a corn dolly from the last sheaf of a local farm, with permission.

## In the southern hemisphere

The southern autumn equinox falls around 20 March. Easter is also in southern autumn; some practitioners there blend harvest thanks and Easter's themes.

> **Safety:** If you make cider or wine, follow safe methods; homemade alcohol can be dangerous if made badly. Wash windfall apples well. Gather leaves and fruit only where allowed.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven calls this festival, and how it keeps the harvest.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the equinox, harvest customs such as the last sheaf, crying the neck and the harvest supper, Michaelmas, the harvest moon.
- **Modern:** the name Mabon (1970s), the church harvest festival (1843), and most equinox rites, including balance and letting go.

docs.title: The anatomy of a ritual
docs.summary: What a ritual is, the parts almost every ritual shares and why they are there, and how a ritual differs from a spell.
docs.body:
## What a ritual is

A **ritual** (or *rite*) is a planned sequence of meaningful actions, words and silences, done with attention, to mark something, honour something, or bring about a change. A birthday party with candles and a song is a ritual. So is a wedding, a funeral, a graduation, or lighting a candle every evening for someone who has died.

In a coven, rituals mark the Moon and the seasons, honour gods, spirits and ancestors, celebrate life events, initiate new members, heal, bless, and work magic together. You have already taken part in your coven’s own ritual form, taught in your tradition’s ritual lessons. This lesson looks underneath it, at the shape that most rituals across many traditions share, so that you can understand any ritual and, by the end of this module, write and lead one yourself.

## Ritual and spell

A **spell** is a working for a particular purpose; you learned its structure in Spellcraft. A **ritual** is the larger frame. Some rituals contain a spell (a full-moon rite with a healing working); many contain none at all (a seasonal celebration, an offering to a god). A ritual is often more about relationship, celebration and meaning than about getting a result.

## The parts of a ritual

Not every ritual has every part, and traditions name and order them differently. But you will recognise most of these in almost any rite.

1. **Purpose.** Every ritual starts, long before the day, with a clear purpose: what is this rite for? A full moon, a festival, a blessing, a farewell? Like a spell’s intention, everything else serves it.
2. **Preparation.** Planning, gathering what is needed, setting up the space, and preparing yourself: bathing, dressing, fasting lightly or not at all, quieting the mind.
3. **Purification.** Cleansing the people and the space, so that everyday concerns are set aside. Washing the hands, sprinkling water, passing through smoke, sweeping, ringing a bell. Almost every tradition has a form of this.
4. **Opening.** Marking the start and making the space sacred: casting a circle, opening a grove, a procession, lighting a hearth fire, a call to the gods, a prayer. You learned the general idea in Sacred space and your tradition’s form in its own lessons.
5. **Statement of purpose.** Someone says aloud why everyone is here. This simple step focuses the whole group.
6. **Welcoming the powers.** Calling, inviting or greeting the gods, spirits, ancestors, elements or quarters honoured in the rite. Often with offerings.
7. **The heart of the rite.** The main action: a seasonal drama, a story told, offerings made, a meditation, a working of magic, a blessing, a divination, an initiation.
8. **Sharing.** Food and drink are shared, often blessed first and with a portion offered to the powers. In Wicca this is called **cakes and ale** (or cakes and wine); in Heathenry the drinking rounds of **sumbel**; in Hellenic and Roman practice the shared feast after sacrifice. It grounds people and binds the group.
9. **Thanks and farewells.** Thanking and bidding farewell to the powers welcomed earlier, in reverse order.
10. **Closing.** Undoing the opening: opening the circle, closing the grove, extinguishing the fire. A clear end so everyone knows the rite is over.
11. **Grounding and aftercare.** Eating, drinking, talking, laughing, grounding any lingering energy. More on this in the last lesson.
12. **Clearing up and recording.** Tidying the space, disposing of offerings properly, and writing down what happened.

## Why this shape works

This shape has lasted because it suits people.

- **A clear beginning and end** lets people move fully into ritual time and fully out again. Leaving a ritual “open” often leaves people feeling unsettled.
- **Purification and opening** help everyone set aside the day’s concerns and arrive.
- **Saying the purpose** aloud brings a group into one focus.
- **Welcoming and thanking** the powers expresses relationship and respect, in the same way you would greet and thank a guest.
- **Sharing food** brings people back into their bodies and to each other.
- **Grounding** prevents the spaced-out, overwrought feeling some people have after intense ritual.

## A small example

Even the simplest solitary rite has this shape. Here is a ten-minute evening offering, mapped onto the parts:

- **Purpose:** to give thanks at the end of the day.
- **Preparation:** clear the altar; pour a little water or juice into a cup.
- **Purification:** wash your hands and face.
- **Opening:** light a candle and say, “I come to my altar.”
- **Statement of purpose:** “I am here to give thanks for this day.”
- **Welcoming:** greet the gods, spirits or ancestors you honour, by name or simply as “you who watch over this house”.
- **The heart:** name three things from the day you are grateful for, and pour a little of the drink into an offering bowl.
- **Sharing:** drink the rest of the cup yourself.
- **Thanks and closing:** “Thank you. Goodnight.” Put out the candle.
- **Grounding:** a breath, your hands on the floor.
- **Clearing up:** in the morning, pour the offering onto soil.

Once you see the shape, you will find it in every rite your coven does, however elaborate.

## Rhythm and pace

Good rituals have a rhythm: a gentle start, a building of focus, a peak at the heart of the rite, and a gentle return. Think of a piece of music. Too fast, and people can’t settle; too slow, and their attention drifts. Most coven rituals run between thirty minutes and an hour and a half, including sharing. A simple solitary rite might be fifteen minutes.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own ritual form, with its own names for each part and its own order. It may leave some parts out or add others. Ask your mentor to walk you through a typical rite and map it onto the parts above.

> **Try this:** Think back to the last coven ritual you attended (or one you saw described in your tradition’s lessons). Write down each part in order and match it to the list above. Which parts were there? Which were missing or different? Why do you think so?

docs.title: Roles and coven etiquette
docs.summary: The roles people take in coven ritual, and the etiquette that makes a coven work: punctuality, confidentiality, consent, sharing the work, and looking after one another.
docs.body:
## Many hands

In a coven, ritual is shared work. Different people take different roles, and over time most members try many of them. Knowing the roles helps you understand what is happening and prepares you to take part.

## Common roles

Names differ between traditions; your coven will have its own.

- **High Priestess and/or High Priest** (or another title, such as gothi or gydja in Heathenry, or simply leader or elder): the coven’s leader or leaders, who often lead major rites, hold the coven’s lore, and carry final responsibility for its wellbeing.
- **Officiant** or **ritual leader:** whoever leads a particular ritual. Not always the High Priestess; many covens rotate this.
- **Quarter callers** or **element callers:** in traditions that use them, the people who call and later dismiss the quarters or elements.
- **Those who make offerings or pour libations:** in many traditions a particular person makes the main offerings.
- **The person who purifies:** carrying water, smoke or salt round the space and the people.
- **Maiden, summoner or steward:** names for a coven officer who helps the leaders, organises, keeps the calendar, or watches over people’s wellbeing during rites.
- **Scribe:** keeps the coven’s records.
- **Participants:** everyone. Taking part fully (singing, responding, focusing, raising energy) is a role in itself, and the most important one.

## Etiquette: how to be a good coven member

Etiquette here isn’t fussy manners. It is the set of habits that lets a group of people do intense, vulnerable work together safely and well.

### Arriving

- **Be on time,** or a little early. Rituals often can’t start until everyone is there, and arriving late can break a circle that has already been cast. If you’re running late, message the coven so they can decide whether to wait.
- **If you can’t come, say so** as early as you can.
- **Come prepared:** read anything you were sent, bring what you agreed to bring, and know your part if you have one.
- **Come sober.** Don’t arrive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. If the rite includes a drink, you may always choose juice or water.

### Confidentiality

- **What happens in the coven stays in the coven.** Never tell anyone outside who the members are, what they said, or personal things they shared, without their permission. Many people have good reasons to keep their practice private: family, work, safety.
- **Never “out” a member** as a witch or pagan, online or off.
- **Some teachings may be oathbound,** meaning you promise not to share them. Keep those promises. But no legitimate coven will ask you to keep secrets about harm, abuse or crime. Safety always comes before secrecy.
- **Don’t photograph or record** rituals or members without everyone’s agreement.

### Consent and care

- **Ask before you touch.** Hand-holding in a circle is common; check that people are comfortable, and say if you are not. Hugs are offered, not assumed.
- **No one may pressure you** into anything you’re uncomfortable with: touch, nudity (some traditions practise “skyclad”, meaning naked, in some rites; it is never required of a trainee who doesn’t want it), drinking, sharing personal things, or any working. You can always step back or leave.
- **Share allergies, health needs and access needs** with the leaders, so the rite can be planned around them. Accept others’ needs without fuss.
- **Look after each other.** If someone seems unwell or distressed during a rite, quietly tell the leader or the person responsible for wellbeing.

### Sharing the work

- **Help set up and clear up.** Offer before being asked.
- **Bring your share** of food and supplies if that is your coven’s custom.
- **Take your turn** at roles as you are ready. Everyone was a beginner once.
- **Contribute honestly** in discussions, and listen.

### In the circle

- **Phones off,** or on silent and put away, unless the rite is online.
- **Follow the leader’s cues.** If you’re unsure what to do, watch, or quietly ask the person beside you.
- **Leaving during a rite:** if you need to leave (unwell, overwhelmed, a call of nature), it is fine. Your coven will have a way to do this; often you signal the leader, or a door is “cut” in the circle. You learned the general idea in Sacred space.
- **Laughter is fine.** Mistakes happen in every ritual: candles go out, words are forgotten, the cat walks through. Smile, carry on.

## Red flags in any group

Every coven has its quirks, but some things are never acceptable. Leave, and seek help from someone you trust, if a leader or member:

- demands money beyond reasonable shared costs, or sex, or secrets about harm;
- pressures anyone into sexual activity, or uses initiation or teaching as leverage for it;
- isolates members from family and friends;
- forbids members from talking about concerns, or punishes questions;
- claims to be beyond criticism or the only true path.

You learned more about these in the Welcome module. Your safety and dignity always come first.

> **Your coven:** Every coven has its own customs about arrival times, what to bring, dress, how to leave a circle, and who does what. Ask your mentor for your coven’s, and note them in your Grimoire.

> **Try this:** Write down your coven’s customs as you understand them so far: when to arrive, what to bring, what to wear, how to leave during a rite, and who to tell if someone is unwell. Check the list with your mentor.

docs.title: Gathering online
docs.summary: How to take part in coven rituals and meetings held through the app: preparing your space, safety at home, timing, presence on camera, and privacy.
docs.body:
## Covens without walls

Many covens now meet online for some or all of their rites: members live far apart, travel is hard, health or caring duties keep people home, or the coven is spread across countries. Online ritual is different from gathering in one room, but it can be very powerful. Many people find that knowing others are lighting their candles at the same moment, in their own homes, creates a strong sense of connection.

Your coven uses the app for its meetings, conversations and shared work, and may hold rites through it or alongside it.

## Before the gathering

1. **Read what you were sent.** The leader may share a ritual script or a list of what to have ready. Read it the day before.
2. **Check the time zone.** If your coven spans time zones, check the start time in yours.
3. **Prepare your space.** Clear a small area, set up a simple altar, and gather what you need: often a candle, a cup of water or juice, a small piece of food, and anything the script asks for.
4. **Test your device.** Charge it, check your connection, and know how to mute and unmute. Prop it up so your hands are free.
5. **Tell your household,** if you live with others, that you need quiet and privacy for the time. Close the door.
6. **Purify yourself** in a simple way: wash your hands and face, ground and centre.

## During the gathering

- **Join a few minutes early,** to settle in and sort out technical problems.
- **Mute yourself** when you are not speaking, unless the leader asks everyone to speak or sing together. (Online, voices often lag, so group chanting may work better muted, each person chanting at home.)
- **Follow the leader’s cues** for when to light candles, speak, or act. The leader will usually say each step aloud.
- **Be present.** Close other apps and notifications. Treat it as you would a gathering in person.
- **Use the chat thoughtfully:** for short responses or practical messages, not side conversations during the rite.
- **If your connection drops,** carry on the rite at home if you know what comes next, or rejoin quietly. Don’t worry; it happens to everyone.

## Safety at home

> **Safety:** You are responsible for fire safety in your own home. Keep candles in safe holders on heat-proof surfaces, away from screens, cables, curtains and pets. Don’t let the screen distract you from the flame. Put candles out properly when the rite ends, before you leave the room. If you can’t safely have a flame (rented rooms, children, pets, smoke alarms), use an LED candle; it is just as good for ritual.

Ground well afterwards, as you would after any rite. It is easy to close the laptop and go straight back to the washing up, and some people find they feel spaced out or flat later. Eat, drink, and take a few minutes before going on with your evening.

## Making online ritual feel real

Some people find online rites flat at first. These help:

1. **Mark the threshold.** Before joining, wash your hands, change into something you keep for ritual, or ring a bell. Your body learns that this is not an ordinary call.
2. **Keep your own altar in view.** Look at your candle, not only the screen, during the quiet parts.
3. **Close your eyes** during meditations and energy work; listen to the leader’s voice.
4. **Use your body.** Stand for the opening if you can, raise your hands when others do, touch the floor to ground.
5. **Share the food at home.** Have your bread and drink ready, and eat and drink at the same moment as everyone else.
6. **Stay for the chat afterwards.** The talk after a rite matters as much online as in person.

## Including everyone

Online gatherings can include people who could never travel to a circle: those with disabilities or chronic illness, carers, parents of small children, people in remote places. Help make that work.

- Be patient with technology and with people who are new to it.
- Turn on captions if anyone needs them, and speak clearly.
- Don’t comment on people’s homes, backgrounds, clothing or interruptions from children and pets.
- If someone must keep their camera off, respect that without question.

## Common difficulties

- **Lag and echo:** mute when not speaking; leaders can pause after each cue to let everyone catch up.
- **Distractions at home:** put a sign on the door, and arrange the time with your household in advance.
- **Feeling disconnected:** speak a response aloud now and then, even when muted, and keep your own candle as your focus.

## Privacy

- **Don’t record or screenshot** the rite or members without everyone’s permission.
- **Check what is behind you** on camera if you want to keep your home private, and be aware of who can hear.
- **Don’t share** links, scripts or members’ details outside the coven.
- Remember that **messages in the app** are part of the coven’s private space; treat them with the same confidentiality as anything said in the circle.

> **Your coven:** Your coven will have its own way of running online rites: whether cameras are on, how people speak in turn, and what to have ready. Ask your mentor, and ask to see a script from a previous online rite.

> **Try this:** Before your coven’s next online gathering, set up your space and test your device as described above. Afterwards, write down what worked and what you would change next time.

docs.title: Aftercare, and bringing it all together
docs.summary: How to look after yourself and others after ritual, signs that someone needs more care, and how the capstone of this course works.
docs.body:
## After the rite

Ritual can be intense. People often feel strong emotions, deep peace, joy, grief, or a buzzing energy during a rite. Afterwards some people feel wonderful; others feel tired, spacey, tearful, flat, or restless. A few days of low mood after a big ritual or festival is common enough to have a name in many communities: a **ritual drop**. Good aftercare makes all of this easier.

## Common after-effects

- **Spaciness:** feeling light-headed, dreamy, not quite here.
- **Buzzing:** restlessness, difficulty sleeping, racing thoughts.
- **Tiredness:** feeling drained, especially after raising energy.
- **Emotion:** tears, sadness, unexpected memories, or great happiness.
- **Hunger and thirst.**
- **The drop:** a day or two later, a low or flat mood.

None of these means anything has gone wrong. They are normal responses to intense experience. But they need looking after.

## Aftercare, step by step

Right after the rite:

1. **Ground.** Use the methods you learned in Grounding: hands on the floor, feet on the ground, breath, imagining excess energy sinking into the earth.
2. **Eat and drink.** Something with substance: bread, biscuits, fruit, and water. This is why sharing food is part of ritual.
3. **Move.** Stretch, stamp your feet, shake out your hands.
4. **Talk.** Light conversation and laughter bring people back.
5. **Wait before driving** if you feel spacey. Sit a while, eat, and ground until you are fully clear.

Over the next day or two:

1. **Rest.** Sleep well, if you can.
2. **Be gentle with yourself.** Don’t plan anything demanding the morning after a big rite, if you can help it.
3. **Write it down.** Journal about the rite: what you felt, saw, learned.
4. **Reach out.** Message a coven friend or your mentor, especially if you feel low.

## Caring for each other

Look after the people beside you in the circle. Notice who is quiet, who is shaky, who leaves quickly. A simple “How are you doing?” matters. Leaders and helpers should make sure everyone is grounded before they go home.

## Aftercare for leaders

Leaders often give so much attention to others that they forget themselves. After leading, you may feel exhausted, elated, or unable to switch off. Ask someone else to lead the grounding or clear up, so you can eat and sit down. Debrief with someone you trust, and allow a quiet day afterwards if you can. It is normal to replay every mistake; write down two things that went well for every one you would change.

## Integrating the experience

Ritual can bring insights, strong feelings, memories, or a sense of contact with something greater. Integration means letting those experiences settle into everyday life, rather than leaving them in the circle.

1. **Write it down** within a day, while it is fresh.
2. **Ask what it means for your life:** a decision to make, a habit to change, a relationship to tend.
3. **Take one small action** that honours it.
4. **Talk it through** with your mentor if it was significant or puzzling.
5. **Don’t force meaning.** Some rites are simply good evenings with friends, and that is enough.

## When to seek more help

> **Safety:** Ritual is not therapy, and magic is never a substitute for medical or psychological care. If after a ritual you or someone else feel very distressed for more than a few days, have intrusive memories or panic, feel disconnected from reality, or have any thoughts of harming yourself, stop ritual practice for a while, tell your mentor or High Priestess, and contact a doctor, therapist or crisis line. If anyone is in immediate danger, call emergency services. Seeking help is wise and strong, and any good coven will support you.

It is always all right to step back from intense practices for a while. The craft will still be there when you are ready.

## Bringing it all together: the capstone

You have now worked through the whole course: the welcome, energy, grounding, raising energy, sacred space and your tradition’s ritual, the altar and tools, your tradition and its devotions, correspondences, the Moon and timing, divination, spellcraft, the holy days, and now ritual craft and coven life.

The capstone brings it together in three parts:

1. **Write a ritual.** Using everything you have learned, write a complete ritual, about thirty to forty-five minutes long, for a real occasion: a full moon, a festival, a blessing, a coven gathering. Use your tradition’s form for opening and closing. Include purification, a clear purpose, welcoming, a heart, sharing, thanks, closing, and aftercare. Plan safety and accessibility. Share it with your mentor for feedback and revise it.
2. **Lead it.** Lead the ritual, for your coven, a small group of members, or, if your coven agrees, with your mentor present online. You lead; they take part.
3. **Reflect.** Afterwards, write a reflection: how the rite went, what you learned, and how you have changed since you began this course.

There is no perfect capstone. Your mentor is not looking for polish; they are looking for care, understanding, safety, and sincerity.

> **Your coven:** Your High Priestess and mentor will decide when you are ready for the capstone, who will attend, and what form it takes. Some covens hold the capstone at a full moon or festival; others in a quiet session with just the mentor. Ask them.

> **Try this:** Before you start writing your capstone ritual, re-read your journal from the beginning of the course. Note three ways your understanding or practice has changed. You will use them in your reflection.

docs.title: Leading a ritual
docs.summary: How to lead a ritual well: preparing yourself and others, using your voice and pace, handling the things that go wrong, and caring for everyone present.
docs.body:
## The leader’s job

Leading a ritual isn’t a performance. It is **holding the space** so that everyone else can go deep. The leader keeps the rite moving, keeps people safe, and helps everyone feel included. You don’t need to be charismatic or word-perfect; you need to be prepared, calm and attentive.

## Before the day

1. **Know the script well.** Read it aloud several times. You don’t have to memorise it (most leaders hold a card or read from notes), but you should know what comes next without hunting for it.
2. **Rehearse the actions.** Walk through any movement, lighting, pouring or handing round. Find where things will go.
3. **Brief everyone with a role.** Make sure each person knows their part, has their words, and knows their cues.
4. **Check the materials.** Use a checklist. Have spares: matches, a lighter, an extra candle, tissues, water.
5. **Check safety.** Fire safety, a clear floor, ventilation, allergies, seating, a first aid kit nearby, and a plan for anyone who becomes unwell or distressed.
6. **Prepare yourself.** On the day, give yourself time to bathe or wash, dress, eat lightly, and ground and centre before people arrive.

## During the rite

### Voice

- **Speak more slowly and more loudly than feels natural.** In ritual, almost everyone speaks too fast.
- **Breathe** before each section.
- **Pause** after important words and let them land.
- **Use cues** so people know what to do: “Now we will each light our candle,” “Please repeat after me.”

### Pace

- **Watch the people, not just the script.** Are they settling, or restless? Engaged, or drifting? Adjust.
- **Leave room for silence,** but not so much that people grow uncomfortable.
- **Keep sections in proportion.** The heart of the rite deserves the most time.

### Presence

- **Ground and centre yourself** at the start, and again whenever you feel flustered.
- **Be warm.** A smile does a great deal.
- **Include everyone.** Make eye contact round the circle, or round the screens.

## When things go wrong

Every ritual has hiccups. Most are invisible to participants if the leader stays calm.

- **You forget your words.** Pause, breathe, look at your notes, or simply say what you mean in plain words. No one minds.
- **A candle won’t light, or goes out.** Relight it, or carry on without it. If it keeps going out in a draught, move it or accept it.
- **Something falls over or catches fire.** Stop the rite. Deal with it calmly and fully: put the fire out, clear up, make sure everyone is safe. Then decide whether to carry on. Safety always comes before finishing a rite.
- **Someone laughs.** Smile and carry on. Laughter is not disrespect.
- **Someone becomes distressed.** Gently check on them, or ask a helper to. Offer to let them step out with someone, sit down, drink water, and ground. Never force anyone to carry on. Afterwards, check in with them privately.
- **Someone feels faint or unwell.** Stop, help them sit or lie down, give water, open a window. If it’s serious, call emergency services.
- **The online connection fails.** Have a plan: who takes over, or everyone carries on alone and rejoins.
- **Someone behaves inappropriately.** Calmly and firmly stop it. If needed, pause the rite and speak to them privately; involve the High Priestess.

## Starting small

Nobody leads a festival rite for the first time without practice. A good path:

1. **Lead a part** of a coven rite: a quarter call, an offering, a reading.
2. **Lead a short solitary rite** at home, aloud, as if others were there.
3. **Lead a short rite for one or two people,** perhaps with your mentor.
4. **Co-lead** a coven rite with an experienced leader, taking half the parts.
5. **Lead a whole rite,** with an experienced member ready to help.

Each step builds confidence. Nerves are normal and often a sign that you care; ground before you begin and they will settle once you start speaking.

## Leading together

Many rites have more than one leader. If you co-lead, agree beforehand who says what, who watches the time, who keeps an eye on participants’ wellbeing, and who handles any problem. Give each other small signals, such as a nod when a section is done. Never contradict a co-leader during the rite; talk afterwards.

## Endings

Close every rite properly, even if it went wrong or ran short. Do the thanks and the closing, so everyone knows the rite is over, then lead the grounding.

## After the rite

1. **Make sure everyone grounds:** food, drink, conversation.
2. **Check in with anyone who seemed affected.**
3. **Clear up together,** and put out every flame.
4. **Debrief.** With your mentor or the coven, talk about what went well and what to change. Invite honest feedback and receive it gracefully.
5. **Write it down:** the script, what actually happened, how it felt, and the feedback.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may ask trainees to lead small parts of rites (a quarter call, an offering) before leading a whole one. Ask your mentor how you will build up to leading.

> **Try this:** Choose a section of a ritual you know (an opening, a blessing, a farewell). Practise reading it aloud, slowly, in your ritual space, five times. Record yourself on your phone if you like, and listen back for pace and volume.

docs.title: Writing a ritual
docs.summary: How to write a ritual step by step, from purpose to script, including accessibility and timing, with a complete sample full-moon rite you can adapt.
docs.body:
## Why write rituals?

Every tradition has rites handed down, and you will learn your coven’s. But almost every coven also writes new rites, for a festival, a life event, a coven anniversary, a member’s need. Writing a ritual is one of the best ways to understand ritual, and by the end of this module you will write and lead one.

## Writing a ritual, step by step

1. **State the purpose** in one sentence. “To give thanks for the harvest and share the year’s gifts.” “To mark Jo’s new job and bless her new start.” Every choice that follows should serve it.
2. **Know your setting.** Who will be there and how many? Indoors or out, in person or online? How long can it be? Check with your mentor what your coven expects.
3. **Choose your form.** Use your tradition’s ritual form as the frame: its way of purifying, opening, welcoming the powers, and closing. You learned it in your tradition’s ritual lessons. Don’t invent new openings for a coven rite unless your coven allows it.
4. **Plan the heart.** This is where most of your creativity goes. What single main action expresses the purpose? Telling a story, sharing gifts, a guided meditation, a blessing, a spell, a song, a procession, a divination, offerings.
5. **Choose the powers.** Which gods, spirits, ancestors or elements are honoured, and why? Make sure they fit the purpose and your tradition.
6. **Plan the sharing.** What food and drink? Offer non-alcoholic and allergy-friendly options.
7. **Assign roles,** if more than one person is involved. Give everyone something to do, if they want it.
8. **Write the script.** Write out every part, with what is said and what is done. Mark who says or does each part. Keep spoken parts short; people listen better to short speeches.
9. **Time it.** Read it aloud and time it. Add time for silences and actions. Cut what isn’t needed.
10. **Check accessibility.** Can everyone take part? Think of people who can’t stand for long, kneel, see in dim light, hear well, read small print, or are sensitive to smoke or scent. Offer alternatives: chairs, larger print, smoke-free cleansing.
11. **Check safety.** Fire, candles, herbs, food allergies, alcohol, weather if outdoors, and emotional safety (rites about grief or trauma need gentle handling and good aftercare).
12. **Get feedback.** Show the script to your mentor before the day.
13. **Prepare the materials list** and send participants what they need to know.

## Writing words for ritual

- **Use plain, strong language.** Ritual words don’t have to be archaic. “We gather tonight under the full moon” is better than awkward “thee” and “thou” you don’t feel.
- **Short lines** are easier to say and to follow.
- **Repetition and call-and-response** let everyone join in: the leader says “Hail and welcome!” and everyone repeats it.
- **Silence is powerful.** Build in pauses.
- **Use your tradition’s traditional words** where they exist (opening phrases, prayers, closings).

## A sample: a simple full-moon rite

This is a short, tradition-neutral rite for three to eight people, about forty minutes, which can be held in person or online. Adapt the opening, welcoming and closing to your tradition’s form.

**Purpose:** to honour the full Moon, give thanks, and send blessing to each person’s intention for the month.

**You will need:** a central candle (or one each, online) in a safe holder; a bowl of water; a small bowl of salt; a plate of biscuits or bread; a jug of juice and cups; a bowl for offerings.

1. **Gathering** (5 minutes). People arrive, settle, and are reminded of the purpose. Phones away.
2. **Purification** (3 minutes). The leader adds three pinches of salt to the water and says: “Salt and water, clear and clean, wash away what lies between.” Each person dips their fingers and touches their forehead (or, online, each does this at home).
3. **Opening** (5 minutes). Open sacred space in your coven’s way.
4. **Statement of purpose.** The leader says: “We meet under the full Moon to give thanks for what this month has brought, and to bless what we hope for.”
5. **Welcoming** (3 minutes). The leader lights the central candle (each person lights their own online) and says: “Moon, bright at the full, lady of tides and of light, we welcome you.” (Adapt to your tradition: a lunar god or goddess, or simply the Moon.) All: “Welcome.”
6. **The heart: thanks** (8 minutes). Going round, each person says one thing they are thankful for this month. After each, all say: “We give thanks.”
7. **The heart: blessing** (8 minutes). Each person in turn says one intention for the coming month, in one sentence. The group raises energy together, with a hum that builds for a slow count of twenty, with hands held out towards that person (or towards the screen), then releases it with a breath out and the words: “So may it be.”
8. **Sharing** (5 minutes). The leader holds up the bread and juice: “The gifts of the earth, shared in thanks.” A portion is put in the offering bowl. Everyone eats and drinks.
9. **Thanks and farewell** (2 minutes). “Moon, bright at the full, thank you for your light. Go if you must, stay if you will. Hail and farewell.” All: “Hail and farewell.”
10. **Closing** (3 minutes). Close sacred space in your coven’s way. The leader says: “The rite is ended.” Candles are put out.
11. **Grounding and aftercare** (as long as needed). Everyone touches the floor, then talks, eats the rest of the food and drinks some water.
12. **Afterwards.** The offerings are put outside on soil or in the garden waste the next day; the salt water is poured down the sink. The leader notes the rite in the coven’s records.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have rules on who may write and lead rites, and on what may change in its traditional forms. Ask your mentor before writing for the coven.

> **Try this:** Choose a purpose for a short ritual you could lead: a full moon, a coming festival, a blessing. Work through steps 1 to 4 and write them in your Grimoire. You will build it into your capstone ritual.

docs.title: What initiation means
docs.summary: What initiation means in an eclectic Wheel coven: a deeper commitment to the coven and its work, not entry into a lineage it does not hold; what changes, what does not, and the honest difference from initiation in traditional Wicca.
docs.body:
## A deeper step

You dedicated yourself to the path, the coven and the land. Initiation is the next step, for those who choose it: a deeper commitment, marked by a rite, after a year and a day of study and service. This lesson explains what it means in an eclectic Wheel coven, what changes, and what doesn't.

## What the word means

"Initiation" comes from the Latin initium, "a beginning". In many religions it means being brought into a community or a body of knowledge through a rite. The ancient Greek mysteries at Eleusis initiated thousands; many cultures initiate young people into adulthood; religious orders initiate members.

In modern witchcraft and paganism, initiation usually means three things at once:

1. **Entry into a group:** you become one of its initiates, with the trust and responsibility that brings.
2. **Transformation:** the rite marks, and many feel causes, a change in you.
3. **Recognition:** the group recognises that you have learned and practised enough to be trusted with more.

## Initiation in an eclectic coven

In your coven, initiation is into **this coven**: its practice, its work, its circle of trust. It recognises that you have kept the full Wheel at least once, studied its roots, served the coven and the land, and are ready to take on more.

It is honest about what it is not:

- **It is not initiation into traditional Wicca.** Traditional initiatory Wicca, such as Gardnerian and Alexandrian Wicca, initiates people into a lineage, a line of initiation going back to its founders, with oathbound rites and teachings that are not shared outside it. An eclectic coven does not hold that lineage and cannot give it. If you want it, you would seek out a traditional coven of that line. The closed and living traditions guide explains more.
- **It is not a degree of superiority.** Initiates are not better people than dedicants or seekers. They have taken on more responsibility.
- **It is not magic power conferred.** Some people experience initiation as a real change in their practice or perception; others don't. What makes an initiate is the year of work behind them and the commitment they take on.
- **It is not a lifelong prison.** Initiation is a serious commitment, often with an oath, but an initiate can still leave the coven, with honesty and care for what they promised.

## Degrees

Some covens have one initiation; others borrow the three degrees of traditional Wicca, or have their own sequence of steps. In an eclectic coven, any degrees are the coven's own: they mean what the coven's agreements say they mean, and they are not recognised by traditional Wiccan lines. That's fine. What matters is that you know what each step asks and offers, before you take it.

## What changes

In most eclectic Wheel covens, an initiate:

- **takes fuller roles** in rites, including leading parts and whole rites;
- **may mentor** newer members, with guidance;
- **is trusted** with more of the coven's own practice and records, such as its Book of Shadows;
- **takes part** in more of the coven's decisions, as its agreements set out;
- **is expected** to keep a steady practice and to keep learning;
- **may go on**, in time and if called, to the elder path.

## What doesn't change

- You are still free to ask questions, to doubt, and to grow.
- You still keep the coven's agreements about consent, confidentiality, money and safety, and so does everyone else.
- You still honour whoever you honour, or no one.
- You are still you.

## The shape of the year

The initiate program is at least a year and a day. In it you will:

1. **Learn deeper craft:** correspondences, the moon and timing, divination, spellcraft, and ritual craft and coven life, in the core modules.
2. **Keep the full Wheel:** every festival, with its lore lesson.
3. **Study:** read and reflect on a set of books and sources.
4. **Build your own wheel:** a seasonal calendar of your own land.
5. **Serve:** the coven and the land.
6. **Write your oath** and prepare for initiation.

## Are you called to this?

Not everyone needs initiation. Many people keep the Wheel as dedicants for years, or all their lives, and that is a full practice. Before you begin, ask yourself:

- **Why do I want this?** For deeper practice, for service, for belonging? Or for status, or because others expect it?
- **Can I give the time?** A year of festivals, study and service.
- **Do I trust this coven** and its leaders enough to make a deeper commitment?
- **Am I willing to take on responsibility** for others' practice and wellbeing, in time?

> **Safety:** No one should be pressured towards initiation, offered it as a reward for personal favours, or charged for it beyond agreed shared costs. No genuine initiation requires sex, nudity, intoxication or anything harmful. If anyone suggests otherwise, speak to someone outside the situation.

> **Your coven:** Covens differ: some have one initiation, others several degrees. Ask your mentor what your coven's path looks like after dedication, and what it means by initiation.

> **Try this:** Write a page on why you want to be initiated, what you hope will change, and what you are afraid of. Keep it to reread at the end of the year.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** initiation into mysteries and communities in many cultures, the idea of a new beginning.
- **Modern:** initiation in pagan covens (from the 1950s), and eclectic covens' honest distinction between initiation into a coven and into a lineage.

docs.title: A year of study and service
docs.summary: What the year and a day asks: keeping the full Wheel and the moons, a reading list of honest sources, building your own land’s calendar, keeping your book, and serving the coven and the land.
docs.body:
## A year of practice

The heart of the initiate's year is simple: keep the Wheel faithfully for a full turn, learn deeply, and serve. This lesson describes each part and gives you a reading list to start from. Your High Priestess or High Priest may adapt all of it.

## Keeping the full Wheel

You will keep all eight festivals in the year, using the lore module's lessons. For each:

- read the lesson and the festival's page ahead of time;
- watch your land in the weeks before;
- keep the festival, with the coven or at home;
- write it up in the app.

You will also keep the moons, if your coven does: at least one phase each month, usually the full moon.

## Study

Read and reflect on a set of sources through the year. Aim for one substantial book or set of sources each quarter, with notes. Start from this list and agree a plan with your mentor.

### On the Wheel's history

- **Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996):** the ritual year in Britain, festival by festival, with the evidence. The single best book for this path.
- **Ronald Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999, new edition 2019):** the history of modern pagan witchcraft, including Gardner, Nichols and the making of the Wheel.
- **Máire MacNeill, The Festival of Lughnasa (1962):** the classic study of a Gaelic festival in folk custom.
- **Bede, The Reckoning of Time, chapter 15:** the short passage on the English months, Modraniht and Eostre. Read it yourself; it is a page long.

### On folk custom and the land

- **Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica (from 1900):** prayers, charms and customs collected in the Scottish Highlands and islands, including Brigid's Day and the seasons. Read with an awareness that Carmichael sometimes polished what he collected.
- **A field guide to your local trees, plants and birds.**
- **A local history** of the land you live on, including its first peoples if you live in a colonised land.

### On practice

- **A good book on modern paganism of a tradition other than yours,** for perspective: for example on Druidry, Heathenry or Hellenic polytheism.
- **Your coven's own Book of Shadows,** as you are given access.

### How to read

For each, write notes: what it teaches, what surprised you, what it changes about how you keep the Wheel, and what questions it raises. Share them with your mentor.

> **Note:** Be wary of books that make big claims about "ancient Celtic" or "ancient pagan" practice without evidence. A good test: does the author say how they know? Hutton, MacNeill and Bede do. Many popular books don't.

## Building your own wheel

Over the year, build a written calendar of your own land: for each of the eight festivals, and for the weeks between, what your land is doing. Include:

- the light: sunrise and sunset times, how they change;
- the weather;
- plants: first flowers, fruit, leaf fall;
- birds and animals: arrivals, departures, nesting;
- local human customs and festivals.

By the end, you will have your land's own Wheel. Many initiates find it the most valuable thing they make in this year. Share it with the coven if you like; it may become part of the coven's own Book.

## Keeping your book

Keep a book of your practice through the year, in the app's Grimoire or on paper: your rites, words, festivals, workings, readings, reading notes and your land's calendar. Near the end of the year, write one page for the coven's shared Book on something you have learned, and send it to your High Priestess or High Priest.

## Service

Service is part of the initiate's year because an initiate takes on responsibility for others.

### In the coven

Help at coven rites through the year: setting up, carrying things, cooking, welcoming newcomers, keeping the fire, clearing away. Take small leading roles as you're ready.

### Beyond the coven

Do something for the land or people beyond the coven: a regular conservation day, tree planting, litter picking, food bank volunteering at harvest, visiting the lonely at midwinter. Many initiates dedicate this to the land or a power they honour.

## A sample year

Here is how one initiate's year might be spread out, beginning at Samhain:

- **Samhain to Imbolc:** keep Samhain and Yule; read Hutton's The Stations of the Sun; start your land's calendar; help set up at two coven rites.
- **Imbolc to Beltane:** keep Imbolc and the spring equinox; read Bede's passage and MacNeill; join a conservation group; take a small leading role in a rite.
- **Beltane to Lughnasadh:** keep Beltane and Midsummer; half-year review; read a book on another tradition; draft your oath.
- **Lughnasadh to Samhain:** keep Lughnasadh and the autumn equinox; finish your land's calendar; write your page for the coven's Book; prepare for initiation.

## Pacing the year

A year is long. Some advice:

- **Plan with your mentor** at the start.
- **Review at six months.**
- **Don't do everything at once.** Spread the reading and service out.
- **Life happens.** If illness, bereavement or a crisis interrupts, pause and talk to your mentor. The year can be extended.

> **Your coven:** Your High Priestess or High Priest may set different reading, service or requirements. Ask your mentor at the start of the year.

> **Safety:** Don't let study and service crowd out rest, family or health. A year of initiation is meant to deepen your life, not exhaust it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** apprenticeship, keeping the year's festivals, service to the community.
- **Modern:** this reading list, the year and a day as a period of study, and the land's calendar as an initiate's work.

docs.title: The oath
docs.summary: What an oath is, what an eclectic Wheel coven’s initiation oath usually promises and never may, how to write yours step by step, and the limits of any oath: no promise binds you to harm, to silence about abuse, or to stay.
docs.body:
## Why an oath

At initiation, most covens ask the initiate to swear an oath: a solemn promise, spoken before witnesses and the powers they honour. An oath gives weight to the commitment. It also protects the coven: initiates are trusted with more of each other's lives and the coven's practice, and an oath marks that trust.

This lesson explains what an oath is, what it may and may not contain, and how to write yours.

## What an oath is

An oath is a promise made more solemn by calling witnesses: people, and often the powers you honour. Oaths are very old. Greek, Roman, Norse and Irish sources all treat oaths as sacred, and breaking them as a serious wrong. In many traditions the witnesses called upon were expected to punish oathbreakers.

Today, an oath in a pagan coven is a serious personal commitment. Whatever you believe about the powers you call to witness, you are giving your word before people who trust you.

## What a Wheel coven's oath usually promises

Most eclectic Wheel covens' initiation oaths include some of these:

1. **To keep the path:** the festivals, your practice, learning.
2. **To keep confidences:** not to share members' names, personal stories, or what they say in confidence, without their permission.
3. **To keep the coven's own material** as the coven asks: some covens ask initiates not to share their own rites or Book outside the coven without permission.
4. **To care for the land.**
5. **To use magic ethically:** consent, no harm, honesty.
6. **To support the coven and its members,** and to take on responsibility as you're able.
7. **To part well,** if you ever leave: honestly, and keeping your confidences.

## What an oath may never contain

No genuine oath can bind you to:

- **obey a person** in everything;
- **keep silent about abuse, harm or crime,** including sexual abuse, abuse of children, or violence;
- **harm yourself or anyone else;**
- **give money** beyond agreed shared costs;
- **anything sexual;**
- **never leave.**

If you are ever told an oath covers any of these, it is not a valid oath, and you are free to speak and to leave. Confidentiality protects members' privacy. It never protects wrongdoing.

> **Safety:** If you have concerns about abuse in any group, you may always report them to the police, a safeguarding body or someone you trust, whatever you have sworn. No coven's oath overrides the law or your safety.

## Writing your oath

Your High Priestess or High Priest will usually share the coven's core oath, and invite you to add your own words. Here is a way to write yours.

### Step by step

1. **Witnesses.** Name whom you call to witness: "Before the spirits of this land, my ancestors, [any god you honour], and my coven, I swear..."
2. **Who you are.** "I, [name], ..."
3. **Your promises.** Three to six specific promises, taken from the list above and your coven's core oath. Each should be something you can keep for years, on bad days as well as good.
4. **Your own promise.** One promise that is yours alone: something your year has taught you that you want to commit to.
5. **The bond.** Many oaths end with what the swearer accepts if they break it: in old oaths, the anger of the gods. Many modern pagans prefer something like "if I break this oath, may I have the courage to make it right."
6. **Closing.** "So I swear." Or "This is my oath."

### Testing it

- **For each promise,** ask: can I keep this in ten years? If my life changes? If I leave this coven?
- **Read it aloud** at your altar.
- **Wait a week,** and read it again.
- **Talk it through** with your High Priestess or High Priest.

## An example

This is one person's oath, to show the shape. Yours will be different, and your coven's core oath may come first.

"Before the spirits of this land, my ancestors of blood and heart, the gods I honour, and my coven, I, Sam, swear: I will keep the turning year, its festivals and its moons, as long as I am able. I will keep the confidences of my coven-mates, and share nothing of their lives without their leave. I will keep this coven's own rites within the coven unless I am given leave to share them. I will work magic only with consent, and never to harm. I will care for the land where I live. And I will remember that I am always learning. If I break this oath, may I have the courage to say so and make it right. So I swear."

Notice what it leaves out: no promise to obey a person, to stay forever, or to keep silent about harm.

## Keeping an oath

An oath is kept day by day. Reread yours at each festival. If you find a promise has become impossible, talk to the coven's leaders honestly. It is far better to renegotiate a promise openly than to break it quietly.

## If you leave

If you leave the coven later, you still keep the promises that concern other people: confidences, and the coven's own material if you promised to. You are released from promises about taking part in the coven. A healthy coven will help you part well.

> **Your coven:** Ask to read your coven's core oath, if it has one, well before your initiation, and ask any questions about it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** sacred oaths sworn before gods and witnesses, and the seriousness of oathbreaking.
- **Modern:** the initiation oath in pagan covens, and the explicit limits that no oath may protect harm.

docs.title: Preparing for initiation
docs.summary: How to prepare in the weeks and days before initiation, what to know about the rite (its meaning and your safety, not its secrets), and how to care for yourself in the weeks after.
docs.body:
## The end of the year

At the end of your year and a day, you and the coven's leaders decide together whether you are ready to be initiated. If you are, this lesson helps you prepare, explains what you can and should know about the rite, and how to care for yourself afterwards.

## Deciding you are ready

Readiness is decided together, usually in a conversation with your mentor and your High Priestess or High Priest. You'll look back at:

- the festivals you kept, and your write-ups;
- your study and notes;
- your land's calendar;
- your service;
- your book;
- the page you wrote at the start, about why you wanted to be initiated.

Either side may say "not yet". That is not failure. Many initiates take longer than a year and a day.

## What you should know about the rite

Some covens keep parts of their initiation rite private, so that the experience is fresh for the initiate. That is a reasonable custom. But you always have a right to know:

- **the date, place and how long it will take;**
- **who will be there;**
- **what you need to wear and bring;**
- **whether there will be any blindfolding, binding, nudity, physical contact, fasting or substances,** and that you can refuse any of them;
- **that you can stop at any point;**
- **the oath you will swear,** in full, beforehand;
- **what happens afterwards.**

A healthy coven will tell you all of this without hesitation. If a coven refuses to tell you whether a rite involves nudity, physical contact or substances, do not go ahead.

> **Safety:** Initiation must never involve sex, sexual contact, unwanted touch, intoxication you haven't agreed to, physical harm, humiliation, or anything you haven't been told about. You may stop at any point. If anything like this is suggested, leave, and talk to someone outside the coven.

## The weeks before

1. **Talk to your High Priestess or High Priest** three or four weeks before about the practicalities and any concerns. Tell them about any health needs: medication, mobility, anxiety, allergies, past trauma that might be affected by parts of the rite.
2. **Read your oath** daily in the final week.
3. **Keep your daily practice.**
4. **Clean your home and altar.**
5. **Spend time on your land:** your sit spot, a favourite walk.
6. **Reflect:** reread your book and your notes.
7. **Rest:** sleep, eat well, avoid heavy drinking.
8. **Keep any agreed preparations** that are safe for you, such as a day of quiet. Fasting, if your coven suggests it, is only ever optional, and never if you are pregnant, diabetic, have a history of eating disorders or are advised against it.

## On the day

1. **Wash or bathe** with attention.
2. **Keep your morning practice.**
3. **Eat** something, unless you've agreed a short fast that is safe for you.
4. **Bring** your oath, and anything you were asked to bring.
5. **Arrange to get home safely** afterwards; you may not feel like driving.

## The rite

Initiation rites differ greatly. Many include, in some form: a challenge or questioning at a threshold; purification; a symbolic journey or ordeal (never harmful); the oath; a presentation to the powers honoured; a new name or token; and a welcome by the initiates. Your coven will keep its own form. Give yourself to it, and remember you may pause or stop.

## Aftercare

The weeks after initiation can be intense. Many initiates feel joy, closeness to the coven, and a sense of change. Many also feel tired, emotional, or low after the high. Look after yourself:

1. **Ground:** eat, sleep, walk, do ordinary things.
2. **Keep your daily practice** simple and steady.
3. **Write** what you can about the experience, keeping private what the coven keeps private.
4. **Talk** to your mentor; they will check in with you.
5. **Be gentle:** don't make big life decisions in the week after.
6. **If low mood or unease lasts more than two weeks,** tell your mentor and see a doctor.

## If you decide not to go ahead

Sometimes, close to the day, an initiate realises they aren't ready, or that they don't want to take this step after all. That is allowed, at any point, including on the day itself. Tell your High Priestess or High Priest as soon as you know. You don't have to give a reason, though talking it through may help you both. You remain a dedicant, with everything that means; you can come back to initiation later, or never. A healthy coven will not pressure you, punish you, or treat you differently.

Equally, the coven's leaders may decide, close to the day, that it isn't the right time: perhaps because of something happening in your life or in the coven. If so, they should tell you why, kindly and clearly, and what would help.

## What comes next

As an initiate, you'll take on more: leading rites, mentoring, helping to run the coven. Some initiates go on, in time, to the elder path. There's no hurry. Many spend years simply being initiates, deepening their practice and serving.

> **Your coven:** Ask your High Priestess or High Priest exactly what you need to know before your initiation, and what support the coven offers in the weeks after.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** preparing for a rite of passage with purification and reflection; the community's welcome afterwards.
- **Modern:** the explicit list of what an initiate has a right to know, and aftercare as a named practice.

quizzes.title: Correspondences: test
quizzes.intro: Fifteen questions on what correspondences are, colours, plants, stones, days and hours, and safety. Most are scored at once; the written answers are scored by your mentor. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can read the lessons again and retake it.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a correspondence in magic?
options: A fixed law of nature that makes a spell work
An agreed link between one thing and an idea or purpose, built up through tradition and experience
A letter you send to a deity
A list of ingredients that must all be used exactly
questions.explanation: A correspondence is an agreed link, such as rosemary with remembrance, built up through folk custom, learned tradition, modern books and personal experience. It is a shared language, not a law of nature, and you can substitute when you need to.

questions.prompt: Most of the specific crystal meanings in modern books are ancient and recorded in Roman sources.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Stones have been worn as amulets for thousands of years, but most specific modern crystal meanings, especially healing claims, come from New Age books of the 1980s onward. Knowing what is old and what is new helps you weigh a source honestly.

questions.prompt: You want to do a working for calm but have no blue, white or purple candle. What is the best choice?
options: Wait until you can buy the right colour
Use any candle you have and tie a ribbon or set it on a cloth of a calm colour, or simply use a plain white tea light if you have one
Use a red candle, because colour doesn’t matter at all
Skip the candle and burn a cinnamon stick instead
questions.explanation: Correspondences are meant to help, not block you. White is the universal substitute, and a ribbon, cloth or coloured ink can carry the colour instead. There is no need to wait or buy anything.

questions.prompt: Which of these stones should never be put in water?
options: Clear quartz
Rose quartz
Selenite
Amethyst
questions.explanation: Selenite is a soft form of gypsum and dissolves, flakes and pits in water. Hematite and pyrite can rust, so don’t soak them either. Clear quartz, rose quartz and amethyst are safe to rinse.

questions.prompt: Which of these stones fade if left in strong sunlight? Choose all that apply.
options: Amethyst
Rose quartz
Hematite
Citrine
questions.explanation: Amethyst, rose quartz and citrine can fade in strong sun. Hematite doesn’t fade, though it shouldn’t be soaked. Remember too that clear quartz can focus sunlight like a lens and start a fire.

questions.prompt: Why does the course recommend garden sage rather than white sage?
options: Garden sage is stronger
White sage is sacred to particular Native American nations and is being over-harvested in the wild
White sage is poisonous
Garden sage is the only sage mentioned in old books
questions.explanation: White sage grows wild only in a small region and is sacred to the nations there; wild stands are being poached for the smudge-kit trade. Garden sage, rosemary, bay or juniper make good cleansing smoke, and we call it smoke cleansing rather than smudging.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much essential oil to a teaspoon (5 ml) of carrier oil gives a gentle dilution for anointing?
options: About one drop
About ten drops
Half and half
None: essential oils go straight on the skin
questions.explanation: One drop to a teaspoon of carrier is roughly a 1 per cent dilution, plenty for anointing. Never use essential oils undiluted on skin, patch test first, and never swallow them.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real dangers to pets? Choose all that apply.
options: Peppermint and tea tree oil around cats
Lilies on an altar in a home with cats
Incense smoke in a room with a pet bird
A plain white candle in a holder on a high shelf with the animal out of the room
questions.explanation: Cats can’t break down many essential oils, and lily pollen can cause fatal kidney failure in cats. Birds can be killed by smoke. A candle safely out of reach, with the pet out of the room and the flame attended, is not in itself a danger.

questions.prompt: A herb that is safe to cook with is also safe to take in large amounts as a remedy, as long as it’s for magic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Culinary amounts are not medicinal amounts. Never eat, drink or put on your skin any herb or oil as part of magic unless it is an everyday food in everyday amounts, or a qualified professional has advised you.

questions.prompt: Which planet rules Friday, and what does it traditionally suit?
options: Mars: courage and protection
Venus: love, friendship and harmony
Saturn: boundaries and endings
Mercury: study and words
questions.explanation: Friday is Venus’s day (vendredi in French, Frigg’s day in English), traditionally for love, friendship, beauty and harmony.

questions.prompt: How are planetary hours counted?
options: Every clock hour from midnight, in alphabetical order of planets
Daylight and night are each split into twelve parts; the first hour after sunrise belongs to the day’s planet, and the rest follow in a fixed order
Each planet rules a whole day and there are no hours
They are chosen freely by each practitioner
questions.explanation: Sunrise to sunset and sunset to sunrise are each split into twelve unequal hours. The first after sunrise belongs to the planet of the day, then Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon in order. The app works them out for where you are.

questions.prompt: If you are pregnant, which of these should you avoid? Choose all that apply.
options: Handling mugwort or rue
Essential oils on your skin
Breathing smoke from burning herbs
Looking at a picture of a herb
questions.explanation: Mugwort, rue, tansy, pennyroyal and wormwood are traditionally avoided in pregnancy, as are essential oils on the skin and herb smoke. Pictures, words and safe substitutes can carry any plant’s meaning.

questions.prompt: Two books give different elements for the same herb. What do you do, and why is that all right?
questions.explanation: Lists disagree because they come from different sources and times. Choose one meaning that makes sense to you, write it down, and be consistent; your own tested experience is a valid source too, as long as you say it is yours.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): says that lists differ because they come from different traditions, periods or authors (1); says to choose one meaning (or the one that fits their experience or coven) and use it consistently, writing it down (1); recognises that correspondences are a language, not a law, so either can be used (1).

questions.prompt: Plan a simple working for an intention of your own using correspondences. Name your intention, then choose a colour, one or two plants, a stone (or a substitute), and a day or hour, saying why you chose each. Include every safety point that applies to what you chose.
questions.explanation: A good plan starts from one clear intention, uses a few well-chosen items that all point the same way, explains the choices, and builds safety in from the start rather than adding it at the end.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): one clear intention in a sentence (1); a colour, at least one plant and a stone or reasonable substitute, each matching the intention, with a reason (1); a day or planetary hour with a fitting planet (1); correct safety points for every item chosen, such as candle safety, not ingesting herbs, smoke ventilation, pets, stone water or sun cautions (1); keeps it simple and affordable, or explains substitutions (1).

quizzes.title: The Moon and magical timing: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the phases, working with them, signs, void-of-course and eclipses, the seasons, and when timing matters. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can retake it.

questions.prompt: Why does the Moon have phases?
options: The Earth’s shadow covers part of it each night
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it travels around the Earth
The Moon’s own light grows and fades
Clouds of dust pass in front of it
questions.explanation: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits the Earth we see more or less of that lit half. The Earth’s shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: About how long is one full cycle of phases, from new moon to new moon?
options: 7 days
14 days
About 29 and a half days
365 days
questions.explanation: A lunation takes about 29 and a half days. The word month comes from moon.

questions.prompt: You live in the northern hemisphere and see a crescent Moon lit on the right, low in the west just after sunset. Which phase is it?
options: Waning Crescent
Waxing Crescent
Last Quarter
Full Moon
questions.explanation: In the northern hemisphere a waxing Moon is lit on the right (a D shape), and the young crescent is seen in the west after sunset. In the southern hemisphere it would be lit on the left.

questions.prompt: A full moon happens at the same moment all over the world, even though local clock times differ.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Phases are moments in the Moon’s orbit, so they happen at the same instant for everyone. Only the clock time differs, which is why a coven can share a full moon online across countries.

questions.prompt: Which phase is traditionally best for release, breaking habits and clearing out?
options: Waxing Crescent
First Quarter
Last Quarter
Waxing Gibbous
questions.explanation: The waning half of the cycle, and the Last Quarter especially, is for release, breaking habits and clearing out. The waxing phases are for beginnings, action and building.

questions.prompt: The Moon is waning, and you want more confidence. What is the best approach?
options: Give up until the Moon is waxing
Word the working as release, for example “my self-doubt shrinks with the Moon”
Do a working to shrink your confidence
Only work at the full moon
questions.explanation: Most intentions can be turned to fit the phase: what should grow, and what should shrink? In a waning Moon, release what stands in the way of what you want.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to make and use moon water? Choose all that apply.
options: Use a clean jar with a lid on it overnight
Use it to wipe the altar or water plants
Drink water left uncovered outside for several days
Put stones in it and drink it
questions.explanation: Keep moon water in a clean, covered jar and use it for cleansing, anointing and watering plants. Uncovered water outdoors can carry bacteria and pollutants, and stones can contain toxic minerals, so never drink those.
