3. **Ask the person.** Being head is a heavy commitment. Ask whether they want it, and give them time to say no without loss of face.
4. **Train them in the open.** Let the coven see the successor taking on more: leading major rites, chairing meetings, sitting in on difficult conversations. This module and the one before it are part of that training.
5. **Share leadership first.** In the app, give the successor a position that carries "Leads the coven", so they can edit pages, positions and details and act on members below them, while you remain the head. A season or a year of shared leadership shows both of you, and the coven, whether it works.
6. **Name a deputy for emergencies.** Even before a successor is ready, name in the rules who steps in if the head is suddenly unable to lead.

## Sharing leadership in the app

The app has one **head** for each coven: the founder, or the person to whom it was handed on. The head always has every power. Others share leadership through their **position**: any position that carries "Leads the coven" lets its holders edit the coven's pages, positions and details, give positions up to their own level, and act on members below them.

A few things stay with the head alone: handing on leadership, archiving the coven, choosing who sees ritual participation and who keeps the members' record, and choosing the position people reach by finishing a program. If two of you lead together, decide in your rules which of you is the head in the app, and what each of you decides.

## Handing over, step by step

When the time comes:

1. **Agree the timing with your successor and elders.** A festival or the turn of the year can be a fitting moment.
2. **Tell the coven before the change, not after.** Explain why, what will change and what will stay the same. Give people the chance to speak with you and with the successor.
3. **Prepare a handover file.** Put it in the coven's Book (members only, or opened only to the successor): the vision, a "who can do what" list, current trainees and their mentors, open concerns (without needless private detail), the calendar for the coming year, and anything only you know how to do.
4. **Hold a rite or a meeting to mark it.** Many covens hold a simple rite of passing: the old head blesses the new, the coven affirms them, the old head steps back to the circle.
5. **Make the change in the app.** Open the coven, tap **Members**, and tap your successor. Under the options, tap **Hand on leadership**. The app asks, "Make (their name) the coven's leader?" and explains that they become its founder, with every power over the coven, and that you stay a member in your current position. Tap **Hand on**. Only the head (or a site moderator) can do this, and the new leader must be an active member.
6. **Sort out your own position.** You keep the position you held before. If that position carries "Leads the coven", you still have those powers. Agree with the new head what position you should now hold, and let them change it. Many outgoing heads take an "Elder" or honorary position with no managing powers, so the new head truly leads.
7. **Check the coven's settings together.** The new head should look through Manage: Who runs training, Ritual participation, the members' record's keepers, Gathering notifications. Some of these were chosen by you for your way of leading.

> **Safety:** Handing on leadership in the app can't be undone by you afterwards; only the new head could hand it back. Make sure it is the right person and the right time, and that you have talked it through, before you tap the button.

## After the handover

The hardest part comes afterwards. A former head who stays in the coven must truly step back:

- Don't countermand the new head, in public or in private.
- When members come to you with complaints about the new head, send them to the new head, or to the coven's complaints process.
- Offer advice when asked, and mostly only then.
- Consider stepping away from the coven entirely for a season, so the new head can find their feet.

If you are the successor, honour what came before, change things slowly, and say thank you often.

## When succession is sudden

If a head dies or becomes unable to lead without having handed on, no member can take over the coven's head role in the app by themselves. Those who hold "Leads the coven" through their position can keep most things running. Contact the Salt & Sovereignty moderators through the app; site moderators can hand on a coven. Have this possibility written into your rules so that the coven knows who should step forward.

> **Try this:** Write a short succession section for your coven's rules: who steps in if the head can't lead, how a successor is chosen, and how the handover happens in the app. Discuss it with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** In some lineaged traditions, only someone of a particular degree may lead a coven, and the line of succession matters greatly. In others, the coven chooses its leader. Ask your head what your tradition requires of a successor.

docs.title: Hiving off a daughter coven
docs.summary: What hiving is, good and less good reasons, planning it step by step, and founding the daughter coven in the app.
docs.body:
## What hiving off is

**Hiving off** is when part of a coven leaves, with blessing, to form a new coven of its own: a **daughter coven**. The word is borrowed from bees, which swarm out of a full hive with a new queen. In modern Wicca, especially British Traditional lines from the mid-twentieth century onwards, it describes a High Priestess (usually of a senior degree) leaving her teacher's coven to found her own, while staying connected to it. Other traditions use other words, but the pattern is common.

Hiving off is a sign of health, not of failure. A coven that trains good leaders will, in time, have more leaders than one circle needs.

## Good reasons, and less good ones

Good reasons to hive off:

- The coven has grown too big for a close circle (many find that ten to thirteen active members is a natural limit).
- An elder is ready to lead and has a calling the current coven can't hold.
- Members live far apart, and a second circle closer to some of them makes sense.
- A distinct focus has grown up (a devotional circle, a study group) that deserves its own space.

Less good reasons, which call for care:

- Conflict with the head. Sometimes parting is the right answer, but call it what it is, and part honestly rather than dressing a split as a hiving.
- Wanting status. Leading a coven is service, and it is hard.

## Planning a hiving, step by step

1. **Talk with the head first, privately.** If you are the elder who wants to hive, ask your head's view before you tell anyone else. If you are the head, raise it with the elder you see as ready.
2. **Agree the relationship.** Will the daughter coven keep the same tradition, rites and Book? Will its trainees be able to come to the mother coven's festivals? Will the heads meet? Write it down.
3. **Agree who goes, and let people choose freely.** No one should feel pressured to go or to stay. Members can belong to more than one coven in the app, so some may stay in both for a while.
4. **Agree what is carried.** Which rites, teachings and Book pages may go with the new coven? Oath-bound material may need the head's specific blessing.
5. **Set a date and a rite.** Many covens hold a rite of hiving: a blessing, the gift of a candle or flame lit from the mother coven's altar, and a farewell.
6. **Found the new coven** (below).
7. **Keep in touch.** A shared festival each year, a call between heads each season.

## Founding the daughter coven in the app

1. Open the Coven tab, choose **Find a coven**, and tap **Found a coven**. Make your coven profile first if asked.
2. Fill in the **Coven name**, its **Web address** (this can't change later, so choose with care), **One line about the coven**, and **Who you are and how you practise**. In the description, say honestly where the coven comes from ("A daughter of the Thistle & Moon Circle, hived in 2026").
3. Add its **Tradition or path**, **When you gather** and **Tags** if you like.
4. Choose **How witches join** and whether it is **Listed** in the directory. Many new covens start unlisted and by invitation, while they settle.
5. Write **Your title as leader**.
6. Agree to lead it by the community guidelines, and tap **Found the coven**.

The app sets up starting positions (Seeker, Dedicant, Initiate, Elder and your own title), empty creed, rules and requirements pages, and a starter member agreement. Then:

1. Under **Manage**, write the creed, rules, requirements and agreement. You may adapt the mother coven's, with permission.
2. Set the **Practice calendar**.
3. Set up **Positions** and their powers.
4. Invite the members who are coming, with an invitation in the app or a single-use link from **Invite**.
5. Begin the programs your new coven will use under **Initiation & training**, **Design and assign**, and assign mentors.
6. Carry over Book material by writing it into the new coven's Book, or by suggesting pages from your own grimoire to it, only where the mother coven has agreed.

The app has no built-in link between a mother and daughter coven. Record the relationship yourself: in the description, in the creed or an "Our lineage" page, and in both covens' Books.

> **Note:** If you were the mother coven's head and are leaving to found the daughter, hand on leadership of the mother coven first (see the lesson on succession). The head can't leave a coven they lead.

## Hiving when it's hard

Sometimes a hiving comes out of disagreement. It can still be done well:

- Agree a short, kind account that both covens give ("We've grown in different directions, and the circle is dividing with blessing").
- Don't recruit. Let people choose.
- Don't take material that wasn't agreed.
- Don't speak ill of the other coven, in person, online or in the coven's chat.
- After some time, reach out. Many hard partings soften into friendship.

## After the hiving

The first year of a daughter coven is fragile. If you lead it:

- Keep it small and simple at first.
- Lean on your mother coven's head for advice.
- Begin training leaders at once.
- Review your rules after six months.

> **Try this:** Imagine your coven needs to hive in two years. Write down who might lead the daughter, what would be carried and what would not, how members would choose, and the rite you'd hold. Discuss it with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** Some lineaged traditions honour a High Priestess whose covens have hived as a "Witch Queen", and keep formal rules about who may hive and what they carry. Ask your head what your tradition expects.

docs.title: Training the trainers
docs.summary: Growing elders into mentors and teachers: shadowing, assigning mentees, supervision, fair scoring and feedback, and looking after trainers.
docs.body:
## Training the trainers

A coven that only the head can teach is limited to what one person can give. A healthy coven has several **trainers**: elders who mentor, teach, lead rites and sign off work. Training those trainers is one of the head's most important tasks, and one of the longest.

## What a trainer needs

An elder who mentors or teaches needs:

- **Knowledge** of the material they're teaching, and honesty about where it comes from.
- **Skill** in explaining step by step, in listening, and in giving feedback.
- **Judgement** about when someone is ready, when to slow down, and when to refer on.
- **Boundaries**: not becoming a counsellor, a parent or a guru to their mentee.
- **Fairness**: holding every trainee to the same standards, and scoring tests and written answers against the rubric, not their feelings about the person.
- **Support**: someone they can bring difficulties to.

## Step by step: growing a mentor

1. **Choose them.** Look for elders who are patient, reliable and kind, and who have finished the training they'll be helping with.
2. **Let them shadow.** For a few months, they sit in on your mentoring conversations (with the mentee's consent) and read the work you sign off.
3. **Give them one mentee.** Choose someone who is likely to do well. In the app, open **Initiation & training**, **Design and assign**, then **Mentors**, tap the mentee and choose the new mentor.
4. **Give them the powers they need.** A mentor signs off tasks and stages left to mentors without any extra power. If they'll also design programs or see everyone's progress, the head can give that under **Manage**, then **Who runs training**, or through their position.
5. **Meet regularly.** Once a month, talk with each mentor about their mentees: what's going well, what's hard, any concerns. These conversations are a kind of supervision.
6. **Look at their scoring.** Read a few test answers they've scored. Are they fair and consistent with the rubric? Too generous or too harsh?
7. **Widen their role slowly.** A second mentee; teaching a session; leading a rite; then perhaps managing a program.

## Teaching trainers to give feedback

Good feedback is specific, kind and useful. Teach trainers a simple pattern:

1. Say what was done well, specifically. "Your account of grounding was clear, and you named three methods."
2. Say what is missing or wrong, specifically. "You didn't say what to do if someone feels dizzy after raising energy."
3. Say what to do next. "Read the section on grounding the excess again and add two sentences."

Avoid vague praise ("Lovely!"), vague criticism ("Not quite there") and comments about the person rather than the work.

## Keeping standards consistent

When several people teach, standards can drift. Help keep them steady:

- Use the same programs for everyone on a path, so every trainee meets the same lessons and tests.
- Agree as elders what "ready for dedication" and "ready for initiation" mean, and write it into the requirements of each position ("What it asks of someone").
- Once or twice a year, meet as trainers to compare: share anonymous examples of answers and how you'd score them.
- Use the members' record and progress views to notice anyone stuck, and talk about them kindly in the trainers' meeting.

## A trainers' meeting, step by step

Once or twice a year, gather everyone who mentors or teaches. In the app, plan a meeting kept to those who manage programs and the mentors, with a Chair and a Secretary.

1. **Open with a short grounding**, as you would any coven gathering.
2. **Review each program.** Is anyone stuck? Is any lesson or task confusing, out of date or too much? Use the progress views to see where people are.
3. **Score together.** Take two or three written answers (with names removed and the trainees' permission) and score them separately against the rubric. Compare. Where you differ, talk about why, and agree what the rubric means.
4. **Share difficulties.** A mentee who has gone quiet; a mentee who wants more than a mentor can give; a mentor who feels out of their depth. Decide together who will do what, respecting confidentiality.
5. **Agree changes** to programs or requirements, and who will make them.
6. **Thank each other**, and save the minutes to the Book (kept to the trainers if they mention individuals).

## When a mentor and mentee don't fit

Not every pairing works. Signs include check-ins that keep being missed, a mentee who seems afraid to ask questions, or a mentor who is frustrated. This is no one's fault. Talk to each privately, then change the pairing under Design and assign, Mentors, without fuss. Tell the trainee that asking for a change is always allowed.

## Looking after trainers

Mentoring takes energy. Protect your trainers:

- No more than three mentees each.
- A break after every year or two of heavy mentoring.
- A clear path for concerns: a mentor who's worried about a mentee comes to the head, not just keeps worrying.
- Thanks, publicly and often.

> **Safety:** Trainers hold power over trainees' progress, which brings the same risks as any other power: favouritism, pressure and, at worst, exploitation. Make sure every trainee knows they can ask for a different mentor without explaining why, and that they can report anything to the site's moderators.

## Passing on the work of training trainers

In time, the head shouldn't be the only one training trainers. Choose an experienced elder to lead the coven's training, give them the power to manage programs, and let them mentor new mentors. Your role becomes overseeing and supporting, not doing everything.

> **Try this:** List the elders in your coven who mentor or could mentor. For each, note one strength and one area to grow. Pick one person you would bring on as a new mentor, and write the first three steps you would take.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions require a particular degree before someone may teach or initiate. Ask your head what your coven requires of its trainers and mentors.

docs.title: The coven’s long-term health and lineage
docs.summary: Signs of health and trouble, a yearly health check, honest lineage, and keeping the coven’s story.
docs.body:
## The coven's long-term health

Individual rites can go well or badly. A coven's **health** is about the longer run: whether it keeps its purpose, its people and its practice over years. Like a garden, a coven needs regular, patient tending more than dramatic interventions.

## Signs of a healthy coven

- Members come because they want to, and leave without drama when it's time.
- Several people can lead rites, teach and moderate.
- New members are welcomed and trained; some become elders.
- Disagreements are spoken about and resolved.
- The practice is deepening, not just repeating.
- The coven's documents match what it actually does.
- The head is not exhausted.
- People outside the coven, partners and friends included, don't feel threatened by it.

## Signs of trouble

- Attendance slowly falling, with no one asking why.
- The same few people do everything.
- An inner circle and an outer circle, with secrets between them.
- Unresolved conflicts that everyone tiptoes around.
- No one new has joined, or no one has risen, in years.
- The head can't imagine anyone else leading.
- Rites have become routine; no one remembers why they're done that way.

## A yearly health check, step by step

Once a year, perhaps at the turn of your tradition's year, hold an elders' meeting (in the app, plan a meeting kept to the elders) to review the coven's health.

1. **Look at the numbers.** How many members? How many joined and left? How many came to the major rites? The members' record shows attendance and studies; use it as a starting point, not a verdict.
2. **Ask members.** Before the meeting, ask everyone two or three simple questions: What do you value most? What would you change? Do you feel heard?
3. **Review the documents.** Do the creed, rules, requirements and agreement still fit? Update them carefully (remember that changing a signed agreement asks everyone to sign again).
4. **Review the leaders.** Who leads what? Who is overstretched? Who is ready for more?
5. **Review training.** Are trainees moving? Are mentors supported? Are programs up to date?
6. **Choose two or three changes** for the coming year. Not ten. Write them in the minutes and save them to the Book.

## Using the app for the health check

The app can give you a picture, though never the whole one:

- **Members' record** (Members, then Members' record): choose a year under "Over", and look at attendance, when people last took part, and the gentle flags.
- **Initiation & training**: everyone's progress shows who is moving and who has stalled.
- **Paths in the coven**: what share of members practise each way and honour each deity. Has the coven's practice drifted from its stated tradition, or broadened in a way the creed should reflect?
- **Book of Shadows**: the meeting minutes and ritual records of the past year.

Numbers raise questions; they don't answer them. A member who has come to fewer rites may be caring for a parent. Ask before you conclude.

## People come and go

Healthy covens have a steady flow: some join, some rise, some leave. Treat each part well.

- **Welcoming.** Give every newcomer a named person to ask, and a mentor once they begin training.
- **Rising.** Recognise growth fairly and publicly; keep the requirements of each position clear and up to date.
- **Leaving.** When someone leaves, thank them, wish them well and, if they're willing, ask what the coven could do better. A member who leaves well may return, or send a friend.

## Lineage: the coven's story

**Lineage** is the coven's line of descent: where its teaching came from, who taught whom, and which covens it gave rise to. In some traditions, especially British Traditional Wicca, lineage is formal and matters a great deal: initiates can trace their line, teacher by teacher, back to the founders of the modern Craft in the mid-twentieth century. In reconstructionist and eclectic traditions, lineage may be looser: the books, teachers and communities that shaped the coven.

Be honest about lineage. Many groups have claimed descent from ancient, unbroken witch cults; historians have found no good evidence for this, and modern Paganism is largely a twentieth century revival drawing on older sources. A real, honest lineage of eighty years, or of eight, is something to be proud of. An invented one of eight hundred is a weakness waiting to be found out.

## Keeping the coven's story

Even a young coven has a story worth keeping:

1. **Make an "Our lineage" page.** In the coven's Book, record who founded the coven, who taught them, which coven it came from (if any), and the daughters it has hived. Keep dates.
2. **Keep the records.** Save rites and meeting minutes to the Book after gatherings, so the coven's history builds up as it goes.
3. **Record the leaders.** A list of heads and elders, with their years of service.
4. **Tell the story.** At an anniversary or a festival, tell new members where the coven came from.
5. **Respect privacy.** Members may not want their names in the coven's history after they leave. Ask, and use coven names, not legal names.

## Traditions that change

Every living tradition changes. Rites are rewritten, new festivals added, old customs dropped. A good steward changes things slowly, explains why, records what was done before, and is honest about what is new. Change is not betrayal; carelessness about what came before can be.

> **Try this:** Write a draft "Our lineage" page for your coven: where its teaching came from, who has led it, and anything you know of its history. Mark anything you're unsure of, and ask your head about it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your head what your coven's lineage is, how it is recorded, and what may be told to non-members.

docs.title: Closing a coven well
docs.summary: When a coven may need to end, the alternatives, closing well step by step, and archiving the coven in the app.
docs.body:
## When a coven ends

Covens end. The head moves away, members drift, a tradition is outgrown, or the coven simply completes what it was for. An ending isn't a failure. A coven that closes well leaves its members blessed and free; one that collapses leaves hurt that can last for years.

## Signs it may be time

- No one is willing or able to lead, and no successor is in sight.
- Attendance has fallen to a handful for a long time.
- The purpose the coven was formed for has been fulfilled.
- The head is burnt out, and there is no one to share or take over.
- Conflict has made the circle unsafe, and repair has failed.

Before closing, consider the alternatives: a season's rest, a smaller rhythm, handing on to an elder, or merging with another coven. Closing should be a considered choice, not a reaction to a bad month.

## Closing well, step by step

1. **Decide with care.** Talk with your elders. Give yourselves time, a month or more, before deciding.
2. **Tell the coven honestly and early.** Explain why, when, and what will happen. Don't announce a closing in a chat message and disappear. A meeting is better.
3. **Give members somewhere to go.** Suggest other covens they might join, or offer introductions. Encourage members to keep practising on their own.
4. **Finish what you can.** Let trainees complete the stage they're in, or give them a written record of what they've done so another coven can recognise it. Tell people in programs what will happen to their progress.
5. **Return what isn't the coven's.** Tools, books or money held for the coven should be returned or distributed fairly, according to the rules.
6. **Decide what happens to the coven's material.** Its Book, rites and records: some may be shared with members, some passed to another coven, some kept by the head. Oath-bound material should be handled as the tradition requires.
7. **Hold a final rite.** Thank the gods, spirits and ancestors the coven has honoured; release what was bound together; close the coven's circle for the last time. Many covens bless each member individually.
8. **Archive the coven in the app.**
9. **Rest and grieve.** Ending something you loved is a loss.

## Telling the coven

How you tell people matters. A simple pattern:

1. Tell the elders first, privately.
2. Then gather the whole coven, in person or in a meeting in the app, rather than posting it in the chat.
3. Say it plainly: "After a lot of thought, the elders and I have decided that the coven will close at Samhain."
4. Say why, honestly but without blaming anyone.
5. Say what will happen: the final rite, the programs, the Book, the chat.
6. Invite questions, and feelings. Some will be sad, some angry, some relieved.
7. Follow up with a short written summary, and offer each member a conversation.

## A simple final rite

Your tradition may have its own form. If not, a simple shape:

1. Gather and ground together, and open sacred space in your coven's usual way.
2. Give thanks to the powers the coven has honoured, by name, with an offering.
3. Remember: each person names a moment from the coven's life they will carry with them.
4. Release: the head says words that free each member from any bond to the coven, while blessing whatever friendships continue.
5. Bless each member in turn, perhaps with water or oil, or simply by name.
6. Put out the coven's candle together, or let it burn down safely while you share food.
7. Close as you always have, for the last time, and ground well.

## Archiving in the app

Only the coven's head can archive it (and site moderators).

1. Open the coven and tap **Manage**.
2. At the foot, under **Archive the coven**, read the note, then tap **Archive the coven**.
3. The app asks, "Archive this coven?" and explains that it leaves the directory, its chat and altars become read-only, and only the site moderators can reopen it. Tap **Archive** to confirm.

Before you archive:

- Tell everyone, and give them time to save anything of their own from the chat or Book.
- Make sure anything members need from the coven's Book has been shared with them.
- Encourage members to keep a copy of any coven altar they love: an altar's "Keep a copy" saves it among their own altars.

> **Note:** Archiving keeps the coven's material, read-only, rather than deleting it. If the coven might one day reopen, the site's moderators can do that, so write down why it was archived and who led it.

## When a coven ends badly

Sometimes a coven ends in conflict or crisis, or a head simply vanishes. If you are an elder in that situation:

- Look after people first: check in with members individually.
- Don't spread blame; say what is known, simply.
- If someone was harmed, make sure it has been reported to the site's moderators and, where needed, to the authorities.
- If the coven still holds members' material and no one can lead it, contact the Salt & Sovereignty moderators through the app.
- Help members find new homes.

## After the ending

Former members may grieve, feel lost, or feel relieved. All are normal. Some will want to keep in touch, start their own practice, or join other covens. Bless all of these. If you led the coven, consider talking with someone outside it, a friend, another head or a counsellor, about what the coven meant and what you learned.

> **Try this:** Write a short "closing well" section for your coven's rules: who decides to close, how members are told, what happens to trainees' progress, the coven's material and any shared money, and the shape of a final rite.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions have a formal rite for "closing" or "dissolving" a coven; others simply release the circle at a final gathering. Ask your head whether your tradition has one.

docs.title: Working with other covens and the wider community
docs.summary: Relations with other covens, guests, the wider Pagan community and closed traditions, and leading by the Salt & Sovereignty coven community guidelines.
docs.body:
## The coven among covens

No coven practises alone. Around it are other covens, solitary practitioners, teachers and authors, festivals and moots, local Pagan and interfaith groups, and online communities like Salt & Sovereignty. A head represents the coven to all of these. Good relations bring friendship, shared learning, safety and support; bad ones bring rivalry and harm.

## Working with other covens

Other covens may share your tradition or differ from it entirely. Either way, some principles help:

1. **Respect their ways.** Their rites and rules are theirs. Don't criticise them to your members, and don't teach their material as your own.
2. **Don't poach.** If a member of another coven wants to join yours, that's their right; but don't recruit from other covens, and if someone is leaving in conflict, encourage them to part well.
3. **Share what's shareable.** Joint public festivals, open rites, workshops and study days. Many regions hold an open celebration at the major festivals that several covens help lead.
4. **Talk head to head.** A call or coffee once a season with heads of nearby covens builds trust. They can be your outside friend when you need one.
5. **Share concerns about safety, carefully.** If someone has harmed members, other covens may need to know. Share facts, not rumours, and in serious cases report through the proper channels rather than spreading word informally.
6. **Honour visits.** When members of another coven visit a rite, explain your ways, invite them to take part only as they wish, and thank them.

## Guests at your rites

When you welcome guests from outside the coven:

- Tell them, before they arrive, what will happen and what is asked of them.
- Never ask a guest to take an oath, give money or do anything they don't freely choose.
- Keep oath-bound material out of open rites.
- Remember that in the app, gatherings and the chat are for members. An open public rite happens in person or elsewhere; guests don't need to join the coven to come.

## The wider Pagan and spiritual community

Beyond covens, you may connect with:

- **Local moots**: informal meetings, often monthly in a café or pub, where Pagans of every kind meet socially.
- **Festivals and conferences.**
- **Interfaith groups**, where Pagan voices are increasingly welcome.
- **Public education**: talks at libraries or schools (be prepared, and stay within what you know).
- **Living and closed traditions**: some practices belong to particular peoples and are not open to outsiders. The app's Living Library has a guide to closed and living traditions. Respect it, and teach your members to.

When you speak publicly, be honest and humble. You speak for your coven, not for all Pagans, and never for a closed tradition you weren't given.

## The Salt & Sovereignty community

Every coven in the app is part of the Salt & Sovereignty community and agrees to its coven community guidelines. As a head, you lead your coven by them. In summary:

- **Covens are for adults.** Everyone must be 18 or older. If you think someone in a coven is under 18, report them.
- **Joining and invitations.** Each coven chooses how people join. Everyone confirms they are 18 or older and signs the agreements before joining, and may decline any invitation. Only invite people you believe will keep the guidelines, and never pressure anyone to accept.
- **Freedom comes first.** Anyone may leave any coven at any time without explaining why. No one may pressure anyone for money, gifts, secrets, private photographs, sexual contact, an address or obedience. A coven may ask members to help with shared costs, but never as a condition of belonging or of rising. No one may tell a member to cut off family or friends, stop medical or mental-health care, or harm themselves. Initiation and advancement must never involve humiliation, danger, nudity or anything not freely consented to.
- **Respect.** No harassment, bullying, threats or curses aimed at members; no hate or discrimination; no sexual content or advances in covens; respect closed and living traditions; no spam, scams or selling unless the coven's rules allow it.
- **Privacy.** What members share in a coven stays in it; no screenshots or reposting without permission; no sharing anyone's real name, address or details. The site's moderators can read every coven to keep covens safe.
- **Leading a coven.** Founders and those they give powers to are trusted with others' safety: write your documents honestly, apply them fairly, and don't use your position to pressure anyone. Coven rules can add to the guidelines but can't override them.
- **Reporting and blocking.** Every message, member, application and coven has a Report button. Reports go to the site's moderators, never to the coven's leaders, and the person reported isn't told who reported them.
- **Danger.** Covens are not a crisis service. If anyone is in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number. The Sanctuary lists support lines.

You can read the full guidelines from your coven profile in the app, where you agreed to them.

## Being a good neighbour in the app

- **Keep the directory honest.** Make the coven's description, tradition and "When you gather" accurate. If you aren't taking members, set "Not taking members".
- **Be careful with links.** Invite links let people join without applying. Share them privately, set a short life and few uses, and revoke them when done.
- **Cooperate with moderators.** If the site's moderators contact you about your coven, answer honestly and promptly. They exist to keep everyone safe, including you.
- **Model the guidelines.** Your members will treat the wider community as they see you treat it.

> **Try this:** Find out what other covens, moots or Pagan groups exist near you or in your tradition online. Write down two you might contact, and what you would offer or ask. Then re-read the coven community guidelines and note one thing in your coven's rules that should mention them.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions have umbrella bodies, councils or networks of covens, with their own codes of conduct; some prefer independence. Ask your head which your coven belongs to, if any, and what it expects of a head.

docs.title: Priesthood without lineage
docs.summary: What it means to be a High Priestess or High Priest of an eclectic Wheel coven: where the titles come from, authority that rests on trust and agreement rather than lineage, the priest as servant, and staying accountable.
docs.body:
## The title

"High Priestess" and "High Priest" are titles most modern pagans know from Wicca. In Gerald Gardner's covens of the 1950s, the High Priestess led the coven, with a High Priest as her partner; she held authority by her initiation into a lineage, passed from initiator to initiate. Many traditional Wiccan covens still work this way.

An eclectic Wheel coven uses the same titles, or others (some prefer "coven leader", "elder", "steward" or "keeper"), but its leaders' authority rests on something different. This lesson explores what that is, and what it asks of you.

## Where authority comes from

In a lineage tradition, a High Priestess's authority comes partly from her place in the line: she was made a High Priestess by someone who was, back to the founder. An eclectic coven has no such line, or only a short one. So where does its leaders' authority come from?

1. **The coven's agreement.** The coven's founding documents and agreements say who leads, how they are chosen, and what they may decide.
2. **Experience and knowledge.** You have kept the Wheel for years, learned its roots, led its festivals and cared for its people.
3. **Trust.** The members trust you to lead well. Trust is earned and can be lost.
4. **Service.** You do the work: planning, teaching, caring, organising.

This is a strong foundation, but a different one. It means your authority is real but limited: it extends as far as the coven's agreements and the members' trust, and no further.

## Honesty about the title

Be honest, inside and outside the coven, about what your title means:

- **Don't claim a lineage** you don't have. "I'm High Priestess of an eclectic coven" is honest. "I'm a third-degree Gardnerian High Priestess", unless you are, is not.
- **Don't claim to be the priestess of a god** in a sense that implies authority over others' relationship with that god.
- **Don't claim ancient authority.** Your coven may be new or old, but the eclectic Wheel is modern.

## The priest as servant

In many traditions, a priest is a servant: of the gods, of the people, of the rites. That is a good model for an eclectic High Priestess or High Priest. You serve:

- **the coven,** by holding it together, planning its year, caring for its members;
- **the rites,** by making sure they are done well and safely;
- **the land,** by leading the coven's care for it;
- **the powers the coven honours,** by keeping its relationships with them;
- **each member's own path,** which is theirs, not yours.

Leading as a servant does not mean having no authority. It means using your authority for the coven's good, not your own.

## Staying accountable

The great danger of any spiritual leadership is unaccountable power. Eclectic covens are especially vulnerable, because there is no wider institution to check a leader. The core module on leading a coven covered accountability in depth. In the Wheel's terms:

- **Have written agreements** that limit your power and say how members can raise concerns.
- **Share leadership:** a High Priestess and High Priest, a council of elders, or rotating roles.
- **Ask for feedback** regularly, and listen.
- **Have someone outside the coven** you can talk to: a peer in another coven, a mentor of your own.
- **Step back** when you are tired, ill or in crisis.
- **Never use your role** for money beyond agreed costs, for sex, or for personal power.

> **Safety:** The most common harms in pagan groups come from leaders who are not accountable: financial exploitation, sexual misconduct, controlling members' lives. Build safeguards into your coven, and accept them for yourself, from the start.

## Priestess and priest, or neither

Gardner's covens paired a High Priestess with a High Priest, reflecting Wicca's Goddess and God, and gave the High Priestess precedence. Eclectic covens vary: some keep a priestess and a priest, some have one leader of any gender, some share leadership among several people, and many use titles that don't depend on gender at all. Whatever your coven chooses, make sure it doesn't exclude members because of their gender, and that the titles serve the coven rather than the other way round.

## Relationships with other traditions

Your coven will meet traditional Wiccans, Druids, Heathens and others. Respect their structures: a Gardnerian coven's lineage matters to it. Don't call your coven Wiccan if it is not initiated into a Wiccan line and doesn't keep Wicca's practice; many traditional Wiccans find this misleading. Equally, expect them to respect your coven's own integrity.

## What you are not

You are not a guru. You are not the voice of the gods. You are not responsible for members' whole lives. You are a person who has been trusted to lead a group of people in keeping the turning year, and who serves them as well as you can.

> **Your coven:** Your coven's founding documents say what its leaders may decide. Read them again with this lesson in mind, and talk with the current leaders about how authority and accountability work in practice.

> **Try this:** Write a short statement, for your coven and for anyone outside who asks, of what your title means: where your authority comes from, what it covers, what it doesn't, and how members can hold you to account.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** priesthood as service to gods and people; the idea that a priest's authority rests on the community's trust.
- **Modern:** the High Priestess and High Priest titles (from 1950s Wicca), eclectic covens without lineage, and written agreements that limit a leader's power.

docs.title: Leading the whole year
docs.summary: How to plan and lead a coven’s whole turn of the Wheel: the festival calendar and its leaders, moons, teaching and rites of passage, the northern or southern wheel, pacing the year to avoid burnout, and reviewing it at its end.
docs.body:
## The year as a whole

An elder leads a festival. A High Priestess or High Priest leads the year: the whole cycle of festivals, moons, teaching, rites of passage, service and ordinary coven life, so that it holds together and the coven thrives. This lesson is about that larger work.

## Planning the year

Most covens plan the year at or after Samhain, the Wheel's new year, or at Yule. A planning meeting with the coven's elders, or the whole coven, works well.

### What to plan

1. **The eight festivals:** for each, the date this year (the app's calendar shows them), where the coven will gather, who will lead, and whether it is open or coven-only.
2. **Moons:** whether the coven gathers at full moons, new moons, both or neither, and how often.
3. **Teaching:** which members are on which programs; when study evenings fall; who mentors whom.
4. **Rites of passage:** dedications, initiations, elevations, handfastings, namings, memorials. Many fit naturally at particular festivals: dedications at Imbolc, handfastings at Beltane, memorials at Samhain.
5. **Service:** land days, food bank collections, open festivals.
6. **Coven business:** meetings, reviews of agreements, elections or appointments.
7. **Rest:** months with less on.

Put the year's dates in the coven's calendar and the ritual builder as soon as they are fixed, so members can plan.

### Sharing the leading

A coven where the High Priestess leads every festival is fragile: she will tire, and others won't learn. Share the festivals among elders and initiates, with support. Many covens give each festival to a different leader, rotating each year.

## The northern or southern wheel

If your coven is in the southern hemisphere, it will have chosen the turned wheel or the northern dates. Revisit this occasionally. If your coven has members in both hemispheres, online, decide how to handle it: some covens keep the season of the majority, others hold two short rites, others let each member keep the local season at home and gather for the astronomical festivals, which happen at the same moment everywhere.

## Pacing the year

The Wheel's festivals come every six or seven weeks, with moons between. That is a lot. Signs a coven's year is too full:

- members missing gatherings because there are too many;
- the same few people doing all the work;
- leaders exhausted after every festival;
- rites becoming routine.

Ways to lighten it:

- **Not every festival needs a big gathering.** Some can be household festivals, with the coven sharing a short rite online.
- **Not every moon needs a gathering.** Monthly is plenty; some covens meet at only some moons.
- **Build in fallow time:** perhaps between Yule and Imbolc, or in the summer holidays.
- **Share the work** widely.

## Keeping the year alive

A coven that keeps the Wheel for many years risks it becoming routine. Some ways to keep it alive:

- **Return to the land.** Each year's season is different. Let the rites respond to what is actually happening.
- **Keep some customs fixed, vary others.** A coven's repeated customs give continuity; a new touch each year gives freshness.
- **Bring in members' gifts:** a musician's song, a baker's bread, a gardener's flowers.
- **Learn something new each year:** a new source, a festival in depth.
- **Ask members** what they love and what feels stale.

## A sample year's plan

To make it concrete, here is the outline of one coven's year:

- **Samhain:** coven-only rite with the names of the dead; led by the High Priestess. Planning meeting the week after.
- **Yule:** all-night vigil, open to members' families; led by an elder.
- **Imbolc:** dedications; Brigid's crosses; led by the High Priest.
- **Spring equinox:** seed blessing and a land day at the coven's wood; led by an initiate with an elder's support.
- **Beltane:** open festival in a hired hall's garden; led by two elders.
- **Midsummer:** sunrise on the hill, then breakfast; a household festival for anyone who can't climb.
- **Lughnasadh:** bread and games, and a food bank collection; led by an initiate.
- **Autumn equinox:** harvest supper and the year's review; led by the High Priestess.
- **Moons:** full moons monthly, online, except in August and January.
- **Fallow:** no coven business between Yule and Imbolc.

## Leading through hard years

Some years are hard: a member dies, the coven goes through conflict, the world is in crisis, you yourself are ill. The Wheel can hold these. Samhain can hold grief; Yule hope; Imbolc beginning again. Let the year's rites speak to what is happening, gently and without forcing. And let yourself lead less when you need to.

## Reviewing the year

At the end of the year, review it with the coven:

1. **Which festivals worked best,** and why?
2. **Who led,** and who would like to lead next year?
3. **Which members progressed** on their paths?
4. **What service did the coven do?**
5. **What was too much,** and what was missing?
6. **What will we keep, change and try next year?**

Write the review in the coven's Book. Over years these reviews become the coven's history.

> **Safety:** Watch your own and others' tiredness through the year. Burnout among leaders is one of the commonest reasons covens fail. Rest is part of leading.

> **Your coven:** Ask the current leaders how the coven plans its year now, and what they'd like to change.

> **Try this:** Draft a plan for the coming year: the eight festivals with their dates and leaders, moons, teaching, rites of passage, service, business and rest.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the festival year kept by a community, with rites of passage at fitting seasons.
- **Modern:** the eight-fold coven year, rotating festival leaders, the southern wheel, and planning it in an app.

docs.title: Building the coven’s own tradition
docs.summary: How an eclectic coven grows its own tradition over years: writing liturgy and customs, keeping them honestly in the coven’s Book, when a custom becomes tradition, handing it on to new members and daughter covens, and never pretending it is ancient.
docs.body:
## Every coven makes tradition

Every coven that keeps the Wheel for more than a few years develops its own tradition: words it always uses, customs at particular festivals, songs, recipes, a place it returns to, stories about its past. This is how all traditions are made. The Wheel itself is the work of people in the 1950s and 1970s building something meaningful from what they had. Your coven is doing the same. As its leader, you shape and keep that tradition. This lesson is about doing it well.

## Writing liturgy

Liturgy is the set words and order of a rite. Many covens develop their own: an opening used at every rite, a welcome for each festival, a blessing for the bread. Good liturgy:

- **is simple** enough to remember after a few years;
- **is beautiful** enough to be worth repeating: rhythm, imagery, plain strong words;
- **includes everyone** in the circle, as the elder lessons taught;
- **is honest:** it says what the coven means, not what sounds impressive;
- **leaves room** for each festival, each year, each person.

Write it with others. Test it in rites. Revise it. Let it settle over several years before fixing it. Watch for words that newer members stumble over or don't understand, and for lines that everyone has quietly stopped saying; both are signs a passage needs rewriting.

## Customs

Customs are the things the coven does: always lighting the Yule candle from last year's stub, always planting a tree at Imbolc, always reading the names of the dead at Samhain. Many arise by accident: something done once that people loved. Notice them. Keep the ones that carry meaning. Let others go.

## Keeping it in the Book

The coven's Book of Shadows (or whatever your coven calls it) is where its tradition is kept. Record:

- **the coven's rites and liturgy,** with dates of when they were written and by whom;
- **customs for each festival,** with when they began;
- **songs, chants, recipes, crafts;**
- **the coven's place** and what is known of it;
- **the history of the coven:** founding, leaders, members (with consent), daughter covens, important events;
- **year reviews.**

Date everything and say who made it. This is the single best protection against the coven's tradition being mistaken, in twenty years, for something ancient.

## Honesty about invention

The great temptation of any growing tradition is to claim more age than it has. It is very common in modern paganism: customs invented in the 1970s were presented as ancient; teachers claimed family traditions going back centuries; founders hinted at secret sources. Much harm has come from this: confusion, disillusion, and broken trust when the truth comes out.

Your coven's tradition doesn't need to be old to be true. Teach it as what it is: "This is how our coven has kept Imbolc since 2015." Members will value it more for the honesty.

## Liturgy in practice

A short example of liturgy grown over years, an opening one coven uses at every rite:

"We gather at the turning of the year. We come from our homes and our work, carrying what we carry. We set it down for a while. Here is fire; here is water; here is the ground beneath us and the sky above. Here are we. Let the rite begin."

It is plain, includes everyone, names no particular god, and is short enough that every member knows it by heart after a year. That is what good liturgy usually looks like.

## When a custom becomes tradition

A custom becomes tradition when it is handed on: when members who weren't there when it started keep it, teach it and love it. That usually takes several years and at least one change of leaders. You can't force it. You can make it more likely by:

- **keeping customs regularly,** so they become familiar;
- **explaining** their meaning to new members;
- **writing them down;**
- **letting others lead them,** so they don't depend on you.

## Handing it on

Your coven's tradition will pass to new members, and perhaps to daughter covens, which the core stewardship module covers. When it does:

- **Hand on the Book,** or copies of it, with its dates and sources.
- **Hand on the reasons,** not just the forms.
- **Allow change.** A daughter coven in another land will keep its own seasons; a new generation will bring new customs. A living tradition changes.
- **Keep what is private** private, as your coven agreed, while never hiding anything that would protect members from harm.

## Sharing with the wider community

Some covens share some of their tradition: publishing a seasonal rite, sharing a ritual through the Sanctuary's Community Rituals, teaching at open festivals. That can be a real gift. Share only what the coven agrees to share, credit those who made it, and say it is your coven's own.

> **Your coven:** Look through your coven's Book with this lesson in mind. Which customs are dated and credited? Which are not? Ask the current leaders about any whose origins are unclear.

> **Try this:** Choose one custom your coven keeps. Write its entry for the Book: what it is, when and how it began, who started it, what it means, and how it is done.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** traditions growing from repeated customs, handed on through generations.
- **Modern:** recording a coven's tradition in its Book with dates and credits, honesty about recent invention, and sharing rites through an app.

docs.title: The ethics of leading worship and divination
docs.summary: The theology and ethics of leading worship in a pluralist coven: speaking for the circle, not for the gods; divination and discernment in a leading role; handling claims of divine messages; consent in magic; and the limits of your role.
docs.body:
## Leading worship for others

When you lead the coven's rites, you stand between the coven and whatever it honours. That is a position of trust. In an eclectic coven, where members honour different powers or none, it raises particular questions. This lesson works through them.

## Speaking for the circle, not for the gods

When you lead, you speak for the circle: you welcome, thank and offer on behalf of everyone present. You do not speak for the gods.

That distinction matters. A leader who says "the Goddess wants us to..." claims an authority no one can check, and that claim can be used to control. Instead:

- **Speak in your own voice:** "I feel..." "I sense..." "My reading of this season is..."
- **Offer, don't command:** "You might find it helpful to..."
- **Leave each member's relationship** with their powers to them.

## Divination for the coven

Many Wheel covens use divination at festivals: a reading for the coven's year at Samhain or Yule, a reading before a big decision, a reading for a member who asks. As High Priestess or High Priest, you may lead these. Some principles:

1. **Be clear about status.** A reading is a tool for reflection, not a command. Present it as "this is what the cards suggest to me", not "this is what will happen".
2. **Don't decide coven matters by divination alone.** Use it alongside discussion and the coven's agreed ways of deciding.
3. **Read with others** where you can: two or three readers, or the whole coven reflecting together, reduces the risk of one person's hopes or fears dominating.
4. **Never use a reading** to pressure a member: "the cards say you should leave your partner" is not acceptable.
5. **Respect consent:** don't read about a member who hasn't asked.
6. **Keep records** of readings for the coven, and look back at them.

## Handling claims of messages

Members, and leaders, sometimes report messages from gods, spirits or ancestors: in meditation, dreams, divination, or during a rite. In an eclectic coven these must be handled with care.

- **Receive them respectfully.** The experience may be deeply meaningful to the person.
- **Apply discernment,** as the devotion module taught: is it consistent, does it hold up over time, could there be an ordinary explanation, does it lead to good?
- **Never let one person's message bind the coven.** A message to one member is for that member. If it concerns the coven, it goes through the coven's usual ways of deciding.
- **Watch for red flags:** messages that make one person special, that call for isolation, money, secrecy or sex, or that frighten.
- **Care for wellbeing.** Some experiences are signs of distress. Kindly encourage medical help where needed.

Apply the same discipline to your own experiences, especially. Leaders who believe they hear the gods directly, and that their messages bind others, are a common source of harm.

## Consent in magic

Covens work magic for members and others: healing, protection, blessing. As leader:

- **Work only with consent:** no magic on anyone who hasn't asked, including members, family, or people in the news.
- **Be honest about what magic can do:** present it as practice and experience, not guaranteed cause and effect.
- **Never as a substitute** for medical, psychological, legal or financial help.
- **No harmful magic:** most covens forbid curses, bindings of others without consent, and manipulative love magic, and your agreements should be clear.

## Leading when you doubt

High Priestesses and High Priests have doubts too: about the gods, about the coven, about themselves. That's human, and it doesn't disqualify you from leading. Lead honestly: you can lead a rite of welcome and thanks wholeheartedly while uncertain what lies behind it. If doubt grows to the point where you can't lead with integrity, talk to a trusted peer, share the leading, or step back for a time. A leader who admits doubt often helps members with their own.

## Money and worship

Leading worship must never become a source of income beyond agreed shared costs. Don't charge for rites, readings, initiation or teaching within the coven. If the coven runs paid public events, be transparent about money.

## The limits of your role

There are things you cannot be for members, however much they need them:

- **their doctor, therapist or counsellor;**
- **their judge or confessor,** in the sense of granting forgiveness;
- **their only source of spiritual truth;**
- **their friend in every sense,** if that compromises your role.

Know where to refer people: doctors, counsellors, crisis lines, legal advice.

## Closed traditions at the leader's level

As leader, you set the coven's practice. Make sure it stays within what is open. If members bring closed practices, address it. If you are ever tempted to borrow something powerful from a closed tradition, don't. The closed and living traditions guide is your reference.

> **Safety:** Spiritual authority can be abused easily, often without meaning to. The safeguards are humility, shared leadership, written agreements, outside advice, and always speaking for yourself rather than for the gods.

> **Your coven:** Ask the current leaders how the coven uses divination together, how it handles members' reports of messages, and what its agreements say about magic for others.

> **Try this:** Write the guidelines you would give your coven for divination at festivals: who reads, how readings are presented, what they may and may not be used for.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** priests and diviners serving communities; oracles consulted for public decisions, and the ancient awareness that oracles could be misread or manipulated.
- **Modern:** explicit ethics of consent, pluralism and accountability in leading pagan worship.

quizzes.title: Leading a coven
quizzes.intro: Fifteen questions on authority, the coven’s documents, running the coven in the app, delegating, crises and sustainability. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a coven head’s authority?
options: A spiritual rank that, once given by initiation, can never be questioned
Trust the members give for particular jobs, which must leave them genuinely free to disagree or leave
The right to guide members in every area of their lives
Whatever the gods tell the head, which members must accept
questions.explanation: Whatever a tradition says about lineage or calling, a head only leads people who are free to leave. Authority is given for particular jobs (safety, purpose, decisions, recognition, speaking for the coven) and never extends to members’ private lives.

questions.prompt: Which are warning signs of a guru dynamic? Choose all that apply.
options: Disagreement with the head is called a spiritual failing
The head keeps rules for themselves that differ from everyone else’s
The head explains why a decision was made
Members ask the head’s permission for ordinary life decisions
Those who leave are spoken of as traitors
questions.explanation: Calling disagreement a failing, special rules for the leader, members deferring on ordinary life and treating leaving as betrayal are all classic signs. Explaining decisions is the opposite: it is a mark of accountability.

questions.prompt: A report a member makes with the app’s Report button goes to the coven’s head first, so the head can deal with it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators, never to the coven’s leaders, and the person reported isn’t told who reported them. That independence is part of what keeps every coven, and its head, accountable.

questions.prompt: You correct a typo in the coven’s member agreement and save it. What happens?
options: Nothing; only the head sees the change
It becomes a new version, and every member must sign it again before they can speak in the chat or tend the altars
Everyone is removed from the coven until they sign
The agreement becomes members-only
questions.explanation: Changing the title or words of a page members sign creates a new version that everyone must sign again before taking part. Gather changes together, tell the coven first, and don’t save a signed page for trivial edits.

questions.prompt: Why must a page that members sign be readable by everyone?
options: So it shows in search engines
Because seekers sign the agreements before they join
Because the site’s moderators can’t read members-only pages
It doesn’t have to be; that is only a suggestion
questions.explanation: Agreements are signed before joining, so a seeker must be able to read them. The app won’t save an agreement set to “Members only”.

questions.prompt: You want members to be able to ask to become Initiates. Which do you set on the Initiate position? Choose all that apply.
options: Tick “Members can apply to rise to it”
Write what it asks of someone, which applicants will see
Tick “New members begin here”
Give it the power “Leads the coven”
questions.explanation: An open position has “Members can apply to rise to it” ticked, and its requirements (“What it asks of someone”) are shown to members applying under My standing and to reviewers. New members don’t begin there, and it shouldn’t carry the power to lead the coven.

questions.prompt: An elder with the “Reviews applications” power but no other powers wants to raise a member to the Warden position, which carries “Moderates the gathering”. What happens?
options: They can, as long as Warden is below their own position
They can’t: reviewers raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers
They can, but only during a ritual
They can, if the member agrees
questions.explanation: Reviewers can raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers. Only those who lead the coven give positions with powers, which keeps powers in the hands of those trusted with them.

questions.prompt: You want everyone who becomes a Dedicant to go through the coven’s initiate training, now and in future. What is the simplest way?
options: Assign the program to each Dedicant by name, and remember to do it for new ones
Assign the program to the Dedicant position
Tick “Any member may begin it themselves”
Post a message in the chat
questions.explanation: Assigning a program to a position enrols everyone in it now and anyone who takes it later. Self-enrolment lets anyone begin it, which isn’t the same thing.

questions.prompt: The coven has a rule that elders hear about every Deipnon rite, but for this month’s Deipnon you want the whole coven told. Where do you change it?
options: Delete the Deipnon rule in Gathering notifications
In that rite’s own details, choose who hears for this one
Ask every member to turn on Reminders
You can’t; the rule always wins
questions.explanation: A gathering’s own choice, in its planner, comes first; then the closest rule. Changing one rite leaves the coven’s rule in place for next time.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses of the members’ record? Choose all that apply.
options: Noticing that someone has been quiet for months and sending them a kind message
Reading what members wrote in their private conversations
Correcting attendance when someone was at a rite in person
Writing brief, fair leaders’ notes that you’d be comfortable for the person to read one day
Publicly listing the least active members in the chat
questions.explanation: The record is a pastoral tool: flags mean “check in kindly”. Leaders can correct attendance and keep brief notes. The record never shows private conversations or what anyone wrote, and shaming people publicly is never right.

questions.prompt: When you delegate leading the Imbolc rite to an elder, what should you also do?
options: Write every word for them so it is done right
Give them the authority to do it, such as a position that lets them plan rites and put them on the calendar
Check their work every day
Keep the delegation secret from the coven
questions.explanation: Responsibility without authority is a trap. Describe the outcome, give the powers the task needs, agree limits and check-ins, then stand back.

questions.prompt: A member tells you she has been thinking about ending her life. What comes first?
options: Offer a healing ritual at the next full moon
Tell the elders so they can pray for her
Ask directly about her safety now, stay with her, and connect her with a crisis line or emergency services if she is in danger
Suggest she takes a break from the coven
questions.explanation: Safety comes first. Ask plainly, listen, and if she is in danger contact emergency services or a crisis line together. Ritual and the coven’s care can support her alongside professional help, never instead of it.

questions.prompt: A member tells you an elder has been pressuring them for money and private photographs. Describe, in order, what you would do.
questions.explanation: This is a safeguarding concern. Take it seriously, don’t promise secrecy, act on any immediate danger, report through the app (the reason “Pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience”), contact authorities where needed, protect the coven (pausing or removing the elder, and taking away their powers) without public accusation, and keep a factual record.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): takes it seriously and listens without promising secrecy; acts on immediate danger (emergency services) if relevant; reports it through the app’s Report button to the site’s moderators; protects members while it is resolved (e.g. changes the elder’s position to remove powers, pauses or removes them) without a public accusation; keeps a factual, dated record; mentions proper authorities where the law or situation requires. 2: most of these, but misses reporting or protecting members. 1: some sensible steps but confronts the elder publicly or investigates alone. 0: dismisses it or keeps it secret.

questions.prompt: Name three things a head should keep (or share only with a co-leader) rather than delegate, and three things that are good to delegate. Say briefly why for one of each.
questions.explanation: Heads keep final responsibility for safety, decisions to remove or ban (except emergencies), changes to the creed, rules and agreements, recognitions their tradition reserves, and handing on the coven. Routine work, teaching within someone’s competence, leading rites by turns and projects with a clear end are good to delegate.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): three sound “keep” items (e.g. safety and safeguarding, removing or banning, changing documents, initiations reserved to the head, handing on) and three sound “delegate” items (e.g. setting up, chat moderation, mentoring, leading some rites, projects), with a sensible reason for one of each. 2: mostly right but no reasons, or one item misplaced. 1: only one list done well. 0: misunderstands delegation.

questions.prompt: Write a short sustainability plan for yourself as head (or future head): your coven’s rhythm, your message hours, who shares leadership, your own practice, your support outside the coven, and what you would do if you noticed signs of burnout.
questions.explanation: A sustainable head sets a realistic rhythm, has boundaries on time, shares leadership, keeps their own practice, has support outside the coven, and plans in advance how to step back when needed, including professional help if burnout becomes depression.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): a realistic gathering rhythm; clear message hours (and what members do in an emergency); named sharing of leadership (co-leader, rota, positions with powers); a personal practice and rites they attend without leading; support outside the coven; concrete steps on noticing burnout (step back, hand over for a season, see a doctor if it becomes depression). 3–4: most present but general. 1–2: vague or missing several. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: Stewardship: the coven over time
quizzes.intro: Fourteen questions on succession, hiving, training trainers, the coven’s health and lineage, closing a coven and the wider community. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head taps “Hand on leadership” for a member and confirms?
options: The member becomes the coven’s head, with every power, and the former head stays a member in their current position
The former head is removed from the coven
Both become heads with equal powers
The coven is archived and a new one is made
questions.explanation: The new leader becomes the coven’s founder, with every power over it. The former head stays a member in the position they held, which may still carry powers, so agree with the new head what position they should now hold.

questions.prompt: Which belong to a good handover? Choose all that apply.
options: Telling the coven before the change, and why
A handover file in the Book: vision, who can do what, trainees and mentors, the coming calendar
The former head quietly keeping the power to overrule the new head
Checking the coven’s settings together after the change
Handing on by surprise, so there is no fuss
questions.explanation: A good handover is open and prepared: the coven is told first, the successor gets what they need to know, and the settings chosen for the old head’s way of leading are reviewed. The former head steps back rather than keeping a shadow veto.

questions.prompt: You want an elder to share leadership with you for a year before you hand on. How do you do this in the app?
options: Give them your password
Give them a position that carries “Leads the coven”, while you remain the head
Hand on leadership and ask them to hand it back if it doesn’t work
There is no way to share leadership in the app
questions.explanation: Positions carry powers. A position with “Leads the coven” lets its holders edit pages, positions and details and act on members below them, while the few head-only actions stay with you. Never share an account.

questions.prompt: A head who wants to leave the coven they lead to found a daughter coven should hand on leadership first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The head can’t leave a coven they lead. Hand on leadership to a successor first, then step back or leave, and found the daughter coven.

questions.prompt: Which are good practice when hiving off a daughter coven? Choose all that apply.
options: Talking with the head privately before telling anyone else
Letting members choose freely whether to go or stay
Taking oath-bound material without asking, since you were taught it
Agreeing what is carried, and the relationship between the covens
Recording the daughter coven’s origin in its description and Book
questions.explanation: A hiving is done with blessing: the head is told first, members choose freely, what is carried and how the covens relate is agreed, and the lineage is recorded (the app has no built-in link, so you record it yourself). Oath-bound material goes only with the head’s blessing.

questions.prompt: Which is the more honest way to describe your coven’s lineage?
options: “Our line goes back unbroken to the witches of the Stone Age.”
“Our coven was founded in 2019 by a priestess trained in a coven founded in the 1980s, drawing on twentieth-century Wicca.”
“We are the only true coven in our tradition.”
“Our history is secret, so we cannot be questioned.”
questions.explanation: Historians have found no good evidence for unbroken ancient witch cults; modern Paganism is largely a twentieth-century revival. An honest lineage of decades is something to be proud of, and it can be checked.

questions.prompt: A new mentor gives every trainee full marks on written answers because they don’t want to discourage anyone. What should the head do?
options: Nothing; kindness matters most
Remove them as a mentor at once
Look at their scoring together against the rubric, and teach specific, kind, useful feedback
Score all the tests themselves from now on
questions.explanation: Training trainers includes supervision: reading the scores they give, checking them against the rubric, and teaching feedback that says what was done well, what is missing and what to do next. Fairness is a kindness to every trainee.

questions.prompt: How many mentees should one mentor usually have at most?
options: One
About three
About ten
As many as they like
questions.explanation: Mentoring takes real time and energy. Around three mentees each keeps check-ins regular and protects mentors from burnout.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head archives a coven in the app? Choose all that apply.
options: It leaves the directory
Its chat and altars become read-only
Everything in it is deleted for good
Only the site moderators can reopen it
questions.explanation: Archiving takes the coven out of the directory and makes its chat and altars read-only; it doesn’t delete them. Only the site moderators can reopen it, so archive only after a considered decision.

questions.prompt: Before deciding to close a coven, what should a head consider first?
options: Archiving it the same day, to avoid a long goodbye
Alternatives such as a season’s rest, a smaller rhythm, handing on to an elder, or merging with another coven
Keeping the decision secret from the members
Deleting the coven’s Book so no one argues over it
questions.explanation: Closing should be a considered choice. Rest, a smaller rhythm, a successor or a merger may keep what is good alive. If it does close, tell members early, help them find new homes, and hold a final rite.

questions.prompt: Under the Salt & Sovereignty coven community guidelines, which of these are never allowed? Choose all that apply.
options: Making a payment a condition of rising to a higher position
Asking members to help with shared costs, if it is never a condition of belonging or rising
Telling a member to stop seeing their therapist
Initiation involving nudity a member hasn’t freely consented to
A coven rule that overrides the guidelines
questions.explanation: Covens may ask for help with shared costs, but never as a condition of belonging or rising. No one may tell a member to stop medical or mental-health care; initiation must never involve anything not freely consented to; and coven rules can add to the guidelines but can’t override them.

questions.prompt: A member of a nearby coven asks to join yours after a falling-out with their head. What is the best response?
options: Welcome them and ask for every detail of the falling-out
Refuse, since they belong to another coven
Welcome their application on its merits, encourage them to part from the other coven well, and don’t speak ill of it
Tell the other coven’s head everything they said
questions.explanation: Anyone may leave a coven and apply to another. A good neighbour doesn’t poach or gossip, encourages a kind parting, and judges the application on its merits.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would found a daughter coven in the app and set it up in its first month.
questions.explanation: Found it from Find a coven → Found a coven (name, web address that can’t change, description including its origin, joining, directory, your title, agreeing to the guidelines). Then write its documents, set its practice calendar and positions, invite its members, begin programs and mentors, and carry over agreed material.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): founding steps (Found a coven, name and permanent web address, honest description naming the mother coven, joining and directory choice, leader title, agreeing to the guidelines); then Manage (creed, rules, requirements, agreement), practice calendar, positions and powers, inviting members by invitation or short-lived link, programs and mentors, and carrying over only material the mother coven agreed. 2: founding plus some setup. 1: only founding. 0: not attempted.

questions.prompt: Write a succession plan for your coven: who would step in if the head were suddenly unable to lead; how a successor would be chosen and prepared; how the handover would happen, including in the app; and what the former head would do afterwards.
questions.explanation: A good succession plan names an emergency deputy, chooses a successor for character with the elders’ support and the person’s consent, prepares them through shared leadership, tells the coven before the change, uses Hand on leadership from Members, sorts out the former head’s position and settings, and has the former head truly step back.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): names an emergency deputy and what they may do (including contacting the site moderators if the head can’t hand on); chooses for character with elders consulted and the successor asked; prepares through shared leadership (a position with “Leads the coven”); tells the coven first; marks it with a rite or meeting; Members → tap the successor → Hand on leadership; agrees the former head’s new position and reviews head-only settings; former head steps back and redirects complaints. 3–4: most of this. 1–2: general ideas only. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: High priesthood of the Wheel: test
quizzes.intro: Eleven questions on priesthood without lineage, leading the whole year, building the coven’s tradition, and the ethics of leading worship and divination. You need 80% to pass. A fellow leader or your own High Priestess or High Priest scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: In an eclectic Wheel coven, what does a High Priestess’s authority rest on? Choose all that apply.
options: The coven’s agreements
Experience and knowledge
The members’ trust
An unbroken lineage back to Gerald Gardner
questions.explanation: An eclectic coven has no Wiccan lineage. Its leaders’ authority rests on agreement, experience, trust and service, and is limited by them.

questions.prompt: Which is an honest way to describe your role outside the coven?
options: "I’m a third-degree Gardnerian High Priestess" (when you are not)
"I’m High Priestess of an eclectic coven that keeps the Wheel of the Year"
"I lead the oldest pagan tradition in Britain"
"I speak for the Goddess"
questions.explanation: Be honest about the title: no false lineage, no ancient authority, no claim to speak for the gods.

questions.prompt: Which are safeguards on a coven leader’s power? Choose all that apply.
options: Written agreements that limit it
Shared leadership
Someone outside the coven to talk to
Members promising to obey the leader in everything
questions.explanation: Agreements, shared leadership, feedback and outside advice keep power accountable. Promises of total obedience do the opposite.
