Start with the most important point: **you don't need any tools to practise.** Everything in this course so far has been done with your breath, your body, your attention and your hands. Tools are aids. They focus the mind, carry meaning, and connect you with a tradition. They don't contain the power on their own.

Many experienced practitioners own very few tools. Some own none. If someone tells you that you must buy a particular set of tools (especially from them) to practise, be wary (see "Red flags in any group").

That said, tools can be a real joy, and learning what they're for helps you understand rituals you'll see. Here's a guide.

## Common tools in modern witchcraft

These are the tools you'll see in most Wiccan and eclectic books. Each is linked to an element in many traditions; the links vary, so don't worry if a book disagrees.

- **Athame** (pronounced variously, often "a-THAH-may" or "ATH-a-may"). A ritual knife, usually double-edged with a black handle, used to direct energy: casting the circle, cutting a door, consecrating. It's **not** used to cut anything physical. The word appears in Gerald Gardner's writings and probably comes from a variant spelling in one version of the *Key of Solomon*. Often linked with fire or air.
- **Wand.** A rod of wood (or other material) used, like the athame, to direct energy, often in gentler work: invoking, blessing, charging. Often linked with air or fire. Your index finger does the same job.
- **Chalice.** A cup or goblet, holding water, wine or juice for blessing and sharing. Linked with water.
- **Pentacle.** A flat disc of wood, metal, clay or stone, inscribed with a pentagram (a five-pointed star in a circle), used as a base for consecrating objects and offerings. Linked with earth. (A **pentagram** is the star; a **pentacle** is the disc or the star in a circle.)
- **Censer.** An incense burner. Linked with air.
- **Candles.** On almost every altar. Linked with fire.
- **Bowls for water and salt.** Used to purify and consecrate. Linked with water and earth.
- **Besom.** A broom of twigs used to sweep the space before ritual.
- **Cauldron.** A small iron pot, used to burn things safely, hold water for scrying, or as a symbol of transformation and the goddess in some traditions.
- **Bell.** Rung to cleanse, to mark the start and end of a ritual, or to call attention.
- **Cords.** Used in knot magic, to measure a circle, or worn as a sign of degree in some covens.
- **Boline.** A practical knife, often white-handled, used for actually cutting herbs, cords and candles.
- **Book of Shadows or Grimoire.** Your book of practice: arguably the most important tool of all.

## Tools in other traditions

Each tradition has its own tools; your tradition module teaches them properly. A taste:

- **Hellenic:** a basin or bowl for **khernips**; a **phiale** (a shallow libation bowl) for pouring drink offerings; a censer for incense (frankincense was widely used); barley grains; a lamp; images of the gods.
- **Roman:** a **patera** (a libation dish, like the phiale); an incense box; a lamp; the household shrine (lararium) with images of the Lares and the family genius.
- **Heathen:** a **drinking horn** or cup for sumbel and blót; a bowl for offerings; sometimes a sprig of evergreen to sprinkle; a hammer pendant or symbols of the gods.
- **Druid and Celtic revival:** a cup, often a sickle or knife, candles, the sacred fire, offerings of water, silver or song.
- **Slavic:** the hearth or stove, bread and salt, an embroidered cloth (a **rushnyk** in Ukrainian tradition), candles, and the "beautiful corner" found in many Slavic homes, a shelf for holy images where Christian and older folk customs have long mingled.
- **Christian folk practice:** the Bible, candles, holy water, oil, a rosary or prayer beads, images of saints.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may use some of these tools, others, or none. It may ask members to make their own, to wait until a certain stage before acquiring some, or to keep certain tools for group ritual only. Ask your mentor what your coven expects before you buy anything.

## Choosing and finding tools

- **Use what you have.** A wine glass makes a chalice. A wooden spoon or a fallen stick makes a wand. A saucer makes a pentacle or an offering dish. A cereal bowl holds water.
- **Make your own.** Many traditions value hand-made tools above bought ones. A stick you've found, stripped and oiled yourself; a clay dish you've shaped; a cord you've braided.
- **Buy second-hand.** Charity shops, flea markets and car boot sales are full of cups, bowls, candle holders, bells and knives. Cleanse them before use (next lesson).
- **Take your time.** Many practitioners acquire tools one at a time, over years, as they're needed or as the right one turns up.
- **Buy ethically.** Some plants, resins and stones raise real sourcing concerns: wild-harvested white sage and palo santo, some sandalwood, some crystals mined with child labour. The Living Library's sourcing notes give alternatives. Choose garden herbs and well-sourced resins; buy stones from sellers who can tell you where they came from, or use local stones.

## Knives and the law

Ritual knives are knives, and the law treats them so.

- In many countries, carrying a knife in public without a good reason is a crime, and "it's for my religion" may not be accepted as a reason for a ritual knife. In the UK, for instance, carrying any fixed-blade or locking knife in public without good reason is an offence.
- **Check the law where you live.** Keep ritual knives at home, and transport them to group rituals only if it's legal, wrapped and out of reach (in a locked box in the boot of a car, for instance). Many covens use a wand or a finger for outdoor rites for exactly this reason.
- An athame is traditionally blunt, since it isn't for cutting, but a blunt knife can still be illegal to carry and can still hurt someone. Keep knives away from children.

## Tools are relationships, not purchases

Many practitioners say a tool becomes powerful through use: the more you work with it, the more it carries your practice. A plain cup used for every offering for ten years becomes more sacred than an expensive chalice used once. So choose simply, use often, and let your tools grow with you.

> **Try this:** Look around your home for three things that could serve as tools: a cup, a dish, a candle holder, a stick, a bell. Set them on or near your altar. In your journal, write what each will be for.

docs.title: Cleansing and consecrating
docs.summary: How to clear an object of what it carries and dedicate it to sacred use, step by step, with methods that are safe for different materials.
docs.body:
## Two steps: clear, then dedicate

Before using a new (or new-to-you) object on your altar or in ritual, most practitioners do two things:

- **Cleansing** clears the object of whatever it has picked up: from its makers, its previous owners, the shop, its journey. In the energy view, it removes old energy. In the spirit view, it removes pollution or unwanted influences. In the psychological view, it marks a clean start: this object's past is behind it.
- **Consecrating** dedicates it to sacred use: you declare what it's for, and (in many traditions) ask the gods or the elements to bless it. After consecration, it belongs to your practice. Many people then keep consecrated tools for sacred use only.

A third idea you've already met, **charging**, fills an object with energy for a particular purpose (see "Directing, releasing and grounding"). You might cleanse, consecrate and then charge a protective pendant, for instance.

## Methods of cleansing objects

Choose a method that's safe for the material. When in doubt, use smoke, sound or visualisation, which suit everything.

### Water

Rinse or wipe the object in clean water, ideally running water (a tap or a stream), with intention: "I wash away all that came before." Dry thoroughly.

Safe for: glass, glazed ceramic, most metal (dry quickly to prevent rust), hard stones such as quartz.
Not safe for: wood (can warp), paper, fabric you can't wash, many soft or porous stones (selenite, malachite, turquoise, opal and others), anything electronic or with glued parts.

### Salt

Bury the object in a bowl of dry salt, or sprinkle salt over it, for a few hours or overnight. Or wipe it with salt water.

Safe for: glass, glazed ceramic, many hard stones.
Not safe for: most metals (salt corrodes them), wood, and many stones (salt can scratch or damage soft and porous stones). Salt water is worse than dry salt.

### Smoke

Pass the object through the smoke of incense or local herbs three times, or hold it in the smoke for a minute, with your words.

Safe for: almost everything. Ventilate, and see the safety notes on smoke in earlier lessons.

### Sound

Ring a bell, strike a singing bowl or clap over the object several times, imagining the sound shaking it clean.

Safe for: everything. Ideal if you can't use smoke.

### Light: sun and moon

Leave the object in sunlight for a few hours, or in the light of the full moon overnight (on a windowsill is fine).

Safe for: most things.
Not safe for: many coloured stones fade in sunlight (amethyst, rose quartz, citrine and others), and some fabrics, photographs and dyes fade too. Moonlight is gentle on everything.

### Earth

Bury the object in a pot of soil or in the garden for a day to a week, so the earth can absorb what it carries.

Safe for: stones, sturdy objects. Mark where you buried it.
Not safe for: anything that rusts, rots or stains.

### Breath and visualisation

Hold the object, ground and centre, and breathe slowly onto it, imagining your breath and a clear light washing it clean. Safe for everything; needs nothing.

## A cleansing, step by step

1. Ground and centre.
2. Hold the object. Notice what it feels like (use your hand-sensing).
3. Choose a safe method and carry it out, saying something like: "I cleanse this [cup] of all that came before. Let it be clean and new."
4. Hold it again and notice whether it feels different.
5. Wash your hands.

## Consecrating, step by step

This is a simple, general consecration using the four elements, suitable for any tool. Your coven may have its own form, or may consecrate tools together in group ritual.

You'll need: the cleansed object; a candle (fire); incense or a feather (air); a bowl of water (water); a dish of salt or a stone (earth). If you can't use smoke or salt, use a feather for air and a stone for earth.

1. **Purify and make sacred space**, in your coven's form or with the simple circle.
2. **Ground and centre.**
3. **Hold the object** and say what it is and what it will be for: "This is my chalice. I dedicate it to hold offerings for the gods and the waters of blessing."
4. **Earth.** Touch it to the salt or stone (or sprinkle a few grains near it): "By earth, I consecrate you."
5. **Air.** Pass it through the incense smoke, or brush it with the feather: "By air, I consecrate you."
6. **Fire.** Pass it carefully above (not through) the candle flame, keeping it well clear: "By fire, I consecrate you."
7. **Water.** Sprinkle it with a few drops of water: "By water, I consecrate you." (Use only a touch on things water can damage.)
8. **Spirit.** Hold it up, or to your heart, and say: "By spirit, and in the presence of [your gods, the powers you honour, or simply the sacred], I consecrate you to my practice. So it is."
9. **Charge it (optional).** Raise energy and direct it into the object, as you learned in the raising module.
10. **Place it on your altar.** Use it for the first time, if you can, right away: pour a little water into your new chalice as an offering, or ring your new bell.
11. **Close and ground.**

> **Safety:** Don't pass anything flammable through a flame: fabric, paper, feathers, wooden tools with varnish, anything with ribbons. Hold it well above the flame, or just name fire while holding it near the candle. Keep long sleeves and hair back.

> **Your coven:** In some traditions, tools are consecrated in the name of particular gods, or by an elder, or only within a coven rite. Hellenic practitioners might purify an object with khernips and dedicate it with a prayer and libation to the god it will serve; Heathens might hallow it with fire. Ask your mentor before consecrating anything you'll use in group ritual.

## How often?

- **Cleanse** new objects before first use; objects others have handled; after a difficult or intense working; and every so often as part of altar care (monthly, or at the new or full moon, is common).
- **Consecrate** once, when an object first becomes a tool. Some people renew consecrations yearly.
- **Recharge** charged objects when they feel "flat", or monthly.

## Living objects and people's things

Don't cleanse or consecrate other people's belongings without their consent. If you're given a gift for your practice, cleanse it if you wish, but honour the giver. Plants are living things: purify them with sound, light or water (if they're happy to be watered), never with salt.

> **Try this:** Choose one object for your altar, perhaps the cup or dish you found in the last lesson. Cleanse it with a safe method, and then consecrate it with the four elements. Write what you did and what you noticed.

docs.title: Caring for your altar, and the app's altar
docs.summary: How to tend an altar day to day and through the seasons, what to do with offerings, wax and old things, and how to use the app's altar alongside a physical one, or instead of one.
docs.body:
## An altar is tended, not just made

An altar is a living thing in the sense that matters: it changes with your practice. Practitioners talk about **tending** an altar: visiting it, cleaning it, renewing offerings, keeping it alive. An altar that's set up and then ignored gathers dust in more ways than one. One that's tended becomes a place you feel drawn to.

## Daily tending (a few minutes)

Many practitioners visit their altar once a day, often in the morning or evening:

1. Stand or sit before it. Ground and centre for a few breaths.
2. Light a candle (or switch on a battery candle).
3. Say a greeting or a short prayer to your gods, spirits or ancestors, or simply a few words of intention for the day.
4. Renew fresh water, or offer a little incense, a flower or a few drops of drink, if your practice includes daily offerings.
5. Sit quietly for a minute or two.
6. Put out the flame before you leave the room.

Even one minute a day, done regularly, builds a strong habit and relationship. Many people find it the anchor of their whole practice.

## Weekly care

1. Remove old offerings, wilted flowers and spent candles.
2. Dust the altar and its objects, and wipe the surface.
3. Wash the offering dishes and the water bowl.
4. Straighten the cloth, or change it.
5. Notice whether anything no longer belongs: things on an altar should mean something to you now.
6. Cleanse the space lightly, with sound, smoke or a sprinkle of water.

## Offerings: what to do with them

Offerings (food, drink, flowers, incense) are given away; they're not for you to take back. What to do with them afterwards varies by tradition, and your tradition module explains your coven's custom. Common modern practices:

- **Food and drink:** leave on the altar for a set time (an hour, a day, overnight), then put them outside on the earth if they're safe for wildlife, pour drink onto the ground or into the garden, or compost or bin them respectfully if you can't. In some traditions (Hellenic offerings to Hestia, for instance, or shared feasts in many traditions), part of an offering is shared and eaten by the worshippers; in others, offerings to certain beings (such as the dead or chthonic gods) are never eaten.
- **Flowers:** compost them, or return them to the earth when they fade.
- **Incense ash:** scatter it outside or bin it.
- **Candle wax:** let it cool and bin it, or keep it if your practice reuses wax. Don't pour hot wax down drains.

> **Safety:** Don't leave food offerings where they'll attract pests or harm pets and wildlife. Chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic and alcohol are toxic to many animals; salty or bready food isn't good for birds in large amounts. Pour drink offerings onto soil, not into ponds or streams.

## Through the year

Many practitioners change their altar with the seasons and the holy days of their calendar: autumn leaves and apples, winter evergreens and candles, spring flowers and eggs, summer herbs and grain. The details depend on your tradition's calendar, which your tradition module covers. Changing the altar is itself a way of marking the turning of the year.

## When an altar needs changing or putting away

- **Moving house:** cleanse the altar's things, pack them with care, and set the altar up again early in the new home; many people find it helps the new place feel like home.
- **Going away:** cover the altar, remove perishable offerings, put out all flames, and let your gods or ancestors know you'll be back. Some people take a small travel altar.
- **Retiring objects:** when a tool or object is broken or no longer belongs, thank it, cleanse it, and then bury it, burn it safely (if it's something that burns cleanly), give it away, or bin it respectfully.
- **Pauses:** if you step back from practice for a while, it's fine to cover or pack away your altar. It'll be there when you return.

## The app's altar

The app has its own altars, on the **Altar** tab. You can build an altar piece by piece from a cabinet of candles, herbs, crystals, offerings, natural finds, tools and seasonal things; light its candles; tend it over time; and keep it with your account. You can also add your own items with photos, and set photographs of ancestors in frames.

You can use the app's altar in several ways:

- **Alongside a physical altar.** Build a twin of your physical altar in the app: the same candle, the same stones, the same offerings. When you tend your physical altar, tend its twin too, and the app keeps a record. Many people find this helps them keep their practice regular, and it's a way to carry your altar with you when you're away from home.
- **Instead of a physical altar.** If you can't keep a physical altar (because of space, safety, privacy, living situation, health, or travel), the app's altar is a real place of practice. You can light its candles, make offerings, and tend it daily. Practitioners have long used images, words and imagination for sacred space; a digital altar continues that tradition.
- **For workings.** Set out an altar for a particular working or holy day, and keep it until the working is done. Today offers "Set tonight's altar", which suggests a starter altar for the day's planet, moon or holiday.
- **With your coven.** Your coven may keep altars together, tended by members, for petitions and for the coven's rituals. You'll find them on the Altar tab under "Coven", or on your coven's page.

Tending reminders (in Settings, under Notifications and reminders) can remind you to tend your altars, water your altar plants, refresh offerings and look after candles.

> **Note:** A digital candle is perfectly safe to leave "burning". A real one never is. If you use both, make sure the real candle is out before you leave it, whatever the app's candle is doing.

## Recording your altar

Your altar changes over time, and recording it lets you look back. Photograph your physical altar now and then and describe it in your Grimoire; the app also lets you record an altar in your Grimoire. Note what's on it, why, and what's changed since last time.

> **Your coven:** Some covens keep their altars private and ask members not to photograph group altars or share images of sacred objects. Others are happy to. Ask before photographing anything in group ritual, and don't share images of other people or their altars without permission.

> **Try this:** Build a twin of your physical altar in the app (or, if you don't have a physical altar, build one in the app as your altar). Tend both, or the app's one, every day for a week.

docs.title: What Wicca is
docs.summary: Wicca as a religion: its shape (the Goddess and God, the sabbats and esbats, the circle, magic and priesthood), the words you will meet, how Wicca relates to witchcraft and to wider paganism, and how this course’s core skills fit it.
docs.body:
## A religion, not only a craft

Wicca is a modern pagan religion. That word, religion, matters. Many people today call themselves witches and practise magic without any particular gods or worship; that is witchcraft as a craft, and it is a fine thing. Wicca is something more specific: a religion of witchcraft, in which magic is practised within a relationship of worship with a Goddess and a God, in a sacred circle, through a cycle of seasonal and lunar rites.

So a Wiccan is a witch, in Wicca's own understanding, but not every witch is a Wiccan. You will meet witches who are Heathens, Hellenic polytheists, Christians, atheists or simply eclectic. Being clear about this saves a great deal of confusion.

## The shape of the religion

Most forms of Wicca have these features in common.

### The Goddess and the God

Wicca sees the divine as having two great faces, a Goddess and a God, whose relationship is the life of the world. The Goddess is often linked with the moon, the earth, the sea, birth and the mysteries of the body; the God with the sun, the horned beasts and the wild, the grain that is cut and grows again, and the journey through death to rebirth. Behind them, some Wiccans speak of a single source of all, beyond names. A later lesson in this module explores the many ways Wiccans understand them.

### The turning year

Wiccans keep eight festivals, the sabbats: Samhain, Yule, Imbolc, the spring equinox, Beltane, Midsummer, Lammas and the autumn equinox. In Wicca these are not only seasonal markers but the chapters of a sacred story: the God born at midwinter, growing with the light, joining with the Goddess in spring, ripening in summer, giving his life in the harvest and passing into the dark to be reborn. The lore module tells this story festival by festival.

### The moon

Wiccans meet at the full moon, and some at the new or dark moon, for rites called esbats. The esbat is especially the Goddess's rite, and the usual time for magic.

### The circle

Wiccan rites take place in a circle cast for the purpose: a space made sacred, set apart from ordinary time and place, often described as "between the worlds". The four directions and the elements (air, fire, water, earth) are called at its edges. The circle both protects and contains: it keeps out what is not wanted and holds in the power raised inside until it is sent out.

### Magic

Wicca includes magic as part of religious life: healing, protection, blessing and the work of changing oneself and the world for the better. It is usually done in the circle, with the gods' blessing, alongside ordinary action, never instead of it.

### Priesthood

In Wicca, every initiate is regarded as a priestess or priest: there is no lay congregation watching a professional clergy. Even in open, eclectic Wicca, each person is expected to meet the gods directly. Covens are led by a High Priestess, often with a High Priest, but leading is a service, not a barrier between members and the divine.

## The vocabulary

You will meet these words often. Each is taught in depth later.

- **Coven:** a small group of Wiccans who work together, traditionally no more than thirteen.
- **Sabbat:** one of the eight seasonal festivals.
- **Esbat:** a rite at the full moon (or another phase).
- **Circle:** the sacred space cast for a rite.
- **Quarters:** the four directions and their elements, called at the circle's edge.
- **Athame** (a-THAH-may or ATH-a-may): the ritual knife, used to cast the circle and direct power, not to cut.
- **Book of Shadows:** a Wiccan's book of rites and teachings. In initiatory Wicca, the coven's book is oathbound and copied by hand; in open Wicca, it is each person's own record.
- **Blessed be:** a common Wiccan blessing, greeting and farewell.
- **Deosil** (JESH-il) and **widdershins:** sunwise (clockwise) and against the sun (anticlockwise).
- **Skyclad:** working naked, as some traditional covens do. Never required of a newcomer.

## Wicca and wider paganism

Wicca is one of the largest and most influential modern pagan religions, and many things that are now common across paganism, including the circle, the calling of quarters, the eight sabbats and the word esbat, spread outwards from it. Your coven may share festivals and friendships with Druids, Heathens and eclectic pagans. Wicca is not the parent of all of these, nor the only true form of witchcraft; it is one tradition among several, with its own particular shape.

The Wheel of the Year, in particular, grew up alongside Wicca, and many eclectic pagans keep it without being Wiccan. If you want the history of the eight festivals themselves, this course links you to the Wheel of the Year lessons rather than repeat them.

## How the core skills fit

The core lessons of this course (energy, grounding, raising and directing power, sacred space, the altar and tools, correspondences, the moon, divination and spellcraft) are tradition-neutral. In Wicca they all have a home:

- **Grounding and centring** come before and after every rite.
- **Sacred space** is, for Wiccans, the cast circle with its quarters, taught in the ritual module.
- **Raising power** is done in the circle, often by chanting and dancing deosil, and sent out at the height of the rite.
- **The altar and tools** have particular Wiccan forms and meanings: the athame, wand, chalice, pentacle and censer.
- **The moon** shapes the esbats; **the seasons** shape the sabbats.

> **Your coven:** Your coven will have its own way of doing almost everything in this module. Where this course describes "most Wiccans", ask your mentor how your coven does it.

> **Try this:** In your Grimoire, start a page called "Words of the Craft". Add each new term as you meet it, with its meaning in your own words.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** many of the materials Wicca was built from, such as ceremonial magic, folk custom and the ancient gods it honours.
- **Modern:** Wicca as a religion, its theology of the Goddess and God, and its rites, from the 1940s onwards.

docs.title: How Wicca began: an honest history
docs.summary: Where Wicca came from, as historians now understand it: Leland’s Aradia and Murray’s witch-cult theory, Gerald Gardner and the New Forest story, Doreen Valiente and the Charge of the Goddess, and how Wicca spread through the Sanders, Buckland and the books of the 1970s and 1980s.
docs.body:
## Why honest history matters

Older books often tell Wicca's story as the secret survival of a Stone Age religion, hidden through the witch trials and handed down in families. Historians, and most Wiccans today, now agree that this is not what happened. The real story is more interesting, and it frees you to love Wicca for what it is: a religion made by gifted, imperfect people in the twentieth century, from older materials, which has since become real in the lives of many thousands. The best book on this history is Ronald Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon (1999).

## The materials

Several things came together before Wicca existed.

- **Ceremonial magic.** The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn (founded 1888) and the magician Aleister Crowley developed rituals with a cast circle, the four elements at the quarters, tools tied to the elements, and invocations of gods. The Wiccan circle owes them a great deal.
- **Freemasonry and its offshoots.** The idea of a secret society with degrees of initiation, oaths and a ritual book came from this world. Gardner himself was a Co-Mason.
- **Charles Godfrey Leland.** In 1899 this American folklorist published Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches, which he said came from an Italian witch called Maddalena. It tells of Aradia, daughter of the goddess Diana, sent to teach witchcraft to the poor, and has the witches meet at the full moon, naked, to worship Diana and share cakes and wine. Whether Maddalena's material was genuine folk tradition, her own invention or Leland's is still debated, but several of its images passed into Wicca.
- **Margaret Murray.** In The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921) and The God of the Witches (1931), this Egyptologist argued that the people accused at the witch trials belonged to an organised pagan fertility religion, worshipping a horned god in covens of thirteen at four great sabbats. Historians have shown that the trial records do not support this, and that she read them selectively. But her picture of the witches shaped Wicca's coven, its sabbats and its Horned God, and she wrote a friendly foreword to Gardner's Witchcraft Today.
- **Romantic paganism and folklore.** Poets and writers such as Robert Graves (The White Goddess, 1948) and Rudyard Kipling, and the folklore of the English countryside, supplied images of the Goddess and the old gods of the land.

## Gerald Gardner

Gerald Brosseau Gardner (1884 to 1964) was a retired civil servant who had spent most of his working life in Malaya and became an enthusiastic amateur folklorist. Settling in the New Forest in the late 1930s, he joined a group of occultists linked with the Rosicrucian Order Crotona Fellowship. Gardner said that through some of them he was initiated in 1939 into a surviving witch coven.

Historians disagree about how much of this is true. Some, such as Philip Heselton, have found evidence that there was a real group of people Gardner worked with; others, such as Hutton, think that whatever Gardner found, the religion he later made public was largely his own work, assembled from the materials above. What is clear is that by the late 1940s Gardner had a coven of his own, meeting near St Albans, and a working book of rites drawing heavily on Crowley, Leland and Masonic ritual.

After the Witchcraft Act of 1735 was repealed in 1951, Gardner went public. He published Witchcraft Today in 1954 and The Meaning of Witchcraft in 1959, and earlier, in 1949, a novel, High Magic's Aid, that showed some of the practices in fictional form. He called the religion "the Wica" (with one c). He sought publicity, and the newspapers obliged, not always kindly.

## Doreen Valiente and the Charge of the Goddess

Doreen Valiente (1922 to 1999) was initiated by Gardner in 1953 and became his High Priestess. She recognised much of Crowley's writing in Gardner's book and, being a gifted poet, set about rewriting it. A great deal of the Wiccan liturgy known today is hers.

Her best-known work is the **Charge of the Goddess**, the words in which the Goddess speaks to her worshippers. Gardner's earlier version had stitched together passages from Leland's Aradia and from Crowley. Valiente rewrote it, first in verse and then in the prose version that became famous, keeping a few of the borrowed lines but making most of it new. The Charge is now read in Wiccan circles around the world, and many people who have never heard of Valiente know its words. Knowing that it was written by a twentieth-century woman, drawing on a nineteenth-century folklorist and an Edwardian magician, does not lessen it. It is honest to say who wrote it.

Valiente left Gardner's coven in 1957 after disagreements, including over Gardner's appetite for publicity and a set of "Laws" he produced as though they were ancient. She went on writing and teaching for the rest of her life, and in later books, such as Witchcraft for Tomorrow (1978), she offered rites of her own for anyone to use, helping make Wicca available outside the initiatory covens.

## How Wicca spread

- **The Alexandrian line.** In the 1960s Alex Sanders and Maxine Sanders, in Manchester and then London, built a tradition on Gardnerian material with more ceremonial magic added. Their students Janet and Stewart Farrar later published much traditional material, with Valiente's help, in Eight Sabbats for Witches (1981) and The Witches' Way (1984).
- **To America.** Raymond and Rosemary Buckland were initiated in Britain in 1963 and brought Gardnerian Wicca to the United States. Raymond Buckland later founded Seax-Wica (1973), an open tradition with its own published book.
- **The 1970s and 1980s.** New traditions grew: Dianic Wicca, centred on the Goddess, through Zsuzsanna Budapest; the Reclaiming tradition, which joined Wicca with political and ecological activism, through Starhawk, whose The Spiral Dance (1979) was hugely influential. Margot Adler's Drawing Down the Moon (1979) described the whole pagan scene for a wide readership.
- **Solitary and eclectic Wicca.** Scott Cunningham's Wicca: A Guide for the Solitary Practitioner (1988) told readers that they could practise Wicca alone, without initiation, and gave them the means. It was followed by a flood of books, and later by websites. Most people who call themselves Wiccan today learned this way.

## What this means for you

1. Wicca is a modern religion from older materials. Ask of any practice: how old is this, and where does it come from?
2. The founders were real people, with gifts and faults. You can honour Gardner's vision and Valiente's poetry without believing every claim either made.
3. Wicca has always grown by people adding to it. Your coven is part of that history.

> **Note:** You will still read that nine million people died in the witch trials, and that they were all pagans. Both are wrong. Estimates of executions in Europe are about 40,000 to 60,000, and almost all of the accused were Christians. Honest history honours them better.

> **Try this:** Choose one Wiccan practice you have met so far (the circle, the Charge, the sabbats, the athame). Write in your Grimoire what you now know of where it came from.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** ceremonial magic's roots, folk custom, the ancient gods and the seasons.
- **Modern:** Leland (1899), Murray (1921), Gardner's Wica (1940s and 1950s), Valiente's Charge (1950s), and every tradition since.

docs.title: How the Wheel was assembled
docs.summary: The honest history of the eight-fold Wheel: Margaret Murray’s four sabbats, Gerald Gardner’s coven, Ross Nichols and the Druids adding the solstices and equinoxes in the 1950s, and Aidan Kelly naming Litha, Ostara and Mabon in the 1970s.
docs.body:
## Why the story matters

Many books and websites say the Wheel of the Year is the ancient pagan calendar of the Celts, or of all northern Europe. It is not. Knowing how it really came together does not spoil it. It frees you: you can love the festivals for what they are, keep the old parts with respect, and feel at liberty to build your own, as the people who made the Wheel did. This lesson draws on the work of historians, especially Ronald Hutton, whose books The Stations of the Sun and The Triumph of the Moon are the best places to read further.

## The old pieces

Long before anyone spoke of a Wheel, the pieces existed separately.

- **The Gaelic quarter days.** Early Irish literature, written down from about the 8th century onward, names four great festivals that began the seasons: Samhain (1 November), Imbolc (1 February), Bealtaine (1 May) and Lughnasadh (1 August). They are well recorded in Ireland, Scotland and the Isle of Man, with customs that lasted into living memory.
- **The solstices and equinoxes.** People have watched the sun's turning points for thousands of years. Newgrange in Ireland, built around 3200 BCE, lets the rising sun into its chamber at the winter solstice. We do not know what its builders believed.
- **Anglo-Saxon month names.** In 725 the English monk Bede wrote about the old English months. He mentions Modraniht, "mothers' night", at midwinter; months called Litha around midsummer; and a month named for a goddess, Eostre, around the spring equinox. He is the only source for Eostre.
- **Folk customs.** Across Britain and Europe, people kept midsummer fires on St John's Eve, brought in May blossom, baked the first loaf at Lammas, held harvest suppers and kept Hallowe'en. Many of these were kept on church holidays and are recorded from the Middle Ages to the twentieth century.

No source joins all of these into one eight-fold cycle.

## Margaret Murray's four sabbats

In 1921 the Egyptologist Margaret Murray published The Witch-Cult in Western Europe. She argued that the people accused of witchcraft in early modern Europe had been members of a surviving pagan fertility religion, which met at four great "sabbats": Candlemas (2 February), May Eve, Lammas (1 August) and Hallowe'en. Her theory was popular for decades. Historians have since shown that it does not fit the evidence: the trial records do not describe an organised pagan religion, and Murray read them selectively. But her four sabbats shaped what came next.

## Gerald Gardner and the 1950s

Gerald Gardner, a retired civil servant, made public in the early 1950s the religion that became known as Wicca, which he said he had been initiated into in 1939. His coven, meeting near St Albans, kept Murray's four great sabbats.

In the late 1950s, members of the coven asked for the solstices and equinoxes to be celebrated too. Gardner was close friends with **Ross Nichols**, a fellow member of a naturist club and later founder of the Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids. Druid groups were already gathering at the solstices and equinoxes; Nichols was interested in adding the Gaelic fire festivals to the Druid year. Around 1958, both groups came to keep all eight. The friendship and conversation of these two men is the best-supported origin of the eight-fold cycle as we know it.

The phrase "Wheel of the Year" came into common use later, in the 1970s and 1980s, as books spread the practice.

## Aidan Kelly's names

For a while the solstices and equinoxes had no special names; they were simply "the summer solstice" and so on, or carried Christian names such as Midsummer. In the early 1970s the American pagan **Aidan Kelly**, preparing a calendar for his own tradition, gave them names:

- **Litha** for the summer solstice, from Bede's month name.
- **Ostara** for the spring equinox, from Jacob Grimm's 1835 German form of Bede's Eostre.
- **Mabon** for the autumn equinox, from Mabon ap Modron, a figure in Welsh legend. Kelly later said he chose it because he wanted a name that sounded right; there is no old link between Mabon and the equinox.

Kelly's names spread through books and calendars and are now used everywhere. Yule was already in use, from the old English and Norse midwinter.

## The Druid names

You will also meet the names Alban Arthan (winter solstice), Alban Eilir (spring equinox), Alban Hefin (summer solstice) and Alban Elfed (autumn equinox). These come from the writings of Edward Williams, known as Iolo Morganwg, a Welsh poet and antiquarian of the late 18th and early 19th centuries who was a brilliant writer and a notorious forger of "ancient" Welsh lore. Modern Druids use them knowing their source.

## What this means for you

1. **The Wheel is a modern creation from old materials.** Every part has its own age and story. When you keep a festival, you can ask of each custom: how old is this, and where does it come from?
2. **The names are choices.** Your coven may use Kelly's names, Gaelic names, English names (Candlemas, May Day, Lammas, Harvest Home, Hallowe'en), Druid names, or simply "the spring equinox". None is more ancient than the others in the way people often claim.
3. **Making new practice is part of the tradition.** The Wheel exists because people in the 1950s and 1970s built something meaningful from what they had. You are invited to do the same, honestly.
4. **Wicca is a sibling, not a parent you must obey.** The Wheel grew up alongside Wicca, and much shared practice comes from it. Some Wiccan rites are oathbound in their traditional forms and are not taught outside their covens; you should not expect to find them in an eclectic course.

> **Note:** Some older books still teach that the witch trials killed nine million people, or that the Wheel is an unbroken pagan survival. Both are wrong. Estimates of executions for witchcraft in Europe are around 40,000 to 60,000, a terrible enough number. Honest history honours the dead better than inflated history.

> **Try this:** Choose one festival. Find its page in the app and read its history. In the answer box for this module's reading task, write which of its parts are old, which are folk custom and which are modern, as far as you can tell.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic festivals, the noticing of solstices, Bede's month names, folk customs.
- **Modern:** Murray's theory (1921), Gardner's coven and Nichols' Druids keeping eight festivals (late 1950s), "Wheel of the Year" as a phrase, and Kelly's names (1970s).

docs.title: Lineages: initiatory, eclectic and other Wiccas
docs.summary: The difference between British Traditional Wicca (Gardnerian and Alexandrian), the open and eclectic Wicca of the books, and other lineages; what is oathbound and why; what this course does and does not teach; and how to recognise a genuine initiatory coven, or a false claim to be one.
docs.body:
## Why this matters

The word Wicca covers several quite different things. Knowing which is which protects you from confusion, from false claims, and from accidentally treating someone else's sacred secrets carelessly. It also lets you be honest about what you are learning.

## British Traditional Wicca

**British Traditional Wicca**, often shortened to BTW, is the name usually given to the initiatory lines that descend from Gerald Gardner's covens: the **Gardnerian** tradition, and the **Alexandrian** tradition founded by Alex and Maxine Sanders. Some other closely related lines, such as Algard (a blend of the two), are often included. Despite the name, BTW covens now exist around the world.

What marks BTW is this:

- **Initiation.** You become a Gardnerian or Alexandrian only by being initiated by a priestess or priest of that line who has the standing to initiate. The phrase often used is "only a witch can make a witch".
- **Lineage.** Each initiate can trace their line of initiators back to the founders. Lineage is taken seriously and can be checked.
- **Oaths.** At initiation, people swear to keep the tradition's secrets.
- **An oathbound Book of Shadows.** The coven's Book of Shadows, holding its rites, the names it uses and its inner teachings, is copied by hand by each initiate from their initiator's copy. Its contents are not shared with outsiders.
- **Coven practice.** BTW is practised in covens, in a priestess-and-priest working partnership, usually with three degrees.
- **No charge for teaching.** Traditional covens do not charge for training or initiation.

Some early material from the Gardnerian Book of Shadows has been published over the years, by Gardner's critics and later, with Doreen Valiente's support, by Janet and Stewart Farrar. But reading published text is not the same as being initiated, and BTW initiates hold that the tradition lives in the relationship between initiator and initiate, not in a text.

## What this course does not teach

This course does **not** teach, reproduce or claim to reproduce the oathbound material of any initiatory tradition: not its secret names of the gods, its initiation rites, its inner teachings or its Book of Shadows. Where it describes things that BTW covens do, such as drawing down the moon or the three degrees, it does so only as they have been publicly described by initiates and historians. Completing this course does not make anyone a Gardnerian or Alexandrian, and no app or book can.

The Sanctuary's closed and living traditions guide has an entry on initiatory Wicca explaining this in more detail.

## Open and eclectic Wicca

**Open Wicca** is Wicca that anyone may learn. Its sources are published books and teachers who share openly. It grew from the 1970s onwards, through writers such as Raymond Buckland (whose Seax-Wica was openly published), Doreen Valiente's later books, Starhawk, and above all Scott Cunningham, whose Wicca: A Guide for the Solitary Practitioner (1988) taught that a person could practise Wicca alone and dedicate themselves without initiation.

**Eclectic Wicca** means drawing on many sources, choosing what speaks to you within the broad shape of Wicca. **Solitary Wicca** means practising alone. Many people are both.

Open Wicca keeps the public shape of the religion: the Goddess and God, the sabbats and esbats, the cast circle and quarters, the tools, cakes and ale, the Rede. It writes its own words for its rites. This course teaches open Wicca, and your coven may be an open Wiccan coven, or an initiatory coven using these lessons for its public, outer teaching.

## Other lineages

Between BTW and solitary eclecticism lie many organised traditions, some initiatory, some open:

- **Seax-Wica,** Buckland's Saxon-flavoured open tradition (1973).
- **Dianic Wicca,** centred on the Goddess; some Dianic groups are for women only.
- **Reclaiming,** founded in San Francisco by Starhawk and others, joining Wicca-derived ritual with activism, and teaching openly.
- **Correllian, Georgian, Blue Star** and many more American traditions, each with its own history and degree of openness.
- **Feri,** from Victor and Cora Anderson, is related to Wicca but is usually counted as a separate witchcraft tradition, and is initiatory.

Each tradition decides what it shares. Respect that.

## Who may call themselves Wiccan

This is a live question, held in good faith on all sides. Some BTW initiates feel that "Wicca" should mean only the initiatory lines, and that others are "Wiccan-inspired" or simply "witches". Many eclectic Wiccans feel the word has grown beyond its first meaning, as words do. Some people solve it by speaking of "traditional Wicca" and "eclectic Wicca". Whatever you call yourself, be accurate about your training: say "I practise eclectic Wicca" or "I was trained in an open Wiccan coven", and never claim an initiation or lineage you do not have.

## Recognising a genuine initiatory coven, and false claims

If one day you seek initiation into a BTW line, these signs help:

- They are open about their lineage when you are serious, and others in that tradition know them.
- They usually meet seekers first through public events, study groups or an outer court, and take time, often a year and a day, before initiating.
- They do not charge for training or initiation.
- They never make sex, nudity, money or cutting off your friends a condition of being taught.

Be wary of anyone who claims a hereditary or ancient secret line they cannot explain, sells "initiations" online, or uses secrecy to discourage questions about how they treat people. A real oath of secrecy covers a tradition's rites, never harm done to a person.

> **Your coven:** Your High Priestess or mentor can tell you where your coven stands: initiatory and in which line, open, or a mixture with an outer court. Ask.

> **Try this:** Open the closed and living traditions guide and read its entry on initiatory Wicca. In the answer box for this module's reading task, describe in your own words what is open to you and what is not.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Modern, all of it:** BTW from the 1950s and 1960s, open Wicca from the 1970s, and the debate about the word from the 1980s onwards.

docs.title: The Goddess and the God
docs.summary: Wiccan theology: the Goddess and the God and the polarity between them, the Triple Goddess and the Horned God, the many ways Wiccans understand them (duotheism, soft and hard polytheism, a Goddess-centred view, the One behind all), and how to approach named gods respectfully.
docs.body:
## The heart of Wicca

Wicca is, at its heart, the worship of a Goddess and a God. Everything else (the circle, the tools, the sabbats, the magic) serves that relationship. This lesson introduces them, and the many honest ways in which Wiccans understand them. You do not need to settle your own view now; it will grow with practice.

## The Goddess

The Wiccan Goddess is often called simply the Goddess or the Lady. She is seen in the moon, waxing, full and waning; in the earth that bears and receives all life; in the sea; and in the turning of birth, love, motherhood, age and death. In the Charge of the Goddess, she speaks as the one who has been with her worshippers from the beginning, and who asks to be worshipped with joy, beauty, strength, mirth and reverence.

Many Wiccans honour her as a **Triple Goddess**: Maiden, Mother and Crone, mirroring the waxing, full and waning moon and the stages of a woman's life. This threefold image is modern. It owes most to Robert Graves's book The White Goddess (1948), a poetic, not a historical, work. Ancient religions did have triple goddesses (Hekate was shown with three bodies), but not the Maiden, Mother and Crone as Graves described them. Many find the image rich and true to experience; others find it limiting, especially for anyone whose life does not fit those three stages. Both are fair responses.

## The God

The Wiccan God, often called the Lord, is frequently pictured as the **Horned God**: lord of the wild, of animals and the hunt, of the woods and of death and what lies beyond. This image owes a good deal to Margaret Murray's theory of a witches' horned god, and to figures such as the Gaulish Cernunnos (known from a few images and one inscription) and the Greek Pan. He is also seen as the **sun**, born at midwinter and at his height at midsummer, and as the **grain**, cut down at harvest and sown again. In the sabbats, he lives, loves, dies and is reborn each year, while the Goddess endures and transforms.

Some covens tell part of the God's year through the story of the **Oak King and the Holly King**, twin rulers of the waxing and waning year, a modern image popularised by Janet and Stewart Farrar from the writings of Robert Graves and James Frazer.

## Polarity

In much traditional Wicca, the relationship between Goddess and God is reflected in the relationship between priestess and priest, and between female and male. This is called **polarity**: the idea that power and life arise from the meeting of complementary forces. Rites are often led by a priestess and a priest together, and cakes and ale is a symbol of their union.

Polarity has been rethought by many Wiccans. Same-sex, transgender and non-binary Wiccans have always been part of the religion, and many covens now understand polarity as something that can arise between any two people, or within each person, rather than tying it to sex or gender. Some traditions work without gendered roles at all. The elder module discusses this further.

## Many ways of understanding them

Wiccans hold a wide range of theologies. Here are the most common, and honest Wiccans hold every one of them:

- **Duotheism.** There is one Goddess and one God. All the goddesses of the world's religions are names and faces of the Goddess, and all the gods of the God. Dion Fortune's line, "All the gods are one god, and all the goddesses are one goddess, and there is one initiator", from her novel The Sea Priestess (1938), is often quoted. This is the classic Wiccan view.
- **Soft polytheism.** The many gods are real, and are also, in some way, aspects of the Goddess and God.
- **Hard polytheism.** The gods are many and distinct persons, and the Wiccan Goddess and God are particular deities, or a convenient way of speaking about the gods a coven honours. Some Wiccan covens honour named gods, such as Diana and Cernunnos, as themselves.
- **A Goddess-centred view.** Some traditions, such as Dianic Wicca, honour the Goddess as the source of all, with the God present as her son or consort, or not at all.
- **The One behind all.** Some Wiccans speak of an unknowable source beyond both the Goddess and God, sometimes called the Dryghtyn or simply the One.
- **Archetypal or naturalistic.** For some, the Goddess and God are powerful symbols of nature and the psyche, worshipped as such, without claims about persons beyond.

You may find your view changes over the years. That is normal.

## Names

In open Wicca, people call the Goddess and God by many names: the Lady and the Lord, the Mother and the Horned One, or the names of particular gods from the ancient world. In initiatory Wicca, each tradition has its own names for them, which are part of its oathbound material and are not taught here.

## Approaching named gods respectfully

If you come to honour a particular god, such as Brigid, Cernunnos, Diana or Hekate, learn about them as their own peoples knew them. Read the Library entries and, where the Sanctuary has one, try the dedication journey. Remember that some gods belong to living, closed traditions (the closed and living traditions guide explains which), and treat them with the respect their own people ask for. Do not fold gods from living religions into "the Goddess" without care.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven speaks of the Goddess and God, which names it uses in the circle, and whether it honours particular deities.

> **Try this:** For a week, at your candle greeting, speak to the Goddess and God by the simplest names: the Lady and the Lord. In the second week, try a particular name that draws you. Write what changed, if anything.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the ancient gods themselves, such as Diana, Pan and Cernunnos, and the honouring of moon, sun and earth.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan Goddess and God as a pair, the Triple Goddess (Graves, 1948), the Horned God of the witches (Murray, 1931), the Oak and Holly Kings, and every theology described here.

docs.title: Wiccan ethics: the Rede, the Threefold Law and beyond
docs.summary: The Wiccan Rede and where it came from, the Threefold Law and how variously it is held, what Wiccan ethics actually asks (responsibility, consent, honour, care for the earth), and what the ethics means for magic and for coven life.
docs.body:
## Ethics, not commandments

Wicca has no book of commandments. Its ethics is a matter of freedom and responsibility: you are free, and you are answerable for what you do with your freedom. This lesson looks at the two sayings most often quoted, where they come from, how differently Wiccans understand them, and the wider values that sit around them.

## The Wiccan Rede

The **Wiccan Rede** is usually given as: "An it harm none, do what ye will." "Rede" is an old word for advice or counsel; "an" means "if". In plain modern English: if it harms no one, do as you will.

### Where it came from

The Rede in this form first appears in public in 1964, in a speech by Doreen Valiente, who called it "eight words the Wiccan Rede fulfil". Gerald Gardner had written something similar in The Meaning of Witchcraft (1959), comparing the witches' morality to that of "the good King Pausol" in a French novel, who said, in effect, "do what you like, so long as you harm no one." The idea also echoes Aleister Crowley's "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law", though its spirit is different.

A much longer poem, often called "The Rede of the Wiccae", with many couplets of advice, was published in 1975 by Gwen Thompson, who attributed it to her grandmother, Adriana Porter. Whether it is that old is uncertain. Many Wiccans love it; it is a later addition, not the source of the short Rede.

### What it means

Wiccans read the Rede in several ways:

- **As permission:** whatever harms no one is allowed. Wicca does not forbid harmless pleasures.
- **As an ideal:** harm none, as far as you can. Since almost every action harms something (we eat, we compete, we say no), many Wiccans read it as "cause the least harm you can, and take responsibility for the harm you do cause".
- **As counsel, not law:** "rede" means advice. It is wisdom to weigh, not a rule to obey blindly.
- **As including yourself:** "none" includes you. Self-harm, burnout and letting others harm you are not what the Rede asks.

It does not mean that a Wiccan may never defend themselves, say no, or act firmly. It asks that you think before you act and own what follows.

## The Threefold Law

The **Threefold Law**, or Law of Return, says that whatever you send out, for good or ill, comes back to you three times over.

### Where it came from

A version appears in Gardner's novel High Magic's Aid (1949), in a scene where an initiate is told that good received must be returned threefold. In the form most people know today, as a universal law of magical consequences, it spread through American books of the late 1960s and 1970s, notably those of Raymond Buckland, and became one of the most quoted ideas in eclectic Wicca.

### How variously it is held

Wiccans hold the Threefold Law in very different ways:

- some believe it literally, as a law of the universe;
- some treat it as a vivid way of saying that what you do shapes who you become and how others treat you;
- some hold a broader idea of return without the number three;
- some initiatory Wiccans regard it as a modern addition, not part of their tradition;
- some reject it, pointing out that good people suffer and harmful people often prosper, and that ethics should not rest on fear of punishment.

It is honest to say that it is relatively recent and not universal. It is also fair to notice its wisdom: magic done in anger tends to keep the one doing it angry.

## The wider values

Around the Rede, most Wiccan covens hold values like these:

- **Responsibility.** You answer for what you do, magically and otherwise.
- **Consent.** No magic is done on or for another person without their consent, including healing. Ask first; if you cannot ask, offer it to the gods "for their highest good, if they would welcome it", or not at all.
- **Honour and truthfulness.** Keep your word; do not claim titles or lineage you do not have; keep confidences.
- **Perfect love and perfect trust.** A phrase widely used in Wicca for the spirit in which members enter the circle together. It is an ideal of how a coven should be, not a demand that you trust anyone blindly. Trust is earned.
- **Care for the earth.** The Goddess is seen in nature, so harming the earth carelessly is seen as a failure of worship.
- **Freedom and joy.** The Charge of the Goddess asks for mirth as well as reverence. Pleasure is not sinful in Wicca.

## Ethics and magic

Most Wiccan covens forbid curses and harmful magic, and many forbid "binding" anyone except, in rare cases, to stop serious harm, and then only after much thought and with the coven's leaders. The core spellcraft lessons discuss this in detail. Wicca's ethics also ask you to do the ordinary things: see the doctor, call the police, apply for the job. Magic works alongside action, never instead of it.

## Ethics and coven life

The same ethics applies to coven leaders. No one may use the Rede, perfect love and perfect trust, or oaths of secrecy to pressure you into anything harmful, sexual or financial. An oath never covers abuse. If anything in your coven feels wrong, speak to someone you trust, inside or outside it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven's own ethical agreements are, and how it understands the Rede and the Threefold Law.

> **Try this:** Think of a decision you face. Write how the Rede would guide it if read as permission, as an ideal and as counsel. Which reading helps most?

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the wish to do no harm, which appears in many ethical traditions.
- **Modern:** the Rede in its eight words (1964), the long Rede (1975), the Threefold Law as a universal law (1960s and 1970s), and "perfect love and perfect trust" as a Wiccan phrase.

docs.title: What a Wiccan coven does
docs.summary: Coven life in Wicca: the sabbats and esbats, training, the High Priestess and High Priest, degrees described in public terms, robes and skyclad working, outer courts, and how the app holds the coven’s rites, Book of Shadows and conversations.
docs.body:
## A small, close group

The coven is the classic unit of Wicca. Traditionally it has no more than thirteen members, a number that comes from Margaret Murray's theory and has stuck, though many covens are smaller. A coven is small on purpose: people who work magic and worship together need to know and trust one another, and that takes time and closeness.

## What a coven does through the year

### The sabbats

The coven gathers for the eight sabbats, often on the nearest weekend. A sabbat is festive: the circle is cast, the season's story is enacted or told, the season's custom is kept, cakes and ale are shared, and there is a feast. Some covens open certain sabbats to guests.

### The esbats

The coven meets at the full moon, or as near as possible, for the esbat. The esbat is more inward than the sabbat: worship of the Goddess, often with the Charge, and the coven's magical work, such as healing for those who have asked for it. Some covens also meet at the new or dark moon.

### Training

Covens train newcomers. In initiatory covens this often happens first in an **outer court** or study group that is not yet part of the coven proper; in open covens, through programs like this one. Training covers the coven's ritual, the craft of magic, devotion, history and ethics.

### Magic and service

Covens do healing work, protection and blessings for members and those who ask, and often service to the wider community or the land. Consent comes first.

### Fellowship

Covens are also friendships. Members eat together, support one another through hard times and celebrate births, handfastings (Wiccan weddings) and lives at their ending.

## Who leads

Most Wiccan covens are led by a **High Priestess**, often with a **High Priest**. In traditional Wicca the High Priestess has the final word in the circle: Wicca has always given women leadership. The High Priest works alongside her. Many covens now have two priestesses, two priests, or leaders of any gender. Leading is a service: planning rites, teaching, caring for members, and holding the coven to its own ethics.

## Degrees, in public terms

Many Wiccan traditions, especially the initiatory ones, use **three degrees**. What follows is only what has been publicly described; the rites and teachings of each degree belong to each tradition.

- **First degree.** Initiation itself: the person becomes a witch and a priestess or priest of the tradition, and a member of the coven.
- **Second degree.** After further training, often a year or more: deeper teachings, and often the ability to initiate others and lead rites under the guidance of the coven's leaders.
- **Third degree.** The fullest standing in the tradition, usually needed to lead a coven independently and to "hive off", that is, found a daughter coven.

Open covens may use degrees, may use only a dedication and an initiation, or may have no degrees at all. In this Sanctuary, covens describe their own positions, such as Dedicant, Initiate, Elder and High Priestess, and the programs raise people to them.

## Robes and skyclad

Some traditional covens work **skyclad**, naked, as Gardner described and as Leland's Aradia had pictured. Those who do it say it removes distinctions of wealth and status and makes everyone equal before the gods. Many other covens wear robes, often black or plain, with a cord at the waist. Others wear ordinary clean clothes. Whatever a coven does, nudity is never required of a newcomer or guest and must never be a condition of being taught. If a coven works skyclad, it should tell you before you are asked to decide anything, and you may choose a coven that robes.

## The coven's Book of Shadows

Every coven keeps its own Book of Shadows: its rites, words, recipes, history and teachings. In initiatory covens it is oathbound and copied by hand. In this Sanctuary, your coven's Book lives in the app, and its leaders decide what is shared with whom. Your own Book of Shadows, your personal record, lives in the Grimoire.

> **Note:** Secrecy in Wicca protects a tradition's rites from being treated carelessly. It never protects harm. Anything that is done to a person against their will, or that would need hiding from the law, is not a coven secret.

## How the app helps

- **The coven's rituals and ritual builder** hold the rites the coven plans, with dates, roles and words.
- **The calendar** shows the sabbats, the moons and the coven's own dates.
- **The coven's Book** holds its shared teaching.
- **The altars** let members tend a shared altar together.
- **The coven's messages** keep members in touch between rites, and online rites let distant members join.

## Your first year

In your first year you will usually keep all eight sabbats and most full moons with the coven, keep a daily practice, study, and slowly take small roles in the circle: calling a quarter, carrying the incense, reading a part. By the end you will know the coven's rite by heart.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven organises its year: which sabbats are open, how often it meets for esbats, whether it has an outer court, and whether it uses degrees.

> **Try this:** Look in the app at the coven's rituals and its Book. Find one rite that has already been planned and read it through.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the image of witches meeting in small groups, from folklore and the trial records, though not as Murray read them.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan coven as it exists today, with its degrees, outer courts and High Priestess, from the 1950s onwards.

docs.title: A daily Wiccan practice
docs.summary: How to build a daily devotion to the Lady and the Lord that lasts: a five-minute morning and evening form, a fuller form for days with time, a household shrine, prayer in your own words, and what to do when you miss days or feel nothing.
docs.body:
## Why daily

Coven rites happen a few times a month. Relationship with the gods happens every day, or it fades. Most experienced Wiccans say that their daily practice, small and unglamorous, is what made the religion real for them. The sabbats and esbats are feasts; daily devotion is the bread.

The aim is not perfection. It is a practice simple enough to keep on your worst days, with room to grow on your best.

## The household shrine

A shrine is a small, permanent place for devotion, separate from (or part of) your working altar. It might be a shelf, a windowsill, or the top of a chest of drawers. On it:

- two candles, or one, for the Lady and the Lord;
- an image of each, or natural things that speak of them: a shell or a white stone for the Goddess, an antler, an acorn or a sunflower head for the God;
- a small offering bowl;
- something of the season.

Keep it clean and tended. Dust it weekly; change the seasonal things at each sabbat.

## A five-minute morning devotion

1. **Stand before the shrine.** Take three slow breaths, in for four and out for six.
2. **Light the candle** (or candles).
3. **Greet the Goddess and God.** For example: "Lady, Lord, I greet you in this new day. Be with me in all I do."
4. **Offer something small:** a few drops of water, a pinch of herbs, a flower, or simply your attention.
5. **Ask for one thing for the day,** or offer the day to them: "Help me to be patient today," or "Let my work today honour you."
6. **Stand quietly** for a minute.
7. **Close:** "Blessed be." Put out the candle before you leave the room.

## A five-minute evening devotion

1. **Light the candle.**
2. **Thank them** for one particular thing from the day. Be specific: "Thank you for the sound of rain this afternoon."
3. **Review the day honestly.** Where did you act well? Where would you act differently? This is not self-punishment; it is the Wiccan habit of taking responsibility.
4. **Ask for rest,** for yourself and anyone you are worried about (with their consent if it is a working; a prayer for someone is different from magic on them).
5. **Close** and put out the candle.

## A fuller devotion, once a week

On a day with more time, keep a longer devotion of twenty or thirty minutes: light incense, read something sacred to you (the Charge of the Goddess, a poem, a passage from a book), sing or chant, meditate in silence, write in your Book of Shadows. Some Wiccans cast a simple circle for this; most do not, for daily devotion.

## Praying in your own words

Wicca has few set prayers outside its rites. Most Wiccans pray in their own words. If that feels strange, a simple pattern helps:

1. **Address:** whom you are speaking to. "Lady of the moon..."
2. **Praise:** something true about them. "...who turns the tides and the seasons..."
3. **Thanks or request:** what you bring. "...thank you for carrying me through this hard week."
4. **Close:** "Blessed be."

Short is fine. Honest is better than beautiful.

## Through the day

Devotion need not stay at the shrine. Many Wiccans greet the moon when they see it, bow slightly to the sun at sunrise, thank the earth when they eat, or say "blessed be" when they pass a tree they love. These small acts weave the gods into ordinary life.

## Living with others

Not everyone lives alone, or with people who share their religion. If your household is not pagan, keep your shrine modest and your devotion quiet; a candle and a few whispered words disturb no one. If you cannot keep a shrine at all, a small box holding your candle and images can be brought out and put away again. Children can be welcomed into devotion simply, by lighting the candle or choosing the flower, without being pressed to believe anything.

## Devotion through the year

Let your daily devotion follow the Wheel. Change the seasonal things on the shrine at each sabbat, greet the Lady and Lord as the season shows them (the young God at Imbolc, the Lady in flower at Beltane, the God in the grain at Lammas), and let your words change with the light. Over a year, you will find that daily devotion and the sabbats teach each other.

## When you miss days

You will. Illness, travel, children, grief and plain forgetting happen to everyone. When you notice, simply start again, without guilt. The gods of Wicca are not keeping a register. If you miss weeks, a simple "I'm back" at the shrine is enough.

If daily is impossible for you, choose a rhythm you can keep: three times a week, or every weekend. Regular is more important than frequent.

## When you feel nothing

Many people go through long periods of feeling nothing in devotion. This is very common in every religion and has many causes: tiredness, depression, a phase of growth, or simply the ordinary rhythm of any relationship. Keep the practice simple and steady. Talk to your mentor. If the dryness comes with low mood that lasts more than a couple of weeks, please see a doctor too: devotion and medical care work well together.

> **Safety:** Daily candles are the commonest cause of fires in pagan homes. Put them out every time you leave the room. An electric candle on a shrine you pass often is a good idea.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have a daily prayer or greeting it shares. Ask your mentor if there is one you might use.

> **Try this:** Keep the five-minute morning and evening devotions for thirty days. Log each day. At the end, write what changed.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** household shrines and daily offerings, kept in ancient Greek, Roman and many other homes.
- **Modern:** Wiccan daily devotion to the Lady and the Lord, much of it shaped by the solitary Wicca books of the 1980s onwards.

docs.title: The esbats and the moon’s month
docs.summary: The Wiccan esbat: where the word comes from, what is done at the full moon, the new and dark moon, the thirteen moons of a year and the popular moon names (and where those names really come from), keeping an esbat alone or with the coven, and magic by the moon.
docs.body:
## What an esbat is

An **esbat** is a Wiccan rite kept at a phase of the moon, most often the full moon. Where the sabbats belong to the turning year and the story of the God, the esbats belong especially to the Goddess, whose sign is the moon. The esbat is also the usual time for a coven's magical work.

## The word

The word esbat was popularised by Margaret Murray in The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921). She found it in a sixteenth-century French account of witches' meetings and took it to mean the ordinary, smaller meetings of a coven, as distinct from the great sabbats. It probably comes from the Old French "s'esbattre", to frolic or amuse oneself. Wicca took up Murray's distinction: sabbats for the seasons, esbats for the moon.

The idea of meeting at the full moon has another source too: in Leland's Aradia (1899), the goddess Diana tells her followers to gather once a month, when the moon is full. Wicca drew on both.

## The moon's month

The moon goes from new to full and back in about twenty-nine and a half days. Wiccans often link its phases with the Goddess:

- **New moon:** the dark, hidden Goddess; beginnings, seeds, rest, inner work.
- **Waxing moon:** the Maiden; growth, drawing things in, building.
- **Full moon:** the Mother; fullness, power, worship, healing, blessing.
- **Waning moon:** the Crone; release, letting go, endings, banishing what harms.
- **Dark moon,** the last days before the new: rest, divination, the mysteries.

The core lessons on the moon and timing teach the phases in more depth. The app's moon page shows tonight's phase.

## What happens at a full moon esbat

A coven's full moon esbat usually follows the Wiccan shape, with the Goddess at its centre:

1. The circle is cast and the quarters called.
2. The Goddess (and often the God) is invited.
3. **Worship:** the Charge of the Goddess may be read or spoken; in some covens, the Goddess is drawn down into the High Priestess.
4. **Magic:** healing for those who have asked, blessings, workings for the coven or its members. Power is raised, often by chanting and dancing deosil, and sent.
5. **Cakes and ale.**
6. Thanks, release, and opening.
7. Often, a social time, and sometimes teaching.

The previous module's "complete esbat" is a full example for one person.

## The new and dark moon

Some covens also meet at the new or dark moon, for quieter work: meditation, divination, inner journeys, banishing and protection, or rest. Many solitary Wiccans keep a short new moon rite to set intentions for the month. Others keep the dark moon simply as a time not to work, letting the Goddess rest.

## Thirteen moons

A solar year holds twelve or thirteen full moons: twelve lunar months take about 354 days, so roughly every two and a half or three years there is a thirteenth. Wiccans often speak of "the thirteen moons" of a year.

A "blue moon" has two meanings: the popular modern one, a second full moon in a calendar month; and an older almanac meaning, the third of four full moons in one season. Either way, it is often treated as a time for long-term wishes.

## Moon names, honestly

You will meet names for each month's full moon: Wolf Moon, Snow Moon, Worm Moon, Pink Moon, Flower Moon, Strawberry Moon, Buck Moon, Sturgeon Moon, Harvest Moon, Hunter's Moon, Beaver Moon, Cold Moon. The app has a ready-made rite for each.

These names came into wide use through twentieth-century American almanacs, especially the Maine Farmers' Almanac from the 1930s and later the Old Farmer's Almanac. They mix colonial American, English and loosely attributed Native American sources, and many claims about which people used which name are uncertain. They fit the seasons of the northern temperate zone. Use them as seasonal folklore, not as an ancient or a single people's calendar, and in the southern hemisphere many Wiccans shift them by six months or make their own names from their land's year.

Some Wiccans name the moons from their own land: the moon of the first frost, the moon of the swifts' return. This is a beautiful practice.

## Keeping an esbat alone

Alone, an esbat can be as short as fifteen minutes or as long as an hour:

1. Look at the moon, if you can see it.
2. Cast a circle, or simply light your candles.
3. Greet the Goddess under her name as the full moon.
4. Read or speak words of praise.
5. Stand or sit in the moonlight, or before her candle, in silence.
6. Do one working, if you have one, with consent.
7. Share cakes and ale with her.
8. Thank her and close.
9. Write in your Book of Shadows.

## Magic by the moon

Wiccans commonly time magic by the moon: drawing things in while it waxes, giving thanks and blessing at the full, releasing while it wanes. The core lessons teach this. It is a help, not a rule: urgent healing need not wait for a full moon.

> **Safety:** Moon-gazing outdoors at night: tell someone where you are, take a torch, stay where you know the ground, and dress warmly. Charging water in moonlight is fine; drinking water left outdoors is not.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor when your coven keeps its esbats (on the night of the full moon, or the nearest convenient evening), whether it keeps the new moon too, and how members ask for healing.

> **Try this:** For three months, keep the full moon with an esbat, alone or with the coven, and the new moon with five minutes of quiet and one intention. Log each.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** honouring the moon, in many ancient religions; the word esbat (from a sixteenth-century French source); Aradia's full moon gatherings (1899).
- **Modern:** the Wiccan esbat, the Triple Goddess reading of the phases, and the popular moon names as they are now listed.

docs.title: The moon between festivals
docs.summary: How the moon’s monthly turning sits inside the year’s: keeping new and full moons at home, esbats as an option, simple moon practices, the Cycle & Moon tracker for those who use it, and not overloading your practice.
docs.body:
## Two wheels

The year turns once around the sun; the moon turns about twelve and a half times inside it. Many Wheel practitioners keep both: the eight festivals for the year, and the moon's phases for the month. This lesson shows how the moon can fit into a seasonal practice without crowding it.

The core course's lesson on the moon and timing teaches the phases in detail. Here we look at moon devotion.

## Esbats, and other words

In Wicca, gatherings at the full moon are called esbats, a word borrowed from Margaret Murray's account of witch meetings. Many eclectic covens use the word too. Others simply say "full moon gathering". Keeping the moon is an option in the Wheel, not a rule.

## Why keep the moon

- **It is regular.** The moon gives a monthly rhythm between festivals six weeks apart.
- **It is visible.** Unlike a date on a calendar, you can see the moon change.
- **It is old.** Many calendars were lunar, including the Greek and the Gaelic Coligny calendar, and the moon has been watched for as long as people have looked up.
- **It suits magic.** Many practitioners time their spells by the moon.
- **It speaks to many.** Some people feel a link between the moon and their own cycles of energy, mood or body.

## Simple moon practices

### At the new moon

The new moon, when the moon is hidden or a first thin crescent appears at dusk, is a time of beginnings.

1. Look for the first crescent in the west after sunset, a day or two after the new moon.
2. Light a candle at your altar.
3. Say: "New moon, first light: I begin again."
4. Write down one thing you want to grow this month.
5. Keep the note on your altar until the full moon.

### At the full moon

The full moon, round and bright all night, is a time of fullness, celebration and power.
