1. Go outside, or to a window where you can see the moon.
2. Stand in its light for a few minutes. Breathe slowly.
3. Greet it: "Full moon, bright moon: I see you."
4. Look back at the note from the new moon. How has it grown?
5. If you work magic, this is a common time for it. Many people leave water out in the moonlight to use later.

### At the dark moon

The dark moon, the day or so before the new moon when nothing is visible, is a time of rest, release and endings. Some practitioners keep it quietly: cleaning, letting go, early to bed.

## The moon and the festivals

Sometimes the moon and a festival fall close together: a full moon at Samhain, a new moon at Yule. Many practitioners notice these as especially strong. You may combine them, or keep them separately.

## The moon and the body

Some practitioners, especially those who menstruate, notice a link between the moon and their own cycle, energy or mood, and like to keep both. Others find no link, and that is fine too: menstrual cycles vary, and science finds no reliable link between the moon and menstruation. The Sanctuary has a private Cycle & Moon tracker for those who want to watch both side by side. It is entirely optional, and what you record there is kept private.

## Moon names

You will meet many names for the full moons of the year: the Wolf Moon in January, the Snow Moon in February, the Harvest Moon nearest the autumn equinox, the Hunter's Moon after it, and so on. Some of these are old: the Harvest Moon and Hunter's Moon are recorded in English from the early eighteenth century. Most of the others were popularised by American almanacs in the twentieth century, which said they came from Native American nations. Some do, from particular nations, but they were collected loosely and often credited to "Native Americans" in general. The app's ready-made moon rites use these popular names.

You are free to use them, or better, to name the moons after what happens on your own land: the Blossom Moon when your apple tree flowers, the Swift Moon when the swifts arrive. Many practitioners find their own names more meaningful.

## Not overloading your practice

Eight festivals, twelve or thirteen full moons, twelve or thirteen new moons, daily practice, a coven, a job, a life. It's easy to feel you're failing to keep up. Some guidance:

- **The festivals come first** in the Wheel. The moon is extra.
- **Choose one phase** to keep each month, if you keep the moon at all: full or new.
- **Shrink it.** A full moon practice can be a minute at the window.
- **Skip it.** Missing a moon is not failure. There will be another in a month.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven gathers at the full moon, the new moon, or neither, and what it does when a moon falls near a festival.

> **Safety:** If you leave water out under the moon to use later, keep it covered and clean, don't drink it unless it was clean drinking water to begin with, and don't add stones or herbs that may be toxic. Be careful going out at night: bring a torch, mind your footing, tell someone where you are.

> **Try this:** For the next three months, keep either the new moon or the full moon with the simple practice above. Log each one.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** watching the moon, lunar calendars, the new crescent as the start of a month in many cultures.
- **Modern:** the esbat (from Murray and Wicca), moon water, and keeping the moon as part of an eclectic seasonal practice.

docs.title: Coming to know the Goddess
docs.summary: Practical ways to build a relationship with the Wiccan Goddess: the moon, the earth and the sea; reading the Charge as devotion; working with a particular goddess; offerings she is traditionally given; and noticing her in your own life.
docs.body:
## Knowing, not only knowing about

The tradition module explained what Wiccans believe about the Goddess. This lesson is about coming to know her: building a relationship through practice, as you would with a person. Like any relationship, it is built through time, attention, gifts and conversation.

## Where she is met

Wiccans meet the Goddess in many places. Choose one or two to begin with.

### The moon

The moon is the Goddess's best-known sign in Wicca. Watch it through a whole month: where it rises, how its shape changes, how it feels to stand under it. Greet it when you see it. Many Wiccans have a small gesture, such as touching the heart and then raising the hand, or a few words: "Hail, Lady."

### The earth

The Goddess is also the earth: the soil, the growing things, the land you live on. Gardening, walking, tending a houseplant, cooking food from the land, and caring for a place can all be devotion to her. The Wheel of the Year course's lesson on the land has more on this.

### The sea and the waters

For many, she is the sea, the tides that follow the moon, rivers and wells. If you live near water, visit it as a place of worship. Bring nothing that pollutes; take away litter.

### The body and life's turnings

Wicca honours the body and its cycles as sacred. The Goddess is met in birth and death, in love and pleasure, in menstruation, pregnancy, menopause and age. You need not be a woman to know her here. Many people find the Sanctuary's Cycle and Moon page helps them notice their own rhythms beside the moon's.

## The Charge as devotion

The Charge of the Goddess, in Doreen Valiente's words, is the nearest thing Wicca has to a scripture spoken by the Goddess. In it, she calls her worshippers to meet her at the full moon, to be free, to find her within themselves, and to keep mirth and reverence, beauty and strength, power and compassion, honour and humility.

Reading it slowly, aloud, as a prayer, is one of the best ways to come to know the Goddess of Wicca. Try reading it at every full moon for a year. Notice which lines catch you differently each time. Copy it by hand into your Book of Shadows; many Wiccans do. It is widely published, in Valiente's own books among others.

## A particular goddess

Many Wiccans come to honour a particular goddess as well as, or as a face of, the Goddess: Diana or Artemis of the moon and the wild; Brigid of the hearth, the forge and poetry; Selene, the moon herself; Isis, Hekate, Cerridwen, Aphrodite, or another. If one draws you:

1. **Learn her story** from good sources: the Library entry, the myths, and scholars' accounts of how she was worshipped.
2. **Learn what she was given:** offerings traditional to her.
3. **Try the dedication journey** in the app if there is one for her.
4. **Speak to her by name** at your shrine for a month, and notice.
5. **Respect her people.** If she belongs to a living religion, honour her in ways that religion would recognise.

## Offerings to the Goddess

Common Wiccan offerings to the Goddess include:

- **milk, water, wine or juice** poured into a bowl or onto the earth;
- **white or silver candles**;
- **flowers,** especially white flowers, and roses;
- **moon cakes** or bread, at the esbat;
- **incense,** such as jasmine, myrrh or sandalwood (from sustainable sources);
- **silver** or **shells** placed on the shrine;
- **acts**: time spent in nature, care for the earth, kindness to those who are vulnerable, art made for her.

Offer what you would want to give a beloved guest, and what you can afford. A sincere small gift is better than a grand one made grudgingly.

## Noticing her

Devotion includes listening. Over weeks, notice:

- dreams of the moon, the sea, or a woman who seems to be more than a woman;
- moments of unexpected comfort or awe;
- the same image or animal turning up repeatedly;
- a deepening sense, during rites, of being met.

Write these down, without deciding at once what they mean. The lesson on discernment will help you weigh them.

## A short full moon devotion to the Goddess

On a full moon when you are not keeping a full esbat, try this simple devotion of ten minutes:

1. Go where you can see the moon, or light a silver or white candle.
2. Stand with your arms raised and palms open towards her, and breathe slowly.
3. Greet her: "Lady of the moon, I see you in your fullness. Hail and welcome."
4. Read a few lines of the Charge, or speak your own praise.
5. Tell her one thing you are grateful for and one thing you need.
6. Pour a little water or milk onto the earth as an offering.
7. Stand in silence, letting the moonlight fall on you.
8. Close: "Thank you, Lady. Blessed be."

## If she feels distant

Some people find the Goddess immediately; others find her hard to reach, especially if they have complicated feelings about mothers, about women, or about their own bodies. If that is you, start with the face of her that feels safest: the moon in the sky, or the earth under your feet, rather than the Mother. Give it time, and talk it through with your mentor.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may honour the Goddess under particular names or with particular offerings. Ask your mentor what is customary.

> **Try this:** For one lunar month, greet the moon each time you see it, and read the Charge aloud at the full moon. At the end of the month, write a letter to the Goddess telling her what you have noticed.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the worship of moon, earth and sea goddesses, and of particular goddesses such as Diana, Selene and Brigid.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan Goddess as one who includes them all, and the Charge of the Goddess (1950s).

docs.title: Coming to know the God
docs.summary: Practical ways to build a relationship with the Wiccan God: the Horned One of the wild, the sun, the grain that dies and is reborn, the Oak and Holly Kings; working with a particular god; offerings; and why some find the God harder to know at first.
docs.body:
## The often-overlooked partner

Many people come to Wicca drawn by the Goddess and find the God harder to know. Some have had difficult experiences of masculine images of God in other religions; some simply find less written about him. Yet Wicca is a religion of both, and many Wiccans say that coming to know the God changed their practice deeply. He is not a stern father in the sky. He is wild, joyful, sacrificial and tender, and he dies every year.

## Where he is met

### The wild

The Horned God is lord of the animals and the untamed places: forests, moors, the hunt, the beasts with antlers and horns. Wiccans meet him outdoors: walking in woods, watching deer at dusk, listening to wind in trees, feeling the animal in their own bodies when they run or dance.

He has ancient relatives. The Gaulish Cernunnos is known from a few images, most famously on the Gundestrup cauldron, and a single inscription; the Greek Pan and Roman Faunus were gods of the countryside and wild music. Herne the Hunter, the antlered ghost of Windsor Forest, is a figure of English folklore first written down by Shakespeare. Wicca gathered these into the Horned God. Knowing their separate stories helps you know him.

### The sun

The God is also the sun, born at the winter solstice, growing through spring, at full strength at midsummer, and waning towards winter. Watching the sunrise and sunset through the year is devotion to him.

### The grain

He is the grain: sown in the earth, growing, cut down at harvest, made into bread, and sown again. The harvest sabbats, especially Lammas, tell this story. Every loaf of bread can remind you of it.

### Death and rebirth

Because he dies and returns, the God is lord of death and what lies beyond, the comforter and guide of the dead. Many Wiccans find in him a gentle face for death.

## The Oak King and the Holly King

Some covens tell the God's year through two kings: the Oak King, who rules the waxing year from midwinter to midsummer, and the Holly King, who rules the waning year from midsummer to midwinter. They fight at the solstices, and each in turn gives way to the other. This is a modern image, popularised by Janet and Stewart Farrar from Robert Graves and James Frazer, and loosely connected with folk plays and the carol "The Holly and the Ivy". Many find it a lively way to dramatise the year. The lore module uses it in some sabbats.

## A particular god

As with the Goddess, many Wiccans come to honour a particular god: Cernunnos, Pan, Lugh, Apollo, Dionysus, Osiris, Herne. If one draws you, learn his story from good sources, learn what he was given, try the dedication journey if the app has one, and speak to him by name. Respect his own people's ways.

## Offerings to the God

Common Wiccan offerings to the God include:

- **ale, beer, cider, mead or wine,** or apple juice;
- **bread,** especially at the harvest;
- **gold, yellow or red candles**;
- **oak leaves, acorns, pine cones, antlers** (shed naturally), **seeds**;
- **incense** such as frankincense, pine or cedar;
- **meat** at a feast, shared;
- **acts:** physical work, protection of wild places, music and dance, courage for others.

## A practice for coming to know him

1. **Watch the sun.** For a week, note the time and place of sunrise or sunset, and greet the sun when you see it.
2. **Go to the wild.** Spend an hour in the most untamed place you can safely reach. Walk slowly. Listen. Greet the God of the place.
3. **Bake or buy bread.** At your shrine, hold the loaf and thank the God for his life, given in the grain. Share it.
4. **Dance.** Put on music with a drum beat and move for ten minutes, as an offering. Notice how it feels.
5. **Write.** Record what you noticed.

## If he is hard to know

If you find the God difficult:

- start with one face of him (the sun, the stag, the grain) rather than all at once;
- notice whether old associations from other religions are getting in the way, and talk about them with your mentor;
- remember that in Wicca he is a partner, not a ruler;
- be patient. Relationships take time.

## The Goddess and God together

Coming to know each separately is a start; Wicca also honours them together. Their relationship is the story of the year: meeting, union, parting and return. At your shrine, try greeting them as a pair, noticing how each changes in the light of the other: the Lady as the earth that receives the God's grain, the Lord as the sun that warms her fields. The sabbats tell this story in full, as the lore module will show.

> **Safety:** In wild places, stay on paths you know, tell someone where you are going, and keep your distance from animals, especially deer in the rut and cattle with calves. Shed antlers may be collected only where it is legal.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven honours the God, whether it uses the Oak and Holly Kings, and whether it honours a particular god.

> **Try this:** Keep the practice above over a fortnight. Then write a letter to the God, as you did to the Goddess, telling him what you have noticed.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** Cernunnos, Pan, Faunus and other gods of the wild; sun and grain gods; Herne in folklore.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan Horned God (shaped by Murray's work), and the Oak and Holly Kings (Farrar, from Graves and Frazer).

docs.title: Offerings, the beloved dead and the Summerland
docs.summary: How Wiccans make offerings and dispose of them well; Wiccan ideas of death, the Summerland and rebirth and where they come from; honouring the beloved dead at home; and a simple Wiccan remembrance.
docs.body:
## Offerings in Wicca

An **offering** is a gift given to the gods, the spirits or the dead. In Wicca, offerings are a way of saying thank you, of honouring, of building relationship and of sharing the good things of life. They are given freely: Wicca does not teach that the gods need feeding or will be angry without them.

## What to offer

Good offerings are things that are real gifts to you, given with attention:

- **food and drink:** bread, cakes, fruit, honey, milk, wine, juice, water, the first portion of a meal;
- **light and scent:** candles, incense, oil lamps;
- **flowers and greenery,** ideally grown or gathered with thanks;
- **things made:** poems, songs, drawings, crafts;
- **acts:** time, service, care for the earth or for people, done in a god's name.

## How to offer

1. Set out the offering in a bowl on your shrine or altar.
2. Say whom it is for and why: "Lady, Lord, I give you this bread in thanks for the harvest."
3. Leave it for a time: an hour, overnight, or until the next day.
4. Then dispose of it respectfully.

## Disposing of offerings

- **Liquids** can be poured onto the earth, into the garden or a plant pot, or, if you have nowhere else, down the sink with thanks.
- **Food** can be left outside where wildlife can eat it safely, buried, or composted. Avoid foods that harm animals (chocolate, grapes and raisins, onions, salty and sugary things for birds and dogs).
- **Flowers** go to the compost or the earth when they fade.
- **Candles and incense** are burned to the end where safe, or the remains are buried or put in the bin with thanks.
- Some Wiccans eat food offerings after a time, believing the gods have taken its essence; others do not. Ask your coven.

Never leave anything that will become litter or harm wildlife, and never leave offerings on private land or in sacred places of other religions without permission.

## Wicca and death

Wicca has no single doctrine of death, but some ideas are widely shared:

- **The Summerland.** Many Wiccans speak of a place of rest and renewal after death, called the Summerland. The name comes from nineteenth-century Spiritualism, especially the American writer Andrew Jackson Davis, and was taken up in Theosophy before Wicca adopted it.
- **Rebirth.** Many Wiccans believe in reincarnation: that after rest, the soul is born again. This idea came into Wicca from Theosophy and Eastern religions as understood in Britain in the early twentieth century, and fits the God's yearly death and rebirth.
- **The God as guide.** The God, as lord of death, is often seen as the one who receives and comforts the dead.
- **The Goddess as the cauldron of rebirth,** from whom all are born again.

Many Wiccans hold these as beliefs; others hold them as hopes, or as poetry. Some do not believe in any afterlife. Wicca does not require one view.

## Honouring the beloved dead

Wiccans honour their own dead: family, friends, teachers, and those of the Craft who have gone before (sometimes called "the Mighty Dead"). Samhain is the great festival of the dead, but you can honour them at any time.

### A place for them

Many Wiccans keep a small place for the dead, separate from the shrine of the gods: a photograph, a candle, a keepsake. The app's ancestors page lets you keep names and memories too.

### Who counts

The beloved dead are those you choose to honour. You do not have to honour relatives who harmed you. You can honour the dead of your choice: chosen family, teachers, those whose lives inspire you.

## A simple Wiccan remembrance

You can keep this on the anniversary of a death, at Samhain, or whenever you wish.

1. Set out a photograph or name of the person, a candle and a small offering of something they loved.
2. Light the candle: "Lord who guides the dead, Lady who receives all into the cauldron of rebirth, I remember [name]."
3. Speak to them: tell them something you remember, something you are grateful for, or news they would want to hear.
4. Sit quietly with them for a few minutes.
5. Offer the food or drink: "This is for you, with my love."
6. Close: "Rest well in the Summerland, and be reborn in joy, if that is your path. Blessed be."
7. Put out the candle, and dispose of the offering the next day.

## Grief

Honouring the dead can bring grief to the surface. That is natural and often healing. If grief is overwhelming, if you cannot function, or if it is very fresh, take care: keep rites short, talk to someone, and seek bereavement support or a doctor if you need to. Wicca does not ask you to be fine.

> **Safety:** Necromancy, trying to summon or speak with the dead in trance, is not a beginner's practice and is not part of this course. Remembrance is speaking to the dead in love; it does not require any reply.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven honours the dead, at Samhain and at members' deaths, and what it believes about the Summerland.

> **Try this:** Set up a place for your beloved dead. Keep the simple remembrance for one person. Write what you felt.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** offerings to the gods and to the dead, in almost every ancient religion.
- **Modern:** the Summerland (Spiritualism, nineteenth century) and the Wiccan blend of rebirth and the God's yearly death.

docs.title: Discernment: telling real from wishful
docs.summary: How to weigh experiences of the Goddess and God honestly: personal gnosis and its limits, simple tests (time, fruit, consistency, others), divination as a check, signs that something is wrong, and when to seek help from your mentor or a professional.
docs.body:
## Why discernment matters

As your practice deepens, you may have experiences that feel like contact with the gods: a voice, an image, a strong feeling, a dream, a sign. Some will be deeply meaningful. Some will be ordinary mind-noise, wishful thinking or tiredness. A few might be signs that something is not well with you. **Discernment** is the skill of telling these apart, with humility and good sense. It is one of the most important skills in any religion that values direct experience, as Wicca does.

## Personal gnosis

Pagans often call personal religious experience **unverified personal gnosis**, or UPG: knowledge that feels true to you but cannot be checked against tradition or shared evidence. "The Goddess wants me to wear blue at the full moon" is UPG. So is "the God came to me as a stag in a dream".

UPG is not worthless. It is how much of anyone's religious life works. But it is personal: it guides you, not others, and it must be held lightly. When several people independently have the same experience, some call it **shared personal gnosis**, which carries a little more weight.

## Simple tests

When you have an experience that seems significant, ask:

1. **Time.** Write it down and wait. Does it still seem meaningful in a week, a month? Wishful experiences often fade; real ones tend to deepen.
2. **Fruit.** What does it lead to? Experiences of the gods in Wicca usually lead towards love, freedom, courage, responsibility, care for the earth and others. Experiences that lead towards fear, cruelty, isolation, grandiosity or harm are suspect.
3. **Consistency.** Does it fit what is known of this god, the tradition and your own experience so far? If it contradicts everything, be cautious, though not dismissive.
4. **Others.** What does your mentor think? What do experienced Wiccans say? A good mentor will neither dismiss nor inflate it.
5. **Ordinary explanations.** Were you tired, hungry, ill, emotional, on medication? Is there a simple, ordinary cause? Taking these seriously is not disbelief; it is honesty.
6. **Divination.** Some Wiccans check experiences with a tarot or rune reading. This can help, as long as you do not keep drawing until you get the answer you want.

## Warning signs

Be cautious, and talk to your mentor, if an experience:

- tells you that you are uniquely chosen, superior to others, or above ordinary rules;
- tells you to harm yourself or anyone else, or to cut yourself off from people;
- demands money, sex, secrecy or obedience to a person;
- brings persistent fear, dread or a sense of being watched;
- keeps you from sleeping, eating, working or caring for yourself;
- comes with voices or visions you cannot stop, outside ritual.

The gods of Wicca do not demand that you harm yourself or others. A coven leader who says "the Goddess told me" to justify pressure or harm is not to be obeyed.

## When to seek help

Religious experience and mental health can overlap, and anyone can become unwell. If you notice:

- low mood that does not lift for two weeks or more;
- anxiety that disrupts daily life;
- hearing or seeing things outside ritual that others do not;
- thoughts of harming yourself;

then please speak to your doctor or a mental health professional, and tell your mentor. Getting medical help does not mean your spiritual life is false; it means you are looking after the body and mind through which you meet the gods. Many devout Wiccans take medication and see therapists. If you are in crisis, contact emergency services or a crisis line straight away.

## Keeping a discernment journal

A simple record helps:

1. **What happened:** date, time, what you were doing, what you experienced.
2. **What you thought it meant** at the time.
3. **Your state:** tired, well, emotional, unwell.
4. **After a week:** does it still seem meaningful? What came of it?
5. **After a month:** the same question.

Over a year, patterns emerge. You learn which of your experiences tend to bear fruit.

## Sharing experiences in a coven

Covens differ in how they handle members' experiences. Some share them freely at the feast; others keep them for private conversation with a mentor. A few things help in any coven:

- share an experience as yours ("I felt the Goddess say..."), not as a message for everyone ("the Goddess says we must...");
- be glad for others' experiences without measuring yours against them;
- never pressure anyone to report an experience they did not have;
- let the coven's leaders help weigh anything that seems to concern the whole group.

## Divination as a check, used well

If you use cards or runes to check an experience, ask one clear question once ("What do I need to understand about this dream?"), read honestly, and write down the answer before you decide what it means. The app's spreads include one for questions about a patron deity and one for checking before a working. Don't keep drawing until you get the answer you hoped for: that is a sign you have already decided.

## Humility and wonder

Discernment is not cynicism. It is possible to hold an experience with wonder and gratitude while not being sure what it was. Many experienced Wiccans say they have had a handful of experiences in their life they would stake everything on, and many more that were lovely and uncertain. That is a healthy place to be.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven approaches personal experiences: whether members share them, and how the leaders help people weigh them.

> **Try this:** Keep a discernment journal for a month alongside your daily devotion. At the end, read it back and write what you have learned about how your own experiences tend to come.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the testing of visions and prophecies, in ancient oracle traditions and in many religions.
- **Modern:** the terms UPG and shared gnosis, from pagan discussion in the 1990s.

docs.title: What dedication means in Wicca
docs.summary: Dedication, self-dedication and initiation: how they differ in Wicca, where self-dedication came from, what the traditional year and a day means, what you promise and what you do not, and how to know whether you are ready.

docs.title: Preparing for dedication
docs.summary: How to prepare: writing your words of dedication step by step, choosing a token, choosing a Craft name if you want one, choosing the time (a new or full moon, a sabbat), and the week of preparation before.
docs.body:
## Preparing well

A dedication is better for being prepared. The weeks before are part of the rite: they let you think through what you are doing, find the words, and arrive ready. This lesson takes you through the preparation step by step.

## Writing your words

Your words of dedication are the heart of the rite. Many covens have set words; many also invite the dedicant to add their own. Write yours even if your coven has set words, so that you understand what you are saying.

### Step by step

1. **Who you speak to.** Begin by naming the Goddess and the God, by the names you use. For example: "Lady of the moon and the earth, Lord of the sun and the wild."
2. **Who you are.** Name yourself: your everyday name, and your Craft name if you are taking one.
3. **What you have done.** Say briefly what brought you here: "I have walked with you through these months, kept your moons and your seasons, and learned at the feet of this coven."
4. **What you promise.** Say what you promise and for how long. For example: "For a year and a day I will honour you, study your ways, keep your festivals, live by the Rede as I understand it, and treat my coven with honour."
5. **What you ask.** Ask for help: "Guide me, teach me, and keep me true."
6. **A closing.** "So mote it be," or "Blessed be."

### Testing your words

- **Can you keep each promise?** If "every day" is not realistic, say "faithfully". Promises you break weigh on you.
- **Is anything vague?** "I will be a good witch" is hard to keep or to know you have kept. Be specific.
- **Is anything too much?** A first dedication is not a lifelong vow.
- **Read them aloud** at your altar. Notice what feels true and what feels forced.
- **Wait a few days,** then read them again and revise.

Show your mentor your draft. They can help you see what you might have missed.

## Choosing a token

Many Wiccans mark their dedication with a **token**: something they keep, wear or use to remember it. Some ideas:

- **a cord,** in a colour your coven uses, or white, to wear at rites;
- **a pentagram** pendant or ring;
- **a stone or shell** from a place that matters to you;
- **a tool** you have made, such as a wand;
- **your Book of Shadows** itself, blessed at the rite.

Choose something meaningful rather than expensive. It will be blessed at the rite.

## A Craft name, if you want one

If you would like a Craft name:

1. Spend some weeks noticing what draws you: plants, animals, stars, qualities, figures from myth.
2. Write a list. Say each name aloud.
3. Ask in your devotion for guidance, and notice your dreams.
4. Check the name's meaning and origins, and avoid names that belong to living religions not your own, or the names of gods.
5. Choose one you could live with for years, and that you will not mind being called in front of others.

You can change it later, and many people do.

## Choosing the time

Wiccans often dedicate:

- **at the new moon,** for a new beginning;
- **at the full moon,** in the fullness of the Goddess;
- **at Imbolc,** the festival of beginnings and of initiation in many covens;
- **at the sabbat nearest** the end of your devotee path.

Your coven will usually choose a time with you. Look in the app's calendar and moon page.

## The week before

In the week before your dedication:

1. **Keep your daily devotion** each morning and evening.
2. **Read your words aloud** each day.
3. **Clean** your home and altar.
4. **Spend time outside,** with the land and sky.
5. **Rest.** Go to bed at a reasonable time; eat well.
6. **Reflect.** Read back over your Book of Shadows and your notes from the devotee path.
7. **Avoid** heavy drinking and anything that would leave you unwell.

On the day, take a ritual bath or shower with attention, put on clean clothes or robes, and keep your morning devotion before you go to the rite.

## Practicalities

Ask your mentor:

- where and when the rite will be, and how long it will take;
- what to wear and bring;
- what you will be asked to say and do;
- whether you can bring a friend (usually not, for coven rites);
- what happens if you need to pause or stop.

Tell them about any health needs: mobility, allergies, anxiety, anything that might affect you in the rite.

> **Safety:** If you have a health condition, or are pregnant, tell your mentor before the rite. Ritual baths should be warm, not hot, and never use essential oils on bare skin or in a bath without proper dilution and advice.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have set words, a set token, or a set time for dedications. Ask your mentor what is fixed and what is yours to choose.

> **Try this:** Write the first draft of your words this week. Read them aloud at your altar each evening for a week, and revise.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** preparing for a sacred rite by washing and fasting, in many ancient religions.
- **Modern:** Wiccan dedication and its preparation.

docs.title: The shape of the dedication rite
docs.summary: The usual shape of a Wiccan dedication, which your coven will adapt: the circle, presenting the dedicant, the questions, the words, the anointing and blessing of the token, the welcome; and a version for a solitary self-dedication.
docs.body:
## A shape, not a script

This lesson describes the shape most Wiccan dedications share. It is not your coven's rite: your coven will have its own, and its leaders will walk you through it beforehand. Knowing the shape helps you feel at home and understand what is happening.

Dedication rites are not usually secret, even in initiatory covens; initiation rites are. Nothing here describes an initiation.

## The shape of a coven dedication

1. **The circle is cast** in the usual way, and the quarters called.
2. **The Goddess and God are invited.**
3. **The dedicant is presented.** Often the dedicant waits outside the circle, or at its edge, and is brought in through a doorway by their mentor or a sponsor. The High Priestess may say who they are and why they have come.
4. **The questions.** The High Priestess or High Priest asks the dedicant a few questions, to be answered freely. For example: "Do you come of your own free will?" "Do you wish to study the Craft of the Wise with this coven for a year and a day?" "Will you honour the Goddess and the God?" The dedicant answers in their own words or with a simple "I do" or "I will".
5. **Purification.** The dedicant may be sprinkled with salt water and censed with incense, to mark the new beginning.
6. **The words.** The dedicant speaks their words of dedication, facing the altar or the coven.
7. **The anointing.** The High Priestess or High Priest may anoint the dedicant with water or oil, often on the forehead, perhaps tracing a pentagram, with a blessing.
8. **The token.** The dedicant's token is blessed on the pentacle, passed through the elements (salt, incense, flame, water), and given to them.
9. **The name,** if one is taken: the dedicant says it, and the coven greets them by it.
10. **The welcome.** The coven welcomes the dedicant, often with "Blessed be" from each person.
11. **Cakes and ale,** shared with the dedicant first or last, as the coven's custom is.
12. **Thanks, release and opening** of the circle.
13. **A feast.**

The whole rite may take thirty minutes to an hour.

## What you will be asked to do

You will usually be asked to:

- arrive prepared, washed and dressed as your coven asks;
- answer a few questions honestly;
- speak your words;
- receive a blessing and your token;
- share cakes and ale.

You will not be asked to undress, to do anything sexual, to harm yourself or anything else, or to keep secret anything that would harm you or others. You may pause or stop at any time. Saying "I need a moment" is always allowed.

## A solitary self-dedication

If you are dedicating alone, or your coven agrees that you may, you can keep a self-dedication. The app has two ready-made versions, "Solitary Self-Dedication" (Wiccan) and a kitchen-witch self-dedication. A simple form:

1. **Prepare** as for a coven rite: bathe, dress, set your altar with your two candles, salt, water, incense, oil (or water) for anointing, and your token.
2. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
3. **Invite the Goddess and God.**
4. **Purify yourself:** sprinkle yourself with salt water and pass through the incense smoke.
5. **Ask yourself the questions** aloud, and answer them: "Do I come of my own free will? I do."
6. **Speak your words** of dedication.
7. **Anoint yourself:** dip a finger in the oil or water and touch your forehead, saying "I am dedicated to the Lady and the Lord," then your heart, "in love," and your hands, "in the work of the Craft."
8. **Bless your token** on the pentacle and through the elements, and put it on or hold it.
9. **Sit in silence** and listen for some minutes.
10. **Cakes and ale,** with an offering.
11. **Thank** the Goddess and God, release the quarters, open the circle.
12. **Write** it in your Book of Shadows.

If you can, ask a trusted friend on the same path to witness, in person or online.

## What people experience

Dedicants describe many things: a rush of emotion when speaking their words, a sense of being welcomed, warmth at the anointing, a quiet certainty, or, quite often, nervousness that makes it all pass in a blur. Some feel the presence of the Goddess and God strongly; others feel little in the moment and find the meaning grows in the weeks after. None of these says anything about whether your dedication was real. It was real because you meant it.

## If something goes wrong

Candles go out, words are forgotten, someone sneezes during the silence. Covens are used to this. If you lose your words, your mentor can prompt you, or you can simply say what is in your heart. If you feel faint or overwhelmed, say so; the rite will pause while you sit, drink water and breathe. A dedication that stopped for a few minutes is no less a dedication.

## In the app

Your coven may hold your dedication in person, or in the app as an online rite, with you at your own altar. Either is real. If online, make sure your space is private, your connection steady, and your candles safe while you look at a screen.

> **Safety:** Anointing oil should be a skin-safe carrier oil such as olive or sunflower, or plain water. Never use undiluted essential oils on the skin, and avoid them altogether if you are pregnant or have sensitive skin.

> **Your coven:** Your coven's dedication may differ in many ways. Ask your mentor to walk you through it, and to tell you which parts are fixed and which are yours.

> **Try this:** Write the shape of your own dedication rite in your Book of Shadows, from the circle to the feast, with your words in their place.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** anointing and purification at a new beginning, in many religions; giving a token or a new name.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan dedication rite, as covens and books from the 1970s onwards have shaped it.

docs.title: After dedication
docs.summary: The weeks after dedication: aftercare for body and mind, what changes in coven life, keeping your promises, the beginning of the year and a day, when doubts come, and what lies ahead on the path to initiation.
docs.body:
## The rite is a beginning

A dedication is not the end of something; it is the beginning of your year and a day, or whatever time your coven has set. This lesson is about the days and weeks after, and how to carry what you promised into ordinary life.

## The first few days

Sacred rites can leave people feeling many things: joy, peace, tiredness, emptiness, tearfulness, a sense of being very open, or very little. All of these are normal. Take care of yourself:

1. **Eat** good food, and drink water.
2. **Rest** and sleep.
3. **Ground yourself:** walk, touch the earth, do something practical with your hands.
4. **Keep your daily devotion,** even if it is short.
5. **Write** in your journal or Book of Shadows: what happened, how you felt, what you remember of what was said.
6. **Wear or keep your token** where you will see it.

If you feel unsettled, talk to your mentor on this step. If low mood or anxiety lasts more than a couple of weeks, please see a doctor as well.

## What changes in coven life

In many covens, dedication brings some changes:

- you may be invited to rites that are open only to dedicants and above;
- you may take small roles in the circle more often: calling a quarter, carrying the incense, reading a part;
- you will begin the next stage of training, often called the initiate path, with deeper study;
- you may have more responsibility: helping set up, preparing food, welcoming newcomers;
- you may begin keeping some of what you learn confidential, as your coven asks.

In the app, your position in the coven will change, and new programs may be open to you.

## Keeping your promises

Promises fade if they are not tended. Some ways to keep yours alive:

- **Reread your words** at each full moon, or at least each sabbat.
- **Mark the date** in your calendar, and remember it each month.
- **Check honestly** every few months: are you keeping what you promised? If not, why? What needs to change, in your practice or in the promise?
- **Talk to your mentor** if you are struggling. That is what they are there for.

If you find you cannot keep a promise, say so. A promise renegotiated honestly is better than one quietly broken.

## The year and a day

If your coven uses the year and a day, it begins now. It is a time to:

- **keep the whole Wheel:** all eight sabbats, as the lore module teaches;
- **keep the moons:** thirteen full moons;
- **study deeply:** correspondences, the moon and timing, divination, spellcraft, and the craft of ritual;
- **serve:** your coven, your community and the land;
- **discern:** whether initiation, if your coven offers it, is right for you.

The next program, the year and a day to initiation, takes you through all of this.

## When doubts come

Doubts after dedication are very common. Perhaps the rite felt less powerful than you hoped, or life got busy, or you wonder whether you believe as much as you thought. Some honest responses:

- **Feelings come and go.** The commitment is what you do, not only what you feel.
- **Doubt is part of religion.** Many experienced Wiccans have periods of doubt; they often lead to a deeper faith, or a more honest one.
- **Talk about it.** Your mentor has almost certainly felt the same.
- **It is all right to change your mind.** If, after time and honest thought, Wicca is not your path, it is better to leave well than to stay unhappily.

## Building your practice now

The months after dedication are a good time to deepen your own practice, not only to follow the coven's. Some Wiccans set themselves small disciplines for the year: a daily devotion kept without fail for a season, learning the coven's rite by heart, reading one serious book each quarter, making one tool with their own hands, learning the plants of their neighbourhood. Choose one or two, write them in your Book of Shadows, and tell your mentor.

It is also a time to begin giving back: welcoming the next newcomers as you were welcomed, helping set up and clear away, and noticing what the coven needs. Service is part of the Wiccan priesthood you are moving towards.

## Your Book of Shadows

If you have not yet begun a proper Book of Shadows, begin now. Record your dedication: the date, the moon, your words, what you were given, what you felt. From now on, write down each sabbat and esbat, each working and its result, what you learn and what you wonder. In a year it will be a record of your path; in ten, a treasure. The app's Grimoire keeps it safe and private, or you may prefer paper.

## Looking ahead to initiation

If your coven offers initiation, it is usually at least a year and a day away, and is not automatic. It depends on your study, your practice, your relationship with the coven, and on both you and the coven's leaders agreeing that you are ready. You may decide not to seek it; many Wiccans live fulfilled religious lives as dedicants, or as solitary practitioners after self-dedication.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what changes for you now: which rites you may attend, what roles you might take, what is confidential, and when the next program begins.

> **Try this:** A month after your dedication, read your words aloud at your altar, and write a short note on how you have kept them so far.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the care of people after a rite of passage, in many religions.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan year and a day after dedication, as covens practise it today.

quizzes.title: Welcome: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on how the course works, what a coven is, consent, safety, looking after yourself and red flags. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: You sat for a breathing practice for ten minutes and noticed nothing in particular. What should you write in the answer box?
options: Nothing; leave it blank until something happens
What you did and that you noticed nothing much, honestly
A description of what you think you were supposed to feel
Skip logging it, since it didn't work
questions.explanation: Honest notes, including "nothing much happened", are what let you and your mentor see real patterns. Most practitioners' early journals are full of quiet sessions.

questions.prompt: To pass a module's test, you need 80 per cent of the points.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each module's test needs 80 per cent. Choice questions are marked at once and written answers are scored by your mentor. If you don't pass, look at the questions you missed, go back over the lessons and talk to your mentor about trying again. The right answers and explanations show once you've passed.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to separate noticing from concluding in your journal?
options: "I felt energy between my hands."
"Noticed: my palms tingled and grew warm as I breathed slowly. I think this may be what my coven calls energy."
"My spirit guide touched my hands."
"Nothing; I don't write conclusions."
questions.explanation: Write what you noticed in plain words first, then your interpretation, kept apart. The noticing is the evidence; the conclusion may change as you learn.

questions.prompt: Modern covens, and Wicca in particular, are an unbroken continuation of an organised pagan religion that survived the witch trials.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. That was Margaret Murray's 1920s theory, which historians have rejected. Wicca was made public in the 1950s by Gerald Gardner and others, drawing on older sources. Modern practice is meaningful without needing to be ancient.

questions.prompt: Which of these respect consent? Choose all that apply.
options: Asking "Is it all right if I anoint your hands?" before doing so
Doing a healing working for a friend who asked you to
Doing a working to make a particular person fall in love with you
Stepping out of a ritual partway through because you're uncomfortable
questions.explanation: Consent means free, informed agreement that can be withdrawn. Asking before touch, working only for those who've asked, and being free to step out all respect it. A love spell aimed at a particular person tries to change their feelings without their agreement.

questions.prompt: You can't safely use a naked flame where you live. What should you do?
options: Use one anyway, but only for short rituals
Use a battery candle; it's perfectly acceptable
Give up on candle practices
Light it outside your door
questions.explanation: Battery candles are fully acceptable and many experienced practitioners use them. Safety always comes first: never leave a flame unattended or use one where it isn't safe.

questions.prompt: Which of these are safe practice with herbs and oils? Choose all that apply.
options: Diluting essential oils in a carrier oil and patch-testing before they touch skin
Drinking a herbal tea from a spell book to make the spell stronger, without asking anyone
Checking every herb and oil with a professional if you're pregnant
Keeping oils away from cats, dogs and birds
questions.explanation: Never ingest a herb or oil for magical purposes without expert advice: many interact with medicines. Dilute and patch-test oils, check everything in pregnancy, and keep oils away from pets, some of which are poisoned by them.

questions.prompt: Libations must be alcoholic to be acceptable.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Alcohol is always optional. Water, juice, milk or tea are acceptable offerings in every tradition this course teaches, and no one should pressure you to drink.

questions.prompt: After a week of evening meditation you've been sleeping badly and feel detached from your surroundings much of the day. What's the right first step?
options: Meditate longer to push through it
Stop the practice, ground yourself, tell your mentor, and see a doctor if it continues
Keep it to yourself so you don't look weak
Stop taking any medication that might be interfering
questions.explanation: These are signs to pause. Stop, ground (food, water, feet on the floor, something ordinary), tell your mentor, and get medical help if it doesn't settle. Never change medication because of a spiritual practice.

questions.prompt: Which of these are red flags in a spiritual group? Choose all that apply.
options: Being told you must pay the leader to be initiated
Being asked to share the cost of candles and room hire, with the costs shown openly
Being told not to talk to former members
Being told sex with the leader is part of advancement
questions.explanation: Open sharing of costs is normal. Paying for advancement, being cut off from people outside the group, and any suggestion that sex is required are serious warning signs.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between confidentiality and harmful secrecy in a coven, with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects people (who is a member, what others share, the coven's own rites). Secrecy that hides harm protects the person doing harm. No promise can require you to hide abuse, crime or danger. Ask: "Who does keeping this secret protect?"
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): explains that confidentiality protects members and the coven's private practice (1); explains that secrecy hiding abuse, crime or danger is never binding (1); gives a fitting example of each, such as not naming members vs. being told not to tell the police or a doctor (1).

questions.prompt: A practice has left you feeling anxious and unsettled for several hours. Describe what you would do, step by step.
questions.explanation: Stop the practice; ground yourself with food, water, feeling your feet and doing something ordinary; tell your mentor; seek medical or crisis help if it's severe or doesn't settle; rest from practice and return gently.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): stops the practice and grounds in a concrete way (1); tells the mentor (1); says they would seek professional or emergency help if it doesn't settle or if they feel unsafe, and returns gently or pauses (1).

quizzes.title: Energy: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on what practitioners mean by energy, the ways of understanding it, and how to perceive it safely and honestly. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: When practitioners of magic talk about "energy", what do they usually mean?
options: The physicist's energy, measured in joules
A felt sense of aliveness, force, mood or presence in the body, between people, in places and objects
Electricity from the body that instruments can measure
Only the energy that comes from food
questions.explanation: In magical practice, "energy" is an old, loose word for a felt sense of aliveness, force, mood or presence, which can be felt, raised, directed, released and grounded. It isn't the physicist's measurable quantity.

questions.prompt: Which of these are ways practitioners understand energy, as taught in this module? Choose all that apply.
options: A subtle life force that flows through living things
Presence and relationship with spirits, gods and the land
What it feels like when attention, imagination, emotion and the body work together
A proven physical force that guarantees results
questions.explanation: The three views are subtle energy, spirit and relationship, and the psychological view. Many practitioners hold a mix. None is a proven physical force guaranteeing results.

questions.prompt: You need to decide which view of energy is true before you can learn the practices.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The practices work the same way whatever you believe: slow down, pay attention, notice, and learn to shift what you notice. Your own view can grow from experience.

questions.prompt: After two weeks of practice, you still feel very little in your hands. What does this most likely mean?
options: You have no ability and should stop
Something is blocking you that needs removing
It's normal; attention is a skill that grows, and some people perceive more through images, moods or a sense of knowing
You should practise for hours at a time to force it
questions.explanation: Noticing little at first is completely normal. Keep practising gently, notice what you do perceive (images, moods, knowing), and talk to your mentor.

questions.prompt: During the four-count breath you start to feel dizzy and your lips tingle. What should you do?
options: Breathe faster to push through it
Hold your breath until it passes
Stop shaping the breath, breathe normally, and rest
Carry on; dizziness means energy is rising
questions.explanation: Dizziness and tingling around the lips are signs of over-breathing, which can bring on panic. Stop, breathe naturally and rest. Breath practices in this course are always gentle.

questions.prompt: In breath awareness, your mind wanders over and over. What's the right attitude?
options: You're failing at the practice
Noticing that you've wandered and coming back is the practice itself
Stop and try again when your mind is clear
Force your thoughts to stop
questions.explanation: No one's mind stops. Each time you notice you've drifted and return to the breath, you're doing the exercise. That's how attention is trained.

questions.prompt: The purpose of the body scan is to learn what your body normally feels like, so you can notice changes during practice.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The body scan gives you a baseline. Once you know what normal feels like, you can recognise the changes that come with grounding, raising energy and ritual.

questions.prompt: A body scan brings up panic and a feeling of being outside your body. Which of these are good responses? Choose all that apply.
options: Open your eyes and press your feet into the floor
Look around and name things you can see
Tell your mentor, so the practice can be adapted
Close your eyes tighter and keep scanning to get through it
questions.explanation: Stop, come back to the room through the senses and the body's contact with the floor, have some water, and tell your mentor. These reactions aren't your fault; they mean the method needs adapting.

questions.prompt: You can't picture images in your mind. How can you do the energy ball exercise?
options: You can't; energy work needs visualisation
Focus on a felt sense of warmth gathering, or a silent word with each breath, instead of a picture
Look at a photo of a ball instead
Skip all energy work
questions.explanation: Energy work doesn't depend on visualisation. Felt sense, breath and words work just as well, and many practitioners can't form mental pictures.

questions.prompt: Which journal entry best keeps perception and interpretation apart?
options: "The room had bad vibes."
"A spirit was in the room."
"My shoulders tightened when I walked in and I wanted to leave. Maybe the room holds the argument from yesterday."
"My aura was attacked."
questions.explanation: Write what you noticed in plain words first, then any interpretation separately and tentatively. Plain words keep you honest and make patterns visible.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would do the "between the palms" exercise, and name three things you might notice.
questions.explanation: Breathe for a couple of minutes, rub the palms to warm them, hold them facing each other about thirty centimetres apart, and very slowly bring them close and apart again for a few minutes while breathing slowly. People notice warmth, tingling, pressure, a push or pull, or nothing at first. Finish by resting and shaking the hands.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): describes preparing (breath and warming or waking the hands) (1); describes the slow movement of the palms towards and away from each other without touching, with slow breathing (1); names three plausible sensations such as warmth, tingling, pressure, push or pull, or says that noticing little is normal (1).

questions.prompt: You sense a room in your home and it feels "heavy". Explain how you would work out whether this is perception or assumption.
questions.explanation: Check your own state first (your baseline), write the raw impression before explaining it, notice whether you expected it, return at other times and in other moods, and compare with someone else's impressions taken separately.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): mentions checking their own state or baseline (tiredness, mood) (1); mentions recording the raw impression before explaining it, or noticing whether it was expected (1); mentions checking consistency over time or comparing with another person's separate impression (1).

quizzes.title: Grounding, centring, shielding and cleansing: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on the four protective skills, when to use them, and what they can't do. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which best describes grounding?
options: Putting a protective boundary around yourself
Settling into your body and the present, letting excess energy drain to the earth and steadiness come in
Washing away what's clinging to you
Raising energy for a spell
questions.explanation: Grounding settles you: attention in the body and the present, excess drained away, steadiness drawn in. Shielding sets a boundary; cleansing clears what's clinging.

questions.prompt: What is centring?
options: Standing in the middle of the ritual space
Gathering your scattered attention and energy back to a still point in your body, such as the belly or chest
Balancing the four elements on the altar
Sending energy to the centre of the earth
questions.explanation: Centring gathers you in to your own middle, usually felt in the belly or chest, so you feel collected and balanced. It's normally done after grounding.

questions.prompt: Which are signs you need to ground? Choose all that apply.
options: Feeling spacey or "not quite here" after practice
Buzzing, jittery energy you can't settle
Clumsiness and bumping into things
Feeling calm, steady and present
questions.explanation: Spaciness, jitteriness, racing thoughts and clumsiness are classic signs you need grounding. Calm and steady is what grounding leads to.

questions.prompt: After a ritual you feel very floaty, and the roots visualisation isn't helping. Which is the best next step?
options: Do more energy work to use up the extra energy
Eat something substantial, drink water, press your feet into the floor, and name things you can see and hear
Drive home quickly before it gets worse
Go straight to sleep without grounding
questions.explanation: Physical grounding (food, water, firm contact with the floor, using your senses) is the fastest method when you're very spacey. Don't drive until you feel fully present.

questions.prompt: You must be able to visualise roots to ground successfully.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Physical grounding and breath-and-words methods work just as well. Use whichever suits you.

questions.prompt: Which of these can a shield NOT do? Choose all that apply.
options: Replace locking your door or leaving a dangerous situation
Replace saying no to someone who is mistreating you
Treat anxiety or depression on its own
Help you feel steadier in a crowded place
questions.explanation: A shield is a practice for your own steadiness. It doesn't give physical protection, replace real-life boundaries, or treat health conditions. It can help you feel steadier in busy places.

questions.prompt: Why do many practitioners prefer a mirror shield that sends things down into the earth, rather than back at the sender?
options: Because it's more powerful
So that nothing is returned to anyone with force: protect yourself without sending harm
Because mirrors only work facing downward
Because the earth needs feeding
questions.explanation: Most covens' ethics allow protecting yourself but not sending harm back. Sending things to the earth protects you without targeting anyone.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to cleanse yourself if someone in your home has asthma? Choose all that apply.
options: Ringing a bell or singing bowl around yourself
Washing your hands and face with intention
Burning a large bundle of herbs in a closed room
Breath and brushing down with your hands
questions.explanation: Smoke can trigger asthma, so choose smoke-free methods: sound, water, breath and brushing, shaking. If you do use smoke, ventilate and use small amounts, and not around anyone with breathing problems.

questions.prompt: What should you call burning herbs to cleanse, and what herbs should you use?
options: Smudging, with wild white sage
Smoke cleansing, with herbs grown locally or in your garden, such as garden sage, rosemary or lavender
Smudging, with palo santo
It doesn't matter what you call it or use
questions.explanation: "Smudging" names a particular practice of some Indigenous nations, and wild white sage is being overharvested. Call it smoke cleansing and use local or garden herbs or reliably sourced resins.

questions.prompt: If you feel under constant psychic attack and are spending more and more time on protection, the right response is to shield harder.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. That's a sign to pause magical practice and talk to your mentor, and to a doctor or mental health professional. Protection practices that take over your day need care, not more protection.

questions.prompt: Describe the two-minute grounding and centring sequence you'll use before and after practice, step by step.
questions.explanation: Three slow breaths; feel your feet and send roots down or press your feet into the floor; let tension and excess drain on the out-breath and draw steadiness up on the in-breath; hand on your centre and gather your attention in; one last breath and notice how you feel.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes slow breathing and contact with the floor or roots (1); includes releasing tension or excess downward and drawing steadiness in (1); includes gathering attention to a centre (belly or chest) and checking how they feel (1). Equivalent physical or verbal methods are fine.

questions.prompt: Give a short daily routine of grounding, shielding and cleansing that would fit your own life, saying when you'd do each part.
questions.explanation: A good routine grounds and centres in the morning, uses quick shields before demanding situations, quick grounds and cleanses during the day, and an evening cleanse and grounding, all fitted to real moments in your day.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes grounding (and ideally centring) at a named time (1); includes a shield at a named time or situation (1); includes a cleansing at a named time, with methods that are realistic and safe for their home (1).

quizzes.title: Raising, directing and releasing: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the arc of a working, the methods of raising energy, directing and releasing it, grounding afterwards, and working in a group. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you raise any energy?
options: Decide your purpose in one sentence and check it against your ethics
Raise as much as you can, then decide what to use it for
Drink something alcoholic to relax
Ask the energy what it wants to do
questions.explanation: Know exactly what a working is for, check that it doesn't harm or override anyone, and pair it with practical action. Energy raised without a purpose tends to leave you unsettled.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for the arc of a working?
options: Raise, prepare, ground, decide the purpose, release, record
Decide the purpose, prepare, raise, focus and hold, direct and release, ground the excess, record
Prepare, release, raise, record, ground
Ground, raise, keep it inside you, record
questions.explanation: Purpose, preparation (cleanse, ground, centre), raise, focus and hold, direct and release, ground the excess, record. Every working, alone or in a group, follows this arc.

questions.prompt: After releasing a working, it's best to keep checking on it and thinking about it so it stays strong.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Releasing is an act of letting go. Holding on tends to leave you jittery and keeps worrying at the working. Do your part, release it, ground, and move on.

questions.prompt: Which describes the breath method of raising energy safely?
options: Breathing as fast and hard as you can until your hands tingle
Holding your breath for as long as possible
Slow, slightly deepened breathing, gathering warmth and fullness in your centre with each breath
Breathing through a cloth to make it harder
questions.explanation: Raise with slow, comfortable breathing and imagery. Fast or forced breathing causes over-breathing, with dizziness, tingling lips and panic. Stop and breathe normally if those appear.

questions.prompt: Which are good ways to adapt raising energy if you live in a shared home and have limited mobility? Choose all that apply.
options: Whispering a chant, or chanting silently with moving lips
Swaying in your chair, building gradually
Tapping a rhythm softly on a cushion
Spinning on the spot as fast as you can
questions.explanation: Quiet chanting, seated movement and soft rhythm all work. Spinning risks falls and isn't needed; seated and quiet methods are fully valid.

questions.prompt: What does "charging" an object mean?
options: Plugging it in
Selling it
Filling it with energy and purpose so that it carries the working
Leaving it in sunlight for a day
questions.explanation: Charging means cleansing an object, raising energy with a clear purpose, and directing it into the object so it carries that purpose. Many people recharge objects regularly.

questions.prompt: A friend is going through a hard time but hasn't asked for help. What's the ethical way to work for them?
options: Send healing energy to them without telling them
Ask them if they'd like you to, or offer a general blessing that doesn't target them
Charge an object and hide it in their home
Do a working to change how they feel
questions.explanation: Direct energy at a person only with their consent. Ask first, or offer a general blessing such as "may all who suffer find ease". Healing work is always alongside medical care, never instead of it.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of overdoing energy work? Choose all that apply.
options: A headache or nausea that doesn't settle with grounding
Being wired and unable to sleep for hours
Feeling drained and flat the next day
Feeling calm and pleasantly tired after grounding
questions.explanation: Persistent headache, sleeplessness, exhaustion, irritability and spaciness are signs to rest, ground thoroughly, raise less next time, and talk to your mentor. Calm tiredness after grounding is normal.

questions.prompt: After a working you're still buzzing and restless ten minutes later. What should you do?
options: Raise more energy to use it up
Keep grounding: palms on the floor, eat and drink, then go for a walk, wash your hands or do something ordinary and physical
Ignore it and go to bed
Drive somewhere to clear your head
questions.explanation: Ground the excess: palms to the floor, food and water, the grounding sequence, then ordinary physical activity. Don't drive while you're not fully present.

questions.prompt: The "cone of power" story of witches in 1940 is well documented by independent historical evidence.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The story comes from Gerald Gardner and later accounts, with no independent evidence. Treat it as a story the tradition tells about itself. The image of the cone is still a useful one for group work.

questions.prompt: In a coven's circle dance, which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
options: Holding hands should be asked for, not assumed
You can step out and sit if you feel unwell
You should know the purpose of the working before you join in
Everyone must dance at full speed, whatever their body
questions.explanation: Group work rests on consent: to the purpose, to touch, and to taking part at all. Anyone can step out, and those who can't dance can drum, chant or hold the centre.

questions.prompt: Describe your first working (charging a candle for a purpose) from start to finish: your purpose, how you prepared, which method you used to raise energy, how you directed and released it, how you grounded, and what you noticed at each stage.
questions.explanation: A full working moves through purpose, safe preparation (space, cleansing, grounding and centring), raising with a chosen method while holding the purpose, directing into the candle, a clear release, lighting the candle safely, grounding the excess, and recording honestly.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): a clear, ethical one-sentence purpose (1); preparation including candle safety and grounding and centring (1); a named raising method described with the purpose held in mind (1); directing into the candle and a clear moment of release (1); grounding afterwards and an honest account of what they noticed, including if little happened (1).

questions.prompt: In a group working, what is the leader's role, and what is yours as a member?
questions.explanation: The leader sets the pace, keeps the group together, senses the peak and calls the release. Members follow the cues, keep the purpose in mind, put in full effort within their limits, release together, and ground afterwards.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): leader sets pace and keeps the group together (1); leader senses the peak and calls the release (1); member follows cues, holds the purpose, releases on the call and grounds afterwards, within their own limits (1).

quizzes.title: Sacred space: test
quizzes.intro: Twelve questions on purification, why boundaries matter, how traditions differ, casting and closing a circle, and leaving safely. You can have the lessons open. You need 80 per cent to pass; your mentor scores the written answers.

questions.prompt: Which are reasons practitioners mark the boundary of sacred space? Choose all that apply.
options: To focus the mind and mark the change from everyday life
To be clean and fit to approach the gods
To hold what's raised until it's released, and keep out unwanted influences
To make sure nothing can ever go wrong in a ritual
questions.explanation: Boundaries help with focus, purity and respect, containment, protection and marking time. They don't guarantee anything, and safety still applies inside them.

questions.prompt: Every pagan tradition casts a circle before ritual.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The circle comes mainly from ceremonial magic and Wicca. Hellenic practice centres on purification with khernips and procession; Heathens may hallow the space; Druids open a grove; Christian folk practice uses prayer and blessing.

questions.prompt: What is khernips, in Hellenic practice?
options: A circle drawn with a knife
Lustral water made by plunging a burning brand into water, used to wash the hands and sprinkle the space and people
A Norse toast
A type of incense
questions.explanation: Khernips is purifying water: a lit match, twig or sprig is plunged into water and the water used to wash the hands and sprinkle. Purification, not a circle, is the heart of Hellenic sacred space.

questions.prompt: What comes first in nearly every tradition's way of making sacred space?
options: Calling the quarters
Purification of yourself and the space
Raising energy
Making an offering
questions.explanation: Purification is shared by almost every tradition: cleaning yourself and the space, physically and symbolically, before marking a boundary or approaching the gods.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to purify a small flat where someone has asthma and there's a cat? Choose all that apply.
options: Cleaning and sweeping with intention
Ringing a bell at the centre, corners and door
Sprinkling a little water around the edges
Burning a large amount of incense with the windows shut
questions.explanation: Sweeping, sound and water are all smoke-free. Smoke can trigger asthma and harm pets; if you use it at all, use a little, with good ventilation, and not around anyone with breathing problems.

questions.prompt: In the most common modern pattern, which element is linked with the east?
options: Air
Fire
Water
Earth
questions.explanation: East is usually air, south fire, west water and north earth. This pattern comes from the Golden Dawn and north-western European geography; many in the Southern Hemisphere swap north and south.

questions.prompt: The idea of four elements (air, fire, water, earth) goes back to the Greek philosopher Empedocles in the fifth century BCE.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Empedocles taught that everything is made of four "roots". The pairing of elements with the four quarters in modern witchcraft is much later, from the Golden Dawn.

questions.prompt: A pan catches fire in the kitchen while you're inside a cast circle. What do you do?
options: Cut a door in the circle carefully first
Close the circle formally, then deal with the fire
Leave immediately and deal with the fire; the circle doesn't matter
Stay in the circle, where you're protected
questions.explanation: Safety always comes first. In any emergency, just go. Nothing terrible happens to someone who leaves a circle in a hurry; you can recast or close it later.

questions.prompt: When closing a circle, in what order are the quarters usually thanked?
options: The same order as they were called: east, south, west, north
In reverse: north, west, south, east
Any order
Only the east is thanked
questions.explanation: Closing usually reverses opening: thank the quarters from the last called back to the first, then take up the circle widdershins (against the direction you cast).

questions.prompt: Which belong in closing sacred space? Choose all that apply.
options: Thanking the gods, spirits or quarters you invited
Grounding and eating something
Making sure every candle and incense is out or safely attended
Leaving the circle open overnight to keep working
questions.explanation: Closing thanks those invited, unwinds the boundary, grounds you, puts out flames and tidies. A space left open tends to leave people spacey and unsettled.

questions.prompt: Describe step by step how you make sacred space at home: either the simple circle from this module, or your coven's own form if it doesn't cast circles. Include purification, opening, what you did inside, and closing.
questions.explanation: A complete answer moves through purification of self and space, grounding and centring, marking the boundary (circle and quarters, or the coven's own opening), the work inside, then thanks, closing in reverse, grounding, putting out flames, tidying and recording.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): purification of self and space (1); grounding and centring (1); a clear opening, either circle and quarters with direction of walking or the coven's own form (1); thanks and closing in reverse, or the coven's closing (1); grounding afterwards, fire safety and tidying or recording (1).

questions.prompt: Why might a coven in the Southern Hemisphere cast its circle anticlockwise and place fire in the north? What does this tell you about the quarters?
questions.explanation: "Sunwise" means following the sun's apparent path: south of the equator it rises in the east, passes through the north at noon and sets in the west, so following it means turning anticlockwise, and the noon sun (fire) is in the north. The usual pattern comes from north-western Europe; quarters are conventions to be applied thoughtfully and consistently, not fixed laws.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): explains that sunwise follows the sun, which moves the other way as seen in the Southern Hemisphere (1); explains that the noon sun (fire) is in the north there (1); concludes that the common pattern reflects north-western European geography and that quarters are adaptable conventions, used consistently (1).

quizzes.title: Wiccan ritual: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the shape of a Wiccan rite, the tools, the circle, the quarters, cakes and ale and drawing down the moon. Most are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers. You need 80% to pass.

questions.prompt: In which order do these come in a Wiccan rite?
options: Cakes and ale, cast the circle, call the quarters, invite the Goddess and God
Cast the circle, call the quarters, invite the Goddess and God, the heart of the rite, cakes and ale
Call the quarters, open the circle, cast the circle, cakes and ale
Invite the Goddess and God, release the quarters, cast the circle
questions.explanation: The circle is cast, the quarters called and the Goddess and God invited; then the heart of the rite, cakes and ale, thanks, releasing and opening, in reverse.

questions.prompt: What is the athame used for in most Wiccan traditions?
options: Cutting herbs and cords
Casting the circle and directing power, not cutting anything physical
Carving candles
Self-defence
questions.explanation: The athame is a tool of will and direction. The boline, or a kitchen knife kept for the purpose, is the one that cuts.

questions.prompt: Wiccan sources all agree that the athame is linked with air and the wand with fire.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The Golden Dawn gives the blade to air and the wand to fire; many Wiccan books reverse them. Learn your coven’s choice and keep it consistently.

questions.prompt: Which are wise ways to keep an athame? Choose all that apply.
options: At home, out of children’s reach
Carried in a pocket to an outdoor rite in a public park
Blunted, as many Wiccans keep it
Wrapped in cloth when not in use
questions.explanation: In many countries carrying a blade in public is an offence. Keep it at home; use a wand or your hand for outdoor rites, or check the law first.

questions.prompt: In which direction is the circle usually cast?
options: Widdershins (anticlockwise)
Deosil (clockwise, sunwise)
Straight lines only
It doesn’t matter
questions.explanation: The circle is cast and walked deosil, sunwise. It is opened widdershins, undoing what was done.

questions.prompt: Someone needs to leave the circle during a coven rite. What usually happens?
options: They must stay until the end
A doorway is cut with the athame, they step through, and it is closed again
They walk straight through the edge
The whole rite is abandoned
questions.explanation: A doorway is cut and closed. Alone in an emergency you can simply go; the circle will not punish you. Ground and recast or close it afterwards.

questions.prompt: In most northern-hemisphere Wicca, which element belongs to the south?
options: Air
Fire
Water
Earth
questions.explanation: East is air, south fire, west water, north earth. Many southern-hemisphere Wiccans place fire in the north, where the noon sun stands.

questions.prompt: In what order are the quarters released at the end of a rite?
options: The same order they were called
In reverse, usually beginning in the north
Only the east is released
