2. **Gather** rushes, straw or paper strips, a white candle, a bowl of milk or water, and a ribbon or cloth.
3. **Weave a Brigid's cross.** There are many guides; the simplest uses folded strips, each one wrapped around the last, until you have four arms.
4. **On the eve, keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
5. Light the white candle and say: "Brigid, if it please you, be welcome in this house." Or if you honour no god: "Welcome, first light of spring."
6. Hold up your cross and bless it, then hang it above your door.
7. Hang the cloth outside overnight for blessing, and bring it in in the morning.
8. Light every candle you can safely watch, one by one, naming something you want to begin this year.
9. **Look for the first signs of spring** on your land in the days around Imbolc.

## With the coven

Many covens make Brigid's crosses together, bless candles for the year, hold dedications of new members, and share dairy foods such as butter, cheese and pancakes. Some visit a holy well.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Imbolc falls on 1 August, in late winter, when wattle begins to bloom in Australia and lambs are born. St Brigid's Day and Candlemas fall in summer there; southern practitioners usually keep the customs at their own Imbolc.

> **Safety:** Lighting every candle is lovely and dangerous. Use stable holders on heat-proof surfaces, keep them away from curtains and children, and never leave them unattended. If you visit a well, take care at the water's edge, and don't leave coins, ribbons or plastic there; they harm the water and the trees.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Imbolc, and whether it honours Brigid, and in which form.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** Imbolc as the Gaelic start of spring, Brigid as saint (and probably goddess), rush crosses, the Brídeóg, Brigid's bed, the brat Bríde, Candlemas candles and weather lore.
- **Modern:** Imbolc as a pagan festival of Brigid in this form, and its use for dedications.

docs.title: The spring equinox in Wicca
docs.summary: The spring equinox as Wiccans keep it: light and dark in balance, the Maiden and the young God meeting in the greening world, seeds and eggs, and a sabbat rite for a coven and for one person, with honesty about Eostre and the hare.
docs.body:
## The equinox in the Wiccan story

The spring equinox falls around 20 March in the northern hemisphere (22 September in the south), when day and night are of equal length. Many Wiccans call it Ostara, a name given in the 1970s from Jacob Grimm's form of Bede's goddess Eostre. The Wheel of the Year lesson on the spring equinox tells its history, and is honest about how little is known of Eostre. Read it alongside this lesson.

In the Wiccan story, light and dark stand in balance, and from now the light will be stronger. The Goddess, as the Maiden, walks the greening earth, and the young God, growing towards manhood, meets her. Some covens tell this as a courtship: the two meet, play and fall in love, and their union will come at Beltane. The earth wakes: buds open, birds pair and build, seeds are sown.

## Themes

- **Balance.** Equal day and night; balance in one's own life between work and rest, giving and receiving.
- **Growth and fertility.** Seeds, eggs, buds, young animals: everything beginning to grow.
- **The meeting of the Maiden and the young God.** Joy, play, attraction, the energy of youth.
- **Planting intentions.** Sowing, literally and in one's life, what you want to grow this year.

## Eggs, hares and honesty

Eggs and hares are everywhere at this season. Eggs as symbols of new life are found in many cultures, and decorated eggs at Easter go back centuries in Christian Europe. The idea that hares and eggs belonged to an ancient goddess Eostre is a nineteenth-century and later invention: Bede, our only source, says nothing of either. Wiccans can enjoy both as symbols of spring without claiming they are ancient to a goddess about whom we know almost nothing.

## Keeping the equinox in a coven

A coven's spring equinox often includes:

1. The usual opening, perhaps outdoors if the weather allows.
2. Inviting the Goddess as the Maiden in the greening world, and the God as the young lord of the woods.
3. **Balance:** a meditation on light and dark, sometimes with a black and a white candle lit together.
4. **The meeting,** in some covens: a light-hearted drama of the Maiden and the young God, or a game or dance.
5. **Blessing seeds:** each member brings seeds to be blessed on the pentacle, to plant afterwards with an intention.
6. **Eggs:** decorated eggs blessed and shared, or hidden for children to find.
7. Cakes and ale, thanks, release, opening, and a spring feast.

## A solitary equinox rite

1. **Set your altar** with spring flowers, a black and a white candle, a small pot of soil, seeds, and eggs (real, painted, or wooden).
2. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
3. **Invite the Goddess and God:** "Lady of the green and growing earth; young Lord of the waking wood: be with me in this time of balance."
4. **Light the black and white candles** together: "Day and night are equal. Dark and light are in balance. From now, the light grows."
5. **Reflect on balance:** sit and consider where your life is out of balance, and one thing you could do about it.
6. **Bless and plant seeds:** hold the seeds, breathe your intention into them ("as these grow, may my courage grow"), bless them on the pentacle, and plant them in the pot.
7. **Bless an egg:** hold it, and give thanks for new life. Eat it later (if it is a real egg, cooked), or bury it in the garden as an offering.
8. **Cakes and ale,** with a portion for the gods.
9. **Thank, release and open.**
10. **Tend your seeds** in the weeks after, and note in your Book of Shadows how they grow, alongside your intention.

The app's ready-made "Ostara: Seed and Egg" is a fuller version.

## Balance in your own life

The equinox invites an honest look at balance. Make two lists in your Book of Shadows: what gives you energy and what drains it; what you give to others and what you receive. Notice where one side is much heavier than the other. Choose one small change for the light half of the year, and bless it at the sabbat. Balance in Wicca is not a fixed point but a movement, like the year itself: day and night are equal for only a moment before the scales tip again.

## Taking it outside

The spring equinox is a good time to begin keeping rites outdoors. Find a quiet place, check whether you need permission, and keep it simple: a cloth, a candle in a jar, a bottle of water for offerings. Take everything away with you.

> **Safety:** Raw eggs carry a risk of salmonella; wash hands after handling, and cook any you eat. If you dye eggs, use food-safe colours. Plant seeds of plants you know: some garden plants are toxic to pets.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps the spring equinox: whether it tells the meeting of the Maiden and young God, blesses seeds, or keeps it outdoors.

> **Try this:** Plant a seed with an intention at the equinox. Keep a short note each week in your Book of Shadows of how both are growing, until Midsummer.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the equinox itself; eggs as symbols of new life; Bede's single mention of Eostre (see the Wheel lesson).
- **Modern:** the name Ostara for the festival (1970s), Eostre's hares and eggs, and the Wiccan story of the Maiden and the young God.

docs.title: The spring equinox
docs.summary: The spring equinox, when day and night stand equal: Bede’s single line on Eostre, how eggs and hares came to Easter, the thin folk record and what modern practitioners have built, and keeping it with seeds and balance.
docs.body:
## When

The spring equinox falls around 20 March in the northern hemisphere and around 22 September in the south. On that day, night and day are nearly equal all over the world, and from then on the days grow longer than the nights.

## The roots

### The equinox

"Equinox" means "equal night". At the equinoxes the sun rises due east and sets due west. Some ancient monuments may be aligned to the equinoxes, though the evidence is weaker than for the solstices.

### Bede's Eostre

The English monk Bede, writing in 725, listed the old English months. He says that Eosturmonath, the month around the spring equinox, "was once called after a goddess of theirs named Eostre, in whose honour feasts were celebrated in that month". That sentence is all we know about Eostre from ancient sources. The English word Easter comes from her name, or at least from the same root, which is related to the words for "east" and "dawn".

In 1835 the German scholar Jacob Grimm suggested that a German goddess Ostara must have existed alongside Bede's Eostre, and imagined her as a goddess of spring and dawn. There is no other evidence for Ostara. Aidan Kelly took Grimm's name for the equinox in the 1970s.

### Eggs and hares

Eggs and hares are everywhere in modern equinox and Easter customs. Their histories:

- **Eggs:** in medieval Europe eggs were forbidden during Lent, the forty days before Easter, so Easter was when people ate them again. Decorated and dyed eggs are recorded from the Middle Ages in many parts of Europe; red eggs are still central to Orthodox Easter. Egg-rolling and "pace-egging" (from Pasch, Easter) were English folk customs.
- **The Easter hare:** first recorded in Germany in 1682, bringing eggs to children. It came to America with German immigrants and became the Easter bunny.
- **Eostre and the hare:** many modern books say the hare was Eostre's sacred animal. There is no ancient evidence for this; it was suggested in the 19th and 20th centuries.

### The thin folk record

In Britain and Ireland there was little traditional folk custom at the equinox itself: spring customs gathered around Easter, Lady Day (25 March, a quarter day for rents and the old new year in England until 1752) and May Day. Elsewhere in Europe, the Slavic custom of drowning Marzanna, a straw figure of winter, was kept in spring, often at the equinox in modern times.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Most of what modern pagans do at the spring equinox is modern, and none the worse for that. Common customs:

- **balance:** marking the moment of equal day and night, often with a light and a dark candle;
- **seeds:** blessing and sowing seeds for the year's garden and the year's goals;
- **eggs:** decorating eggs, eating them, hunting for them with children;
- **greening:** bringing in spring flowers and budding branches;
- **spring cleaning;**
- **honouring** spring deities, including Eostre in her modern form, for those drawn to her.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Decorate your altar** with spring flowers, budding twigs, eggs (real, blown or wooden), and two candles, one white and one black or dark.
2. **Gather** a few seeds and a pot of compost.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Light the dark candle and say: "Night, you have held us through the winter." Light the white candle: "Day, now you grow." Sit for a moment between them, noticing balance in your own life.
5. Hold the seeds and name one thing you want to grow this year for each seed.
6. Plant them, water them, and set the pot in a sunny window.
7. Decorate an egg with a symbol of what you hope for, and keep it on your altar or eat it.
8. **Tend your seeds** through the spring, and notice how your intentions grow alongside them.

## Food and family

Eggs are the obvious food: boiled, painted, rolled down a hill, or baked into breads and cakes. Spring greens, the first shoots of wild garlic (identified with care, since it looks like poisonous lily of the valley), sprouted seeds, honey and fresh cheese all suit the season. With children, egg painting, planting cress in an eggshell, and a walk to find the first lambs, catkins or blossom are good ways to keep the day. If an egg hunt clashes with a family's Easter, hold it on another day; nobody minds two egg hunts.

## With the coven

Covens often bless seeds together, decorate eggs, hold egg hunts for members' children, and walk outside to see the spring. Some make a straw figure of winter and send it away, after the Slavic custom.

## In the southern hemisphere

The southern spring equinox falls around 22 September, when spring flowers are opening. Easter falls in southern autumn; southern practitioners usually keep eggs and seeds at their own September equinox.

> **Safety:** If you blow eggs for decorating, wash them well and wash your hands; raw egg can carry salmonella. Wash your hands after handling seeds, some of which are treated with chemicals. Keep candles stable and attended.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven calls this festival, and how it keeps it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the equinox itself, Bede's one line on Eostre, Easter eggs from the Middle Ages, the Easter hare from 1682, Lady Day, the Slavic Marzanna.
- **Modern:** Ostara as a name (Grimm's form, chosen by Kelly in the 1970s), the hare as Eostre's animal, and most equinox rites.

docs.title: Beltane in Wicca
docs.summary: Beltane as Wiccans keep it: the sacred marriage of the Goddess and God, the fertility of the earth, the maypole and the fires, handfastings, the Great Rite in token, and keeping it joyful with clear consent; with a rite for a coven and for one person.
docs.body:
## Beltane in the Wiccan story

Beltane is kept on May Eve and May Day, 30 April and 1 May in the northern hemisphere (the turn of October into November in the south). The Wheel of the Year lesson on Beltane tells its history: the Gaelic Bealtaine and its fires, May Day customs, the maypole, May blossom and the May Queen. Read it alongside this lesson.

In the Wiccan story, Beltane is the **sacred marriage**. The Goddess, now in the full bloom of her womanhood, and the God, now grown, join in love, and from their union the earth becomes fertile. Everything flowers. In the Wiccan year this is the festival of love, desire, pleasure and joy, as the Charge of the Goddess says: all acts of love and pleasure are her rituals.

## Themes

- **Union and love.** The joining of the Goddess and God, and of all opposites that make life.
- **Fertility.** Of the earth, of animals, of people and of creative projects.
- **Joy and pleasure.** Dancing, flowers, music, feasting, the body.
- **Fire.** The Beltane fires of Gaelic custom; leaping a small fire for luck and blessing.
- **Handfasting.** Beltane is a favourite time for Wiccan weddings, called handfastings.

## Consent first

Because Beltane celebrates love and desire, it needs clear boundaries. In any coven:

- no one is ever expected to kiss, touch, pair off or do anything sexual;
- flirting is welcome only where it is welcome;
- dances are joined freely, and anyone may step out;
- the Great Rite at Beltane, as at any sabbat, is enacted **in token**, with athame and chalice, unless a committed couple choose otherwise in private.

> **Safety:** No genuine coven requires sex of anyone at Beltane or any other time. If you feel pressured, leave, and tell someone you trust.

## Keeping Beltane in a coven

A coven's Beltane often includes:

1. The circle cast outdoors if possible, with flowers and greenery everywhere.
2. Inviting the Goddess as the bride and Queen of May, and the God as the bridegroom, often the Green Man or the Horned God in his fullness.
3. **The sacred marriage:** enacted in token, often with the athame and chalice, with great joy, perhaps with a crowning of a May Queen and King.
4. **The maypole,** if the coven has one: members dance in and out with ribbons, weaving them round the pole.
5. **The fire:** a small fire or a cauldron with a candle, which members may leap over (carefully) or pass their hands over for blessing.
6. **Blessing:** flowers, crowns, handfasting cords, or couples who ask for it.
7. Cakes and ale, thanks, release, opening, and a feast with music.

## A solitary Beltane rite

1. **Gather flowers** in the days before, with thanks, from your garden or where it is allowed. Make a flower crown if you like.
2. **Set your altar** with flowers, greenery, red and white ribbons, your athame and chalice, and a small fire or a candle in your cauldron or a fireproof dish.
3. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
4. **Invite the Goddess and God:** "Lady in your flowering, Queen of May; Lord of the greenwood, in your strength: be with me on this day of joy."
5. **Honour their union:** hold up the athame and chalice, then lower the blade into the cup: "Lady and Lord, in your joining all life is blessed. As above, so below; as within, so without."
6. **Wear your crown,** or tie a ribbon on a tree or a branch, with a wish for what you want to flourish this summer.
7. **Pass your hands over the flame** (not through it) and ask for blessing, health and joy.
8. **Celebrate:** dance, sing, or simply enjoy the flowers and the light. Pleasure is the point.
9. **Cakes and ale,** with a portion for the gods.
10. **Thank, release and open.**

The app's ready-made "Beltane Flower Crown" is a fuller version.

## Handfastings

A **handfasting** is a Wiccan or pagan wedding, in which the couple's hands are bound together with a cord. Some couples are handfasted "for a year and a day", some for life, and some "for as long as love shall last". A handfasting can be a legal marriage in some countries if performed by an authorised celebrant; elsewhere it is religious only, and couples who want a legal marriage need a separate ceremony. Check the law where you live.

## Beltane on your own terms

Not everyone feels like celebrating love and desire. If you are single and sad about it, grieving, asexual, recovering from harm, or simply not in that mood, Beltane can be kept as a festival of flowering, creativity and joy in the earth. The Goddess and God's union is the union that makes all life; it belongs to everyone.

> **Safety:** Leaping fires is for small, low flames only, with loose clothing and hair tied back, and never after drinking. A candle in a cauldron that you pass your hands over is safer and keeps the meaning. Never pick protected wild flowers.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Beltane: whether it is held outdoors, whether there is a maypole or a fire, how it marks the sacred marriage, and whether it holds handfastings.

> **Try this:** Spend an hour outdoors on Beltane morning looking for every flower in bloom. Write down what you find.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Bealtaine fires, May Day customs, maypoles, the May Queen (see the Wheel lesson).
- **Modern:** the sacred marriage of the Goddess and God as Wiccans tell it, the Great Rite in token at Beltane, and the Wiccan handfasting.

docs.title: Beltane
docs.summary: The beginning of summer on May Eve and May Day: the Gaelic Bealtaine fires and cattle, May dew, hawthorn and the May bush, maypoles, May queens, Jack-in-the-Green and the hobby horse, and keeping it as a festival of fire, flowers and life.
docs.body:
## When

Beltane is kept from the evening of 30 April into 1 May in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 October into 1 November in the south.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Bealtaine

Bealtaine (in modern Irish, the name of the month of May) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the beginning of summer. Cormac's Glossary, compiled around 900, says that on this day two fires were lit with incantations, and cattle were driven between them to protect them from disease before they went out to summer pasture. The name has often been explained as "bright fire" or "fire of Bel", from a supposed god Belenus, but its meaning is uncertain.

Beltane fires were recorded in the Scottish Highlands into the 18th and 19th centuries. The traveller Thomas Pennant described in 1769 how people in some places cooked a custard and an oatcake on the fire, and threw pieces of the cake over their shoulders as offerings to protect their animals from foxes and eagles. In Ireland, May Eve was a dangerous time when the fairies were active and butter or milk might be stolen by magic. People hung rowan or primroses at the door, and were careful not to give fire or milk away.

### May Day in England and beyond

May Day customs were widespread across Britain and Europe:

- **Bringing in the May:** young people went out on May Eve or at dawn to gather flowering branches, especially hawthorn (called "may"), to decorate houses and the village.
- **May dew:** washing your face in the dew on May morning was said to bring beauty.
- **The maypole:** a tall pole, recorded in England from the 14th century, set up on the village green, decorated with greenery and danced around. The ribbon dance familiar today was popularised in the 19th century.
- **The May queen:** a girl crowned with flowers, a custom popular in Victorian times.
- **Jack-in-the-Green:** a figure covered in a frame of leaves, carried in May Day processions by chimney sweeps from the 18th century; revived in many towns today.
- **Hobby horses:** at Padstow in Cornwall, the 'Obby 'Oss dances through the town on May Day, a custom recorded from the early 19th century.
- **The May bush:** in Ireland, a hawthorn or other small tree decorated with ribbons, flowers and eggshells.

In German lands, the night of 30 April is Walpurgis Night, when witches were said to gather. In Rome, the Floralia for the goddess of flowers ran from late April into May.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Beltane is a festival of the full flowering of spring: life, fertility, love, joy and fire. Common modern customs:

- **a Beltane fire,** jumped over (small and safe) or danced around;
- **gathering flowers** and making garlands and crowns;
- **maypole dancing;**
- **washing in May dew** at dawn;
- **honouring the fairy folk** with care;
- **celebrating love and life,** including handfastings, which are pagan weddings or commitments.

Some Wiccan traditions treat Beltane as the sacred marriage of the Goddess and God. In an eclectic coven that's one story among others, and Beltane is never an occasion for pressure about sex or partners.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **On May Eve,** hang a sprig of rowan or a few primroses over your door, after the Irish custom.
2. **Decorate your altar** with flowers, green branches and ribbons.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Light a candle or small fire for Beltane and say: "Summer begins. Fire of life, burn bright."
5. Weave a ring or crown of flowers and greenery, naming what makes you feel alive.
6. If you have a safe, small fire (or a candle in a lantern), step past it or over it, saying what you want to bring into the summer.
7. **At dawn on May Day,** go out and wash your face in the dew, if you can. Bring in a flowering branch, and greet the summer.

## Food and family

Beltane food is fresh and festive: oatcakes or bannocks after the Scottish custom, dairy, honey, the first green herbs, and anything you can eat outdoors. With children, gathering flowers for crowns, dancing round a simple maypole (a broom handle with ribbons will do), and getting up early for the dew are joyful ways to keep the day.

## With the coven

Covens often keep Beltane outdoors with a fire, a maypole or ribbon dance, flower crowns, and a feast. Some go out at dawn for May dew, or join a local May Day celebration.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Beltane falls on 31 October and 1 November, in late spring, when much is in flower. Hallowe'en falls on the same night in the calendar, which can be confusing; southern practitioners usually keep Beltane then, and Samhain in April.

> **Safety:** Jumping over fire is optional and must be done only over a very small fire, with loose clothing and hair secured, no alcohol beforehand, and someone watching with water ready. A candle in a lantern is a good substitute. Check fire rules before lighting any fire outdoors. Some say hawthorn blossom brings bad luck indoors; whether you keep that belief or not, some people are sensitive to its scent. Never pick protected flowers.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Beltane, and what it does about fire and dancing.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Bealtaine fires and cattle, May Eve protection and fairy lore, bringing in the May, May dew, maypoles, the May bush, Walpurgis Night, the Floralia.
- **Modern:** the ribbon maypole dance (Victorian), May queens (largely Victorian), and Beltane as a pagan festival of fertility and the sacred marriage.

docs.title: Midsummer in Wicca
docs.summary: Midsummer as Wiccans keep it: the God at the height of his power, the Holly King taking the year from the Oak King, the Goddess carrying the harvest, herbs gathered for the year, and a sabbat rite for a coven and for one person.
docs.body:
## Midsummer in the Wiccan story

Midsummer is kept at the summer solstice, around 21 June in the northern hemisphere (21 December in the south): the longest day, when the sun is at its highest and strongest. Many Wiccans call it Litha, a name given in the 1970s from Bede's month name. The Wheel of the Year lesson on Midsummer tells its history: St John's Eve fires, rolling wheels, herbs gathered on the eve. Read it alongside this lesson.

In the Wiccan story, the God is at the **height of his power**: the sun at noon on the longest day, the lord in his full strength and glory. But the height is also the turning point: from now on the days shorten, and the God begins his long journey towards the harvest and the dark. The Goddess, joined with him at Beltane, carries within her the coming harvest. In covens that tell the **Oak King and the Holly King**, this is the second battle of the year: the Oak King, who has ruled the waxing year, yields to the Holly King, lord of the waning year.

## Themes

- **The fullness of light.** Strength, success, abundance, joy at the height of summer.
- **The turning.** Every height is also a beginning of descent; celebrating what is, while knowing it will change.
- **The sun's power.** Healing, vitality, courage.
- **Herbs.** In folk custom, herbs gathered at Midsummer were thought especially powerful, and St John's wort is named for the saint's day.
- **The fairies.** In English folklore (and Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream), Midsummer Eve was a time of fairy mischief.

## Keeping Midsummer in a coven

A coven's Midsummer often includes:

1. A rite outdoors, often at noon, sunrise or sunset, or around a bonfire on the eve.
2. Inviting the God in his full glory as the sun king, and the Goddess as the fruitful Mother.
3. **The battle of the kings,** in some covens: the Oak King yields to the Holly King.
4. **A sun wheel:** a wheel or wreath of flowers and greenery, sometimes set alight and rolled downhill (in folk custom), more often blessed and hung up for the year.
5. **Gathering herbs:** members gather herbs for the year's healing and magic, with thanks.
6. **A bonfire,** where it is safe and permitted: members may cast herbs into it with wishes.
7. Cakes and ale, thanks, release, opening, and a long summer feast.

## A solitary Midsummer rite

1. **Rise for the sunrise,** if you can, or plan the rite for noon or sunset.
2. **Set your altar** outdoors or in the brightest room, with sunflowers or yellow and gold flowers, a gold candle, and a small sun wheel or wreath if you have made one.
3. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
4. **Invite the Goddess and God:** "Lord of the sun, in your full glory; Lady of the fruitful earth: be with me on this longest day."
5. **Greet the sun:** face it (never look directly at it), raise your arms and say: "Hail, Lord of light, at the height of your power. I honour your strength, and I know your turning."
6. **Reflect** on what in your life is at its height now, and what you are ready to let begin to change.
7. **Gather herbs,** if you have a garden or permission: take a little of each with thanks, and leave plenty. Bind them in a bundle to dry and hang them up for the year.
8. **Bless your sun wheel** and hang it in your home.
9. **Cakes and ale,** with a portion for the gods.
10. **Thank, release and open.**
11. **Stay outside** as long as you can in the long evening light.

The app's ready-made "Litha: Noon Herb Gathering" is a fuller version.

## The height and the turning

Midsummer carries a quiet lesson that many Wiccans value: every height is also a turning. The God is never stronger than today, and from today his light begins to wane. It is a good moment to celebrate fully what is going well in your life, without holding on to it as if it could last forever. Some Wiccans write a letter at Midsummer to the self who will read it at Yule, describing the fullness of this season, so that in the dark they remember the light will come again.

## The far north and the tropics

In the far north, Midsummer brings nights that never quite darken; in the tropics, day length barely changes. Wiccans in these places adapt the sabbat to what their land actually does, as the Wheel lessons discuss. The story of the God's height and turning can be told wherever you are.

> **Safety:** Never look directly at the sun. Use sunscreen, water and shade at outdoor rites. Bonfires only where permitted, with water to hand, and never in dry weather or on peat. Know your herbs before you pick: some, like foxglove, are poisonous, and St John's wort can interact with many medicines if taken.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Midsummer: at sunrise, noon or night; whether it tells the battle of the kings; whether it gathers herbs together.

> **Try this:** Note the time of sunrise and sunset on Midsummer Day. Compare them with what you noted at Yule.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the solstice; St John's Eve fires, wheels and herbs; English midsummer fairy lore (see the Wheel lesson).
- **Modern:** the name Litha for the festival (1970s), the God at his height, and the Oak and Holly Kings as Wiccans tell them.

docs.title: Midsummer
docs.summary: The summer solstice, the longest day: Stonehenge and the solstice sun, St John’s Eve fires and burning wheels, gathering midsummer herbs, love divination, Kupala Night and the Scandinavian midsummer pole, and keeping the height of the light.
docs.body:
## When

Midsummer is kept at the summer solstice, around 21 June in the northern hemisphere and 21 December in the south: the longest day and shortest night. In much of Europe the traditional celebration was on St John's Eve, 23 June.

## The roots

### The solstice

At the summer solstice the sun rises and sets at its furthest north (in the northern hemisphere), climbs highest at noon, and gives the longest day. After it, the days begin to shorten. Stonehenge's main axis is aligned to the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset. Crowds have gathered there at midsummer since at least the 19th century; we do not know what its builders did.

Bede's names for the months around midsummer were Ærra Liþa and Æfterra Liþa, "before Litha" and "after Litha". We know the name, not the festival.

### St John's Eve

In Christian Europe, midsummer was kept on St John's Eve, 23 June, the eve of the birth of John the Baptist. It was one of the most widespread festivals in Europe, from Ireland to Russia:

- **Bonfires** were lit on hills and in villages, and people danced around them, leapt through them, and drove cattle past them for protection.
- **Burning wheels** were rolled down hills in parts of Germany and France, sometimes said to show the sun turning.
- **Herbs** gathered on St John's Eve were thought especially powerful: St John's wort above all, hung over doors against evil, and also yarrow, vervain, mugwort and others.
- **Divination,** especially for love: young women looked for a future husband in dreams, or in water, on midsummer night.
- **Fairies** were active on midsummer night, as Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream reflects.

In Slavic lands, Kupala Night, on the same night, was kept with fires, flower wreaths floated on rivers, and a search for the magical fern flower. In Scandinavia, midsummer is still a great festival with a decorated pole (in Sweden, the midsommarstång), dancing and feasting.

### The Oak King and Holly King

Many modern pagans tell a story at midsummer and midwinter of an Oak King and a Holly King who fight for the year. This is a modern story, drawing on Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) and popularised by Wiccan writers in the 1980s. It is a good story, not an old one.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Midsummer celebrates the sun at its height: abundance, strength, joy, and, as the days begin to shorten, the first turn towards the dark. Common customs:

- **watching the sunrise or sunset** on the longest day;
- **midsummer fires** and candles at dusk;
- **gathering herbs** at their peak, to dry for the year;
- **making sun water**, water left in the sun;
- **flower wreaths,** floated on water or hung on the door;
- **spending the long evening outdoors** with food and friends.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Decorate your altar** with summer flowers, a sun wheel (a circle of twigs or straw with spokes), golden candles and a bowl of water.
2. **At sunrise or sunset,** go outside and watch the sun. Greet it: "Sun at your height, I see you."
3. **Gather a few herbs** you can identify, such as St John's wort, yarrow, lavender or mint, with thanks, and hang them to dry.
4. **Keep the seasonal rite** at dusk, with this at its heart:
5. Light a candle or a small, safe fire and say: "The longest day. The light is full."
6. Name what has grown and flowered in your life since spring.
7. Then say: "From now, the light turns towards the dark," and name something you want to carry gently into the second half of the year.
8. **Share food outdoors** if you can: strawberries, honey, bread, something grilled.

## Food and family

Midsummer food is light and outdoor: strawberries and cream, salads, fresh bread, honey, elderflower cordial, anything grilled. With children, staying up late to see how long the light lasts, making a sun wheel from sticks and string, and floating flower boats on a pond (natural materials only, and retrieved afterwards) are good ways to keep the day. Many families simply eat outside on the longest evening and watch the sun go down together, which is a full festival in itself.

## With the coven

Covens often gather outdoors for midsummer: a sunrise vigil, an evening fire, a picnic, herb gathering. Some float flower wreaths on water, after the Kupala custom, using only natural materials.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Midsummer falls at the December solstice, close to Christmas. Many southern practitioners keep it with a beach day, a barbecue, a fire at dusk and the long light, and blend it with Christmas celebrations with family.

> **Safety:** St John's wort can make skin sensitive to sunlight and interacts with many medicines, including antidepressants and the contraceptive pill. Don't take it internally without advice from a doctor or pharmacist. Mugwort is unsafe in pregnancy. Wear sun protection at sunrise and sunset vigils that run long, and drink water. Fires: check the rules, especially in dry summers, when lanterns are safer.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Midsummer, and whether it watches the sunrise or the sunset.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the solstice and monuments aligned to it, Bede's Litha months, St John's Eve fires, burning wheels, midsummer herbs and divination, Kupala Night, the Scandinavian midsummer.
- **Modern:** Litha as a festival name (1970s), the Oak King and Holly King story, and sun water.

docs.title: Lammas in Wicca
docs.summary: Lammas as Wiccans keep it: the first harvest, the God who gives his life in the grain, John Barleycorn, bread blessed and shared, and gratitude and sacrifice; with a rite for a coven and for one person.
docs.body:
## Lammas in the Wiccan story

Lammas, also called Lughnasadh, is kept on 1 August in the northern hemisphere (the start of February in the south): the beginning of the harvest. Many Wiccans use the English name Lammas, "loaf mass", from the Anglo-Saxon church custom of blessing bread from the first grain; others use the Gaelic Lughnasadh, the festival of the god Lugh. The Wheel of the Year lesson on Lughnasadh and Lammas tells the history of both. Read it alongside this lesson.

In the Wiccan story, Lammas is the festival of **sacrifice**. The God, who reached his height at Midsummer, now gives his life in the grain: he is the corn that is cut down so that the people may eat. His death is not a defeat but a gift, and he will be reborn. The Goddess is the Mother of the harvest, the earth that has borne the grain, and she will mourn him as the year darkens.

## John Barleycorn

Many Wiccan covens tell the Lammas story through the folk song "John Barleycorn", known in English broadside ballads from the seventeenth century, in which John Barleycorn (the barley) is "killed": cut down, beaten, ground and made into ale and bread, yet "proves the strongest man at last". The song was almost certainly a joking drinking song, not a survival of pagan ritual. But Wiccans, following writers like Frazer, have found in it a moving image of the God in the grain, and many covens sing it at Lammas.

## Themes

- **The first harvest.** The first fruits of the year's work, literal and personal.
- **Sacrifice.** The God gives himself; what must be given up or cut away for something to be gained.
- **Gratitude.** Thanks for food, for the land, and for those who grow and harvest it.
- **Bread.** The God's body in the grain, baked and shared.
- **Skill and games,** from the Gaelic Lughnasadh with its fairs and contests, honouring Lugh, god of many skills.

## Keeping Lammas in a coven

A coven's Lammas often includes:

1. A rite outdoors, near fields if possible.
2. Inviting the Goddess as Mother of the harvest, and the God as the lord of the grain.
3. **The cutting of the grain:** in some covens, a sheaf or a figure of John Barleycorn is "cut down" with the boline, in a small drama of the God's sacrifice.
4. **The loaf:** a loaf baked by members, often in the shape of a man or a sun or a sheaf, is blessed and broken, and shared as the God's gift.
5. **First fruits:** members bring the first fruits of their own year's work (a finished project, a skill learned, a harvest from the garden) and offer thanks for them.
6. **Games or contests,** in some covens, honouring Lugh.
7. Cakes and ale (often the loaf itself), thanks, release, opening, and a harvest feast.

## A solitary Lammas rite

1. **Bake bread** the day before, or on the day, if you can: a simple loaf, perhaps shaped like a sun or a sheaf. As you knead, think of the grain, the sun and rain that grew it, and the people who harvested it. A bought loaf is fine.
2. **Set your altar** with the bread, wheat or other grain, early fruits, a gold or orange candle, and a corn dolly if you have one.
3. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
4. **Invite the Goddess and God:** "Mother of the harvest, Lady of the fruitful earth; Lord of the grain, who gives his life that we may live: be with me."
5. **Honour the sacrifice:** hold up the loaf: "Lord of the grain, you were cut down that we might eat. I thank you for your life, given in this bread."
6. **First fruits:** name the first harvests of your own year, the things you have achieved or grown, and give thanks for each.
7. **What to give up:** consider what you might need to sacrifice or let go of for a greater harvest. Write it down.
8. **Break the bread:** break the loaf, set the first piece aside for the gods, and eat a piece with thanks.
9. **Cakes and ale,** with the loaf as the cake.
10. **Thank, release and open.**
11. **Offer** the first piece outside afterwards, for the birds.

The app's ready-made "Lammas Bread Offering" is a fuller version.

## Gratitude in practice

Lammas is a good time for practical thanks: give to a food bank, support local farmers, learn where your food comes from, or volunteer at a community garden. In Wicca, worship and right action go together.

> **Safety:** If you or anyone sharing has coeliac disease or a wheat allergy, bake a gluten-free loaf or use oatcakes or rice cakes. Keep the boline away from hands when cutting sheaves; children should not handle it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Lammas: whether it enacts the cutting of the grain, sings John Barleycorn, holds games, and who bakes the loaf.

> **Try this:** Bake bread for Lammas, from scratch if you can. Write in your Book of Shadows how it felt to make it as an offering.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Lughnasadh and Lugh; the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass; harvest customs and corn dollies; the John Barleycorn ballads (see the Wheel lesson).
- **Modern:** the God's sacrifice in the grain as Wiccans tell it, and John Barleycorn sung as a sacred song.

docs.title: Lughnasadh and Lammas
docs.summary: The first harvest at the start of August: Lugh and Tailtiu, Máire MacNeill’s record of Lughnasa hilltop gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, and keeping it with bread, thanks and the fruits of work.
docs.body:
## When

Lughnasadh, also called Lammas, is kept from the evening of 31 July into 1 August in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 January into 1 February in the south.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Lughnasadh

Lughnasadh (LOO-na-sa; Lúnasa in modern Irish, the name of the month of August) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the beginning of the harvest. Medieval Irish texts say it was founded by the god Lugh, a god of many skills, in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, who died after clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. The Óenach Tailten, a great assembly with games, horse races, trading and marriages, was held at Teltown in County Meath at this time.

### Máire MacNeill's Lughnasa

In 1962 the Irish folklorist Máire MacNeill published The Festival of Lughnasa, a study of how the festival survived in folk custom across Ireland. She found nearly two hundred places where people gathered at the start of August, usually on the last Sunday of July or the first of August, often called Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday or Height Sunday:

- **climbing hills** and mountains together;
- **picking bilberries** (also called fraughans or whortleberries), the first wild fruit, and eating or bringing them home;
- **visiting holy wells** and lakes;
- **dancing, music, courting** and sometimes faction fights;
- **the first new potatoes** dug and eaten.

The pilgrimage up Croagh Patrick on the last Sunday of July, and Puck Fair at Killorglin, where a wild goat is crowned king, are among the customs she linked to Lughnasa.

### The Anglo-Saxon Lammas

In England, 1 August was Hlafmæsse, "loaf mass", recorded from the 10th century. Bread baked from the first ripe grain was blessed in church. One Old English charm instructs that the blessed Lammas loaf be broken into four and the pieces put in the four corners of the barn to protect the stored grain. Lammas was also a quarter day for rents in Scotland.

### Harvest customs

Across Britain and Ireland, the end of the grain harvest (often later, in late August or September) had many customs: cutting the last sheaf, sometimes by throwing sickles at it so no one person "killed" it; plaiting it into a corn dolly or "kern baby" to keep through the winter; and a harvest supper for the workers. These belong to the harvest season as a whole, shared between Lammas and the autumn equinox.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Lughnasadh is a festival of the first harvest: gratitude for what has ripened, the fruits of work, and the first turn towards autumn. Common customs:

- **baking bread** from new grain, blessing it and sharing it;
- **giving the first piece** as an offering;
- **honouring Lugh** as a god of skill, for those drawn to him;
- **games and contests,** after the Óenach Tailten;
- **climbing a hill** and picking wild fruit;
- **making corn dollies** or wheat weavings;
- **giving thanks** for the work of the year, your own and others'.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Bake or buy a loaf,** ideally one you have made with your own hands. Even a simple soda bread counts.
2. **Decorate your altar** with ears of wheat or other grain, early fruit such as blackberries or bilberries, and a golden candle.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Hold up the loaf and say: "First bread of the harvest, gift of the land, the sun, the rain and many hands."
5. Name what you have harvested this year so far: the fruits of your work, learning, relationships.
6. Break off the first piece and give it as an offering. Break the rest and share it.
7. Name the people whose work feeds you: farmers, bakers, drivers, shop workers. Thank them.
8. **If you can, climb a hill** or walk somewhere with a view, and pick a few wild berries you can identify.

## Food and family

This is the festival of bread above all, so bake if you can: soda bread needs no yeast and takes under an hour. Shape the dough into a sheaf, a sun, a person or a simple plait. Early fruit, especially blackberries, bilberries and the first apples, and new potatoes with butter, suit the day. With children, baking together, making a simple corn dolly from a handful of wheat or long grass, and going blackberrying (with care about what they pick) all keep the festival. Games and races, after Lugh's games, are a good excuse to be outside.

Lugh himself is called Samildánach, "skilled in all the arts", in Irish legend. Some practitioners use Lughnasadh to show or celebrate a skill they have worked on this year: a craft, a song, a piece of writing. That fits the festival well.

## With the coven

Covens often bake bread together, hold a harvest feast, play games, or climb a hill. Many also give to a food bank, sharing the harvest with those in need.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Lughnasadh falls on 1 February, in late summer, at the height of many grain and fruit harvests. It suits the season well.

> **Safety:** Never eat wild berries you can't identify with certainty: some, such as deadly nightshade and yew, are poisonous. Hill walks need good shoes, water and an eye on the weather. Have gluten-free bread for those who need it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Lughnasadh, and whether it calls it Lammas, Lughnasadh or another name.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Lughnasadh, Lugh and Tailtiu, the Óenach Tailten, the folk Lughnasa gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, harvest customs and corn dollies.
- **Modern:** Lughnasadh as a pagan festival of the first harvest in this form, and corn dollies as altar decorations.

docs.title: The autumn equinox in Wicca
docs.summary: The autumn equinox as Wiccans keep it: balance again, the second harvest and thanksgiving, the God’s descent towards the underworld and the Goddess’s mourning, and a sabbat rite for a coven and for one person, with honesty about the name Mabon.
docs.body:
## The equinox in the Wiccan story

The autumn equinox falls around 22 September in the northern hemisphere (20 March in the south), when day and night are again equal, and from now the dark grows longer. Many Wiccans call it Mabon, a name given by Aidan Kelly in the 1970s from Mabon ap Modron, a figure in Welsh legend. As the Wheel of the Year lesson on the autumn equinox explains, there is no old link between Mabon and the equinox; Kelly chose the name because it sounded right. Read that lesson alongside this one for the history and customs.

In the Wiccan story, the equinox is the **second harvest**: the fruits, the apples, the last of the grain gathered in. Light and dark stand in balance once more, but now the dark is winning. The God, who gave his life at Lammas, begins his journey into the underworld, the land of the dead. The Goddess, Mother of the harvest, prepares to mourn him and to become the Crone. Some covens borrow the Greek story of Persephone, who goes down to the underworld at this season while her mother Demeter grieves, though the Greek festivals kept it differently.

## Themes

- **Thanksgiving.** Gratitude for the harvest of the year: food, friendship, work, growth.
- **Balance.** Equal day and night; weighing up the year.
- **Descent.** Going inward; preparing for the dark half of the year.
- **Sharing.** Harvest suppers, giving to those in need.
- **Letting go.** As the leaves fall, releasing what is finished.

## Keeping the equinox in a coven

A coven's autumn equinox often includes:

1. The usual opening, perhaps with an altar heaped with fruit, gourds, nuts and grain.
2. Inviting the Goddess as the Mother of the harvest, turning towards her Crone aspect, and the God as the one who departs.
3. **Balance:** a black and a white candle, as at the spring equinox, but now with the dark one lit first or left burning last.
4. **The descent,** in some covens: a short drama or meditation on the God's journey into the underworld, and the Goddess's grief.
5. **Thanksgiving:** each member names what they are grateful for from the year's harvest.
6. **Apples:** an apple cut crosswise to show the five-pointed star within (a favourite Wiccan teaching), shared, and seeds kept or planted.
7. **Giving:** food collected for a food bank.
8. Cakes and ale, thanks, release, opening, and a harvest supper.

## A solitary equinox rite

1. **Set your altar** with autumn fruit, nuts, gourds, leaves, a black and a white candle, and an apple and your boline.
2. **Cast your circle** and call the quarters.
3. **Invite the Goddess and God:** "Mother of the harvest, Lady of the turning year; Lord who journeys into the dark: be with me in this time of balance."
4. **Light the white candle, then the black:** "Day and night are equal. From now, the dark grows. I give thanks for the light, and I welcome the dark."
5. **Give thanks:** name aloud, one by one, at least five things you are grateful for from this year. Take your time.
6. **Weigh the year:** sit with the question: what has this year's harvest been? What did I sow that did not grow? What do I take into the dark?
7. **Cut the apple** crosswise and look at the star within: "The star of the Goddess, hidden in the fruit." Eat half and set half aside as an offering.
8. **Let go:** gather a few fallen leaves; name something you are ready to release with each, and let them go into the wind or onto the earth.
9. **Cakes and ale,** with a portion for the gods.
10. **Thank, release and open.**
11. **Give:** in the week after, give food or time to someone in need.

The app's ready-made "Mabon: Thanks and Balance" is a fuller version.

## Preparing for the dark half

The autumn equinox opens the dark half of the year, which Wicca does not treat as something to be endured but as a season with its own gifts: rest, reflection, study, dreams, and the company of the dead. In the weeks after, many Wiccans turn their practice inward: longer evening devotions, more reading, divination, and time with their Book of Shadows. Prepare your altar for the change: put away the summer flowers, bring in dark cloth, seeds, nuts and candles for the long evenings.

## Gratitude as a practice

Gratitude is one of the simplest and most powerful Wiccan practices. Many Wiccans keep a gratitude list through the autumn, adding one thing each day until Samhain. It is a good way to enter the dark half of the year.

> **Safety:** Wild fruits, nuts and fungi gathered for the altar must not be eaten unless you are certain what they are. Conkers (horse chestnuts), yew berries and many fungi are poisonous. Keep autumn decorations away from candles: dry leaves catch fast.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps the autumn equinox: whether it tells the God's descent or Persephone's, holds a harvest supper, or gathers food for others.

> **Try this:** From the autumn equinox until Samhain, write one thing you are grateful for each day in your Book of Shadows.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the equinox; harvest home suppers and thanksgiving; the Greek myth of Persephone (see the Wheel lesson).
- **Modern:** the name Mabon (1970s), the second harvest as a sabbat, and the God's descent and the Goddess's mourning as Wiccans tell them.

docs.title: The autumn equinox
docs.summary: The autumn equinox, when day and night stand equal again: the name Mabon and why it was chosen, Harvest Home, the last sheaf, the church harvest festival, Michaelmas and the harvest moon, and keeping it with gratitude, balance and letting go.
docs.body:
## When

The autumn equinox falls around 22 September in the northern hemisphere and around 20 March in the south. Day and night are nearly equal; from then on, the nights grow longer than the days.

## The roots

### The name Mabon

In the 1970s Aidan Kelly named the autumn equinox Mabon, after Mabon ap Modron, "Mabon son of Modron", a figure in the medieval Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, where he is a prisoner who must be rescued. Kelly later explained he chose the name because he liked its sound and wanted a Celtic-sounding name; there is no old connection between Mabon and the equinox. Some modern writers have linked Mabon's imprisonment to the waning year. That is a modern reading. Many practitioners prefer to call this festival Harvest Home, the autumn equinox, or Alban Elfed (the Druid name, from Iolo Morganwg).

### Harvest Home

In Britain and Ireland, there was no traditional folk festival at the equinox itself. But the weeks around it were the end of the grain harvest, and that had many customs:

- **The last sheaf:** the last of the grain to be cut was often treated specially: cut by all the reapers together, decorated, plaited into a figure called the corn dolly, the kern baby, the maiden or the hag, and kept until spring.
- **Crying the neck:** in Devon and Cornwall the reapers held up the last handful of wheat and cried out, a custom revived in some places today.
- **The harvest supper:** the farmer gave a feast for everyone who had worked the harvest, with drinking and songs.
- **Gleaning:** the poor were allowed to gather what was left in the fields.

### The church harvest festival

In 1843 the Reverend Robert Hawker of Morwenstow in Cornwall invited his parishioners to a service of thanksgiving for the harvest, with bread made from the new corn. The idea spread quickly, and the harvest festival, with churches decorated with produce later given to the poor, became one of the best-loved festivals in Britain. It is a Victorian creation, not a pagan survival.

### Michaelmas and the harvest moon

Michaelmas, 29 September, the feast of St Michael, was a quarter day for rents and the end of the farming year. Goose was eaten, and folklore said you must not pick blackberries after Michaelmas, because the devil had spat on them. The full moon nearest the autumn equinox is the harvest moon, which rises at almost the same time for several nights, giving light for harvesting late into the evening. The name is recorded in English from the early 18th century.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Because there is so little traditional equinox custom, this is the festival where modern practitioners have built the most. Common customs:

- **giving thanks** for the whole harvest of the year;
- **balance:** marking equal day and night, often with a light and a dark candle;
- **letting go:** releasing what you don't want to carry into the dark half of the year;
- **sharing:** giving to food banks, feeding others;
- **apples and the garden:** making cider, apple dishes, putting the garden to bed;
- **honouring the harvest's gods** for those drawn to them, such as Demeter and Persephone.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Decorate your altar** with apples, gourds, the last flowers of the garden, autumn leaves, and two candles, one light and one dark.
2. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
3. Light both candles: "Day and night, equal again."
4. Name, one by one, everything you are grateful for from this year's harvest: in your life, your work, your relationships, the land. Say thank you after each.
5. Then name something you want to let go of as the nights lengthen. Write it on a leaf, and later put it on the compost or bury it.
6. Share an apple: cut it across to show the five-pointed star of seeds inside, eat half, and give half as an offering.
7. **In the days around the equinox,** give food or time to someone in need, or to a food bank.

## Food and family

The autumn equinox is a time for apples, pears, plums, blackberries (before Michaelmas, if you keep the old saying), squash, nuts and the last of the garden: crumbles, pies, soups and cider or apple juice. With children, apple picking, pressing apples for juice, making a leaf crown and collecting conkers are good ways to keep the day. Taking a box of food together to a food bank teaches the heart of the festival: that a harvest is meant to be shared.

## With the coven

Covens often hold a harvest feast, give to a food bank, put a garden to bed together, or go apple picking. Some make a corn dolly from the last sheaf of a local farm, with permission.

## In the southern hemisphere

The southern autumn equinox falls around 20 March. Easter is also in southern autumn; some practitioners there blend harvest thanks and Easter's themes.

> **Safety:** If you make cider or wine, follow safe methods; homemade alcohol can be dangerous if made badly. Wash windfall apples well. Gather leaves and fruit only where allowed.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven calls this festival, and how it keeps the harvest.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the equinox, harvest customs such as the last sheaf, crying the neck and the harvest supper, Michaelmas, the harvest moon.
- **Modern:** the name Mabon (1970s), the church harvest festival (1843), and most equinox rites, including balance and letting go.

docs.title: The anatomy of a ritual
docs.summary: What a ritual is, the parts almost every ritual shares and why they are there, and how a ritual differs from a spell.
docs.body:
## What a ritual is

A **ritual** (or *rite*) is a planned sequence of meaningful actions, words and silences, done with attention, to mark something, honour something, or bring about a change. A birthday party with candles and a song is a ritual. So is a wedding, a funeral, a graduation, or lighting a candle every evening for someone who has died.

In a coven, rituals mark the Moon and the seasons, honour gods, spirits and ancestors, celebrate life events, initiate new members, heal, bless, and work magic together. You have already taken part in your coven’s own ritual form, taught in your tradition’s ritual lessons. This lesson looks underneath it, at the shape that most rituals across many traditions share, so that you can understand any ritual and, by the end of this module, write and lead one yourself.

## Ritual and spell

A **spell** is a working for a particular purpose; you learned its structure in Spellcraft. A **ritual** is the larger frame. Some rituals contain a spell (a full-moon rite with a healing working); many contain none at all (a seasonal celebration, an offering to a god). A ritual is often more about relationship, celebration and meaning than about getting a result.

## The parts of a ritual

Not every ritual has every part, and traditions name and order them differently. But you will recognise most of these in almost any rite.

1. **Purpose.** Every ritual starts, long before the day, with a clear purpose: what is this rite for? A full moon, a festival, a blessing, a farewell? Like a spell’s intention, everything else serves it.
2. **Preparation.** Planning, gathering what is needed, setting up the space, and preparing yourself: bathing, dressing, fasting lightly or not at all, quieting the mind.
3. **Purification.** Cleansing the people and the space, so that everyday concerns are set aside. Washing the hands, sprinkling water, passing through smoke, sweeping, ringing a bell. Almost every tradition has a form of this.
4. **Opening.** Marking the start and making the space sacred: casting a circle, opening a grove, a procession, lighting a hearth fire, a call to the gods, a prayer. You learned the general idea in Sacred space and your tradition’s form in its own lessons.
5. **Statement of purpose.** Someone says aloud why everyone is here. This simple step focuses the whole group.
6. **Welcoming the powers.** Calling, inviting or greeting the gods, spirits, ancestors, elements or quarters honoured in the rite. Often with offerings.
7. **The heart of the rite.** The main action: a seasonal drama, a story told, offerings made, a meditation, a working of magic, a blessing, a divination, an initiation.
8. **Sharing.** Food and drink are shared, often blessed first and with a portion offered to the powers. In Wicca this is called **cakes and ale** (or cakes and wine); in Heathenry the drinking rounds of **sumbel**; in Hellenic and Roman practice the shared feast after sacrifice. It grounds people and binds the group.
9. **Thanks and farewells.** Thanking and bidding farewell to the powers welcomed earlier, in reverse order.
10. **Closing.** Undoing the opening: opening the circle, closing the grove, extinguishing the fire. A clear end so everyone knows the rite is over.
11. **Grounding and aftercare.** Eating, drinking, talking, laughing, grounding any lingering energy. More on this in the last lesson.
12. **Clearing up and recording.** Tidying the space, disposing of offerings properly, and writing down what happened.

## Why this shape works

This shape has lasted because it suits people.

- **A clear beginning and end** lets people move fully into ritual time and fully out again. Leaving a ritual “open” often leaves people feeling unsettled.
- **Purification and opening** help everyone set aside the day’s concerns and arrive.
- **Saying the purpose** aloud brings a group into one focus.
- **Welcoming and thanking** the powers expresses relationship and respect, in the same way you would greet and thank a guest.
- **Sharing food** brings people back into their bodies and to each other.
- **Grounding** prevents the spaced-out, overwrought feeling some people have after intense ritual.

## A small example

Even the simplest solitary rite has this shape. Here is a ten-minute evening offering, mapped onto the parts:

- **Purpose:** to give thanks at the end of the day.
- **Preparation:** clear the altar; pour a little water or juice into a cup.
- **Purification:** wash your hands and face.
- **Opening:** light a candle and say, “I come to my altar.”
- **Statement of purpose:** “I am here to give thanks for this day.”
- **Welcoming:** greet the gods, spirits or ancestors you honour, by name or simply as “you who watch over this house”.
- **The heart:** name three things from the day you are grateful for, and pour a little of the drink into an offering bowl.
- **Sharing:** drink the rest of the cup yourself.
- **Thanks and closing:** “Thank you. Goodnight.” Put out the candle.
- **Grounding:** a breath, your hands on the floor.
- **Clearing up:** in the morning, pour the offering onto soil.

Once you see the shape, you will find it in every rite your coven does, however elaborate.

## Rhythm and pace

Good rituals have a rhythm: a gentle start, a building of focus, a peak at the heart of the rite, and a gentle return. Think of a piece of music. Too fast, and people can’t settle; too slow, and their attention drifts. Most coven rituals run between thirty minutes and an hour and a half, including sharing. A simple solitary rite might be fifteen minutes.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own ritual form, with its own names for each part and its own order. It may leave some parts out or add others. Ask your mentor to walk you through a typical rite and map it onto the parts above.

> **Try this:** Think back to the last coven ritual you attended (or one you saw described in your tradition’s lessons). Write down each part in order and match it to the list above. Which parts were there? Which were missing or different? Why do you think so?

docs.title: Roles and coven etiquette
docs.summary: The roles people take in coven ritual, and the etiquette that makes a coven work: punctuality, confidentiality, consent, sharing the work, and looking after one another.
docs.body:
## Many hands

In a coven, ritual is shared work. Different people take different roles, and over time most members try many of them. Knowing the roles helps you understand what is happening and prepares you to take part.

## Common roles

Names differ between traditions; your coven will have its own.

- **High Priestess and/or High Priest** (or another title, such as gothi or gydja in Heathenry, or simply leader or elder): the coven’s leader or leaders, who often lead major rites, hold the coven’s lore, and carry final responsibility for its wellbeing.
- **Officiant** or **ritual leader:** whoever leads a particular ritual. Not always the High Priestess; many covens rotate this.
- **Quarter callers** or **element callers:** in traditions that use them, the people who call and later dismiss the quarters or elements.
- **Those who make offerings or pour libations:** in many traditions a particular person makes the main offerings.
- **The person who purifies:** carrying water, smoke or salt round the space and the people.
- **Maiden, summoner or steward:** names for a coven officer who helps the leaders, organises, keeps the calendar, or watches over people’s wellbeing during rites.
- **Scribe:** keeps the coven’s records.
- **Participants:** everyone. Taking part fully (singing, responding, focusing, raising energy) is a role in itself, and the most important one.

## Etiquette: how to be a good coven member

Etiquette here isn’t fussy manners. It is the set of habits that lets a group of people do intense, vulnerable work together safely and well.

### Arriving

- **Be on time,** or a little early. Rituals often can’t start until everyone is there, and arriving late can break a circle that has already been cast. If you’re running late, message the coven so they can decide whether to wait.
- **If you can’t come, say so** as early as you can.
- **Come prepared:** read anything you were sent, bring what you agreed to bring, and know your part if you have one.
- **Come sober.** Don’t arrive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. If the rite includes a drink, you may always choose juice or water.

### Confidentiality

- **What happens in the coven stays in the coven.** Never tell anyone outside who the members are, what they said, or personal things they shared, without their permission. Many people have good reasons to keep their practice private: family, work, safety.
- **Never “out” a member** as a witch or pagan, online or off.
- **Some teachings may be oathbound,** meaning you promise not to share them. Keep those promises. But no legitimate coven will ask you to keep secrets about harm, abuse or crime. Safety always comes before secrecy.
- **Don’t photograph or record** rituals or members without everyone’s agreement.

### Consent and care

- **Ask before you touch.** Hand-holding in a circle is common; check that people are comfortable, and say if you are not. Hugs are offered, not assumed.
- **No one may pressure you** into anything you’re uncomfortable with: touch, nudity (some traditions practise “skyclad”, meaning naked, in some rites; it is never required of a trainee who doesn’t want it), drinking, sharing personal things, or any working. You can always step back or leave.
- **Share allergies, health needs and access needs** with the leaders, so the rite can be planned around them. Accept others’ needs without fuss.
- **Look after each other.** If someone seems unwell or distressed during a rite, quietly tell the leader or the person responsible for wellbeing.

### Sharing the work

- **Help set up and clear up.** Offer before being asked.
- **Bring your share** of food and supplies if that is your coven’s custom.
- **Take your turn** at roles as you are ready. Everyone was a beginner once.
- **Contribute honestly** in discussions, and listen.

### In the circle

- **Phones off,** or on silent and put away, unless the rite is online.
- **Follow the leader’s cues.** If you’re unsure what to do, watch, or quietly ask the person beside you.
- **Leaving during a rite:** if you need to leave (unwell, overwhelmed, a call of nature), it is fine. Your coven will have a way to do this; often you signal the leader, or a door is “cut” in the circle. You learned the general idea in Sacred space.
- **Laughter is fine.** Mistakes happen in every ritual: candles go out, words are forgotten, the cat walks through. Smile, carry on.

## Red flags in any group

Every coven has its quirks, but some things are never acceptable. Leave, and seek help from someone you trust, if a leader or member:

- demands money beyond reasonable shared costs, or sex, or secrets about harm;
- pressures anyone into sexual activity, or uses initiation or teaching as leverage for it;
- isolates members from family and friends;
- forbids members from talking about concerns, or punishes questions;
- claims to be beyond criticism or the only true path.

You learned more about these in the Welcome module. Your safety and dignity always come first.

> **Your coven:** Every coven has its own customs about arrival times, what to bring, dress, how to leave a circle, and who does what. Ask your mentor for your coven’s, and note them in your Grimoire.

> **Try this:** Write down your coven’s customs as you understand them so far: when to arrive, what to bring, what to wear, how to leave during a rite, and who to tell if someone is unwell. Check the list with your mentor.

docs.title: Gathering online
docs.summary: How to take part in coven rituals and meetings held through the app: preparing your space, safety at home, timing, presence on camera, and privacy.
docs.body:
## Covens without walls

Many covens now meet online for some or all of their rites: members live far apart, travel is hard, health or caring duties keep people home, or the coven is spread across countries. Online ritual is different from gathering in one room, but it can be very powerful. Many people find that knowing others are lighting their candles at the same moment, in their own homes, creates a strong sense of connection.

Your coven uses the app for its meetings, conversations and shared work, and may hold rites through it or alongside it.

## Before the gathering

1. **Read what you were sent.** The leader may share a ritual script or a list of what to have ready. Read it the day before.
2. **Check the time zone.** If your coven spans time zones, check the start time in yours.
3. **Prepare your space.** Clear a small area, set up a simple altar, and gather what you need: often a candle, a cup of water or juice, a small piece of food, and anything the script asks for.
4. **Test your device.** Charge it, check your connection, and know how to mute and unmute. Prop it up so your hands are free.
5. **Tell your household,** if you live with others, that you need quiet and privacy for the time. Close the door.
6. **Purify yourself** in a simple way: wash your hands and face, ground and centre.

## During the gathering

- **Join a few minutes early,** to settle in and sort out technical problems.
- **Mute yourself** when you are not speaking, unless the leader asks everyone to speak or sing together. (Online, voices often lag, so group chanting may work better muted, each person chanting at home.)
- **Follow the leader’s cues** for when to light candles, speak, or act. The leader will usually say each step aloud.
- **Be present.** Close other apps and notifications. Treat it as you would a gathering in person.
- **Use the chat thoughtfully:** for short responses or practical messages, not side conversations during the rite.
- **If your connection drops,** carry on the rite at home if you know what comes next, or rejoin quietly. Don’t worry; it happens to everyone.

## Safety at home

> **Safety:** You are responsible for fire safety in your own home. Keep candles in safe holders on heat-proof surfaces, away from screens, cables, curtains and pets. Don’t let the screen distract you from the flame. Put candles out properly when the rite ends, before you leave the room. If you can’t safely have a flame (rented rooms, children, pets, smoke alarms), use an LED candle; it is just as good for ritual.

Ground well afterwards, as you would after any rite. It is easy to close the laptop and go straight back to the washing up, and some people find they feel spaced out or flat later. Eat, drink, and take a few minutes before going on with your evening.

## Making online ritual feel real

Some people find online rites flat at first. These help:

1. **Mark the threshold.** Before joining, wash your hands, change into something you keep for ritual, or ring a bell. Your body learns that this is not an ordinary call.
2. **Keep your own altar in view.** Look at your candle, not only the screen, during the quiet parts.
3. **Close your eyes** during meditations and energy work; listen to the leader’s voice.
4. **Use your body.** Stand for the opening if you can, raise your hands when others do, touch the floor to ground.
5. **Share the food at home.** Have your bread and drink ready, and eat and drink at the same moment as everyone else.
6. **Stay for the chat afterwards.** The talk after a rite matters as much online as in person.

## Including everyone

Online gatherings can include people who could never travel to a circle: those with disabilities or chronic illness, carers, parents of small children, people in remote places. Help make that work.

- Be patient with technology and with people who are new to it.
- Turn on captions if anyone needs them, and speak clearly.
- Don’t comment on people’s homes, backgrounds, clothing or interruptions from children and pets.
- If someone must keep their camera off, respect that without question.

## Common difficulties

- **Lag and echo:** mute when not speaking; leaders can pause after each cue to let everyone catch up.
- **Distractions at home:** put a sign on the door, and arrange the time with your household in advance.
- **Feeling disconnected:** speak a response aloud now and then, even when muted, and keep your own candle as your focus.

## Privacy

- **Don’t record or screenshot** the rite or members without everyone’s permission.
- **Check what is behind you** on camera if you want to keep your home private, and be aware of who can hear.
- **Don’t share** links, scripts or members’ details outside the coven.
- Remember that **messages in the app** are part of the coven’s private space; treat them with the same confidentiality as anything said in the circle.

> **Your coven:** Your coven will have its own way of running online rites: whether cameras are on, how people speak in turn, and what to have ready. Ask your mentor, and ask to see a script from a previous online rite.

> **Try this:** Before your coven’s next online gathering, set up your space and test your device as described above. Afterwards, write down what worked and what you would change next time.

docs.title: Aftercare, and bringing it all together
docs.summary: How to look after yourself and others after ritual, signs that someone needs more care, and how the capstone of this course works.
docs.body:
## After the rite

Ritual can be intense. People often feel strong emotions, deep peace, joy, grief, or a buzzing energy during a rite. Afterwards some people feel wonderful; others feel tired, spacey, tearful, flat, or restless. A few days of low mood after a big ritual or festival is common enough to have a name in many communities: a **ritual drop**. Good aftercare makes all of this easier.

## Common after-effects

- **Spaciness:** feeling light-headed, dreamy, not quite here.
- **Buzzing:** restlessness, difficulty sleeping, racing thoughts.
- **Tiredness:** feeling drained, especially after raising energy.
- **Emotion:** tears, sadness, unexpected memories, or great happiness.
- **Hunger and thirst.**
- **The drop:** a day or two later, a low or flat mood.

None of these means anything has gone wrong. They are normal responses to intense experience. But they need looking after.

## Aftercare, step by step

Right after the rite:

1. **Ground.** Use the methods you learned in Grounding: hands on the floor, feet on the ground, breath, imagining excess energy sinking into the earth.
2. **Eat and drink.** Something with substance: bread, biscuits, fruit, and water. This is why sharing food is part of ritual.
3. **Move.** Stretch, stamp your feet, shake out your hands.
4. **Talk.** Light conversation and laughter bring people back.
5. **Wait before driving** if you feel spacey. Sit a while, eat, and ground until you are fully clear.

Over the next day or two:

1. **Rest.** Sleep well, if you can.
2. **Be gentle with yourself.** Don’t plan anything demanding the morning after a big rite, if you can help it.
3. **Write it down.** Journal about the rite: what you felt, saw, learned.
4. **Reach out.** Message a coven friend or your mentor, especially if you feel low.

## Caring for each other

Look after the people beside you in the circle. Notice who is quiet, who is shaky, who leaves quickly. A simple “How are you doing?” matters. Leaders and helpers should make sure everyone is grounded before they go home.

## Aftercare for leaders

Leaders often give so much attention to others that they forget themselves. After leading, you may feel exhausted, elated, or unable to switch off. Ask someone else to lead the grounding or clear up, so you can eat and sit down. Debrief with someone you trust, and allow a quiet day afterwards if you can. It is normal to replay every mistake; write down two things that went well for every one you would change.

## Integrating the experience

Ritual can bring insights, strong feelings, memories, or a sense of contact with something greater. Integration means letting those experiences settle into everyday life, rather than leaving them in the circle.

1. **Write it down** within a day, while it is fresh.
2. **Ask what it means for your life:** a decision to make, a habit to change, a relationship to tend.
3. **Take one small action** that honours it.
4. **Talk it through** with your mentor if it was significant or puzzling.
5. **Don’t force meaning.** Some rites are simply good evenings with friends, and that is enough.

## When to seek more help

> **Safety:** Ritual is not therapy, and magic is never a substitute for medical or psychological care. If after a ritual you or someone else feel very distressed for more than a few days, have intrusive memories or panic, feel disconnected from reality, or have any thoughts of harming yourself, stop ritual practice for a while, tell your mentor or High Priestess, and contact a doctor, therapist or crisis line. If anyone is in immediate danger, call emergency services. Seeking help is wise and strong, and any good coven will support you.

It is always all right to step back from intense practices for a while. The craft will still be there when you are ready.

## Bringing it all together: the capstone
