questions.explanation: Respect other traditions’ oaths as you would want yours respected. Reading text is not initiation in any case.

questions.prompt: Which is the best-known modern history of Wicca to read during your year and a day?
options: Margaret Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe
Ronald Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon
Charles Leland, Aradia
A website claiming Wicca is from the Stone Age
questions.explanation: Hutton’s 1999 history is the standard. Murray and Leland are sources for Wicca, to be read critically, not histories of it.

questions.prompt: The year and a day is a deadline: if you have not finished in time, you have failed.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It is a minimum. Illness, work and life happen; tell your mentor, and the year can be paused or extended.

questions.prompt: Which are wise in the week before initiation? Choose all that apply.
options: Reading your oath aloud each day
Telling someone you trust where you will be
Fasting for days without medical advice
Resting and keeping your devotion
questions.explanation: Prepare body and mind with rest, devotion and reflection. Never fast without medical advice if you have a health condition.

questions.prompt: Three weeks after initiation you still feel low and unsettled. What should you do?
options: Hide it: it means you failed
Tell your mentor and see a doctor
Do more intense rituals alone
Leave the coven at once
questions.explanation: Reactions vary, but low mood lasting more than two weeks deserves care from your mentor and a doctor.

questions.prompt: Write the promises you intend to make at initiation (as much as you are willing to share), and explain how you tested them and what they do and do not cover.
questions.explanation: A good oath is one you can keep for years, that you understand fully, and that contains nothing an oath should never contain.
questions.rubric: Full marks (4): promises are clear and specific (1); includes a personal promise of their own (1); explains at least one test they applied and a revision made (1); states that the oath does not cover harm, crime or obedience to a person, or shows this clearly (1).

questions.prompt: What will initiation in your coven make you, and what will it not? Explain in your own words, after talking with your High Priestess.
questions.explanation: Knowing exactly what an initiation confers is part of honesty in Wicca.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): states correctly whether the coven is in an initiatory lineage (1); describes what the initiation confers in this coven, such as priesthood and membership (1); states what it does not confer, such as membership of a lineage they are not entering (1).

programs.title: Wicca: Becoming an elder
programs.summary: For initiates called to lead, teach and care for others.
programs.description: Leading ritual and gatherings, teaching and mentoring (and scoring tests fairly), pastoral care with its boundaries and limits, the coven’s governance, and the tradition’s own leadership.

stages.title: Learning to hold space
stages.intro: Leading begins with watching closely and helping well. In this stage you learn what holding space, timing and group energy ask of a leader, and you assist at rites with those eyes open, before you lead one yourself.

tasks.title: Read: holding space, timing and group energy
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Holding space", "Timing and pacing a rite" and "Managing energy in a group".
2. In the answer box, write about a rite you have attended where you felt completely safe, and what the leader did to make it so.
3. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder
Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)

tasks.title: Time a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Take a rite your coven uses (ask your mentor for one).
2. Write it out in its parts and estimate each part’s time.
3. Read it aloud alone, slowly, timing each part with your phone.
4. In the answer box, write your estimates and your timings side by side, and what surprised you.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)

tasks.title: Assist at a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Ask the person leading a coming rite if you may assist: as the carer, the candle-watcher, or leading one step.
2. Before it, agree exactly what your part is.
3. During it, watch the leader: how they greet, cue, pace, read the room and bring people down.
4. Log each rite. In the answer box, write what your part was, three things the leader did well, and one thing you would do differently.
5. Do this at two rites.

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Prepare for when things go wrong
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "When things go wrong".
2. At the space your coven uses (or your own home, for online rites), find the exits, the fire blanket or extinguisher, the first-aid kit, and the address you would give an ambulance.
3. Ask the High Priestess whether the coven has a written emergency plan and who its first-aiders are.
4. In the answer box, write what you found, and the steps you would take if a robe caught fire during a rite.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)

stages.title: Leading a gathering
stages.intro: Now you lead. You will plan a rite in the app, run a meeting, lead a rite with your mentor beside you, and talk it through afterwards. Expect it to feel strange the first time; that is normal.

tasks.title: Read: running gatherings and leading online
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Running gatherings in person and in the app" and "Leading online and hybrid rites".
2. Ask the High Priestess which kinds of gathering your position lets you plan, and how she likes rites written in the app.
3. Tap "Mark done".

links.label: Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Run a meeting
tasks.instructions:
1. With the High Priestess’s agreement, plan a coven meeting (a planning, teaching or business meeting) of up to an hour.
2. Share a short agenda beforehand.
3. Run it: open, go through the items, hear everyone, record decisions, close on time.
4. In the answer box, write the agenda, the decisions made, and what you would do differently.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Plan and lead a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Agree with your mentor which rite you will lead, and when.
2. Plan it in the app: intention, what to know or bring, steps with full words, and parts given to people (ask them first). Put it on the calendar at least a week ahead.
3. Prepare the space and yourself, and name a carer.
4. Lead it, with your mentor present.
5. In the answer box, write how it went: the timing, the energy, anything that went wrong and how you handled it.
6. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Plan a coven ritual (the ritual builder)
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Talk it through with your mentor
tasks.instructions:
1. Within a week of leading, talk with your mentor on this step’s conversation or in person.
2. Ask for one thing you did well and one thing to work on.
3. In the answer box, write what you learned and what you will change next time.
4. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Look back over the six lessons.
2. Take the test. Choice questions are scored straight away; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor on this step, and try again.

stages.title: Learning to teach
stages.intro: Teaching is a craft of its own. In this stage you learn how adults learn, how to give feedback that helps, and how to score written answers fairly, and you practise each on real or sample work.

tasks.title: Read: teaching adults
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Teaching adults: lessons and practice".
2. In the answer box, describe one technique from your own training and how you would teach it using explain, show, try and reflect, with a visual, a physical and a spoken way of doing it.
3. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Teach a short session
tasks.instructions:
1. With the High Priestess’s agreement, teach one technique (for example grounding or a simple offering) to a newer member or a small group, in person or in the app.
2. Use explain, show, try, reflect, and check understanding without asking "Does that make sense?".
3. In the answer box, write what you taught, how they responded, and what you’d change.
4. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Practise feedback
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Giving feedback that helps".
2. Ask your mentor for two pieces of past work (practice logs or answers), with the writers’ permission or with names removed.
3. Write feedback on each using the four-part shape: what worked, one thing to work on, a next step, an open door.
4. Paste both pieces of feedback in the answer box and send it for sign-off. Your mentor will give you feedback on your feedback.

tasks.title: Practise scoring
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Scoring tests and written answers fairly", including the worked example.
2. Ask your mentor for three written test answers with their rubrics (with names removed).
3. Score each against its rubric, point by point, and write a short note explaining each score.
4. In the answer box, give your scores and notes. Your mentor will compare them with their own scores and talk through any differences on this step.
5. Send it for sign-off.

stages.title: Mentoring in practice
stages.intro: Now you learn the app’s mentor tools and what it means to be a good mentor, and you mentor a trainee alongside an experienced mentor before you take someone on alone.

tasks.title: Read: the mentor tools and being a good mentor
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The app’s mentor tools" and "Being a good mentor".
2. In the answer box, write the availability you could honestly offer a trainee (when you’ll check messages and how quickly you’ll reply), and the boundaries you will keep.
3. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Co-mentor a trainee
tasks.instructions:
1. With the High Priestess’s agreement, and the trainee’s, share the mentoring of one trainee with an experienced mentor for at least a month.
2. Reply on their step conversations, give feedback, and suggest sign-offs and scores for your fellow mentor to review.
3. Log each fortnight. In the answer box, note what you did, one thing that went well and one thing you are learning.
4. Send each log for sign-off.

tasks.title: Reflect on power
tasks.instructions:
1. Re-read the sections on power and not being a guru in "Being a good mentor".
2. In the answer box, write honestly about the power you hold as an elder, the ways you might misuse it without meaning to, and what you will do to guard against that.
3. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Look back over the five lessons.
2. Take the test. Choice questions are scored straight away; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the High Priestess.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor on this step, and try again.

stages.title: Listening, power and consent
stages.intro: Care begins with listening well and knowing the power you hold. In this stage you learn to listen, to keep boundaries, to see power in spiritual groups clearly, and to make consent part of every rite.

tasks.title: Read: listening and boundaries
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Listening and boundaries".
2. Practise the listening steps in an ordinary conversation with a friend or family member this week, without telling them. Notice how hard it is not to fix or tell your own story.
3. In the answer box, write what you noticed, and the boundaries (time, role, limits) you will keep as a carer.
4. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Practise listening
tasks.instructions:
1. With your mentor or another elder, take turns: one talks for ten minutes about something real but not too heavy; the other listens using the steps from the lesson.
2. Afterwards, the talker says what helped and what didn’t.
3. Log each session. In the answer box, note one thing you did well and one thing to practise.
4. Do this twice, once in person or by voice and once in writing in the app.

tasks.title: Read: power and consent
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Power in spiritual groups" and "Consent in ritual".
2. Take one rite your coven uses. Mark every place where touch, trance, alcohol, nudity or photographs could arise, and how consent is (or should be) asked.
3. In the answer box, list what you found and suggest any changes to the rite.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Reflect on your own power
tasks.instructions:
1. In the answer box, write honestly: which kinds of power do you hold in this coven? Where might a newer member find it hard to say no to you? What dual relationships do you have, and how will you handle them?
2. Send it for sign-off. Your mentor will talk it through with you on this step.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

stages.title: Safety, crisis and care for the carer
stages.intro: This stage covers the hardest parts of care: spotting abuse, responding to someone in crisis, knowing when confidentiality must give way, and looking after yourself. Take it slowly, and talk to your mentor if any of it stirs up your own experiences.

tasks.title: Read: safeguarding
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Safeguarding: spotting abuse and coercion".
2. Ask the High Priestess whether the coven has a safeguarding policy and who deals with concerns.
3. In the answer box, write the ten steps for responding to a disclosure in your own words, and what you learned about your coven’s arrangements.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Know your crisis routes
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Crisis and referral".
2. Open More → Support in the app and find the crisis lines for the countries where your coven’s members live.
3. Find your local emergency number, the out-of-hours doctor or mental health line, and a domestic abuse helpline.
4. In the answer box, list them, and write what you would do, step by step, if a member told you in the chat that they had harmed themselves.
5. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Read: confidentiality and caring for yourself
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Confidentiality and its limits" and "Caring for yourself as a carer".
2. Practise saying aloud the words for explaining the limits of confidentiality until they feel natural.
3. Do the weekly self check-in from the lesson and write a line in your own journal.
4. Tap "Mark done".

tasks.title: Talk through a case
tasks.instructions:
1. Ask your mentor for an invented case (a member in crisis, a disclosure, a consent problem in a rite).
2. Talk it through together on this step’s conversation or in person: what you would do, in what order, and why.
3. In the answer box, write the case and your plan.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Look back over the seven lessons.
2. Take the test. Choice questions are scored straight away; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the High Priestess.

stages.title: How a coven is governed
stages.intro: Governance is how a coven decides, sets its rules and keeps its records. In this stage you learn how decisions are made well, study your coven’s own documents, and learn what records the coven keeps and how to keep them fairly.

tasks.title: Read: decisions, documents and rules
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Decisions, documents and rules".
2. Read your coven’s creed, rules, requirements and agreements again, with an elder’s eye.
3. In the answer box, write how decisions are made in your coven in practice, and whether the rules cover consent, confidentiality and its limits, alcohol, conduct online, money, complaints, leaving, and what happens if rules are broken. Note any gaps.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Read: records and privacy
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Records and privacy".
2. Look at your own record under My standing, so you know what members see.
3. Ask the High Priestess who keeps the coven’s records and who reads the private notes.
4. In the answer box, write three principles you will follow whenever you note anything about a member.
5. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Welcome a newcomer
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Welcoming, parting and succession".
2. With the High Priestess’s agreement, act as a guide to a seeker or new member for their first weeks: a personal welcome, an introduction in the chat, and a check-in every week or so.
3. In the answer box, write what you did and what you learned about how the coven welcomes people.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

stages.title: Fairness in hard times
stages.intro: The test of a coven’s governance comes when things go wrong: a quarrel, a broken rule, a complaint about a leader, a leader who must step down. In this stage you learn to handle each fairly, and you help strengthen your coven’s written processes.

tasks.title: Read: conflict and removal
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Resolving conflict" and "Removing someone fairly".
2. Practise a facilitated conversation with your mentor and another elder, using an invented disagreement: you facilitate, they play the two sides.
3. In the answer box, write how it went, and the ground rules you used.
4. Send it for sign-off.

tasks.title: Read: ethics and accountability
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Ethics, accountability and complaints about leaders".
2. In the answer box, list any conflicts of interest you have in the coven, and how you will handle them. Then write who a member could go to with a concern about you, and about the High Priestess.
3. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Draft a process for the coven
tasks.instructions:
1. With the High Priestess, choose one process the coven hasn’t written down yet: resolving conflict, handling complaints (including about leaders), removal and review, record keeping, or succession.
2. Draft it in plain words, in no more than a page, using the steps from the lessons.
3. Paste the draft in the answer box and send it for sign-off. If the High Priestess approves, it can go into the coven’s rules or Book of Shadows.

stages.title: Leading in Wicca
stages.intro: Here you learn the tradition’s own leadership: standing as priestess or priest for the coven, teaching Wicca with honesty, holding a circle where everyone can stand as themselves, and caring for those who take part in strong rites. You plan and lead a rite, teach, and work with your High Priestess on the coven’s practice.

tasks.title: Plan a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Priestess and priest in the circle".
2. Plan a sabbat or esbat for the coven in the ritual builder: purpose, shape, words, roles and what's needed.
3. Ask your High Priestess to look it over, and in the answer box note what you changed after her feedback.

tasks.title: Lead the rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Lead the rite you planned, as High Priestess or High Priest or in the role agreed with the coven's leaders.
2. Afterwards, ask people how it was for them.
3. In the answer box, write what went well, what you'd change, and what you learned about holding a circle.

Ritual: Casting and Closing the Circle

tasks.solitary: Lead the rite you planned for friends or a moot, or, if that isn’t possible, keep it alone in full as though leading others, and write what you would need to do differently with a group.

tasks.title: Teach honestly
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Teaching Wicca honestly".
2. Teach a newcomer or a devotee one topic from this course (the circle, a sabbat, the Rede, the history), in person or in the app.
3. In the answer box, write what you taught, one myth you corrected or might have, and how you kept public and oathbound clear.

docs.title: Holding space
docs.summary: What holding space means, and how to do it before, during and after a gathering, including looking after your own state.
docs.body:
## What "holding space" means

When people speak of someone "holding space" in ritual, they mean something simple but demanding: the person leading takes responsibility for the whole gathering, so that everyone else can let go and take part. The leader keeps track of time, of the order of the rite, of the safety of the room and of how each person is doing, so that nobody else has to.

You have already been on the other side of this. Think of a rite where you could relax completely: you knew someone had it in hand, the candles were watched, the words came at the right moment, and if anything had gone wrong it would have been dealt with calmly. That feeling of safety was made by someone holding space. Now it is your turn to make it.

Holding space has three parts:

- **Attention:** noticing what is happening, in the rite and in the people.
- **Containment:** keeping the gathering within its shape: its time, its purpose, its boundaries.
- **Steadiness:** staying calm and present yourself, so that others can borrow your calm.

None of these needs a commanding voice or a magnetic personality. Some of the best leaders are quiet people who simply pay attention.

## Before the gathering

Holding space begins well before anyone arrives.

1. **Know the rite thoroughly.** Read it through at least twice, aloud. Know what comes next without looking. Mark anything that needs an object or a person.
2. **Know who is coming.** Look at who has answered Going in the app. Is anyone new? Anyone you know has had a hard month? Anyone with access needs, allergies or who doesn’t drink?
3. **Prepare the space.** Check it is clean, warm enough, lit, and safe: candles on heatproof surfaces, a clear path to the door, fire blanket or extinguisher to hand, water nearby.
4. **Brief your helpers.** Who calls the quarters or makes the offerings, who watches the candles, who will look after anyone who needs to step out?
5. **Prepare yourself.** Eat something light. Take ten minutes alone to ground and centre: feet on the floor, three slow breaths, your attention gathered into your body. Leave your own worries at the door; you can pick them up afterwards.

> **Try this:** Before your next gathering, write a one-line answer to each of these: What is this rite *for*? What should people feel or carry away? What is the one thing that must not go wrong? Keep the card in your pocket.

## As people arrive

The rite begins when the first person walks in or joins in the app, not when you light the first candle.

1. Greet everyone by name. Welcome newcomers personally and tell them, in a sentence, what will happen.
2. Say the safety basics out loud, briefly, every time: where the exits and toilets are; that anyone may step out of anything at any time; that there is a non-alcoholic choice; who to go to if they need help.
3. Tell newcomers what is expected of them ("Just follow along; you don’t need to speak unless you want to").
4. Notice how people are. A quick "How are you tonight?" with real attention tells you a lot.

## During the rite

Keep your attention moving in three circles:

- **The rite itself:** where you are in it, what comes next, how the time is going.
- **The room:** candles, heat, noise, doors, the weather if you are outside.
- **The people:** who is engaged, who has drifted, who looks uneasy or unwell.

Practical habits:

1. **Speak clearly and slowly,** slower than feels natural. Nerves speed everyone up.
2. **Give clear cues.** "Now we’ll each light a candle, one at a time, starting from the north." People relax when they know what to do.
3. **Use silence on purpose.** A pause after a prayer lets it land. Don’t rush to fill it.
4. **Keep your own practice light.** You can’t lose yourself in deep trance and also hold the room. Your job tonight is to serve the rite.
5. **Make small corrections quietly.** If someone misses a cue, prompt them gently, or simply carry on.

## After the rite

Holding space doesn’t end with the closing words.

1. **Bring people back.** Food and drink, lights up, ordinary talk. People coming out of a strong rite can be dazed, emotional or giddy.
2. **Check on anyone you noticed.** A quiet "You seemed moved tonight; how are you doing?" is often enough.
3. **Make the space safe.** Every candle out, every flame checked, before anyone leaves.
4. **Debrief, briefly,** with your helpers: what went well, what didn’t, what you’d change.
5. **Look after yourself.** Ground, eat, rest. Leading takes more out of you than you notice at the time.

## Practising holding space

You can practise before you ever lead a rite.

1. **At the next rite you attend,** spend the first ten minutes watching the three circles (rite, room, people) as if you were leading. Notice how much there is to track.
2. **Hold a small space first:** lead grounding for two or three friends, or open a coven meeting with a minute of quiet.
3. **Ask for feedback** from one person afterwards: "Did you feel looked after? Was anything unclear?"

## Your own state

You can only lend calm that you have. If you are exhausted, ill, grieving or upset with someone in the group, think honestly about whether you should lead tonight. Handing the rite to someone else is a mark of good leadership, not weakness.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own customs for who leads which rites and how a leader prepares. Ask the High Priestess what she expects of an elder leading in her coven, and whether there are rites only she leads.

docs.title: Timing and pacing a rite
docs.summary: The usual shape of a rite, how to plan its time, how to pace and read the room, and what to do when you run over or rush.
docs.body:
## Why timing matters

A rite has a shape, like a piece of music. It opens, builds, reaches its heart and comes back to rest. When the pace is right, people move through that shape almost without noticing. When it is wrong, the rite drags, or rushes past its heart, or runs so long that people are tired, cold and thinking about the last bus by the end.

Timing is a skill you can learn. It comes from planning well and from watching the room.

## The usual shape of a rite

Most rites, in most traditions, have something like these parts. Their names and forms differ, but the shape is common:

1. **Gathering and preparation** (5–15 minutes): arriving, settling, purifying.
2. **Opening** (5–15 minutes): marking the beginning, making the space sacred, calling those who are honoured.
3. **The heart** (10–40 minutes): the purpose of the rite: an offering, a working, a story, a seasonal act.
4. **Sharing** (5–20 minutes): food and drink blessed and shared, or words from each person.
5. **Closing** (5–10 minutes): thanks, releasing, marking the end.
6. **Returning** (10–30 minutes): grounding, food, conversation.

A typical coven rite runs sixty to ninety minutes from opening to closing. For a group of newcomers, or online, shorter is better: forty-five minutes is plenty.

## Planning the time

1. **Write the rite out in its parts,** and put a time next to each.
2. **Time yourself reading the spoken parts aloud,** slowly. Most people read ritual text at about 100–130 words a minute when they read it well.
3. **Add time for actions:** each person lighting a candle takes 20–40 seconds; passing a cup round twelve people takes four or five minutes.
4. **Add 15–20% for the unexpected.**
5. **Look at the total.** If it is too long, cut. The heart of the rite is the part to protect; openings and speeches are the parts to trim.
6. **Mark your checkpoints.** Know roughly what time you should reach the heart and the closing. Glance at a clock, discreetly, at each.

## Pacing in the moment

Planning gives you a map. Pacing is how you walk it.

- **Slow the openings.** People are still arriving inwardly. Let them settle.
- **Give the heart room.** This is the part people came for. Don’t hurry it, even if you are behind.
- **Keep transitions short and clear.** The gaps between parts are where rites sag. "Now we come to the offering" moves everyone on.
- **Let silence work, but not too long.** A silence of ten to thirty seconds feels deep. Three minutes of unplanned silence feels lost.
- **Speed up gently if the room is restless.** Shorten a speech; skip an optional part.
- **Slow down if the room is moved.** Let a strong moment breathe.

## Reading the room

You learn more from bodies than words. Notice:

- **Engaged:** still, facing the centre, breathing slowly, joining in.
- **Restless:** shifting, looking at phones or the door, whispering. Usually means too long, too cold, or unclear.
- **Overwhelmed:** tears, shaking, very still or very far away. Check on them quietly (see the lesson on when things go wrong).
- **Flat:** polite but distant. The rite may not have connected. Don’t force it; finish well and talk about it afterwards.

## When you run over

1. Decide what to cut before you start, so you aren’t deciding in the moment.
2. Cut from the edges: a longer reading, a second round of sharing, an extra song.
3. Never cut the closing, the thanks to those you called, or the grounding afterwards. Leaving a rite unclosed leaves people unsettled.
4. If people must leave, let them go kindly: "If you need to go, go with our blessing."

## When it goes too fast

Nerves make leaders rush. If you realise you are ten minutes ahead:

1. Breathe. Slow your speech.
2. Lengthen a silence, or invite a second round of sharing.
3. Let the shared food and talk afterwards take the extra time. A short rite done well is better than a padded one.

## An example

A full moon rite for eight people, planned for 75 minutes:

1. Gathering and purification: 10 minutes.
2. Opening: 10 minutes.
3. The heart: a moon prayer read aloud (3 minutes), each person lighting a candle with a spoken intention (8 people at about 40 seconds: 5–6 minutes), a shared chant building to release (8 minutes), grounding (3 minutes).
4. Sharing the cup and cakes: 8 minutes.
5. Closing: 7 minutes.

That adds up to about 55 minutes, plus 10 minutes of margin, leaving room before 75. Checkpoints: reach the heart by 20 minutes in, and begin the closing by about 50. If the candle round runs long, the leader has decided in advance to shorten the chant, not the grounding.

## Practising timing

1. Take a rite your coven uses. Write it out in parts and estimate each part’s time.
2. Read it aloud alone, timing each part with your phone.
3. Compare your estimate with your timing. Most people are 20–30% out at first.
4. After you lead or assist at a real rite, note how long each part really took. Over a few rites you will learn your own pace.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have customs about time: rites that begin at a fixed hour, festivals that last all evening, or online rites kept short. Ask your mentor how long your coven’s usual rites run and which parts must never be shortened.

docs.title: Managing energy in a group
docs.summary: Matching energy to purpose, raising it together, keeping everyone with you, bringing it down, and signs of too much.
docs.body:
## Energy in a group

Earlier in your training you learned to feel, raise, direct and release energy yourself, and you learned that "energy" can be understood in several honest ways: as subtle force, as the presence of gods and spirits, or as shared attention and emotion. In a group, all of these meet. Whatever your model, you will notice that a group has a mood, a pitch and a momentum of its own, and that the person leading can shape it.

Managing group energy means helping the gathering reach the intensity its purpose needs, keeping everyone together, and bringing everyone safely back down.

## Matching energy to purpose

Not every rite should build to a peak.

- **Celebrations** want warmth and joy, often rising and staying high.
- **Workings** (magic towards a goal) often build to a clear peak and release.
- **Devotions** (offerings, prayers) usually want steadiness and focus, not excitement.
- **Mourning or healing rites** want gentleness, slow pace and safety.

Before you plan, ask: what should this gathering feel like at its heart? Then choose your methods to match.

## Raising energy together

Common methods, from gentle to strong:

1. **Shared breath.** Everyone breathes in time: in for four, out for four, led aloud. Calming and unifying.
2. **Humming or toning.** A single held sound, building in volume. Easy for shy people, since no one is heard alone.
3. **Chant.** A short repeated phrase, starting slow and quiet and gradually getting faster and louder.
4. **Movement.** Swaying, walking in a circle, clapping. Keep it simple enough that nobody feels foolish or unsafe.
5. **Drumming.** A steady beat that others follow; the drummer can lead the pace.

How to lead a build:

1. Explain beforehand what will happen and how it will end: "We’ll chant together, getting louder, and when I raise my hands we’ll stop and send it into the candle."
2. Start slow and quiet so everyone can join.
3. Build gradually. Watch the group and keep everyone with you.
4. Give a clear signal for the peak and release. Everyone needs to know the moment.
5. Lead the grounding straight afterwards.

## A sample build

A simple chant build that works for most groups:

1. Teach the words first, spoken, twice: a short line of six to ten syllables.
2. Begin seated, chanting softly together, at a walking pace.
3. After a minute, invite people to stand, and raise the volume a little.
4. After two or three minutes more, quicken the pace gradually, with clapping or a drum if you use one.
5. When the group sounds as one and the energy is clearly high, give the agreed signal: raised arms and a single word, then silence.
6. Hold the silence for a few breaths, then lead the grounding.

Six to eight minutes from start to release is plenty for most groups.

## Keeping everyone together

Groups drift. Some people race ahead, some hang back. You can help:

- **Lead with your voice and body.** People follow the leader’s pace more than the leader’s words.
- **Make eye contact around the circle** so people feel included.
- **Slow down for the slowest,** within reason. A peak that half the group never reached isn’t a shared peak.
- **Don’t let one person take over.** If someone is louder or wilder than the group, move closer to them, lower your own volume, and bring the group back to the shared rhythm. If needed, quietly ask them afterwards to keep with the group.

## Bringing energy down

The release is not the end. People who have raised a lot of energy, or been deeply moved, need help to come back.

1. **Ground together.** "Put your hands on the floor. Let the extra go down into the earth. Feel your feet, your weight, your breath." Give it two or three minutes.
2. **Eat and drink.** Shared food is the oldest grounding there is.
3. **Turn the lights up** and let ordinary talk begin.
4. **Watch for anyone still "up":** giddy, spacey, shaky, or unable to settle. Sit with them, have them eat, press their feet into the floor, talk about ordinary things.

## Signs of too much

Stop building, or bring the group down sooner, if you notice:

- Someone dizzy, faint, hyperventilating or in pain.
- Someone very distressed, frightened or detached.
- Movement getting unsafe: people stumbling, candles at risk.
- The group splitting: some intense, others clearly uncomfortable.

Simply say, calmly, "Let’s slow down now," and lead the grounding. Nothing is lost by stopping early; plenty can be lost by pushing on.

## Low energy

Sometimes the room is flat. People are tired, or the rite didn’t connect. Don’t try to whip it up artificially. Instead:

1. Acknowledge it lightly, if it helps: "We’re a quiet group tonight, and that’s fine."
2. Choose gentler methods: shared breath, a simple song.
3. Let the rite be what it is. A quiet rite done sincerely still counts.
4. Ask afterwards, without blame, what might help next time.

## In the app

Online, you lose most of the cues of the body, but you can still lead energy: speak or write a clear rhythm ("Breathe in… and out…"), use short repeated words, and use the altar together. Everyone seeing candles lit one by one, or the release step marked, gives a shared moment. Give clear starts and ends, and always lead grounding before people close the app and walk off into their evening.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own ways of raising and releasing energy, and its own words for it. Some traditions don’t speak of energy at all but of presence, blessing or relationship with the gods. Ask your mentor how your coven builds a rite to its heart and how it brings people back.

docs.title: When things go wrong
docs.summary: Step-by-step plans for distress, disruption, candle fires and medical emergencies, and what to do afterwards.
docs.body:
## Things will go wrong

Sooner or later, in every coven, something goes wrong during a rite. Someone becomes distressed. Someone disrupts. A candle sets light to a sleeve. Someone faints. These moments are frightening, but almost all of them are manageable if you know what to do and stay calm. This lesson gives you plans you can follow step by step.

The first rule in every case: **people’s safety comes before the rite.** You can always stop a rite. The gods, spirits and the work will keep. Nothing magical is ever a reason to ignore someone’s distress or a physical danger.

## Before anything happens: be prepared

1. **Know the space.** Exits, toilets, the nearest phone signal, the address (for an ambulance), where the light switches are.
2. **Have the kit:** a fire blanket or suitable extinguisher, a first-aid kit, water, a torch.
3. **Name a carer.** For every in-person rite, agree one person (not the leader) who will look after anyone who needs to step out. Tell the group who it is.
4. **Know your people.** If someone has told you of a medical condition or a mental health difficulty, and given you permission, know what they want you to do.

## Someone is distressed

Strong rites can bring up grief, fear, old memories or overwhelming feeling. Tears are common and often healthy. Distress becomes a concern when someone seems frightened, panicky, detached, or unable to come back.

1. **Notice and decide.** Is this ordinary emotion that the rite can hold, or does the person need care? If in doubt, check.
2. **Send the carer,** or go yourself if you can hand the rite to someone. Approach quietly, at their side, not looming.
3. **Ask, simply:** "Would you like to step out with me for a moment?" Respect their answer.
4. **Somewhere quieter,** sit with them. Speak slowly. Offer water.
5. **Ground them gently.** "Can you feel your feet on the floor? Let’s breathe together: in for four… out for six." Name ordinary things: the room, the time, the date.
6. **Listen, don’t interpret.** This is not the moment to explain what spirit they encountered. Just be with them.
7. **Don’t leave them alone** until they are settled, and don’t let them drive if they are still shaken.
8. **If they don’t settle,** or they say anything about harming themselves, follow the crisis steps you will learn in the pastoral care course, and call emergency services if there is immediate danger.
9. **Follow up** the next day with a message.

## Someone disrupts the rite

Disruption can be innocent (a newcomer who doesn’t know the form, someone who is tipsy, a child or pet wandering in) or deliberate (someone heckling, arguing, or trying to take over).

1. **Small things: carry on.** A dropped cup, a giggle, a missed cue. Smile, prompt, continue. Making a fuss is worse than the slip.
2. **Repeated or larger disruption: pause and name it calmly.** "Let’s pause for a moment." Then, kindly and briefly: "Could we keep silence during this part, please?"
3. **If it continues, take it outside the circle.** Ask your carer or another elder to speak with the person privately, away from the group.
4. **If someone is aggressive, threatening or intoxicated and unsafe:** stop the rite. Your job now is everyone’s safety. Ask them to leave; if they won’t and you feel unsafe, call the police.
5. **Close properly once things are calm,** even if briefly, and ground the group.
6. **Talk to the person later,** when everyone is calm, and tell the High Priestess.

Online, a disruptive member can be dealt with in the app: you can ask them by message to stop, and those who moderate can pause someone’s messages or remove a message. Report serious behaviour so the coven’s leaders and, if needed, the app’s moderators know.

## A candle fire

Candles are the most common hazard in ritual. Most candle fires start with robes, long hair, sleeves, paper, dried herbs or altar cloths.

Prevention:

- Candles in stable, heatproof holders, on heatproof surfaces, away from curtains, shelves and paper.
- Long hair tied back and loose sleeves kept clear when reaching over flames.
- Nobody walks or dances near the altar while candles burn.
- Never leave a candle burning in an empty room.

If something catches fire:

1. **Stay calm and act fast.** Shout clearly: "Fire! Stand back."
2. **Small fire on the altar or a cloth:** smother it with a fire blanket, a damp towel or a heavy lid. Don’t pick up a burning thing and run with it.
3. **Never throw water on burning wax or oil.** It can flare violently. Smother it instead.
4. **Clothing or hair on fire:** the person must *stop, drop and roll*, or you smother the flames with a blanket or coat, wrapping from the head downward.
5. **Burns:** cool the burn under cool (not icy) running water for twenty minutes. Remove rings and tight things near it. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag. Don’t use butter, creams or ice. Seek medical help for anything larger than the person’s palm, on the face, hands or genitals, or if you are unsure.
6. **If the fire spreads beyond what one blanket can cover:** get everyone out, close the door, and call the fire service from outside. Don’t go back in.

## A medical emergency

If someone faints, has a seizure, has chest pain, struggles to breathe, has an allergic reaction or is badly hurt:

1. Stop the rite. Turn the lights up.
2. Call the emergency number for your country (for example 999 or 112 in the UK, 112 across Europe, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia). Give the address clearly.
3. Give first aid if you are trained. Follow the call handler’s instructions.
4. Have one person meet the ambulance; have another keep the rest of the group calm and out of the way.

## Afterwards

1. **Close the rite**, however briefly, and ground the group. People will be shaken.
2. **Check on everyone,** not only the person involved.
3. **Write down what happened** soon afterwards: what, when, who, what you did. Keep it factual.
4. **Tell the High Priestess,** and the person’s emergency contact if appropriate and agreed.
5. **Review** with the other leaders: what helped, what to change.
6. **Look after yourself.** Handling an emergency is draining, even when it goes well.

> **Your coven:** Ask the High Priestess whether your coven has a written plan for emergencies, who its first-aiders are, and where the fire blanket and first-aid kit are kept. If there isn’t a plan, offer to help write one.

docs.title: Running gatherings in person and in the app
docs.summary: Planning rites and meetings in the app, notifications, running a meeting, leading on the day, and attendance.
docs.body:
## The work behind a gathering

A rite that feels effortless has usually been planned with care. As an elder you will plan gatherings of every kind: full moon rites, festivals, teaching evenings, business meetings, social nights. This lesson takes you through planning them step by step, in person and in the app.

## Rites and meetings

The app knows two kinds of gathering:

- A **rite**: a ceremony with steps, held together on the coven’s altar. Members can follow each step in the app.
- A **meeting**: a gathering for talking, teaching, planning or socialising, without ritual steps.

Both go on the coven’s calendar, both can notify members, and members answer whether they will be there.

## Planning a rite in the app, step by step

You can plan rites if your position allows you to lead rituals.

1. **Open the coven, then Rituals and rites, and tap Plan a ritual.**
2. **Name it, and write its intention.** One or two sentences: what the rite is for. Members read this first.
3. **Write what members should know or bring.** Be specific: "Bring a white candle and something to eat. There will be mead and apple juice. We’ll be outside for twenty minutes; dress warmly."
4. **Choose its occasion and day.** Pick from the coming moons and holidays, or choose a day yourself.
5. **Add the steps.** For each step write what happens, any instructions, the words to be spoken, and what it sets on the altar (a candle lit, an offering placed). You can copy steps from one of your earlier rituals to save time.
6. **Give steps to people.** Choose who leads each step: a person, a position, or everyone. Ask people before you give them a step, and give newcomers small, easy parts or none.
7. **Tap Plan the ritual, then Put it on the calendar** when it is ready. Until it is on the calendar, members aren’t told about it and can’t answer whether they’ll come.

> **Note:** Write the spoken words in full in the steps. On the night, people reading from the app shouldn’t have to improvise unless the step says so.

## Notifications

When a gathering goes on the calendar, is moved or is taken off, the app can tell members on their phones. The coven’s leaders decide, for each kind of gathering, who hears: the whole coven, certain positions, certain people, or no one. For one gathering you can also choose differently, for example telling only those who have a part.

Good habits:

- Put gatherings on the calendar **at least a week ahead**, two or more for festivals.
- **Don’t move a gathering at the last minute** unless you must. If you do, send a message as well as the notice.
- **Don’t over-notify.** If every small change pings everyone, people turn notifications off and miss what matters.

## Running a meeting

Meetings matter as much as rites. A coven that can’t meet well can’t make decisions, plan festivals or sort out problems.

1. **Set a purpose and an agenda.** Three to five items is plenty. Share it beforehand, in the meeting’s notes or the coven’s chat.
2. **Set a time limit** and keep to it. Sixty to ninety minutes is usually the most people can manage.
3. **Open simply.** A moment of quiet, a candle, or just "Let’s begin."
4. **Go through the items in order.** For each: say what the question is, let people speak (round the circle, so quiet voices are heard), summarise, and decide or agree the next step.
5. **Write down decisions and who will do what.** Share them afterwards.
6. **Close on time,** with thanks.

## An example agenda

A planning meeting for the next festival, 60 minutes:

1. Welcome and a minute of quiet: 5 minutes.
2. How did the last festival go? One thing that worked, one to change, from each person: 15 minutes.
3. The coming festival: date, place, who leads which part: 20 minutes.
4. Costs and food: 10 minutes.
5. Anything else, then decisions read back and thanks: 10 minutes.

## On the day of a rite

1. Arrive or open the app early. Check the space or the altar.
2. Check who has answered Going and who has a part. Message anyone with a part who hasn’t confirmed.
3. When it is time, tap **Start the ritual**.
4. Move through the steps with **Skip to the next step**, and **Back a step** if you need to.
5. When a step belongs to someone else, give them a moment; the app tells them it is theirs.
6. Finish with **End the ritual**.

## Attendance and record

The app notes who took part: someone counts as there when they open the ritual while it is under way. For in-person rites, those who keep the coven’s record can mark people as there in person, or excuse an absence when someone sent word. Keep this fair and accurate; it is part of how the coven sees who is engaged and who may need a kind check-in. Never use it to shame people.

## After a gathering

1. Thank those who had parts, by name.
2. Post a short note in the coven’s chat: thanks, anything to follow up, the next date.
3. Note what you would change next time, in your own journal or for the High Priestess.

> **Your coven:** Your coven decides who may plan rites, who may put gatherings on the calendar, and who hears about each kind. Ask the High Priestess which of these your position allows, and how she likes rites to be written in the app.

docs.title: Leading online and hybrid rites
docs.summary: What changes online, how to prepare and lead an online or hybrid rite, technical trouble, and safety.
docs.body:
## Online rites are real rites

Some people treat online rites as second best. They don’t have to be. A well-led online rite can be focused, moving and deeply shared, and for members who live far away, are ill, disabled, caring for others or not yet open about their practice, it may be the only way they can take part. Leading online well is a skill of its own.

## What changes online

- **You can’t see bodies.** You lose most of the cues you rely on in a room: posture, breath, a tear, a restless foot.
- **People are in their own spaces,** with their own distractions: family, pets, phones, noise.
- **Timing is harder.** Delays, typing and reading at different speeds mean people drift apart.
- **The altar is shared.** Everyone sees the same coven altar change as it happens, which gives a strong common focus.
- **Endings are abrupt.** People close the app and are instantly in their kitchen. Grounding matters even more.

## Preparing an online rite

1. **Keep it shorter.** Thirty to sixty minutes is usually right.
2. **Write the steps fully** in the app, with words to speak and clear instructions for each person.
3. **Tell people how to prepare** in the "what to know or bring" notes: a quiet place, a candle in a safe holder or none, a glass of water, something to eat afterwards, phone charged.
4. **Give parts to people who are confident with the app,** or walk newcomers through it beforehand.
5. **Open the altar early** and check it.

## Leading the rite

1. **Begin with a welcome in the chat** or a short message: how the rite will run, that anyone can step away at any time, that there is no need to light a real flame.
2. **Give clear cues** for each part: "Now we light the candles: each person in turn, starting with Sam." Wait for each person.
3. **Keep a steady rhythm.** Don’t wait too long for stragglers, but don’t race. If someone falls behind, a gentle "Take your time, we’re on the offering now" helps.
4. **Use the altar as the shared focus.** Candles lit, offerings placed, papers released: everyone sees them at once.
5. **Mark the heart clearly.** Online, people may not know when the peak has come. Tell them.
6. **Ground before you end.** "Before we close: put your hands flat on the floor or the table. Feel your feet. Take three slow breaths. Have a drink of water."
7. **End warmly,** and invite people to stay in the chat for a few minutes.

## Hybrid rites

Some rites are held in a room while others join in the app. These are the hardest to lead well.

- **Have two leaders if you can:** one for the room, one for those in the app.
- **Move the app’s steps in time with the room,** so people at home aren’t left behind.
- **Name the people joining from afar** at the opening, so they are part of the circle.
- **Give app members real parts:** calling a quarter, lighting a candle on the altar.

## Making online rites accessible

Online rites can welcome people who could never reach a room, but only if you think of them.

- **Write the words in the steps,** so people who are hard of hearing or can’t speak aloud can follow by reading.
- **Don’t rely on sound alone** for cues; say in the step text what happens.
- **Keep steps short** for people who tire easily or find long reading hard.
- **Allow for different speeds.** Some people read slowly or use screen readers; leave a little more time than you would need yourself.
- **Make it fine to take part quietly:** reading along without speaking, or simply being present at the altar.
- **Time zones:** if members live far apart, say the time in more than one zone, or rotate times so the same people aren’t always up at midnight.

## When the technology goes wrong

1. **Stay calm.** Technical trouble is nobody’s fault.
2. **If your connection drops,** have a second leader ready to carry on. Agree this beforehand.
3. **If someone can’t join,** send them the order of the rite in a message so they can follow at home.
4. **If the rite can’t continue,** close it briefly in the chat ("We’ll close here, with thanks to all who were present") and arrange another time.

## Safety online

- **Candles at home.** Remind people: stable holder, heatproof surface, away from curtains and pets, never left alone. A candle on the app’s altar is a fine alternative.
- **Privacy.** Not everyone can be heard practising at home. Never pressure anyone to speak aloud or to show their space.
- **Distress.** You can’t see someone crying. Watch for people who go quiet or leave suddenly, and send a private message afterwards: "I noticed you left early; are you all right?"
- **Behaviour.** The same rules apply as in person. Those who moderate can pause someone’s messages or remove a message, and anyone can report.

## After

1. Post thanks and a short note in the chat.
2. Message anyone you were worried about.
3. Ask one or two people what worked and what didn’t. Online rites improve fastest when you ask.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may hold most of its rites online, most in person, or a mixture. Ask the High Priestess how she wants online and hybrid rites led, and who is your second leader if the connection fails.

docs.title: Teaching adults: lessons and practice
docs.summary: How adults learn, the explain–show–try–reflect pattern, holding lessons and practice together, checking understanding, and teaching different learners.
docs.body:
## You are teaching adults

The people you will teach are grown-ups with jobs, families, histories and opinions. Many come to the Craft with years of reading behind them; others know nothing at all. All of them learn best when they are treated as capable equals who happen not to know this particular thing yet.

Adults learn well when:

- **They know why.** "We ground after raising energy because otherwise many people feel jittery or drained" sticks far better than "Always ground."
- **They can connect it to their own life.** Link new ideas to things they already know.
- **They try it themselves.** Reading about grounding teaches very little; grounding ten times teaches a great deal.
- **They reflect on what happened.** Writing down what they noticed turns an experience into understanding.
- **They are respected.** Adults stop learning fast when they feel talked down to or embarrassed.

## The four-step pattern: explain, show, try, reflect

Almost anything in the Craft can be taught with this simple pattern.

1. **Explain.** Say what the thing is, what it is for, and why it is done this way. Keep it short: five minutes of explanation is plenty before people need to do something.
2. **Show.** Do it yourself, slowly, while they watch. Say aloud what you are doing and what you are paying attention to. "I’m breathing in for four… I’m noticing my feet… now I imagine roots going down."
3. **Try.** Let them do it, with you there. Expect it to be clumsy. Encourage, and correct only the most important thing.
4. **Reflect.** Ask what they noticed. Answer their questions. Then send them off to practise on their own and log it.

The courses in the app already follow this pattern: the lessons explain and describe, the practice tasks ask the trainee to try and to log, and the answer box and step conversation are where they reflect with you. Your job as a teacher is to bring the "show" part, and to make the reflection a real conversation.

## Lessons and practice together

A trainee who reads every lesson but never practises will pass tests and know nothing. One who practises without reading may build strange habits. Hold both together:

1. **Read first.** Make sure they have read the lesson before you meet to practise. A quick question ("What did you make of the part about shielding?") tells you whether they did.
2. **Practise soon.** The best time to try a technique is within a day or two of reading about it.
3. **Practise often, briefly.** Ten minutes a day for a week beats seventy minutes once. The tasks ask for a number of times for this reason.
4. **Log every time.** Logging (minutes, what they noticed) builds the habit and gives you something to talk about.
5. **Review the log together** every week or two. Look for patterns: "You noticed more on mornings when you’d slept well."

## Checking understanding

Don’t ask "Does that make sense?" Almost everyone says yes. Instead:

- **Ask them to explain it back:** "How would you describe grounding to a friend?"
- **Ask for an example:** "When might you need to cleanse a space?"
- **Ask what they’d do:** "What would you do if you felt dizzy after a working?"
- **Watch them do it.** Practice shows understanding better than words.

If their answer is muddled, the explanation probably was. Try again a different way.

## People learn differently

Some people think in pictures, some in words, some through the body. In the Craft this shows up clearly: one person "sees" energy as light, another feels warmth in their hands, another hears nothing and feels nothing but finds the words of a prayer powerful. None is better.

- **Offer more than one method.** A visual grounding (roots), a physical one (pressing feet into the floor, eating), a verbal one (a short spoken charm).
- **Don’t insist on your way.** What worked for you may not work for them.
- **Adapt for access.** Someone with chronic pain may not kneel or stand long; someone with ADHD may need shorter practices; someone dyslexic may prefer to listen or talk rather than write long answers. Ask what helps, and adapt. A coven that only teaches one body and one kind of mind loses good people.
- **Accept "I didn’t notice anything".** It is common and normal at first. Help them keep practising without pretending.

## Pace

Let the trainee set much of the pace. Some will race; slow them down, because skipping practice leaves gaps. Some will stall; find out why. Life gets in the way, and a kind "How are things? Would a lighter month help?" often does more than a reminder.

## Teaching a group

When you teach several people at once:

1. **Plan a short session:** fifteen minutes of explaining and showing, thirty of trying, fifteen of reflecting.
2. **Keep the explanation short** and invite questions throughout.
3. **Pair people up** for practice, so they can help each other.
4. **Go round the circle** at the end so everyone speaks.
5. **Follow up** with a note in the chat: the main points, and what to practise.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own customs for teaching: some keep strictly to the program; others add their own lessons from the Book of Shadows. Ask the High Priestess what she wants taught in person, and what she is happy for trainees to learn from the app alone.

docs.title: Giving feedback that helps
docs.summary: What good feedback looks like, a simple four-part shape, writing it well, sending work back, and praising well.
docs.body:
## Feedback is how people improve

When a trainee writes an answer, logs a practice, or leads their first rite, what you say next shapes what they do next. Good feedback helps them improve and keeps them motivated. Poor feedback, whether harsh, vague or simply missing, leaves them discouraged or confused. Feedback is one of the most important things a mentor does.

## What good feedback looks like

Good feedback is:

- **Specific.** "Your description of how the grounding felt in your legs was clear and careful" is useful. "Great work!" is pleasant but teaches nothing.
- **Timely.** Within a few days. Feedback on a practice log three weeks later is hardly feedback at all.
- **Balanced.** It says what is working as well as what to improve. People need to know what to keep doing.
- **Focused.** One or two things to work on, not ten. Choose what matters most.
- **Actionable.** It says what to do next. "Try counting your breath for the first minute before you start the visualisation."
- **About the work, not the person.** "This answer doesn’t mention fire safety" not "You’re careless."
- **Kind.** Honest and kind are not opposites. You can say something clearly and gently at once.

## A simple shape to use

For most written answers and practice logs, this shape works well:

1. **What worked.** One or two specific things they did well.
2. **One thing to work on.** The most important improvement, said plainly.
3. **A next step.** Something concrete to try.
4. **An open door.** An invitation to ask or reply.

An example, replying to a trainee’s grounding log:

"Thank you for logging all seven sessions; that consistency is exactly how this gets easier. I liked how you noticed that the grounding felt stronger outdoors. One thing to work on: you’ve been stopping after two or three minutes, before it has time to settle. Next week, try staying with it for five minutes, even if nothing seems to change. Tell me what you notice. Any questions, just ask here."

## Feedback in writing

Most of your feedback will be written, in the step conversations and when you sign off or send back work. Writing loses tone of voice, so:

- **Read it back before you send** as if you were a nervous beginner receiving it.
- **Use their name** and warm, plain words.
- **Avoid sarcasm and jokes** at their expense; they read far worse in writing.
- **Keep it short:** three to six sentences is usually right.
- **If it’s hard news,** offer to talk by voice or in person.

## Sending work back

Sometimes work isn’t ready to sign off: it misses the point, skips the safety, or shows the practice wasn’t done. Sending it back is part of teaching, not a punishment.

1. **Say what is good** first, if anything is.
2. **Say exactly what is missing,** referring to the task or rubric. "The task asks what you would do if a candle fell over, and that isn’t in your answer yet."
3. **Say what would make it complete.**
4. **Reassure.** "This is normal; most people need a second go at this one."

## When feedback isn’t welcome

Some people bristle at any correction. Some go quiet. Some argue every point.

- **Stay calm and don’t take it personally.** Feedback often touches old wounds about school or work.
- **Listen to their side.** Sometimes they have a point; sometimes the task was unclear.
- **Hold to what matters,** especially safety and consent. You can be flexible about style, never about those.
- **Ask what kind of feedback helps them.** Some people want it short and direct; others want more encouragement. Adjust where you can.
- **If it keeps going badly,** talk to the High Priestess. A different mentor may suit them better, and that is nobody’s failure.

## Praise well

Praise is feedback too, and it is easy to do badly.

- **Praise effort and practice,** not talent. "You kept practising even when it felt like nothing was happening" encourages persistence. "You’re a natural" encourages people to give up when it gets hard.
- **Be specific and sincere.** Empty praise is soon ignored.
- **Don’t over-praise beginners’ experiences.** Telling someone their first meditation vision means they are gifted can set up unhealthy expectations. Receive it warmly, and encourage them to keep observing.

## Feedback on a rite someone led

When a trainee leads their first rite, feedback matters doubly: they are exposed, tired and often anxious about how it went.

1. **Wait a little.** Straight after the rite, say only something warm and true: "Thank you; that was lovely to be part of."
2. **Within a few days, ask them first:** "How do you feel it went? What would you change?" Most people already know what went wrong.
3. **Add what they missed,** kindly: one or two things at most.
4. **Name specific strengths:** "Your pacing in the candle round was just right; nobody felt rushed."
5. **Agree one thing to work on next time.**

Never critique a rite in front of the coven. Talk to the person who led it, privately.

## Receiving feedback yourself

You will also get feedback: from the High Priestess, from other elders, and from your trainees. Model what you hope they will do: listen, thank them, think about it, and change what needs changing.

> **Try this:** Take the last three messages you sent to someone you were helping (in the coven or elsewhere). For each, check: was it specific, balanced, focused and actionable? Rewrite one using the four-part shape.

docs.title: Scoring tests and written answers fairly
docs.summary: Rubrics, scoring step by step, consistency, bias awareness, borderline answers, and a worked example.
docs.body:
## Why fair scoring matters

The tests in the coven’s courses are scored in two ways. Choice questions (single answer, several answers, true or false) are scored by the app at once. Written answers, short and long, are scored by a person: usually the trainee’s mentor or the coven’s head. That may now be you.

Scoring written answers is a real responsibility. A trainee who is marked harshly may give up; one marked too generously may go on without understanding something important, such as fire safety or consent. And if different mentors score the same answer differently, trainees rightly feel the system is unfair. Fair scoring is consistent, honest, and focused on understanding.

## What a rubric is

A **rubric** is a short guide for scoring one question. Every written question in the courses has one. It says what a full-marks answer includes, usually as a list of points each worth a mark. For example:

"Full marks (3): explains what grounding is (1); gives one method in steps (1); says when to use it, such as after raising energy or when feeling spacey (1)."

The rubric is your anchor. It stops you from scoring by mood, by how well you like the trainee, or by how polished the writing is.

## Scoring step by step

1. **Read the question and the rubric first,** before you read the answer. Know what you are looking for.
2. **Read the whole answer once** without scoring, to understand what they are saying.
3. **Go through the rubric point by point.** For each point, ask: is this clearly present in the answer, in any words? Mark it yes or no.
4. **Credit meaning, not wording.** If the rubric says "describes grounding" and the trainee writes "letting the extra buzz drain down into the floor through your feet", that counts. They don’t need to use the course’s words.
5. **Add up the points.** Use the rubric’s guidance for part marks, if it gives any.
6. **Check for anything harmful.** If an answer contains something unsafe (for example, suggesting ingesting an essential oil, or working magic on someone without consent), don’t give credit for that part even if other points are covered, and always address it in your feedback.
7. **Write a short note** explaining the score: which points were there, which were missing, and what to look at again.

## Consistency

Scoring the same quality of answer the same way, every time, for everyone, is the heart of fairness.

- **Score one question at a time across several trainees,** if you mentor more than one, rather than one trainee’s whole test at a time. You will compare like with like.
- **Keep a note of borderline decisions:** "I gave the mark for 'when to use it' to an answer that only said 'after rituals'." Next time, decide the same way.
- **Compare with another scorer** now and then. Ask another mentor to score the same answer without seeing your mark, then compare. If you differ, talk it through and agree.
- **Don’t drift.** Your hundredth answer should be scored by the same standard as your first. Re-read the rubric every time.

## Bias awareness

Everyone has biases. Good scorers know theirs and guard against them. The common ones:

- **The halo effect:** a trainee you like, or who did well before, gets the benefit of the doubt. One who annoys you doesn’t.
- **Fluency bias:** polished, confident writing scores higher than awkward writing saying the same thing. This penalises people writing in a second language, people with dyslexia, and people who simply don’t write much.
- **Length bias:** long answers look more thorough. They aren’t always. A short answer that hits every point earns full marks.
- **Agreement bias:** answers that match your own views or practice score higher. The rubric, not your preference, decides.
- **Mood and fatigue:** answers scored late at night or after a bad day come out harsher. Score when you are fresh.
- **Order effects:** an ordinary answer after a brilliant one looks worse than it is.

Practical guards:

1. **Score against the rubric, not against the trainee.** Ask "Is the point there?", not "Is this person good?"
2. **Ignore spelling, grammar and style** unless the rubric asks for them. They almost never matter here.
3. **When unsure, re-read the answer slowly,** asking what they meant.
4. **If you know your judgement is clouded** (you are in conflict with the trainee, or very close to them), ask someone else to score it.

## Borderline answers

When a point is half there:

- **If the rubric allows part marks,** use them as it says.
- **If not, ask yourself:** would a fair reader agree that the point is made? If yes, give it; if genuinely no, don’t.
- **Be consistent** with how you decided last time.
- **Use the feedback,** not the score, to push for more precision: "You got the mark, but say a bit more next time about *why* we ground."

## When a trainee doesn’t pass

The pass mark is usually 80%. A trainee below it should:

1. Get a clear, kind note: which answers fell short and why.
2. Be pointed to the lessons to read again.
3. Be invited to talk on the step conversation.
4. Try again when ready.

Never pass someone who hasn’t understood safety or consent points simply because they are nearly there, or because you like them. Those points protect people.

## Worked example

Question: "What would you do if a candle fell over during a rite at home?" Rubric: "Full marks (3): stay calm and act at once (1); smother a small fire, never water on wax (1); if it spreads, get out and call the fire service (1)."

- **Answer A:** "Throw my drink on it quickly and carry on." Score: 0. Acting fast is implied but water on wax is unsafe; this needs a clear safety note in feedback.
- **Answer B:** "Smother it with a towel or the lid of a pot. If it was getting bigger I’d leave the room, shut the door and ring 999." Score: 3. Calm, immediate action is implied by the steps, the method is right, and spreading fire is handled.
- **Answer C:** "Put it out with a fire blanket." Score: 1 or 2, depending on how you decide "stay calm and act at once" is shown. Decide, note your rule, and keep to it. In feedback, ask what they’d do if it spread.

> **Your coven:** The High Priestess may want to review scores, or score some tests herself, especially for steps that lead to a new position. Ask how she wants scoring shared, and who to ask when you’re unsure.

docs.title: The app’s mentor tools
docs.summary: Programs and tasks, step conversations, signing off and sending back, confirming stages, scoring tests, progress, check-ins and handover.
docs.body:
## The app as your mentoring room

Much of your mentoring will happen in the app: reading answers, replying on step conversations, signing off work, scoring tests and keeping track of how each trainee is doing. This lesson walks you through the tools and how to use them well. The exact buttons may change as the app grows; the habits will not.

## Programs, stages and tasks

A coven’s training is organised into **programs** (for example, "Becoming a devotee"). Each program has **stages**, and each stage has **tasks**. A task may have lessons to read, a practice to do a number of times, an answer box, and a test.

Each task says who checks it:

- **Self:** the trainee marks it done themselves. Usually for routine reading or logging.
- **Mentor:** you sign it off.
- **Manager:** the coven’s head, or whoever runs training, signs it off.

Each stage also says who confirms it is complete, and may have a least time (for example thirty days) before it can be.

## Being assigned as a mentor

The High Priestess, or whoever manages training, assigns programs to people and chooses their mentors (under **Initiation & training**, in the program’s Assign and Mentors settings). When you are a mentor, the trainee’s work comes to you. Make sure you know:

1. Which trainees you mentor, and in which programs.
2. Which tasks you sign off, and which go to the coven’s head.
3. How the coven’s head wants to hear about progress or concerns.

## The step conversation

Every step of a program has its own conversation between the trainee and those who mentor and lead them. It is the most important tool you have.

Use it for:

- **Welcoming** them to a new stage, and saying what to focus on.
- **Answering questions** about the lessons or the practice.
- **Feedback** on their answers and logs.
- **Checking in** when they’ve gone quiet.

Good habits:

1. **Reply within the time you’ve agreed** (see the next lesson). Two or three days is a reasonable standard.
2. **Keep it on the step.** Questions about grounding go on the grounding step. This keeps a clear record and helps anyone who takes over mentoring later.
3. **Keep it about the training.** Personal matters can be handled with care, but a step conversation is not the place for private counselling (see the pastoral care course).
4. **Remember who can read it.** Those who lead the coven’s training may be able to see step conversations. Tell your trainee so, and don’t write anything you wouldn’t want them to see.

## Signing off

When a trainee finishes a task you check, they send it for sign-off. You then read their answer or log and either:

- **Sign it off,** with a short note of what was good; or
- **Send it back,** with a clear note of what is missing and how to complete it.

Before signing off, check:

1. Did they do what the task asked, the number of times it asked?
2. Does their answer show they understood the lesson, especially any safety points?
3. Is there anything in it that worries you (distress, unsafe practice, signs of pressure from someone)? If so, address it before or alongside signing off.

Don’t sign off work you haven’t read, and don’t leave work waiting for weeks. Both tell the trainee their effort doesn’t matter.

## Confirming a stage

When every task in a stage is done and any least time has passed, the stage can be confirmed by whoever its "passed by" names. If that is you, take a moment to look over the whole stage: is the trainee ready for the next one? If not, talk to them about what they need first.

## Scoring tests

When a trainee takes a test, the app scores the choice questions immediately. The written answers wait for a person to score them against their rubrics. When you score:

1. Open the trainee’s test answers.
2. For each written answer, read the rubric, then the answer, and score as you learned in the lesson on fair scoring.
3. Add a short note to each, especially where points were missed.
4. If the total reaches the pass mark, they pass. If not, tell them kindly what to look at, and invite them to try again.

## Seeing progress

Those whom the coven’s head allows can see everyone’s progress in the coven’s programs. The coven’s **members’ record** also shows, for each member, rites attended, studies and mentoring. Mentors can log **check-ins** there: a short note each time you meet or talk with a trainee about how they’re doing. The coven’s head decides whether mentees can read their mentor’s check-ins.

Use these tools to notice, not to police:

- A trainee who hasn’t logged anything for three weeks may need a kind message, not a warning.
- A trainee racing through without much in their answers may need slowing down.
- A pattern of missed rites may be about life, health or money; ask gently.

## Handing over

If you need to stop mentoring someone (moving, illness, too many commitments, or the pairing isn’t working), tell the High Priestess early. Write a short handover note for the new mentor: where the trainee is, what they find easy and hard, anything agreed. Tell the trainee yourself, kindly, so they don’t feel dropped.

> **Your coven:** Every coven sets up its training a little differently. Ask the High Priestess which tasks you will sign off, which she keeps for herself, whether mentees can read your check-ins, and how often she wants to hear from you about each trainee.

docs.title: Being a good mentor
docs.summary: Availability, boundaries, power, not being a guru, discernment about experiences, and ending mentoring well.
docs.body:
## What a mentor is for

A mentor walks alongside someone as they learn. You are not their master, their therapist, their parent or their guru. You are an experienced companion who knows the path a little further ahead, can answer questions, can show them how, and can tell them honestly how they’re doing. The best mentors make themselves gradually less necessary.

## Availability

Trainees need to know when and how they can reach you, and you need time for your own life.

1. **Agree it at the start.** "I check the step conversations on Tuesday and Friday evenings, and I’ll reply within three days. If it’s urgent, message me directly."
2. **Keep to it.** Reliability matters more than speed. A mentor who always replies in three days is better than one who sometimes replies in an hour and sometimes in three weeks.
3. **Say when you’re away.** "I’m away next week; if you need anything, ask the High Priestess."
4. **Set a rhythm of check-ins.** A short conversation every two to four weeks, even when nothing is wrong, keeps things moving.
5. **Know your limit.** Most people can mentor two or three trainees well. Beyond that, quality drops. Say no to more if you need to.

## Boundaries

Boundaries keep both of you safe and keep mentoring about learning.

- **Time:** you are not on call around the clock. Urgent matters, especially crises, go to the right services, not to you alone (see the pastoral care course).
- **Topics:** you will hear about their lives, because spiritual practice touches everything. Listen kindly, but you are not their counsellor. When something needs a professional, say so.
- **Money:** never lend or borrow money with a trainee, and never take payment for mentoring.
- **Relationships:** no romantic or sexual relationship with someone you mentor, ever, while you hold that role. The power difference makes real consent impossible to be sure of. If feelings arise on either side, hand the mentoring to someone else and talk to the High Priestess.
- **Touch:** ask before any touch, every time, even a hug.
- **Privacy:** what they tell you stays with you, within the limits you will learn in the pastoral care course.

## Power, and why it matters
