Initiation and advancement must never involve humiliation, danger, nudity or anything not freely consented to.
- **Respect.** No harassment, bullying, threats or curses aimed at members; no hate or discrimination; no sexual content or advances in covens; respect closed and living traditions; no spam, scams or selling unless the coven's rules allow it.
- **Privacy.** What members share in a coven stays in it; no screenshots or reposting without permission; no sharing anyone's real name, address or details. The site's moderators can read every coven to keep covens safe.
- **Leading a coven.** Founders and those they give powers to are trusted with others' safety: write your documents honestly, apply them fairly, and don't use your position to pressure anyone. Coven rules can add to the guidelines but can't override them.
- **Reporting and blocking.** Every message, member, application and coven has a Report button. Reports go to the site's moderators, never to the coven's leaders, and the person reported isn't told who reported them.
- **Danger.** Covens are not a crisis service. If anyone is in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number. The Sanctuary lists support lines.

You can read the full guidelines from your coven profile in the app, where you agreed to them.

## Being a good neighbour in the app

- **Keep the directory honest.** Make the coven's description, tradition and "When you gather" accurate. If you aren't taking members, set "Not taking members".
- **Be careful with links.** Invite links let people join without applying. Share them privately, set a short life and few uses, and revoke them when done.
- **Cooperate with moderators.** If the site's moderators contact you about your coven, answer honestly and promptly. They exist to keep everyone safe, including you.
- **Model the guidelines.** Your members will treat the wider community as they see you treat it.

> **Try this:** Find out what other covens, moots or Pagan groups exist near you or in your tradition online. Write down two you might contact, and what you would offer or ask. Then re-read the coven community guidelines and note one thing in your coven's rules that should mention them.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions have umbrella bodies, councils or networks of covens, with their own codes of conduct; some prefer independence. Ask your head which your coven belongs to, if any, and what it expects of a head.

docs.title: The High Priestess and High Priest in Wicca
docs.summary: What it means to lead a Wiccan coven: the High Priestess’s place in Wicca, the High Priest beside her, the third degree in public terms, representing the Goddess and God without claiming their authority, accountability, and the limits every coven leader must keep.
docs.body:
## A religion led by priestesses

From its beginning, Wicca has given women the leading place. In Gardner's covens, and in the traditions that grew from them, the **High Priestess** is the head of the coven: she leads its rites, decides who is trained and initiated, and holds the final word in the circle. The **High Priest** works beside her, as partner and support. In the 1950s this was remarkable; it remains one of Wicca's distinctive features.

Today, covens are led in many ways: by a High Priestess and High Priest together, by two priestesses or two priests, by one leader, or by a small group. In this Sanctuary the coven's leading position is whatever your coven calls it. This module speaks of the High Priestess and High Priest because those are Wicca's traditional titles, and you can read them as your coven's own.

## The third degree, in public terms

In the initiatory traditions, coven leadership usually requires the **third degree**: the fullest standing in the tradition. What happens in a third-degree rite is oathbound and is not described here. What has been publicly said is that it marks full priesthood, completes the initiate's training in the tradition's mysteries, and gives the standing to lead a coven independently and to found daughter covens.

In open and eclectic covens, leaders may have no degrees, or may use their coven's own stages. What matters is not the title but the training, experience and character behind it, and honesty about what that training was.

## Representing the Goddess and God

In Wicca, the High Priestess represents the Goddess in the circle, and the High Priest the God. At drawing down, the High Priestess may become, for a time, a vessel through which the Goddess speaks. This is a great honour and a great responsibility.

It is also the point at which coven leadership can go wrong. A High Priestess **represents** the Goddess in ritual; she is not the Goddess outside it. A High Priest stands for the God in the circle; he does not command members in daily life. Leaders who blur this, who expect members to treat them as divine, to obey them in personal matters, or to accept "the Goddess wills it" as the end of a discussion, have lost the meaning of the role. Teach your coven to tell the difference, and live by it yourself.

## Authority and its limits

A High Priestess's authority covers the coven's religious life:

- leading and planning its rites;
- deciding, with others where the coven's agreements say so, who is trained, dedicated and initiated;
- teaching, and keeping the tradition;
- keeping the coven's Book and confidences;
- upholding the coven's agreements.

It does not cover members' lives outside the coven: their relationships, jobs, money, medical choices, politics or friendships. And it never includes:

- **sex** with members as part of any rite or as a condition of anything;
- **money** beyond fair shared costs;
- **secrecy about harm;**
- **cutting members off** from family, friends or outside help.

## Accountability

Good Wiccan leaders are accountable:

- **to the gods,** in their own conscience;
- **to their coven,** through its agreements, open decisions, and members' freedom to raise concerns and to leave;
- **to their own teachers and elders,** in initiatory lines, who can be consulted when something is wrong;
- **to the wider community,** whose trust in Wicca depends on leaders behaving well;
- **to the law,** which applies inside the circle as outside it.

Build accountability into your coven: a written set of agreements, an elder or two who can speak frankly to you, a way for members to raise concerns about you with someone other than you, and the humility to listen.

## The High Priest

The High Priest's role in traditional Wicca is to support, partner and balance the High Priestess: to invoke the Goddess into her at drawing down, to lead the God's part in the sabbats, to share the teaching and care of the coven, and to speak honestly to her when she needs it. In some traditions, the High Priest has particular responsibility for the coven's men, or for its practical life. He is a priest in his own right, not a deputy.

## The Witch Queen

In some initiatory traditions, a High Priestess from whose coven daughter covens have hived off is honoured with the informal title **Witch Queen**. It is a mark of respect for a teacher of teachers, not a rank of command over other covens, which in most Wicca are independent.

## Leading without burning out

Leading a coven is demanding. The core lessons on leading a coven covered burnout and sustainability. In Wicca specifically: share the leading of rites, train your Maiden and Summoner to take parts, take a sabbat off now and then, and keep your own daily devotion, so that you meet the gods for yourself and not only on others' behalf.

> **Your coven:** Talk with your current High Priestess about how leadership will pass or be shared, what titles your coven uses, and what accountability your coven has in place.

> **Try this:** Write a page in your Book of Shadows: what the title High Priestess (or your coven's name for it) will mean for you, what you will never do with it, and who you will ask to hold you to that.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** priestesses leading worship in many ancient religions; priestesses speaking for a goddess.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan High Priestess and High Priest, the third degree and the Witch Queen, from the 1950s onwards.

docs.title: Lineage, hiving and daughter covens
docs.summary: How lineage works in Wicca and how to keep it honestly, hiving off a daughter coven (when, how, and the relationship afterwards), the autonomy of covens, and what an open coven can say truthfully about where its teaching comes from.
docs.body:
## Lineage

In initiatory Wicca, **lineage** is the line of initiators that runs from each initiate back to the founders: "I was initiated by A, who was initiated by B, who was initiated by C..." back to Gerald Gardner's or Alex Sanders's covens. Lineage is how initiatory Wiccans recognise one another, and how a seeker can check that a coven is what it says it is.

Open and eclectic covens may have no lineage in this sense, or may trace a line of teachers. Both are honourable; the only dishonour is in claiming a lineage you do not have.

## Keeping lineage honestly

As a coven leader, you are responsible for the coven's lineage record:

- **Record initiations** accurately: who was initiated, by whom, when, and into which degree.
- **Keep the record safely,** and private where members' identities need protecting.
- **Answer honestly** when serious seekers or other initiates ask about your lineage, within the bounds of your tradition's customs.
- **Never invent or inflate** a lineage: no hereditary lines you cannot trace, no initiations you did not receive.
- **If you are an open coven,** say so plainly: "We're an eclectic Wiccan coven; our founder trained with X, and we draw on published sources."

## Hiving

When a coven grows large, or when an experienced member is ready to lead, the coven may **hive off**: a new, daughter coven is founded, led by someone trained in the mother coven. The word comes from bees, who swarm to form a new hive when the old one is full.

### When to hive

A coven might hive when:

- it has grown beyond the size where everyone can know and trust each other (often around ten to thirteen);
- a member has the training, experience and standing to lead, and the wish to;
- members live far apart and a second coven would serve them better;
- a member's calling differs from the coven's in a way that is best served by a new coven, with goodwill.

Hiving should never be a way to push someone out, and a split in anger is not a hive, though even that can, with time and care, be healed.

### How to hive well

1. **Talk early and openly** with the member who will lead, and with the coven.
2. **Make sure the new leader is ready:** training, degree (in initiatory traditions), experience leading rites, and good character.
3. **Agree who goes:** members choose freely which coven to join.
4. **Agree what goes:** the new coven's Book of Shadows, its tools, and what it may teach.
5. **Mark the hiving** with a rite: a blessing of the new coven and its leaders, often with a gift.
6. **Set up the new coven** in the app as a daughter coven, so the line between them is kept.

## Preparing the new leader

Before a hiving, the person who will lead the daughter coven needs more than the right degree. In the months before, give them real practice:

- let them lead whole sabbats and esbats in the mother coven, with you present but not leading;
- let them mentor a newcomer through a program, with your support;
- talk through hard situations they may meet: a member in crisis, a conflict, a request they should refuse;
- help them write their coven's agreements and plan their first year;
- agree how they can reach you for advice, and how often you will meet in the first year.

A daughter coven that begins with a confident, well-supported leader is far more likely to flourish.

## Autonomy

In most Wicca, each coven is **autonomous**: it governs itself. A mother coven does not command its daughters. The relationship is more like that of a parent and an adult child: respect, friendship, advice when asked, and perhaps shared rites at the great sabbats. Some initiatory traditions keep more formal ties, with the Witch Queen or elders consulted on serious matters. Agree the relationship at the time of hiving, and revisit it as the years pass.

## When a daughter coven goes wrong

Sometimes a daughter coven develops problems: a leader who abuses their position, teaching that departs badly from the tradition, harm to members. Because covens are autonomous, the mother coven usually cannot simply step in. But it can:

- speak frankly to the daughter coven's leaders;
- offer support and a safe place to members who leave;
- in initiatory traditions, make clear that the daughter coven no longer represents the line, if things are serious;
- encourage anyone harmed to seek help from the authorities where harm is a crime.

## Working with other covens

Beyond your own line, you will meet covens of other traditions. Good relations help everyone:

- join open sabbats, pagan federations and moots;
- share teaching and support with neighbouring covens;
- respect each tradition's own customs and oaths;
- warn others, carefully and fairly, about genuine dangers, such as a person known to have harmed members, and never spread gossip.

> **Your coven:** Ask your High Priestess about the coven's lineage or line of teachers, how it records initiations, and how it has hived, or would hive, in the past.

> **Try this:** Write your coven's line, as far as you know it and may share it, in your Book of Shadows. If you don't know it, ask.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** chains of teachers and initiators in many religions and esoteric orders.
- **Modern:** Wiccan lineage and hiving, from the 1950s and 1960s onwards.

docs.title: Keeping the coven’s Book of Shadows
docs.summary: The coven’s Book of Shadows as the coven’s memory: what goes in it, how it grows and is revised, what belongs only on paper (oathbound material and an online book), who may read what, crediting authors and respecting copyright, and handing it on.
docs.body:
## The coven's memory

Every Wiccan coven keeps a **Book of Shadows**: the book of its rites, teachings and history. In initiatory traditions, the core of it is copied by hand from initiator to initiate, and each coven adds its own pages. In open covens, it is the coven's own creation. Either way, the High Priestess is its keeper.

The origin of the name is uncertain. Gardner's early manuscript was titled Ye Bok of ye Art Magical; the name "Book of Shadows" appeared in the 1950s, perhaps from a magazine article Gardner read. It now means any Wiccan's or coven's book of the Craft.

## What goes in it

A coven's Book usually holds:

- **the coven's rites:** the shape and words of its circle, quarters, sabbats, esbats, dedications and other rites, as the coven keeps them;
- **teachings:** the coven's understanding of the Goddess and God, its ethics, its customs;
- **liturgy:** the Charge, invocations, chants, poems, with their authors;
- **craft knowledge:** tested correspondences, recipes for incense and oils, herb lore, with safety notes;
- **the coven's history:** its founding, its leaders, its hivings, its great rites;
- **its agreements:** the coven's rules and what members have agreed.

It does not usually hold members' personal confidences, which belong in private records if anywhere.

## Growing and revising

A living coven's Book grows. As High Priestess:

- **date every page,** and note who wrote it;
- **keep old versions** when you revise a rite, so the coven's history is not lost;
- **invite contributions:** members write pages, which you review before adding;
- **correct errors openly,** especially historical ones: "We used to teach that this was ancient; we now know it dates from the 1970s."

In initiatory traditions, the core material is kept as received, and changes are made in additional pages, not by editing what was handed down.

## Paper and the app

The coven's Book in this app lives online, and its leaders decide which members can read which pages. This makes it easy to share, search and keep safe from fire or loss. But think about what belongs there:

- **Open material** (your coven's own rites, public teachings, recipes, history) is well suited to the app.
- **Oathbound material** from an initiatory tradition may have its own rules: many traditions require it to be copied by hand and kept on paper, and not stored online at all. Follow your tradition's rules. If in doubt, keep it on paper.
- **Members' identities and confidences** need the most care. Keep them out of the Book, and use the members' record only for what the coven truly needs.

Whatever you keep online, remember that anything stored on a server can, in principle, be exposed. Write as though a page might one day be read by someone outside the coven, and keep the truly secret on paper.

## Your own book and the coven's

Each member keeps their own Book of Shadows as well as reading the coven's. Encourage it. A member's own book is theirs: their experiences, workings, dreams and doubts. The coven's Book is shared: its rites and teaching. When a member copies coven material into their own book, remind them that the coven's confidentiality still applies to those pages, and that their own reflections belong to them alone. A High Priestess never asks to read a member's private book.

## Who may read what

Many covens have levels: pages for everyone, pages for dedicants, pages for initiates, pages for each degree. Decide this deliberately, record it, and review it when people's standing changes. When someone leaves the coven, remove their access with courtesy, and remind them gently of what they agreed to keep private.

## Crediting authors and respecting copyright

Much Wiccan liturgy has authors: Doreen Valiente's Charge and many of her poems, the Farrars' rites, Starhawk's chants, and many more. Good practice:

- **credit the author** on every page that uses their work;
- **respect copyright:** copying a published text into a private coven book for worship is common practice, but republishing it in public (on a website, in a printed booklet for sale) usually needs permission;
- **write your own:** a coven that writes its own liturgy alongside the classics has a living tradition.

## Safety in the Book

Craft knowledge passed down in books has sometimes included dangerous advice: herbs taken internally that are toxic, oils used undiluted on skin, fire practices that are unsafe indoors. As keeper, review recipes and practices for safety, add clear warnings, and remove or correct anything that could hurt someone. A coven's Book should never be the reason a member was harmed.

## Handing it on

A Book of Shadows outlives its keepers. Plan for it:

- name who will keep the Book if you step down or die;
- when a daughter coven hives, agree what it takes;
- if the coven closes, decide what happens to the Book: given to a trusted coven, kept by a member, or, for oathbound material, destroyed according to the tradition's custom.

> **Your coven:** Ask your High Priestess what is kept in the coven's Book, what is kept on paper only, who may read which pages, and who will keep it after her.

> **Try this:** Choose one rite the coven keeps often. Write it up properly for the coven's Book: date, author, sources and credits, safety notes, and the words. Ask your High Priestess to review it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** handwritten books of magic, the grimoires, from the Middle Ages onwards.
- **Modern:** the Wiccan Book of Shadows (1950s onwards), and keeping it online (now).

docs.title: Leading the Wiccan year and its rites of passage
docs.summary: Holding the whole Wiccan year for a coven: planning the sabbats and esbats, drawing down and divination as the coven’s leader, and the rites of passage a High Priestess is asked to lead (Wiccanings, handfastings, croning and saging, and rites for the dead), with the ethics of leading worship.
docs.body:
## The whole year

As High Priestess, you hold the Wiccan year for your coven: eight sabbats, twelve or thirteen esbats, training, dedications and initiations, and the rites that mark members' lives. Holding it well means planning ahead, sharing the work, and keeping the gods, not the calendar, at the centre.

## Planning the year

At Samhain, the Wiccan new year, many High Priestesses sit down with their High Priest and elders to plan:

1. **The sabbats:** dates, places (indoors or out), who leads, which are open to guests, which story each will tell.
2. **The esbats:** dates, the coven's workings, who will draw down, if your coven does.
3. **Training:** who is on which program, who mentors whom, when dedications and initiations might fall.
4. **Rites of passage** already known: handfastings, Wiccanings, rites for elders.
5. **Rest:** months with fewer demands, a sabbat the leaders will attend without leading.

Put it in the coven's calendar in the app, so everyone can plan. Review it at each sabbat.

## Drawing down as leader

If your coven practises drawing down, the High Priestess is usually the one in whom the Goddess is invoked. This asks particular care:

- **keep your own practice** deep, so you come to the rite grounded;
- **have a trusted watcher,** every time;
- **hold inspired words lightly,** as the elder lessons taught: never use them to direct members' lives, and never let anyone treat them as commands;
- **be honest** with yourself and your coven when a drawing down was strong and when it was mostly the Charge spoken well. Both are fine.

## Divination as leader

Covens often look to their High Priestess for divination: for the coven's year, for members, for decisions. Divination can be a fine servant of discernment. As leader:

- **read for the coven openly,** sharing the cards or runes, not only your interpretation;
- **never make a decision** about a member's training or standing by divination alone;
- **ask consent** before reading for any member, and keep their readings confidential;
- **say what you don't know.**

## Rites of passage

Members will ask you to mark the great moments of their lives. These rites are among the most meaningful a High Priestess leads. Your coven may have its own forms; these are the common ones in public Wiccan practice.

### Wiccaning

A **Wiccaning** (or naming) welcomes a baby or child to the community and asks the Goddess and God's blessing on them. It is not an initiation: Wiccans traditionally hold that a child should choose their own religion when grown. A simple form: the circle cast, the child presented to the quarters and the gods, a name given, blessings and gifts from those present, and a promise from the parents and community to love and support the child.

### Handfasting

A **handfasting** is a Wiccan wedding, in which the couple's hands are bound with a cord. It may be "for a year and a day", "for life" or "for as long as love shall last". Check whether a handfasting can be a legal marriage where you live, and if so, whether you are authorised to perform one; if not, couples will need a civil ceremony too. Marry only couples who choose each other freely. A **handparting** is the Wiccan rite for a couple who separate, releasing each other with goodwill.

### Croning and saging

Many Wiccan covens mark the passage into elderhood with a **croning** (for women) or **saging** (for men), and some now with rites for anyone, often at around fifty or sixty, or at menopause or retirement. It honours wisdom and the Crone or Sage aspect of the gods. Let the person choose whether and when.

### Rites for the dead

When a member dies, the coven may hold a **requiem**: a rite of farewell, in which the dead member is remembered, their journey to the Summerland is blessed, and the coven comforts one another. Respect the family's wishes, and the member's own, which it helps to ask about in life. Many Wiccans now write down their wishes for their funeral.

## The ethics of leading worship

Some principles for every High Priestess:

- **The gods first.** The rite is for them and the coven, not for your reputation.
- **Consent always.** In every rite, every member can say no.
- **Honesty.** Teach what is old as old and what is new as new; never claim more than you know.
- **Inclusion.** Make room in the circle for everyone the coven welcomes.
- **Care.** Watch over people before, during and after rites.
- **Humility.** You will make mistakes. Own them.

> **Safety:** Rites of passage often involve families, children and guests who don't know Wiccan ways. Explain what will happen beforehand, keep fire safe around children, provide seats, and keep alcohol optional.

> **Your coven:** Ask your High Priestess how the coven plans its year, who draws down, and what rites of passage it has held and how.

> **Try this:** Plan the coven's next full year in outline, from Samhain to Samhain, in the coven's calendar or your Book of Shadows, and ask your High Priestess to review it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** naming, marriage, elder and funeral rites in every culture; the binding of hands in some old marriage customs.
- **Modern:** Wiccanings, handfastings, handpartings, croning and saging, and the requiem as Wiccan rites, from the 1960s onwards.

quizzes.title: Leading a coven
quizzes.intro: Fifteen questions on authority, the coven’s documents, running the coven in the app, delegating, crises and sustainability. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a coven head’s authority?
options: A spiritual rank that, once given by initiation, can never be questioned
Trust the members give for particular jobs, which must leave them genuinely free to disagree or leave
The right to guide members in every area of their lives
Whatever the gods tell the head, which members must accept
questions.explanation: Whatever a tradition says about lineage or calling, a head only leads people who are free to leave. Authority is given for particular jobs (safety, purpose, decisions, recognition, speaking for the coven) and never extends to members’ private lives.

questions.prompt: Which are warning signs of a guru dynamic? Choose all that apply.
options: Disagreement with the head is called a spiritual failing
The head keeps rules for themselves that differ from everyone else’s
The head explains why a decision was made
Members ask the head’s permission for ordinary life decisions
Those who leave are spoken of as traitors
questions.explanation: Calling disagreement a failing, special rules for the leader, members deferring on ordinary life and treating leaving as betrayal are all classic signs. Explaining decisions is the opposite: it is a mark of accountability.

questions.prompt: A report a member makes with the app’s Report button goes to the coven’s head first, so the head can deal with it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators, never to the coven’s leaders, and the person reported isn’t told who reported them. That independence is part of what keeps every coven, and its head, accountable.

questions.prompt: You correct a typo in the coven’s member agreement and save it. What happens?
options: Nothing; only the head sees the change
It becomes a new version, and every member must sign it again before they can speak in the chat or tend the altars
Everyone is removed from the coven until they sign
The agreement becomes members-only
questions.explanation: Changing the title or words of a page members sign creates a new version that everyone must sign again before taking part. Gather changes together, tell the coven first, and don’t save a signed page for trivial edits.

questions.prompt: Why must a page that members sign be readable by everyone?
options: So it shows in search engines
Because seekers sign the agreements before they join
Because the site’s moderators can’t read members-only pages
It doesn’t have to be; that is only a suggestion
questions.explanation: Agreements are signed before joining, so a seeker must be able to read them. The app won’t save an agreement set to “Members only”.

questions.prompt: You want members to be able to ask to become Initiates. Which do you set on the Initiate position? Choose all that apply.
options: Tick “Members can apply to rise to it”
Write what it asks of someone, which applicants will see
Tick “New members begin here”
Give it the power “Leads the coven”
questions.explanation: An open position has “Members can apply to rise to it” ticked, and its requirements (“What it asks of someone”) are shown to members applying under My standing and to reviewers. New members don’t begin there, and it shouldn’t carry the power to lead the coven.

questions.prompt: An elder with the “Reviews applications” power but no other powers wants to raise a member to the Warden position, which carries “Moderates the gathering”. What happens?
options: They can, as long as Warden is below their own position
They can’t: reviewers raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers
They can, but only during a ritual
They can, if the member agrees
questions.explanation: Reviewers can raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers. Only those who lead the coven give positions with powers, which keeps powers in the hands of those trusted with them.

questions.prompt: You want everyone who becomes a Dedicant to go through the coven’s initiate training, now and in future. What is the simplest way?
options: Assign the program to each Dedicant by name, and remember to do it for new ones
Assign the program to the Dedicant position
Tick “Any member may begin it themselves”
Post a message in the chat
questions.explanation: Assigning a program to a position enrols everyone in it now and anyone who takes it later. Self-enrolment lets anyone begin it, which isn’t the same thing.

questions.prompt: The coven has a rule that elders hear about every Deipnon rite, but for this month’s Deipnon you want the whole coven told. Where do you change it?
options: Delete the Deipnon rule in Gathering notifications
In that rite’s own details, choose who hears for this one
Ask every member to turn on Reminders
You can’t; the rule always wins
questions.explanation: A gathering’s own choice, in its planner, comes first; then the closest rule. Changing one rite leaves the coven’s rule in place for next time.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses of the members’ record? Choose all that apply.
options: Noticing that someone has been quiet for months and sending them a kind message
Reading what members wrote in their private conversations
Correcting attendance when someone was at a rite in person
Writing brief, fair leaders’ notes that you’d be comfortable for the person to read one day
Publicly listing the least active members in the chat
questions.explanation: The record is a pastoral tool: flags mean “check in kindly”. Leaders can correct attendance and keep brief notes. The record never shows private conversations or what anyone wrote, and shaming people publicly is never right.

questions.prompt: When you delegate leading the Imbolc rite to an elder, what should you also do?
options: Write every word for them so it is done right
Give them the authority to do it, such as a position that lets them plan rites and put them on the calendar
Check their work every day
Keep the delegation secret from the coven
questions.explanation: Responsibility without authority is a trap. Describe the outcome, give the powers the task needs, agree limits and check-ins, then stand back.

questions.prompt: A member tells you she has been thinking about ending her life. What comes first?
options: Offer a healing ritual at the next full moon
Tell the elders so they can pray for her
Ask directly about her safety now, stay with her, and connect her with a crisis line or emergency services if she is in danger
Suggest she takes a break from the coven
questions.explanation: Safety comes first. Ask plainly, listen, and if she is in danger contact emergency services or a crisis line together. Ritual and the coven’s care can support her alongside professional help, never instead of it.

questions.prompt: A member tells you an elder has been pressuring them for money and private photographs. Describe, in order, what you would do.
questions.explanation: This is a safeguarding concern. Take it seriously, don’t promise secrecy, act on any immediate danger, report through the app (the reason “Pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience”), contact authorities where needed, protect the coven (pausing or removing the elder, and taking away their powers) without public accusation, and keep a factual record.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): takes it seriously and listens without promising secrecy; acts on immediate danger (emergency services) if relevant; reports it through the app’s Report button to the site’s moderators; protects members while it is resolved (e.g. changes the elder’s position to remove powers, pauses or removes them) without a public accusation; keeps a factual, dated record; mentions proper authorities where the law or situation requires. 2: most of these, but misses reporting or protecting members. 1: some sensible steps but confronts the elder publicly or investigates alone. 0: dismisses it or keeps it secret.

questions.prompt: Name three things a head should keep (or share only with a co-leader) rather than delegate, and three things that are good to delegate. Say briefly why for one of each.
questions.explanation: Heads keep final responsibility for safety, decisions to remove or ban (except emergencies), changes to the creed, rules and agreements, recognitions their tradition reserves, and handing on the coven. Routine work, teaching within someone’s competence, leading rites by turns and projects with a clear end are good to delegate.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): three sound “keep” items (e.g. safety and safeguarding, removing or banning, changing documents, initiations reserved to the head, handing on) and three sound “delegate” items (e.g. setting up, chat moderation, mentoring, leading some rites, projects), with a sensible reason for one of each. 2: mostly right but no reasons, or one item misplaced. 1: only one list done well. 0: misunderstands delegation.

questions.prompt: Write a short sustainability plan for yourself as head (or future head): your coven’s rhythm, your message hours, who shares leadership, your own practice, your support outside the coven, and what you would do if you noticed signs of burnout.
questions.explanation: A sustainable head sets a realistic rhythm, has boundaries on time, shares leadership, keeps their own practice, has support outside the coven, and plans in advance how to step back when needed, including professional help if burnout becomes depression.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): a realistic gathering rhythm; clear message hours (and what members do in an emergency); named sharing of leadership (co-leader, rota, positions with powers); a personal practice and rites they attend without leading; support outside the coven; concrete steps on noticing burnout (step back, hand over for a season, see a doctor if it becomes depression). 3–4: most present but general. 1–2: vague or missing several. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: Stewardship: the coven over time
quizzes.intro: Fourteen questions on succession, hiving, training trainers, the coven’s health and lineage, closing a coven and the wider community. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head taps “Hand on leadership” for a member and confirms?
options: The member becomes the coven’s head, with every power, and the former head stays a member in their current position
The former head is removed from the coven
Both become heads with equal powers
The coven is archived and a new one is made
questions.explanation: The new leader becomes the coven’s founder, with every power over it. The former head stays a member in the position they held, which may still carry powers, so agree with the new head what position they should now hold.

questions.prompt: Which belong to a good handover? Choose all that apply.
options: Telling the coven before the change, and why
A handover file in the Book: vision, who can do what, trainees and mentors, the coming calendar
The former head quietly keeping the power to overrule the new head
Checking the coven’s settings together after the change
Handing on by surprise, so there is no fuss
questions.explanation: A good handover is open and prepared: the coven is told first, the successor gets what they need to know, and the settings chosen for the old head’s way of leading are reviewed. The former head steps back rather than keeping a shadow veto.

questions.prompt: You want an elder to share leadership with you for a year before you hand on. How do you do this in the app?
options: Give them your password
Give them a position that carries “Leads the coven”, while you remain the head
Hand on leadership and ask them to hand it back if it doesn’t work
There is no way to share leadership in the app
questions.explanation: Positions carry powers. A position with “Leads the coven” lets its holders edit pages, positions and details and act on members below them, while the few head-only actions stay with you. Never share an account.

questions.prompt: A head who wants to leave the coven they lead to found a daughter coven should hand on leadership first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The head can’t leave a coven they lead. Hand on leadership to a successor first, then step back or leave, and found the daughter coven.

questions.prompt: Which are good practice when hiving off a daughter coven? Choose all that apply.
options: Talking with the head privately before telling anyone else
Letting members choose freely whether to go or stay
Taking oath-bound material without asking, since you were taught it
Agreeing what is carried, and the relationship between the covens
Recording the daughter coven’s origin in its description and Book
questions.explanation: A hiving is done with blessing: the head is told first, members choose freely, what is carried and how the covens relate is agreed, and the lineage is recorded (the app has no built-in link, so you record it yourself). Oath-bound material goes only with the head’s blessing.

questions.prompt: Which is the more honest way to describe your coven’s lineage?
options: “Our line goes back unbroken to the witches of the Stone Age.”
“Our coven was founded in 2019 by a priestess trained in a coven founded in the 1980s, drawing on twentieth-century Wicca.”
“We are the only true coven in our tradition.”
“Our history is secret, so we cannot be questioned.”
questions.explanation: Historians have found no good evidence for unbroken ancient witch cults; modern Paganism is largely a twentieth-century revival. An honest lineage of decades is something to be proud of, and it can be checked.

questions.prompt: A new mentor gives every trainee full marks on written answers because they don’t want to discourage anyone. What should the head do?
options: Nothing; kindness matters most
Remove them as a mentor at once
Look at their scoring together against the rubric, and teach specific, kind, useful feedback
Score all the tests themselves from now on
questions.explanation: Training trainers includes supervision: reading the scores they give, checking them against the rubric, and teaching feedback that says what was done well, what is missing and what to do next. Fairness is a kindness to every trainee.

questions.prompt: How many mentees should one mentor usually have at most?
options: One
About three
About ten
As many as they like
questions.explanation: Mentoring takes real time and energy. Around three mentees each keeps check-ins regular and protects mentors from burnout.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head archives a coven in the app? Choose all that apply.
options: It leaves the directory
Its chat and altars become read-only
Everything in it is deleted for good
Only the site moderators can reopen it
questions.explanation: Archiving takes the coven out of the directory and makes its chat and altars read-only; it doesn’t delete them. Only the site moderators can reopen it, so archive only after a considered decision.

questions.prompt: Before deciding to close a coven, what should a head consider first?
options: Archiving it the same day, to avoid a long goodbye
Alternatives such as a season’s rest, a smaller rhythm, handing on to an elder, or merging with another coven
Keeping the decision secret from the members
Deleting the coven’s Book so no one argues over it
questions.explanation: Closing should be a considered choice. Rest, a smaller rhythm, a successor or a merger may keep what is good alive. If it does close, tell members early, help them find new homes, and hold a final rite.

questions.prompt: Under the Salt & Sovereignty coven community guidelines, which of these are never allowed? Choose all that apply.
options: Making a payment a condition of rising to a higher position
Asking members to help with shared costs, if it is never a condition of belonging or rising
Telling a member to stop seeing their therapist
Initiation involving nudity a member hasn’t freely consented to
A coven rule that overrides the guidelines
questions.explanation: Covens may ask for help with shared costs, but never as a condition of belonging or rising. No one may tell a member to stop medical or mental-health care; initiation must never involve anything not freely consented to; and coven rules can add to the guidelines but can’t override them.

questions.prompt: A member of a nearby coven asks to join yours after a falling-out with their head. What is the best response?
options: Welcome them and ask for every detail of the falling-out
Refuse, since they belong to another coven
Welcome their application on its merits, encourage them to part from the other coven well, and don’t speak ill of it
Tell the other coven’s head everything they said
questions.explanation: Anyone may leave a coven and apply to another. A good neighbour doesn’t poach or gossip, encourages a kind parting, and judges the application on its merits.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would found a daughter coven in the app and set it up in its first month.
questions.explanation: Found it from Find a coven → Found a coven (name, web address that can’t change, description including its origin, joining, directory, your title, agreeing to the guidelines). Then write its documents, set its practice calendar and positions, invite its members, begin programs and mentors, and carry over agreed material.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): founding steps (Found a coven, name and permanent web address, honest description naming the mother coven, joining and directory choice, leader title, agreeing to the guidelines); then Manage (creed, rules, requirements, agreement), practice calendar, positions and powers, inviting members by invitation or short-lived link, programs and mentors, and carrying over only material the mother coven agreed. 2: founding plus some setup. 1: only founding. 0: not attempted.

questions.prompt: Write a succession plan for your coven: who would step in if the head were suddenly unable to lead; how a successor would be chosen and prepared; how the handover would happen, including in the app; and what the former head would do afterwards.
questions.explanation: A good succession plan names an emergency deputy, chooses a successor for character with the elders’ support and the person’s consent, prepares them through shared leadership, tells the coven before the change, uses Hand on leadership from Members, sorts out the former head’s position and settings, and has the former head truly step back.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): names an emergency deputy and what they may do (including contacting the site moderators if the head can’t hand on); chooses for character with elders consulted and the successor asked; prepares through shared leadership (a position with “Leads the coven”); tells the coven first; marks it with a rite or meeting; Members → tap the successor → Hand on leadership; agrees the former head’s new position and reviews head-only settings; former head steps back and redirects complaints. 3–4: most of this. 1–2: general ideas only. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: Wiccan high priesthood: test
quizzes.intro: Eleven questions on the High Priestess and High Priest, lineage and hiving, the coven’s Book of Shadows, and leading the Wiccan year and its rites of passage. Most are scored at once; the written answers are scored against a rubric. You need 80% to pass.

questions.prompt: What is the right understanding of a High Priestess representing the Goddess?
options: She is the Goddess, in and out of the circle, and must be obeyed
She represents the Goddess in ritual, but holds no divine authority over members’ lives
She may speak for the Goddess on members’ personal decisions
Representation means nothing at all
questions.explanation: Representing the Goddess in the circle is an honour and a responsibility. Leaders who expect to be treated as divine outside it have lost the meaning of the role.

questions.prompt: Which lie outside a High Priestess’s authority? Choose all that apply.
options: Members’ relationships and jobs
Planning and leading the coven’s rites
Members’ medical choices
Asking members for sex as part of a rite
questions.explanation: Her authority covers the coven’s religious life, never members’ private lives, and never sex, money beyond fair costs, or secrecy about harm.

questions.prompt: What is "hiving" in Wicca?
options: Expelling a member
Founding a daughter coven, led by someone trained in the mother coven
Keeping bees for mead
Merging two covens
questions.explanation: As bees swarm from a full hive, a coven may hive off a daughter coven when it grows or a member is ready to lead.

questions.prompt: In most Wicca, a mother coven commands its daughter covens.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Covens are usually autonomous; the relationship is one of respect and friendship, agreed at the hiving.

questions.prompt: An open, eclectic coven is asked about its lineage. What is the honest answer?
options: Claim descent from Gardner to sound credible
Say plainly that it is eclectic, and where its teaching comes from
Refuse to discuss it
Invent a hereditary line
questions.explanation: Open covens have nothing to hide. The only dishonour is in claiming a lineage you do not have.

questions.prompt: Which are good practice for the coven’s Book of Shadows? Choose all that apply.
options: Dating pages and noting who wrote them
Crediting authors such as Doreen Valiente
Storing a tradition’s oathbound material online against its rules
Correcting historical errors openly
questions.explanation: Follow your tradition’s rules for oathbound material, which often require it to be kept on paper. Credit authors and correct errors openly.

questions.prompt: What is a Wiccaning?
options: The initiation of a child into Wicca
A welcome and blessing of a child, not an initiation; the child may choose their own religion when grown
A Wiccan wedding
A funeral
questions.explanation: Wiccans traditionally hold that a child should choose their own path when grown; a Wiccaning welcomes and blesses them.

questions.prompt: A handfasting is always a legal marriage.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It depends on the law where you live and whether the celebrant is authorised; otherwise couples need a civil ceremony too.

questions.prompt: How should a High Priestess use divination about a member’s readiness for initiation?
options: Decide by the cards alone
As one aid to discernment, never the sole basis, with consent and confidentiality
Never for anything at all
Publicly, for the whole coven to discuss
questions.explanation: Divination can serve discernment, but decisions about people rest on their practice, conversation and the coven’s agreements.

questions.prompt: Describe the accountability you would put in place as High Priestess (or your coven’s leading position): to whom you would answer, how members could raise concerns about you, and what you would never do with the role.
questions.explanation: Good leaders build accountability into their covens and know the limits of their authority.
questions.rubric: Full marks (4): names at least two forms of accountability, such as written agreements, elders, outside teachers, the law (1); describes a way for members to raise concerns about the leader with someone other than the leader (1); names clear limits, including sex, money and secrecy about harm (1); shows humility and understanding of representing the gods without claiming their authority (1).

questions.prompt: Outline your plan for the coven’s next year, from Samhain to Samhain: the sabbats, esbats, training and rest.
questions.explanation: A good plan holds the whole year, shares the work and leaves room to rest.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes all eight sabbats and regular esbats (1); shares leading among members and includes training milestones (1); includes rest or reduced demands for the leaders (1).

programs.title: Celtic: Your first thirty days
programs.summary: For someone new, in their first month, deciding whether this coven is right for them.
programs.description: A gentle first month: what the coven is and does, its tradition in brief, what membership asks and what your rights are, a first taste of practice, and a rite to attend. It ends with a decision, made openly with the coven’s head or your mentor: to carry on as a devotee, to take longer, or to part well.

stages.title: Arriving
stages.intro: Welcome. This first stage is short: read how these thirty days work, what a coven is and isn’t, and the rights you keep in any group, then say hello to your mentor or the High Priestess on this step.

tasks.title: Read: what a coven is, and how this month works
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "What a coven is, and what it isn’t".
2. Try the exercise at the end: write three lines in your own journal or Book of Shadows (why you looked for a coven, what you hope to find, what you fear). Keep them private; you will read them again at the end.
3. Tap "Mark done".

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Know your rights
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Your rights, red flags and green flags".
2. Say the five short "no" phrases aloud once each, so they feel familiar.
3. In the answer box, write in your own words the three rights that matter most to you, and one red flag you will keep an eye out for this month.
4. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Say hello
tasks.instructions:
1. Open the conversation on this step.
2. Send your mentor or the High Priestess a short hello: your coven name, how you came to the coven, and what you hope to learn this month. Share only what you are comfortable sharing.
3. Ask who to talk to if you have questions, and which rite would be a good first one to attend.
4. In the answer box, note what they suggested, then send it for sign-off.

stages.title: Taking part
stages.intro: Now get to know the coven as it really is: read its own documents, go to a rite, and talk with its members. Take your time with this stage; it is the heart of the month.

tasks.title: Read the coven’s documents
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Getting to know this coven: attend, ask, read" and "What membership will ask of you".
2. Open the coven’s pages in the app and read its creed, rules, requirements and agreements, slowly, all the way through.
3. Note what you agree with gladly, what you are unsure of, and anything you disagree with or don’t understand.
4. In the answer box, write: the coven’s creed in two or three sentences of your own; what membership would ask of you in time, commitments and money; and your questions.
5. Send it for sign-off. Your mentor will answer your questions on this step’s conversation.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Learn how the coven gathers, online and in person
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Coven life online and in person".
2. Open each part of the coven in the app once: Rituals and rites, Altars, Messages, Petitions, Book of Shadows, and My standing.
3. Check Settings → Notifications & reminders → Covens and choose what you want to hear about.
4. Tap "Mark done".

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Attend a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Choose a rite with your mentor’s help and answer "Will you be there?" in the app.
2. Ask beforehand about anything you need to know: what to bring or wear, whether there is alcohol, access, smoke or pets.
3. Attend, in person or in the app. Follow quietly, and sit out any part you wish to.
4. Afterwards, while it is fresh, write in the answer box: what happened, what you liked, what puzzled you, how you felt before, during and after, and how people treated each other and you.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Meet members
tasks.instructions:
1. Start a conversation with a member (Messages → New message), or talk with them before or after a rite.
2. Ask open questions: how long they have been in the coven, what a typical month is like, what surprised them, what they would change.
3. Log each conversation. In the answer box, write a few lines on what you learned and how they spoke about the coven.
4. Do this with at least two different members.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder

tasks.title: Ask the High Priestess your questions
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Questions to ask the High Priestess".
2. Choose five to eight questions that matter most to you, from the lesson or your own.
3. Ask them on this step’s conversation, or in a call or meeting she agrees to.
4. In the answer box, write down her answers in your own words, and what reassured you or left you uneasy.
5. Send it for sign-off.

stages.title: Deciding
stages.intro: You have seen the coven from the inside. Now weigh it honestly, talk it through with the High Priestess, and choose: continue as a devotee, take longer, or part well. Every one of these is a good choice when it is made with care.

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Look back over the lessons, especially "Your rights, red flags and green flags" and "What membership will ask of you".
2. Take the test. Choice questions are scored straight away; your mentor scores the written answers.
3. You need 80% to pass. If you don’t pass, look at the questions you missed, talk to your mentor on this step, and try again.

tasks.title: Reflect on fit
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Does it fit? Values, people, practice, logistics".
2. Read again the three lines you wrote at the start, and your notes from the month.
3. Do the fit exercise: write what you have seen under Values, People, Practice and Logistics, and give each a mark from 1 to 5.
4. In the answer box, write your marks, a few lines on each, and one sentence on how you feel imagining yourself in this coven a year from now.
5. Send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Talk it through with the High Priestess
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "The decision: continue, take longer, or part well".
2. On this step’s conversation, write to the High Priestess: thank her for the month, say what you valued, say honestly what you are unsure of, and which way you are leaning. Ask any last questions.
3. Read her reply, and talk further if you need to.
4. In the answer box, note what you discussed, then send it for sign-off.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

tasks.title: Make your choice
tasks.instructions:
1. Sleep on it at least one night.
2. In the answer box, write your choice: "I will continue as a devotee", "I would like more time, until [date], because …" or "I will part with the coven".
3. Send it for sign-off. The High Priestess will confirm what happens next.
4. If you are parting, follow the steps for parting well in the lesson, and leave from My standing → Leaving when you are ready.
5. Mark the moment in your own way: a candle, a few lines in your journal, or a quiet minute.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements

stages.title: A first taste of Celtic paganism
stages.intro: In your first thirty days you get a feel for the Celtic practice your coven keeps. Read three short lessons, try one simple practice at home, come to a rite if you can, and talk openly with your mentor or the coven’s head about whether this path is for you.

tasks.title: Celtic paganism in brief
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "Celtic paganism in brief".
2. Open the app's calendar and find the next of the four Celtic fire festivals, and read its page.
3. Note anything that surprised you or that you want to ask, such as which stream your coven leans towards, and mark this task done.

tasks.title: A light and a gift at the hearth
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "A first practice: a light and a gift at the hearth".
2. Keep the practice step by step, safely, and give the gift back to the earth afterwards.
3. Write what you noticed in the app's journal, and log each time. Do it three times on different days during your first month.

links.label: Ritual: Offering to the House Spirit

tasks.title: Come to a rite
tasks.instructions:
1. Read "What a Celtic rite is like, and what is asked of a devotee".
2. Ask your mentor which rite you could come to (often one of the fire festivals), and what to wear and bring.
3. Attend, in person or in the app. Watch and follow; you can say no to anything and leave at any time.
4. Send your mentor a message on this step afterwards with anything that puzzled you.

links.label: The coven’s rituals and ritual builder
Your standing and the coven’s agreements
Ritual: Brigid’s Cross and Well Blessing

tasks.solitary: Keep the next fire festival, or the next full moon, simply at home: read the holy day’s page in the app, kindle your hearth candle, greet the land, the ancestors and the gods, give a gift of milk or oatcake, keep one of the festival’s customs from the page, and write what you did.

tasks.title: Is this path for you?
tasks.instructions:
1. Reread the section "What is asked of a devotee".
2. In the answer box, write honestly: what draws you, what feels hard, how you feel about practising from incomplete sources, how you will treat the living cultures, whether the time fits your life, and what you'd like to ask before deciding.
3. Talk it through with your mentor or the coven's head.

links.label: Your standing and the coven’s agreements
The coven’s rituals and ritual builder
Ritual: Brigid’s Cross and Well Blessing

tasks.title: Take the test
tasks.instructions:
1. Take the short test. The choice questions are scored at once; your mentor reads the written answers.
2. You need 80% to pass. If you don't pass, look at the questions you missed and try again; it's a check of understanding, not a hurdle.

docs.title: What a coven is, and what it isn’t
docs.summary: How these thirty days work, what a coven offers, what it should never be, and the people you’ll meet.
docs.body:
## Welcome

You have found a coven, and the coven has let you in to look around. For the next thirty days or so you are a *seeker*: someone who is getting to know this group, and letting the group get to know you, before either of you makes a promise. Nothing is expected of you yet except honesty and good manners. You are not on trial, and you are not signing up for anything by reading this.

This short course is here to help you decide well. Some people know within a week that they have found their people. Others need the whole month, or longer. Some realise it is not the right group, and that is a good outcome too: it is far better to find out now than after a year of half-hearted attendance.

## How these thirty days work

Everything in this course happens in the app, and the practice happens in your own life.

1. **Read.** Each step has short lessons like this one. Read them in your own time. Ten or twenty minutes is plenty for most.
2. **Take part.** You will be asked to attend a rite, read the coven’s own documents, and talk with some of its members.
3. **Write.** Some steps have an answer box. Write as much or as little as is true for you; there are no clever answers, only honest ones.
4. **Talk.** Every step has its own conversation, where you can message your mentor or the coven’s High Priestess about that step. Use it. A question asked is worth ten wondered about.
5. **Test.** There is one short test, mostly multiple choice, about your rights, what a healthy group looks like and what membership asks. Choice questions are scored straight away; the written answers are read and scored by your mentor or the High Priestess against a clear guide. You need 80% to pass, and you can try again.
6. **Decide.** At the end you choose: continue as a devotee, take longer, or part well.

> **Note:** "High Priestess" is the usual name for a coven’s leader in many modern traditions, and this course uses it throughout. Your coven may say High Priest, Elder, Gothi, Hierophant, Leader or something else. The person who leads the coven is who we mean.

## What a coven is

A **coven** is a small group of people who practise a magical or religious path together, regularly, under agreed ways of working. Most covens are between three and thirteen people, small enough that everyone knows everyone. They meet to hold **rites** (ceremonies with a purpose: marking a full moon or a festival, honouring gods or ancestors, working magic together), to learn, and to support one another’s practice.

The word is old, but the kind of group it now names is mostly modern. One of the earliest recorded uses is in the 1662 confessions of Isobel Gowdie in Scotland, given under interrogation in a witch trial, which speak of witches meeting in "covens" of thirteen. Whether such organised groups really existed then is doubtful; historians treat trial confessions with great caution. The covens you will meet today mostly descend, directly or by inspiration, from the revival of witchcraft and paganism in Britain and America from the 1950s onward, and from the many reconstructed traditions (Norse, Hellenic, Roman, Celtic, Slavic and others) that grew alongside it. Many of those groups use other words: grove, kindred, hearth, household, circle. It is all the same idea: people who choose to practise together.

A good coven usually offers:

- **Shared practice.** Rites are different with others. Many people find group ritual stronger, steadier or simply more joyful than practising alone.
- **Teaching.** Most covens train newer members, often through programs like this one, with a mentor who walks alongside.
- **Continuity.** A coven keeps its own customs, its calendar of holy days and its own Book of Shadows (its shared book of rites and lore).
- **Friendship and support.** Not always, and not with everyone, but often.
- **Accountability.** Practising with others keeps you honest and keeps you practising.

## What a coven isn’t

It helps just as much to know what a coven is not, because disappointment usually comes from expecting the wrong thing.

- **It isn’t a cult.** A healthy coven has no claim on your whole life, your money, your body, your relationships or your mind. You keep your own judgement. You can leave. A later lesson shows you how to tell the difference.
- **It isn’t therapy.** Members may care for each other well, but the coven cannot replace a doctor, counsellor or crisis service, and should never try to.
- **It isn’t a family you can’t leave.** It may come to feel like family, and that is lovely, but membership is always a choice you renew.
- **It isn’t a shop.** Shared costs (candles, room hire, food) are normal and should be open and modest. Paying for rank, for secrets or for "advancement" is not.
- **It isn’t a guarantee.** No group can promise you power, healing, wealth, love or enlightenment. Practice is something you do and experience; it is not a purchase.
- **It isn’t the only way.** Many people practise alone all their lives, and practise well. Joining a coven is one good path among several.

## The people you’ll meet

You will hear words for positions in the coven. They vary, but roughly:

- **The High Priestess** leads: she (or he, or they) holds the coven’s rites, keeps its customs and has the last word on who joins and who rises.
- **Elders** are experienced members who help lead, teach and care for others.
- **Initiates** have made the coven’s deeper commitment, usually after a year and a day of study.
- **Devotees** (or dedicants) have chosen the coven and are training in it.
- **Your mentor** is the person assigned to walk with you through your training: answering questions, reading your answers and signing off your work.
- **Seekers**, like you now, are looking around.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own names for its positions, and some covens have fewer or more of them. Look at the coven’s page in the app, or ask your mentor on this step: "What are the positions here, and what does each one do?"

## A word about pace and pressure

Thirty days is a guide, not a test of speed. If you are busy, unwell, grieving or simply slow to warm up, say so on the step’s conversation. A good coven will tell you to take your time. If anyone hurries you, makes you feel you will "miss your chance", or tells you that doubt is a sign of weakness, notice it: that is one of the red flags you will read about later.

> **Try this:** Before you go on, write three lines in your own journal (or in the app’s Book of Shadows): why you looked for a coven, what you hope to find, and what you are afraid of. Keep it. You will read it again at the end of the month, and it will help you decide.

docs.title: Your rights, red flags and green flags
docs.summary: The rights you keep in any group, how to use them in the moment, and the signs of a healthy or harmful coven.
docs.body:
## Your rights, here and in any group

Whatever coven you join, whatever tradition, whatever position anyone holds, these are yours. They are not favours; they are the floor beneath every healthy group. The app’s community guidelines expect every coven to honour them.

1. **Consent.** Nobody may touch you, work magic on you, or involve you in anything (a ritual act, a trance, a drink, a photograph) without your clear, freely given agreement. You may say no, and you may change your yes to no at any moment, even halfway through. You don’t owe anyone a reason.
2. **Privacy.** Your name, face, address, workplace, health, relationships and history are yours to share or keep. Nobody may demand them, and nobody may share what you’ve told them without your permission (with one narrow exception: when someone is in danger, which a later course for elders covers).
3. **Leaving.** You may leave at any time, for any reason or none, without permission, penalty or punishment. That includes magical punishment: threats of curses, bad luck or spiritual harm if you leave are a form of coercion, whatever words are used.
4. **Never pressured for money.** No one may demand payment, gifts or loans beyond the coven’s open, modest shared costs, and certainly not for rank, initiation, healing or secrets.
5. **Never pressured for sex.** No rank, rite, teaching or initiation ever requires sexual contact, nudity you have not freely chosen, or sending intimate images. A leader who suggests otherwise is abusing their position. This is true in every tradition.
6. **Never pressured for secrets.** No one may require you to reveal private things about yourself as a test of loyalty, or to hand over passwords, messages or information about others.
7. **To ask questions** and get honest answers about how the coven works.
8. **To be safe.** To step out of any rite, to have a non-alcoholic choice, and to be told about fire, herbs and anything else that could hurt you.

> **Safety:** Covens in the app are for adults only. If you believe someone in a coven may be under 18, report it (press and hold one of their messages and choose Report, with the reason "Someone may be under 18").

## How to use your rights in the moment

Knowing your rights is one thing; saying no in a room full of people is another. Practise these simple words until they feel natural:

- "No, thank you."
- "I’ll sit this part out."
- "I’m not comfortable with that."
- "I need to step out for a minute."
- "I’d like to think about it first."

Then do it:

1. Say the words, calmly. You don’t need to explain.
2. Step back physically if you need to.
3. If you are pressed, repeat the same words. You don’t have to find new reasons.
4. Afterwards, write down what happened.
5. Tell your mentor or the High Priestess, unless they were the one pressing you; then tell someone else you trust.

If something serious happens in the app (harassment, pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience, sexual advances, or someone at risk), press and hold the message and choose **Report**. Reports go to Salt & Sovereignty’s moderators, outside the coven. You can also **block** someone. If you are ever in danger, call your local emergency number; crisis and support lines are in the app under **More → Support**.

## Red flags

These are warning signs. One alone may be a misunderstanding; several together, or any of the serious ones, mean you should step back and talk to someone outside the group.

- **Pressure** to commit quickly, sign without reading, or decide before you are ready.
- **Secrecy about the basics:** how decisions are made, money, what happens to complaints, how to leave.
- **Money for rank, secrets, healing or access** to the leader.
- **Sexual pressure** of any kind, including "it’s part of the tradition".
- **Isolation:** being told your friends or family "won’t understand" and you should see less of them.
- **Fear of leaving:** stories about what happened to people who left, threats of curses or bad luck, or ex-members never spoken of.
- **A leader who can’t be questioned,** who claims special authority from the gods that overrides others’ consent, or who punishes doubt.
- **Love-bombing:** overwhelming warmth and flattery at first, which turns cold when you disagree.
- **Discouraging medical or psychological care,** or claiming magic can replace it.
- **Alcohol or drugs pressed on people,** or no non-alcoholic option.
- **Gossip and factions:** members running each other down, especially to newcomers.
- **Rules that apply to everyone but the leader.**

## Green flags

These are signs of a healthy group. You won’t find every one, but you should find most.

- You are encouraged to take your time, ask questions and look at other groups too.
- The documents say plainly how things work, and practice matches them.
- Consent is asked for, out loud, before touch, trance or anything personal.
- There is always a non-alcoholic choice, and nobody comments on what you choose.
- Costs are open, modest and optional for those who can’t pay.
- Members speak well of each other and can disagree respectfully.
- People who have left are spoken of kindly.
- The leader admits mistakes and has someone to answer to.
- Members have lives, friends and interests outside the coven, and that is welcomed.
- Mental and physical health are taken seriously, and professionals are recommended when needed.
- You leave gatherings feeling more yourself, not less.

> **Try this:** Take the two lists and, for each item, note "seen", "not seen" or "don’t know yet" for this coven. Every "don’t know yet" is something to watch or ask about over the rest of the month.

docs.title: Getting to know this coven: attend, ask, read
docs.summary: How to read the coven’s documents, go to a rite as a newcomer, and talk with members, step by step.
docs.body:
## Three ways to get to know a coven

You cannot judge a group from its description, any more than you can judge a person from their profile. You find out by spending time with it. There are three good ways, and you will use all of them this month:

- **Attend:** go to its gatherings and see what really happens.
- **Ask:** talk to the High Priestess, your mentor and the members, and listen to how they answer.
- **Read:** read what the coven has written down about itself: its creed, rules, requirements and agreements.

Each tells you something the others can’t. Documents say what a group intends; attendance shows what it does; conversation shows how it treats people. When all three agree, you can trust what you see. When they don’t, pay attention to the gap.

## Read: the coven’s documents

Every coven in the app can keep pages about itself. They usually come in four kinds:

- **Creed:** what the coven believes or holds sacred, and why it exists.
- **Rules:** how members are expected to behave, at rites and online.
- **Requirements:** what is asked of members: attendance, study, contributions.
- **Agreements:** things you sign. You may already have signed some to join; others may be asked of you later.

How to read them well:

1. Open the coven from the Coven tab and find its pages. Agreements you have signed, or are asked to sign, are also under **My standing → Agreements**.
2. Read each one slowly, all the way through, in a quiet moment. Give it twenty minutes rather than skimming on the bus.
3. As you read, note three kinds of thing on paper or in your journal: what you agree with gladly, what you are unsure about, and anything you disagree with or don’t understand.
4. Look especially for: how decisions are made, how complaints are handled, what is confidential, what costs money, and how someone leaves. Good documents answer these plainly.
5. Take your notes to the step’s conversation and ask about everything in the second and third lists.

> **Note:** Never sign an agreement you have not read or do not understand. It is always acceptable to say "I’d like to ask about this before I sign". A coven that pushes you to sign quickly is showing you something about itself.

## Attend: going to a rite as a newcomer

You will be asked to attend at least one rite this month. It might be in person, held online in the app, or both at once.

Before you go:

1. Find it under **Rituals and rites** on the coven’s page, and answer "Will you be there?" with Going, Maybe or Can’t make it, so the person leading knows who to expect.
2. Read what it says members should know or bring. If anything is unclear (what to wear, whether to bring food, whether there will be alcohol), ask on the step’s conversation or in the coven’s chat.
3. Ask your mentor what will happen, roughly, and whether there is anything a newcomer should not do. Most covens are glad to explain.

While you are there:

- **Arrive on time,** or a little early. Late arrivals can disturb a rite once it has begun.
- **Follow, don’t lead.** Watch what others do. If you are unsure, it is always fine to stand quietly.
- **You may sit out any part.** You never have to speak words you don’t mean, drink anything, be touched, or take part in anything that makes you uncomfortable. Simply step back. A good coven expects this of guests and will not mind.
- **Notice how you feel,** in your body and your mood, before, during and after. That is useful information.
- **Notice how people treat each other,** and how they treat you.

Afterwards, write down what happened while it is fresh: what you saw, what you liked, what puzzled you, how you felt.

## Ask: talking with members

Members are the people you would be practising with for years. Get to know some of them, not only the leader.

1. Use the coven’s chat to say hello, and reply when people talk to you.
2. Start a one-to-one conversation with two or three members (tap **Messages**, then **New message**). A simple opener works: "Hello, I’m new and looking around. How long have you been in the coven, and what do you like about it?"
3. Ask open questions: "What’s a typical month like?", "What surprised you when you joined?", "What would you change?"
4. Listen to *how* they answer as well as what they say. Do they talk freely, or nervously? Do they speak warmly of each other? Can they say something critical without looking over their shoulder?

You never have to share your phone number, address, real name or anything else personal to talk in the app. Share what you’re comfortable with, when you’re ready.

> **Your coven:** Some covens pair every seeker with a member who acts as a friendly guide. Others prefer that you talk mostly with the High Priestess or your mentor at first. Ask what your coven’s custom is.

## Bringing it together

At the end of each week, take ten minutes to ask yourself three questions and write the answers down:

1. What did I learn about this coven this week, from reading, attending and asking?
2. Did what they say, what they wrote and what they did agree?
3. How do I feel about it, honestly, in my body as well as my head?

By the end of the month you will have four short entries, and a much clearer picture than any first impression can give.

docs.title: What membership will ask of you
docs.summary: Time, commitments, confidentiality and money: what is usual, what isn’t, and how to check you have room.
docs.body:
## Knowing the cost before you commit

Every worthwhile commitment costs something: time, attention, a little money, some flexibility. It is far kinder to yourself and to the coven to know what membership asks *before* you say yes than to discover it later and quietly drift away. This lesson sets out the usual asks. Your coven’s own requirements are in its documents; read them alongside this.

## Time

Most covens ask for some mix of these:

- **Rites.** Often each full moon and the main holy days of the tradition: anywhere from eight to twenty-six gatherings a year, usually one to three hours each, plus travel if in person.
- **Training.** As a devotee you will probably read lessons, practise at home and log your practice in the app. Most programs expect between one and four hours a week.
- **Personal practice.** Many traditions ask for a short daily or weekly devotion: five to twenty minutes of prayer, meditation or an offering.
- **Service.** Covens run on volunteers. You may be asked to help set up, bring food, tidy, or later teach and lead.

A simple way to check whether you have room:

1. Look at your last two ordinary weeks. Where did the time go?
2. Find where three or four hours a week could realistically come from. Be honest: if it would come from sleep, it won’t last.
3. Look at the coven’s calendar for the next three months in the app. How many of its rites could you actually reach?
4. If the numbers don’t work, say so. Many covens can adapt, or suggest you take longer.

## Commitments

Beyond time, covens often ask for:

- **Reliability.** If you say you are Going to a rite, go, or tell the person leading as early as you can that you can’t. In the app you can change your answer to Can’t make it; that counts as sending word.
