3. Carry it carefully around the edge of the space, letting the smoke drift into the corners. Hold the dish by its base or on a tile; it gets hot.
4. Set it down safely on the altar.

> **Safety:** Ventilate. Avoid smoke if anyone present has asthma or breathing problems, and around birds and small pets. Never leave burning charcoal or incense unattended, and keep it away from curtains and clothing. Use smoke cleansing, not "smudging", and don't use wild white sage or palo santo (see "Cleansing yourself").

### Sound

1. Ring a bell, strike a singing bowl, clap or drum at the centre of the space, then at each corner, then at the door.
2. Listen to the sound fade. Imagine it clearing the space as it spreads.

### Light

1. Light a single candle (or switch on a battery candle) at the centre or on the altar.
2. Say, "Light fill this place."
3. Some practitioners carry the light around the edge of the space.

## A full purification, step by step

Here is a complete purification you can use before any practice. Allow about fifteen minutes.

1. **Clean** the space physically, as above. Set out what you need.
2. **Prepare yourself:** wash your hands and face, put on clean clothes, ground and centre.
3. **Sweep** from the centre outward, with your words.
4. **Sprinkle** water (with salt, or as khernips, if your tradition uses them) around the edges and on the altar.
5. **Smoke or sound:** carry incense around the edges, or ring a bell at the centre, corners and door.
6. **Light** a candle on the altar.
7. **Stand at the centre** and feel the space. Does it feel different from before? Clearer, quieter, brighter? Note it.

This purification alone makes the space ready for simple practice. For ritual, you'd then go on to mark the boundary in your coven's way, which for some covens is a circle (next lesson) and for others is something else.

## Purifying outdoors

Outdoors, keep to light-touch methods: sound, a little clean water (no salt on soil or plants), a spoken purification, a slow walk around the edge. Pick up litter. Never light fires or charcoal where it isn't safe and allowed.

## How often?

Before every ritual, a full purification. Before daily practice, a quick version (wash your hands, ring a bell, light a candle) is enough. Your home space will feel easier to settle in over time.

## How you'll know it's working

- the space feels quieter, clearer or more "ready" afterwards
- you feel the shift from everyday to sacred more easily
- it becomes part of how you arrive: your body and mind start to settle as soon as you begin

> **Try this:** Do the full purification in the room where you practise, and once in a different room. Notice and write how each feels before and after.

docs.title: Casting a simple circle and calling the quarters
docs.summary: What a magic circle is, what the four elements and quarters are, and a simple circle casting you can do at home, step by step, with words you can use or change.
docs.body:
## Before you begin

This lesson teaches a simple, general-purpose circle in the Wiccan and eclectic style. If your coven doesn't cast circles (Hellenic, Roman, Heathen and some other traditions don't), read it to understand what your friends in other traditions do, and to learn the ideas of the elements and directions, which appear in many places. Then practise your coven's own opening instead, as your mentor shows you.

## What is a circle?

A **circle**, in modern witchcraft, is a boundary drawn around the space where you'll work. It isn't drawn on the floor (though some people mark it with cord, stones or candles); it's drawn with your attention, movement and words. Practitioners describe it as a sphere rather than a flat ring, extending above and below. Inside it, many say, you're "between the worlds": neither wholly in the everyday nor wholly elsewhere.

The circle does all the jobs of sacred space: focus, containment, protection and marking time.

## What are the elements?

The **four elements** are **air, fire, water and earth**. The idea comes from the Greek philosopher Empedocles in the fifth century BCE, who taught that everything is made of these four "roots" in different mixtures. It became the basis of Western science, medicine and magic for two thousand years. We now know chemistry works differently, but the four elements remain a rich way of thinking about qualities in life and magic:

- **Air:** breath, thought, words, communication, beginnings, the mind. Often linked with incense and feathers.
- **Fire:** energy, passion, will, courage, transformation. Often linked with candles.
- **Water:** emotion, intuition, love, healing, dreams. Often linked with a bowl or cup of water.
- **Earth:** the body, stability, growth, home, money, the material world. Often linked with salt, stone or soil.

Many traditions add a fifth, **spirit** (sometimes called aether), which unites the others.

## What are the quarters?

The **quarters** are the four directions (east, south, west, north) at the edges of the circle, each linked with an element. The most common pattern in modern witchcraft, which comes from the Golden Dawn, is:

- **East:** air (the rising sun, new beginnings)
- **South:** fire (the noon sun, heat)
- **West:** water (the setting sun, the sea, for those in Britain looking at the Atlantic)
- **North:** earth (darkness, mountains, the cold)

These links come from the geography and climate of north-western Europe. Practitioners elsewhere often adjust them. In the Southern Hemisphere, many swap north and south (fire in the north, where the sun is at noon, and earth in the south). Others place water towards their nearest sea. There's no single correct pattern; consistency within your practice matters more.

**Calling the quarters** means turning to each direction in turn and inviting its element, or the spirits or guardians associated with it, to be present and to guard the circle.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may use different directions, call different beings at the quarters (elements, winds, guardians, animals, gods), or call no quarters at all. Use your coven's form in group ritual, and ask your mentor which you should practise at home.

## What you'll need

Nothing is required except yourself. If you'd like, you can have:

- a small table as an altar, at the centre or in the north (or east)
- four objects to mark the quarters: a stick of incense or a feather (east), a candle (south), a bowl of water (west), a stone or a dish of salt (north)
- a compass, or a compass app, to find the directions
- a candle on the altar, with safe holders for every candle

## Casting the circle, step by step

This takes about ten to fifteen minutes. Read the steps through before you begin; you can keep this lesson open beside you the first few times.

1. **Purify.** Do the full purification from the previous lesson, or at least wash your hands, sweep and sprinkle.
2. **Ground and centre.** Stand at the centre of the space. Use your favourite method.
3. **Light the altar candle.** Say: "I light this flame to begin."
4. **Walk the boundary.** Go to the east edge of your space. Hold out your hand with your index finger pointing, or the first two fingers together (some use a wand or a ritual knife; neither is required). Walk slowly sunwise (clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere; many in the Southern Hemisphere walk anticlockwise) all the way around, back to the east.
5. **As you walk, draw the boundary.** Imagine a line of light flowing from your fingertip along the edge of the space: blue, white, gold or any colour that suits you. Feel the energy you've learned to raise flowing from your centre down your arm and out. You can say:

"I cast this circle as a place between the worlds,
a boundary to hold what is raised within,
and to keep out all that would do harm."

6. **Walk it twice more**, so you go round three times in all, the line growing brighter and firmer each time. (Some traditions walk once, some three times.)
7. **Feel the sphere.** Back in the east, stand still and imagine the line rising into a dome above and a bowl below, forming a sphere of light around the whole space.
8. **Call the quarters.** Turn to face each direction in turn, starting in the east and moving sunwise. At each, raise your hand in greeting (or light its candle, or hold up its object) and say something like:

East: "Spirits of the East, powers of Air, of breath and thought, I call you to guard this circle. Be welcome."
South: "Spirits of the South, powers of Fire, of energy and will, I call you to guard this circle. Be welcome."
West: "Spirits of the West, powers of Water, of feeling and intuition, I call you to guard this circle. Be welcome."
North: "Spirits of the North, powers of Earth, of body and stability, I call you to guard this circle. Be welcome."

At each, pause, and notice what you feel: a breeze, warmth, coolness, steadiness, or nothing in particular.

9. **Invite your gods (optional).** If you honour particular deities, or your coven does, you might invite them now, at the altar, in your own words or your tradition's. Never feel you must; a circle works without it.
10. **Declare it.** Return to the centre and say: "The circle is cast. I am between the worlds."

Your sacred space is ready. The next lesson covers what you do inside and how to close it.

## Other ways to cast

- **Quiet casting:** if you can't walk around the room, stand or sit at the centre and turn slowly, pointing, while you draw the circle in imagination.
- **Physical marking:** lay a cord, a line of salt (indoors only, on a hard floor), stones or candles around the edge, and walk the circle along it.
- **Verbal casting:** some practitioners cast entirely with words and breath, eyes closed, imagining the circle forming as they speak.
- **Small circles:** cast just around yourself and your altar, an arm's length away.

> **Safety:** Walk slowly, especially in a small room, and keep candles away from where you'll walk. Never walk circles round lit candles on the floor with loose clothing. If you're unsteady on your feet, cast seated.

## Common difficulties

**"I feel silly speaking aloud."** Start by whispering, or speak in your head. It becomes natural with practice.

**"I can't feel the circle."** Many people don't feel it strongly at first. Notice subtler signs: the room seems quieter, you feel more focused. Practise regularly and compare with how the room feels without a circle.

**"I forgot the words."** Use your own. The words matter less than your attention and intention. Write a version you like in your Grimoire.

**"I don't know where north is."** Use a compass app, or note where the sun rises (roughly east) and sets (roughly west).

> **Try this:** Practise casting this circle (or your coven's opening) five times over the next two weeks, closing it each time as the next lesson teaches. Keep it simple: cast, sit for five minutes, close.

docs.title: Working inside, leaving, and closing
docs.summary: What you do inside sacred space, how to leave it safely if you must (and when to just go), and how to close it step by step, including thanking the quarters and grounding.
docs.body:
## Inside sacred space

Once sacred space is made, by circle or by your coven's own form, it's where you do the work of the ritual. That might be:

- prayers, hymns and offerings to gods, spirits or ancestors
- raising and directing energy, as you learned in the last module
- meditation, journeying or divination
- celebrating a holy day
- simply sitting in quiet, to notice what's different

Some customs many practitioners keep inside a circle:

- **Move sunwise.** Walk clockwise (or the sunwise direction your coven uses) when moving around inside, as you did when casting. Moving against it (called **widdershins** or tuathal) is traditionally reserved for unwinding and closing.
- **Stay inside.** Avoid crossing the boundary until the circle is closed. This keeps it whole and keeps you focused.
- **Keep it focused.** Avoid ordinary chatter, phones and interruptions.
- **Keep it safe.** Fire, smoke and movement need the same care as anywhere else.

## Preparing so you won't need to leave

Most interruptions come from forgetting something. Before you begin:

- set out everything you'll need: matches, the snuffer, water, a lighter, the offering, your words
- go to the toilet
- silence your phone and let anyone you live with know you're not to be disturbed (unless it's urgent)
- put pets in another room if they'll be a distraction or a fire risk
- keep a glass of water and a snack nearby for after

## If you need to leave: cutting a door

Sometimes you need to leave a circle briefly: a forgotten item, a child calling, a pet. Many covens use a **door**: a gap cut in the circle and resealed.

1. Go to the edge of the circle, usually in the east or north-east, or wherever your coven puts its door.
2. With your finger (or wand or knife, if you use one), "cut" a doorway in the boundary: draw a line up from the floor, across at head height, and back down, imagining the light of the circle parting like a curtain.
3. Step through. Some people then close the door behind them; others leave it open for a quick return.
4. When you come back, step through and seal the door: trace the doorway again in reverse, imagining the light closing seamlessly.
5. Pause, ground, and pick up where you left off.

In group ritual, only one person (often the leader) cuts the door, or members ask the leader before leaving. If you need to leave, catch the leader's eye or follow your coven's custom.

## When to just go

**Your safety and the safety of others always come before the circle.** If there's a fire, a medical emergency, a child or pet in danger, someone at the door you must answer, or you feel faint, panicked or unwell: **just go.** Step across the boundary, deal with what needs dealing with, and don't give the circle a second thought.

Nothing terrible happens to a person who leaves a circle in a hurry. Some practitioners feel the circle is broken and needs recasting; some feel it holds; some feel a little jarred and need to ground. When you return, you can recast, or simply close it formally and start again another time.

> **Safety:** No ritual is ever worth staying in a dangerous situation. If anyone ever tells you that leaving a circle will bring harm or a curse, that's a red flag (see the welcome module).

## Closing sacred space

Closing is as important as opening. It thanks those you invited, unwinds the boundary, and brings you fully back to everyday life. Skipping it can leave you feeling spacey, unsettled or "half in, half out" for hours. Practitioners also consider it courteous: you don't invite guests and then walk out on them.

### Closing a circle, step by step

1. **Finish the work.** Complete any working, prayer or offering. Ground any raised energy.
2. **Thank the gods (if you invited them).** At the altar, thank them in your own words: "Thank you for your presence and your blessing. Go if you must, stay if you will. Hail and farewell." (Many covens say "Hail and farewell" or "Go in peace".)
3. **Thank the quarters, in reverse.** Turn to each direction in the opposite order from opening: north, west, south, east. At each, raise your hand (or snuff its candle) and say: "Spirits of the North, powers of Earth, thank you for guarding this circle. Go in peace. Hail and farewell." Then the west, the south, and finally the east.
4. **Take up the circle.** Go to the east. Point your finger as when casting, and walk once around **widdershins** (anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere; the reverse of however you cast). Imagine the line of light being drawn back into your fingertip, or fading, or sinking into the earth.
5. **Declare it open.** Back in the east or at the centre, say: "The circle is open, but unbroken. May the peace of the gods (or simply: peace) go in our hearts. Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again." That last line is a traditional Wiccan closing; use your coven's words, or simply, "The circle is open. It is done."
6. **Ground.** Kneel and put your palms on the floor. Let anything left over drain away. Eat and drink.
7. **Put out the flames.** Snuff every candle and make sure incense and charcoal are out or safely burning down in a heat-proof dish, never left unattended.
8. **Tidy.** Put things away. Deal with offerings according to your tradition (your tradition module explains how; a common modern custom is to leave them on the altar for a while, then put food or drink outdoors on the earth if it's safe for wildlife, or compost or bin it respectfully).
9. **Record.** Write in your journal what you did and what you noticed.

### Closing other forms

If your coven doesn't cast circles, its closing will be different: perhaps a final prayer and libation, thanks to the gods and spirits, extinguishing the sacred fire, or a closing blessing. The same principles apply: finish, thank, release the space, ground, tidy and record.

## Signs a space wasn't properly closed

- feeling spacey, buzzy or unsettled long afterwards
- the room still feeling "charged" or strange hours later
- trouble sleeping after evening ritual

If this happens, go back to the space, ground and centre, say a short closing in your own words ("Thank you to all who came. This place returns to ordinary use. It is done."), ring a bell or clap, open a window, and ground again. Then eat something.

## A complete practice session

Put together, a simple practice at home now looks like this:

1. Purify yourself and the space.
2. Ground and centre.
3. Make sacred space (cast a circle, or your coven's opening).
4. Do the work: a prayer, an offering, a meditation, an energy practice.
5. Ground any energy raised.
6. Thank and close.
7. Ground again, eat and drink, tidy, record.

Allow forty-five minutes to an hour at first. It gets quicker as it becomes familiar.

> **Your coven:** Every coven has its own words, order and customs for opening and closing. Ask your mentor to walk you through your coven's form step by step, and write it in your Grimoire. In group ritual, follow the leader and your coven's customs over anything in this lesson.

> **Try this:** After each practice in this stage, write down: how the space felt when opened, during the work, and after closing. Over five sessions, you'll learn what closing well feels like.

docs.title: The shape of a Celtic rite
docs.summary: Why no ancient Celtic liturgy survives, what the sources do give us for building a rite, the shape this course uses (gathering, saining, kindling, honouring the powers, praise and offering, the heart, omen, hospitality, thanks), and how it compares with Druid and Wiccan rites.
docs.body:
## Starting honestly

No complete pagan Celtic rite survives. We have no prayer book of the druids, no temple calendar of offerings, no order of service. What we have are pieces: Roman descriptions of sacrifices and sacred groves; archaeological traces of offerings; medieval tales in which people swear by the elements, feast at Samhain or meet the gods at a ford; and a great wealth of folk custom around fire, water, the hearth and the dead, recorded from Christian communities.

So every Celtic rite you will take part in is **modern**, built from those pieces by people who have studied them. That is not a weakness. It means each part should be there for a reason you can explain. This lesson gives the shape this course uses, and where each part comes from.

## What the sources give us

A few patterns run through the evidence and shape most modern Celtic rites:

- **Hospitality.** Feeding the guest, and the duty of the host, are central to early Irish and Welsh society. A rite can be understood as hospitality between people and the powers: we welcome, feed and honour them, and they bless us.
- **The hearth and the fire.** The household fire, kindled in the morning and smoored at night, and the great fires of Bealtaine and Samhain.
- **Water.** Offerings in lakes, rivers and springs over thousands of years, and the holy wells.
- **Sunwise movement.** Turning deiseal, with the sun, for luck and blessing.
- **The three realms.** Oaths in the Ulster tales are sworn by sky, earth and sea. Many modern rites honour land, sea and sky because of this.
- **Gods, ancestors and spirits of place.** The sources show all three receiving honour or offerings.
- **Poetry.** The poet's praise was a gift of great value; satire was a weapon.

## The shape this course uses

1. **Gathering and preparing.** Arriving, washing hands and face, quieting down, agreeing roles.
2. **Saining.** Blessing and cleansing people and place, with water and, where safe, the smoke of juniper or another herb. Moving sunwise.
3. **Kindling.** Lighting the fire or candle at the centre, with words.
4. **Honouring the powers.** Greeting the land and its spirits, the ancestors, and the gods, often with the three realms of land, sea and sky.
5. **Praise and offering.** Invoking the gods of the occasion by their names and deeds, and giving gifts.
6. **The heart of the rite.** The festival's customs, a devotion, a blessing, a working, a story told.
7. **An omen,** if the coven takes one: asking whether the offerings were welcome, or what counsel the powers give.
8. **Hospitality.** Blessing food and drink, giving the first portion, and sharing.
9. **Thanks and closing.** Thanking each power in reverse order, putting out or banking the fire, and later giving the offerings away.

The next lessons teach each part.

## How it differs from other rites

You may know Wiccan or eclectic rites. A Celtic rite in this style is different in a few ways:

- **No circle is cast.** The sources do not show one. Sacred space is made by saining, by the fire at the centre, and by the welcome given. Some Celtic covens do cast a circle; ask yours.
- **No quarters are called** with elements at each direction. The four directions do appear in Irish tradition (a medieval tale gives each province of Ireland a quality, which the app's five-stave ogham spread uses), but not as guardians to be summoned.
- **No single Goddess and God.** Many gods, each with their own name and story.
- **The gift matters more than the power raised.** Most of the rite is relationship: welcome, praise, gift, blessing. Magic may be part of it, but is not its centre.

**ADF Druid** rites share much of this shape: ADF's public Core Order of Ritual includes purifying, honouring the Earth Mother, establishing the fire, well and tree, opening a gate, inviting the Three Kindreds, offerings, an omen and the return of blessing. **OBOD** rites are held in a circle with the quarters, and use the revival's Druid's Prayer and the awen chant. Both are modern; both are fine; they are simply different.

## Who does what

In a coven rite, roles are often shared:

- **a leader** who speaks for the coven and keeps the rite moving;
- **a fire-keeper** responsible for the fire, its safety and putting it out;
- **a sainer** who carries water and smoke;
- **a poet or speaker** who gives the praise;
- **a host** who sees to the food, drink and hospitality.

In a solitary rite you do all of these yourself, simply. Keep the parts in order, even when each is only a sentence or two: the shape carries you, and over time it becomes something you can do from memory, in the dark, at a fire or by a candle.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor for your coven's order of rite, written out. Compare it with the shape here: what is the same, what is different, and why?

> **Try this:** For each of the nine parts above, write one sentence in your book saying where it comes from: a source, a folk custom, a modern order, or the coven's own making.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** hospitality, the hearth, offerings to water and fire, sunwise turning, oaths by the realms, praise poetry, folk saining.
- **Modern:** the order of rite as a whole, and the absence or presence of a circle in any given group.

docs.title: Saining, sunwise and the threshold
docs.summary: Saining, the Scots word for blessing and protecting, as recorded in Highland folk custom with water and juniper smoke; how to sain people and places safely today; moving sunwise and never against the sun in a rite; and the threshold as a place of care.
docs.body:
## What saining is

**Saining** is an old Scots word meaning to bless, to protect and to make holy; it is related to the word "sign", as in signing with the cross. In the Highlands and Islands, people sained cattle, houses, children and themselves at the turning points of the year and of life. Folklorists recorded the custom from the eighteenth century to the twentieth.

Two of the best recorded forms use water and smoke. F. Marian McNeill, in The Silver Bough (1950s), describes the New Year saining of a Highland house: water was fetched in silence from a ford "over which the living and the dead pass", sprinkled over the household and the house, and then juniper was burned until the house filled with smoke, with the windows shut, before they were opened to let the fresh air in. Other sources record sprinkling with water from a holy well, and carrying fire sunwise round a house, a field or a child.

Modern Celtic pagans have taken up saining as the way to begin a rite: blessing the people and the place before the fire is kindled. It is a good choice, rooted in recorded Gaelic custom, and it replaces the "cleansing" or "casting" of other traditions.

## Saining with water

Water is the simplest and safest way.

1. **Fetch the water.** Ideally from running water, a spring or a well, taken with a word of thanks. Rain water or tap water blessed at your hearth is fine.
2. **Bless it.** Hold the bowl and say what it is for: "Water of the land, bless and protect us and this place."
3. **Sprinkle sunwise.** Walk sunwise round the space, flicking a few drops from your fingers or a sprig of a green plant (rowan, juniper, heather, rosemary). Then go round the people, sprinkling each lightly, or let them dip their fingers and touch their brow.
4. **Return the water.** Afterwards, pour it on the earth.

## Saining with smoke

Smoke saining is powerful but must be done with care.

> **Safety:** Juniper and other herbs make thick, irritating smoke. The old custom of filling a closed house with it is not safe today, and would set off smoke alarms. Use a small amount in a heat-proof dish, with a window open; never disable a smoke alarm; keep it away from anyone with asthma, from pregnant people if they would rather avoid it, and from pets and babies. Outdoors, mind dry grass and wind. Never take smoke near someone who has not agreed to it.

1. Light a little dried juniper, or another herb, on a charcoal disc in a heat-proof dish, or simply use a candle flame as the sign of fire.
2. Carry it sunwise round the space, and offer it to each person, who may waft it towards themselves or decline.
3. Put it out completely afterwards, in sand or water.

If smoke is not possible, water alone is enough, or water followed by carrying a candle sunwise round the space.

## Sunwise

**Sunwise** means moving in the direction the sun travels across the sky: in Irish deiseal, in Scottish Gaelic deiseil, in Welsh, gyda'r haul ("with the sun"). For someone in the northern hemisphere facing south at noon, the sun moves from left to right, so sunwise is clockwise. Martin Martin, describing the Western Isles of Scotland in 1703, recorded people walking sunwise round those they wished to bless, round fires and round holy wells. Rounds at Irish holy wells are still walked sunwise.

The opposite direction, **tuathal** in Irish, "widdershins" in Scots, was unlucky in folk custom and associated with cursing. In a rite, move sunwise: walk sunwise round the fire, pass food and drink sunwise, and when you go round the space, go with the sun.

> **Note:** In the southern hemisphere the sun moves the other way across the northern sky, so some Celtic pagans there walk anticlockwise as their sunwise. Others keep clockwise. Both reasons are good; ask your coven which it keeps.

## The threshold

The threshold, the doorway and the boundary of a place, was a place of special care in Gaelic and Welsh custom. Rowan crosses bound with red thread were hung over doors and byres at Bealtaine; iron was set by the door; Brigid was welcomed in over the threshold on her eve; water was not thrown out of the door at night without warning in case the good folk were passing. A rite often begins at a threshold, real or marked: a gate, a door, two stones.

You can mark the threshold of your rite by:

- pausing at the door or edge, and saying why you have come;
- sprinkling a little water across it;
- setting a sprig of rowan or a piece of iron there.

> **Try this:** Sain your home this week. Bless a bowl of water at your hearth candle, then walk sunwise through every room, sprinkling a few drops in each and at each outside door, saying a short blessing of your own. Pour what is left on the earth outside. Write how it felt.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** saining with water from a ford or well and with juniper smoke, sunwise turning, and threshold protections, all recorded in Gaelic folk custom (in Christian communities).
- **Modern:** saining as the opening of a pagan coven rite, and the safety adjustments above.

docs.title: Fire, well and tree: the sacred centre
docs.summary: The three great features of Celtic sacred places in the sources and in modern practice: the sacred fire (Bealtaine, Kildare, the household hearth), the sacred well and waters, and the sacred tree (the bile); ADF’s modern use of all three; and how to build a simple shrine with them at home.
docs.body:
## A centre to stand at

Every rite needs a centre: a place to face, to give to, to gather round. In Celtic sources three things stand out as sacred centres: the **fire**, the **well** or water, and the **tree**. Modern Celtic pagans use one, two or all three.

## The fire

Fire is everywhere in Gaelic custom. A tenth-century glossary describes the Bealtaine fires through which cattle were driven. Later writers put a great Samhain fire at Tlachtga and a Bealtaine fire at Uisneach. In folk custom the household hearth was the centre of the home, its fire never allowed to go out, banked at night with a blessing and kindled each morning with another. In the 1180s Gerald of Wales described a fire at Kildare kept burning by nineteen nuns in turn, with Saint Brigid tending it herself on the twentieth night; the Brigidine Sisters relit a flame there in 1993.

In a rite the fire is the hearth of the gathering: the place where offerings are given, light by which to see one another, and the presence of the gods' warmth. Indoors it is a candle or a lamp; outdoors, a fire pit, a brazier or a small fire on safe ground.

> **Safety:** Outdoor fires need permission where you are, a safe site away from overhanging branches and dry grass, water or sand to hand, a named fire-keeper, and a plan for putting it out completely. Indoors, keep candles on a heat-proof surface and never leave them unattended.

## The well

Water was where the Celtic peoples gave their best things: swords, shields, cauldrons and jewellery have been found in lakes, rivers and bogs across Europe. Medieval Irish tales place the source of wisdom in a well (Connla's Well, or the well of Segais), surrounded by hazels whose nuts fall into it and feed the salmon of knowledge. Boann, goddess of the Boyne, was said to have made the river when the waters of such a well rose against her. And there are around three thousand holy wells in Ireland alone, most of them dedicated to saints, visited still.

In a rite the well is the way to the depths, to the land, the ancestors and the Otherworld beneath. Indoors it is a bowl of water, or a cauldron; outdoors, a spring, a river, the sea, or a bowl set on the earth.

## The tree

The early Irish knew certain great trees as **bile** (plural bileda), sacred trees standing at royal and assembly sites. The Dindshenchas names five legendary great trees of Ireland. Tree names fill the landscape. The Gaulish word nemeton, a sacred place or grove, appears in place-names across Europe, and Roman writers speak of druids' groves cut down by Roman armies. Folklore keeps the lone hawthorn as a fairy tree not to be cut, and the rowan as a protector.

In a rite the tree is the axis between the worlds, joining the depths and the heights, and a living presence of the land. Indoors it may be a branch, a staff, a potted plant or a carved post; outdoors, a living tree.

## Fire, well and tree together

**ADF Druidry** built its public ritual on these three as the "Sacred Centre": the fire carries offerings to the gods above, the well reaches the depths and the ancestors, and the tree stands between, joining them. This is a **modern** synthesis, made by Isaac Bonewits and others from Irish, Vedic and other sources, not a recovered ancient pattern. It is also a fine one, and many Celtic covens use it.

Other covens use only the fire, as the hearth of hospitality; or fire and water, as at a holy well where a candle is lit beside the spring. What matters is that you know why each is there.

## A shrine at home

You can build a simple Celtic shrine with these three:

1. **Choose a place:** a shelf, a table or a corner where it can stay.
2. **The fire:** a candle or lamp at the centre.
3. **The well:** a small bowl of water, changed often, to one side.
4. **The tree:** a branch, a sprig of a native tree, a piece of wood, or a small plant, to the other side or behind.
5. **The offering dish:** a small bowl or plate in front, for gifts.
6. **The powers:** an image or a stone for a god you honour, a photograph or name of an ancestor, a stone or shell from the land where you live.

Keep it clean. Change the water. Take the offerings away before they spoil. Dust it. A shrine is a place you tend, not a display.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven makes its centre: fire alone, fire and well, or fire, well and tree. Look at the coven's altar in the app, if it keeps one.

> **Try this:** Set up a fire, well and tree shrine at home for one week. Each day, light the candle, change the water and touch the branch, and greet the gods, ancestors and land. Take a photo of it for your mentor if you'd like them to see it, and note which of the three feels most alive to you.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** sacred fires, offerings in water, holy wells, sacred trees and groves, all in the sources.
- **Modern:** putting the three together as a ritual centre (ADF, from the 1980s), and shrines in modern homes.

docs.title: Offering and hospitality
docs.summary: How to give offerings in a Celtic way: hospitality as the frame (host, guest and the gods), what to offer and to whom, how to give to fire, water and earth, the first portion, words to say, what not to do, and how to dispose of offerings well.
docs.body:
## Hospitality as the frame

In early Ireland, hospitality was law as well as custom. Certain landholders, the **briugu** or hospitallers, were bound to keep open house for any traveller, and in the tales their hostels stand at crossroads with a cauldron always on the fire. To refuse a guest food shamed the household. To harm a guest under your roof was among the worst crimes. The Welsh laws and tales value hospitality just as highly: in the First Branch of the Mabinogi, a great feast is the setting for Pwyll's meeting with Rhiannon, and how a host treats guests decides much of the story.

Many Celtic pagans understand offering through this lens. In a rite we are hosts and the gods, ancestors and spirits are honoured guests; or we are guests in their land and bring a gift. Either way, the relationship is one of giving and receiving, with honour on both sides. A gift creates a bond. That is why you give first, give well, and give freely.

## What to offer

The best offerings are good, real things, given with care:

- **dairy:** milk, cream and butter, the wealth of an old Gaelic farm, and in folk custom the first of the churning left for the good folk;
- **grain:** oatcakes, bannocks, bread, porridge, a pinch of oats or barley;
- **honey,** apples, berries and other fruits of the season;
- **drink:** ale, mead, cider, whiskey, or (always just as good) water, milk or juice;
- **made things:** a poem, a song, a piece of craft, a woven cross;
- **work:** clearing litter from a spring, planting a tree, learning a language, given in a god's name.

Archaeology shows the ancients gave their finest metalwork to the waters. A coin or a small handmade object can carry that tradition, but think about where it goes; many wells and rivers are harmed by coins and metal.

## To whom

A common pattern is to give to each of the three kinds of power:

- **the gods:** the first and best, often to the fire;
- **the ancestors:** often to the earth or set at the table;
- **the spirits of the land:** to the earth, a tree or water, often kept separate from the gods' gifts.

## How to give

1. **Prepare it.** Put the offering in a clean dish or cup.
2. **Name it.** Say what you are giving and to whom: "Brigid, I give you this butter, from my hand, with thanks for your blessing on my work."
3. **Give it.** To **fire**, by placing a little in the flames of a fire or on a heat-proof dish beside a candle; to **water**, by pouring it into running water or a bowl; to **earth**, by pouring or burying it, or placing it at the foot of a tree.
4. **Pause.** Let it be received. Many people stand quietly for a breath or two.
5. **Leave it.** Food given is not taken back or eaten.

## The first portion

The old custom was to give the **first** and best portion, not the leftovers: the first of the milk, the first of the harvest at Lughnasadh, the first drop of a drink. At a coven feast, set aside a portion of each dish for the powers before anyone eats. At home, pour the first drop of your evening drink for the house.

## What not to do

- **Don't offer what isn't yours to give.** A stolen or borrowed gift shames the giver.
- **Don't harm wildlife or pets.** No chocolate, grapes, raisins, onion or garlic left outside; nothing in plastic; nothing that will attract rats near houses.
- **Don't pollute waters.** Pour liquids, not oil or wine in quantity, into running water; never throw glass, plastic or synthetic things into wells, rivers or the sea.
- **Don't give blood or harm any creature.** Modern Celtic paganism does not sacrifice animals.
- **Don't bargain greedily.** "I give so that you may give" is an old principle of gift exchange, but a gift that is only a payment is a poor gift.

## Disposing of offerings

Offerings on a shrine are usually taken away at the end of the day or the next morning: poured or buried outside, placed under a tree, composted, or burned in a fire. If you live without a garden, a pot plant's soil takes a liquid; food can go into food waste, wrapped, with a word of thanks. What matters is respect.

## When it feels one-sided

Many people worry, at first, that they are giving into silence. That is normal. Hospitality in the old sense was not a trade with instant returns; it built a bond over years, and honour on both sides. Keep giving small, regular gifts, keep your word, and notice over months rather than days whether your life with the gods, the dead and the land feels any different. Write it down, so that you can look back.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven offers, to whom, and what it does with the offerings after a rite.

> **Try this:** For two weeks, give the first drop of a drink or the first bite of a meal to the house, once a day, with a few words. Note how it changes, if at all, the way you sit down to eat.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** hospitality law and custom, offerings in waters, dairy and food for the good folk and the dead, the first portion.
- **Modern:** the pattern of three kinds of offering to gods, ancestors and land spirits in one rite, and the environmental care.

docs.title: Prayer, praise and the spoken word
docs.summary: Why words matter so much in Celtic tradition: the poets, praise and satire; what we can learn from the shape of Gaelic prayer in Carmina Gadelica without taking it; invoking a god by names, deeds and places; the threefold blessing; and writing your own praise.
docs.body:
## The power of words

In early Ireland and Wales, the poet was one of the most honoured people in society. The **file** (plural filid) in Ireland and the **bardd** in Wales trained for years, kept the genealogies and the lore, and composed praise for kings. A poet's praise could raise a person's honour; a poet's satire could ruin it, and the tales say a true satire could raise blisters on the face of an unjust king. Brigid, says Cormac's Glossary, was the goddess whom the poets worshipped. Cerridwen's cauldron gave Taliesin the awen, poetic inspiration.

So in Celtic practice, words are not filler between actions. Speaking well to the gods is itself an offering, perhaps the best one.

## What we can learn from Gaelic prayer

Alexander Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica (from 1900) gathers hundreds of prayers, blessings and charms from Gaelic-speaking Scotland: for kindling the fire, smooring it at night, milking, weaving, setting out on a journey, going to sleep. They are Christian prayers, addressed to God, Christ, Mary, Brigid and Michael, and Carmichael polished them. They are not pagan texts, and the respectful way to use them is to learn from them rather than to rewrite them.

What they teach is a **way of praying**:

- **Short lines,** often only two or three words, easy to say from memory while working.
- **Threes.** "To save, to shield, to surround." Repetition in threes runs through Gaelic and Welsh speech, and through the triads.
- **Everyday tasks.** Prayer is woven into kindling, milking and travelling, not kept for special occasions.
- **Encircling.** Many prayers ask for a protecting circle, a caim, around a person or a house.
- **The named day and the named thing.** "This eve, this night, and every night."

## Invoking a god

When you call on a god in a rite, the old way of praise suggests a pattern:

1. **Their names.** Call them by name, and by their bynames: "Lugh, Samildánach, Lugh of the long arm."
2. **Their kin.** Name their father, mother or people: "son of Cian, grandson of Balor and of Dian Cécht".
3. **Their deeds.** Tell what they did in the stories: "who came to Tara's door and was master of every art".
4. **Their places.** Name where they are honoured: "you whose feast is at Tailtiu".
5. **The asking.** Invite them, and say why: "come to our fire, receive our gift, bless our work".

This pattern of names, kin, deeds and places is common in praise across many old religions, and fits the Irish and Welsh love of genealogy and place-lore. The words themselves should be yours, drawn from the stories you have read.

## The threefold blessing

A simple form many Celtic pagans use is a blessing in threes, in the manner of Gaelic prayer. For example, at a hearth:

"Fire of the hearth,
warm us, light us, guard us,
this day, this night,
and every day and night."

You can write these for any purpose: a journey, a meal, a new home, a friend who is ill.

## Writing praise

1. **Choose a god** whose stories you have read.
2. **Gather their names, kin, deeds and places** in your book.
3. **Write six to twelve short lines,** speaking to them directly.
4. **Use threes,** and repeat a line at the end, as an echo.
5. **Read it aloud** at your shrine. Change any line that feels false or clumsy.
6. **Keep it** in your book, and use it in your rites.

It does not need to rhyme or be clever. Honest, specific words are worth more than borrowed grand ones.

## Speaking aloud

Many people find speaking to the gods aloud awkward at first. That is common, and it passes. A few things help:

- **Practise alone first,** quietly, then at a normal speaking voice.
- **Learn the opening lines by heart,** so you are not reading while you look at the fire.
- **Slow down.** Old praise was spoken or chanted, not rushed. Leave a breath between lines.
- **Mean it.** If a line feels false to you, change it. A plain "thank you" said with feeling is better than a fine phrase you do not believe.
- **In a coven,** the poet or speaker may read from a card. That is fine; most people do at first.

## Silence

Words are not the whole of prayer. After you have spoken, leave a time of quiet: a minute or two of listening, watching the flame or the water. Some of the most important moments in a rite come in that silence. Notice what comes, and do not hurry to fill it.

## The languages

If you are learning Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Welsh, try saying a line of your praise in that language: a god's name in its own form, a greeting, a blessing. Be humble about pronunciation and check with a teacher or a recording.

> **Note:** Some well-known "Celtic" prayers are modern. The Song of Amergin, from the Lebor Gabála, is a genuine medieval Irish poem, though its meaning is debated; many prayers sold as "ancient Celtic blessings" were written in the last century.

> **Try this:** Write a praise of six to twelve lines for a god whose stories you have read, using names, kin, deeds and places. Read it aloud at your shrine three times over a week, revising each time.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the honour of poets, praise and satire, the Gaelic prayer forms of Carmina Gadelica (Christian), threefold patterns.
- **Modern:** pagan praise written in those forms, and its use in coven rites.

docs.title: A complete rite, from start to finish, with an omen
docs.summary: A full sample Celtic rite to learn and adapt: preparing, saining, kindling, honouring land, sea and sky, the ancestors, the spirits of place and a god, praise and offering, an omen with ogham, hospitality and closing; for a coven and for one person alone.
docs.body:
## Using this rite

Here is a complete rite for a coven, with notes for keeping it alone. It is a **modern** rite in the shape this module teaches. It can serve as a monthly devotion, a welcome for a newcomer, or the frame for a festival, with that festival's customs at its heart. Learn it well enough to lead it without reading, then change it to suit your coven.

This example honours Lugh. Put in the god of your own occasion.

## What you need

- a fire or a candle at the centre; a bowl of water; a branch or plant, if you use the tree;
- a bowl of water for saining, and a sprig of green;
- offerings: milk or butter, oatcakes or bread, and a drink (with juice or water for those who prefer);
- food and drink to share;
- a set of ogham staves, or the app's ogham spreads, for the omen;
- the words, written out for whoever speaks.

## The rite

1. **Gathering.** Everyone washes hands and face, and stands quietly at the edge of the space. The leader says why you have come: "We gather to honour Lugh of the many skills, at his feast."

2. **Saining.** The sainer blesses the water ("Water of the land, bless and protect us") and walks sunwise round the space, sprinkling it, then round the people, sprinkling each who wishes. If smoke is used, it follows, carried sunwise and offered to each person.

3. **Kindling.** The fire-keeper lights the fire or candle and says: "We kindle this fire, hearth of our gathering, light of the gods. Let it burn for welcome." All may answer, "Let it burn for welcome."

4. **Land, sea and sky.** The leader, or three people in turn, face the earth, the water and the sky: "We honour the land beneath us. We honour the sea around us. We honour the sky above us." A modern form, built on the old oath by sky, earth and sea.

5. **The spirits of the land.** Someone pours milk on the earth or into the land's dish: "Spirits of this place, good neighbours, we are guests here. Take this gift, and let there be peace between us." No more is asked of them.

6. **The ancestors.** Someone places bread for the dead: "Ancestors of blood, of place and of spirit, you who went before us, be welcome at our fire." People may speak names quietly.

7. **The god.** The poet speaks the praise of Lugh, with his names, kin, deeds and places, and invites him: "Lugh, come to our fire, receive our gift." The offering is given to the fire: a piece of oatcake and a little butter, and a drink poured.

8. **The heart.** At a festival, its customs; for Lugh, perhaps each person names a skill they are learning and asks for his help, or the first fruits are blessed. At a devotional rite, quiet time, a story read aloud, or each person's own short prayer.

9. **The omen.** The leader asks, "Lugh, have our gifts been welcome? What counsel do you give us?" and draws one ogham stave, or three, in silence. The stave's meaning is read aloud and talked over briefly. If the omen seems poor, a further gift may be given and the omen asked again, once, or the coven may simply take the counsel to heart. Ogham divination is **modern**; there is a medieval tale of a druid using ogham on yew wands to find someone lost, but no surviving rite of omen-taking.

10. **Hospitality.** The host blesses the food and drink: "Bless this food and those who share it." The first portion of each is set aside for the powers. Food and drink are passed sunwise.

11. **Thanks.** In reverse order, the leader thanks Lugh, the ancestors, the spirits of the land and the three realms: "Lugh, thank you. Ancestors, thank you. Good neighbours, thank you. Land, sea and sky, thank you."

12. **Closing.** The fire-keeper banks or puts out the fire: "The fire is banked, but not quenched in our hearts." The leader ends: "The rite is ended. Go in peace." Afterwards, the offerings are given to the earth, water or fire.

## Keeping it alone

Alone, keep every step, simply: one candle, one bowl of water, one dish. Sain yourself with water, kindle, greet the three realms, the land, the dead and the god, give your gift, keep a few minutes of quiet or your festival's custom, draw a stave if you wish, eat a little with the first bite set aside, thank and close. It takes twenty to thirty minutes.

## Common difficulties

- **Too long.** Shorten the praise or the heart, not the welcome and thanks.
- **The fire won't light.** Have a candle ready as a backup, and don't take it as an omen.
- **Unsure of the omen.** Treat it as counsel, not command, and write it down; meaning often becomes clear later.
- **Someone unwell.** Pause. The fire-keeper or another member cares for them; the rite can wait.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor for your coven's own words for each part, and which parts it adds or leaves out.

> **Try this:** Keep this rite once alone and, if you can, once with the coven. Afterwards, write in your book what each part did, which part felt strongest, and what you would change.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** each element's roots (saining, sunwise turning, the hearth, gifts of food and drink, praise, the oath by sky, earth and sea, hospitality).
- **Modern:** this rite as a whole, and ogham omens.

docs.title: What an altar is for, and setting one up
docs.summary: What an altar is and what it's for, a little of its history, the different kinds, and how to set one up step by step with little money or space, safely and discreetly if you need to.
docs.body:
## A place to meet

An **altar** is a surface set aside for religious or magical practice: a place where you make offerings, pray, work magic, and keep the objects that matter to your practice. It might be a grand table in a temple, a shelf in your bedroom, a windowsill, a tray you bring out and put away, or a flat stone in your garden.

What an altar does depends on who you ask, and usually it does several things at once:

- **A place of meeting.** In many religions, the altar is where people meet their gods, spirits or ancestors: where offerings are given and prayers spoken.
- **A focus.** It gathers your attention. Seeing it reminds you of your practice; sitting at it helps you settle.
- **A workbench.** For magical work, it's where you set out what you need: candles, herbs, the objects you're charging.
- **A record of your path.** Over time, an altar comes to reflect your life and practice: the season, your gods, your loved dead, your hopes.

You don't need an altar to practise. But most people find it helps a great deal, and nearly every tradition this course teaches uses one in some form.

## A little history

- In **ancient Greece**, the main altar (**bomos**) usually stood **outside** the temple, in the open air, where fire burned and offerings were made. Inside homes, people kept small shrines to household gods such as Hestia (the hearth) and Zeus Ktesios (protector of the storeroom).
- In **ancient Rome**, many households had a **lararium**, a shrine to the household gods (the Lares and Penates) and the family's guardian spirit, where daily offerings of food, wine and incense were made.
- **Norse and Germanic** peoples made offerings at outdoor sacred places and at the **hörgr**, a heap of stones used as an altar, and in halls and homes.
- **Christian** churches have altars for the Eucharist, and many Christian homes have had prayer corners, holy pictures and household shrines.
- The **modern Wiccan altar**, set with the tools you'll meet in the next lesson, took shape in the 1940s and 1950s, drawing on ceremonial magic and older folk practice.

So the household altar, a small shrine in the home where daily offerings are made, is one of the oldest and most widespread religious practices there is.

> **Your coven:** Your tradition module explains your coven's altar customs in full. In Hellenic practice, for instance, a household shrine often honours Hestia first, and offerings are often made with a libation and incense; Roman practitioners may keep a lararium; Heathens may keep an altar to their gods and ancestors with a drinking horn and bowl.

## Kinds of altar

Many practitioners have more than one:

- **A devotional altar** for one or more gods or spirits, with their images or symbols and a place for offerings.
- **An ancestor altar** with photographs, names and mementos of your loved dead (more on ancestors in your tradition's devotion module).
- **A working altar** where you do spells and energy work, often cleared and reset for each working.
- **A seasonal altar** that changes with the holy days of your calendar.
- **A general altar** that combines some or all of these. This is where most beginners start.

## Choosing a place

Think about:

- **Safety.** Away from curtains, shelves above, and draughts if you'll burn candles. Out of reach of small children and pets, or without flames if they can reach it.
- **Stability.** A steady surface that won't be knocked.
- **Privacy.** Somewhere you're comfortable having it seen, or that can be covered or put away.
- **Use.** Somewhere you can sit or stand in front of it, ideally where you'll pass it daily.
- **Direction.** Some traditions face their altar in a particular direction: many Wiccans east or north, many Hellenic practitioners east, towards the rising sun. If your space doesn't allow it, don't worry.

## Setting up an altar with little money

You can set up a meaningful altar today with things you already have.

1. **Choose your surface.** A shelf, the top of a chest of drawers, a windowsill, a small table, a tray or a wooden board.
2. **Clean it.** Dust and wipe it with intention: this is the first step in making it sacred.
3. **Lay a cloth (optional).** A scarf, a napkin, a piece of fabric in a colour you love or one that suits the season.
4. **Add a light.** A candle in a stable holder, or a battery candle. Light is at the heart of most altars.
5. **Add something for each element (optional but common):** a stone or a dish of salt (earth), a stick of incense or a feather (air), the candle (fire), a small bowl or glass of water (water).
6. **Add something for your gods, spirits or path.** An image (a printed picture, a postcard, a drawing), a symbol, a statue if you have one, or simply a word written on a card. Ask your mentor what's fitting for your tradition.
7. **Add a dish or cup for offerings.** Any small bowl or cup that you keep for this purpose.
8. **Add something from nature:** a leaf, a seed head, a shell, flowers, an acorn. Gather responsibly: take only what's fallen, plentiful, and allowed.
9. **Add something personal:** a photo, a stone from a meaningful place, a gift.
10. **Step back and look.** Move things until it feels right. There's no correct layout: balance, simplicity and meaning are what matter.

Things that cost almost nothing: tea lights, a jam-jar lid as a candle holder (on a heat-proof surface), a saucer as an offering dish, a printed image, a stone from your garden, a glass of water, a sprig from a herb pot.

## A discreet altar

If you live with people who wouldn't understand, or you're not ready to be open about your practice, an altar can be discreet:

- a shelf with a candle, a plant and a few stones that looks like decoration
- a box or tin with your items inside, which you open and set out when you practise
- a tray you bring out and put away
- a single object (a pendant, a stone, a photograph) that stands for your altar
- a corner of a drawer
- the app's altar, which you'll learn about in the last lesson of this module

Discreet altars are a long tradition in themselves. Many people in many times have practised quietly.

## Safety on the altar

- Candles: in stable holders, on heat-proof surfaces, never left unattended. Use battery candles if pets, children or your living situation make flames unsafe.
- Incense: in a proper holder, with ventilation, away from anything that can catch.
- Plants: many common altar plants and flowers (lilies especially) are poisonous to cats and dogs. Check before you put them where pets can reach.
- Stones and small objects: keep out of reach of small children, who may swallow them.
- Water: change it regularly so it doesn't go stale.
- Food offerings: remove them before they go off, and keep them away from pets if they're harmful (chocolate, grapes, raisins and onions are toxic to dogs, for example).

> **Try this:** Choose a place for your altar today, clean it, and set out at least a light and one meaningful object. You can add to it over the coming weeks.

docs.title: Tools and their uses
docs.summary: The tools you'll hear about, what each is used for, the tools of different traditions, why none of them is required, and how to find tools cheaply, ethically and legally.
docs.body:
## None of this is required

Start with the most important point: **you don't need any tools to practise.** Everything in this course so far has been done with your breath, your body, your attention and your hands. Tools are aids. They focus the mind, carry meaning, and connect you with a tradition. They don't contain the power on their own.

Many experienced practitioners own very few tools. Some own none. If someone tells you that you must buy a particular set of tools (especially from them) to practise, be wary (see "Red flags in any group").

That said, tools can be a real joy, and learning what they're for helps you understand rituals you'll see. Here's a guide.

## Common tools in modern witchcraft

These are the tools you'll see in most Wiccan and eclectic books. Each is linked to an element in many traditions; the links vary, so don't worry if a book disagrees.

- **Athame** (pronounced variously, often "a-THAH-may" or "ATH-a-may"). A ritual knife, usually double-edged with a black handle, used to direct energy: casting the circle, cutting a door, consecrating. It's **not** used to cut anything physical. The word appears in Gerald Gardner's writings and probably comes from a variant spelling in one version of the *Key of Solomon*. Often linked with fire or air.
- **Wand.** A rod of wood (or other material) used, like the athame, to direct energy, often in gentler work: invoking, blessing, charging. Often linked with air or fire. Your index finger does the same job.
- **Chalice.** A cup or goblet, holding water, wine or juice for blessing and sharing. Linked with water.
- **Pentacle.** A flat disc of wood, metal, clay or stone, inscribed with a pentagram (a five-pointed star in a circle), used as a base for consecrating objects and offerings. Linked with earth. (A **pentagram** is the star; a **pentacle** is the disc or the star in a circle.)
- **Censer.** An incense burner. Linked with air.
- **Candles.** On almost every altar. Linked with fire.
- **Bowls for water and salt.** Used to purify and consecrate. Linked with water and earth.
- **Besom.** A broom of twigs used to sweep the space before ritual.
- **Cauldron.** A small iron pot, used to burn things safely, hold water for scrying, or as a symbol of transformation and the goddess in some traditions.
- **Bell.** Rung to cleanse, to mark the start and end of a ritual, or to call attention.
- **Cords.** Used in knot magic, to measure a circle, or worn as a sign of degree in some covens.
- **Boline.** A practical knife, often white-handled, used for actually cutting herbs, cords and candles.
- **Book of Shadows or Grimoire.** Your book of practice: arguably the most important tool of all.

## Tools in other traditions

Each tradition has its own tools; your tradition module teaches them properly. A taste:

- **Hellenic:** a basin or bowl for **khernips**; a **phiale** (a shallow libation bowl) for pouring drink offerings; a censer for incense (frankincense was widely used); barley grains; a lamp; images of the gods.
- **Roman:** a **patera** (a libation dish, like the phiale); an incense box; a lamp; the household shrine (lararium) with images of the Lares and the family genius.
- **Heathen:** a **drinking horn** or cup for sumbel and blót; a bowl for offerings; sometimes a sprig of evergreen to sprinkle; a hammer pendant or symbols of the gods.
- **Druid and Celtic revival:** a cup, often a sickle or knife, candles, the sacred fire, offerings of water, silver or song.
- **Slavic:** the hearth or stove, bread and salt, an embroidered cloth (a **rushnyk** in Ukrainian tradition), candles, and the "beautiful corner" found in many Slavic homes, a shelf for holy images where Christian and older folk customs have long mingled.
- **Christian folk practice:** the Bible, candles, holy water, oil, a rosary or prayer beads, images of saints.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may use some of these tools, others, or none. It may ask members to make their own, to wait until a certain stage before acquiring some, or to keep certain tools for group ritual only. Ask your mentor what your coven expects before you buy anything.

## Choosing and finding tools

- **Use what you have.** A wine glass makes a chalice. A wooden spoon or a fallen stick makes a wand. A saucer makes a pentacle or an offering dish. A cereal bowl holds water.
- **Make your own.** Many traditions value hand-made tools above bought ones. A stick you've found, stripped and oiled yourself; a clay dish you've shaped; a cord you've braided.
- **Buy second-hand.** Charity shops, flea markets and car boot sales are full of cups, bowls, candle holders, bells and knives. Cleanse them before use (next lesson).
- **Take your time.** Many practitioners acquire tools one at a time, over years, as they're needed or as the right one turns up.
- **Buy ethically.** Some plants, resins and stones raise real sourcing concerns: wild-harvested white sage and palo santo, some sandalwood, some crystals mined with child labour. The Living Library's sourcing notes give alternatives. Choose garden herbs and well-sourced resins; buy stones from sellers who can tell you where they came from, or use local stones.

## Knives and the law

Ritual knives are knives, and the law treats them so.

- In many countries, carrying a knife in public without a good reason is a crime, and "it's for my religion" may not be accepted as a reason for a ritual knife. In the UK, for instance, carrying any fixed-blade or locking knife in public without good reason is an offence.
- **Check the law where you live.** Keep ritual knives at home, and transport them to group rituals only if it's legal, wrapped and out of reach (in a locked box in the boot of a car, for instance). Many covens use a wand or a finger for outdoor rites for exactly this reason.
- An athame is traditionally blunt, since it isn't for cutting, but a blunt knife can still be illegal to carry and can still hurt someone. Keep knives away from children.

## Tools are relationships, not purchases

Many practitioners say a tool becomes powerful through use: the more you work with it, the more it carries your practice. A plain cup used for every offering for ten years becomes more sacred than an expensive chalice used once. So choose simply, use often, and let your tools grow with you.

> **Try this:** Look around your home for three things that could serve as tools: a cup, a dish, a candle holder, a stick, a bell. Set them on or near your altar. In your journal, write what each will be for.

docs.title: Cleansing and consecrating
docs.summary: How to clear an object of what it carries and dedicate it to sacred use, step by step, with methods that are safe for different materials.
docs.body:
## Two steps: clear, then dedicate

Before using a new (or new-to-you) object on your altar or in ritual, most practitioners do two things:

- **Cleansing** clears the object of whatever it has picked up: from its makers, its previous owners, the shop, its journey. In the energy view, it removes old energy. In the spirit view, it removes pollution or unwanted influences. In the psychological view, it marks a clean start: this object's past is behind it.
- **Consecrating** dedicates it to sacred use: you declare what it's for, and (in many traditions) ask the gods or the elements to bless it. After consecration, it belongs to your practice. Many people then keep consecrated tools for sacred use only.

A third idea you've already met, **charging**, fills an object with energy for a particular purpose (see "Directing, releasing and grounding"). You might cleanse, consecrate and then charge a protective pendant, for instance.

## Methods of cleansing objects

Choose a method that's safe for the material. When in doubt, use smoke, sound or visualisation, which suit everything.

### Water

Rinse or wipe the object in clean water, ideally running water (a tap or a stream), with intention: "I wash away all that came before." Dry thoroughly.

Safe for: glass, glazed ceramic, most metal (dry quickly to prevent rust), hard stones such as quartz.
Not safe for: wood (can warp), paper, fabric you can't wash, many soft or porous stones (selenite, malachite, turquoise, opal and others), anything electronic or with glued parts.

### Salt

Bury the object in a bowl of dry salt, or sprinkle salt over it, for a few hours or overnight. Or wipe it with salt water.

Safe for: glass, glazed ceramic, many hard stones.
Not safe for: most metals (salt corrodes them), wood, and many stones (salt can scratch or damage soft and porous stones). Salt water is worse than dry salt.

### Smoke

Pass the object through the smoke of incense or local herbs three times, or hold it in the smoke for a minute, with your words.

Safe for: almost everything. Ventilate, and see the safety notes on smoke in earlier lessons.

### Sound

Ring a bell, strike a singing bowl or clap over the object several times, imagining the sound shaking it clean.

Safe for: everything. Ideal if you can't use smoke.

### Light: sun and moon

Leave the object in sunlight for a few hours, or in the light of the full moon overnight (on a windowsill is fine).

Safe for: most things.
Not safe for: many coloured stones fade in sunlight (amethyst, rose quartz, citrine and others), and some fabrics, photographs and dyes fade too. Moonlight is gentle on everything.

### Earth

Bury the object in a pot of soil or in the garden for a day to a week, so the earth can absorb what it carries.

Safe for: stones, sturdy objects. Mark where you buried it.
Not safe for: anything that rusts, rots or stains.

### Breath and visualisation

Hold the object, ground and centre, and breathe slowly onto it, imagining your breath and a clear light washing it clean. Safe for everything; needs nothing.

## A cleansing, step by step

1. Ground and centre.
2. Hold the object. Notice what it feels like (use your hand-sensing).
3. Choose a safe method and carry it out, saying something like: "I cleanse this [cup] of all that came before. Let it be clean and new."
4. Hold it again and notice whether it feels different.
5. Wash your hands.

## Consecrating, step by step

This is a simple, general consecration using the four elements, suitable for any tool. Your coven may have its own form, or may consecrate tools together in group ritual.

You'll need: the cleansed object; a candle (fire); incense or a feather (air); a bowl of water (water); a dish of salt or a stone (earth). If you can't use smoke or salt, use a feather for air and a stone for earth.

1. **Purify and make sacred space**, in your coven's form or with the simple circle.
2. **Ground and centre.**
3. **Hold the object** and say what it is and what it will be for: "This is my chalice. I dedicate it to hold offerings for the gods and the waters of blessing."
4. **Earth.** Touch it to the salt or stone (or sprinkle a few grains near it): "By earth, I consecrate you."
5. **Air.** Pass it through the incense smoke, or brush it with the feather: "By air, I consecrate you."
6. **Fire.** Pass it carefully above (not through) the candle flame, keeping it well clear: "By fire, I consecrate you."
7. **Water.** Sprinkle it with a few drops of water: "By water, I consecrate you." (Use only a touch on things water can damage.)
8. **Spirit.** Hold it up, or to your heart, and say: "By spirit, and in the presence of [your gods, the powers you honour, or simply the sacred], I consecrate you to my practice. So it is."
9. **Charge it (optional).** Raise energy and direct it into the object, as you learned in the raising module.
10. **Place it on your altar.** Use it for the first time, if you can, right away: pour a little water into your new chalice as an offering, or ring your new bell.
11. **Close and ground.**

> **Safety:** Don't pass anything flammable through a flame: fabric, paper, feathers, wooden tools with varnish, anything with ribbons. Hold it well above the flame, or just name fire while holding it near the candle. Keep long sleeves and hair back.

> **Your coven:** In some traditions, tools are consecrated in the name of particular gods, or by an elder, or only within a coven rite. Hellenic practitioners might purify an object with khernips and dedicate it with a prayer and libation to the god it will serve; Heathens might hallow it with fire. Ask your mentor before consecrating anything you'll use in group ritual.

## How often?

- **Cleanse** new objects before first use; objects others have handled; after a difficult or intense working; and every so often as part of altar care (monthly, or at the new or full moon, is common).
- **Consecrate** once, when an object first becomes a tool. Some people renew consecrations yearly.
- **Recharge** charged objects when they feel "flat", or monthly.

## Living objects and people's things

Don't cleanse or consecrate other people's belongings without their consent. If you're given a gift for your practice, cleanse it if you wish, but honour the giver. Plants are living things: purify them with sound, light or water (if they're happy to be watered), never with salt.

> **Try this:** Choose one object for your altar, perhaps the cup or dish you found in the last lesson. Cleanse it with a safe method, and then consecrate it with the four elements. Write what you did and what you noticed.

docs.title: Caring for your altar, and the app's altar
docs.summary: How to tend an altar day to day and through the seasons, what to do with offerings, wax and old things, and how to use the app's altar alongside a physical one, or instead of one.
docs.body:
## An altar is tended, not just made

An altar is a living thing in the sense that matters: it changes with your practice. Practitioners talk about **tending** an altar: visiting it, cleaning it, renewing offerings, keeping it alive. An altar that's set up and then ignored gathers dust in more ways than one. One that's tended becomes a place you feel drawn to.

## Daily tending (a few minutes)

Many practitioners visit their altar once a day, often in the morning or evening:

1. Stand or sit before it. Ground and centre for a few breaths.
2. Light a candle (or switch on a battery candle).
3. Say a greeting or a short prayer to your gods, spirits or ancestors, or simply a few words of intention for the day.
4. Renew fresh water, or offer a little incense, a flower or a few drops of drink, if your practice includes daily offerings.
5. Sit quietly for a minute or two.
6. Put out the flame before you leave the room.

Even one minute a day, done regularly, builds a strong habit and relationship. Many people find it the anchor of their whole practice.

## Weekly care

1. Remove old offerings, wilted flowers and spent candles.
2. Dust the altar and its objects, and wipe the surface.
3. Wash the offering dishes and the water bowl.
4. Straighten the cloth, or change it.
5. Notice whether anything no longer belongs: things on an altar should mean something to you now.
6. Cleanse the space lightly, with sound, smoke or a sprinkle of water.

## Offerings: what to do with them

Offerings (food, drink, flowers, incense) are given away; they're not for you to take back. What to do with them afterwards varies by tradition, and your tradition module explains your coven's custom. Common modern practices:

- **Food and drink:** leave on the altar for a set time (an hour, a day, overnight), then put them outside on the earth if they're safe for wildlife, pour drink onto the ground or into the garden, or compost or bin them respectfully if you can't. In some traditions (Hellenic offerings to Hestia, for instance, or shared feasts in many traditions), part of an offering is shared and eaten by the worshippers; in others, offerings to certain beings (such as the dead or chthonic gods) are never eaten.
- **Flowers:** compost them, or return them to the earth when they fade.
- **Incense ash:** scatter it outside or bin it.
- **Candle wax:** let it cool and bin it, or keep it if your practice reuses wax. Don't pour hot wax down drains.

> **Safety:** Don't leave food offerings where they'll attract pests or harm pets and wildlife. Chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic and alcohol are toxic to many animals; salty or bready food isn't good for birds in large amounts. Pour drink offerings onto soil, not into ponds or streams.

## Through the year

Many practitioners change their altar with the seasons and the holy days of their calendar: autumn leaves and apples, winter evergreens and candles, spring flowers and eggs, summer herbs and grain. The details depend on your tradition's calendar, which your tradition module covers. Changing the altar is itself a way of marking the turning of the year.

## When an altar needs changing or putting away

- **Moving house:** cleanse the altar's things, pack them with care, and set the altar up again early in the new home; many people find it helps the new place feel like home.
- **Going away:** cover the altar, remove perishable offerings, put out all flames, and let your gods or ancestors know you'll be back. Some people take a small travel altar.
- **Retiring objects:** when a tool or object is broken or no longer belongs, thank it, cleanse it, and then bury it, burn it safely (if it's something that burns cleanly), give it away, or bin it respectfully.
- **Pauses:** if you step back from practice for a while, it's fine to cover or pack away your altar. It'll be there when you return.

## The app's altar

The app has its own altars, on the **Altar** tab. You can build an altar piece by piece from a cabinet of candles, herbs, crystals, offerings, natural finds, tools and seasonal things; light its candles; tend it over time; and keep it with your account. You can also add your own items with photos, and set photographs of ancestors in frames.

You can use the app's altar in several ways:

- **Alongside a physical altar.** Build a twin of your physical altar in the app: the same candle, the same stones, the same offerings. When you tend your physical altar, tend its twin too, and the app keeps a record. Many people find this helps them keep their practice regular, and it's a way to carry your altar with you when you're away from home.
- **Instead of a physical altar.** If you can't keep a physical altar (because of space, safety, privacy, living situation, health, or travel), the app's altar is a real place of practice. You can light its candles, make offerings, and tend it daily. Practitioners have long used images, words and imagination for sacred space; a digital altar continues that tradition.
- **For workings.** Set out an altar for a particular working or holy day, and keep it until the working is done. Today offers "Set tonight's altar", which suggests a starter altar for the day's planet, moon or holiday.
- **With your coven.** Your coven may keep altars together, tended by members, for petitions and for the coven's rituals. You'll find them on the Altar tab under "Coven", or on your coven's page.

Tending reminders (in Settings, under Notifications and reminders) can remind you to tend your altars, water your altar plants, refresh offerings and look after candles.

> **Note:** A digital candle is perfectly safe to leave "burning". A real one never is. If you use both, make sure the real candle is out before you leave it, whatever the app's candle is doing.

## Recording your altar

Your altar changes over time, and recording it lets you look back. Photograph your physical altar now and then and describe it in your Grimoire; the app also lets you record an altar in your Grimoire. Note what's on it, why, and what's changed since last time.

> **Your coven:** Some covens keep their altars private and ask members not to photograph group altars or share images of sacred objects. Others are happy to. Ask before photographing anything in group ritual, and don't share images of other people or their altars without permission.

> **Try this:** Build a twin of your physical altar in the app (or, if you don't have a physical altar, build one in the app as your altar). Tend both, or the app's one, every day for a week.

docs.title: Who were the Celts? Languages, peoples and two streams
docs.summary: Where the word “Celt” comes from, why it means a family of languages rather than one people, the Gaulish, Gaelic and Brythonic worlds, and why this course keeps the Gaelic and Brythonic streams distinct while honouring both.
docs.body:
## A word with a long history

The first writers to use the word were Greeks. Around 500 BCE Hecataeus and, a little later, Herodotus wrote of the Keltoi, a people living far to the north and west, near the source of the Danube and beyond the Pillars of Heracles. Roman writers later spoke of Galli, the Gauls, and Julius Caesar wrote that the people of central Gaul called themselves Celtae in their own tongue. These were outsiders' words for peoples they barely knew, used loosely.

The modern meaning was fixed much later. In 1707 the Welsh scholar Edward Lhuyd showed that Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx, Welsh, Cornish and Breton were related languages, and that they were related to the ancient language of the Gauls.
