He called the family Celtic. From then on, "Celtic" came to mean, most carefully, a family of languages and the peoples who spoke them.

That is the meaning this course uses. It matters, because the word has gathered a great deal of romance. There was never a Celtic empire, a single Celtic people or one Celtic religion. The people of early Ireland called themselves Gaels (Goídil) or simply the men of Ireland; the Britons called themselves something like Cymry, "fellow countrymen", which is still the Welsh name for the Welsh. Nobody in early medieval Ireland or Wales thought of themselves as a Celt.

## The ancient Celtic world

Archaeologists once linked the Celtic languages to two great cultures of central Europe: the Hallstatt culture (from around 800 BCE) and the La Tène culture (from around 450 BCE), with its swirling, curving art. La Tène art spread across much of Europe, including Ireland and Britain, but whether art styles and languages travelled together is now much debated. Some scholars argue that Celtic languages first spread along the Atlantic coasts, not from the centre of Europe. The honest answer is that we do not know exactly where or when the Celtic languages began.

At their widest, Celtic languages were spoken from Ireland and Iberia to northern Italy, the Danube and, through the Galatians, central Anatolia. Most of these continental languages, Gaulish, Celtiberian, Lepontic and Galatian, died out under Roman rule and are known only from inscriptions and names. One remarkable Gaulish object, the bronze Coligny calendar of the second century CE, sets out the months of a lunar year in Gaulish; the app's calendars include it.

## The two living branches

What survives are the **Insular Celtic** languages of the islands of Britain and Ireland, and of Brittany, in two branches.

- **Gaelic (Goidelic):** Irish (Gaeilge), Scottish Gaelic (Gàidhlig) and Manx (Gaelg). Gaelic speakers carried their language from Ireland to western Scotland in the early Middle Ages; Manx grew from the same root on the Isle of Man.
- **Brythonic (Brittonic):** Welsh (Cymraeg), Cornish (Kernewek) and Breton (Brezhoneg). Before the English, a Brythonic language was spoken over most of Britain; Breton was taken to Armorica, now Brittany, by migrants from Britain in late Roman and early medieval times.

All six are alive today, though some only just. Irish is an official language of Ireland and of the European Union. Welsh is spoken daily in many communities in Wales. Scottish Gaelic is spoken in the Hebrides and western Highlands and by learners across Scotland. Manx lost its last native speaker in 1974 and has been revived by learners, as has Cornish. Breton is spoken mostly by older people and by a growing number of schoolchildren in Breton-language schools.

## Two streams, kept distinct

This course speaks of a **Gaelic stream** and a **Brythonic stream**. They share a great deal: related gods (the Irish Lugh and the Welsh Lleu, the Irish Manannán mac Lir and the Welsh Manawydan fab Llŷr), an Otherworld close at hand, the high place of poets, and the start of winter and of summer as great turning points. But they also differ:

- **The sources.** Irish literature is far larger and older in its written form. The Welsh have the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, a few other tales and a body of poetry and triads.
- **The festivals.** The four Gaelic fire festivals, Samhain, Imbolc, Bealtaine and Lughnasadh, are richly documented in Ireland, Scotland and Man. Welsh tradition keeps Calan Gaeaf and Calan Mai, the calends of winter and of May, strongly, and the others less so.
- **The gods.** Irish gods are the Tuatha Dé Danann. Welsh tales speak of the Children of Dôn and the Children of Llŷr, of Rhiannon and of Cerridwen, in quite a different setting.
- **The languages and communities** today are separate, with their own histories and their own sensitivities.

Many Celtic pagans keep one stream as their home. Others honour both, but do not blend them into a single "Celtic" soup. When this course teaches a custom, it says where it was recorded.

> **Note:** "Celtic" is also used for things that are not Celtic at all: medieval Christian knotwork is often called Celtic, and so is music from places where no Celtic language was spoken. Neither is wrong as everyday speech; just be aware of it.

## The Gauls and the Britons

Behind both streams lie the ancient peoples of Gaul and Britain. From them we have names of gods on altars and in Roman writers, such as Lugus, Taranis, Epona, Sucellos, Belenus, Sulis and Cernunnos; shrines and offerings; and the Roman accounts of the druids. Many Celtic pagans honour these gods too, but the evidence is thin: often a name, an image and a Roman equation with a Roman god.

## Heritage and belonging

Many people come to Celtic paganism through family: Irish, Scottish or Welsh grandparents, or a surname. That is a good and natural way in. But this practice is not owned by bloodlines, and genetic tests do not make anyone more or less Celtic. Celtic identity today is about language, place and culture. Someone who learns Welsh and lives in Wales has a stronger claim to it than someone with a Welsh great-great-grandmother who has never been. The gods, as far as anyone can tell, take people as they come.

> **Try this:** Find out what Celtic language was, or is, spoken nearest to where you or your family come from, if any. Learn to say "hello" and "thank you" in it, and the name of one place in it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the languages, the Gaulish inscriptions and calendar, the Irish and Welsh peoples and their literature.
- **Modern:** the word Celtic for the language family (1707), and the idea of a single Celtic people, which grew in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

docs.title: The sources and their limits
docs.summary: The four kinds of evidence for Celtic religion, each with its strengths and limits: Greek and Roman ethnography, archaeology, the medieval Irish and Welsh literature written by Christian scribes (the Lebor Gabála, the Mabinogi, Cath Maige Tuired), and the folklore collections such as Carmina Gadelica. How to read them honestly.
docs.body:
## Why sources matter

A Celtic pagan cannot open a holy book. Everything we know about the old gods and customs comes from four kinds of evidence, all of them partial. Learning to read them is the most important skill in this tradition: it lets you tell what is old from what is new, and build a practice that is honest.

## 1. Greek and Roman writers

From the fourth century BCE to the fourth century CE, Greek and Roman authors wrote about the Celtic peoples. The most important are:

- **Posidonius,** a Greek philosopher who travelled in Gaul around 100 BCE. His work is lost but quoted by later writers, among them Strabo, Diodorus Siculus and Athenaeus.
- **Julius Caesar,** whose account of the Gallic War (written in the 50s BCE) has the fullest description of the druids and the Gaulish gods.
- **Pliny the Elder,** who describes druids cutting mistletoe from an oak.
- **Tacitus,** who describes the Roman attack on the druids of Anglesey in 60 CE.
- **Lucan,** a poet who names three Gaulish gods, Teutates, Esus and Taranis.

**Their strength:** they are early, written while Celtic paganism was alive.

**Their limits:** they were outsiders, often enemies. Caesar was conquering Gaul and wanted his readers to see its people as dangerous and in need of Roman order. Writers copied one another and repeated stereotypes about wild northern barbarians. They also used **interpretatio Romana**: Caesar says the Gauls worship Mercury above all, then Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva, giving Gaulish gods Roman names, so we do not always know who he meant.

## 2. Archaeology

Archaeology gives us what people actually did, without anyone's story about it: sanctuaries with ditches and posts, weapons and cauldrons thrown into lakes and rivers, carved stones, figures of gods, and inscriptions on altars from Roman times naming gods, often beside a Roman god (Sulis Minerva at Bath, for example). Some famous finds are the hoard from Llyn Cerrig Bach on Anglesey, the Gundestrup cauldron found in a Danish bog (with its antlered figure, though it was probably made in south-eastern Europe), and the Pillar of the Boatmen from Paris, the only inscription that names Cernunnos.

**Its strength:** it is direct evidence of practice, and new finds keep coming.

**Its limits:** objects do not speak. We can see that swords were thrown into a lake; we cannot know the prayers said, or the god it was for, unless something is written. Much of it is Roman-era and shows Celtic and Roman religion mixed.

## 3. Medieval Irish and Welsh literature

This is the richest source, and the one most loved. In Ireland, monks and lay scholars wrote down a vast literature in Irish from about the seventh century onwards, most of it surviving in manuscripts from the twelfth century and later. It includes:

- **Lebor Gabála Érenn,** "the Book of the Taking of Ireland", compiled in the eleventh century: a learned history of Ireland's settlement by waves of invaders, among them the Tuatha Dé Danann, fitted into biblical history from Noah onwards.
- **Cath Maige Tuired,** "the Second Battle of Mag Tuired": the war of the Tuatha Dé Danann against the Fomoire, with Lugh, the Dagda, Nuada, Brigid's son Ruadán and the Morrígan.
- **The Ulster Cycle,** with the Táin Bó Cúailnge and Cú Chulainn; the tales of Fionn mac Cumhaill; tales of kings; place-lore (the Dindshenchas); laws; glossaries such as Cormac's Glossary (around 900); and wisdom texts.

In Wales, the **Four Branches of the Mabinogi** (Pwyll, Branwen, Manawydan and Math) survive in manuscripts of around 1350 and 1400, though they were composed earlier, perhaps in the eleventh or twelfth century. Other sources include the Welsh triads, the poems of the Book of Taliesin, and the tale of Cerridwen and Gwion Bach, which survives only in sixteenth-century versions.

**Their strength:** they keep the names, stories and characters of gods, and many details of law, custom and belief. Much of what modern Celtic pagans know of the gods comes from here.

**Their limits:** these texts were written by Christians, centuries after the conversion. The writers were not pagans preserving scripture; they were scholars and storytellers in a Christian culture, interested in their past. They usually present the gods as people, a race of skilled ancient invaders or Otherworld folk, not as gods being worshipped. They borrowed from the Bible and classical learning. Where a tale preserves something pre-Christian, and where it was invented or reshaped by a medieval author, is debated by scholars, often fiercely. And the literature is about kings, heroes and poets, not ordinary farmers.

## 4. Folklore

From the late seventeenth century, and above all in the nineteenth and twentieth, collectors gathered customs, sayings, prayers and stories from Gaelic-speaking and Welsh-speaking country people. Key collections include **Carmina Gadelica**, the hymns and charms collected in the Scottish Highlands and Islands by Alexander Carmichael and published from 1900; the work of the **Irish Folklore Commission** (1935 to 1971), including the Schools' Collection, written down by Irish schoolchildren in the 1930s; Kevin Danaher's The Year in Ireland (1972); Máire MacNeill's The Festival of Lughnasa (1962); and Trefor Owen's Welsh Folk Customs (1959).

**Its strength:** it shows what people actually did at the festivals, at wells, at the hearth and at death: the fires, the crosses, the dew, the food left out. It is often the closest we can get to how ordinary people lived with the seasons and the Otherworld.

**Its limits:** the people recorded were Christian, often devout Catholics or Presbyterians, and their customs were part of their faith. Carmina Gadelica's prayers address the Trinity, Mary and the saints, and Carmichael is known to have polished, and sometimes rewritten, what he heard. Customs change over time, and we cannot simply assume a nineteenth-century custom is two thousand years old. Some may be; some certainly are not.

## Reading honestly

A few habits help:

1. **Ask who wrote it, when and why.** A Roman general, a twelfth-century monk and a 1930s schoolchild are all valuable, in different ways.
2. **Prefer patterns to single details.** A custom recorded in Ireland, Scotland and Man is more likely to be old than one recorded once.
3. **Separate the evidence from the interpretation.** "A medieval glossary describes Brigid as a goddess of poets" is evidence. "Brigid was the great mother goddess of all the Celts" is interpretation, and a shaky one.
4. **Say "we don't know"** when we don't.
5. **Mark your own creations as yours.** Modern practice is legitimate; it simply needs labelling.

> **Try this:** Open the app's page for Imbolc and read its "What we know" and "What we don't" sections. Which of the four kinds of source does each statement come from?

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** all four kinds of evidence, at very different dates.
- **Modern:** the critical reading of them, which scholars have developed mostly since the twentieth century, and which this course follows.

docs.title: Druids: what we know and what we don’t
docs.summary: What Greek, Roman and early Irish sources say about the druids, how much is outsiders’ guesswork, the hard question of sacrifice, how the eighteenth-century revival and Iolo Morganwg shaped modern ideas, and why no modern druid descends from the ancient ones.
docs.body:
## The druids in the ancient writers

The druids are the most famous figures of the Celtic past, and among the least known. Almost everything we read about them comes from Greek and Roman authors and from early medieval Irish texts.

Julius Caesar, writing in the 50s BCE, gives the fullest account. He says that in Gaul there were two honoured classes, the druids and the warriors. The druids, he says, presided over sacrifices and religion, judged disputes, and taught the young; they were excused from war and taxes; they met once a year at a sacred place in the land of the Carnutes, thought to be the centre of Gaul; some trained for twenty years, learning great numbers of verses by heart, because they would not commit their teaching to writing. He says they taught that souls do not die but pass from one body to another, and that the discipline was thought to have begun in Britain.

Other writers add details. Some Greek authors speak of three learned classes: bards (poets), vates or ouateis (seers and sacrificers) and druids (philosophers and priests). Pliny the Elder, in the first century CE, describes druids in white robes climbing an oak on the sixth day of the moon, cutting mistletoe with a golden sickle, and sacrificing two white bulls; he says the druids held the oak and the mistletoe most sacred. Tacitus describes the Roman invasion of Mona (Anglesey) in 60 CE: druids raising their hands to the sky and calling down curses, women in black running among the ranks with torches, and the destruction of sacred groves afterwards.

## The druids in early Ireland

Ireland was never conquered by Rome, so its druids appear later, in Irish texts written by Christians. There the druí (plural druíd) is a seer, adviser to kings and maker of magic: he foretells, casts spells, raises mists. Early Irish laws mention druids, mostly with low status by then. An early Irish hymn ascribed to Patrick asks protection "against the spells of women and smiths and druids". By the seventh century the druids had faded as a class; the poets, the filid, and the lawyers, the brehons, carried on much of the old learning in a Christian setting.

## The hard question

Classical writers say the druids carried out human sacrifice. Some of this is surely propaganda: the Romans used it to justify suppressing them, though Rome itself had killed people in public spectacles. But not all of it can be waved away. Some bog bodies, such as Lindow Man found in Cheshire in 1984, may have been killed in rituals, though the evidence is debated. An honest Celtic pagan does not deny the question and does not romanticise it. Whatever the ancients did, **modern Celtic paganism rejects harm to any person or animal**. Our offerings are food, drink, objects, words and work.

## What we do not know

Despite all this, we know almost nothing of what the druids actually taught. We have no prayer, hymn or rite in their words. Caesar's summary of their teaching on the soul is one sentence. The idea that they were gentle nature mystics, that they built Stonehenge (built two thousand years before any druid), or that their secret wisdom survives in some lineage, has no evidence behind it.

## The revival

From the seventeenth century antiquarians became fascinated with the druids. John Aubrey and later William Stukeley linked them to Stonehenge and Avebury. In 1781 the Ancient Order of Druids was founded in London as a fraternal society. The most influential figure was the Welsh stonemason and poet Edward Williams, known as **Iolo Morganwg** (1747 to 1826). He held the first Gorsedd of the Bards of the Island of Britain on Primrose Hill in London in 1792, and wrote a whole druidic philosophy, rites, prayers, triads and the three-rayed awen symbol, which he presented as ancient Welsh tradition. Much of it he invented, and some manuscripts he forged. They were published after his death, above all as Barddas (1862), and shaped Druidry for two centuries. Scholars, notably G. J. Williams in the twentieth century, untangled his inventions.

Iolo was also a gifted poet and a real scholar of Welsh literature, and the Gorsedd he founded is today an honoured part of Wales's National Eisteddfod: a cultural institution celebrating Welsh language and arts, not a pagan religion.

## Druids today

Modern Druidry grew from the revival and became a religion and a spiritual path in the twentieth century. It is a living tradition in its own right, and the good orders say plainly that they are not a continuation of the ancient druids. The next lesson describes the main orders.

> **Note:** Use the word "druid" with care. In this course, "the druids" means the ancient learned class, and "Druids" or "Druidry" the modern movement. Do not call yourself a druid in the ancient sense; no one living can.

## Why it matters

Druids attract fantasy, and fantasy breeds false claims: "the ancient druids taught this", "this ritual is two thousand years old". Being clear about the evidence protects you from people who would sell you a secret, and it frees you to make modern practice honestly.

> **Try this:** In your book, make two columns headed "Ancient sources say" and "Modern Druidry says". Fill in three things in each from this lesson. Where do they meet?

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the druids as a learned, priestly class in Gaul, Britain and Ireland, known only through outsiders and later Christians.
- **Modern:** the druid revival (from the 1700s), Iolo Morganwg's druidic philosophy and the awen symbol, and every Druid order today.

docs.title: Modern paths: Reconstructionism, Druidry and Celtic-flavoured practice
docs.summary: The main modern ways of being a Celtic pagan, what each values and how each practises: Celtic Reconstructionism and Gaelic Polytheism, Druidry (OBOD and ADF), and Celtic-flavoured Wicca and witchcraft; some popular ideas to treat with caution; and what a Celtic coven does.
docs.body:
## Three families

Celtic paganism today is not one religion but a family of approaches. Each is modern; each takes the old sources seriously in its own way. You will meet people who move between them, and covens that mix them. Knowing the differences helps you understand where a practice comes from.

## Celtic Reconstructionism and Gaelic Polytheism

**Celtic Reconstructionism** (CR) grew in the late 1980s and 1990s among people who wanted a practice grounded as firmly as possible in the evidence and the living cultures. On the Irish, Scottish and Manx side many now call it **Gaelic Polytheism**; there are smaller Welsh and Gaulish reconstructionist communities. The CR FAQ, written collectively in 2007, is still a good introduction.

Its hallmarks:

- **Study of the sources,** read critically, including in translation and, for many, in the original languages.
- **Learning a Celtic language,** because language carries a culture's way of seeing, and because it is a way of giving something back.
- **Keeping the festivals** by their recorded folk customs: the crosses and the brat Bríde at Imbolc, the fires and dew at Bealtaine, the hill-climbing at Lughnasadh, the dead at Samhain.
- **Honouring gods, ancestors and spirits of place,** with offerings and hospitality, at a household shrine.
- **Support for the living cultures,** their languages and their communities.

CR does not forbid new practice, but asks that it be in keeping with the old, and marked as new. It usually does not cast circles, call quarters or honour a single Goddess and God in the Wiccan way.

## Druidry

Modern **Druidry** draws on the old sources and on two centuries of revival. The two largest orders are:

- **The Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids (OBOD),** founded in 1964 by Ross Nichols and grown worldwide under Philip Carr-Gomm. It teaches a nature spirituality through three grades, Bard, Ovate and Druid, by correspondence course, with an initiation at each. Its rituals take place in a circle, keep the eight festivals of the modern Wheel of the Year, and use the revival's Druid's Prayer and the chanting of the awen. It welcomes members of any religion or none.
- **Ár nDraíocht Féin (ADF),** "Our Own Druidism", founded in the United States in 1983 by Isaac Bonewits. It is explicitly polytheist and scholarly, and draws on many Indo-European cultures, Irish, Welsh and Gaulish among them. Its public Core Order of Ritual works at a sacred fire, well and tree, opens a gate to the Otherworld, honours the Three Kindreds (the gods, the ancestors and the nature spirits), makes offerings and takes an omen. Its first study programme is called the Dedicant Path.

Other groups include the Ancient Order of Druids in America (AODA) and The Druid Network in Britain. Druids tend to welcome personal inspiration more freely than reconstructionists, and many are less tied to one culture.

## Celtic-flavoured eclectic practice

Wicca took several of its festival names from the Gaelic year, and many witches and Wiccans work with Brigid, the Morrígan, Cerridwen or Cernunnos in a framework of circle, quarters and a Goddess and God. This is a legitimate modern practice. The honest thing is to call it what it is, witchcraft or Wicca with Celtic elements, rather than "the old Celtic religion", and to learn the gods' own stories rather than fitting them into a maiden, mother and crone or a horned god pattern they do not have in the sources.

## Ideas to treat with caution

Some popular notions come from modern books, not from the Celts:

- **The Celtic tree calendar** of thirteen tree-months was devised by Robert Graves in The White Goddess (1948), building on a misreading of the ogham letters. "Celtic tree astrology" came later still.
- **The eight-festival "Celtic" Wheel of the Year** is a twentieth-century creation of Wicca and Druidry. The Gaelic year had four quarter days; the solstices and equinoxes are hardly mentioned in Irish or Welsh sources, though Neolithic monuments such as Newgrange, far older than any Celtic language in Ireland, are aligned on the solstice sun.
- **The triple goddess** of maiden, mother and crone is a modern idea, largely from Graves. Irish sources do have goddesses in threes (three Brigids, the three Morrígna, Ériu, Banba and Fódla), but not in that pattern.
- **Ogham divination** is modern in its present forms, though a medieval tale does show a druid using ogham on yew wands to find someone lost.
- **"Celtic shamanism"** is a modern synthesis.
- **Iolo Morganwg's triads and Barddas** are eighteenth-century work, not ancient Welsh tradition.

None of this makes these things wrong to use. It means saying where they come from.

## What a Celtic coven does

"Coven" is a word from witchcraft, and some Celtic groups use other names: a grove (Druidry), a hearth or kindred, or a group named after a place. Whatever its name, a Celtic coven on this app usually:

- keeps the **four fire festivals**, and often the moon and other days its members choose;
- holds **devotional rites** to its gods, with offerings and praise, and honours the ancestors and the land;
- **studies** together: the stories, the sources, often a language;
- **teaches** newcomers through programs like this one;
- **cares** for its members and the places where it meets;
- keeps its own **book** of rites, prayers and learning.

In the app you will find the coven's rites in its calendar, its book, its altars and its messages.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which of these families your coven belongs to, or how it mixes them, and why.

> **Try this:** Write a paragraph in your book on which approach draws you most, and one practice you love that you now know is modern. How do you want to hold it?

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the sources each approach draws on.
- **Modern:** Celtic Reconstructionism (1980s and 1990s), OBOD (1964), ADF (1983), Celtic-flavoured Wicca, the tree calendar (1948) and the eightfold Wheel.

docs.title: The gods of the two streams
docs.summary: An introduction to the gods as the sources show them: the Tuatha Dé Danann of Ireland (the Dagda, Brigid, Lugh, the Morrígan, Nuada, Ogma, Manannán, Boann, Aengus), the Welsh Children of Dôn and Llŷr with Rhiannon and Cerridwen, the Gaulish gods known from inscriptions, and how to approach them without flattening them.
docs.body:
## Meeting the gods through stories

The Celtic gods come to us not through hymns or temple records but through stories, place-names, inscriptions and folk memory. The medieval writers usually present them as a people: wise, skilled and long-lived, sometimes as Ireland's earlier inhabitants, sometimes as the folk of the Otherworld hills. Celtic pagans honour them as gods. This lesson introduces the best known, with where each is found. It is a beginning, not a complete list.

## The Gaelic stream: the Tuatha Dé Danann

In Irish tradition the gods are the **Tuatha Dé Danann**, usually translated "the peoples of the goddess Danu", though the name of the goddess is uncertain: medieval texts speak of Anu or Ana, "mother of the gods of Ireland", and the form Danu is largely a modern reconstruction. The Lebor Gabála says they came to Ireland in a cloud, fought the Fir Bolg and the Fomoire, and finally yielded the land to the sons of Míl, the ancestors of the Gaels, withdrawing into the síde, the hollow hills.

- **The Dagda,** "the good god", meaning good at everything. Father-figure and chief of the Tuatha Dé, with a cauldron from which no one goes away unsatisfied, a great club that kills with one end and brings back to life with the other, and a harp that calls the seasons. In Cath Maige Tuired he meets the Morrígan at Samhain by a river.
- **Brigid,** described in Cormac's Glossary as a goddess "whom poets worshipped", daughter of the Dagda, with two sisters of the same name for healing and smithcraft. She is also Saint Brigid of Kildare, and the relation between goddess and saint is debated.
- **Lugh,** called Samildánach, "skilled in many arts together". In Cath Maige Tuired he wins entry to Tara by mastering every craft, and kills his grandfather Balor of the Fomoire. Lughnasadh bears his name. His Gaulish counterpart was Lugus, and his Welsh, Lleu.
- **The Morrígan,** "great queen" or "phantom queen", often with Badb and Macha as a group of three. She is a goddess of battle, prophecy, sovereignty and the land, appearing as a crow, a woman washing armour at a ford, or a seer chanting a prophecy after the great battle. She is not simply a goddess of death, and not a crone.
- **Nuada,** king of the Tuatha Dé, who lost his hand in battle and was given a silver one by the physician Dian Cécht, and could rule again only once whole.
- **Ogma,** a champion, credited in medieval learned tradition with inventing the ogham letters.
- **Manannán mac Lir,** "son of the sea", lord of the sea and of the Otherworld isle of Emain Ablach, who gives his name to the Isle of Man, where he is honoured still.
- **Boann,** goddess of the river Boyne, and **Aengus Óg,** her son by the Dagda, god of youth and love, living at Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange).
- Others include **Ériu, Banba and Fódla,** sovereignty goddesses who give Ireland its names; **Dian Cécht** and **Airmed,** healers; **Goibniu,** the smith; and, in folklore rather than the medieval tales, the **Cailleach,** the old woman of winter, and **Áine** of Knockainey.

## The Brythonic stream

Welsh tradition is smaller but rich. Its gods are seldom called gods in the texts, which treat them as people of power in an ancient Britain.

- **The Children of Dôn:** Gwydion the magician and storyteller, Arianrhod of the silver wheel, Math son of Mathonwy, and Gilfaethwy. The Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi tells of Arianrhod's sons, Lleu Llaw Gyffes and Dylan, and of Blodeuwedd, the woman made of flowers.
- **The Children of Llŷr:** Brân the Blessed (Bendigeidfran), the giant king whose head kept his companions company after death; his sister Branwen; and Manawydan, the patient, crafty counterpart of Manannán.
- **Rhiannon,** who rides out of the Otherworld on a white horse in the First Branch, chooses Pwyll as her husband, and endures a cruel punishment with dignity. Many scholars link her with the Gaulish horse goddess Epona and the name Rigantona, "great queen", though this is a theory.
- **Cerridwen,** whose cauldron brewed a year and a day to make her son wise, and whose servant Gwion Bach swallowed the three drops and was reborn as the poet Taliesin. Her tale survives only in sixteenth-century versions, but she is mentioned in older poems, and modern Celtic pagans honour her as a goddess of inspiration, the awen.

## The Gaulish and British gods

From Roman-era altars and writers we know **Lugus, Taranis** (thunder), **Esus, Teutates, Epona** (horses, widely honoured by Roman cavalry), **Sucellos** (with his mallet) and **Nantosuelta, Belenus, Sulis** (the hot springs of Bath), **Brigantia** and **Cernunnos**, the antlered god named only once, on the Pillar of the Boatmen in Paris, though antlered figures appear elsewhere. Often we have a name, an image and a few dedications, and little else.

## Approaching the gods well

A few principles:

1. **Learn their stories first.** Read the tales in which a god appears before you decide what that god is "the goddess of". The Morrígan read in the sources is far more than a goddess of war.
2. **Keep them in their place.** Lugh and Lleu are related, but not the same figure; Brigid of Ireland is not the Welsh Ffraid in every way. Honour each as the sources show them.
3. **Avoid flattening them into archetypes.** "Every goddess is one Goddess" is a modern theology some people hold; it is not the view of these sources.
4. **Be modest about epithets.** Many "Celtic god of" labels on websites are modern guesses.
5. **Respect the saint.** Brigid is a living Catholic saint as well as a pagan goddess to many. You can honour the goddess without claiming the saint, or the Catholic devotion to her, as secretly yours.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which gods your coven honours most, and which stories it reads first.

> **Try this:** Choose one god from this lesson. Find their Library entry in the app, and read one story in which they appear. Write three things the story shows you about them that the short summaries do not.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the gods' names and stories, from inscriptions, medieval literature and folklore.
- **Modern:** worshipping them as gods again in a living religion, and many of the shorthand "god of" labels.

docs.title: Living languages, living cultures: practising with respect
docs.summary: Why Celtic paganism is open but borrows from living people; the Gaelic and Brythonic languages and communities today; the difference between practising a tradition and taking someone’s living Catholic or Christian folk custom; how to learn, give back and avoid appropriation; and the Sanctuary’s guide to closed and living traditions.
docs.body:
## Open, but living

Celtic paganism is an **open** tradition. No one needs to be born into it, initiated by a particular people or given permission by a community to honour Brigid or keep Samhain. The gods of the Tuatha Dé and the Mabinogi belong to no single living group.

But this practice is built from the inheritance of **living** peoples. The languages are spoken. The festivals are kept. The holy wells are visited. Many of the customs this course teaches, Brigid's crosses, the brat Bríde, the rounds at a holy well, the Reek Sunday climb, wakes and the blessing of graves, are part of the living Christian faith of Irish, Scottish, Manx, Welsh, Cornish and Breton people today, most of all Catholic communities in Ireland and the Gaelic Hebrides. People who keep them are not keeping pagan survivals in disguise. They are keeping their own religion.

The Sanctuary's guide to closed and living traditions explains the difference between closed traditions, which require initiation or belonging, and open but living ones, which ask for respect. Read it alongside this lesson.

## The languages today

Each Celtic language has a history of loss. Irish was pushed out by English over centuries, and the famine of the 1840s and the emigration that followed devastated its heartlands. Scottish Gaelic was suppressed after 1745 and emptied from much of the Highlands by the Clearances. Welsh children were punished for speaking it at school in the nineteenth century. Manx and Cornish lost their last native speakers and were brought back by learners. Breton was discouraged by the French state for much of the twentieth century.

Today all six have revival movements, schools, broadcasters and writers, and all need speakers. For a Celtic pagan, learning even a little of a language is one of the best things you can do: it opens the sources, it gives you the true names of festivals and places, and it supports the communities that kept this inheritance alive.

## Where respect is needed most

**Living Catholic and Christian folk practice.** Saint Brigid's Day, the patterns at holy wells, the blessing of the sea, Reek Sunday on Croagh Patrick: these are acts of Christian devotion. You may well be welcome to join, as a guest. Do not hold pagan rites in someone's church or churchyard, take over a pattern day, or tell the people keeping it that their custom is "really pagan". Even where a custom may have pre-Christian roots, the people keeping it now have the first claim to its meaning.

**The saints.** Brigid the goddess and Brigid the saint are linked in ways scholars still debate. You may honour the goddess. Do not claim that Catholic devotion to the saint is secretly worship of the goddess, or use Catholic prayers to the saint as though they were pagan.

**Carmina Gadelica and other Christian prayers.** These are Christian prayers. Some Celtic pagans rewrite them, putting gods where the Trinity was; others find that disrespectful. The more honest way is to learn from their shape and spirit (the short lines, the threefold blessings, the prayers for each task of the day) and write your own.

**Place.** Ringforts, standing stones and wells sit on farms and in parishes. Ask permission, close gates, leave nothing that does not rot, and take nothing away.

**Heritage claims.** Do not claim a special right to Celtic tradition because of ancestry, and never claim to belong to a "hereditary line of Celtic witches" or "druid family". No such lines are known to exist.

**Selling.** Be wary of anyone selling "ancient Celtic" spells, initiations or secrets. Buy crosses, books and art from makers in the cultures themselves where you can.

## Giving back

Respect is not only what you avoid. Ways to give back include:

- learning a Celtic language, even slowly, and using it;
- buying books by Irish, Scottish, Welsh, Manx, Cornish and Breton scholars and writers;
- supporting language schools, local heritage groups and the care of holy wells and monuments;
- visiting with courtesy, spending money locally, and listening more than you speak;
- crediting your sources when you teach.

## A simple test

When you are unsure whether something is respectful, ask three questions. Would I be comfortable doing this in front of the people whose custom it is? Am I telling the truth about where it comes from? Am I taking something away, or adding something back? If the answer to the first is no, or you cannot answer the second, pause and ask your mentor. Most of the time the respectful way is also the simpler one: go as a guest, speak honestly, and leave things as you found them.

## The diaspora

Many people of Irish, Scottish and Welsh descent live far from those countries, in North America, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere. Their families' customs, wakes, Halloween guising, Saint Brigid's crosses, are a real inheritance. If that is you, your family's memory is precious; ask your elders what they remember. And if your Celtic practice happens on land with its own Indigenous peoples, remember that you are a guest there too; the closed traditions guide has more on this.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven has any agreements about visiting holy sites, using Christian prayers, or learning a language.

> **Try this:** Read the Sanctuary's closed and living traditions guide. Then write in your book one custom from this course that is still part of someone's living faith, and how you will treat it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the languages, the customs and the faith of the communities that kept them.
- **Modern:** Celtic paganism's relationship with those communities, still being worked out, and better for being careful.

docs.title: The hearth: a daily practice of kindling and smooring
docs.summary: A daily Celtic devotion built on the Gaelic custom of kindling the fire in the morning and smooring it at night: what the folk sources record, how to keep a modern morning and evening practice at a candle, how to learn from the Carmina Gadelica prayers without taking them, and how to keep going.
docs.body:
## The fire that never went out

In the Gaelic-speaking Highlands and Islands of Scotland, and in much of rural Ireland, the household fire was kept alive for years, sometimes for generations. Before matches were common, letting it die was a misfortune; it was not lightly given away to a neighbour on May Day or at the New Year, for the household's luck went with it. Each night the woman of the house raked the embers together and covered them with ash, so they would glow slowly till morning. This was **smooring**, in Scottish Gaelic smàladh. Each morning she uncovered them and blew them into flame: the **kindling**.

Alexander Carmichael, collecting in the Outer Hebrides in the later nineteenth century, recorded prayers said at both. In one smooring, the embers were divided into three, in the name of the Three of the Trinity, and covered with a blessing asking them to "save, shield and surround the hearth, the house, the household" through the night. In a kindling prayer, the woman asks to kindle in her heart a flame of love for her neighbour, as she kindles the fire on the hearth. The app's ready-made Smooring the Fire uses Carmichael's public-domain translation.

These are **Christian prayers**, from devout Christian households. They show us how central the hearth was, and how naturally prayer was woven into daily work. A Celtic pagan can learn from that, and build a pagan practice in the same spirit, without taking the prayers themselves.

## A modern hearth practice

Here is a daily practice in two parts, morning and evening. It is **modern**, built on the shape of the old custom. It takes five to ten minutes each time.

**In the morning: kindling**

1. **Go to your shrine** or hearth before the day's business. Wash your hands and face first if you can.
2. **Light the candle** and say a short kindling blessing of your own, for example: "I kindle this flame as the gods kindle the day. Warm this house, light this work, guard these people."
3. **Greet the powers:** the gods (or one god you honour), the ancestors and the spirits of the place, in a line each.
4. **Give a small gift,** if this is a day for it: a drop of milk, a pinch of oats, the first drop of your tea.
5. **Name the day.** Say what you have to do today, and ask for help with it.
6. **Leave a moment of quiet,** then put out the candle or let it burn while you are in the room.

**In the evening: smooring**

1. **Return to your shrine** before bed.
2. **Light the candle,** if it is out, and sit for a moment.
3. **Look back.** Say what happened today, what you are grateful for, and anything you regret. Some people say aloud three thanks.
4. **Bank the fire.** Say a smooring blessing of your own over the candle, in threes, asking protection for the house and those in it through the night.
5. **Put the candle out,** with a snuffer or by pinching it. In the old way the fire was banked, not quenched; you can think of putting out the flame as banking it, ready to rekindle in the morning.
6. **Take away** any offering from the day, to the earth.

> **Safety:** Never leave a candle burning overnight or when you leave the house. If you have a real fire or stove, follow its safety guidance, use a fireguard and keep a working smoke alarm.

## Writing your own blessings

Learn from the shape of the Gaelic prayers:

- short lines, easy to remember;
- threes: "guard, guide and keep"; "the hearth, the house, the household";
- naming the day and the night: "this day, this night, and every day and night";
- the task itself: kindling, banking, waking, sleeping.

Write a kindling and a smooring blessing for yourself in your book. Address them to the gods you honour, or simply to the fire and the house. Keep them short enough to say half-awake.

## Keeping going

Daily practice is the backbone of devotion, and also the easiest thing to drop. A few things help:

- **Tie it to something you already do:** making the first cup of tea, brushing your teeth at night.
- **Keep it small.** Two minutes kept every day is worth more than half an hour kept once a month.
- **Miss days without guilt.** When you notice you have stopped, start again. The hearth welcomes you back.
- **Notice the seasons.** In winter the candle is a real light in the dark; in summer you may keep it at a window.
- **Write a line in your journal** once a week, not every day: what has changed, what has not.

## What people notice

Over weeks, many people find the hearth practice steadying. Some notice a sense of being kept company, or of the house feeling different. Others notice little beyond a quiet habit, and find that the meaning comes later. Both are normal.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have a kindling or smooring blessing of its own, or a day of the week for a fuller offering. Ask your mentor.

> **Try this:** Keep the morning and evening hearth practice for thirty days. Write your own kindling and smooring blessings in the first week, and revise them at the end.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the ever-burning hearth fire, kindling and smooring, and prayers said at both (Christian, recorded in the nineteenth century).
- **Modern:** this pagan hearth practice at a candle, and blessings to the old gods in the Gaelic manner.

docs.title: The land, the Otherworld and the good neighbours
docs.summary: The spirits of the land and the Otherworld in Gaelic and Welsh tradition: the síd, Tír na nÓg and Annwn, the aos sí or good neighbours and the Tylwyth Teg, the old courtesy towards them and the old cautions; why this course keeps to courtesy and offering, not summoning; and how to get to know the land where you live.
docs.body:
## The land is not empty

In Celtic tradition, the land is full of presence. Rivers have goddesses: Boann of the Boyne, Sinann of the Shannon, Sabrina of the Severn. Hills and mounds are dwellings of the Otherworld folk. Wells and springs are holy. The sovereignty of a kingdom was pictured as a woman, married to the rightful king. And in folk belief across Ireland, Scotland, Man, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, certain places belonged to beings who were not human, not dead, and not quite gods.

Celtic pagans honour the **spirits of the land** as one of the three kinds of power, beside the gods and the ancestors. This lesson teaches how the tradition approached them, and why it counsels courtesy and caution.

## The Otherworld

Irish and Welsh stories describe an Otherworld that lies very close: inside the mounds, beneath lakes, across the western sea, or through a mist that falls on the road. In Ireland it has many names: the **síd** (plural síde), the mound-dwellings; **Tír na nÓg**, the Land of the Young; **Mag Mell**, the Plain of Delight; **Emain Ablach**, the Isle of Apples, ruled by Manannán. In Wales it is **Annwn**, whose king Arawn exchanges places with Pwyll for a year in the First Branch of the Mabinogi.

Time runs differently there: in a later tale, Oisín returns from Tír na nÓg after what seems three years and finds three hundred have passed. The Otherworld comes nearest at the edges: at dusk and dawn, at fords and shores, and at Samhain and May Eve.

## The good neighbours

In the Irish tradition, after the Tuatha Dé Danann yielded the land to the Gaels, they withdrew into the síde and became the **aos sí**, the people of the mounds. In later folk belief the aos sí blur with the dead and with spirits of nature, and the folklore mixes all three. People who believed in them avoided naming them directly: in Ireland they were **the Good People** (na daoine maithe), the Gentry, the Other Crowd or simply Them; in Scotland **the Good Neighbours** or the people of peace (daoine sìth); on Man, **themselves** or the little people; in Wales the **Tylwyth Teg**, the Fair Family, or Bendith y Mamau, the Mothers' Blessing.

Those polite names are a clue. You speak well of them because they are not always well disposed. They are not small or sweet. Folk tradition credits them with beauty and music, but also with blighting cattle, taking people away, leaving changelings and leading travellers astray.

## The old courtesy

Rural families kept a few simple customs, widely recorded:

- leaving a little milk or the first of the butter for the good folk;
- warning before throwing water out of the door at night;
- leaving lone hawthorns and ringforts (in Irish ráth and lios) untouched, never cutting a fairy thorn or taking stones from a fort;
- treating food left out or fallen on the floor on Samhain night as theirs;
- keeping iron, rowan, salt and red thread as protection, especially at the turning of the year.

You can keep these customs today as good neighbourliness. Leave the lone thorn alone. Don't take stones from ancient sites. Be polite to the land: greet a place when you arrive and thank it when you leave. Keep a small dish for the spirits of place, separate from the gods' offerings.

## Caution, and what this course will not teach

Some modern books treat the good folk as friendly guides to be called up, bargained with or "worked with". The folk tradition would think that very unwise. Its stories are about respect, distance and protection, not friendship cultivated lightly. This course keeps to the courtesy and the protections. It does not teach summoning, bargaining or trance work with the Otherworld folk.

There is a darker reason for care. Belief in changelings sometimes led to real cruelty: in 1895, in County Tipperary, Bridget Cleary was killed by her husband, who claimed she had been taken by the fairies and a changeling left in her place. Her death is a reminder that Otherworld beliefs, held without care, can be used to excuse harm, and that illness of body or mind needs doctors, not folklore.

> **Safety:** If any practice involving spirits leaves you frightened, sleepless or unable to tell what is real, stop, ground yourself, talk to your mentor, and see a doctor if it continues. Spiritual practice is never a substitute for medical or psychological care.

## Getting to know your land

Most of us do not live near a síd mound. But every place has its own life: its rivers and their old names, its hills, its trees, its weather, the creatures that live there, the people who were there before. Getting to know your land is a devotion in itself.

1. **Learn the names.** What were the river, the hill and the town called in older languages? Many place-names in Britain and Ireland have Celtic roots; elsewhere, learn the names given by the people of the land, and remember you are a guest.
2. **Walk it.** Go to the same place often: a park, a stream, a hill. Greet it each time.
3. **Notice.** Which plants grow there each month? Which birds come and go?
4. **Give.** Leave a small biodegradable offering, or better, pick up litter, plant something native, or join a conservation group.
5. **Listen.** Sit quietly and notice what you feel.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven honours the land where it meets, and whether it keeps a dish for the spirits of place.

> **Try this:** Choose one outdoor place near you. Visit it four times over a month, greeting it each time, leaving a small gift or picking up litter, and sitting quietly for ten minutes. Write what you notice.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Otherworld of the medieval tales, the aos sí and Tylwyth Teg of folk belief, and the old courtesies and protections.
- **Modern:** honouring the spirits of the land as one of three kinds of power in a pagan rite.

docs.title: The ancestors and the dead
docs.summary: The dead in Celtic tradition: what the sources hint about the afterlife (Caesar’s note on the soul, Tech Duinn, the Otherworld), the folk customs of wakes, Samhain and the blessing of graves, who counts as an ancestor (blood, place and spirit), a simple ancestor shrine and practice, and how to approach hard ancestors and grief.
docs.body:
## The dead are near

Honouring the dead is one of the strongest threads in Celtic tradition, from ancient burials to living custom. Celtic pagans honour the **ancestors** as one of the three kinds of power, beside the gods and the spirits of the land.

## What the sources hint

We have no ancient Celtic teaching on the afterlife in its own words, but there are clues:

- **Caesar** says the druids taught that souls do not die but pass from one body to another after death, and that this made Gaulish warriors fearless. Some Greek writers say much the same. How far this is accurate, and what it meant, we do not know.
- **Archaeology** shows careful burials with food, drink, weapons and ornaments, suggesting a journey or life beyond.
- **Medieval Irish tradition** speaks of **Tech Duinn**, the House of Donn, a gathering place of the dead, placed on a rocky island off the south-west coast, where Donn, an ancestor-figure of the Gaels, welcomes his descendants. The source is a medieval poem and later tradition; it is not a full theology.
- **The Otherworld** of the tales is sometimes a land of the dead and sometimes of the living immortals; the folklore of the good neighbours often mixes the two.

Honestly, then: the sources show that the dead were cared for and thought to continue in some way, but give no single doctrine. Celtic pagans today hold many views: rebirth, an Otherworld, a gathering of the ancestors, or simply remembering.

## The folk customs

Folk custom is much richer, and much of it is still alive, in Christian communities:

- **The wake.** In Ireland and Gaelic Scotland, the dead were watched over at home for a night or more before burial, with company, food, drink, stories and sometimes games. The **keen** (caoineadh), a lament sung by women, was part of the wake into the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and is now rare.
- **Samhain.** The night when the dead come home: a place left at the table, the door unlatched, food left out, the fire kept bright. Its Christian neighbour, All Souls' Day, kept the dead in prayer.
- **Graves.** Irish "cemetery Sundays" in summer, when graves are tidied, decorated and blessed by a priest, are a living custom.
- **The house.** Food that fell on the floor was sometimes left for the dead or the good folk.

As with all living customs, these belong to the communities that keep them. A Celtic pagan can learn from them and keep their own dead in a similar spirit.

## Who are your ancestors?

Many Celtic pagans think of ancestors in three kinds:

- **Ancestors of blood:** your family, back through the generations, whoever they were and wherever they came from. You do not need Celtic ancestors.
- **Ancestors of place:** those who lived and died on the land where you live, known and unknown.
- **Ancestors of spirit:** teachers, poets, people whose work shaped yours, the people who kept the stories and the languages.

Adopted and chosen family are ancestors too. So are people whose names you do not know. If you know little of your family history, that is common; you can honour "those whose names I do not know" just as truly, and learning about them can become part of the practice.

## A simple ancestor shrine

1. **Make a place:** a shelf, part of your hearth shrine, or a corner of a table.
2. **Put something there for them:** photographs, names written on a card, an heirloom, a stone from a family place.
3. **Add a candle** and a small dish or cup.
4. **Visit it:** once a week, or on anniversaries, light the candle, say their names, give a little food or drink they liked (or water), and tell them your news.
5. **Take the offering away** the next day, to the earth.

## Hard ancestors and grief

Not every ancestor was good. Some did harm, perhaps to you. You do not have to honour anyone who harmed you. Many people honour "the well and wise among my dead" rather than everyone, or keep a hard ancestor at a distance with a simple wish for peace. That is your choice.

Grief can rise when you begin ancestor work, especially for those you knew. Go gently. Ancestor practice can be a comfort, but it is not a replacement for grieving with people who love you, or for help from a counsellor or doctor when grief overwhelms you.

> **Safety:** If ancestor practice leaves you persistently low, haunted or unable to sleep, stop for a while, ground yourself, and talk to your mentor. If low mood lasts more than two weeks, please see a doctor.

## Samhain

At Samhain, many Celtic pagans keep a fuller rite for the dead: a candle in the window, a place at the table with food and drink, names spoken aloud, stories told. The lore module teaches Samhain in depth.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven honours its dead, and whether it keeps a shared ancestor shrine or remembers members who have died.

> **Try this:** Make a small ancestor shrine. Over a month, visit it four times, speaking the names of those you remember and one ancestor of place or of spirit. Write in your book what it was like.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** care for the dead, burials, the hints of rebirth and Tech Duinn, and the wake, keen, Samhain and grave customs.
- **Modern:** the three kinds of ancestor (blood, place and spirit), and ancestor shrines as part of a pagan practice.

docs.title: Holy wells, waters and offerings to the land
docs.summary: Water in Celtic tradition: offerings in lakes and rivers, the wells of wisdom, river goddesses and Sulis at Bath; holy wells, rounds, patterns and rag trees as living Christian practice; how to visit with respect and care for the water; and offerings to the land and its waters at home.
docs.body:
## Gifts to the water

For thousands of years, people across the Celtic world gave their best things to water. Archaeologists have found swords, shields, cauldrons, brooches and coins in lakes, rivers, bogs and springs, from the Bronze Age to Roman times. At Llyn Cerrig Bach on Anglesey, a great hoard of weapons, chariot fittings and slave chains was thrown into a lake over two or three centuries before the Roman conquest. At Bath, the hot spring was the shrine of **Sulis**, honoured with Minerva, and over a hundred curse tablets, small lead sheets asking the goddess to punish thieves, were found in it.

We cannot know all that these gifts meant. But the pattern is clear: water was a place to meet the powers.

## Wells of wisdom and river goddesses

In medieval Irish tales, wisdom springs from a hidden well, surrounded by nine hazels whose nuts fall into it and feed the salmon of knowledge. When the goddess **Boann** approached the well against its rules, the tale says, its waters rose and rushed after her, becoming the river Boyne. Sinann did the same for the Shannon. Rivers across Britain, Ireland and Gaul carry goddess names, some still in use. **Manannán mac Lir** rules the sea, and the Isle of Man keeps his memory.

## Holy wells today

There are said to be around three thousand holy wells in Ireland, and many more across Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Man and Brittany. Most are dedicated to saints, Brigid above all, and many may have been sacred before Christianity, though that is rarely provable. Famous examples include St Winefride's Well at Holywell in Wales, Madron Well in Cornwall, and the Clootie Well at Munlochy on the Black Isle in Scotland.

At many wells people still come, often on the saint's feast day (the **pattern**, from the Irish patrún, "patron"), to make the **rounds**: walking sunwise around the well a set number of times, praying at stations, drinking or washing with the water, and leaving a small token. At some, people tie a strip of cloth to a nearby tree, a **rag tree** or, in Scotland, a **clootie** tree, as a prayer for healing: as the cloth rots, the illness fades.

These are **living Christian practices**, cared for by local people. A Celtic pagan can visit, and may be welcome, as a guest.

## Visiting a well with respect

1. **Find out about it first:** who cares for it, whether there is a pattern day, whether visitors are welcome.
2. **Go quietly.** Behave as you would in a church or someone's garden.
3. **Follow local custom.** If people walk rounds, walk them sunwise, or simply stand aside.
4. **Don't hold a pagan rite** at a well that is a Christian site, especially on a pattern day. Say your own prayer quietly, if you wish.
5. **Take little or nothing.** A small bottle of water, if it is the custom. Most well water is untested; wash with it rather than drink it.
6. **Leave nothing that harms.** Many rag trees are smothered in synthetic cloth that never rots. If you tie a cloth, use a short strip of undyed cotton or wool. Never leave plastic, ribbons, coins in fragile wells, or anything else.
7. **Leave it cleaner.** Pick up litter as an offering.

> **Safety:** Wells, springs and rivers can be deep, slippery or fast. Go with someone, mind children, and never drink untested water.

## Offerings to waters near you

You do not need a famous well. Any spring, stream, river, lake or the sea can be honoured.

1. **Greet the water** by name, if it has one.
2. **Give a gift that does no harm:** pour clean water, milk or a little mead; place a flower or a few petals; speak a poem.
3. **Give work:** clear rubbish from its banks, join a river clean-up, or report pollution.
4. **Thank it,** and go.

At home, a bowl of fresh water on your shrine can stand for the well. Change it often, and pour the old water on the earth.

## Water and the Otherworld

In the tales, water is also a doorway. Heroes reach the Otherworld across the sea or beneath a lake; Otherworld women appear at fords and springs; the Morrígan is seen washing armour at a ford before a battle. Many Celtic pagans feel that a spring or a well is a place where the depths come close. That is a good reason for quiet and respect at water, and a reason not to treat it as somewhere to perform. Go to listen as much as to give.

## Offerings to the land

The land itself receives offerings too: milk poured on the earth, bread or oats at the foot of a tree, the first of the garden's harvest. Keep the land's gifts separate from the gods'. Better still, give the land what it needs: native plants, food for birds in winter, less waste.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven visits a particular well, spring or river, and what customs it keeps there.

> **Try this:** Find a well, spring or natural water near you. Visit it, greet it, give a harmless gift or clear some litter, and sit for ten minutes. Write in your book what the place is like, who cares for it, and what you noticed.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** offerings in water across the Celtic world, wells of wisdom and river goddesses in the tales, and holy wells with rounds, patterns and rag trees (living Christian practice).
- **Modern:** pagan devotion at wells and waters, and environmental care as an offering.

docs.title: Coming to know a god
docs.summary: How to build a relationship with one god of the Gaelic or Brythonic stream: choosing or being drawn, reading their stories closely, learning their places and names, a shrine and regular offerings, keeping their feast, and what changes over time. With short guides to Brigid, the Morrígan, Lugh, the Dagda, Manannán, Rhiannon and Cerridwen.
docs.body:
## One god at a time

Many Celtic pagans honour many gods, but come to know them one at a time. A close relationship with one god, built over months and years, teaches you more than a little time with many. Some people feel drawn to a particular god from the start; others choose one to learn about and see what grows.

## Being drawn, and choosing

You might feel drawn because a story moves you, because a god's concerns match your life (a poet to Brigid, a sailor to Manannán), because of a dream or a sign, or because of your family or the land you live on. All are good starts. You do not have to have a sign.

Be wary of the idea that a god has "claimed" you and now demands something of you. That can happen, in people's experience, but it is also a common way for anxiety or wishful thinking to speak. The discernment lesson teaches how to test it. A relationship is two-sided, and you may always go slowly.

## Read the stories

The most important step is to **read the stories** in which the god appears, in good translations, more than once. Look for:

- what they do and how they speak;
- who their kin and companions are;
- the places named with them;
- what they value, and what angers them;
- what surprises you, or contradicts the summaries you have read.

Then read what scholars say about the god, and the app's Library entry. Notice where scholars disagree.

## A few gods to begin with

These short notes point you to the main sources. They are a beginning.

- **Brigid.** Cormac's Glossary; the Lives of Saint Brigid, which show what the saint's devotees valued (hospitality, milk, fire, healing); and the folk customs of Imbolc. A god of poetry, healing and smithcraft, of fire and wells. Remember the living saint.
- **The Morrígan.** Cath Maige Tuired (her meeting with the Dagda at Samhain, and her prophecy after the battle), the Táin Bó Cúailnge (her encounters with Cú Chulainn), and tales of Badb and Macha. A god of battle, prophecy, sovereignty and the land. She is demanding in many people's experience; approach with respect, and not only for her darkness.
- **Lugh.** Cath Maige Tuired (his arrival at Tara and the battle), and the lore of Lughnasadh. A god of skill, craft, kingship and the harvest. People who honour him often take up a new skill.
- **The Dagda.** Cath Maige Tuired, and the Dindshenchas. A god of abundance, the cauldron, the club and the harp; a father, warrior and lover, earthy and generous.
- **Manannán mac Lir.** The Voyage of Bran, the tales of Cormac's cup, and Manx tradition. A god of the sea, the Otherworld, mists and passage.
- **Rhiannon.** The First and Third Branches of the Mabinogi. A woman of the Otherworld, with her horse and her birds, who chooses her own husband and bears injustice with patience.
- **Cerridwen.** The tale of Gwion Bach and Taliesin, and the poems of the Book of Taliesin. A god of the cauldron, transformation and the awen.

The app has a dedication journey for each of these, which can carry you further.

## Building the relationship

1. **A place.** Give the god a place at your shrine: an image, a stone, a candle, a symbol from their stories.
2. **Regular offerings.** Weekly, or on a day that feels right, light their candle, speak to them, give a gift they might like from the stories (milk and butter for Brigid, apples or a sea-shell for Manannán, a good meal shared for the Dagda).
3. **Praise.** Write and speak a praise of them, from their names, kin, deeds and places.
4. **Their work.** Do something in their honour that fits them: write a poem for Brigid, learn a craft for Lugh, help at sea-rescue fundraising for Manannán, cook for others for the Dagda.
5. **Their feast.** Keep a festival associated with them: Imbolc for Brigid, Lughnasadh for Lugh, Samhain for the Morrígan and the Dagda.
6. **Listen.** After each offering, sit quietly. Write down what comes.

## What changes over time

Over months, many people find a god becomes a familiar presence: thought of during the day, felt at the shrine, met in dreams or in the land. Others feel little, and find meaning in the faithfulness itself. Sometimes a god seems to step back, or another comes forward. All of this is normal.

## Common difficulties

- **"I can't choose."** Choose the god whose story you most enjoyed reading. You are not making a lifelong vow.
- **"The stories are confusing."** Medieval tales are often strange to modern readers. Read a good retelling first, then the translation, and keep notes on who is who.
- **"I'm afraid of getting it wrong."** Courtesy, honesty and steady gifts are rarely wrong. If you are unsure, ask your mentor.
- **"Two gods seem to pull me."** Many people honour more than one. Give each their own time and place.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may honour certain gods together. Ask your mentor how members come to know their own gods within the coven's practice.

> **Try this:** Choose one god. Over a month, read one of their stories closely, write a praise, give a weekly offering, and do one piece of work in their honour. Write what you learned about them that you did not know before.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the gods' names, stories and places, in medieval literature, inscriptions and folklore.
- **Modern:** personal devotion to them in a living pagan religion, and every practice in this lesson.

docs.title: Discernment: the sources, experience and the gods
docs.summary: How to tell real experience from wishful thinking, and both from what the sources say: the difference between evidence, scholarship, shared community practice and personal experience (UPG); testing experiences with time, omens, sense and others; when an experience contradicts the sources; and when to ask for help.
docs.body:
## Why discernment matters

As you practise, things will happen: a dream of a crow before you have read of the Morrígan, a strong feeling at a well, a sense that Brigid wants a candle lit, a word that comes in the quiet. Some of these may be the gods; some may be your own mind; some may be both. **Discernment** is the skill of weighing them honestly. It protects you from fooling yourself, and from people who would fool you.

## Four kinds of knowing

It helps to keep four kinds of knowing apart:

1. **The evidence.** What the sources say: "Cormac's Glossary calls Brigid a goddess whom poets worshipped."
2. **Scholarship.** What scholars infer from the evidence, often with disagreement: "Many scholars think Rhiannon was once a horse goddess."
3. **Shared practice.** What a modern community has come to do and believe together, often marked as modern: "Many Celtic pagans offer butter to Brigid."
4. **Personal experience.** What you have experienced yourself. Many pagans call this **UPG**, unverified personal gnosis: knowledge that comes through your own experience and cannot be checked by the sources.

All four are valuable. The trouble comes when they are mixed up, when someone's personal experience is taught as "what the ancient Celts believed", or when a modern community custom is called ancient.

## Testing an experience

When something seems to come from a god, an ancestor or the land, test it gently:

- **Time.** Write it down and wait. Does it still seem true in a week, a month?
- **Sense.** Does it make sense? Does it ask anything harmful, unkind or out of character for the god as the stories show them?
- **Your state.** Were you tired, anxious, longing for something? That does not make it false, but it is worth noting.
- **The sources.** Does it fit, contradict or go beyond what the sources say? Going beyond is common and fine. Contradicting is worth a second look.
- **Others.** Have others had similar experiences? Shared experiences across many people, independently, carry more weight. Talk it over with your mentor.
- **An omen.** Some people ask for a sign, or draw an ogham stave or a tarot card. Treat the result as one voice, not the final word.

## When an experience contradicts the sources

Sometimes your experience of a god will not match the stories: a gentle Morrígan, a stern Dagda. Do not throw it away, and do not teach it as fact. Hold it as your own experience. Over time, it may make sense, or fade. The sources are the shared ground; personal experience is your path across it.

## Red flags

Be cautious of any experience, or any person, that tells you:

- to harm yourself or anyone else;
- to cut off your friends, family or doctor;
- to give money, sex or secrets to someone;
- that you alone have been chosen and others must obey you;
- that you must act at once, without time to think.

These are not the voice of a god worth following. Stop, ground yourself and talk to someone you trust.

> **Safety:** If you hear voices, see things others don't, or feel that spirits are controlling you, and it frightens you or disrupts your life, please see a doctor. Many good pagans also take medication or see therapists; it is not a failure of faith. Spiritual practice is never a substitute for medical or psychological care.

## Keeping a record

Keep a section of your journal or book for experiences: the date, what happened, what you were doing, your state, and what you made of it then. Come back to it months later and add what you think now. Over years, this record becomes one of the most valuable things you own.

## Sharing experience

When you share an experience in the coven or online, mark it: "In my experience...", "This came to me in meditation...", "This is my UPG". It is honest, and it lets others weigh it fairly.

## An example

Suppose that while honouring Brigid at your hearth, you have a strong sense that she would like a bowl of water placed beside her candle. How might you weigh it?

- **The evidence:** Brigid is linked with holy wells in the saint's cult and folk custom, and with healing. So a bowl of water fits the sources well.
- **Your state:** you were calm, not anxious or wishing for anything in particular.
- **Time:** a week later, it still feels right.
- **Harm:** none; it is a simple, kind act.
- **Others:** your mentor says several members of the coven keep water beside Brigid's candle.

This is an experience you can act on with confidence, while still calling it yours. Now suppose instead you felt she demanded that you give up your job and move to Kildare at once. The same tests would rightly make you pause, wait, and talk it over before doing anything.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven handles personal experience: whether members share it, and how the coven weighs it against the sources.

> **Try this:** Look back over your notes from the hearth practice and your offerings. Choose one experience and write it up as the lesson suggests: what happened, your state, how it fits the sources, and what you think now. Draw one ogham stave for it if you wish, and write what it adds.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** omens, dreams and seers in the Irish tales, and the folk caution about the Otherworld.
- **Modern:** the term UPG and the habit of separating evidence, scholarship, community practice and personal experience.

docs.title: What dedication means in this tradition
docs.summary: What a dedication is in a Celtic coven: a promise freely made to learn and practise with the coven, honouring the gods, the ancestors and the land; why it is modern, how it differs from initiation and from ordination in a Druid order, and how to know if you are ready.
docs.body:
## A promise freely made

You have come through the foundations of practice, the coven's ritual, the tradition and its devotion. The devotee path ends in **dedication**: a promise, made before the coven and the powers it honours, to study and practise this tradition with this coven for a time.

Dedication is a beginning, not an arrival. It says: I have chosen this path and these people, and I will give it my honest effort. It does not make you an expert, a priestess or a druid. It makes you a committed member of a learning community.

## Is it old?

Be clear about this: **dedication, as this coven keeps it, is a modern practice.** We do not know how, or whether, the pagan Gaels and Britons marked someone's entry into the worship of their gods; most people were simply born into their community's religion. The sources do show solemn promises and their weight (oaths sworn by sky, earth and sea in the Ulster tales; the honour lost by breaking one's word; the binding force of a geis in the stories), and they show foster-children and pupils bound to their teachers. A modern dedication draws on that seriousness about the spoken word.

Many modern Celtic paths have something similar. ADF's first course of study is called the Dedicant Path and ends with a dedicant oath. OBOD's first grade, the Bardic grade, begins with an initiation. Many reconstructionists make a personal dedication at their shrine to a god or to the practice. The app's Celtic Path journey ends in a self-dedication at the hearth.

## What dedication is not

- **It is not initiation.** If your coven offers initiation, it comes later, after a year and a day of further study, and is a separate decision.
- **It is not ordination.** It does not make you a priest or priestess with authority to lead others.
- **It is not lifelong** unless you choose to make it so. A dedication in this coven is usually for a stated time, often a year and a day, and can be renewed.
- **It is not a surrender.** You keep your judgement, your rights, your other relationships and your freedom to leave. No one may ask you to promise obedience to a person, secrecy that would hide harm, money, sex, or cutting off your family.

## To whom, and to what

A Celtic dedication can include several promises, each to someone:

- **to the gods:** to all the gods of your people, or to one god you have come to know;
- **to the ancestors:** to honour and remember them;
- **to the land:** to care for the place where you live;
- **to the coven:** to learn, to take part, to keep its confidences and to treat its members with honour;
- **to yourself:** to practise honestly and keep your word.

You do not have to include all of these. A dedication is better with a few promises you can keep than many you cannot.

## Why a year and a day?

The phrase "a year and a day" appears often in medieval Irish and Welsh literature and law as a full term: Cerridwen's cauldron boils for a year and a day; some legal arrangements run for that time. Modern pagans use it as a term for commitments. It is a good length: long enough to see a full turn of the festivals, short enough to promise honestly.

## Are you ready?

Some questions to ask yourself:

- Have I kept a regular practice, even imperfectly, for some months?
- Do I understand what this coven asks, and what it does not?
- Can I honour the gods, ancestors and land in a way that is true for me?
- Do I trust the coven's leaders and my mentor enough to make a promise before them?
- Am I free to choose this, without pressure from anyone?
- Can I keep the promises I want to make for the time I will make them?

If the answer to any of these is "not yet", that is worth knowing. You may take longer. Many people do, and it is no failure. Your mentor would far rather you dedicate a season late, with a whole heart, than on time with doubts you have not spoken.

## Honour and the word

In early Irish society every free person had an honour price, the "price of the face". Breaking your word cost you honour. That may seem a harsh standard, but it points to something true: a promise is valuable because it is kept. In this tradition, it is better to make one small promise and keep it than to make a grand one and let it fall.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what dedication means in this coven: how long it lasts, what it is made to, whether it uses a particular form of words, and what changes afterwards.

> **Try this:** Write a page in your book on why you want to dedicate, what you hope it will mean, and what you are unsure about. Keep it; you will read it again at the end of the year.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the weight of the spoken word and of honour, oaths by sky, earth and sea in the tales, and "a year and a day" as a term in medieval literature and law.
- **Modern:** dedication as a rite of entry into a Celtic pagan coven, and every form of it in use today.

docs.title: Preparing for dedication
docs.summary: How to prepare: writing your words of dedication step by step, choosing a token and a gift for the gods, the old oath by land, sea and sky and how to use it honestly, whether to take a name, and preparing body, home and shrine in the week before.
docs.body:
## Your words

At the heart of your dedication are words you will speak aloud. Writing them is part of the preparation, and it may take a few weeks.

1. **List what you want to promise.** Look back at the lesson on what dedication means. Under each of the gods, the ancestors, the land, the coven and yourself, write what you want to promise, if anything.
2. **Test each promise.** For each, ask: can I keep this for the whole time? Is it specific enough to know whether I have kept it? Does it harm anyone, or ask me to give up my judgement? Cross out any that fail.
3. **Write it plainly.** Use short sentences, in the first person: "I will keep my hearth." "I will learn the stories of the gods." "I will honour my dead at Samhain." "I will keep the confidences of this coven."
4. **Add who and how long.** Begin with who you are and to whom you speak, and end with the term: "for a year and a day, from this day".
5. **Read it aloud** at your shrine. Listen to how it sounds. Change anything that feels false or overblown.
6. **Wait a few days,** then read it again and revise.
7. **Show your mentor,** and listen to their thoughts.

Your words might be ten lines or forty. Shorter is often stronger.
