4. Close the lid. If you seal it with drips of candle wax, do so over a plate, carefully.
5. Hold it, charge it, release, ground.
6. Keep it on your altar, by the door, in a cupboard, wherever suits the intention.

**Disposal:** when the work is done, thank it, empty the plant matter into compost or the garden waste, rinse the jar and recycle or reuse it.

## Charm bags and sachets

A **charm bag** (or sachet) is a small cloth bag of herbs, stones and other items, carried with you or kept in a particular place.

1. Use a small bag or a square of cloth tied up with thread, in a colour that suits the intention.
2. Add two or three herbs and a small stone or token, naming each.
3. Tie it closed with three knots, saying your intention once for each knot.
4. Charge it and carry it in a pocket or bag, or hang it somewhere.
5. Refresh it about once a month by holding it and restating your intention.

## Written petitions

A **petition** is a written request or intention. It may be kept, put under a candle, folded into a jar, or burned safely.

1. Write your intention in your own words, clearly and specifically. Some people write it three times, or sign it.
2. Fold it, place it under your candle, inside your jar, or on your altar.
3. If you burn it, hold it with tongs over a fire-safe bowl containing sand, with a window open and water nearby. Let it burn out completely, and make sure the ash is cold before disposing of it.

## Knot magic

Tying knots in a cord to “bind in” a spell is one of the oldest forms of magic, found in many cultures.

1. Take a length of cord or thread in a suitable colour.
2. Tie a series of knots (often three, seven or nine), saying a line of your intention with each one.
3. Keep the cord. Some practitioners untie the knots one by one to release the spell when it is needed, or when it is done.

## Sigils

A **sigil** is a symbol you design to stand for an intention. The modern method was developed by the English artist Austin Osman Spare in the early twentieth century and is now widely used.

1. Write your intention as a short sentence: “I SLEEP DEEPLY.”
2. Cross out repeated letters, and (in Spare’s method) vowels, leaving a handful of letters: S, L, P, D.
3. Combine the remaining letters into a single design, overlapping, turning and simplifying them until the result no longer reads as letters and pleases your eye.
4. Charge the sigil: gaze at it while raising energy, then release.
5. Many practitioners then put it away, burn it safely, or hide it, and try to forget it, so the conscious mind doesn’t interfere. Others draw it on candles or carry it.

## Kitchen and household magic

Everyday tasks become spells when done with intention: stirring a soup clockwise while thinking of health, sweeping the house from the back to the front door to clear it out, baking bread for abundance, simmering a pot of water with rosemary, orange peel and cinnamon to bless the home. The app’s craft pages have many of these. They are gentle, practical and easy to fit into a busy life.

> **Safety:** Never leave a simmer pot or anything on the stove unattended, and don’t let it boil dry. Only eat what is ordinary food in ordinary amounts.

## Disposal and the environment

What you do with the remains of a spell matters, magically and practically.

- **Plant matter:** compost, bury, or put in the garden waste.
- **Candle wax:** let it cool and put it in the household rubbish, or keep a jar for remnants. Don’t pour hot wax down the sink.
- **Ash:** when completely cold, scatter on soil or put in the bin.
- **Salt:** don’t pour it on soil or plants you want to grow; put it down the sink with running water, or in the bin.
- **Jars, stones and cords:** cleanse and reuse, or recycle.
- **Never** leave glass, plastic, wax, foil or non-native plants in rivers, the sea, woods or parks, even as an offering. If you leave something outdoors, it should be biodegradable and harmless to wildlife.

Some practitioners dispose of the remains of banishing spells away from home, at a crossroads or in a public bin, to “send them away”. That is fine, as long as you follow the same rules.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have its own preferred forms, materials, or ways of disposing of remains. Ask your mentor.

> **Try this:** Choose one form from this lesson (not a candle spell) and make it for the intention you have been working on, following every step and safety note. Record it.

docs.title: The Gaelic year: four quarter days
docs.summary: How the Gaelic year was divided: the four quarter days named in the medieval texts, the winter and summer halves, days reckoned from sunset, the Coligny calendar of Gaul, the Welsh calends and the Scottish term days; where the solstices fit; and keeping the year in the southern hemisphere.
docs.body:
## Four days that turn the year

The Gaelic year turned on four great days, the **quarter days**, at the beginning of each season:

- **Samhain,** 1 November, the beginning of winter;
- **Imbolc,** 1 February, the beginning of spring;
- **Bealtaine,** 1 May, the beginning of summer;
- **Lughnasadh,** 1 August, the beginning of autumn.

They are named together in medieval Irish literature. In the tale Tochmarc Emire, "the Wooing of Emer", the heroine Emer sets the hero Cú Chulainn riddles that name the four: Samain, Imbolc, Beltaine and Brón Trogain, an old name for Lughnasadh, often translated "the sorrow" or "the labour of the earth" as the harvest begins. Other tales place assemblies, feasts and battles on them, above all at Samhain.

Each is not a single day but an eve and a day: the festival begins at sunset the evening before. That is why Halloween is 31 October and the eve of Brigid's day is 31 January.

## Days from sunset

Julius Caesar noted that the Gauls counted time by nights rather than days, and kept birthdays and the beginnings of months and years with the night first. Medieval Irish practice also treated the eve as part of the feast. In modern Irish the night before a feast is its oíche: Oíche Shamhna, Samhain night. Many Celtic pagans begin their festivals at sunset for this reason.

## The two halves

The quarter days divide the year in two great halves as well as four seasons: the **winter half**, from Samhain to Bealtaine, and the **summer half**, from Bealtaine to Samhain. The Irish words geimhreadh (winter) and samhradh (summer) cover these halves loosely. Herds went up to summer pastures at Bealtaine and came down at Samhain. The dark half came first, as night comes before day; many scholars and modern pagans speak of Samhain as the Gaelic New Year, though the evidence for this is suggestive rather than certain.

## The Coligny calendar

The one surviving pagan Celtic calendar is the bronze tablet found at Coligny in eastern France in 1897, made in the late second century CE. It sets out five years of lunar months in Gaulish, each month split into two halves, with intercalary months to keep the moon and sun in step. Its first month is Samonios, a name linked with the word for summer, and one of its days reads TRINVX SAMONI, often understood as "three nights of Samonios". Whether Samonios fell near Samhain or at the start of summer is still argued. The app's calendars include the Coligny months as a reconstruction. It shows that at least one Celtic people kept a careful lunar-solar calendar; it does not tell us their festivals.

## Wales, Scotland, Man and Brittany

- **Wales** keeps the calends, **calan**: Calan Gaeaf (1 November, the calends of winter) and Calan Mai (1 May), each with an eve, a nos galan, counted among the **ysbrydnosau**, the spirit nights. Gŵyl Awst, the feast of August, and Gŵyl Fair y Canhwyllau, Mary's feast of the candles (Candlemas, 2 February), stand at the other quarters.
- **Scotland** kept the Gaelic festivals in the Highlands and Islands, and Scots law kept four **term days**, on which rents and wages fell due: Candlemas, Whitsunday, Lammas and Martinmas, near the old quarter days.
- **The Isle of Man** kept Hop-tu-Naa at Samhain, Laa'l Breeshey at Imbolc, Laa Boaldyn at Bealtaine and Laa Luanys at Lughnasadh.
- **Brittany** kept Kala-Goañv, the calends of winter, and Kala-Mae, the calends of May.

## And the solstices?

The solstices and equinoxes are hardly mentioned in early Irish or Welsh sources. That does not mean no one noticed them: the great Neolithic tomb at Newgrange, built over five thousand years ago, long before any Celtic language reached Ireland, is aligned so that the rising sun at midwinter lights its inner chamber. And Midsummer Eve, the feast of Saint John, was kept with bonfires across Ireland, Man, Wales and Brittany in folk custom, as it still is in parts of the west of Ireland. But the eight-festival Wheel of the Year, with solstices and equinoxes between the quarter days, is a twentieth-century creation. A Celtic coven may keep Midsummer as a folk feast, but should not call the eightfold Wheel ancient Celtic.

## Calendar changes

When Britain and Ireland moved from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, eleven days were dropped. Some communities went on keeping festivals by the old reckoning, so you will find "Old May Day" on 12 May and "Old Halloween" in mid-November in some records. Some Celtic pagans also keep the festivals by the land rather than the date: Bealtaine when the hawthorn flowers, Lughnasadh with the first harvest. Both have good reasons. This coven's calendar in the app keeps the fixed dates.

## In the southern hemisphere

The Gaelic festivals belong to the seasons of Ireland and Scotland. In Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and South America, the seasons are reversed. Many southern Celtic pagans keep Samhain at the start of May and Bealtaine at the start of November, to follow the land; others keep the Irish dates, to stay with the communities and calendars of the homelands. Both are honest choices. Ask your coven which it keeps; the app's Celtic calendar shows the northern dates.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which festivals your coven keeps besides the four, whether it begins them at sunset, and whether it keeps them by date or by the land.

> **Try this:** Draw the Gaelic year in your book as a circle split into two halves and four quarters. Mark the four festivals, the winter and summer halves, and three things that happen on your own land in each quarter.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the four quarter days in medieval Irish literature, days from sunset, the Coligny calendar, the Welsh calends, the Scottish term days, and Midsummer fires in folk custom.
- **Modern:** the eightfold Wheel, and keeping the Gaelic festivals by the southern seasons.

docs.title: The turning year: dates, names and keeping a festival
docs.summary: How the eight festivals are dated (fixed days and the sun’s own turning points), the many names each goes by, the southern and northern wheels, and how to keep a festival well as a beginner or a coven.
docs.body:
## A year of eight festivals

This module gives one lesson to each of the eight festivals of the Wheel, in the order the year turns from Samhain, which many practitioners treat as the beginning. Each lesson tells you the festival's roots honestly, its old and folk customs, how modern practitioners keep it, and a way to keep it yourself. You will keep each festival as it comes, so this module takes a full year.

## How the dates work

The festivals are dated in two different ways.

### The sun's turning points

The solstices and equinoxes are astronomical events. They happen when the sun reaches a particular point in its yearly path across the sky, so their dates shift by a day or so from year to year:

- **winter solstice:** 20 to 23 December (northern hemisphere);
- **spring equinox:** 19 to 21 March;
- **summer solstice:** 20 to 22 June;
- **autumn equinox:** 21 to 24 September.

They even happen at a particular moment, which may fall in the night. Many practitioners keep the festival on the day, or the evening before, rather than at the exact minute.

### The cross-quarter days

Imbolc, Beltane, Lughnasadh and Samhain are usually kept on fixed days: 1 February, 1 May, 1 August and 1 November (with their eves, the evenings before, often the main celebration). These follow the old Gaelic calendar, whose festivals began at sunset on the evening before.

The true astronomical midpoints between the solstices and equinoxes fall a few days later: around 4 February, 5 May, 7 August and 7 November. Some practitioners prefer these. Others keep the festival when the land shows its signs: the first lambs, the hawthorn in flower, the first grain harvested, the first hard frost.

You don't have to calculate any of this. The app's calendar shows each year's dates, and each festival has its own page.

## The names

Every festival has several names. Here they are, so you will recognise them:

- **Samhain** (SOW-in): Hallowe'en, All Hallows, Calan Gaeaf (Welsh).
- **Yule:** the winter solstice, Midwinter, Alban Arthan (Druid).
- **Imbolc** (IM-bolk): Imbolg, St Brigid's Day, Lá Fhéile Bríde, Candlemas, Oimelc.
- **Ostara:** the spring equinox, Eostre, Alban Eilir.
- **Beltane:** Bealtaine, May Day, May Eve, Walpurgis Night (in German lands, 30 April), Calan Mai.
- **Litha:** the summer solstice, Midsummer, St John's Eve, Alban Hefin.
- **Lughnasadh** (LOO-na-sa): Lammas, Lúnasa, Garland Sunday, the first harvest.
- **Mabon:** the autumn equinox, Harvest Home, Alban Elfed.

The names Litha, Ostara and Mabon date from the 1970s, as the tradition module explained. In the app's calendar, the festivals carry their most common names.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which names your coven uses. Some covens prefer the Gaelic names, some English folk names, some the 1970s names.

## The southern wheel

In the southern hemisphere, most practitioners turn the wheel by six months, as the tradition module explained. The Sanctuary keeps a southern Wheel calendar with the dates turned: Samhain at the end of April, Yule at the June solstice, Imbolc at the start of August, the spring equinox in September, Beltane at the end of October, Midsummer in December, Lughnasadh at the start of February, and the autumn equinox in March. Each lesson in this module notes the southern date. Where a festival's customs are tied to church holidays (Candlemas, Easter, St John's Eve, Christmas, All Saints), southern practitioners usually keep the customs with the season, not the church date.

## Keeping a festival as a beginner

Each festival lesson gives a way to keep the day. In general:

1. **Read ahead.** Read the lesson and the festival's page a week or two before.
2. **Watch your land.** What is the season doing where you are?
3. **Choose one thing** you can do: one custom done well is a full festival.
4. **Prepare.** Gather what you need. Change your seasonal altar.
5. **Keep the rite.** The complete seasonal rite from the ritual module, with the festival's custom at its heart, works for every festival.
6. **Share food,** with your coven, family or friends if you can.
7. **Write it up** in the app afterwards.

## Keeping a festival with a coven

Covens usually gather for most festivals. A coven festival follows the coven's rite at greater length, often outdoors, with a shared meal and roles for many members. Online gatherings in the app let members who live far apart keep the day together, each at their own altar.

## Honesty about what we know

Every festival lesson separates what is old from what is folk custom and what is modern. Some festivals, like Samhain and Beltane, are richly recorded; others, especially the equinoxes, have little traditional custom in Britain and Ireland, and modern practitioners have built most of what is done. That is fine. What matters is not pretending our inventions are ancient.

> **Safety:** Several festivals involve fire: bonfires, candles, burning wheels and logs. Never leave a flame unattended; check local rules on fires; in dry weather, use lanterns instead. Several involve drink: alcohol is never required. Several involve gathering plants: identify them, take little, and never eat what you can't identify.

> **Try this:** Before the next festival, use the app's year-ahead spread, or simply sit and write, to set out what you hope for from this full turn of the Wheel. Read it again at the same festival next year.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic quarter days and their eves, the solstices and equinoxes, many of the names.
- **Modern:** keeping all eight as one cycle, the 1970s names, and the southern wheel.

docs.title: The great stories: the Mythological Cycle and the Mabinogi
docs.summary: A reader’s guide to the stories of the gods: the Lebor Gabála and the invasions of Ireland, Cath Maige Tuired, the Wooing of Étaín and other tales of the Tuatha Dé, the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Culhwch and Olwen and the Taliesin tradition; what each is, when it was written, and how to read them for practice.
docs.body:
## Why read the stories

For a Celtic pagan, the medieval stories are the nearest thing to scripture, though they are not scripture. They are where the gods speak and act. Reading them closely, and more than once, is the best way to come to know the gods and the world-view of the tradition. This lesson is a guide to the main ones.

Scholars sort the Irish tales into four groups: the **Mythological Cycle** (the Tuatha Dé Danann), the **Ulster Cycle** (Cú Chulainn and the Táin), the **Fenian Cycle** (Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna) and the **Cycles of the Kings**. These groupings are modern. For the gods, the Mythological Cycle matters most, though the gods appear in all four.

## Lebor Gabála Érenn

"The Book of the Taking of Ireland" is an eleventh-century compilation, in prose and verse, telling how Ireland was settled by a series of peoples: Cessair before the Flood, then Partholón, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the **Tuatha Dé Danann**, and finally the sons of Míl, ancestors of the Gaels. It fits Irish tradition into the Bible's history, tracing the Gaels back to Noah.

It is a work of medieval learning, not a pagan myth, and modern scholars read it with great caution. But it keeps the names and kinships of the Tuatha Dé, their arrival in Ireland, and their withdrawal into the síde after they were defeated by the Gaels. It is also the source of the poem known as the Song of Amergin, spoken by the poet of the sons of Míl as he sets foot in Ireland: "I am a wind on the sea, I am a wave of the ocean...". Its meaning and age are debated.

## Cath Maige Tuired

"The Second Battle of Mag Tuired" survives in a sixteenth-century manuscript, in language that suggests an earlier text, perhaps of the ninth to twelfth centuries. It is the great story of the gods: the Tuatha Dé under the oppressive half-Fomorian king Bres; the healing of Nuada's hand; the arrival of Lugh at Tara, master of every art; the Dagda's labours and his meeting with the Morrígan at Samhain; the preparations, in which each god promises their craft; the battle, in which Lugh slays Balor of the baleful eye; and the Morrígan's prophecies at the end, one of peace and one of the end of the world.

If you read only one Irish tale, read this one.

## Other tales of the Tuatha Dé

- **Tochmarc Étaíne,** "the Wooing of Étaín": the love of Midir of the síd for Étaín, her transformation into a fly, her rebirth as a mortal woman and Midir's winning her back. It includes the druid Dalán's use of ogham on yew wands to find her.
- **Aislinge Óenguso,** "the Dream of Aengus": Aengus falls in love with a woman in a dream and finds her, Caer, as a swan at Samhain.
- **Oidheadh Chlainne Lir,** "the Fate of the Children of Lir": the children turned into swans for nine hundred years. It is a later medieval tale, with a Christian ending.
- **The Dindshenchas,** the lore of places: poems and prose explaining place-names, full of gods and goddesses, including Boann and the Boyne.

## The Four Branches of the Mabinogi

The Four Branches are the great Welsh stories, in manuscripts of around 1350 and 1400, probably composed in the eleventh or twelfth century by one or more skilled authors.

- **Pwyll, Prince of Dyfed:** Pwyll trades places for a year with Arawn, king of Annwn; Rhiannon rides out of the Otherworld to choose him; their son Pryderi is stolen, and Rhiannon is falsely accused and punished, until he is found.
- **Branwen, daughter of Llŷr:** Branwen's marriage to the king of Ireland, her mistreatment, Brân the Blessed's war, the cauldron of rebirth, and Brân's head, which keeps his companions company for eighty years.
- **Manawydan, son of Llŷr:** Manawydan and Rhiannon, an enchantment that empties Dyfed, and patience and craft that win it back.
- **Math, son of Mathonwy:** Gwydion's trickery, Arianrhod's curses on her son Lleu, the making of Blodeuwedd from flowers, her betrayal of Lleu, and her transformation into an owl.

## Other Welsh sources

- **Culhwch and Olwen,** perhaps the oldest Arthurian tale, full of Otherworld figures and impossible tasks.
- **The Book of Taliesin,** a manuscript of the fourteenth century with poems of various dates, including Preiddeu Annwfn, "the Spoils of Annwn", in which Arthur sails to the Otherworld for a cauldron.
- **Hanes Taliesin,** the story of Cerridwen, Gwion Bach and the birth of Taliesin, in sixteenth-century versions.
- **Trioedd Ynys Prydein,** "the Triads of the Island of Britain", lists of three that preserve names and story-fragments, many now lost.

## How to read them

1. **Read a good modern translation,** with notes, and if possible a retelling first to learn the plot.
2. **Read slowly,** and keep a list of names and kin.
3. **Notice what is strange.** The odd, unexplained details are often the oldest or most revealing.
4. **Ask what it shows of the gods:** what they do, value and refuse.
5. **Remember the authors:** Christians, often learned, writing for their own audiences.
6. **Don't flatten the story** into an allegory or a set of archetypes. Let it be what it is.
7. **Read it aloud,** as these stories were once told.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which stories your coven reads together, and which translations it prefers.

> **Try this:** Read Cath Maige Tuired or the First Branch of the Mabinogi in full. In your book, list the gods who appear, one thing each does, and the strangest detail you noticed.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the stories themselves, as written by medieval authors, and the older material they may preserve.
- **Modern:** the four "cycles" of scholarship, and reading the tales as sources for a living religion.

docs.title: Samhain (Oíche Shamhna)
docs.summary: Samhain in the Gaelic and Brythonic world: the medieval tales of assemblies, Otherworld encounters and kings’ deaths, the folk customs of fires, guising, divination and the dead across Ireland, Scotland, Man, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, what is not known, and a Celtic Samhain rite for a coven and alone.
docs.body:
## Summer's end

Samhain, in Scottish Gaelic Samhainn and in Manx Sauin, is the first day of winter, 1 November, kept from sunset on 31 October. Its name is usually explained as "summer's end", though the word's origins are debated. For the general history of the festival and of Halloween, read the Wheel of the Year lesson on Samhain alongside this one. This lesson goes deeper into the Gaelic and Brythonic sources and customs.

## Samhain in the medieval tales

In early Irish literature Samhain is the great assembly time, and the time when the Otherworld is open.

- **Assemblies and feasts.** The tales place the great Feast of Tara at Samhain, with the king and the men of Ireland gathered for days. Seventeenth-century historian Geoffrey Keating describes a fire lit at Tlachtga (the Hill of Ward in County Meath) at Samhain, from which others were kindled; his source and its age are uncertain.
- **The Otherworld opens.** In Echtra Nerai, "the Adventure of Nera", a young warrior goes out on Samhain night at the court of Crúachan, follows a host of the síd into their mound, and lives there for a time. In Aislinge Óenguso, "the Dream of Aengus", the god Aengus finds his beloved Caer at Samhain in the form of a swan, and flies away with her.
- **The gods meet.** In Cath Maige Tuired, the Dagda meets the Morrígan at Samhain, at a river in Connacht, before the great battle, and she promises her help.
- **Danger and death.** Fionn mac Cumhaill guards Tara on Samhain night against Aillén, a fire-breathing being of the síd who burns it every year. Several kings meet their deaths at Samhain in the tales.

These are stories written by Christian authors. They show that Samhain was remembered as a time of gathering, of the Otherworld close at hand, and of fate. They do not describe pagan rites.

## Samhain in folk custom

- **Ireland.** Bonfires on hills; guisers in straw masks and costumes going from house to house; the barmbrack, a fruit loaf with a ring baked in (whoever finds it will marry); colcannon with charms; games of divination with apples and nuts; a place left at the table and the door unlatched for the dead; turnip lanterns. Food left out that night, or fallen to the floor, was not eaten.
- **Scotland.** Samhainn fires in the Highlands, and guising in the Lowlands and Highlands alike; divination with apples, kale stalks and nuts, as Robert Burns describes in his poem "Halloween" (1785).
- **The Isle of Man.** **Hop-tu-Naa**, with turnip lanterns and children going round singing the Hop-tu-Naa songs, still kept today.
- **Wales.** Nos Galan Gaeaf, a spirit night, with bonfires (coelcerthi); people marked stones and threw them into the fire, and looked for them in the morning, a missing stone being an ill omen; and everyone ran home before "the tailless black sow" (yr hwch ddu gwta) caught the last one.
- **Cornwall.** Allantide, with large, polished "Allan apples" given as gifts and placed under pillows for dreams of love.
- **Brittany.** The night of the dead, when the souls (an Anaon) are thought to return, with food left out and graves visited at All Saints.

Much of this is still alive, in Christian families and communities. All Saints and All Souls stand right beside Samhain, and for most Irish, Scottish, Manx, Welsh and Breton people the dead are remembered at Mass and at the graves.

## What we don't know

We have no reliable description of pagan Samhain worship. Stories of druids' Samhain sacrifices, or of a "lord of death" called Samhain, are modern errors. That Samhain began the year is likely but not proven.

## The gods of Samhain

From the tales, the Dagda and the Morrígan meet at Samhain; Aengus finds Caer; the people of the síd ride out. Many Celtic pagans honour these gods, the Cailleach as winter begins, and above all their own dead.

## A Celtic Samhain rite

**With the coven,** perhaps outdoors by a fire:

1. **Gather** at sunset. Sain everyone with water.
2. **Kindle** the fire.
3. **Honour** the land, sea and sky, and the spirits of the place, with a gift left apart for the good neighbours, and a word of courtesy.
4. **The dead.** Each person speaks the names of their dead, and gives a little food or drink to the fire or the earth for them.
5. **The gods.** Praise and an offering to the Dagda and the Morrígan, or the coven's gods of the season.
6. **The customs.** Divination games with apples and nuts, done with laughter as well as meaning; stories of the year past.
7. **A feast** with a place set and a plate served for the dead.
8. **Thanks and closing.** The dead's plate is given to the earth in the morning.

**Alone:** light a candle in the window, set a place at your table, speak your dead's names, give them food, play one old game, and write in your book what you are leaving behind with the summer.

> **Safety:** Bonfires need permission and care; guising should be kind, never frightening for the vulnerable. Respect graveyards: they belong to living families.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Samhain: indoors or out, with which gods, and whether it remembers members who have died.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** Samhain as an Otherworld-haunted assembly time in the tales, and the fires, guising, divination and care for the dead in folk custom.
- **Modern:** pagan Samhain rites to the old gods, and calling Samhain "the Celtic New Year" with certainty.

docs.title: Samhain
docs.summary: The end of harvest and the beginning of winter, kept from the evening of 31 October: what the Irish sources say, the Hallowe’en folk customs of guising, lanterns, apples and divination, All Saints and All Souls, and keeping it as a festival of the dead.
docs.body:
## When

Samhain (pronounced SOW-in) is kept from the evening of 31 October into 1 November in the northern hemisphere, and from 30 April into 1 May in the south. Many practitioners treat it as the beginning of the Wheel's year.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Samhain

Samhain is the best recorded of the Gaelic festivals. In early Irish literature, written down by monks from about the 8th century, it marks the end of the harvest and the beginning of winter. Kings held great assemblies and feasts at Samhain, such as the Feast of Tara. Many tales are set at Samhain because it was a time when the boundary between this world and the Otherworld opened: the sídhe, the fairy mounds, stood open, and their people walked abroad. Heroes met strange beings, and the dead were close.

Whether Samhain was the pre-Christian "Celtic new year" is often said and is plausible, but scholars disagree; the evidence is indirect. There was no god called Samhain, "lord of the dead"; that is an eighteenth-century mistake still repeated online.

### All Saints and All Souls

In the 8th and 9th centuries, the church in Rome came to keep All Saints' Day on 1 November, and in the late 10th century the monastery of Cluny began All Souls' Day on 2 November, praying for all the dead. Whether these dates were chosen to replace Samhain is debated: All Saints moved to 1 November in Rome, not Ireland. Either way, in Ireland and Britain the old festival and the Christian days of the dead came together, and the eve, All Hallows' Eve, became Hallowe'en.

### Hallowe'en folk customs

From the eighteenth to the twentieth century, Hallowe'en in Ireland, Scotland, Wales and northern England was rich in custom:

- **Guising:** children and young people went from house to house in disguise, performing for food or coins. This, and the English custom of souling (begging for soul cakes in return for prayers for the dead), are the roots of trick-or-treating.
- **Lanterns:** turnips or mangel-wurzels hollowed out and carved with faces, lit with a candle. Pumpkins replaced them in America.
- **Apples and nuts:** bobbing for apples in water, snapping at apples hung on strings, and roasting nuts in the fire.
- **Divination:** especially for love and marriage. Robert Burns's poem "Halloween" (1785) describes many of these customs in Scotland: pulling kale stalks, burning nuts in pairs, eating an apple before a mirror to see a future spouse.
- **The dead:** in many places, a place was set at the table or the fire left burning for the family's dead, and food left out.

## How modern practitioners keep it

For most modern pagans, Samhain is the great festival of the dead and of endings: the last harvest is in, the year is dying back, and it is time to remember those who have gone and to rest. Common modern customs include:

- a **silent supper** (often called a dumb supper), a meal eaten in silence with a place set for the dead;
- an **ancestor altar** with photographs, candles and the dead's favourite foods;
- **reading the names** of the dead aloud;
- **divination** for the year ahead;
- **letting go** of what the year has ended, often by writing it on paper and burning it;
- **carving lanterns** to guide the dead and keep away the unwelcome;
- **Hallowe'en fun:** costumes, apples and sweets, for and with children.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Prepare your altar:** a dark cloth, autumn leaves, apples, photographs or names of your dead, a candle, a glass of water.
2. **Carve a lantern** from a turnip, swede or pumpkin, and set it at your door or window.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Light a candle for the dead. Say the names you know, and "all those whose names I do not know".
5. Tell them something of your year. Leave a little of their favourite food or drink.
6. Sit in silence for a few minutes.
7. Write on a slip of paper something the year has ended for you. Burn it safely in a fireproof dish, or tear it and bury it.
8. **Eat a meal,** with a place set for the dead if you like, in silence for a while or in remembrance.
9. **Afterwards,** dispose of the offerings kindly, and ground well. Ancestor work can stir grief.

## With the coven

Many covens hold a silent supper, read the names of members' dead, and do divination for the coming year. Some hold a public Hallowe'en gathering for families as well as the coven's own rite. Online, members light candles at their own altars and read names in turn.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Samhain falls at the end of April, in autumn, when leaves are turning and nights lengthening, which suits it well. Hallowe'en itself, at the end of October, falls in southern spring; many southern practitioners enjoy it as a secular holiday and keep their Samhain in April or May.

> **Safety:** Ancestor work can bring up grief. Ground well afterwards, and talk to your mentor if it stays heavy. Never leave candles or lanterns burning unattended. Divination is for reflection, not for frightening yourself or others about death.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Samhain, and whether you may bring a name to be read.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Samhain as the start of winter and a time when the Otherworld opened; All Saints and All Souls; Hallowe'en guising, lanterns, apples and divination.
- **Modern:** Samhain as the pagan new year and festival of the dead in this form, the silent supper, and the ancestor altar as a modern pagan practice.

docs.title: Imbolc (Lá Fhéile Bríde)
docs.summary: Imbolc and Brigid’s feast across the Gaelic world: the name and its uncertain meaning, Brigid as goddess and saint, the crosses, the brat Bríde, the Brídeog and Brigid’s bed in Ireland, Scotland and Man, the Cailleach and the serpent, the living Christian feast and how to honour it, and a Celtic Imbolc rite.
docs.body:
## The first day of spring

Imbolc, 1 February, kept from the eve of 31 January, is the first day of spring in the Gaelic year and the feast of Brigid: Lá Fhéile Bríde in Irish, Là Fhèill Brìghde in Scottish Gaelic, Laa'l Breeshey in Manx. For the festival's wider history read the Wheel of the Year lesson on Imbolc as well. This lesson goes into the Gaelic customs, Brigid herself, and the respect the day asks for.

## The name

Imbolc is named in Tochmarc Emire among the four quarter days. Its meaning is uncertain. Cormac's Glossary, around 900, explains it as oímelc, "ewe's milk", for the lambing season; many modern scholars prefer i mbolg, "in the belly", for the pregnant ewes. Neither is certain. Both point to the same thing: the first stirring of new life in the farming year, lambs and milk after the hungry winter.

## Brigid, goddess and saint

Cormac's Glossary describes a goddess Brigid, daughter of the Dagda, "a goddess whom poets worshipped", with two sisters of the same name, one of healing and one of smithcraft. Saint Brigid of Kildare, who died around 525, is one of Ireland's three patron saints. Her early Lives are full of miracles of milk, butter, fire, healing and hospitality. Gerald of Wales described the fire kept by her nuns at Kildare in the 1180s.

How the goddess and the saint are related is one of the great open questions of Irish religious history. Some scholars think the saint's cult took up much of the goddess's; others think the saint was simply a remarkable woman whose cult gathered folk customs. People hold this in different ways, and it cannot be proved either way. A Celtic pagan honours the goddess, and treats the saint, and those who love her, with respect.

## The customs

**In Ireland:**

- **Brigid's crosses** of rushes or straw are woven on the eve and hung over doors and in byres, the old ones burned or kept. There are many regional forms: the four-armed cross with a woven centre, the three-armed cross, diamond "lozenge" forms.
- **The brat Bríde,** a cloth or ribbon, is left outside overnight for the saint to touch as she passes, and kept for healing headaches and sore throats through the year.
- **The Brídeog,** a doll or figure of Brigid, is carried from house to house by young people, the Biddy boys in some places, who are given food or money.
- **Brigid is welcomed in:** in some places a member of the family went out and knocked three times, asking to be let in "for Brigid", and was welcomed in with the rushes for the crosses.

**In Scotland,** Carmina Gadelica records the women of the house dressing a sheaf of oats as Bride and laying her in a basket bed, **leabaidh Bhrìde**, by the hearth with a white wand, crying "Bride is welcome", and checking the ashes in the morning for her footprint as a sign of a good year. A rhyme says the serpent will come out of its hole on Bride's day, a sign of spring. And in Highland folklore, if Imbolc is fine, the **Cailleach**, the hag of winter, is out gathering firewood to make winter last longer; if it is foul, she is asleep, and spring is near.

**On the Isle of Man,** rushes were gathered and the family stood at the door to invite Brigid in to spend the night.

**In Wales** the day after, 2 February, is Gŵyl Fair y Canhwyllau, the Christian feast of Candlemas, with candles blessed in church.

## A living feast

Saint Brigid's Day is a living Christian feast. Since 2023 Ireland has had a public holiday in Brigid's honour on the first Monday of February (or 1 February when it falls on a Friday). The Brigidine Sisters relit Brigid's flame in Kildare in 1993 and keep it at Solas Bhríde, which welcomes visitors of any faith. Crosses are made in Irish schools and blessed in churches.

So at Imbolc, more than at any other festival, a Celtic pagan is keeping a day that others keep as their own. You may weave a cross, leave out a cloth and welcome Brigid as goddess at your hearth. Do not claim the Catholic customs as secretly pagan, and if you visit a church, a holy well or Kildare, go as a respectful guest.

## A Celtic Imbolc rite

**With the coven:**

1. **Gather** at sunset on the eve. One person waits outside with the rushes.
2. **The welcome.** The one outside knocks three times and asks to come in with Brigid; the coven answers, "Come in, and welcome." The rushes are brought in sunwise.
3. **Sain** with water from a well or spring if you can get it, and **kindle** the fire.
4. **Honour** the land, the ancestors and Brigid, with praise and an offering of milk, butter and bread.
5. **Weave crosses** together, with talk, stories and poems. Read or speak something new for Brigid as goddess of poets.
6. **Make Brigid's bed** by the hearth: a basket with a small figure or sheaf and a white stick. Smooth the ashes, or a dish of sand, beside it.
7. **Put out the brat Bríde,** a strip of cloth from each person, to stay out overnight.
8. **Feast** on dairy, oatcakes, colcannon or barmbrack.
9. **Thanks and closing.** In the morning, look at the ashes, take in the cloths, and hang the crosses.

**Alone:** weave one cross, make a small bed for Brigid, leave a ribbon outside overnight, light a candle and say a poem to her, and give milk to the earth in the morning.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor which form of cross your coven weaves, and whether the coven visits a holy well at Imbolc.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the quarter day, Brigid in Cormac's Glossary, the saint and her cult, and the crosses, brat Bríde, Brídeog and Brigid's bed in folk custom (Christian).
- **Modern:** honouring Brigid as goddess with these customs in a pagan rite.

docs.title: Imbolc
docs.summary: The first stirring of spring at the start of February: the uncertain name, Brigid as goddess and saint, rush crosses, the Brídeóg and Brigid’s bed, holy wells, Candlemas and weather lore, and keeping it as a festival of hearth, light and beginnings.
docs.body:
## When

Imbolc is kept from the evening of 31 January into 1 February in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 July into 1 August in the south. In Ireland it is St Brigid's Day, and since 2023 it has been a public holiday there.

## The roots

### The name

Imbolc (IM-bolk) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the start of spring. The meaning of its name is uncertain. A glossary compiled in Ireland around 900, called Cormac's Glossary, explains it as oimelc, "ewe's milk", the time when sheep came into milk before lambing. Modern scholars more often suggest i mbolc, "in the belly", perhaps also about pregnant ewes. Either way, it seems to have been a festival of the first signs of new life in the farming year.

### Brigid, goddess and saint

Cormac's Glossary also describes a goddess, Brigit, worshipped by poets, with two sisters of the same name, one of healing and one of smithcraft; all three were daughters of the Dagda. St Brigid of Kildare, said to have died around 525, was one of Ireland's patron saints, with a feast on 1 February. At Kildare, the 12th-century writer Gerald of Wales reported a fire kept burning by nuns, which no man might approach. How much of the saint's story borrowed from a goddess is unknowable and much debated; modern practitioners honour Brigid in both forms, or either. The Sanctuary has a page and a dedication journey for Brigid.

### Folk customs

St Brigid's Day customs were kept in Ireland and Scotland into living memory:

- **Brigid's crosses:** woven from rushes or straw, often with four arms around a square centre, hung above doors and in byres for protection through the year. The old one was burned or kept when the new was made.
- **The Brídeóg:** a doll made from straw or a churn dash, dressed and carried from house to house by girls (and in some places young men called Biddy Boys) who were welcomed and given food or coins.
- **Brigid's bed:** in the Hebrides, a sheaf of oats was dressed as Brigid and laid in a basket called her bed, with a wand beside it. In the morning people looked in the ashes of the fire for her footprint as a sign of a good year. A traveller, Martin Martin, recorded this around 1703.
- **The brat Bríde:** a cloth or ribbon left outside on the eve for Brigid to bless as she passed; kept for healing through the year.
- **Holy wells:** visited on her day, especially the many wells named for her.

### Candlemas and weather lore

The next day, 2 February, is Candlemas, the church's feast of the Presentation, when candles for the year were blessed. It was also a day for weather lore: an English rhyme says "If Candlemas be fair and bright, winter will have another flight". In Scotland, the hag of winter, the Cailleach, was said to gather firewood on that day; if the day was fine, she gathered plenty for a long winter. America's Groundhog Day comes from the same family of lore.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Imbolc is a festival of the first light of spring: cleaning out winter, kindling new beginnings, honouring Brigid as patron of poetry, healing and smithcraft, and noticing the first snowdrops. Common customs:

- **weaving Brigid's crosses;**
- **lighting candles,** sometimes every candle in the house;
- **making a bed for Brigid** and inviting her in;
- **leaving out a cloth** for her blessing;
- **spring cleaning** the house and altar;
- **writing poetry** or starting a creative project;
- **dedications,** since it's a festival of beginnings.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Clean your altar** and house: sweep out the winter.
2. **Gather** rushes, straw or paper strips, a white candle, a bowl of milk or water, and a ribbon or cloth.
3. **Weave a Brigid's cross.** There are many guides; the simplest uses folded strips, each one wrapped around the last, until you have four arms.
4. **On the eve, keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
5. Light the white candle and say: "Brigid, if it please you, be welcome in this house." Or if you honour no god: "Welcome, first light of spring."
6. Hold up your cross and bless it, then hang it above your door.
7. Hang the cloth outside overnight for blessing, and bring it in in the morning.
8. Light every candle you can safely watch, one by one, naming something you want to begin this year.
9. **Look for the first signs of spring** on your land in the days around Imbolc.

## With the coven

Many covens make Brigid's crosses together, bless candles for the year, hold dedications of new members, and share dairy foods such as butter, cheese and pancakes. Some visit a holy well.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Imbolc falls on 1 August, in late winter, when wattle begins to bloom in Australia and lambs are born. St Brigid's Day and Candlemas fall in summer there; southern practitioners usually keep the customs at their own Imbolc.

> **Safety:** Lighting every candle is lovely and dangerous. Use stable holders on heat-proof surfaces, keep them away from curtains and children, and never leave them unattended. If you visit a well, take care at the water's edge, and don't leave coins, ribbons or plastic there; they harm the water and the trees.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Imbolc, and whether it honours Brigid, and in which form.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** Imbolc as the Gaelic start of spring, Brigid as saint (and probably goddess), rush crosses, the Brídeóg, Brigid's bed, the brat Bríde, Candlemas candles and weather lore.
- **Modern:** Imbolc as a pagan festival of Brigid in this form, and its use for dedications.

docs.title: Bealtaine
docs.summary: Bealtaine in the Gaelic and Brythonic world: Cormac’s Glossary and the two fires, Uisneach, the protective customs of fire, dew, rowan, the May bush and the first water, butter luck and its thieves, the Beltane bannock and Pennant’s Highland account, Calan Mai in Wales and May Eve on Man, what is not known, and a Celtic Bealtaine rite.
docs.body:
## The first day of summer

Bealtaine, 1 May, kept from the eve of 30 April, is the first day of summer in the Gaelic year: Lá Bealtaine in Irish, Latha Bealltainn in Scottish Gaelic, Laa Boaldyn in Manx, and Calan Mai in Welsh. For the wider history of May Day, read the Wheel of the Year lesson on Beltane as well. This lesson goes into the Gaelic and Welsh sources and customs.

## In the medieval sources

Bealtaine is one of the four quarter days in Tochmarc Emire. Cormac's Glossary, around 900, gives the fullest early description: it explains the name as "lucky fire" or "bright fire", and says that two fires were made by druids with great incantations, and cattle were driven between them each year against disease. The glossary was written by a Christian scholar long after the druids, and what he describes may be memory, custom of his own day, or learned guesswork; but the driving of cattle past fire for protection is well recorded in later folk custom.

Later writers, among them Keating in the seventeenth century, placed a great Bealtaine assembly at the Hill of **Uisneach** in County Westmeath, the symbolic centre of Ireland. In recent years a Bealtaine fire has again been lit there as a public festival.

## The name and Belenus

You will often read that Bealtaine means "the fire of Bel" or honours a god Belenus or Bel. Belenus was a real Gaulish and British god, known from inscriptions, often linked with Apollo. But most scholars doubt the connection with Bealtaine; the name's first part probably means "bright" or "lucky". Honour Belenus if you are drawn to him, but don't teach that Bealtaine is his feast.

## The customs of protection

Bealtaine customs are above all about **protecting** the household, the herds and the dairy as summer begins and the cattle go out to pasture, and about guarding the household's luck.

- **Fire.** In Ireland and Scotland, the household fire was put out and relit from a bonfire. Cattle were driven past the flames or singed with a burning bush. People jumped the fire or walked round it sunwise.
- **Rowan and red thread.** Sprigs or crosses of rowan, often bound with red thread, were put over doors, on byres and in the cattle's tails.
- **The May bush.** In Ireland a branch or small tree, often hawthorn, was set up and decorated with flowers, ribbons and eggshells. (Cutting hawthorn was otherwise unlucky; customs differed by place.)
- **The May dew.** Washing the face in May morning dew brought beauty and health.
- **The first water.** The first water drawn from a well on May morning, "the flower of the well", was prized, and could carry away a neighbour's luck.
- **Butter luck.** It was unlucky to give away fire, milk or salt on May Day, lest the household's luck went with them. Tales tell of butter-stealing witches, sometimes in the shape of hares, skimming the dew or the well to steal the neighbours' butter for the year.
- **Primroses and marigolds** were strewn on doorsteps and windowsills.

## Scotland and the Beltane bannock

In the Highlands a special **Bealltainn bannock** was baked. Thomas Pennant, describing a Beltane gathering in Perthshire in his Tour in Scotland (1769), tells of a caudle of eggs, butter, oatmeal and milk poured on the ground, and of oatcakes with nine knobs, each broken off and thrown over the shoulder with words given to a protector of the herds or to a creature that might harm them, asking it to spare the flocks. Other accounts tell of a cake divided by lot, with one piece blackened, and its taker made to leap the fire.

## Wales and Man

In **Wales**, Nos Galan Mai, May Eve, was another spirit night. May carols, **carolau Mai**, were sung from house to house, and in some places a birch maypole (bedwen Fai) was raised. Calan Mai began the summer, and the summer and winter "fought" in folk plays.

On the **Isle of Man**, crosses of rowan, crosh cuirn, were placed over doors, gorse was burned to drive out witches, and in some places the May Queen and the Queen of Winter fought a mock battle.

## What we don't know

We do not know which gods, if any, were honoured at Bealtaine. The maypole and the May Queen are mostly English customs, found in Wales and Man but not in Gaelic Ireland or Scotland. The modern Wiccan idea of Beltane as a sacred marriage of Goddess and God is not in the Celtic sources.

## A Celtic Bealtaine rite

**With the coven,** outdoors if you can:

1. **On May Eve,** put rowan and red thread over each door, and set up a May bush.
2. **Gather** at the fire. **Sain** with water from a spring.
3. **Kindle** the Bealtaine fire, with words of protection for the summer.
4. **Honour** the land, the ancestors and the gods of the coven, with praise and offerings of milk, butter and bannock.
5. **Walk the fire** sunwise, three times, asking protection for people, animals and homes. Those who wish may carry a candle lit from the fire home.
6. **Share the bannock,** with the first piece given to the fire.
7. **Thanks and closing.**
8. **At dawn,** those who can go out and wash their faces in the dew.

**Alone:** hang rowan and red thread on May Eve, light a candle and walk round it sunwise, bless your home and animals, eat an oatcake with butter, and wash your face in the dew at sunrise.

> **Safety:** Never jump a fire that is more than embers, and never with loose clothing or after drinking. Hawthorn is thorny, and some of its folklore warns against bringing it indoors; follow your coven's custom.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven keeps Bealtaine with a fire, and whether it walks between two fires or round one.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the quarter day, Cormac's two fires, and the folk customs of fire, rowan, dew, the May bush, butter luck and the bannock.
- **Modern:** the link with Belenus, and pagan Bealtaine rites to the old gods.

docs.title: Beltane
docs.summary: The beginning of summer on May Eve and May Day: the Gaelic Bealtaine fires and cattle, May dew, hawthorn and the May bush, maypoles, May queens, Jack-in-the-Green and the hobby horse, and keeping it as a festival of fire, flowers and life.
docs.body:
## When

Beltane is kept from the evening of 30 April into 1 May in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 October into 1 November in the south.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Bealtaine

Bealtaine (in modern Irish, the name of the month of May) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the beginning of summer. Cormac's Glossary, compiled around 900, says that on this day two fires were lit with incantations, and cattle were driven between them to protect them from disease before they went out to summer pasture. The name has often been explained as "bright fire" or "fire of Bel", from a supposed god Belenus, but its meaning is uncertain.

Beltane fires were recorded in the Scottish Highlands into the 18th and 19th centuries. The traveller Thomas Pennant described in 1769 how people in some places cooked a custard and an oatcake on the fire, and threw pieces of the cake over their shoulders as offerings to protect their animals from foxes and eagles. In Ireland, May Eve was a dangerous time when the fairies were active and butter or milk might be stolen by magic. People hung rowan or primroses at the door, and were careful not to give fire or milk away.

### May Day in England and beyond

May Day customs were widespread across Britain and Europe:

- **Bringing in the May:** young people went out on May Eve or at dawn to gather flowering branches, especially hawthorn (called "may"), to decorate houses and the village.
- **May dew:** washing your face in the dew on May morning was said to bring beauty.
- **The maypole:** a tall pole, recorded in England from the 14th century, set up on the village green, decorated with greenery and danced around. The ribbon dance familiar today was popularised in the 19th century.
- **The May queen:** a girl crowned with flowers, a custom popular in Victorian times.
- **Jack-in-the-Green:** a figure covered in a frame of leaves, carried in May Day processions by chimney sweeps from the 18th century; revived in many towns today.
- **Hobby horses:** at Padstow in Cornwall, the 'Obby 'Oss dances through the town on May Day, a custom recorded from the early 19th century.
- **The May bush:** in Ireland, a hawthorn or other small tree decorated with ribbons, flowers and eggshells.

In German lands, the night of 30 April is Walpurgis Night, when witches were said to gather. In Rome, the Floralia for the goddess of flowers ran from late April into May.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Beltane is a festival of the full flowering of spring: life, fertility, love, joy and fire. Common modern customs:

- **a Beltane fire,** jumped over (small and safe) or danced around;
- **gathering flowers** and making garlands and crowns;
- **maypole dancing;**
- **washing in May dew** at dawn;
- **honouring the fairy folk** with care;
- **celebrating love and life,** including handfastings, which are pagan weddings or commitments.

Some Wiccan traditions treat Beltane as the sacred marriage of the Goddess and God. In an eclectic coven that's one story among others, and Beltane is never an occasion for pressure about sex or partners.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **On May Eve,** hang a sprig of rowan or a few primroses over your door, after the Irish custom.
2. **Decorate your altar** with flowers, green branches and ribbons.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Light a candle or small fire for Beltane and say: "Summer begins. Fire of life, burn bright."
5. Weave a ring or crown of flowers and greenery, naming what makes you feel alive.
6. If you have a safe, small fire (or a candle in a lantern), step past it or over it, saying what you want to bring into the summer.
7. **At dawn on May Day,** go out and wash your face in the dew, if you can. Bring in a flowering branch, and greet the summer.

## Food and family

Beltane food is fresh and festive: oatcakes or bannocks after the Scottish custom, dairy, honey, the first green herbs, and anything you can eat outdoors. With children, gathering flowers for crowns, dancing round a simple maypole (a broom handle with ribbons will do), and getting up early for the dew are joyful ways to keep the day.

## With the coven

Covens often keep Beltane outdoors with a fire, a maypole or ribbon dance, flower crowns, and a feast. Some go out at dawn for May dew, or join a local May Day celebration.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Beltane falls on 31 October and 1 November, in late spring, when much is in flower. Hallowe'en falls on the same night in the calendar, which can be confusing; southern practitioners usually keep Beltane then, and Samhain in April.

> **Safety:** Jumping over fire is optional and must be done only over a very small fire, with loose clothing and hair secured, no alcohol beforehand, and someone watching with water ready. A candle in a lantern is a good substitute. Check fire rules before lighting any fire outdoors. Some say hawthorn blossom brings bad luck indoors; whether you keep that belief or not, some people are sensitive to its scent. Never pick protected flowers.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Beltane, and what it does about fire and dancing.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Bealtaine fires and cattle, May Eve protection and fairy lore, bringing in the May, May dew, maypoles, the May bush, Walpurgis Night, the Floralia.
- **Modern:** the ribbon maypole dance (Victorian), May queens (largely Victorian), and Beltane as a pagan festival of fertility and the sacred marriage.

docs.title: Lughnasadh
docs.summary: Lughnasadh across the Gaelic world: Lugh and Tailtiu and the Óenach Tailten in the medieval texts, Máire MacNeill’s study of the hill gatherings and Crom Dubh, Garland Sunday, Reek Sunday and Puck Fair, Lùnastal and Laa Luanys, Gŵyl Awst, the first fruits, and a Celtic Lughnasadh rite.
docs.body:
## The first day of autumn

Lughnasadh, 1 August, is the first day of autumn in the Gaelic year and the start of the harvest: Lúnasa in modern Irish (the name of the month of August), Lùnastal in Scottish Gaelic, Laa Luanys in Manx. In Wales the day is Gŵyl Awst, the feast of August, and in England Lammas, "loaf-mass". For the wider history of Lammas and the harvest, read the Wheel of the Year lesson on Lammas as well. This lesson goes into the Gaelic sources and customs.

## Lugh and Tailtiu

The name means "the assembly of Lugh". Medieval Irish texts say that Lugh founded the **Óenach Tailten**, the assembly at Tailtiu (Teltown, County Meath), as funeral games for his foster-mother Tailtiu, who died after clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. Her labour made the harvest possible; her death is remembered at its beginning. Assemblies were held there at the start of August, with horse races, contests, trading, the settling of laws and the making of marriages. Similar gatherings took place at other royal sites.

In Tochmarc Emire the festival is called Brón Trogain, often understood as "the sorrow of the earth" or "the earth's labour", the land in travail as it gives up its harvest.

Lugh himself is the bright, many-skilled god of Cath Maige Tuired, who came to Tara and was admitted because he alone held every art. Many Celtic pagans honour him at Lughnasadh as master of skills and as the god who wins the harvest.

## MacNeill and the hill gatherings

The great study of this festival is Máire MacNeill's The Festival of Lughnasa (1962). Working through the archives of the Irish Folklore Commission, she found records of summer gatherings at nearly two hundred sites, mostly on hills and mountains or by lakes and rivers, held on the last Sunday of July or the first of August. People climbed, picked bilberries (fraughans), danced, courted, raced horses, held faction fights, and in many places brought home the first new potatoes. She found a recurring story behind many of them: Lugh, or a saint such as Patrick, defeats a dark figure, Crom Dubh, who has held back the harvest, or tames a bull.

MacNeill's work is careful and widely respected, but her reconstruction of a single ancient Lughnasadh myth is interpretive. Use it, and say so.

## The living customs

- **Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday, Height Sunday** and many other local names for the hill gatherings, some still kept.
- **Reek Sunday,** the last Sunday of July, when thousands of pilgrims climb Croagh Patrick in County Mayo, some barefoot, in honour of Saint Patrick. It is a Catholic pilgrimage.
- **Puck Fair** at Killorglin, County Kerry, in August, when a wild goat is crowned king of the town for three days. Its origins are argued over.
- **The first fruits:** the first new potatoes dug and eaten with ceremony, a sheaf brought to the table, bread from the new grain.
- **Teltown marriages:** a folk tradition said that couples could be joined at Teltown for a year and a day and part by walking away from each other. It is a nineteenth-century folk memory, not a recorded ancient law.

In **Scotland**, Lammas fairs were held, and in **Man** people climbed hills on the first Sunday of August, Laa Luanys. In **Wales**, Gŵyl Awst was kept with gatherings on hills in some places, and Lammas with bread.

## Respect

Reek Sunday is a Catholic pilgrimage; pilgrims climb as an act of penance and prayer. If you climb Croagh Patrick, climb as a guest among pilgrims, not to hold a pagan rite. Many of the hill gatherings are local community events with their own life. Join in, enjoy them, and don't claim them.

## A Celtic Lughnasadh rite

**With the coven,** on a hill if you can:

1. **Climb together,** at an easy pace, with water, food and a little of the first harvest: new potatoes, a loaf from new flour, berries.
2. **At the top, sain** with water and **kindle** a candle in a jar or lantern (no open fire on hills).
3. **Honour** the land and Tailtiu who cleared it, the ancestors who farmed it, and Lugh, with praise.
4. **First fruits.** Break the bread, share the berries, and leave a small portion on the earth for Tailtiu and the land.
5. **Games.** A race, a contest of skill, a poem or song competition, in Lugh's honour.
6. **Skills.** Each person names a skill they will learn or practise this season, and asks Lugh's help.
7. **Thanks and closing.** Take every scrap of rubbish home.

**Alone:** walk somewhere high, or into your garden; eat the first fruits of the season with a portion given to the earth; name a skill to learn; and do something with your hands in Lugh's honour.

> **Safety:** Hills need proper shoes, water and weather sense. Tell someone where you are going. Pick berries only where it is allowed and where you are sure what they are.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven climbs a hill at Lughnasadh, and which skills or games it keeps.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the quarter day, Lugh and Tailtiu and the Óenach Tailten in the medieval texts, and the hill gatherings, bilberries and first fruits in folk custom.
- **Modern:** pagan Lughnasadh rites to Lugh, and the use of MacNeill's reconstruction as a myth for the festival.

docs.title: Lughnasadh and Lammas
docs.summary: The first harvest at the start of August: Lugh and Tailtiu, Máire MacNeill’s record of Lughnasa hilltop gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, and keeping it with bread, thanks and the fruits of work.
docs.body:
## When

Lughnasadh, also called Lammas, is kept from the evening of 31 July into 1 August in the northern hemisphere, and from 31 January into 1 February in the south.

## The roots

### The Gaelic Lughnasadh

Lughnasadh (LOO-na-sa; Lúnasa in modern Irish, the name of the month of August) is one of the four Gaelic quarter days, marking the beginning of the harvest. Medieval Irish texts say it was founded by the god Lugh, a god of many skills, in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, who died after clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. The Óenach Tailten, a great assembly with games, horse races, trading and marriages, was held at Teltown in County Meath at this time.

### Máire MacNeill's Lughnasa

In 1962 the Irish folklorist Máire MacNeill published The Festival of Lughnasa, a study of how the festival survived in folk custom across Ireland. She found nearly two hundred places where people gathered at the start of August, usually on the last Sunday of July or the first of August, often called Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday or Height Sunday:

- **climbing hills** and mountains together;
- **picking bilberries** (also called fraughans or whortleberries), the first wild fruit, and eating or bringing them home;
- **visiting holy wells** and lakes;
- **dancing, music, courting** and sometimes faction fights;
- **the first new potatoes** dug and eaten.

The pilgrimage up Croagh Patrick on the last Sunday of July, and Puck Fair at Killorglin, where a wild goat is crowned king, are among the customs she linked to Lughnasa.

### The Anglo-Saxon Lammas

In England, 1 August was Hlafmæsse, "loaf mass", recorded from the 10th century. Bread baked from the first ripe grain was blessed in church. One Old English charm instructs that the blessed Lammas loaf be broken into four and the pieces put in the four corners of the barn to protect the stored grain. Lammas was also a quarter day for rents in Scotland.

### Harvest customs

Across Britain and Ireland, the end of the grain harvest (often later, in late August or September) had many customs: cutting the last sheaf, sometimes by throwing sickles at it so no one person "killed" it; plaiting it into a corn dolly or "kern baby" to keep through the winter; and a harvest supper for the workers. These belong to the harvest season as a whole, shared between Lammas and the autumn equinox.

## How modern practitioners keep it

Lughnasadh is a festival of the first harvest: gratitude for what has ripened, the fruits of work, and the first turn towards autumn. Common customs:

- **baking bread** from new grain, blessing it and sharing it;
- **giving the first piece** as an offering;
- **honouring Lugh** as a god of skill, for those drawn to him;
- **games and contests,** after the Óenach Tailten;
- **climbing a hill** and picking wild fruit;
- **making corn dollies** or wheat weavings;
- **giving thanks** for the work of the year, your own and others'.

## Keeping it as a beginner

1. **Bake or buy a loaf,** ideally one you have made with your own hands. Even a simple soda bread counts.
2. **Decorate your altar** with ears of wheat or other grain, early fruit such as blackberries or bilberries, and a golden candle.
3. **Keep the seasonal rite,** with this at its heart:
4. Hold up the loaf and say: "First bread of the harvest, gift of the land, the sun, the rain and many hands."
5. Name what you have harvested this year so far: the fruits of your work, learning, relationships.
6. Break off the first piece and give it as an offering. Break the rest and share it.
7. Name the people whose work feeds you: farmers, bakers, drivers, shop workers. Thank them.
8. **If you can, climb a hill** or walk somewhere with a view, and pick a few wild berries you can identify.

## Food and family

This is the festival of bread above all, so bake if you can: soda bread needs no yeast and takes under an hour. Shape the dough into a sheaf, a sun, a person or a simple plait. Early fruit, especially blackberries, bilberries and the first apples, and new potatoes with butter, suit the day. With children, baking together, making a simple corn dolly from a handful of wheat or long grass, and going blackberrying (with care about what they pick) all keep the festival. Games and races, after Lugh's games, are a good excuse to be outside.

Lugh himself is called Samildánach, "skilled in all the arts", in Irish legend. Some practitioners use Lughnasadh to show or celebrate a skill they have worked on this year: a craft, a song, a piece of writing. That fits the festival well.

## With the coven

Covens often bake bread together, hold a harvest feast, play games, or climb a hill. Many also give to a food bank, sharing the harvest with those in need.

## In the southern hemisphere

Southern Lughnasadh falls on 1 February, in late summer, at the height of many grain and fruit harvests. It suits the season well.

> **Safety:** Never eat wild berries you can't identify with certainty: some, such as deadly nightshade and yew, are poisonous. Hill walks need good shoes, water and an eye on the weather. Have gluten-free bread for those who need it.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor how your coven keeps Lughnasadh, and whether it calls it Lammas, Lughnasadh or another name.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Gaelic Lughnasadh, Lugh and Tailtiu, the Óenach Tailten, the folk Lughnasa gatherings and bilberries, the Anglo-Saxon loaf mass, harvest customs and corn dollies.
- **Modern:** Lughnasadh as a pagan festival of the first harvest in this form, and corn dollies as altar decorations.

docs.title: The anatomy of a ritual
docs.summary: What a ritual is, the parts almost every ritual shares and why they are there, and how a ritual differs from a spell.
docs.body:
## What a ritual is

A **ritual** (or *rite*) is a planned sequence of meaningful actions, words and silences, done with attention, to mark something, honour something, or bring about a change. A birthday party with candles and a song is a ritual. So is a wedding, a funeral, a graduation, or lighting a candle every evening for someone who has died.

In a coven, rituals mark the Moon and the seasons, honour gods, spirits and ancestors, celebrate life events, initiate new members, heal, bless, and work magic together. You have already taken part in your coven’s own ritual form, taught in your tradition’s ritual lessons. This lesson looks underneath it, at the shape that most rituals across many traditions share, so that you can understand any ritual and, by the end of this module, write and lead one yourself.

## Ritual and spell

A **spell** is a working for a particular purpose; you learned its structure in Spellcraft. A **ritual** is the larger frame. Some rituals contain a spell (a full-moon rite with a healing working); many contain none at all (a seasonal celebration, an offering to a god). A ritual is often more about relationship, celebration and meaning than about getting a result.

## The parts of a ritual

Not every ritual has every part, and traditions name and order them differently. But you will recognise most of these in almost any rite.

1. **Purpose.** Every ritual starts, long before the day, with a clear purpose: what is this rite for? A full moon, a festival, a blessing, a farewell? Like a spell’s intention, everything else serves it.
2. **Preparation.** Planning, gathering what is needed, setting up the space, and preparing yourself: bathing, dressing, fasting lightly or not at all, quieting the mind.
3. **Purification.** Cleansing the people and the space, so that everyday concerns are set aside. Washing the hands, sprinkling water, passing through smoke, sweeping, ringing a bell. Almost every tradition has a form of this.
4. **Opening.** Marking the start and making the space sacred: casting a circle, opening a grove, a procession, lighting a hearth fire, a call to the gods, a prayer. You learned the general idea in Sacred space and your tradition’s form in its own lessons.
5. **Statement of purpose.** Someone says aloud why everyone is here. This simple step focuses the whole group.
6. **Welcoming the powers.** Calling, inviting or greeting the gods, spirits, ancestors, elements or quarters honoured in the rite. Often with offerings.
7. **The heart of the rite.** The main action: a seasonal drama, a story told, offerings made, a meditation, a working of magic, a blessing, a divination, an initiation.
8. **Sharing.** Food and drink are shared, often blessed first and with a portion offered to the powers. In Wicca this is called **cakes and ale** (or cakes and wine); in Heathenry the drinking rounds of **sumbel**; in Hellenic and Roman practice the shared feast after sacrifice. It grounds people and binds the group.
9. **Thanks and farewells.** Thanking and bidding farewell to the powers welcomed earlier, in reverse order.
10. **Closing.** Undoing the opening: opening the circle, closing the grove, extinguishing the fire. A clear end so everyone knows the rite is over.
11. **Grounding and aftercare.** Eating, drinking, talking, laughing, grounding any lingering energy. More on this in the last lesson.
12. **Clearing up and recording.** Tidying the space, disposing of offerings properly, and writing down what happened.

## Why this shape works

This shape has lasted because it suits people.

- **A clear beginning and end** lets people move fully into ritual time and fully out again. Leaving a ritual “open” often leaves people feeling unsettled.
- **Purification and opening** help everyone set aside the day’s concerns and arrive.
- **Saying the purpose** aloud brings a group into one focus.
- **Welcoming and thanking** the powers expresses relationship and respect, in the same way you would greet and thank a guest.
- **Sharing food** brings people back into their bodies and to each other.
- **Grounding** prevents the spaced-out, overwrought feeling some people have after intense ritual.

## A small example

Even the simplest solitary rite has this shape. Here is a ten-minute evening offering, mapped onto the parts:

- **Purpose:** to give thanks at the end of the day.
- **Preparation:** clear the altar; pour a little water or juice into a cup.
- **Purification:** wash your hands and face.
- **Opening:** light a candle and say, “I come to my altar.”
- **Statement of purpose:** “I am here to give thanks for this day.”
- **Welcoming:** greet the gods, spirits or ancestors you honour, by name or simply as “you who watch over this house”.
- **The heart:** name three things from the day you are grateful for, and pour a little of the drink into an offering bowl.
- **Sharing:** drink the rest of the cup yourself.
- **Thanks and closing:** “Thank you. Goodnight.” Put out the candle.
- **Grounding:** a breath, your hands on the floor.
- **Clearing up:** in the morning, pour the offering onto soil.

Once you see the shape, you will find it in every rite your coven does, however elaborate.

## Rhythm and pace

Good rituals have a rhythm: a gentle start, a building of focus, a peak at the heart of the rite, and a gentle return. Think of a piece of music. Too fast, and people can’t settle; too slow, and their attention drifts. Most coven rituals run between thirty minutes and an hour and a half, including sharing. A simple solitary rite might be fifteen minutes.

> **Your coven:** Your coven has its own ritual form, with its own names for each part and its own order. It may leave some parts out or add others. Ask your mentor to walk you through a typical rite and map it onto the parts above.

> **Try this:** Think back to the last coven ritual you attended (or one you saw described in your tradition’s lessons). Write down each part in order and match it to the list above. Which parts were there? Which were missing or different? Why do you think so?

docs.title: Roles and coven etiquette
docs.summary: The roles people take in coven ritual, and the etiquette that makes a coven work: punctuality, confidentiality, consent, sharing the work, and looking after one another.
docs.body:
## Many hands

In a coven, ritual is shared work. Different people take different roles, and over time most members try many of them. Knowing the roles helps you understand what is happening and prepares you to take part.

## Common roles

Names differ between traditions; your coven will have its own.

- **High Priestess and/or High Priest** (or another title, such as gothi or gydja in Heathenry, or simply leader or elder): the coven’s leader or leaders, who often lead major rites, hold the coven’s lore, and carry final responsibility for its wellbeing.
- **Officiant** or **ritual leader:** whoever leads a particular ritual. Not always the High Priestess; many covens rotate this.
- **Quarter callers** or **element callers:** in traditions that use them, the people who call and later dismiss the quarters or elements.
- **Those who make offerings or pour libations:** in many traditions a particular person makes the main offerings.
- **The person who purifies:** carrying water, smoke or salt round the space and the people.
- **Maiden, summoner or steward:** names for a coven officer who helps the leaders, organises, keeps the calendar, or watches over people’s wellbeing during rites.
- **Scribe:** keeps the coven’s records.
- **Participants:** everyone. Taking part fully (singing, responding, focusing, raising energy) is a role in itself, and the most important one.

## Etiquette: how to be a good coven member

Etiquette here isn’t fussy manners. It is the set of habits that lets a group of people do intense, vulnerable work together safely and well.

### Arriving

- **Be on time,** or a little early. Rituals often can’t start until everyone is there, and arriving late can break a circle that has already been cast. If you’re running late, message the coven so they can decide whether to wait.
- **If you can’t come, say so** as early as you can.
- **Come prepared:** read anything you were sent, bring what you agreed to bring, and know your part if you have one.
- **Come sober.** Don’t arrive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. If the rite includes a drink, you may always choose juice or water.

### Confidentiality

- **What happens in the coven stays in the coven.** Never tell anyone outside who the members are, what they said, or personal things they shared, without their permission. Many people have good reasons to keep their practice private: family, work, safety.
- **Never “out” a member** as a witch or pagan, online or off.
- **Some teachings may be oathbound,** meaning you promise not to share them. Keep those promises. But no legitimate coven will ask you to keep secrets about harm, abuse or crime. Safety always comes before secrecy.
- **Don’t photograph or record** rituals or members without everyone’s agreement.

### Consent and care

- **Ask before you touch.** Hand-holding in a circle is common; check that people are comfortable, and say if you are not. Hugs are offered, not assumed.
- **No one may pressure you** into anything you’re uncomfortable with: touch, nudity (some traditions practise “skyclad”, meaning naked, in some rites; it is never required of a trainee who doesn’t want it), drinking, sharing personal things, or any working. You can always step back or leave.
- **Share allergies, health needs and access needs** with the leaders, so the rite can be planned around them. Accept others’ needs without fuss.
- **Look after each other.** If someone seems unwell or distressed during a rite, quietly tell the leader or the person responsible for wellbeing.

### Sharing the work

- **Help set up and clear up.** Offer before being asked.
- **Bring your share** of food and supplies if that is your coven’s custom.
- **Take your turn** at roles as you are ready. Everyone was a beginner once.
- **Contribute honestly** in discussions, and listen.

### In the circle
