- **Phones off,** or on silent and put away, unless the rite is online.
- **Follow the leader’s cues.** If you’re unsure what to do, watch, or quietly ask the person beside you.
- **Leaving during a rite:** if you need to leave (unwell, overwhelmed, a call of nature), it is fine. Your coven will have a way to do this; often you signal the leader, or a door is “cut” in the circle. You learned the general idea in Sacred space.
- **Laughter is fine.** Mistakes happen in every ritual: candles go out, words are forgotten, the cat walks through. Smile, carry on.

## Red flags in any group

Every coven has its quirks, but some things are never acceptable. Leave, and seek help from someone you trust, if a leader or member:

- demands money beyond reasonable shared costs, or sex, or secrets about harm;
- pressures anyone into sexual activity, or uses initiation or teaching as leverage for it;
- isolates members from family and friends;
- forbids members from talking about concerns, or punishes questions;
- claims to be beyond criticism or the only true path.

You learned more about these in the Welcome module. Your safety and dignity always come first.

> **Your coven:** Every coven has its own customs about arrival times, what to bring, dress, how to leave a circle, and who does what. Ask your mentor for your coven’s, and note them in your Grimoire.

> **Try this:** Write down your coven’s customs as you understand them so far: when to arrive, what to bring, what to wear, how to leave during a rite, and who to tell if someone is unwell. Check the list with your mentor.

docs.title: Gathering online
docs.summary: How to take part in coven rituals and meetings held through the app: preparing your space, safety at home, timing, presence on camera, and privacy.
docs.body:
## Covens without walls

Many covens now meet online for some or all of their rites: members live far apart, travel is hard, health or caring duties keep people home, or the coven is spread across countries. Online ritual is different from gathering in one room, but it can be very powerful. Many people find that knowing others are lighting their candles at the same moment, in their own homes, creates a strong sense of connection.

Your coven uses the app for its meetings, conversations and shared work, and may hold rites through it or alongside it.

## Before the gathering

1. **Read what you were sent.** The leader may share a ritual script or a list of what to have ready. Read it the day before.
2. **Check the time zone.** If your coven spans time zones, check the start time in yours.
3. **Prepare your space.** Clear a small area, set up a simple altar, and gather what you need: often a candle, a cup of water or juice, a small piece of food, and anything the script asks for.
4. **Test your device.** Charge it, check your connection, and know how to mute and unmute. Prop it up so your hands are free.
5. **Tell your household,** if you live with others, that you need quiet and privacy for the time. Close the door.
6. **Purify yourself** in a simple way: wash your hands and face, ground and centre.

## During the gathering

- **Join a few minutes early,** to settle in and sort out technical problems.
- **Mute yourself** when you are not speaking, unless the leader asks everyone to speak or sing together. (Online, voices often lag, so group chanting may work better muted, each person chanting at home.)
- **Follow the leader’s cues** for when to light candles, speak, or act. The leader will usually say each step aloud.
- **Be present.** Close other apps and notifications. Treat it as you would a gathering in person.
- **Use the chat thoughtfully:** for short responses or practical messages, not side conversations during the rite.
- **If your connection drops,** carry on the rite at home if you know what comes next, or rejoin quietly. Don’t worry; it happens to everyone.

## Safety at home

> **Safety:** You are responsible for fire safety in your own home. Keep candles in safe holders on heat-proof surfaces, away from screens, cables, curtains and pets. Don’t let the screen distract you from the flame. Put candles out properly when the rite ends, before you leave the room. If you can’t safely have a flame (rented rooms, children, pets, smoke alarms), use an LED candle; it is just as good for ritual.

Ground well afterwards, as you would after any rite. It is easy to close the laptop and go straight back to the washing up, and some people find they feel spaced out or flat later. Eat, drink, and take a few minutes before going on with your evening.

## Making online ritual feel real

Some people find online rites flat at first. These help:

1. **Mark the threshold.** Before joining, wash your hands, change into something you keep for ritual, or ring a bell. Your body learns that this is not an ordinary call.
2. **Keep your own altar in view.** Look at your candle, not only the screen, during the quiet parts.
3. **Close your eyes** during meditations and energy work; listen to the leader’s voice.
4. **Use your body.** Stand for the opening if you can, raise your hands when others do, touch the floor to ground.
5. **Share the food at home.** Have your bread and drink ready, and eat and drink at the same moment as everyone else.
6. **Stay for the chat afterwards.** The talk after a rite matters as much online as in person.

## Including everyone

Online gatherings can include people who could never travel to a circle: those with disabilities or chronic illness, carers, parents of small children, people in remote places. Help make that work.

- Be patient with technology and with people who are new to it.
- Turn on captions if anyone needs them, and speak clearly.
- Don’t comment on people’s homes, backgrounds, clothing or interruptions from children and pets.
- If someone must keep their camera off, respect that without question.

## Common difficulties

- **Lag and echo:** mute when not speaking; leaders can pause after each cue to let everyone catch up.
- **Distractions at home:** put a sign on the door, and arrange the time with your household in advance.
- **Feeling disconnected:** speak a response aloud now and then, even when muted, and keep your own candle as your focus.

## Privacy

- **Don’t record or screenshot** the rite or members without everyone’s permission.
- **Check what is behind you** on camera if you want to keep your home private, and be aware of who can hear.
- **Don’t share** links, scripts or members’ details outside the coven.
- Remember that **messages in the app** are part of the coven’s private space; treat them with the same confidentiality as anything said in the circle.

> **Your coven:** Your coven will have its own way of running online rites: whether cameras are on, how people speak in turn, and what to have ready. Ask your mentor, and ask to see a script from a previous online rite.

> **Try this:** Before your coven’s next online gathering, set up your space and test your device as described above. Afterwards, write down what worked and what you would change next time.

docs.title: Aftercare, and bringing it all together
docs.summary: How to look after yourself and others after ritual, signs that someone needs more care, and how the capstone of this course works.
docs.body:
## After the rite

Ritual can be intense. People often feel strong emotions, deep peace, joy, grief, or a buzzing energy during a rite. Afterwards some people feel wonderful; others feel tired, spacey, tearful, flat, or restless. A few days of low mood after a big ritual or festival is common enough to have a name in many communities: a **ritual drop**. Good aftercare makes all of this easier.

## Common after-effects

- **Spaciness:** feeling light-headed, dreamy, not quite here.
- **Buzzing:** restlessness, difficulty sleeping, racing thoughts.
- **Tiredness:** feeling drained, especially after raising energy.
- **Emotion:** tears, sadness, unexpected memories, or great happiness.
- **Hunger and thirst.**
- **The drop:** a day or two later, a low or flat mood.

None of these means anything has gone wrong. They are normal responses to intense experience. But they need looking after.

## Aftercare, step by step

Right after the rite:

1. **Ground.** Use the methods you learned in Grounding: hands on the floor, feet on the ground, breath, imagining excess energy sinking into the earth.
2. **Eat and drink.** Something with substance: bread, biscuits, fruit, and water. This is why sharing food is part of ritual.
3. **Move.** Stretch, stamp your feet, shake out your hands.
4. **Talk.** Light conversation and laughter bring people back.
5. **Wait before driving** if you feel spacey. Sit a while, eat, and ground until you are fully clear.

Over the next day or two:

1. **Rest.** Sleep well, if you can.
2. **Be gentle with yourself.** Don’t plan anything demanding the morning after a big rite, if you can help it.
3. **Write it down.** Journal about the rite: what you felt, saw, learned.
4. **Reach out.** Message a coven friend or your mentor, especially if you feel low.

## Caring for each other

Look after the people beside you in the circle. Notice who is quiet, who is shaky, who leaves quickly. A simple “How are you doing?” matters. Leaders and helpers should make sure everyone is grounded before they go home.

## Aftercare for leaders

Leaders often give so much attention to others that they forget themselves. After leading, you may feel exhausted, elated, or unable to switch off. Ask someone else to lead the grounding or clear up, so you can eat and sit down. Debrief with someone you trust, and allow a quiet day afterwards if you can. It is normal to replay every mistake; write down two things that went well for every one you would change.

## Integrating the experience

Ritual can bring insights, strong feelings, memories, or a sense of contact with something greater. Integration means letting those experiences settle into everyday life, rather than leaving them in the circle.

1. **Write it down** within a day, while it is fresh.
2. **Ask what it means for your life:** a decision to make, a habit to change, a relationship to tend.
3. **Take one small action** that honours it.
4. **Talk it through** with your mentor if it was significant or puzzling.
5. **Don’t force meaning.** Some rites are simply good evenings with friends, and that is enough.

## When to seek more help

> **Safety:** Ritual is not therapy, and magic is never a substitute for medical or psychological care. If after a ritual you or someone else feel very distressed for more than a few days, have intrusive memories or panic, feel disconnected from reality, or have any thoughts of harming yourself, stop ritual practice for a while, tell your mentor or High Priestess, and contact a doctor, therapist or crisis line. If anyone is in immediate danger, call emergency services. Seeking help is wise and strong, and any good coven will support you.

It is always all right to step back from intense practices for a while. The craft will still be there when you are ready.

## Bringing it all together: the capstone

You have now worked through the whole course: the welcome, energy, grounding, raising energy, sacred space and your tradition’s ritual, the altar and tools, your tradition and its devotions, correspondences, the Moon and timing, divination, spellcraft, the holy days, and now ritual craft and coven life.

The capstone brings it together in three parts:

1. **Write a ritual.** Using everything you have learned, write a complete ritual, about thirty to forty-five minutes long, for a real occasion: a full moon, a festival, a blessing, a coven gathering. Use your tradition’s form for opening and closing. Include purification, a clear purpose, welcoming, a heart, sharing, thanks, closing, and aftercare. Plan safety and accessibility. Share it with your mentor for feedback and revise it.
2. **Lead it.** Lead the ritual, for your coven, a small group of members, or, if your coven agrees, with your mentor present online. You lead; they take part.
3. **Reflect.** Afterwards, write a reflection: how the rite went, what you learned, and how you have changed since you began this course.

There is no perfect capstone. Your mentor is not looking for polish; they are looking for care, understanding, safety, and sincerity.

> **Your coven:** Your High Priestess and mentor will decide when you are ready for the capstone, who will attend, and what form it takes. Some covens hold the capstone at a full moon or festival; others in a quiet session with just the mentor. Ask them.

> **Try this:** Before you start writing your capstone ritual, re-read your journal from the beginning of the course. Note three ways your understanding or practice has changed. You will use them in your reflection.

docs.title: Leading a ritual
docs.summary: How to lead a ritual well: preparing yourself and others, using your voice and pace, handling the things that go wrong, and caring for everyone present.
docs.body:
## The leader’s job

Leading a ritual isn’t a performance. It is **holding the space** so that everyone else can go deep. The leader keeps the rite moving, keeps people safe, and helps everyone feel included. You don’t need to be charismatic or word-perfect; you need to be prepared, calm and attentive.

## Before the day

1. **Know the script well.** Read it aloud several times. You don’t have to memorise it (most leaders hold a card or read from notes), but you should know what comes next without hunting for it.
2. **Rehearse the actions.** Walk through any movement, lighting, pouring or handing round. Find where things will go.
3. **Brief everyone with a role.** Make sure each person knows their part, has their words, and knows their cues.
4. **Check the materials.** Use a checklist. Have spares: matches, a lighter, an extra candle, tissues, water.
5. **Check safety.** Fire safety, a clear floor, ventilation, allergies, seating, a first aid kit nearby, and a plan for anyone who becomes unwell or distressed.
6. **Prepare yourself.** On the day, give yourself time to bathe or wash, dress, eat lightly, and ground and centre before people arrive.

## During the rite

### Voice

- **Speak more slowly and more loudly than feels natural.** In ritual, almost everyone speaks too fast.
- **Breathe** before each section.
- **Pause** after important words and let them land.
- **Use cues** so people know what to do: “Now we will each light our candle,” “Please repeat after me.”

### Pace

- **Watch the people, not just the script.** Are they settling, or restless? Engaged, or drifting? Adjust.
- **Leave room for silence,** but not so much that people grow uncomfortable.
- **Keep sections in proportion.** The heart of the rite deserves the most time.

### Presence

- **Ground and centre yourself** at the start, and again whenever you feel flustered.
- **Be warm.** A smile does a great deal.
- **Include everyone.** Make eye contact round the circle, or round the screens.

## When things go wrong

Every ritual has hiccups. Most are invisible to participants if the leader stays calm.

- **You forget your words.** Pause, breathe, look at your notes, or simply say what you mean in plain words. No one minds.
- **A candle won’t light, or goes out.** Relight it, or carry on without it. If it keeps going out in a draught, move it or accept it.
- **Something falls over or catches fire.** Stop the rite. Deal with it calmly and fully: put the fire out, clear up, make sure everyone is safe. Then decide whether to carry on. Safety always comes before finishing a rite.
- **Someone laughs.** Smile and carry on. Laughter is not disrespect.
- **Someone becomes distressed.** Gently check on them, or ask a helper to. Offer to let them step out with someone, sit down, drink water, and ground. Never force anyone to carry on. Afterwards, check in with them privately.
- **Someone feels faint or unwell.** Stop, help them sit or lie down, give water, open a window. If it’s serious, call emergency services.
- **The online connection fails.** Have a plan: who takes over, or everyone carries on alone and rejoins.
- **Someone behaves inappropriately.** Calmly and firmly stop it. If needed, pause the rite and speak to them privately; involve the High Priestess.

## Starting small

Nobody leads a festival rite for the first time without practice. A good path:

1. **Lead a part** of a coven rite: a quarter call, an offering, a reading.
2. **Lead a short solitary rite** at home, aloud, as if others were there.
3. **Lead a short rite for one or two people,** perhaps with your mentor.
4. **Co-lead** a coven rite with an experienced leader, taking half the parts.
5. **Lead a whole rite,** with an experienced member ready to help.

Each step builds confidence. Nerves are normal and often a sign that you care; ground before you begin and they will settle once you start speaking.

## Leading together

Many rites have more than one leader. If you co-lead, agree beforehand who says what, who watches the time, who keeps an eye on participants’ wellbeing, and who handles any problem. Give each other small signals, such as a nod when a section is done. Never contradict a co-leader during the rite; talk afterwards.

## Endings

Close every rite properly, even if it went wrong or ran short. Do the thanks and the closing, so everyone knows the rite is over, then lead the grounding.

## After the rite

1. **Make sure everyone grounds:** food, drink, conversation.
2. **Check in with anyone who seemed affected.**
3. **Clear up together,** and put out every flame.
4. **Debrief.** With your mentor or the coven, talk about what went well and what to change. Invite honest feedback and receive it gracefully.
5. **Write it down:** the script, what actually happened, how it felt, and the feedback.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may ask trainees to lead small parts of rites (a quarter call, an offering) before leading a whole one. Ask your mentor how you will build up to leading.

> **Try this:** Choose a section of a ritual you know (an opening, a blessing, a farewell). Practise reading it aloud, slowly, in your ritual space, five times. Record yourself on your phone if you like, and listen back for pace and volume.

docs.title: Writing a ritual
docs.summary: How to write a ritual step by step, from purpose to script, including accessibility and timing, with a complete sample full-moon rite you can adapt.
docs.body:
## Why write rituals?

Every tradition has rites handed down, and you will learn your coven’s. But almost every coven also writes new rites, for a festival, a life event, a coven anniversary, a member’s need. Writing a ritual is one of the best ways to understand ritual, and by the end of this module you will write and lead one.

## Writing a ritual, step by step

1. **State the purpose** in one sentence. “To give thanks for the harvest and share the year’s gifts.” “To mark Jo’s new job and bless her new start.” Every choice that follows should serve it.
2. **Know your setting.** Who will be there and how many? Indoors or out, in person or online? How long can it be? Check with your mentor what your coven expects.
3. **Choose your form.** Use your tradition’s ritual form as the frame: its way of purifying, opening, welcoming the powers, and closing. You learned it in your tradition’s ritual lessons. Don’t invent new openings for a coven rite unless your coven allows it.
4. **Plan the heart.** This is where most of your creativity goes. What single main action expresses the purpose? Telling a story, sharing gifts, a guided meditation, a blessing, a spell, a song, a procession, a divination, offerings.
5. **Choose the powers.** Which gods, spirits, ancestors or elements are honoured, and why? Make sure they fit the purpose and your tradition.
6. **Plan the sharing.** What food and drink? Offer non-alcoholic and allergy-friendly options.
7. **Assign roles,** if more than one person is involved. Give everyone something to do, if they want it.
8. **Write the script.** Write out every part, with what is said and what is done. Mark who says or does each part. Keep spoken parts short; people listen better to short speeches.
9. **Time it.** Read it aloud and time it. Add time for silences and actions. Cut what isn’t needed.
10. **Check accessibility.** Can everyone take part? Think of people who can’t stand for long, kneel, see in dim light, hear well, read small print, or are sensitive to smoke or scent. Offer alternatives: chairs, larger print, smoke-free cleansing.
11. **Check safety.** Fire, candles, herbs, food allergies, alcohol, weather if outdoors, and emotional safety (rites about grief or trauma need gentle handling and good aftercare).
12. **Get feedback.** Show the script to your mentor before the day.
13. **Prepare the materials list** and send participants what they need to know.

## Writing words for ritual

- **Use plain, strong language.** Ritual words don’t have to be archaic. “We gather tonight under the full moon” is better than awkward “thee” and “thou” you don’t feel.
- **Short lines** are easier to say and to follow.
- **Repetition and call-and-response** let everyone join in: the leader says “Hail and welcome!” and everyone repeats it.
- **Silence is powerful.** Build in pauses.
- **Use your tradition’s traditional words** where they exist (opening phrases, prayers, closings).

## A sample: a simple full-moon rite

This is a short, tradition-neutral rite for three to eight people, about forty minutes, which can be held in person or online. Adapt the opening, welcoming and closing to your tradition’s form.

**Purpose:** to honour the full Moon, give thanks, and send blessing to each person’s intention for the month.

**You will need:** a central candle (or one each, online) in a safe holder; a bowl of water; a small bowl of salt; a plate of biscuits or bread; a jug of juice and cups; a bowl for offerings.

1. **Gathering** (5 minutes). People arrive, settle, and are reminded of the purpose. Phones away.
2. **Purification** (3 minutes). The leader adds three pinches of salt to the water and says: “Salt and water, clear and clean, wash away what lies between.” Each person dips their fingers and touches their forehead (or, online, each does this at home).
3. **Opening** (5 minutes). Open sacred space in your coven’s way.
4. **Statement of purpose.** The leader says: “We meet under the full Moon to give thanks for what this month has brought, and to bless what we hope for.”
5. **Welcoming** (3 minutes). The leader lights the central candle (each person lights their own online) and says: “Moon, bright at the full, lady of tides and of light, we welcome you.” (Adapt to your tradition: a lunar god or goddess, or simply the Moon.) All: “Welcome.”
6. **The heart: thanks** (8 minutes). Going round, each person says one thing they are thankful for this month. After each, all say: “We give thanks.”
7. **The heart: blessing** (8 minutes). Each person in turn says one intention for the coming month, in one sentence. The group raises energy together, with a hum that builds for a slow count of twenty, with hands held out towards that person (or towards the screen), then releases it with a breath out and the words: “So may it be.”
8. **Sharing** (5 minutes). The leader holds up the bread and juice: “The gifts of the earth, shared in thanks.” A portion is put in the offering bowl. Everyone eats and drinks.
9. **Thanks and farewell** (2 minutes). “Moon, bright at the full, thank you for your light. Go if you must, stay if you will. Hail and farewell.” All: “Hail and farewell.”
10. **Closing** (3 minutes). Close sacred space in your coven’s way. The leader says: “The rite is ended.” Candles are put out.
11. **Grounding and aftercare** (as long as needed). Everyone touches the floor, then talks, eats the rest of the food and drinks some water.
12. **Afterwards.** The offerings are put outside on soil or in the garden waste the next day; the salt water is poured down the sink. The leader notes the rite in the coven’s records.

> **Your coven:** Your coven may have rules on who may write and lead rites, and on what may change in its traditional forms. Ask your mentor before writing for the coven.

> **Try this:** Choose a purpose for a short ritual you could lead: a full moon, a coming festival, a blessing. Work through steps 1 to 4 and write them in your Grimoire. You will build it into your capstone ritual.

docs.title: What initiation means in a Celtic coven
docs.summary: Why no ancient Celtic initiation rite is known, what the sources say of the long training of druids and poets, how modern Druid orders and reconstructionists approach initiation, and what an initiation in this coven does and does not confer.
docs.body:
## An honest beginning

You may be thinking about initiation: a deeper commitment to the tradition and the coven, marked by a rite. Before you begin the year and a day towards it, it is worth being clear about what initiation can honestly mean in a Celtic coven.

**No ancient Celtic initiation rite is known.** We have no description of how a druid, a poet or a worshipper of the gods was initiated in pagan Gaul, Britain or Ireland. Anyone who offers you "the ancient druidic initiation" is offering something modern, whether they know it or not.

That does not make initiation meaningless. It means that, like dedication, it is a modern rite, made with care from what the sources do tell us, and from the experience of modern communities.

## What the sources tell us about learning

The sources say a good deal about **long training**:

- **The druids.** Julius Caesar says that some trained for twenty years, learning great numbers of verses by heart, because they would not write their teaching down.
- **The poets.** In medieval Ireland the **filid** trained for many years, often said to be twelve, learning hundreds of tales, the genealogies, place-lore, law and the many metres of poetry. They rose through grades, from the lowest to the highest, the ollam. Later bardic schools, which lasted in Ireland and Gaelic Scotland into the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, were described by a writer of 1722 as teaching students to compose lying in the dark, in windowless rooms, a stone on their bellies; that description is late, and its details are debated.
- **The Welsh poets** had their own grades and training, and the medieval laws of Wales give the court poet an honoured place.
- **Fosterage.** Children of noble families in early Ireland were fostered by others, who taught them; the bond between fosterer and foster-child was strong, and teaching created a kind of kinship.

So the sources give us a model: initiation as the fruit of long, demanding study, entering a body of learning, and binding teacher and student.

## Modern initiation

Modern Celtic communities approach initiation differently:

- **OBOD** initiates members into each of its three grades, Bard, Ovate and Druid, with rites shared with members as they reach them.
- **ADF** has no initiation into its basic membership; its Dedicant Path ends with an oath, and its clergy training leads to ordination.
- **Many reconstructionists** do not practise initiation at all, seeing the household religion of the gods, the ancestors and the land as open to all without a rite of entry. Some groups have roles of learning and service, such as a priest or a poet, entered by training.
- **Celtic witchcraft covens** often have initiations shaped by Wicca, sometimes with degrees.

## What initiation means in this coven

In this coven, initiation marks a member who has spent at least a year and a day in study and service, has kept the festivals and the devotions, and is ready to take on more: deeper rites, more responsibility, and a share in the coven's teaching and care. It is a rite of commitment to the tradition and the coven, and of recognition by the coven.

It is honest about what it does not do. It does not make you a druid in the ancient sense, enter you into an ancient lineage, or give you secret knowledge passed down from the pagan Celts. It does not make you better than anyone who is not initiated, or give you power over others.

> **Your coven:** Ask the coven's leaders exactly what initiation means here: what it makes you, what it allows and asks, whether it connects you to a wider line or order, and whether there is a later initiation or degree.

## Why seek it?

People seek initiation for many reasons: a wish to go deeper, to serve, to belong more fully, to mark a change in themselves. Some reasons are worth questioning: wanting status, wanting secret knowledge, wanting to be told you are special. Honest reflection now saves pain later.

## What the year is for

The year and a day before initiation is not a waiting room. It is where the real change happens: in the festivals kept through cold and rain, the reading done slowly, the words of a language learned one at a time, the service given without thanks. The rite at the end recognises what the year has made. If the year is skimped, the rite means little; if the year is kept faithfully, the rite is a celebration of something already true.

The medieval poets did not become poets on the day they were made ollam. They became poets through years of learning, and the title said so. That is the spirit of this path.

## Your freedom

You may stop at any point on this path. You may decide that dedication is enough. You may take longer than a year and a day. Initiation is never owed to you, and it is never forced on you. The coven's leaders will decide with you, not for you.

> **Try this:** Write a page in your book on why you want to be initiated, what you hope will change, and what you are afraid of. Keep it sealed or set aside, and read it again at the end of the year.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the long training of druids and poets as the sources describe it, the grades of the filid, and fosterage.
- **Modern:** every Celtic initiation rite in use today, including this coven's.

docs.title: A year and a day of study and service
docs.summary: What the year and a day asks: reading the sources and good scholarship, beginning a Celtic language, keeping every festival and a monthly devotion, learning the coven’s rite, keeping your book, and serving the coven, the land and people; with a reading list to choose from.
docs.body:
## The shape of the year

The year and a day towards initiation is not a test of endurance. It is a year of deepening in five ways:

1. **Study:** reading the sources and good scholarship, and beginning a language.
2. **Practice:** keeping every festival, a monthly devotion and your daily hearth.
3. **Ritual:** learning the coven's rite by heart, part by part.
4. **Your book:** keeping a record of all of it.
5. **Service:** to the coven, the land and people beyond.

Your High Priestess or mentor may adapt any of it to your life.

## Study

Choose a reading plan with your mentor: about one book or set of sources each season. A plan might include:

**Primary sources in translation:**

- Cath Maige Tuired, and other tales of the Tuatha Dé (Tochmarc Étaíne, Aislinge Óenguso);
- the Four Branches of the Mabinogi;
- the Táin Bó Cúailnge, or a selection of Ulster tales;
- the Triads of Ireland, and the Welsh triads;
- a selection of Carmina Gadelica, read as Christian folk prayer;
- Caesar on the Gauls (book six of the Gallic War).

**Scholarship and history:**

- Ronald Hutton, Blood and Mistletoe (the druids) and The Stations of the Sun (the festivals);
- Kevin Danaher, The Year in Ireland;
- Máire MacNeill, The Festival of Lughnasa;
- Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology;
- Fergus Kelly, A Guide to Early Irish Law;
- Miranda Aldhouse-Green's books on the archaeology of Celtic religion.

**Modern practice:**

- the CR FAQ (2007) and writing by Gaelic Polytheists;
- Erynn Rowan Laurie, Ogam: Weaving Word Wisdom;
- a modern Druid book, such as those of Philip Carr-Gomm or Isaac Bonewits, read with an eye for what is old and what is new.

For each, write notes: what it teaches, what surprised you, what you question, and how it changes your practice.

## A language

Begin, or continue, a Celtic language: Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx, Welsh, Cornish or Breton, whichever is closest to your coven's stream or your own life. You are not expected to become fluent in a year. Aim to:

- learn the sounds and how to say the names of the gods, festivals and places correctly;
- learn simple greetings, blessings and thanks;
- read a short prayer or poem in the language, with help;
- use a few words in your rites.

There are good courses, classes and apps for every Celtic language, many free, run by the language communities themselves. Using them is also a way of giving back.

## Practice

- **The four festivals:** keep each, fully, with the coven or alone (the lore module guides you).
- **A monthly devotion:** once a month, at the full moon, the first of the month, or another day you choose, keep a full rite at your shrine.
- **The hearth:** keep your morning kindling and evening smooring.

## Learning the coven's rite

Over the year, take each part of the coven's rite at least once: saining, kindling, greeting the land, the ancestors, the gods, giving the offering, the omen, hosting the feast, thanks and closing. By the end you should be able to lead the whole rite without reading.

## Your book

Keep your book through the year, in the app's Grimoire or on paper: rites, praises, offerings, festivals, readings, reading notes, language notes, experiences weighed. Near the end of the year, write one page for the coven's shared book on something you have learned, for the coven's leaders to approve.

## Service

The tradition values hospitality and service. Over the year:

- **serve the coven:** help set up rites, cook for the feast, welcome newcomers, keep the shrine, clear away;
- **serve the land:** join a conservation group, a river clean-up, tree planting, or care for a holy well or monument with its keepers' blessing;
- **serve people:** a food bank, a hospice, a language group, a community garden.

You may dedicate your service to a god, the ancestors or the land, or simply do it.

## Half-way

At about six months, read back through your book and logs. Write a short review: what has gone well, what has been hard, what has changed, what you want next. Talk it through with your mentor.

## When life gets in the way

A year is long. Illness, work, family, grief and moves happen. If you fall behind, tell your mentor early. The year can be paused or lengthened; parts can be adapted. What matters is honest effort over time, not a perfect record. Many people find that the practice they kept through a hard season meant more to them than any other part of the year.

## Keeping it in balance

Study can swallow practice. If you find yourself reading every night and no longer keeping your hearth, put the book down for a week and go back to the fire, the gifts and the land. The sources serve the practice, not the other way round.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what your coven expects in particular: certain texts, a level of language, particular roles or service.

> **Try this:** Make your reading plan now: four sources, one for each season, with the festival that falls in each.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the sources you read, and the value of learning, hospitality and service in them.
- **Modern:** this year of study as a path towards initiation, and the scholarship you read.

docs.title: Ogham: the stones, the letters and divination
docs.summary: What ogham is: an early Irish alphabet carved on standing stones from about the fourth to the seventh centuries, its twenty letters in four groups, the medieval tracts that name the letters and link some to trees, what is not known, and how modern ogham divination works, marked as modern, with the app’s ogham spreads.
docs.body:
## Letters in stone

**Ogham** (in modern Irish ogham, in Old Irish ogam) is an alphabet made of strokes and notches cut along a line, usually the edge of a standing stone. Around four hundred ogham inscriptions survive, most in Ireland, especially the south and west, with others in Wales, Scotland, the Isle of Man and south-west England. The stones date from about the fourth to the seventh centuries CE.

Almost all the inscriptions are short: a name, often with a family, such as "of X, son of Y". Many stones probably marked graves or boundaries of land. Some in Wales have the same name in Latin letters too, which helped scholars read the alphabet.

Nobody knows exactly where or why ogham was invented. Most scholars think it was devised in Ireland in the early centuries CE by people who knew the Latin alphabet and grammar, as a way to write the Irish language. Medieval Irish learned tradition says it was invented by **Ogma**, the god, a champion and man of letters.

## The letters

The core alphabet has twenty letters, called **feda** (singular fid), arranged in four groups of five, called **aicmí** (singular aicme), each named after its first letter:

- **Aicme Beithe:** B, L, F (V), S, N, cut on one side of the line;
- **Aicme hÚatha:** H, D, T, C, Q, on the other side;
- **Aicme Muine:** M, G, NG, Z (ST), R, as strokes across the line;
- **Aicme Ailme:** A, O, U, E, I, the vowels, as notches on the line.

Later scholars added five more letters, the **forfeda**, mostly for sounds borrowed from Latin and Greek.

Each letter has a name. Some are tree names: beith (birch), fern (alder), sail (willow), dair (oak), coll (hazel), and others. Some are not trees at all, or not certainly: muin may mean a neck or a ruse, gort means a field, úr means earth or fresh. The app's Library has an entry for each letter.

## The medieval tracts

What we know of the letter names comes from medieval Irish learned texts written centuries after the stones:

- **Auraicept na nÉces,** "the Scholars' Primer", a grammar for poets, which describes ogham and calls the letters by tree names, giving every letter a tree even where the name was not one.
- **In Lebor Ogaim,** "the Book of Ogams", which lists nearly a hundred kinds of ogham (bird ogham, colour ogham, cow ogham and more), probably learned games and memory systems.
- **The word oghams,** the **bríatharogaim**: short kennings, or poetic riddles, for each letter, preserved in three lists attributed to Morann, Mac ind Óc and Cú Chulainn. For beith, for example, one says "withered foot with fine hair", perhaps the birch's pale bark.

These tracts are invaluable, but they are medieval learning, not pagan scripture. The tree names were partly a scholarly scheme; the original meanings of some letter names are unknown.

## What is not known

- Whether ogham was ever used for magic or divination in pagan times. There is one striking medieval scene: in **Tochmarc Étaíne**, the druid Dalán cuts four wands of yew, writes ogham on them, and by them finds where the lost Étaín has been taken. The Ulster tales also mention ogham cut on wood as messages and warnings. These are stories, but they show that medieval authors could imagine ogham used for seeking.
- The meaning of most letters beyond their names.
- Whether ogham had any connection with a calendar. The "Celtic tree calendar" of thirteen tree-months was Robert Graves's invention in The White Goddess (1948).

## Ogham divination today

Ogham divination as practised now is **modern**, developed from the 1970s onwards, drawing on the letter names, the word oghams and the medieval tracts, and sometimes on Graves. It is a good modern practice when it is honest about its sources. It usually works like this:

1. **Make or buy a set of staves:** twenty (or twenty-five) small sticks or tiles, each with one letter.
2. **Ask a clear question.**
3. **Draw one or more staves,** or cast them and read those that fall nearest.
4. **Read each letter** through its name, its word oghams and, if you use them, its tree, asking what it says about your question.
5. **Write the reading** and come back to it.

The app has three ogham spreads: **one stave**, for a question or the day; **three staves**, for what has been, what is and what may come; and **five staves**, for the four quarters and the centre, each with the quality a medieval Irish tale gives it (battle in the north, plenty in the east, music in the south, learning in the west, sovereignty at the centre). The app's notes say plainly that casting staves this way is modern.

## Learning the letters

1. **Learn the four aicmí** by heart, with their names.
2. **Write your name** in ogham, from bottom to top, as on the stones.
3. **Read about one letter a week:** its name, its word oghams, its tree if it has one; go and find the tree.
4. **Draw one stave a day** for a month, and write what it says to you.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven uses ogham for omens in its rites, and which book on ogham it trusts.

> **Try this:** Learn the four aicmí and write your name in ogham in your book. Then draw a stave a day for two weeks with the app's one-stave spread, noting each letter's name and what you made of it.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the ogham stones (fourth to seventh centuries), the letters and their names, the medieval tracts and word oghams, and Dalán's yew wands in a medieval tale.
- **Modern:** ogham divination as practised today, and the tree calendar (1948).

docs.title: Triads, memory and the poet’s way of learning
docs.summary: The triads of Ireland and Wales: what they are, when they were written, examples, and how the poets used them to remember; Iolo Morganwg’s forged triads; learning by heart in the old way; and writing triads of your own as a modern practice.
docs.body:
## The love of three

Irish and Welsh learning loves to put things in threes. Gods appear in threes (three Brigids, three sons of Tuireann, three queens of battle). Blessings come in threes. Prayers repeat in threes. And both Ireland and Wales kept collections of **triads**: short sayings that group three things under one heading.

Triads were a way of remembering. A heading and three items are easy to hold in the mind and easy to recite. For poets and lawyers who learned great quantities by heart, they were a tool of the trade.

## The Triads of Ireland

The Irish collection, **Trecheng Breth Féne**, "a triad of judgements of the Irish", was compiled around the ninth century, and translated by Kuno Meyer in 1906 as The Triads of Ireland. It has some two hundred and fifty triads, beginning with lists of places (three this, three that of Ireland), and going on to wisdom about people, law, behaviour and the world. Some are wise, some funny, some sharp.

Among them:

- "Three candles that illume every darkness: truth, nature, knowledge."
- "Three cauldrons that are in every fort: the cauldron of running, the cauldron of Gúba, the cauldron of guests." (The cauldron of guests is the cauldron of hospitality, always on the fire.)

Others list the three things that make a good household, the three signs of a fop, or the three things that are best for a chief. They are the voice of a Christian, learned, often aristocratic medieval Ireland, but they keep values that run deep in the tradition: truth, hospitality, honour, and the right ordering of things.

## The Welsh triads

The Welsh **Trioedd Ynys Prydein**, "the Triads of the Island of Britain", are different. They are lists of names and story-fragments: three great queens, three powerful swineherds, three unfortunate disclosures, three frivolous battles. They were a storyteller's index, reminding a poet of tales he knew. Many of the tales are now lost, so the triads are a tantalising glimpse of a much larger Welsh tradition. The standard edition is Rachel Bromwich's.

Wales also has triads of law and of poetry, and a few of wisdom.

## The forged triads

You will meet many "druidic triads" in modern books, especially triads about the soul, the circles of existence and the bardic way. Most come from **Iolo Morganwg**, the eighteenth-century Welsh poet and forger, published as Barddas in 1862. They are often beautiful, and they shaped Druidry; but they are not ancient. If you quote them, say where they come from.

## Learning by heart

The druids and the poets learned by heart. Caesar says the druids learned great numbers of verses; the filid learned hundreds of tales. You will not need to learn so much, but learning some things by heart is a real part of this tradition. It frees you from the page in a rite, and it changes how a text lives in you.

Ways to learn:

1. **Choose something short:** a triad, a praise, a blessing, the opening of a tale.
2. **Say it aloud,** many times, in a rhythm.
3. **Learn it line by line,** adding one line at a time.
4. **Use the threes.** A triad's shape is its own memory aid.
5. **Say it at a fixed time:** at your hearth in the morning, walking, before sleep.
6. **Recite it to someone,** or in a rite.

Over the year, aim to learn by heart your coven's rite, a praise for your god, a handful of triads, and a short passage from a tale.

## Writing your own triads

Writing triads is a good **modern** practice: it makes you think about what matters, in a form the tradition loves. For example:

- "Three things a guest is owed: a seat, a meal and a welcome."
- "Three gifts of the hearth: warmth, light and company."

Write them about your practice, your values, your land, your coven. Keep them short and true. Mark them as yours.

## Triads in teaching

Triads are useful in a coven: a simple way to teach values and practice. Many Celtic groups have triads of their own, written by their members, about hospitality, honour and the duties of members. If your coven has some, learn them; if not, perhaps you will write one.

## Other old ways of remembering

Triads are one of several memory tools the poets used. Others you can borrow:

- **Genealogies:** learning a god's kin, a hero's line, or your own ancestors, as a chain of names.
- **Place-lore:** tying a story to a place, as the Dindshenchas does, so that walking past the place recalls the tale.
- **Metre and sound:** poems with strong rhythm and alliteration are easier to remember than prose.
- **Lists of three, five and nine:** sacred numbers in the tradition that also make good memory shapes.

You might, for example, learn the gods of Cath Maige Tuired by their kin, or tie each of the four festivals to a place you know.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven has triads of its own, or ones it loves from the old collections.

> **Try this:** Learn three of the Triads of Ireland by heart. Then write three triads of your own about your practice, and keep them in your book.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the Triads of Ireland (around the ninth century), the Welsh triads, and learning by heart.
- **Modern:** Iolo Morganwg's druidic triads (eighteenth century), and writing new triads for practice.

docs.title: The oath, and the geis as story
docs.summary: The weight of oaths in the sources (by sky, earth and sea; by the gods one’s people swear by), what an initiation oath in this coven may and may never cover, how to write it, and the geis: what it is in the tales (Conaire, Cú Chulainn, Diarmaid), why it is a literary motif, and why any personal geis today must be small, modern and freely chosen.
docs.body:
## The weight of a word

In early Irish and Welsh society, a person's word was their honour. The tales are full of oaths: warriors swearing to keep their word "unless the sky falls, the earth opens or the sea rises", heroes swearing "by the god my people swear by", kings bound by promises they cannot break. Breaking an oath brought shame and loss of honour, and in the stories often death.

Initiation in this coven includes an oath: promises you make before the coven, the gods, the ancestors and the land. This lesson teaches what such an oath should and should not be.

## What the oath may cover

An initiation oath in this coven may include promises:

- **to the gods, ancestors and land:** to honour them, keep the festivals, keep your hearth;
- **to the tradition:** to keep learning honestly, to teach truthfully, to mark what is modern;
- **to the coven:** to take part, to serve, to treat its members with honour, to keep its confidences, to support its leaders in good faith;
- **to the wider community:** to practise with respect for the living cultures.

It may include a promise to keep private what is shared in the coven: members' personal lives and difficulties, and any rites the coven chooses to keep within itself.

## What the oath may never cover

No oath, in this coven or any other, may bind you to:

- **harm** yourself or anyone else;
- **obey a person without question,** or give up your conscience;
- **keep secret** any abuse, crime or harm; no confidence ever covers that;
- **stay** in the coven when you want to leave;
- **give money, sex** or anything else in return for teaching or rank;
- **cut off** your family, friends or doctor.

If anyone asks for such an oath, do not make it, and speak to someone outside the coven.

> **Safety:** An oath that would hide harm is not binding, in this tradition or in any decent one. If something wrong happens in any coven, you may always speak, to the coven's leaders, to someone outside it, or to the police.

## Writing your oath

1. **Ask to see** your coven's core oath, if it has one, and ask what it covers.
2. **List** what you want to promise, under each heading above.
3. **Test** each promise: can you keep it for life, or for the term it is made for? Is it specific? Does it harm anyone?
4. **Write it plainly,** in the first person.
5. **Choose the close.** The oath by sky, earth and sea is the strongest in the sources; use it only if you are sure. Calling the realms to witness is gentler.
6. **Read it aloud,** wait a week, and revise.
7. **Agree the final words** with the coven's leaders.

## The geis

You will meet the word **geis** (plural geasa) in Irish stories, and in some modern Celtic practice. A geis is a prohibition or an obligation laid on a person, often from birth or by a druid or a woman of power, and binding on them. Breaking it brings disaster.

In the tales:

- **Conaire Mór,** in Togail Bruidne Dá Derga, "the Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel", is a king with many geasa: among them, not to go round Tara with his right hand towards it, not to let three Reds go before him to the house of Red, not to stay in a house whose firelight can be seen from outside after sunset. One by one, through no great fault of his own, he breaks them, and goes to his death.
- **Cú Chulainn** has a geis never to eat the flesh of a dog, his namesake, and another never to refuse food offered at a hearth. When three hags at the roadside offer him dog meat, he cannot keep both; he eats, his strength fails, and he dies soon after.
- **Diarmaid** is put under geis by Gráinne to elope with her, against his loyalty to Fionn; the tale of their pursuit follows.

## Reading the geis honestly

The geis is above all a **literary motif**: a device of the storytellers, used to make fate visible, to trap heroes between duties, and to bring tragedy. We do not know how far real people in early Ireland lived under geasa, or what they would have been. It is a mistake to treat the stories as a manual of ancient practice.

Some modern Celtic pagans take on a small personal **geis** or **búada** (the positive side, a gift or advantage) as a devotional practice: a promise kept for a god's sake, such as never refusing someone food, always pouring the first drop for the house, or never cutting a hawthorn. This is **modern**. If you do it:

- choose something small, kind and possible to keep for life;
- choose it freely: no one else may lay a geis on you;
- never choose something that harms you or others, or could become a source of anxiety or compulsion;
- tell your mentor.

The tales' geasa are tragedies. A modern one should be a quiet discipline, not a trap.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor whether your coven's initiation includes a personal promise or geis, and how members choose it.

> **Try this:** Read the opening of Togail Bruidne Dá Derga, where Conaire's geasa are laid on him. In your book, write what the story suggests a geis is for, as a storyteller's device.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the weight of oaths, oaths by sky, earth and sea, and geasa in the medieval tales.
- **Modern:** initiation oaths in Celtic covens, and personal geasa as a devotional practice.

docs.title: Preparing for initiation
docs.summary: The end of the path: deciding together that you are ready, practical preparation and consent, the week before, what you may and may not be asked in the rite, and care for body and mind in the weeks after.
docs.body:
## Deciding together

At the end of the year and a day, you and the coven's leaders decide together whether you are ready. It is a conversation, not an exam. Before it:

1. **Reread the page** you wrote at the start of the year.
2. **Look back through your book:** the festivals, the monthly devotions, the reading notes, the language, the service, the parts of the rite you learned.
3. **Ask yourself honestly:** have I kept faith with this path, imperfectly but truly? Do I understand what initiation here means? Can I make the oath I have written? Am I choosing this freely?

Then meet your mentor and the coven's leaders to talk it through. They may suggest more time, a gap to fill, or that you are ready. You may decide to wait. Either is honourable. Waiting a season, or another full turn of the year, is common, and no one who waits for good reason should feel they have failed.

## Practicalities and consent

About three or four weeks before, talk with the coven's leaders about the practical side:

- **When and where.** A festival is a common time, Samhain or Imbolc above all, but any day may be chosen.
- **What to bring:** your oath, a gift for the gods, perhaps a token or a robe.
- **What to wear,** and whether you will be outdoors.
- **What will happen,** in as much detail as the coven shares. Many covens keep some parts of an initiation as a surprise, so that they are experienced rather than anticipated. That is reasonable. But you must be told enough to consent: nothing involving nudity, sex, pain, drugs, alcohol, being restrained or being left alone in danger. None of these belong in this coven's initiation.
- **Health:** tell the leaders of any physical or mental health needs, medication, allergies, mobility needs or fears, so the rite can be made safe for you.
- **A support person:** someone in or outside the coven you can talk to afterwards.

You may stop at any point, before or during the rite. A good coven will honour that without question.

> **Safety:** If anything in your coven's plans for the rite makes you uneasy, say so. If you are pressured, or asked to keep the plans from people who care about you in a way that feels wrong, stop and speak to someone outside the coven.

## The week before

1. **Read your oath** at your shrine each day.
2. **Keep your hearth,** morning and evening.
3. **Clean and sain** your home and shrine.
4. **Spend time on your land,** and with water if you can.
5. **Give an offering** to the gods, the ancestors and the land, asking for their blessing on what is coming.
6. **Rest and eat well,** and go lightly on alcohol and late nights.
7. **Tell someone you trust** where you will be on the day.

Some people take an omen in the days before, drawing an ogham stave or a card. If you do, treat it as counsel for how to go, not a judgement on whether to go.

## The rite

Your initiation is held by the coven's leaders in the coven's way. This course does not describe it; the coven keeps its own form. It will usually be in the shape of the coven's rite, with saining, kindling and the honouring of the powers, and at its heart your oath, spoken before the coven and the powers, and the coven's recognition of you.

## The weeks after

Initiation can stir a great deal, sometimes more than people expect. In the days and weeks after:

- **Eat, drink water, rest.**
- **Ground yourself:** walk, garden, cook, put your hands in water or earth.
- **Keep your hearth** and your daily practice.
- **Write** in your journal what you can, keeping private what the coven keeps private.
- **Talk** to your mentor or support person within a week.
- **Be gentle** with yourself if you feel flat, tearful, elated, unsettled or nothing at all.

> **Safety:** If low mood, anxiety, sleeplessness or a sense of unreality lasts more than two weeks, please tell your mentor and see a doctor. A strong rite can bring things to the surface; there is no shame in getting help.

## Being initiated

Afterwards, life goes on, and so does the practice. You may take on new roles, and you will be asked to help newcomers. The tradition's values remain the measure: truth, hospitality, honour and keeping your word.

Some initiates expect to feel transformed and are disappointed when ordinary life resumes the next morning. That is normal. Initiation, like a wedding or a graduation, marks a change that unfolds over months and years. Many people say they only understood their initiation long after. Keep your hearth, keep your oath, and let it grow.

If you find, after initiation, that something about the rite troubles you, or that you made a promise you cannot keep, speak to your mentor or the coven's leaders. An honest conversation is always better than silent distress or a broken word.

> **Your coven:** Ask your mentor what changes for an initiate in this coven, and when.

> **Try this:** Write a short letter to yourself to open a month after your initiation: what you hope you will remember, and what you want to keep doing.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the value of a kept word, hospitality and honour.
- **Modern:** this coven's initiation, and the care and consent around it.

quizzes.title: Correspondences: test
quizzes.intro: Fifteen questions on what correspondences are, colours, plants, stones, days and hours, and safety. Most are scored at once; the written answers are scored by your mentor. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can read the lessons again and retake it.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a correspondence in magic?
options: A fixed law of nature that makes a spell work
An agreed link between one thing and an idea or purpose, built up through tradition and experience
A letter you send to a deity
A list of ingredients that must all be used exactly
questions.explanation: A correspondence is an agreed link, such as rosemary with remembrance, built up through folk custom, learned tradition, modern books and personal experience. It is a shared language, not a law of nature, and you can substitute when you need to.

questions.prompt: Most of the specific crystal meanings in modern books are ancient and recorded in Roman sources.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Stones have been worn as amulets for thousands of years, but most specific modern crystal meanings, especially healing claims, come from New Age books of the 1980s onward. Knowing what is old and what is new helps you weigh a source honestly.

questions.prompt: You want to do a working for calm but have no blue, white or purple candle. What is the best choice?
options: Wait until you can buy the right colour
Use any candle you have and tie a ribbon or set it on a cloth of a calm colour, or simply use a plain white tea light if you have one
Use a red candle, because colour doesn’t matter at all
Skip the candle and burn a cinnamon stick instead
questions.explanation: Correspondences are meant to help, not block you. White is the universal substitute, and a ribbon, cloth or coloured ink can carry the colour instead. There is no need to wait or buy anything.

questions.prompt: Which of these stones should never be put in water?
options: Clear quartz
Rose quartz
Selenite
Amethyst
questions.explanation: Selenite is a soft form of gypsum and dissolves, flakes and pits in water. Hematite and pyrite can rust, so don’t soak them either. Clear quartz, rose quartz and amethyst are safe to rinse.

questions.prompt: Which of these stones fade if left in strong sunlight? Choose all that apply.
options: Amethyst
Rose quartz
Hematite
Citrine
questions.explanation: Amethyst, rose quartz and citrine can fade in strong sun. Hematite doesn’t fade, though it shouldn’t be soaked. Remember too that clear quartz can focus sunlight like a lens and start a fire.

questions.prompt: Why does the course recommend garden sage rather than white sage?
options: Garden sage is stronger
White sage is sacred to particular Native American nations and is being over-harvested in the wild
White sage is poisonous
Garden sage is the only sage mentioned in old books
questions.explanation: White sage grows wild only in a small region and is sacred to the nations there; wild stands are being poached for the smudge-kit trade. Garden sage, rosemary, bay or juniper make good cleansing smoke, and we call it smoke cleansing rather than smudging.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much essential oil to a teaspoon (5 ml) of carrier oil gives a gentle dilution for anointing?
options: About one drop
About ten drops
Half and half
None: essential oils go straight on the skin
questions.explanation: One drop to a teaspoon of carrier is roughly a 1 per cent dilution, plenty for anointing. Never use essential oils undiluted on skin, patch test first, and never swallow them.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real dangers to pets? Choose all that apply.
options: Peppermint and tea tree oil around cats
Lilies on an altar in a home with cats
Incense smoke in a room with a pet bird
A plain white candle in a holder on a high shelf with the animal out of the room
questions.explanation: Cats can’t break down many essential oils, and lily pollen can cause fatal kidney failure in cats. Birds can be killed by smoke. A candle safely out of reach, with the pet out of the room and the flame attended, is not in itself a danger.

questions.prompt: A herb that is safe to cook with is also safe to take in large amounts as a remedy, as long as it’s for magic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Culinary amounts are not medicinal amounts. Never eat, drink or put on your skin any herb or oil as part of magic unless it is an everyday food in everyday amounts, or a qualified professional has advised you.

questions.prompt: Which planet rules Friday, and what does it traditionally suit?
options: Mars: courage and protection
Venus: love, friendship and harmony
Saturn: boundaries and endings
Mercury: study and words
questions.explanation: Friday is Venus’s day (vendredi in French, Frigg’s day in English), traditionally for love, friendship, beauty and harmony.

questions.prompt: How are planetary hours counted?
options: Every clock hour from midnight, in alphabetical order of planets
Daylight and night are each split into twelve parts; the first hour after sunrise belongs to the day’s planet, and the rest follow in a fixed order
Each planet rules a whole day and there are no hours
They are chosen freely by each practitioner
questions.explanation: Sunrise to sunset and sunset to sunrise are each split into twelve unequal hours. The first after sunrise belongs to the planet of the day, then Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon in order. The app works them out for where you are.

questions.prompt: If you are pregnant, which of these should you avoid? Choose all that apply.
options: Handling mugwort or rue
Essential oils on your skin
Breathing smoke from burning herbs
Looking at a picture of a herb
questions.explanation: Mugwort, rue, tansy, pennyroyal and wormwood are traditionally avoided in pregnancy, as are essential oils on the skin and herb smoke. Pictures, words and safe substitutes can carry any plant’s meaning.

questions.prompt: Two books give different elements for the same herb. What do you do, and why is that all right?
questions.explanation: Lists disagree because they come from different sources and times. Choose one meaning that makes sense to you, write it down, and be consistent; your own tested experience is a valid source too, as long as you say it is yours.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): says that lists differ because they come from different traditions, periods or authors (1); says to choose one meaning (or the one that fits their experience or coven) and use it consistently, writing it down (1); recognises that correspondences are a language, not a law, so either can be used (1).

questions.prompt: Plan a simple working for an intention of your own using correspondences. Name your intention, then choose a colour, one or two plants, a stone (or a substitute), and a day or hour, saying why you chose each. Include every safety point that applies to what you chose.
questions.explanation: A good plan starts from one clear intention, uses a few well-chosen items that all point the same way, explains the choices, and builds safety in from the start rather than adding it at the end.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): one clear intention in a sentence (1); a colour, at least one plant and a stone or reasonable substitute, each matching the intention, with a reason (1); a day or planetary hour with a fitting planet (1); correct safety points for every item chosen, such as candle safety, not ingesting herbs, smoke ventilation, pets, stone water or sun cautions (1); keeps it simple and affordable, or explains substitutions (1).

quizzes.title: The Moon and magical timing: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on the phases, working with them, signs, void-of-course and eclipses, the seasons, and when timing matters. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can retake it.

questions.prompt: Why does the Moon have phases?
options: The Earth’s shadow covers part of it each night
We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it travels around the Earth
The Moon’s own light grows and fades
Clouds of dust pass in front of it
questions.explanation: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits the Earth we see more or less of that lit half. The Earth’s shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: About how long is one full cycle of phases, from new moon to new moon?
options: 7 days
14 days
About 29 and a half days
365 days
questions.explanation: A lunation takes about 29 and a half days. The word month comes from moon.

questions.prompt: You live in the northern hemisphere and see a crescent Moon lit on the right, low in the west just after sunset. Which phase is it?
options: Waning Crescent
Waxing Crescent
Last Quarter
Full Moon
questions.explanation: In the northern hemisphere a waxing Moon is lit on the right (a D shape), and the young crescent is seen in the west after sunset. In the southern hemisphere it would be lit on the left.

questions.prompt: A full moon happens at the same moment all over the world, even though local clock times differ.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Phases are moments in the Moon’s orbit, so they happen at the same instant for everyone. Only the clock time differs, which is why a coven can share a full moon online across countries.

questions.prompt: Which phase is traditionally best for release, breaking habits and clearing out?
options: Waxing Crescent
First Quarter
Last Quarter
Waxing Gibbous
questions.explanation: The waning half of the cycle, and the Last Quarter especially, is for release, breaking habits and clearing out. The waxing phases are for beginnings, action and building.

questions.prompt: The Moon is waning, and you want more confidence. What is the best approach?
options: Give up until the Moon is waxing
Word the working as release, for example “my self-doubt shrinks with the Moon”
Do a working to shrink your confidence
Only work at the full moon
questions.explanation: Most intentions can be turned to fit the phase: what should grow, and what should shrink? In a waning Moon, release what stands in the way of what you want.

questions.prompt: Which are safe ways to make and use moon water? Choose all that apply.
options: Use a clean jar with a lid on it overnight
Use it to wipe the altar or water plants
Drink water left uncovered outside for several days
Put stones in it and drink it
questions.explanation: Keep moon water in a clean, covered jar and use it for cleansing, anointing and watering plants. Uncovered water outdoors can carry bacteria and pollutants, and stones can contain toxic minerals, so never drink those.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional advice about the void-of-course Moon?
options: It is the best time to start anything new
Things begun then tend to go off course, so some avoid starting important new workings then
It is when the Moon is invisible
It means the Moon has left the zodiac
questions.explanation: The void-of-course Moon runs from the Moon’s last major aspect in one sign until it enters the next. Astrologers advise against starting important things then. How much weight to give it is up to you and your coven, and it should never stop you acting when something is urgent.

questions.prompt: It is safe to look at a partial solar eclipse through ordinary sunglasses.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Never look at the Sun without certified eclipse glasses or a safe projection method. Ordinary sunglasses and phone screens are not safe, and eye damage can happen in seconds. Lunar eclipses, by contrast, are safe to watch.

questions.prompt: Around 21 June, what is happening in the southern hemisphere?
options: The summer solstice
The winter solstice
The spring equinox
The autumn equinox
questions.explanation: The seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres. Around 21 June the north has its summer solstice and the south its winter solstice.

questions.prompt: A friend is frightened and needs protection tonight, but the Moon is in the “wrong” phase and void of course. What should you do?
options: Wait for a better time
Help them in practical ways now (and get emergency help if they are in danger), and do a protection working now if you wish, worded to suit the phase
Tell them magic can’t help until the new moon
Do nothing, because the void-of-course Moon will spoil it
questions.explanation: Timing is a tool, not a gate. Urgent needs come first, and practical help and emergency services come before magic. Any working can be worded to suit any phase.

questions.prompt: Choose an intention of your own. Write it once worded for a waxing Moon and once for a waning Moon.
questions.explanation: For the waxing Moon, word the intention as something growing; for the waning Moon, as something shrinking or being released. The same goal can be reached from either side.
questions.rubric: Full marks (2): a waxing wording that clearly grows or draws in something (1); a waning wording of the same intention that clearly releases or shrinks what stands in the way (1).

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words when timing matters in magic and when it doesn’t. Include what you have noticed in your own moon journal or seasonal observations so far.
questions.explanation: Timing adds meaning and focus when you can plan ahead, for larger workings, for coven rites and when your tradition asks for it. It matters less for urgent needs, daily practice, and when waiting would mean not acting at all. Your own records are the best guide.
questions.rubric: Full marks (4): gives at least two situations where timing is worth considering (1); gives at least two situations where it matters less, including urgent needs (1); says that magic never replaces practical help or that timing is a tool, not a gate (1); refers to their own observations from their journal or seasonal spot with at least one specific detail (1).

quizzes.title: Divination: test
quizzes.intro: Fourteen questions on what divination is, the tarot deck, reading a spread, other systems, journaling and ethics. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can retake it.

questions.prompt: Which question is best suited to a divination reading?
options: Will I get the job? Yes or no?
What do I need to know about applying for this job?
What is my manager secretly thinking about me?
Will my test results be clear?
questions.explanation: Good questions are open, about you, and about the present or near future. Yes-or-no questions give little to read, questions about other people’s private thoughts invade their privacy, and health questions belong with a doctor.

questions.prompt: Tarot cards were invented in ancient Egypt to preserve secret wisdom.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Tarot first appears in fifteenth-century Italy as a card game. The Egyptian theory was proposed by Court de Gébelin in 1781 and is not supported by any evidence. Divinatory use dates from the eighteenth century.

questions.prompt: How many cards are in a tarot deck, and how are they divided?
options: 52 cards in four suits
78 cards: 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana
78 cards: 56 Major Arcana and 22 Minor Arcana
22 cards only
questions.explanation: A tarot deck has 78 cards: 22 Major Arcana (0 The Fool to 21 The World) and 56 Minor Arcana in four suits of fourteen cards each.

questions.prompt: In most modern decks, which suit corresponds to water and feelings?
options: Wands
Cups
Swords
Pentacles
questions.explanation: Cups are water: feelings, love, relationships and intuition. Wands are fire, Swords air, and Pentacles earth (though a few decks swap Wands and Swords).

questions.prompt: You draw the Death card. What does it most often mean?
options: Someone is going to die
Endings, transformation and clearing the way for something new
A curse has been placed on you
You should stop reading tarot
questions.explanation: Death almost never means a physical death. It stands for endings, change and clearing. Dramatic cards show what is happening so you can respond; they are not curses.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good habits when reading for yourself? Choose all that apply.
options: Writing down the question before you start
Looking at each picture before reading its meaning
Drawing again until you get an answer you like
Recording the reading and checking it later
questions.explanation: Writing the question, looking before reading, and recording and reviewing readings all make you a better reader. Re-drawing until you like the answer teaches nothing.

questions.prompt: What does the court card the Page usually suggest?
options: Mature leadership
A learner, messenger or beginning curiosity
Rushing into action
Completion
questions.explanation: Pages are learners and messengers; Knights are action and pursuit; Queens are inward mastery; Kings are outward mastery and leadership.

questions.prompt: Reading reversed cards is required in tarot, and a reading without reversals is incomplete.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reversals are optional. Many good readers never use them. You can turn every card upright as a beginner and add reversals later if you choose.

questions.prompt: Which statement about runes is most accurate?
options: Rune divination methods, including reversed readings and the blank rune, are recorded in detail in Viking sources
The runes are an old alphabet; most modern divination methods with them, including reversed readings and the blank rune, are twentieth-century
Runes were invented in 1982
Runes come from ancient Ireland
questions.explanation: The Elder Futhark was used from about the second to the eighth century. The rune poems give old meanings, but most divination methods, reversed readings and the blank rune (1982) are modern. Ogham, not the runes, is Irish.

questions.prompt: What is the ideomotor effect, and why does it matter for pendulum work?
options: A spirit that moves pendulums
Tiny, unnoticed muscle movements, driven by expectation, that can move a pendulum; so its answers reflect what something in you inclines towards, not certain fact
A magnetic force from crystals
A rule that pendulums only work at the full moon
questions.explanation: Small unconscious movements move a pendulum. Some see this as the deeper mind speaking, others believe more is involved, but either way it is not a medical test or lie detector.

questions.prompt: While scrying you start to feel disoriented and frightened. What should you do? Choose all that apply.
options: Stop at once and put the lights on
Ground yourself firmly
Keep going until you see something clearly
Talk to your mentor about it
questions.explanation: Stop, put the lights on, ground, and talk to your mentor. Keep sessions short. If you have a history of dissociation, psychosis or seizures, check with your mentor and doctor first.

questions.prompt: A friend asks you to read on whether their partner is cheating. What is the most ethical response?
options: Read on it, since they asked
Refuse and end the conversation
Explain you don’t read on other people’s private lives, and offer to read on what would help them with their worries about trust
Tell them what you think the partner is doing
questions.explanation: Reading on someone who hasn’t consented invades their privacy and rarely helps. Turning the question back to the person asking respects everyone and gives something they can act on.

questions.prompt: A reader tells someone they have a curse that only a costly working can lift. Explain why this is a red flag and what the person should do.
questions.explanation: Claiming a curse that only paid work can remove is a classic exploitation pattern. No genuine reader or coven demands money, sex or secrets. The person should stop, not pay, and talk to someone they trust, such as their mentor or High Priestess.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): names it as a common scam or exploitation pattern using fear (1); says genuine readers and covens don’t pressure for money, sex or secrets (1); says what to do: stop, don’t pay, and talk to a trusted person such as the mentor or High Priestess (1).

questions.prompt: Describe one three-card reading you did during this stage: the question, the spread, the three cards, what you saw in each picture, and your summary. Then say what you would do differently next time.
questions.explanation: A good reading starts from an open question, uses a clear spread, looks at the pictures before the meanings, reads the cards together, and sums up in something useful. Reflecting on it is how you improve.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): an open question about themselves (1); a named spread with the three cards in their positions (1); describes what they saw in the pictures, not only keywords (1); a summary that reads the cards together and ends on something actionable (1); a thoughtful note on what to do differently (1).

quizzes.title: Spellcraft: test
quizzes.intro: Fourteen questions on intention, the structure of a spell, forms, ethics, and results. Choice questions are scored at once; your mentor scores the written answers. You need 80 per cent to pass, and you can retake it.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest, best-shaped intention?
options: I want my life to be better
I speak calmly and clearly at Thursday’s meeting
I want my manager to like me whether they want to or not
I don’t want to fail
questions.explanation: A good intention is specific, about one thing, about you, realistic and positively worded. Trying to change someone else’s feelings against their will is manipulation.
