6. Invite questions, and feelings. Some will be sad, some angry, some relieved.
7. Follow up with a short written summary, and offer each member a conversation.

## A simple final rite

Your tradition may have its own form. If not, a simple shape:

1. Gather and ground together, and open sacred space in your coven's usual way.
2. Give thanks to the powers the coven has honoured, by name, with an offering.
3. Remember: each person names a moment from the coven's life they will carry with them.
4. Release: the head says words that free each member from any bond to the coven, while blessing whatever friendships continue.
5. Bless each member in turn, perhaps with water or oil, or simply by name.
6. Put out the coven's candle together, or let it burn down safely while you share food.
7. Close as you always have, for the last time, and ground well.

## Archiving in the app

Only the coven's head can archive it (and site moderators).

1. Open the coven and tap **Manage**.
2. At the foot, under **Archive the coven**, read the note, then tap **Archive the coven**.
3. The app asks, "Archive this coven?" and explains that it leaves the directory, its chat and altars become read-only, and only the site moderators can reopen it. Tap **Archive** to confirm.

Before you archive:

- Tell everyone, and give them time to save anything of their own from the chat or Book.
- Make sure anything members need from the coven's Book has been shared with them.
- Encourage members to keep a copy of any coven altar they love: an altar's "Keep a copy" saves it among their own altars.

> **Note:** Archiving keeps the coven's material, read-only, rather than deleting it. If the coven might one day reopen, the site's moderators can do that, so write down why it was archived and who led it.

## When a coven ends badly

Sometimes a coven ends in conflict or crisis, or a head simply vanishes. If you are an elder in that situation:

- Look after people first: check in with members individually.
- Don't spread blame; say what is known, simply.
- If someone was harmed, make sure it has been reported to the site's moderators and, where needed, to the authorities.
- If the coven still holds members' material and no one can lead it, contact the Salt & Sovereignty moderators through the app.
- Help members find new homes.

## After the ending

Former members may grieve, feel lost, or feel relieved. All are normal. Some will want to keep in touch, start their own practice, or join other covens. Bless all of these. If you led the coven, consider talking with someone outside it, a friend, another head or a counsellor, about what the coven meant and what you learned.

> **Try this:** Write a short "closing well" section for your coven's rules: who decides to close, how members are told, what happens to trainees' progress, the coven's material and any shared money, and the shape of a final rite.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions have a formal rite for "closing" or "dissolving" a coven; others simply release the circle at a final gathering. Ask your head whether your tradition has one.

docs.title: Working with other covens and the wider community
docs.summary: Relations with other covens, guests, the wider Pagan community and closed traditions, and leading by the Salt & Sovereignty coven community guidelines.
docs.body:
## The coven among covens

No coven practises alone. Around it are other covens, solitary practitioners, teachers and authors, festivals and moots, local Pagan and interfaith groups, and online communities like Salt & Sovereignty. A head represents the coven to all of these. Good relations bring friendship, shared learning, safety and support; bad ones bring rivalry and harm.

## Working with other covens

Other covens may share your tradition or differ from it entirely. Either way, some principles help:

1. **Respect their ways.** Their rites and rules are theirs. Don't criticise them to your members, and don't teach their material as your own.
2. **Don't poach.** If a member of another coven wants to join yours, that's their right; but don't recruit from other covens, and if someone is leaving in conflict, encourage them to part well.
3. **Share what's shareable.** Joint public festivals, open rites, workshops and study days. Many regions hold an open celebration at the major festivals that several covens help lead.
4. **Talk head to head.** A call or coffee once a season with heads of nearby covens builds trust. They can be your outside friend when you need one.
5. **Share concerns about safety, carefully.** If someone has harmed members, other covens may need to know. Share facts, not rumours, and in serious cases report through the proper channels rather than spreading word informally.
6. **Honour visits.** When members of another coven visit a rite, explain your ways, invite them to take part only as they wish, and thank them.

## Guests at your rites

When you welcome guests from outside the coven:

- Tell them, before they arrive, what will happen and what is asked of them.
- Never ask a guest to take an oath, give money or do anything they don't freely choose.
- Keep oath-bound material out of open rites.
- Remember that in the app, gatherings and the chat are for members. An open public rite happens in person or elsewhere; guests don't need to join the coven to come.

## The wider Pagan and spiritual community

Beyond covens, you may connect with:

- **Local moots**: informal meetings, often monthly in a café or pub, where Pagans of every kind meet socially.
- **Festivals and conferences.**
- **Interfaith groups**, where Pagan voices are increasingly welcome.
- **Public education**: talks at libraries or schools (be prepared, and stay within what you know).
- **Living and closed traditions**: some practices belong to particular peoples and are not open to outsiders. The app's Living Library has a guide to closed and living traditions. Respect it, and teach your members to.

When you speak publicly, be honest and humble. You speak for your coven, not for all Pagans, and never for a closed tradition you weren't given.

## The Salt & Sovereignty community

Every coven in the app is part of the Salt & Sovereignty community and agrees to its coven community guidelines. As a head, you lead your coven by them. In summary:

- **Covens are for adults.** Everyone must be 18 or older. If you think someone in a coven is under 18, report them.
- **Joining and invitations.** Each coven chooses how people join. Everyone confirms they are 18 or older and signs the agreements before joining, and may decline any invitation. Only invite people you believe will keep the guidelines, and never pressure anyone to accept.
- **Freedom comes first.** Anyone may leave any coven at any time without explaining why. No one may pressure anyone for money, gifts, secrets, private photographs, sexual contact, an address or obedience. A coven may ask members to help with shared costs, but never as a condition of belonging or of rising. No one may tell a member to cut off family or friends, stop medical or mental-health care, or harm themselves. Initiation and advancement must never involve humiliation, danger, nudity or anything not freely consented to.
- **Respect.** No harassment, bullying, threats or curses aimed at members; no hate or discrimination; no sexual content or advances in covens; respect closed and living traditions; no spam, scams or selling unless the coven's rules allow it.
- **Privacy.** What members share in a coven stays in it; no screenshots or reposting without permission; no sharing anyone's real name, address or details. The site's moderators can read every coven to keep covens safe.
- **Leading a coven.** Founders and those they give powers to are trusted with others' safety: write your documents honestly, apply them fairly, and don't use your position to pressure anyone. Coven rules can add to the guidelines but can't override them.
- **Reporting and blocking.** Every message, member, application and coven has a Report button. Reports go to the site's moderators, never to the coven's leaders, and the person reported isn't told who reported them.
- **Danger.** Covens are not a crisis service. If anyone is in immediate danger, contact your local emergency number. The Sanctuary lists support lines.

You can read the full guidelines from your coven profile in the app, where you agreed to them.

## Being a good neighbour in the app

- **Keep the directory honest.** Make the coven's description, tradition and "When you gather" accurate. If you aren't taking members, set "Not taking members".
- **Be careful with links.** Invite links let people join without applying. Share them privately, set a short life and few uses, and revoke them when done.
- **Cooperate with moderators.** If the site's moderators contact you about your coven, answer honestly and promptly. They exist to keep everyone safe, including you.
- **Model the guidelines.** Your members will treat the wider community as they see you treat it.

> **Try this:** Find out what other covens, moots or Pagan groups exist near you or in your tradition online. Write down two you might contact, and what you would offer or ask. Then re-read the coven community guidelines and note one thing in your coven's rules that should mention them.

> **Your coven:** Some traditions have umbrella bodies, councils or networks of covens, with their own codes of conduct; some prefer independence. Ask your head which your coven belongs to, if any, and what it expects of a head.

docs.title: Sovereignty: the goddess, the ruler’s truth and leading a coven
docs.summary: The sovereignty goddess in the Irish and Welsh tales (Ériu and her sisters, Medb, the hag at the well who becomes Sovereignty, the feast of kingship) and the ruler’s truth; what scholars do and don’t agree on; and what these old ideas, handled carefully, can teach the head of a modern, voluntary coven.
docs.body:
## The land as a woman

One of the most striking ideas in early Irish literature is that the **sovereignty** of a kingdom, its right rule and its fruitful land, is pictured as a woman, often a goddess, who chooses and marries the rightful king. When she is wed to a true king, the land flourishes; when the king is false, she leaves him, or the land withers.

Scholars call her the **sovereignty goddess**. Here are some of the tales in which she appears.

- **Ériu, Banba and Fódla.** In the Lebor Gabála, when the sons of Míl come to Ireland, three goddesses meet them, each asking that the island be named after her. Ériu is promised the chief name: Éire, Ireland, comes from her.
- **The hag at the well.** In a medieval tale, Echtra mac nEchach Muigmedóin, the five sons of a king go hunting and grow thirsty. They find a well guarded by a hideous old woman, who will give water only for a kiss. Four refuse. Niall, the youngest, kisses her and lies with her, and she becomes the most beautiful woman in the world. She tells him her name is **Flaithius**, Sovereignty, and that he and his descendants will rule. Niall of the Nine Hostages becomes the ancestor of the great Uí Néill kings.
- **Medb.** Medb of Connacht, queen of the Táin, is said to have had many husbands, and a later text says that no king could rule in Tara unless Medb had first slept with him. Many scholars see her as a sovereignty figure turned, in the tales, into a formidable human queen.
- **The feast of kingship.** Early Irish sources speak of the **banais ríghi**, the wedding feast of kingship, and of a king's inauguration as a marriage to the land; at Tara, the feast was called Feis Temro. What happened at such inaugurations is not well known.
- **Wales.** Some scholars read Rhiannon, who chooses Pwyll in the First Branch and is linked with horses, as a sovereignty figure. This is an interpretation, not a statement of the text.

## The ruler's truth

Alongside the goddess runs the idea of **fír flathemon**, the ruler's truth, set out in the **Audacht Morainn**, a text of advice to a king from perhaps about 700. Through the ruler's truth, it says, the land is fruitful, the weather mild, the rivers full of fish, the cattle give milk, and plagues and enemies are kept away. A false judgement brings blight. The king's justice and the land's health are one.

## What we don't know

These are literary and learned texts, written by Christians, often with political purposes: the tale of Niall and the hag, for example, gives a royal dynasty a divine right to rule. Scholars agree the sovereignty theme is real and important; they disagree on how far it reflects pagan religion, and on whether there was ever a real rite of marriage to a goddess. Be careful not to claim more.

## What this can teach a coven's head

You are not a king, and a coven is not a kingdom. A modern coven is small, voluntary and equal in dignity; its members can leave at any time; its head leads by consent. Any idea of sovereignty that gives the head power over members' lives, bodies or consciences must be rejected outright. But read carefully, the old ideas say something true about leadership:

1. **Leadership is a relationship, not a possession.** In the tales, sovereignty is given, and can be withdrawn. A coven's head leads because the coven accepts them, and should hold that lightly.
2. **The right leader serves the land and the people.** The test of a king was whether the land flourished. The test of a coven's head is whether the coven and its members flourish: grow in practice, feel safe, learn, care for one another.
3. **Truth and justice are the foundation.** The ruler's truth asks for honesty, fair judgement, keeping one's word, and not favouring friends. Without it, the coven withers.
4. **The hag and the beauty.** Niall alone accepts the hard, unlovely part of sovereignty, and finds its beauty. Leading a coven includes much that is unglamorous: difficult conversations, admin, conflict, care. Accepting it is part of the work.
5. **Sovereignty can leave.** In the tales, a false king loses his kingship. A coven's head who fails in truth, generosity or care should expect to lose the coven's trust, and should step aside rather than cling on.

## The land itself

Many Celtic coven heads also take the sovereignty theme as a reminder that the coven is in relationship with the **land** where it meets: its spirits, its waters and its people. Leading the coven includes caring for that relationship.

## Rejecting the misuses

Be alert to misuses of sovereignty language: a leader claiming to be "wedded to the goddess" and so beyond question; a "sacred marriage" used to pressure anyone into sex; a claim that the coven's head embodies the land and must be obeyed. None of these has any place in this coven. The coven's agreements, and the core lessons on authority and accountability, set the limits.

> **Your coven:** Talk with the coven's current head about how leadership is given, held and handed on in this coven, and how the coven can withdraw it if needed.

> **Try this:** Read the tale of Niall and the hag at the well in translation. In your book, write what it suggests about the cost and the gift of leadership, and one misuse of the idea you would guard against.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the sovereignty goddess in the tales (Ériu, the hag at the well, Medb), the feast of kingship, and the ruler's truth in the Audacht Morainn.
- **Modern:** applying these ideas, carefully and without their hierarchy, to leading a voluntary coven.

docs.title: Druid, poet and priestess: priesthood old and new
docs.summary: The learned orders of the past as the sources show them (druids, filid and brehons, Welsh poets) and what they did; modern Celtic clergy (ADF’s ordained clergy, OBOD’s grades, reconstructionist roles, coven heads); the honest use of titles; and what a Celtic High Priestess or High Priest actually does.
docs.body:
## The learned of the past

The pagan Celtic peoples had learned specialists who served their communities. What we know of them comes from outsiders and from Christian-era texts, so we must be careful, but the outline is this:

- **Druids:** in Gaul and Britain, according to Caesar and others, priests, judges, teachers and philosophers; in early Ireland, seers, advisers to kings and makers of magic. They faded in Ireland by the seventh century.
- **Bards, seers and poets:** Greek writers speak of bards (singers of praise) and vates (seers). In Ireland the **filid**, poets, became the great learned class after the druids: keepers of genealogy, place-lore and tales, composers of praise, feared for their satire, trained for many years and ranked in grades up to the ollam. In Wales the **beirdd** held a similar place.
- **Brehons,** the jurists of early Irish law, who kept and interpreted the law.

These roles were for the few, often inherited, and closely tied to kings and nobles. We know little of any priesthood that served ordinary households; the household's religion, then as in folk custom later, was probably kept largely by the household itself.

## Modern Celtic clergy

Modern Celtic paganism has many kinds of religious leader:

- **ADF** trains and ordains **clergy** through a long study programme, with a priesthood that serves its groves and the public.
- **OBOD** has three grades, Bard, Ovate and Druid. Its Druid grade is a path of study and practice, not quite a priesthood in the church sense, though many OBOD Druids lead rites for others.
- **Reconstructionist** communities often avoid formal priesthood, keeping religion at the household's hearth, while recognising people who serve as priests, poets or seers for a group because of their learning and practice.
- **Celtic covens** usually have a head, often called High Priestess or High Priest (a title from Wicca), sometimes with other titles, and elders.

## Titles and honesty

Titles in this tradition need care. "Druid" in particular carries the weight of the ancient learned class, and no one alive inherits it. If you call yourself a Druid, mean the modern movement, and say so if asked. If your coven uses "High Priestess" or "High Priest", be clear that it means the coven's leader, not the holder of an ancient office. Avoid titles like "Arch-druid of the Celts", "keeper of the ancient Gaelic mysteries" or "hereditary priestess", which claim far more than anyone can honestly hold.

Many Celtic coven heads prefer plain words: the coven's head, its keeper, its host, its fire-keeper. Whatever your coven's titles, hold them lightly.

## What a Celtic coven's head does

The core lessons cover the general work of leading a coven. In a Celtic coven, the head's particular work includes:

1. **Keeping the year:** making sure the four fire festivals, and the coven's other rites, are kept, and kept well.
2. **Keeping the sources:** making sure the coven teaches honestly, names its sources and marks the modern, and keeps learning.
3. **Keeping the hearth:** the coven's shared devotion to its gods, its ancestors and its land, including its shrine, its offerings and its relationships with places.
4. **Hospitality:** welcoming newcomers, guests and visitors, and caring for members.
5. **Fair judgement:** settling disputes, deciding with others, holding the coven to its agreements.
6. **Teaching and raising up others:** training elders and future leaders through these programs.
7. **Relations with others:** Druid groves, other covens, local communities, and the living Gaelic and Brythonic cultures.
8. **Keeping the book:** the coven's record of its rites, its learning and its people.

## Serving, not ruling

The filid had great honour, and they also had duties: their praise had to be true, their learning sound, their judgements fair. A satirist who satirised unjustly was himself shamed. The same applies to the head of a coven: honour comes from service, and is lost by its abuse. You are accountable to the coven, and through it to the gods, the ancestors and the land.

## Your own practice

Leading a coven can crowd out your own devotion. Keep your hearth. Keep your own relationship with your gods. Keep studying. A coven's head who has stopped practising leads from memory, and it shows.

## Working with other groups

A Celtic coven rarely stands alone. Nearby there may be a Druid grove, a reconstructionist hearth, a Wiccan coven keeping the Gaelic festivals in its own way, a language class, a folk music session, a heritage society. A coven's head is often the one who builds those relationships. Some guidance:

- **Be generous.** Visit others' open rites as a guest, and invite them to yours.
- **Respect differences.** A grove that casts a circle, or a hearth that never would, is not doing it wrong; it is doing it differently.
- **Don't poach.** If someone from another group wants to join yours, talk openly, and part well with the group they are leaving.
- **Share learning.** Recommend good books, correct myths kindly, and learn from others in turn.
- **Speak carefully in public.** When the coven is asked about Celtic paganism by the press or a school, speak honestly, mark the modern, and never speak for the Irish, Scots or Welsh.

## When you are wrong

Every coven head makes mistakes: a poor judgement, an unkind word, a rite that went badly. The filid were held to their own standard of truth. Hold yourself to it. Admit the mistake, make amends, and let the coven see you do it. It will trust you more, not less.

> **Your coven:** Talk with the coven's current head about the titles this coven uses, what they mean, and what you would want to keep or change.

> **Try this:** Write a short statement, for the coven's book, of what the coven's head does and does not do in this coven, using the list above as a start.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** the druids, filid, brehons and Welsh poets, as far as the sources show them.
- **Modern:** every Celtic clergy, grade and coven title in use today.

docs.title: Leading the Celtic year and its rites of passage
docs.summary: Planning a coven’s whole year around the four fire festivals and its devotions; rites of passage in a Celtic coven (welcoming a child, handfasting, death, mourning and remembering) with what the sources and folk customs show, what is modern, and respect for living Irish, Scottish and Welsh custom; and keeping the coven’s book.
docs.body:
## Planning the year

A coven's head plans the year, usually at Samhain, the start of the Gaelic year, or soon after. A good plan includes:

- **the four fire festivals,** with who will lead each, and where;
- **regular devotions:** monthly, at the full moon or another day;
- **study:** a story or source the coven will read together, perhaps one each season;
- **teaching:** who is in which program, and who mentors them;
- **care for the land:** a regular act of service to a place the coven loves;
- **social time:** meals, walks, festivals in the wider community;
- **rest:** months with less, especially in the dark of winter or the busy summer.

Put it in the app's calendar and the coven's book, and share it early. The year-ahead spread can be a good companion for the coven's planning.

## Rites of passage

Members will ask the coven to mark the great moments of life: a birth, a marriage or partnership, a death. These are among the most important things a coven does, and they need special care, because they often involve families and friends who are not pagan, and because many of the customs drawn on are part of living Irish, Scottish and Welsh culture.

## Welcoming a child

We know almost nothing of pagan Celtic birth rites. Folk custom in Ireland and Scotland recorded many protections for mother and child: iron, rowan, salt and red thread by the cradle, and fear of the child being taken by the good folk before baptism. Carmina Gadelica records a "birth baptism", in which the midwife sprinkled water on the newborn with a blessing, before the Christian baptism.

A modern Celtic welcoming might include saining the child with water, naming them before the hearth, a blessing in threes from each person present, the gift of a protective token (rowan and red thread, kept safely away from the baby's mouth), and an offering to the ancestors. It is **modern**. Always shape it with the parents, and include non-pagan family kindly.

## Handfasting

Many Celtic pagan couples marry or bless their partnership with a **handfasting**. The word is old: in Scotland and northern England it meant a betrothal or a marriage by joining hands and making promises, sometimes without a priest. The popular idea that the ancient Celts had "trial marriages" of a year and a day, ending with handfasting, owes much to later writers; the Teltown marriages of folk memory are a nineteenth-century tradition. The binding of hands with cords is a modern pagan rite, now widely used.

A Celtic handfasting might include saining, kindling, honouring the powers, the couple's own vows, the binding of hands, an offering together, and a feast in the spirit of hospitality. Check the law where you are: in many places a handfasting is not a legal marriage unless performed by a legally recognised celebrant; in Scotland, some pagan organisations can solemnise legal marriages. Make sure couples know what is and is not legal.

## Death, mourning and remembering

Here more than anywhere, living custom matters. The Irish and Scottish **wake**, watching with the dead at home with company, food and stories, is still alive in many places, as are funeral Masses, month's minds and anniversary Masses, and cemetery Sundays. The **keen**, the women's lament, was sung at wakes into the twentieth century and is now very rare.

When a member dies, the coven's place is usually beside the family, not in charge. Many members' families will hold a Christian or secular funeral. The coven can:

- offer its own rite of remembrance, separately, with the family's blessing;
- keep the member's name at the coven's Samhain and on their anniversary;
- support the bereaved, practically and in care;
- keep the member in the coven's book.

If a member has asked for a pagan funeral, and the family agrees, a Celtic rite might include saining, kindling, honouring the ancestors, speaking the person's names and deeds as in a praise, and an offering for their journey. Do not attempt a keen unless you have learned the tradition properly; better to read a poem or sing a lament of your own making.

> **Safety:** Grief can bring people to crisis. Know where to send someone for bereavement support, and watch over members after a death in the coven.

## Respect for living custom

When you draw on Irish, Scottish or Welsh rites of passage, remember that families still keep them, with their own faith. Learn from them; do not stage them as pagan survivals; and include non-pagan relatives with warmth, so that a rite of passage brings people together.

## The coven's book

The coven's book should keep a record of its year: the festivals and how they were kept, the sources read, the rites of passage, members welcomed, initiated and remembered. Over time it becomes the coven's own tradition, and the best thing you can hand to those who come after.

> **Your coven:** Ask the coven's current head how the coven has marked births, partnerships and deaths, and what it has learned.

> **Try this:** Draft the coven's plan for the next Celtic year, from Samhain to Samhain, with festivals, devotions, study, service and rest. Show it to the coven's head.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** handfasting as a Scottish and northern English word for betrothal or marriage, folk protections for mother and child, the wake and the keen.
- **Modern:** pagan welcomings, handfastings with cords, and Celtic pagan funerals.

docs.title: Stewardship: succession, daughter covens and the living cultures
docs.summary: Caring for the coven beyond your own time: training successors, handing on leadership in the spirit of the tradition, founding daughter covens, keeping the coven’s book and credit honest, money, and the coven’s long relationship with the living Gaelic and Brythonic languages, cultures and communities.
docs.body:
## Beyond your own time

A coven's head is a steward, not an owner. The coven existed before you led it, or will outlive you if you founded it. Stewardship is caring for it so that it can thrive after you: its people, its practice, its book and its relationships.

## Fosterage and succession

Early Irish society valued **fosterage**: children raised and taught by another family, forming bonds as strong as blood. A teacher and student were bound in a similar way. That is a good picture of how a coven raises its future leaders: not by appointing a successor at the last minute, but by fostering several people over years, through the elder and high priest or priestess programs, teaching them, trusting them with more, and letting them lead.

Some practical steps:

- **Share the work** now: let elders lead festivals, teach, mentor and care for members.
- **Write it down:** the coven's rites, agreements, calendar, contacts and how things are done, in the coven's book.
- **Talk openly** about succession before it is urgent: how a new head will be chosen, and what happens if you are suddenly unable to lead.
- **Step back gracefully.** When it is time, hand over fully, and support your successor without second-guessing them.

Remember the lesson of sovereignty: leadership is given, and a good leader knows when to give it back.

## Daughter covens

When a coven grows too large, or members move away, a new coven may form from it: a daughter coven. The app's daughter covens page records these relationships. In a Celtic coven, a daughter coven might:

- keep the same core rite and festivals, adapted to its own land and members;
- carry a share of the parent coven's book, with credit;
- honour the parent coven's founders as ancestors of spirit;
- be fully independent in its decisions.

Founding one well takes time: an elder trained to lead, members who want to go, a blessing from the parent coven, and honesty about what is shared and what is new. This is a **modern** custom; it does not make either coven part of an ancient line.

## Credit and honesty

Over years, a coven's book gathers rites, prayers, praises, triads and teachings, written by members or adapted from published sources. Keep credit honest: name who wrote what, and where adaptations come from. Do not present members' work, or published authors' work, as "traditional" or "ancient". Respect copyright, especially of modern translators and authors. When you share material with daughter covens or others, share the credit too.

## Money

Running a coven costs something: candles, food, sometimes a room. Share costs fairly and openly. Never charge for initiation or for rank, and never make money a condition of belonging. If the coven runs paid public events or courses, keep accounts open to members, and avoid selling "ancient Celtic" secrets of any kind.

## Closing a coven

Sometimes a coven comes to an end: its head moves, members drift, a season of life closes. Ending well is part of stewardship. Tell members honestly and in good time; help those in programs find another teacher or a solitary path; decide together what happens to the coven's book, its shrine objects and its shared offerings; and hold a last rite to thank the gods, the ancestors and the land, and to release the coven's promises. A coven that ends with gratitude leaves good memories and, often, the seeds of new groups.

## The coven and the living cultures

Over the long term, a Celtic coven has a relationship with the living Gaelic and Brythonic cultures, whether it means to or not. A good steward makes that relationship one of respect and giving back:

- **Language.** Encourage members to learn a Celtic language, and use it in the coven's rites with care. Support language classes, schools and media.
- **Credit the communities.** When you teach a custom, say where it was recorded and who keeps it now.
- **Support heritage.** Give to the care of wells, monuments and archives; join local heritage groups; buy books by scholars and writers from the cultures.
- **Visit well.** When the coven visits Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Man, Cornwall or Brittany, go as respectful guests: spend locally, listen, learn, and never hold rites where they would offend.
- **Listen.** Irish, Scottish, Welsh, Manx, Cornish and Breton people, including pagans among them, sometimes have strong views on how outsiders use their heritage. Listen, and change where you should.
- **Stand with them.** Where language and heritage communities ask for support, give it.

The Sanctuary's guide to closed and living traditions is a good touchstone. Return to it, and teach it.

## The coven's long health

Signs of a healthy Celtic coven over years: members who keep their hearths and festivals faithfully; honest teaching; newcomers welcomed and trained; elders who lead; disputes settled fairly; good relations with its land and neighbours; a book that grows; and leaders who can step aside without the coven falling apart. Signs of trouble: one person who cannot be questioned, secrets that protect someone, teaching that has drifted into fantasy, members leaving hurt. Review the coven's health each year, perhaps at Samhain, with the elders.

> **Your coven:** Talk with the coven's current head about succession, daughter covens, and how the coven gives back to the cultures it draws on.

> **Try this:** Write a stewardship plan for the coven: how leaders are raised, how succession will work, what the book holds, how credit is kept, and one way the coven will give back to a living Celtic culture in the coming year.

## What's old and what's modern

- **Old:** fosterage and the bonds of teaching, and the value of honour and generosity.
- **Modern:** covens, daughter covens, succession plans, and the coven's relationship with living Celtic cultures.

quizzes.title: Leading a coven
quizzes.intro: Fifteen questions on authority, the coven’s documents, running the coven in the app, delegating, crises and sustainability. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a coven head’s authority?
options: A spiritual rank that, once given by initiation, can never be questioned
Trust the members give for particular jobs, which must leave them genuinely free to disagree or leave
The right to guide members in every area of their lives
Whatever the gods tell the head, which members must accept
questions.explanation: Whatever a tradition says about lineage or calling, a head only leads people who are free to leave. Authority is given for particular jobs (safety, purpose, decisions, recognition, speaking for the coven) and never extends to members’ private lives.

questions.prompt: Which are warning signs of a guru dynamic? Choose all that apply.
options: Disagreement with the head is called a spiritual failing
The head keeps rules for themselves that differ from everyone else’s
The head explains why a decision was made
Members ask the head’s permission for ordinary life decisions
Those who leave are spoken of as traitors
questions.explanation: Calling disagreement a failing, special rules for the leader, members deferring on ordinary life and treating leaving as betrayal are all classic signs. Explaining decisions is the opposite: it is a mark of accountability.

questions.prompt: A report a member makes with the app’s Report button goes to the coven’s head first, so the head can deal with it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reports go to the Salt & Sovereignty moderators, never to the coven’s leaders, and the person reported isn’t told who reported them. That independence is part of what keeps every coven, and its head, accountable.

questions.prompt: You correct a typo in the coven’s member agreement and save it. What happens?
options: Nothing; only the head sees the change
It becomes a new version, and every member must sign it again before they can speak in the chat or tend the altars
Everyone is removed from the coven until they sign
The agreement becomes members-only
questions.explanation: Changing the title or words of a page members sign creates a new version that everyone must sign again before taking part. Gather changes together, tell the coven first, and don’t save a signed page for trivial edits.

questions.prompt: Why must a page that members sign be readable by everyone?
options: So it shows in search engines
Because seekers sign the agreements before they join
Because the site’s moderators can’t read members-only pages
It doesn’t have to be; that is only a suggestion
questions.explanation: Agreements are signed before joining, so a seeker must be able to read them. The app won’t save an agreement set to “Members only”.

questions.prompt: You want members to be able to ask to become Initiates. Which do you set on the Initiate position? Choose all that apply.
options: Tick “Members can apply to rise to it”
Write what it asks of someone, which applicants will see
Tick “New members begin here”
Give it the power “Leads the coven”
questions.explanation: An open position has “Members can apply to rise to it” ticked, and its requirements (“What it asks of someone”) are shown to members applying under My standing and to reviewers. New members don’t begin there, and it shouldn’t carry the power to lead the coven.

questions.prompt: An elder with the “Reviews applications” power but no other powers wants to raise a member to the Warden position, which carries “Moderates the gathering”. What happens?
options: They can, as long as Warden is below their own position
They can’t: reviewers raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers
They can, but only during a ritual
They can, if the member agrees
questions.explanation: Reviewers can raise members only to positions below their own that carry no powers. Only those who lead the coven give positions with powers, which keeps powers in the hands of those trusted with them.

questions.prompt: You want everyone who becomes a Dedicant to go through the coven’s initiate training, now and in future. What is the simplest way?
options: Assign the program to each Dedicant by name, and remember to do it for new ones
Assign the program to the Dedicant position
Tick “Any member may begin it themselves”
Post a message in the chat
questions.explanation: Assigning a program to a position enrols everyone in it now and anyone who takes it later. Self-enrolment lets anyone begin it, which isn’t the same thing.

questions.prompt: The coven has a rule that elders hear about every Deipnon rite, but for this month’s Deipnon you want the whole coven told. Where do you change it?
options: Delete the Deipnon rule in Gathering notifications
In that rite’s own details, choose who hears for this one
Ask every member to turn on Reminders
You can’t; the rule always wins
questions.explanation: A gathering’s own choice, in its planner, comes first; then the closest rule. Changing one rite leaves the coven’s rule in place for next time.

questions.prompt: Which are good uses of the members’ record? Choose all that apply.
options: Noticing that someone has been quiet for months and sending them a kind message
Reading what members wrote in their private conversations
Correcting attendance when someone was at a rite in person
Writing brief, fair leaders’ notes that you’d be comfortable for the person to read one day
Publicly listing the least active members in the chat
questions.explanation: The record is a pastoral tool: flags mean “check in kindly”. Leaders can correct attendance and keep brief notes. The record never shows private conversations or what anyone wrote, and shaming people publicly is never right.

questions.prompt: When you delegate leading the Imbolc rite to an elder, what should you also do?
options: Write every word for them so it is done right
Give them the authority to do it, such as a position that lets them plan rites and put them on the calendar
Check their work every day
Keep the delegation secret from the coven
questions.explanation: Responsibility without authority is a trap. Describe the outcome, give the powers the task needs, agree limits and check-ins, then stand back.

questions.prompt: A member tells you she has been thinking about ending her life. What comes first?
options: Offer a healing ritual at the next full moon
Tell the elders so they can pray for her
Ask directly about her safety now, stay with her, and connect her with a crisis line or emergency services if she is in danger
Suggest she takes a break from the coven
questions.explanation: Safety comes first. Ask plainly, listen, and if she is in danger contact emergency services or a crisis line together. Ritual and the coven’s care can support her alongside professional help, never instead of it.

questions.prompt: A member tells you an elder has been pressuring them for money and private photographs. Describe, in order, what you would do.
questions.explanation: This is a safeguarding concern. Take it seriously, don’t promise secrecy, act on any immediate danger, report through the app (the reason “Pressure for money, secrets, photos or obedience”), contact authorities where needed, protect the coven (pausing or removing the elder, and taking away their powers) without public accusation, and keep a factual record.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): takes it seriously and listens without promising secrecy; acts on immediate danger (emergency services) if relevant; reports it through the app’s Report button to the site’s moderators; protects members while it is resolved (e.g. changes the elder’s position to remove powers, pauses or removes them) without a public accusation; keeps a factual, dated record; mentions proper authorities where the law or situation requires. 2: most of these, but misses reporting or protecting members. 1: some sensible steps but confronts the elder publicly or investigates alone. 0: dismisses it or keeps it secret.

questions.prompt: Name three things a head should keep (or share only with a co-leader) rather than delegate, and three things that are good to delegate. Say briefly why for one of each.
questions.explanation: Heads keep final responsibility for safety, decisions to remove or ban (except emergencies), changes to the creed, rules and agreements, recognitions their tradition reserves, and handing on the coven. Routine work, teaching within someone’s competence, leading rites by turns and projects with a clear end are good to delegate.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): three sound “keep” items (e.g. safety and safeguarding, removing or banning, changing documents, initiations reserved to the head, handing on) and three sound “delegate” items (e.g. setting up, chat moderation, mentoring, leading some rites, projects), with a sensible reason for one of each. 2: mostly right but no reasons, or one item misplaced. 1: only one list done well. 0: misunderstands delegation.

questions.prompt: Write a short sustainability plan for yourself as head (or future head): your coven’s rhythm, your message hours, who shares leadership, your own practice, your support outside the coven, and what you would do if you noticed signs of burnout.
questions.explanation: A sustainable head sets a realistic rhythm, has boundaries on time, shares leadership, keeps their own practice, has support outside the coven, and plans in advance how to step back when needed, including professional help if burnout becomes depression.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): a realistic gathering rhythm; clear message hours (and what members do in an emergency); named sharing of leadership (co-leader, rota, positions with powers); a personal practice and rites they attend without leading; support outside the coven; concrete steps on noticing burnout (step back, hand over for a season, see a doctor if it becomes depression). 3–4: most present but general. 1–2: vague or missing several. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: Stewardship: the coven over time
quizzes.intro: Fourteen questions on succession, hiving, training trainers, the coven’s health and lineage, closing a coven and the wider community. Choice questions are scored at once; your written answers are scored by your mentor or the coven’s head. You need 80% to pass, and you can take it again.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head taps “Hand on leadership” for a member and confirms?
options: The member becomes the coven’s head, with every power, and the former head stays a member in their current position
The former head is removed from the coven
Both become heads with equal powers
The coven is archived and a new one is made
questions.explanation: The new leader becomes the coven’s founder, with every power over it. The former head stays a member in the position they held, which may still carry powers, so agree with the new head what position they should now hold.

questions.prompt: Which belong to a good handover? Choose all that apply.
options: Telling the coven before the change, and why
A handover file in the Book: vision, who can do what, trainees and mentors, the coming calendar
The former head quietly keeping the power to overrule the new head
Checking the coven’s settings together after the change
Handing on by surprise, so there is no fuss
questions.explanation: A good handover is open and prepared: the coven is told first, the successor gets what they need to know, and the settings chosen for the old head’s way of leading are reviewed. The former head steps back rather than keeping a shadow veto.

questions.prompt: You want an elder to share leadership with you for a year before you hand on. How do you do this in the app?
options: Give them your password
Give them a position that carries “Leads the coven”, while you remain the head
Hand on leadership and ask them to hand it back if it doesn’t work
There is no way to share leadership in the app
questions.explanation: Positions carry powers. A position with “Leads the coven” lets its holders edit pages, positions and details and act on members below them, while the few head-only actions stay with you. Never share an account.

questions.prompt: A head who wants to leave the coven they lead to found a daughter coven should hand on leadership first.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The head can’t leave a coven they lead. Hand on leadership to a successor first, then step back or leave, and found the daughter coven.

questions.prompt: Which are good practice when hiving off a daughter coven? Choose all that apply.
options: Talking with the head privately before telling anyone else
Letting members choose freely whether to go or stay
Taking oath-bound material without asking, since you were taught it
Agreeing what is carried, and the relationship between the covens
Recording the daughter coven’s origin in its description and Book
questions.explanation: A hiving is done with blessing: the head is told first, members choose freely, what is carried and how the covens relate is agreed, and the lineage is recorded (the app has no built-in link, so you record it yourself). Oath-bound material goes only with the head’s blessing.

questions.prompt: Which is the more honest way to describe your coven’s lineage?
options: “Our line goes back unbroken to the witches of the Stone Age.”
“Our coven was founded in 2019 by a priestess trained in a coven founded in the 1980s, drawing on twentieth-century Wicca.”
“We are the only true coven in our tradition.”
“Our history is secret, so we cannot be questioned.”
questions.explanation: Historians have found no good evidence for unbroken ancient witch cults; modern Paganism is largely a twentieth-century revival. An honest lineage of decades is something to be proud of, and it can be checked.

questions.prompt: A new mentor gives every trainee full marks on written answers because they don’t want to discourage anyone. What should the head do?
options: Nothing; kindness matters most
Remove them as a mentor at once
Look at their scoring together against the rubric, and teach specific, kind, useful feedback
Score all the tests themselves from now on
questions.explanation: Training trainers includes supervision: reading the scores they give, checking them against the rubric, and teaching feedback that says what was done well, what is missing and what to do next. Fairness is a kindness to every trainee.

questions.prompt: How many mentees should one mentor usually have at most?
options: One
About three
About ten
As many as they like
questions.explanation: Mentoring takes real time and energy. Around three mentees each keeps check-ins regular and protects mentors from burnout.

questions.prompt: What happens when the head archives a coven in the app? Choose all that apply.
options: It leaves the directory
Its chat and altars become read-only
Everything in it is deleted for good
Only the site moderators can reopen it
questions.explanation: Archiving takes the coven out of the directory and makes its chat and altars read-only; it doesn’t delete them. Only the site moderators can reopen it, so archive only after a considered decision.

questions.prompt: Before deciding to close a coven, what should a head consider first?
options: Archiving it the same day, to avoid a long goodbye
Alternatives such as a season’s rest, a smaller rhythm, handing on to an elder, or merging with another coven
Keeping the decision secret from the members
Deleting the coven’s Book so no one argues over it
questions.explanation: Closing should be a considered choice. Rest, a smaller rhythm, a successor or a merger may keep what is good alive. If it does close, tell members early, help them find new homes, and hold a final rite.

questions.prompt: Under the Salt & Sovereignty coven community guidelines, which of these are never allowed? Choose all that apply.
options: Making a payment a condition of rising to a higher position
Asking members to help with shared costs, if it is never a condition of belonging or rising
Telling a member to stop seeing their therapist
Initiation involving nudity a member hasn’t freely consented to
A coven rule that overrides the guidelines
questions.explanation: Covens may ask for help with shared costs, but never as a condition of belonging or rising. No one may tell a member to stop medical or mental-health care; initiation must never involve anything not freely consented to; and coven rules can add to the guidelines but can’t override them.

questions.prompt: A member of a nearby coven asks to join yours after a falling-out with their head. What is the best response?
options: Welcome them and ask for every detail of the falling-out
Refuse, since they belong to another coven
Welcome their application on its merits, encourage them to part from the other coven well, and don’t speak ill of it
Tell the other coven’s head everything they said
questions.explanation: Anyone may leave a coven and apply to another. A good neighbour doesn’t poach or gossip, encourages a kind parting, and judges the application on its merits.

questions.prompt: Describe, step by step, how you would found a daughter coven in the app and set it up in its first month.
questions.explanation: Found it from Find a coven → Found a coven (name, web address that can’t change, description including its origin, joining, directory, your title, agreeing to the guidelines). Then write its documents, set its practice calendar and positions, invite its members, begin programs and mentors, and carry over agreed material.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): founding steps (Found a coven, name and permanent web address, honest description naming the mother coven, joining and directory choice, leader title, agreeing to the guidelines); then Manage (creed, rules, requirements, agreement), practice calendar, positions and powers, inviting members by invitation or short-lived link, programs and mentors, and carrying over only material the mother coven agreed. 2: founding plus some setup. 1: only founding. 0: not attempted.

questions.prompt: Write a succession plan for your coven: who would step in if the head were suddenly unable to lead; how a successor would be chosen and prepared; how the handover would happen, including in the app; and what the former head would do afterwards.
questions.explanation: A good succession plan names an emergency deputy, chooses a successor for character with the elders’ support and the person’s consent, prepares them through shared leadership, tells the coven before the change, uses Hand on leadership from Members, sorts out the former head’s position and settings, and has the former head truly step back.
questions.rubric: Full marks (5): names an emergency deputy and what they may do (including contacting the site moderators if the head can’t hand on); chooses for character with elders consulted and the successor asked; prepares through shared leadership (a position with “Leads the coven”); tells the coven first; marks it with a rite or meeting; Members → tap the successor → Hand on leadership; agrees the former head’s new position and reviews head-only settings; former head steps back and redirects complaints. 3–4: most of this. 1–2: general ideas only. 0: not attempted.

quizzes.title: Celtic high priesthood: test
quizzes.intro: Thirteen questions on sovereignty and leadership, priesthood old and new, leading the year and its rites of passage, and stewardship. Most are scored at once; the coven’s head reads the written answers. You need 80% to pass, and you can try again.

questions.prompt: In the tale of Niall and the hag at the well, who does the hag turn out to be?
options: The Morrígan
Sovereignty (Flaithius)
Brigid
Rhiannon
questions.explanation: She becomes beautiful and names herself Sovereignty, promising the kingship to Niall and his line.

questions.prompt: Which goddess gives Ireland its name in the Lebor Gabála?
options: Banba
Ériu
Medb
Boann
questions.explanation: Ériu is promised the chief name: Éire comes from her. Banba and Fódla are her sisters.

questions.prompt: Scholars agree that pagan Irish kings were certainly married to a goddess in a known rite.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The sovereignty theme is real in the literature, but how far it reflects pagan rite is debated, and the rites are not well known.

questions.prompt: Which are misuses of sovereignty language in a coven? Choose all that apply.
options: A head claiming to be wedded to the goddess and beyond question
Using “sacred marriage” to pressure someone into sex
Seeing leadership as given by the coven and able to be withdrawn
Claiming members must obey because the head embodies the land
questions.explanation: Leadership given and withdrawable is the healthy reading. The others are abuses with no place in this coven.

questions.prompt: In early Ireland, who became the great learned class after the druids faded?
options: The brehons only
The filid, the poets
The briugu
The monks only
questions.explanation: The filid kept genealogy, lore and tales, composed praise, and were ranked in grades up to the ollam.

questions.prompt: Which titles claim more than anyone can honestly hold? Choose all that apply.
options: Hereditary priestess of the ancient Gaelic mysteries
Arch-druid of all the Celts
The coven’s head
Keeper of the unbroken druid line
questions.explanation: “The coven’s head” is honest. Claims of ancient hereditary offices and unbroken lines are not.

questions.prompt: What was “handfasting” originally, in Scotland and northern England?
options: An ancient druid wedding with cords
A betrothal or marriage by joining hands and making promises
A trial marriage recorded in the Mabinogi
A Samhain game
questions.explanation: The word is old, meaning betrothal or marriage by handclasp. Binding hands with cords is a modern pagan rite.

questions.prompt: A pagan handfasting is always a legal marriage.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. It depends on the law where you are and who performs it. Make sure couples know what is legal.

questions.prompt: When a member dies and their family holds a Christian funeral, what is usually the coven’s place?
options: To take over the funeral
To stand beside the family, offering its own remembrance separately with their blessing
To hold a keen at the church
To do nothing
questions.explanation: The coven supports the family and remembers its member in its own rites, with the family’s blessing.

questions.prompt: Which are good stewardship? Choose all that apply.
options: Training several possible successors over years
Writing the coven’s rites and agreements in its book
Keeping all leadership in one person’s hands
Talking about succession before it is urgent
questions.explanation: Like fosterage, stewardship raises others up over time. Keeping everything in one person’s hands is a sign of trouble.

questions.prompt: Which are ways a Celtic coven can give back to living Gaelic and Brythonic cultures? Choose all that apply.
options: Encouraging members to learn a Celtic language
Supporting the care of wells and monuments
Selling “ancient Celtic” initiations
Crediting where customs were recorded and who keeps them
questions.explanation: Language, heritage and honest credit give back. Selling invented “ancient” initiations does harm.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would lead this coven in the spirit of sovereignty and the ruler’s truth, and how you would guard against the misuses of those ideas.
questions.explanation: Old ideas, carefully read, can guide modern leadership.
questions.rubric: Full marks (4): accurately draws on at least one sovereignty tale or the Audacht Morainn (1); explains leadership as given and accountable, judged by the coven’s flourishing (1); names concrete practices of truth and fair judgement (1); names specific misuses and how they would be prevented (1).

questions.prompt: Share the main points of your plan for the coven’s next Celtic year, from Samhain to Samhain.
questions.explanation: A good year plan keeps the festivals, devotion, study, service and rest in balance.
questions.rubric: Full marks (3): includes all four fire festivals with leaders (1); includes devotions, study and service (1); includes rest and realistic pacing (1).
